My opinion of this game has varied throughout, and I'll do my best to explain how that's gone.
After the first chapter (or thereabouts), I was pretty sure that I was playing a generic action game, starring Generic Angry White Man and Irritating 'Can't Do Anything Myself' Girl. The story seemed to be littered with Deus Ex Machina after Deus Ex Machina, and I was not expecting much more than a mindless fight-the-robots romp. But during the game, this completely changed - I'm not sure whether the game got better or if I suddenly 'got' something I hadn't noticed before, but I started to really enjoy it.
The story got a lot stronger as it went on, and the character development is perfectly paced. As I learnt more about the characters, I became more fond of them, and by the last couple of chapters, I was completely invested in them. The actors did a fine job with the voice work, and even though there are only three characters in the entire game, it doesn't suffer for it in the least. The story itself was excellent, with humour balancing the more emotional parts nicely. My only complaint is that the epilogue felt a little bit rushed as an end to the story, but it did tie things up nicely.
Combat in the game is a great mix of hand-to-hand and shooting with Monkey's staff, and the flow between each style is really good. While the hand-to-hand reminds me a little of Remember Me, it's nowhere near as complex, and it can often be the best option to button mash until you defeat the enemies.
The one thing that I really didn't like was the parkour-style elements. Sure, it looked nice, and hopping between hand-holds, bars and other things was fluid, but I would have liked a bit more freedom. There seems to always be one way, and one way only, to reach where you are going, and most of the time you are railroaded into that way by being completely unable to even try and jump anywhere else.
I'm honestly surprised that I hadn't really heard of this game before I played it - it's got some big names behind it, and it's so well-made. Definitely worth playing.

is an action adventure game that caught me by surprise. Purchased on sale sometime ago, it stayed in my backlog while my expectations of it were quite low and had completely forgotten about it. Trying it out today for the first time, I have to say
in such a way that Resident Evil 4 did 10 years ago on the Wii and its introduction of motion controls.
Being a console port of course the usual gripes follow it, such as no screen/gpu options to fine-tune, bearable keyboard/mouse controls, fixed fps, some awkward camera views etc. I found that my modest/dated laptop (nVidia GTX860m) managed to deliver the 60fps @ 1080p resolution with just few and afar fps drops when there was a lot of action going on (xsplit indicated drops to 45fps). To add to that, initially playing with the keyboard/mouse combo it was unsatisfying and switching to DS4 gamepad it made a noticeable difference.
Despite the above, I thoroughly enjoyed ENSLAVED: Odyssey to the West. The scripted action was well placed, with a number of almost "on the rails" events that unfold to tell the story and the graphics galore sequences that accompany each step, were a pleasure to watch. Not to forget the enemy finishing moves (takedowns) which were great fun when the timing would trigger them!! On normal difficulty I found Enslaved relative easy, with over 2.5hrs non-stop immersion gaming till the first death and only a couple sticky points to require multiple re-runs (
). Part of the game's charm for me was the amazing motion and voice acting of Monkey by Andy Serkis (Gollum?) along with Lindsay Shaw (Tripitaka), which brought the story of Wu Cheng'en's excellent novel, Journey to the West, into it's futuristic re-imagination. Having read the original, I was pleasantly surprised remembering all the references, roles and parallels of the original story.
Not a game for everyone but highly recommended nevertheless.

A hillarious run-and-gun game featuring plenty of caricatures based on movie heroes? That´s pretty much what you´ll find in Broforce.
Pros:
* Fast paced run-and gun action!
* Nice graphic style and fitting heroic music (the voicework is limited but quite hillarious!)
* Plenty of characters with many varied styles! (how many of them can you recognize without a guide?)
* Destructible enviroments give you more options to tackle any given mission!
* Infinite ammo just like in the movies! :)
* Multiplayer is a total riot!
* Don´t like any level in particular? Build your own with the level editor!
Cons:
* Some of the characters are meant for very specific scenarios... (Wrong bro for the job = Dead bro...)
* You get a random character every time you die. (this makes gameplay varied, but it can be difficult to master any bro in particular!)
* Controls may seem a little restrictive at first (You can't shoot upwards nor crouch, just like in the early megaman games!)
* Most of the references and jokes are meant for the older gamers that grew up in the 80's!
The game is certainly fun and an easy recommendation for gamers that are on the lookout for a fun action game. Step into the shoes of your favorite hero and blast evil with excessive movie-like force! :)

TL;DR
8.5/10 if you like any 2 of the following there's no reason not to get this game:
Space
The 90's
RTS
being the nomadic fleet that wrecks everybody's good day
explosions
Retro gaming
updated retro gaming
getting what is technically four, but in reality is two drastically different iterations of 2 classic games
Seriously though I would've gave them $30 for the first game by itself and felt satisfied since it has multiplayer, and skirmishes. So heck the 2nd game AND their original versions for the price of one???? Shut up and take my Resource Units.
Long Version:
I started my gaming career in 1999 at the age of 5. Though I played other genres, RTS is the kind I most consider 'My roots' in video gaming. Despite this, somehow I missed out on the three homeworld games when they were first launched, and never managed to get around to playing them. This remastering offered me a chance to right the wrong i had allowed to persist throughout my life, and for that I am thankful.
HW remastered is something you don't get to experience everyday: a true blue 90's RTS that has the graphics and UI of a modern title. and make no mistake-- the game(s) are absolutely beautiful. The UI improvements are a god send, and if you take time just to play as far as the first mission in the Original games you will have tears brought to your eyes when you feel the difference.
The differences between the 2 games have never been vast, but the differences in the remastered versions are basically not even there and telling 1 from 2 would be dificult outside of the campaign. Thats a good thing. it means both titles were given the same love and care and both games were updated to an equal level, so there is no reason to skip the first in favor of always playing the second.
At time of writing I have not progressed far into 2, so I can only really speak on the story of 1. It is a very simple story told through a few in-engine, and animated-artwork cutscenes. The radio chatter also helps it along a bit. Despite this the story is gripping, and you'll always look forward to that next intermission. You'll literally feel every sacrifice made by your fleet as rescources are scarce along the journey to the homeworld and any ship lost during the trek is a bit like losing a classmate: You may not have hung out with them everyday, or even seen them everyday, but they were there, and now their not and it feels wong to you. And if it was a ship that's been with you for a long time it's a little bit stronger of a loss. to both your efforts ingame, and your personal morale. you will do evrything you can to keep losses as low as possible. Your worst enemy in this game is impatience.
It's not perfect however. there are some glitches I personally encountered. 1 in the second mission where the salvage corvettes had taken control of a frigate but it wouldn't move. Restarting this very short mission fixed it.
Another one where the Salvage corvettes just spun the captured ship along the Y-axis and didn't move. eventually it straightened itself out and everytjing worked. (Neither of these bugs happened again)
the most common glitches were graphical. Some captured ships would change skin to reflect their affiliation change, while others would not, and some would only do it after several missions. other times ships would randomly change skins altogether going from Taidain Imperial Navy to Taidain Elite unexspectedly. and these were ships that had been in my fleet for several missions.
Another thing that kinda bothered me, but I'm alright with was the tutorial. Homeworld 1's tutorial uses Homeworld 2 era ships, and mechanics, some of which you never experience in Homeworld 1... Why? It really kinda threw me for a loop at first, and I feel a seperate tutorial would not have been that much to ask for. also... "Press Okay to continue" got really dang old when it didn't matter if you pressed it or not, the tutorial would continue without input the moment  the line was finished.
Those are literally the only complaints I have. the game work fine, it's beautiful, and at an age where I have hung up my RTS hat in favor for Sandboxes and Grand-Strategies... It was nice returning to the era of gaming that made me a gamer to begin with. Just a simple, challenging, good experience.
This is one of my favorite series, and I am so happy that this got remastered. It's like a dream come true.  The new models are great, and well done. I love everything about this game.

An overlong but satisfying survival horror game, Alien: Isolation is the closest a video game has come to capturing the tension of the Alien films since the marine campaign in AvP2.
Playing as Ellen Ripley's daughter, your training as an engineer does little to protect you from the threats you'll face aboard Sevastopol station, so you'll find yourself spending the majority of your time hiding in a closet or sneaking around. I know this may read like a negative but it's a positive; this is the first time in a very long time that a survival horror game has actually felt like it required the use of brains over brawn, the way it should do,
The one and only problem with this title starts to set in about halfway through, when it becomes abundantly clear that the developers ran out of ideas and are artificially padding things out to stall for time. This wouldn't have been too much of a issue if they hadn't overdone it to the degree that they did. No joke, some of the second act and most of the third could have been cut and you'd still have a congruent narrative and well-paced gameplay at the end of it.
As stated, the game's excessive length is the only real issue here and much of the rest of it is flawless. The retro-futuristic stylings mirror those of the original films down to the smallest detail, completely immersing you in their world from the start. The AI has the odd hiccup every now and then but overall it's believable, and hilarious after you learn how to lure the xenomorph into a group of enemies.
One of the most surprisingly great things about A: I, however, is just how well optimised it is. The devs must have a wizard in their team or something, because even on my fairly average PC this runs with max settings across the board without so much as a stutter. Even with its dodgy anti-aliasing, A: I looks eye-poppingly gorgeous in its own dark, dingy sort of way.
If you're a fan of the film Alien or survival horror, this is the best representation of either in years.
10/10 would run like a little kid and hide in lockers from the Alien again.

+ Spectacular visuals & lighting; there is also a meticulous, franchise-loyal attention to detail
+ Environments are designed so well that it is absolutely jaw-dropping; level design, too, is excellent in every way
+ Voice-acting is superb, with virtually every actor delivering their lines with a professionalism that complements the game nicely; lip-syncing is less than admirable in comparison, but isn't so bad as to detract from the overall experience
+ Audio-design is literally perfect; soundtrack is appropriate and used well, & the ambient noises make for a deep and satisfying sensation of immersion
+ Everything stays true & loyal to the aesthetics & overall atmosphere of the first film
+ Engine is very well optimized, even on maximum settings; my PC seemed to barely notice it was running a game, & GPU temps were barely above idle figures
+ Atmosphere is rich, & postively pregnant with tension
+ Personnel logs, audio logs, and collectibles are enjoyable to collect, & do well to further tell the nuances of the game's story
+ Alien AI behavior is wildly unpredictable, therefore adding to the title's challenge & replayability
+ Crafting allows for a multitude of useful gadgets, traps & distractions
+ Game includes a challenging survival mode, puffing up the replayablity & competitiveness a bit
- Crafting UI feels awkward & unpolished, particularly when selecting components to commit
- Tons of tedious backtracking in the second-half of the game

This game was one of the best experiences I've had in gaming.
The design was a fascinating 80's look into what space travel ought to be--with very interesting (to me) large single-purpose electronics/machinery that makes me wish the 80's never ended.  Navigating the rather large station is also perfection, as it's sections and their purpose are memorable and logical (a long shot from the seemingly arbitrary design of other games).
The gameplay was quite rewarding, as your character acquires the firepower to transform from prey hiding under the bed into the predator, eventually making the alien your b!tch and exacting revenge on the rather annoying robotic helpers lurking the area.  This transformation is a wonderful validation of all the hard work you put into the game.
Manipulating the alien(s) can be fun at times, but the sometimes dangerous remains of the crew bring the situation together.  The incredible textures allowed by the sometimes cramped quarters of a space station is a quite welcome bonus for those with a decent system.
But most of all, when I encounter a door or mechanism in a video game, I often wonder why it was designed as such, most often the answer is because an "artist" decided it looked cool.  The Alien: Isolation mechanisms, doors, and functional pieces appear viable to me, as if an engineer had designed these objects instead of an "artist".  It is the singular thing that increases immersion, and made me love the station, and it's switches, buttons, and doors--even it's layout!
Highly recommended, I hope they keep making good games.

Pineapple Smash Crew is a fun top down run n gun. Smash Crew presents an excellent retro pixel art style combined with with a most fantastic soundtrack by Amiga artist Syphus (aka EchoLevel.) The game controls well, with WASD being used to move and the mouse used to aim and shoot, giving it a twin stick feeling but it lacks controller support (made in 2011, not gonna hold it against them.) Smash Crew also contains some Rogue-like elements with levels being randomly generated as you go and leveling up gives you the option of one of two grenade upgrades. It's a very impressive game and certainly needs more love.

Is's not clear at first how good this is.. The engine sure as hell feels nice to handle, easy  and a pleasure to use  and I would wager that they have play tested this pretty decently,
It seems a simple game, but apart from when it becomes harder in the later levels (and perhaps hard difficulty) the effort to kill things and to frag your way through level feels what I would describe as 'Pleasantly taxing' and the action is quite enjoyable.
The grenade system is infact one of the best aprts of this game, as the guns are not upgradeable (whcih this game could benfit from having) and can be a bit boring to use ALL the time;  the grenades on the other hand add a very nice amount of variety and fun.  You can create combos, set up multikills and manipulate your enemy fatally, which is seldom seen in many games, and I think that was the best part of Doom, where enemies could be manipulated to kill each other and die at your environment's hands, not yours(at least directly)...
The decor at time does change,  but subtly, although the random generated levels are different and many levels dont look EXACTLY alike with all the differnet layouts and wall design(which normally consist of different colour schemes)(reminds me alot of Phantasy Star II actually:) )).. The props themselves consist of a set of doors and a number of crates, although many of them can be used to blow up and evaporate your enemy which is anotehr  good thing.  Generally everything here is quite simple, though not TOO simple.
The sound is retro style, although the guns and explosions are satisfying enough, but the music side of things really good... I remember watching a You tube vdeo of Total biscuit talking about another game... and mentioning Syphus; and I totally agree that the drum and bass influenced electronica (or chiptune as I read in other places) really is nice and a pleasure to listen to, making the most frantic levels throughly enjoyable! I like electronica and DnB  so I really enjoyed his wall to wall sound and elaborately colourful melodies :3
All in all I was not inpressed at first but got a bit hooked.. I may return to play this again, perhaps for 10-20 mins a time inbetween other things, as that is possible with this game... Don't overlook this game if at first it seems boring, as there is much more of worth in there; which is pretty good for what is essentially a simple game.

Pineapple Smash Crew is a squad-based top-down shooter, with a strong retro style (models, fonts and music). The pace is frantic, the controls are witty and the game fluid. So much for the positive points.
Unfortunately, the randomized levels cannot beat that feeling of repetitiveness and fatigue. If you like to play the same thing over and over again to reach a transe-like state of flow, Pineapple Smash Crew might be a good candidate.
Since I prefer a certain amount of novelty and surprise, this one is not for me in spite of its qualities (a great piece of code and a genuine love for retro).

This is an Early Access review of Eden Star. This review will contain what I've learned from my 15+hrs of playing the game.
Eden Star is, currently, an Early Access game about a character who crashes on an alien planet and must find specific parts from an object called the Eden Kit. The tutorial gives you everything you need to know on how to play the game from start to finish.
The game is created through the Unreal 4 Engine. The engine has great potential, and the developers have given the game rather nice texures for obvious reasons.
You begin the game falling from the sky and landing in a pod of some kind. As the door shoots open you are greeted to the alien planet along with a fiery sky show of fallen ship parts. Your goal is to go and retrieve an Eden Kit to call your home.
After building a base out of trees, rocks and other minerals you can gather, it should soon be night time. During this time you will want to stay near  your Eden Kit and inside of your bubble to keep your shield up and to stay safe from enemies that will come for your Eden Kit's power. Once your power is destroyed so is your respawn point.
You are able to build guns, augments, upgrades, and eventually armor for your character to defend themselves with. You may also build defence weapons for your base like turrents and electrified fencing.
Pros:
+Great controles and rebinding capability
+Ajustable resolutions
+Great crafting system/UI
+Amazing replayability
+Perfect atmosphere
+Multiplayer
+Range of graphics options
+Beautiful visuals/graphics
Cons:
+Can sometimes lag on max settings (980ti GPU)
Bugs/Glitches:
+Specific area of the map that allows your Eden Kit to never be attacked.
Overall this game is a lot like Subnautica but, better in my opinion. It is a very fun game to waste time or let's play for a YouTube channel. If this game was played by a famous let's player it would get a lot of traffic.

ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS is a game with the simple concept of being control of a small rocket with the idea being that you have to eliminate up to 3 other rockets (PvP or PvC) using Missles, Mines, and Bombs. Sounds simple, but the way the game presents itself, and how it makes use of what it has it what makes it such a blast to pIay!
The game's enviroments (Maps) consist of simple neon colored shapes that can be used as cover from incoming attacks from enemy rockets. There aren't many maps in the game at the moment but the maps that are currently availible still manage to offer a grand time with friends
The game's graphics consist of the use of simple neon colors that can be seen in the enviroment as mentioned, but dispite being simple the game still manages to look amazing even though there are no use of any background images. The game allows you to use your rockets exaust trails in order to paint the enviroment, even though you may be left with scribbles because of the fact that you'll be dogfighting with other players, but the game offers a Zen mode that lets fly around, drawing in the enviroment, while listening to the game's music.
Speaking of the music. It consists of Dubstep that DEMANDS your attention, even though there isn't much of it (The Soundtrack only consists of nine songs, but they're all good)
lastly, the game's weapons (Missles, Mines, and Bombs) work like you may expect them to in other dogfighting games (Missles can be shot directly towards an enemy rocket and is the primary weapon you will be using, Mines are bombs that can be dropped behind you to stop any Rockets tailing you, and Bombs can be dropped and blow up any enemy rockets from below.) But a quick thing to note on the weapons is that all of them have the secondary ability to be fired in a barrage attack (which is what I call them at least) which fires mutilple rounds from the gun you're using, this can be done by pressing and holding the fire button for that weapon.
In the end, the game is really simple in design but it offers a fun and challenging experience for those who decide to get this game.
9/10

I've spent a considerable amount of time with this game, both modded and unmodded and I wanted desperately to love it. You don't always get what you want. I did get the game as a gift from a friend though, and our desperation to love the game enough to play together led to many a wasted hour trying to find happiness.
This game may be summed up in one word – Shallow
The strategic map has more in common with Settlers of Catan than Risk. The cities are nothing more than a series of slots you can put buildings into that provide a flat military, public order and/or economic boost. 6 per major city, no more, as has been the case since Empire. There is never any sort of feeling of progression or accomplishment that comes from building the finest city in the world and this is due in no small part to how terrible the AI is at handling the strategic layer.
The AI will march with its armies in the 'double time' stance virtually everywhere, literally forcing you to ambush them in order to engage as ambushes are automatic when attacking an army in this stance. You will never see properly developed cities anywhere that you haven't built yourself as the AI is also incapable of even feeding itself by building enough farms.
The diplomacy is also a joke on normal - wherein everyone wants to be your friend no matter what and your borders simply are never threatened - and virtually every other faction conspires against you on any setting higher than normal. I had some small Spanish tribe declare war on my Seleucids because of how I treated the Persians. It never makes sense, and even modded it is still a complete pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥
The fleets thrown against you, if you can call them that, consist of the lightest, cheapest, smallest possible ships which are incapable of posing any real threat. The armies are made of 10 slingers and 10 hoplites if you're fighting against the Greeks and 10 spearmen and 10 slingers if you're fighting against anyone else. That is not a joke or hyperbole. The AI never constructs the proper buildings to field good armies even when they have the technology to do so. Enjoy seeing a lot of really advanced artillery along side sack-wearing peasants forming the army core. It got so bad they had to 'rebalance' the building chains. All this did was add military units to the city center to hide the fact the AI is such a ♥♥♥♥ing joke that after more than a year it still couldn't/can't build a decent settlement.
When it comes time to actually play the battles you're in for your biggest disappointment yet, as they are by far the worst of any total war game. Remember Spider Man climbing your walls in Empire? Imagine the Human Torch at the gates of Rome... Throwing torches. Even now, after countless patches, even modded, the battles suck. They are terrible. I have never witnessed the AI do anything other than stretch its forces into the longest line possible and simply march toward you. No skirmishing - the ranged units merely stop and fire at you when in range until the melee have made contact. No holding the melee back to inflict casualties, nope, they just keep going forward until they route. Every battle. Never holding any units as reserves. Nothing but march forward and die.
Unless, of course you are playing a defensive siege battle. Those will make you wonder how the hell they thought this game was even finished. If you're defending all you need to do is put units in front of the gates and at the stairwells leading up to the wall. If the enemy takes the wall or breaches the gate they simply run on in and get slaughtered. They won’t flank around off the wall, they will simply walk down the stairs, one at a time, until the unit routes and you win. And that's if you're lucky and the AI actually used its siege equipment. More often than not it will simply run its army forward to throw burning torches at the main gates, one unit at a time, until the towers of your city have routed them all. If they actually do manage to get through the gates, the entire enemy army will attempt to enter simultaneously and all die due to the burning oil poured down from the gatehouse.
Things get far, far worse if there is more than a single army being commanded by the AI in a battle. Take the above example of the entire army rushing through one gate and add a second army, which started on the other side of your city, which will march around your city, as close to the walls as possible suffering horrific losses, just to charge into the same gate. No flanking, no tactics, nothing but a sad disappointment, which is exactly what this game turned out to be.
Oh, and the naval battles are the same as the land battles. No differences what so ever in tactics needed to win or those used by the AI.
TL:DR – Game is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reskin of Fall of the Samurai.

After having read tons of reviews here on Steam I decided to give it a go and got it during one of the innumerable crazy-for-whatever-reason-on-steam-sales. Then it got stuck on my library for ages until I found the time to actually play it (which was the past week during autumn vacation) - and I loved almost every part of it. I'm not a fan of console ports and usually avoid them. This game was clearly designed with controllers in mind and when you fire it up, you get a nice welcome message remembering you "not to shut down the console, because this game saves automatically". PC gamer pride aside and some initial struggle playing with mouse & keyb I quickly fell in love with it. It's basically a sci-fi hack'n'slay with a nice plot and some AC badass climbing (with pre-fixed anchor points you can't miss mind you) in a Mad Max'isch environment. The characters are likeable though I lack the background information about the universe, the past of it, how everyone got where they are and who they are basically. Think of entering LOTR on the last chapter, where you figure the Ring is evil, you understand who's good and bad and you know it has to be destroyed - you just don't know how everyone got there.
Pro's
Con's
Despite some minor flaws it was just plain fun and diverse and never really felt repetitive. Though from a graphical perspective it doesn't live up to today's standards, it's an utter delight in colors and fireworks.

Short and sweet single-player game. The opening chapters and the final chapter are great. The middle chapters slump a bit the story is fairly well-paced overall.
Platforming is a little too low-risk, but the parkour animations are very well-done. Combat is not always very engaging, although there is a decent amount of offensive options (some combo attacks and ranged abilities and defensive options (evading and blocking with counter-attacks). Enemy variety is very low, there are maybe 5 types of enemy in the game, with a couple variants of each. Boss battles are straightforward but make for decent set-pieces and memorable story beats.
The areas where this game really shines is in art direction and characterization. The levels are gorgeous, full of bright greens and deep blues, and are very refreshing to look at. The characters are believable and the way that their personalities and relatonships develop over the course of the story is convincing and feels natural.

This has to be the greatest horror game I've ever played. As well as the best sequel to the original 1979 Alien. I highly recomend this game for anyone that loves horror games or is a fan of the Alien movies.

This game is so immersive, the sounds and build-up of atmosphere has been excellently done. The graphics are pretty decent and I like that it has an excellent options menu. There are many graphics options and fully remappable controls. What I also like in this game is once the alien has been released he roams wherever he wants. There's no scripted rubbish, so you've got to be constantly aware of where he is. The AI of the alien is excellent, much better than most AAA AI. If you make too much sound you can guarantee he will get there as fast as possible. You have to be clever with your hiding and with the tools you choose to use. It's very well done. There were a couple of things I didn't like. There are parts of the game where you have to sneak around groups of humans which I thought didn't fit in the game at all. I also thought the whole ending was dragged out for way too long. It was a bit of a get to the exit. Oh no the exit is blocked, find an alt route. Oh no the alt route needs you to power on something, find that. It just felt a little dragged out at the end and it wasn't necessary in my opinion. However, it takes nothing away from how excellent this game is. It really is a very immersive and scary experience, great game and worth the money.

Homeworld is, hands down, one of the best RTS games of all time. Not only are the gameplay mechanics amazing, but it possesses one of the best narratives in the genre. The story is emotional and moving -- but without the forced melodrama you'd find in some other games. It's a straightforward tale told with sincerity.
The classic version of both games play like the original release, so check them out for the original experience.
The Remastered Editions enhance the graphics... but they also rebalance gameplay mechanics. This is most apparent in Homeworld 1. Strike craft are rendered all but useless, forcing you to use corvettes as your "fighter wings." You also no longer have to refuel them. Frigates and capital ships have been variously nerfed or overpowered. So, if you're a veteran of the series, your "old school" tactics may no longer work. These changes angered some people, though I actually appreciated having a new twist on an old classic. It made the gameplay feel fresh, even though I've beaten the original version a dozen times.
So, whether you're a new player or a veteran returning home, there's something for everybody. Want the original experience? Play the classic editions. Want a new twist? Play the remastered editions. Either way, Homeworld is still one of the best strategy games ever produced.

Okay, let's dive right into why you should buy this game:
1) If you loved both Homeworld games, then you'll love this. By the way, the game includes both the Remastered versions of 1 and 2, the original versions, and the MP (currently in Beta).
2) Clearly a great effort was made to refine the visuals and audio of the game. The gameplay mechanics and UI have also been altered, but do not interfere heavily from the original concept. It's non-intrusive in my opinion and makes the game just that much more enjoyable.
3) A growing modding community. I have high hopes for the community, but at the moment some creative, useful, and just overal interesting sets of mods are available from the Workshop. Some include reskins, reinterfacing, unofficial patches (some of these are specific to the hardcore fans of the originals), and even a multiplayer map pack (which claims to have 130+ maps!).
Please note that there is much more that could be said, but it is fruitless explaining it all in text like this.
I recommend that you watch some gameplay footage if you'd like more info, or even feel free to ask me. I'm sure to put more hours into this game.

Eden Star is an early-access game with a sci-fi setting. It belongs to the genres of sandbox, ego-shooter and has roleplay elements.
So, first off, this game is in a very early early state and most of the gameplay is not implemented, this review is based on the 0.04 pre-alpha update.
I can only speak positive of this game so far, the stability is frightening for a game in a this early state, I only encountered 4 crashes so far and the FPS are stable (i7, 760gtx), the game runs on Unreal Engine 4. The graphics are really good, feel well composed and the art-style is appealing(imo).
Now let's come to the gameplay aspect: Some upgrades are already in, 3 weapons and basic construction. Most of it feels well implemented, it just seems that the devs know exactly what they want, this is not some project of some unorganized garage-devs(*huh*starforge*huhhuhu*). Shooting is still a bit inaccurate. The cool thing is the power of UE4, resource mining feels really awesome and the world is really immersive. The fighting is based on shooting and using your tools like lifting enemies and samshing them into the ground, all paired with parcours elements and wallrunning.
So, EDEN STAR has a lot of potential, but we still have to see how it will become but it definitely has better chances of becoming something. The devs are also very responsive and explain why they implement what.

For years I've spoken praises for the Total War franchise; and I can say that I have played hundreds of hours of Medieval 2 alone, not to mention similar investments in Empire, Shogun, and Rome II. But alas, the time has come where I can confidently state that I will not buy another Total War title, for Rome II was the last straw. The Franchise has been devolving since Medieval II.
TL;DR at bottom.
I was originally hooked back in 2007 on the first incarnation of Rome: Total War, and I was completely STRICKEN with it until I was exposed to the "hotseat" variant for Medieval II: Kingdoms. To this day, many of my friends and I continue these hotseat campaigns through the Retrofit mod, and it has become somewhat of a ritual for us. Since, we have hoped for a Total War experience that would capitalize on this feature and maximize the idea of a "multiplayer campaign." Since, we have been disappointed time and time again.
Empire came promising a new multiplayer campaign that could be played on a massive scale that included three entirely separate theaters! Unfortunately, unlike the hotseat function, only two players could be present, and this alone was enough to shy my friends from buying it (not to mention a very limited selection of factions, and no ability to edit the descr_strat.txt to unlock all factions. . . but no matter! A simple mod fix, I thought!) but I had to try it. After having my all-time favorite campaign as Prussia, Empire had my praise. I persuaded a friend to play this "Beta" campaign. We did, and indeed we found it to be exceptional. We could even play as the enemy faction during battles to surmount the jagged AI which for YEARS was found to be lacking. Then, after 10 turns of greatness, the dreaded DESYNC. We trouble-shot for hours on end, digging through the internet to find answers- to no avail. Plenty of others had the same issue, but there were no answers? How curious. Even following "a one-month delay for the release of Empire" (Quote Wikipedia) they couldn't fashion a working version of the Multiplayer campaign? No matter, I thought; a failed project. Perhaps they will fix it in the near future. Unfortunately, despite taking my money and making a promise, to this day no fix has been issued. A "Beta" they called it- not worthy of a fix, despite having delayed the game launch. Buy Napoleon, they said. Quote the Creative Assembly; "This beta programme was designed to offer a taste of the exciting multiplayer gameplay we were integrating into recent titles, such as Total War: Shogun 2 and Napoleon: Total War,"
I ignored Napoleon entirely (although I was foolish enough to buy it) because of the puny map size and the pathetic faction diversity. These facts did not convince any of 'my party' to buy it, either. Despite a supposed "working" multiplayer campaign, where was the fun if you could not be Venice, Spain, or Greece? What about an African or Anatolian or, for that matter, any "small" faction whatsoever? I supposed it was because there was no audience for such things. I supposed that all of my desires were a niche and that only my group of friends were the audience.
Then came Shogun offering another attempt at a multiplayer campaign; still no hotseat, mind you. Again I felt hope that it could be everything I had wished, and again I gave the Creative Assembly my money. PLENTY of "small" factions, but little unit diversity! You could play with Samurai, or with Samurai; Japan is a very small place, after all. By the way, where were the nearby Eastern Korean or Chinese shores? Once more, Shogun did not interest the majority of my friends (for there was no hotseat function! No separate theaters of war! How difficult could it be to BRING BACK an old, yet fantastic idea? It could even be modernized and perfected!) but one other decided to take the plunge with me. I wasn't impressed by the lack of unit diversity, but I found myself well at home with the culture and the new agent system. The campaign AI was still clanky and had an absurd handicap budget, but at least the multiplayer campaign didn't desync! Or, thus I thought, until ALAS! The dreaded DYSYNC AGAIN! We were halted until we discovered the problem; each turn that passed seemed to bring the .sav file to a bigger size (just like in Medieval) and these new "packets" of data would build upon each other until finally, after enough turns had passed, our (I and my campaign partner's) .sav files were no longer identical. The fix? exchange .sav files via E-mail and replace. Thus, the desync was defeated- but only temporarily. It would come back to haunt us every twenty or thirty turns and we would have to repeat the process.
NBD, I played Shogun with this friend of mine for many hours. We completed several multiplayer campaigns on Legendary (cooperating and surviving) and tried a multitude of factions to mix up our geographical positioning. I wanted more so I reluctantly bought the Fall of the Samurai campaign for both myself and my friend, whom is an adamant boycotter of DLC- fearing that each sale to The Creative Assembly is another encouragement for MORE DLC. I foolishly purchased and gifted him a copy. We went on to play two more Legendary Coop campaigns both for and against the Imperials. Even with the presence of the Westerners, there STILL was no Korea and no China.
I must admit over the years my desire to play SP campaigns has died down, and I've been looking for something to do with friends more than to do with myself. That said, I've played ample SP campaigns for each title, with the exception of Napoleon. I've played ample MP campaigns on Shogun and Rome II, and I've invested hours of effort into attempting the Empire Beta, both LAN and online. As I said earlier I still do Hotseat campaigns with my mates to this day, and we have one rotating right now.
TL;DR
ROME II REVIEW:
My rating: 5/10 MP campaign, 3/10 SP campaign
PROS
- Decent/good battle AI
- Armies/Navies more personal/customizable
- Decent campaign AI
- IF YOU PAY FOR IT, reasonable unit diversity,
CONS
- OVER HALF AVAILABLE FACTIONS ARE DLC. TERRIBLE FACTION DIVERSITY.
- MORE THAN HALF CAMPAIGNS ARE DLC. INCOMPLETE GAME THROUGH and THROUGH.
- Non tradable tech tree. Uninteresting tech.
- No multiple theaters
- Army units are glued to their generals, unlike previously
- Battle AI still somewhat reliant on stat handicaps
- *nonfrequent* Desyncing multiplayer campaign, limited 2 players
CONCLUSION
So, what's my point? Each game had its admirable traits, but the Creative Assembly continues to swing and miss. Gradually they have lost their innovation and they are trying to get away with selling more DLC. IT IS UNBELIEVABLE and honestly quite INSULTING to me that the GREEK STATES are DLC. (Or preorder contents in my case.)
To be honest, I DO have fun playing Rome II, but I think it is an UNFINISHED product. There are tears in the graphics, many unit animations look mechanical, the load times are substantial, and half the game is DLC. IF none of the game were DLC, I would rate it 9/10 and call it a fantastic game, even if it was at the expense of my ideal Rome II.
SO what would be my ideal Rome II? A blend of traits from each total war.
Medieval II: Hotseat campaign / Unit and faction roster diversity
Empire: 3 theater world map / political, systems / gamechanging, tradable tech
Shogun: Good agent system
Rome II: Customizable armies / Dynamic naval application / Good AI / cultural differences
NO FACTIONS DLC. NO CAMPAIGNS DLC. DESYNC FREE MULTIPLAYER CAMPAIGN. HOTSEAT WITH REALTIME PLAYABLE BATTLES.
I have NO reason to believe ATTILA will be anything but a graphical UI revamp, and thus NO REASON to believe the Creative Assembly deserves another dollar of mine. They are selling content that is in every respect UNFINISHED.

Do you have friends that play smite already? Here's a little tip from me, don't play with them yet.
I was first introduced to smite mid 2014, my first experience with a moba. My friends were already at a much higher level than myself and I got stomped. I thought, "it's not for me," and moved on.
November last year I was invited to try again and since it had been a while I thought things might've changed, they hadn't, abuse was thrown at me and it became the first game where I had rage quit after being told to leave by team mates. This left me feeling bad.
I eventually got back into the game around February after I bought the founders pack for Paladins which gave a skin for Ares. I redeemed the skin and decided to create a new account.
I re-did the tutorials, worked my way up, understood the gods and how to work effectively before I switched back to my actual account. I'm not the best player at my level but I'm not exactly the worst, my win:lose is about 1:1 which is how I like it.
The game controls well, looks decent and has some good music and sound effects. Although I did like Heroes of the Storm for peaking my interest on the MOBA genre I have to say the 3rd person view makes you feel like you are doing a lot more than just pointing at things with a mouse cursor like in AoE.

Differently form dota and lol game is in third person view and in smite you can pick yourself 2 relics aswell each game which grant you extra 2 simple but often useful abilitys. Good things :

* lots of events with rewards (gems, ip, skins ect) - i havent spent real money for this game yet as it is easy to get both in game and purchasable currency over time

From there, you build up your mega-factory-complex-of-awesome by building increasinly complex stuff from 6 base resources (copper, iron, oil, coal, wood, water). It's beautiful.

Dark Souls 2 is a sequel i have mixed feelings about (i suppose its hard to beat what is in my opinion one of the best games, if not the best game i've played). Mechanically its superior to Dark Souls 1: Graphics are better, framerate is smoother, online coop and invading is reliable. At the same time Dark Souls 1 has the superior design: Lore, Bosses, Enemies and Environments are infinitely more intersting in that game.
At its core its still a very strong Souls game: The game is tough but fair and there are alot of different builds that play completely different from eachother.
All in all if you liked Souls games for their gameplay you'll love Dark Souls 2. if you're new to Souls games, this is a pretty good place to start since knowledge from DS1 is not required. But if you're unsure if Dark Souls is up your alley, go with DS1 first. If youre hungry for more then DS2 definitely has you covered.

I watched tons of Monkey King in Chinese growing up and loved it even though I didn't understand it.    It was great to see how the staff, cloud, monkey, pig and the even the crown were re-imagined and fit in the world.
You start with a whole world where you're trying to figure out who are these people, why are there murder robots everywhere, why did the world "end"? Unfortunately by the end of the game you don't really know that much more about the people, some plot points felt super blunt while others felt too vague.  The pacing towards the end feels rushed and is probably the worst part of the game.  Nothing really feels really resolved and it was a very deus ex machina ending.
Traversal was bearable at first and made sense with the monkey king influences but, after a while it became a boring hold direction/mash jump until you're done.  Even worse than say an Assassin's Creed because most of the climbing sections were linear vs the more open nature of AC.  Using the cloud was great though, it felt good and looked good while using it though transitioning
The gameplay kinda followed the story with a solid premise.  An okay Arkham Knight like combat with basic shooting but, as the game went on it the mechanics on top of it didn't feel great.  Offensively the upgrade tree didn't provide much variety or even options.  The limited options it did provide felt super inefficient compared the the standard mash quick attack.
Shooting in this game felt pretty unwelcome. It was slow and clunky and unfortunately became more mandatory as the game progressed. There were segments later on in the game where I'm basically <travolta.gif> because I'm being shot at by by enemies I can't melee and ammo is somehow scarcer than health.
Honestly I think the game is worth an hour or two of your time but, it isn't worth seeing through to the  end.

A surprisingly fun overhead shooter. Tough enemies and gigantic explosions provide ample difficulty, but it's the relatively strict time limit that makes Pineapple Smash Crew the game that it is. The player is forced to develop an efficient strategy and work quickly to accomplish objectives, though the temptation to wander and collect the loot necessary to level up can at times be overwhelming. Randomly generated levels and three modes of difficulty provide some amount of replayability and variety, but realistically, you'll probably only get a few hours out of this game before the whole thing starts to get stale. Still, I can see this game becoming a fun diversion to revisit on occasion.

Eden Star is a game with potential. Big potential. Fun, engaging, and challenging I recommend it. That said, in its current state it is A) little more than clean functioning fundamentals and B) A base defense game at it's core. It may be one of the most immersive, pretty, and well crafted tower defense games but it is still about hustling to get the materiel you need and craft (and place) the items you need before night falls and all hell breaks loose.
Things to Know:
The game is functional, very functional right now. Limited in scope (maybe 10 hours of fun right now, big patch coming soon), but plays like a final game.
The dev's have addressed past problems such as no save system (still waiting on randomly generated worlds)
The game seems well thought out, and the content they plan to add will be what fills out the potential of the game.
Conclusions
Most of the early release games on steam are steaming piles of crap, Eden Star seems different. The game as it currently  stands is the most playable and functional Early Access games I have ever played. The game plan of the future, adding more content, such as new building options, defenses, items, and enemies is exactly what this game needs  to make it great....and that is just the start of what they plan. I check my updates every day waiting for the April patch, and i cannot remember the last time I was so eager for a game update.

If Attila: Total War didn't exist, I'd recommend this game. Unfortunately, Attila: Total War exists, and includes many of the things this game does not, like: family trees (more advanced than ever), in depth governor management system (think Crusader Kings 2 lite), the ability to play as a migratory faction, the ability to go to a war of attrition by burning your enemy's cities to the ground, and so on, so forth. This isn't the successor to Rome 1, Attila is. Rome 2 is fun for a few factions, like the Greek cities, but everything else is busted compared to its companion game, Atilla.

I only show to have a few hours into the game since it recently released to Steam, but have played since release & have over 1500 total played hours over the years.  I enjoy both Hunting & Gaming, so finding & playing the best hunting game comes natural to me.
First things first...this is not a shoot-em'-up game where you sprint through the woods guns-a-blazin'.  You will often be crouching through the woods or sitting in a stand, if that's your preference.  Some will see this game style as a bit slow or even boring at times, especially if they're used to playing a FPS.  That being said, theHunter is a good compromise between Hunting Simulation & video game.
There are currently 18 different species that you can hunt in theHunter, and that number continues to grow as they add new content.  There are the small deer species (roe, blacktail, whitetail, mule deer), larger deer species (roosevelt elk, moose, red deer), waterfowl (mallards & Canadian geese), canines (fox & coyote), hogs (wild boar & feral hogs), bear (black & brown), birds (pheasant & turkey), and small game (rabbits).  There are also 7 different maps for you to hunt these animals, containing anywhere from 4 to 6 different species in each map.  You also have access to 32 different weapons with which to choose from, which allows you to hunt with a variety of rifles, pistols, primitive bows, compound bows, shotguns, a flintlock muzzleloader, or even an air rifle, each with different scopes for you to use.  Further adding to the variety offered in theHunter are the different types of camo & large equipment, such as treestands, blinds, feeders, bear bait barrels, etc.
When you start a new game in theHunter, the animals are randomly generated on the map.  This only happens once, which is right when the game starts.  There are no “respawns” as you harvest animals throughout the course of your game.  Nobody knows exactly how this works, but suffice to say that you have close to an equal number of each species on the map that you selected.  There will always be animals that are trophy worthy, and it is up to you to use your skill & patience to find them.  Along with the trophy animals are rare variations of almost every species offered.  This gives you a real sense of accomplishment when you find an albino bull elk, that trophy piebald whitetail, or the rarest of rare bears.  All of the deer species use a system called TruRacs that generates the antlers that you see in-game, and it is different every time.  All of these things, combined with the variety above, give this game a great amount of addictive replayability.  In one hunt, you might be shooting for a red deer muzzleloading competition in Hirschfelden wearing the trapper outfit & in the next you might be hunting mallard ducks in the swamps of the Rougarou Bayou online with your friends.  Even if you start in the same location & hunt the same species repeatedly, no two animals you kill will be identical & no two hunts will be the same.
Adding to the replayability in theHunter are Competitions, Missions, Achievements, & Skills.  There is at least one Competition available every day for each species, most often lasting a day or two each.  There are also 250 different Missions available.  These are optional, but now earn you a currency called gm$, which can be spent on some consumable items, such as scent eliminator spray.  You can also increase your Hunter score by earning Achievements, which are mostly earned through killing x number of species or x number of kills with each weapon.  You also increase your skills along the way, making you better at tracking & spotting game.  An expert tracker can tell the sex of the animal, along with good estimates of the track’s age & the weight of the animal, while an expert spotter can give you a really good estimate of the animal’s score.
This is easily the best gaming community that I have ever had the pleasure of playing & communicating with.  The developers are actively involved in the Forums, and allow the community to make suggestions for future content.  They send out surveys regularly & then deliver the content that the community wants.  The community also hosts their own competitions that pay out significantly more than the official ones.
theHunter throws out some pretty cool special events for certain holidays.  Sometimes, it’s just a special item (see Xmas beanie or St Patty’s Day hat) but sometimes it can be weeks’ long competitions that award guns or special trophies that are only awarded during that time.
All in all, the game is absolutely beautiful, with nice water & weather effects.  Inside 200m the game is breathtaking.  The graphics do show their weakness if you’re zooming in with binoculars or a scope beyond 250m or so.  That is an engine issue, which I will talk about below.
The biggest weakness in theHunter is it’s dated game engine.  Specifically, the draw range of animals & most objects is limited to somewhere around 250m.  While the game boasts realistic ballistics & has beautiful scenery, that immersion is broken when you reach the summit of a mountain in Hammerfel and can’t spot animals on the opposite mountain.  You see, due to the limited nature of the engine, the game doesn’t draw those animals.  They exist, but you can’t see them until they come inside that 250m range.

I personally don’t agree with this being a weakness, but I’ve been around theHunter long enough to know that most do view this as an area of concern.  First, let me say that the “Free to Play” is extremely limiting, and it should be.  I wish they wouldn’t even market it this way, as it gives people the wrong impression from the outset.  The bottom line is the game offers you a ton of content, much of which is not necessary, but costs money.  You can hunt every species in the game with the basic single shot shotgun that can be purchased with your gm$ earned through Missions, you can spend a little extra for gold engraved shotguns & rifles, or you can land somewhere in between.

Purchasing the Trailrunner membership is easily the best bet for the new player, giving you all you need to hunt every species on every map for a year for $43.99, and is my advice for anybody that is just starting out.  If you still want to play after that year has expired, then in my opinion, it’s well worth the money to extend your membership.
theHunter is an addictive blend of hunting simulation & gaming, offering high replayability through randomly generated animals, enormous maps, variety in hunting methods & species.  You always have a carrot to chase, whether it’s finding that next trophy animal, looking for rare variations, trying to win competitions, reach the leaderboards & hall of fame, or completing achievements, missions, and increasing your skills.  If you can afford the Trailrunner ($43.99) membership and don’t mind the slower playstyle of a hunting simulation, then I wouldn’t hesitate to pick this game up.

I thought I was being smart by buying this during the Summer sale instead of at launch. Surely they've fixed the bugs, and it's only $20! Even at that price point, this game stinks.
Fundamentally, it's a stealth game where even on normal difficulty, the AI is part-bloodhound with incredible vision, tracking you down from 100 yards and behind a stack of crates. Once the alarm sounds and fifteen guards converge on your crates, the framerate drops and you're left watching what's essentially an animated cut-scene that occasionally reflects the choices you've made on your controller. Fun!
Maybe the AI being the world's greatest trackers wouldn't be so bad if it was balanced by good level design to go with good production design, but multiple levels involve jumping around open city blocks on beautifully clear afternoons. Full disclosure, I didn't get too far into the game; when a guard's response to his mate not being at his post was a full-on panic that led to him finding and killing me, I decided Dishonored 2 just wasn't for me; I don't need a game punishing me for doing its stealth out of order. But despite that, I didn't really prioritize buying Dishonored 2, and it wasn't until I got it as a birthday gift many months later that I actually got around to playing this.

This is one of the most refreshing stealth/FPS games I've played in years. The the start, the game shakes things up by not just making you play through as Corvo and his familiar - but revamped - powers, but also to play as Emily and her own unique power set. After a brief starting/tutorial mission to get the hang of the game, you unlock your first power and get thrown into the first of several large levels. While many other games say that there are different ways to get something done, Dishonored 2 truly means it. Just in that first level alone, trying to get into a secure area has multiple different routes you can take, rather than just having one stealth option and one assault option.
The gameplay itself is great too. The combat feels fast, fluid, and pulse-pounding when you get to it, especially in a pseduo-stealth run where you're not gearing up to fight. The stealth gameplay features all sorts of ledges, vents, guard routes, and use of the environment. The powers themselves cause things to be radically different as well. Corvo has an ability that lets him possess something, like a rat, a corpse, or even a living person, which he can use for his own unique stealth approaches. Emily meanwhile has the ability to 'link' targets together, up to four at the max upgrade, and have what happens to one target happen to all the other linked targets as well. This opens up some really fun navigating of the levels as you sneak around trying to link a few people, then jump on one guard and bash his head into the ground, causing three other guards to collapse simultaneously.
Movement in the game is also very good. You have your standard array of parkour abilities, and you can get upgrades (which I highly recommend) that let you jump a dozen feet high, or survive massive falls. Corvo has the simple Blink ability, which functions like a teleport, but can be chained with his other abilities. Emily doesn't have that, instead having the Far Reach power that lets her shoot some sort of weird spiritual grappling hook at a ledge, and yank her towards it. The upgrade paths further the difference between these two, as while Corvo gains the ability to be even more stealthy while teleporting around, Emily's Far Reach gains the ability to yank other things towards her - including unsuspecting guards. Once I had that ability, I wasted a lot of time in the rest of the game engineering the perfect situations for her to be able to yank a guard towards her, screaming loudly all the way towards her, and then choke them out and put their unconscious body in a bathroom.
On a related note, if you play as Emily and yank a guard towards her, they scream VERY loudly all the way towards her. As the other guards have ears, it can be quite a mess.
And then nearly each level shakes things up by having its own unique gimmick. I will avoid spoiling anything, but in a nutshell there is a level that involves a unique environmental effect, a level that features a constantly-shifting map, a level where there is a lot of vertical connection between everything, and then my favorite one, which I can't actually describe without spoiling the whole mission.
All in all, a great game with a lot of heart, gumption, and replay value.

More or less, I play this like a single player game.  That is not really by choice, I haven't found a group of like minded players to guild up with yet, but a couple friends and the occasional stranger will party up with me to tackle some dungeons or difficult bosses. For now I am content to wander Tamriel, learning as many crafts as I am able in order to better my own equipment, forging alliances, completing quests, and I hope to find a group of guild mates because that, I believe, will be the thing to keep me coming back regularly.

This has to be the greatest horror game I've ever played. As well as the best sequel to the original 1979 Alien. I highly recomend this game for anyone that loves horror games or is a fan of the Alien movies.

This game is so immersive, the sounds and build-up of atmosphere has been excellently done. The graphics are pretty decent and I like that it has an excellent options menu. There are many graphics options and fully remappable controls. What I also like in this game is once the alien has been released he roams wherever he wants. There's no scripted rubbish, so you've got to be constantly aware of where he is. The AI of the alien is excellent, much better than most AAA AI. A variety of usability improvements and overall better optimization and PC porting give this an edge over the first game for both new players, and PC players with less-than-top-tier hardware.
That being said, there is an argument to be made for the original Dark Souls' world, enemies, and story being more interesting in comparison to it's sequel.  There is a plethora of "large-humanoid" type bosses and normal enemies, with a few less monsters than you may have seen in Dark 1 and Demon's.  The lore is also heavily reliant on callbacks to the first game, and there are some areas that feel less interesting, or just annoying in their gameplay mechanics.  Namely the areas where one of the primary hazards is cursed jars and statues that shoot poison projectiles at you.  I do consider these to be minor complaints and can still say that I enjoyed every single area of the game, and when I finished, jumped right into new game +, which still feels fresh and exciting thanks to many events which only occur in subsequent playthroughs.
There are a large number of small changes in Dark Souls 2.  It is now possible to respec your character 4 or 5 times per playthrough, and to pay 3,000 souls after dying while keeping your humanity and the rest of your souls.  Random invasions in the world seem much less common.  Movement springs to cardinal directions, (which is not a terrible thing, and barely noticeable.)  It is a different game, but it's still unforgiving, deep, and incredibly rewarding. There's nothing else like it.
If you have the perseverance, guts, and patience to stick with it, I think this is one of the best games ever made.  Buy it, buy the first one, buy Bloodborne when it comes out.

Some of the recent Disney hand drawn animated releases have fallen short of expectations. I have to say that I was extremely impressed by the plot and character development in this movie. The story, while it is a relatively simple one, is one that draws you in and makes you care about the characters. And while many of us can see where the plot is going, the journey is highly enjoyable with some unexpected twists along the way.
For those of you who don't know what the movie is about, it is a coming of age movie about a boy who becomes a man by becoming a bear. Beyond that, it is about breaking stereotypes, and developing a respect for life. It is about dealing with anger and loss. The emotional intensity of this movie is much more similar to Lilo and Stitch or Finding Nemo, than it is to older hand animated movies such as Aladdin or The Little Mermaid. My four year old is very sensitive and had to be held at several points during the movie. But my six year old loved it, and learned some valuable lessons as well.
If I had anything negative to say, it would be that the music is not as memorable as I would have liked. I wish that they had asked Sir Elton John to contribute to the music for the picture. I like Phil Collins, but the music is too reminiscent of Tarzan for me. Still, it's not enough of a negative in this movie to make me change my rating.
Overall, I think that if they made more hand animated movies like this, they could continue to put them out forever. CGI is nice, but part of what makes Pixar movies memorable is the care given to the plot. This movie will probably be one of the great animated sleeper movies of all time--definitely can't wait to own it on DVD as well.

I've spent about 8 hours with Homeworld remastered re-living one of the best game experiences I can remember, and have to say that there are ups and downs to the remastered version.
The good:
The graphics are beautiful yet look like I remember them. That is to say Gearbox has done a great job of updating the graphics so that the game looks as it should through my rose tinted glasses of fond memories :)
They stripped out some mechanics that were a real pain in the original, specifically fuel for fighters.
The Bad:
Stripping out some of those features had unintended consequences. For example, strike craft used to automatically fly home to refuel from time to time and would automatically be repaired and re-armed. Now since they don't have fuel they don't return to base on their own and die very easily left to their own devices.
Gearbox removed the 'aggressive' and 'evasive' posture from the original which used to be very handy for keeping your ships alive longer. In the original game you could re-position your forces, withdraw, or wait for reinforcements without taking crippling losses, but now these situations lead to crippling losses.
Formations don't seem to be working right... you can put your ships in formation but they break that formation if so much as an enemy fighter shows up.
Automatic harvesting was added but works inconsistently. This was a Homeworld 2 feature meant to be a time saver so you could hyperspace out when the mission was done instead of waiting for 40 minutes for your harvesters to finish gathering resources. It's broken though so it seems to harvest random amounts and not everything on the map.
Another homeworld 2 feature they seem to have dabbled with is dynamic difficulty, which I personally hate. It basically punishes you for playing smart on prior missions and removes most of the incentive to do a good job rather than just scrape by. They should have left it out or put in a difficulty level selection.
The Ugly:
Frequent crashes to desktop even with updated drivers and directX. There are some bugs in the graphical portion.
Myriad scripting errors including...
Some missions can't be completed about 1/3 of the time. For example the mission diamond shoals has a nasty bug where after you clear the minefield the bentusi may or may not show up making the mission un-finish-able. As if this wasn't bad enough the bug also exists in the automatically made quicksave at the start of the mission, so if you get stung by this error you have to reload in the previous mission.
In the previous mission there's a scripted event where fleet command tells you about enemy defender ships and how you should research your own... in my game the research option didn't show up, so I literally cannot build this type of ship for the rest of the game.
On later missions similar bugs appear where you finish all the objectives but just can't finish the mission.
Some AI seems to have been lobotomized in transition. The garden of kadesh used to be very tough, but now most of the enemy ships don't do anything...

tl;dr 1/1 - buy it
You know how things you remember from your younger years seem to have an almost mystical glow about them?  For me it is The OG Transformers series.  To my 6-year-old mind, those Robots in Disguise (tm) cme to life every afternoon on the small screen.  They were sooo real.  Now, 30 years later when I watch an episode...  well, lets say Optimus has not aged well.
Not so with Homeworld Remastered.  The new edition looks even better than I remember the old one being, and for years, I used that game (visuals and sounds) as my standard, at least for spave sims, by which other games are judged.  HWR does not dissapoint!
My one beef is that some of the remastered soundtrack seems a bit out of place.  The noises are mainly present between levels and so do not seem to impact the immersion while playing.

On the positive side: The game is very, very pretty when it works correctly, and it includes the complete untouched originals as a bonus, except they actually work correctly on Windows 7 64-bit from what I'm seeing. Homeworld remains one of the greatest PC games ever made. The uniqueness and originality of Relic's game is still unmatched and it required very little touch-up work to remain breathtakingly beautiful.
On the negative side: Homeworld Remastered has many bugs which you will discover rapidly. I certainly did, in my first few minutes of play. The tutorials do not work; the voice instruction speeds by without waiting for you to hit 'ok' to continue, and hitting 'ok' will in fact skip a section of voice. The tutorial in HW1R is in fact for HW2, not HW1; it includes HW2's ships. Achievements do not work; they only unlock when you leave the game, and even then it seems to be a fifty-fifty tossup whether you get ones that you earned in your last play session. The game is highly unstable; I had to uninstall and reinstall it multiple times due to the game entering a state of crashing whenever you did anything at the launcher, and I'm still not sure what's causing the instability. If you have any sort of desktop overlay software running, for example MSI Overdrive, AMD Raptr, Stardock's Windowblinds and Deskscapes, or even apparently the steam overlay(!) you will suffer graphical glitches including transparent ships, broken UI effects and broken HDR effects.
I'm keeping the game because I like having a version of HW classic that works on my machine. I wish the remastered edition worked equally as well. Hopefully in the future patches will fix this, at which point I will change my opinion to positive.

The game itself looks amazing it almost feels like a real world in which you have two characters to play for: empress and her father. The game doesn't dictate how you need to play it, it's completely up to you and each way is definitely possible to play. You can play stealth or try to fight everything you see in each case using your super powers or you can play without super powers at all only with your weapons. If you choose to play with abilities you can upgrade them to make yourself even more powerful.
Combat itself is realistic which means you can't just mash the attack button and hope the game will do everything. Enemies can knock you back and you die in three shots. Though you can also perform special attacks and cut enemies in half in slow motion watching a kill-cam.
The story is very interesting and well-developed, lots of interesting notes around the area to help you complete missions or explain life around you as you progress. Every step you make counts towards the ending of the story, every kill you make will result in changes around you. This allows you to have the story which you are actually part of and have lots of different endings.
There's really nothing wrong with the game except one small thing, to enjoy the game on high graphics

Have you ever noticed how those games with severe gameplay issues are the ones that somehow end up with a significant price reduction?  Duh.  I paid $30, half price for this game and feel I should have waited for a better sale. Better yet, I should have paid attention to the many negative reviews from my fellow gamers. The gameplay mechanics are typical of console ports; they’re like threading a needle with a pair of plyers and a vise.  It's proably just me but I don’t recall JC2 being anywhere near this difficult to play.  For example, it’s too easy to end up in grappling hook h311 during those heavy action sequences.  During one of the missions, “Abandon Ship” the absurdly poor AI has the character “Mario,” whom the object is to protect, is out walking in the middle of the firefight waiting to get whacked. During this time you’re evading airstrikes, shooting down helicopters, etc.  You’re half a second from mission completion and wham, Mario dies …or worse the game’s well-documented memory leak takes hold and crashes the game completely.  Once that happens, the player is forced to replay the mission from the beginning since there is no built-in resume checkpoint feature.  Didn’t any of the developers test their product?
The game's map is a couple steps up from useless.  The map should give the player all they need in terms of status, potential targets and so on.  Nope, the player is forced to turd hunt in order to "discover" said targets.
I'll say it again, I should have paid attention to this game's less than stellar reviews.

I'v been playing factorio now for a good 2 years almost 3 now, and so far its been an amazing game that has some really good replayability as well. you start off small manually mining ores, but quickly begin to do basic automation. which then becomes a snowball effect untill you have mega processing areas that just pump out goods, which are then used to make even more things and so on. This game is extremly stable, through out my play time i'v only had the game crash once. but other than that one small bump in the road it has ran extremly well.
Pros:
- lots of replayability
- very good progression/tech system
- nice graphics (my opinion)
- trains!!!! and robots to move stuff around
- can create blueprints then have robots build stuff based on blueprints
- good map generation as well as lots of options for the map generator
- in game map editor/scenario editor
- large variety of ways to reach end game ( IE kill all the natives and take their oil and rapidly expand, or build small and compact base and try to deffend from the natives if you p*** them off)
- Ai are well balanced but could do with a few more variety
- lots of ways to deal with the natives such has tanks, rocket launchers, or gas grenades
Cons
- end game isn't fully completed altho its still being developed
- As I said before could use a few more types of natives
All in all its a really good game for the price they are asking for and they have a friday facts where they talk about everything they have done in the week so you can get an idea of what the next update is going to be about. if you have the money and you think you'd like this then buy it, and its even more fun if you can get a server going with a few friends.
