I can't recommend this title and it pains me to do so.
The good:
-Large map, probably the largest in any Total War game to date.
-It's set during the great Roman era.
-There's not a lot of bugs at present.
-Battles seem relatively untouched from previous titles although there is a lack of variety in units per faction.
The bad:
-It's completely lackluster.
-Stripped features.
-Overly simplistic management of cities/provinces with no dept at all.
-Zero dept to the game.
-Limited amount of armies and naval marines.
-Gold balanced around forcing you to have as few active armies as possible.
-Poor AI.
The good, the bad and the ugly...
It's just poorly done in all regards and overly simplified with some really bad AI. Regularly you'll see the AI abandon their only city and leave it wide open for players or NPCs to just walk in and take. Every game i've started in Grand Campaign the surrounding factions have done stupid things like this. One faction left their strongly fortified city free for the taking. An enemy of theirs, my allies, was on their territory and the AI just upped and left despite knowing there would be an attack. This was a territory I had my eye on and was fighting towards then my allies just walk in and take it without a bother as it's pretty much given to them as a gift.
Other than this allies are annoying. They constantly spam you with war proposals against other factions nowhere near your location. If you accept and attack another enemy you'll have a full troop of enemy soldiers whom your allies asked you to go to war with just appear on the last day of your siege and wipe out your remaining forces(Because your forces take damage over time while besieging a city). They usually come in full force to defend those who aren't even their allies, wipe you out then disappear never to be seen again.
What's there to say about the gameplay other than the fact it's been simplified in every aspect... City management is barebones. Each city is part of a province. In each province you share every stat. This means upgrades, unit production, buffs, happiness, taxation(No individual taxing of cities, just whether or not you can or can not tax the entire province), you get the picture. Everything is shared in a province instead of cities being managed independently. Building up a city or town is very poor. You have three, four or five slots to choose a building placement and how to upgrade it from there. You can't build walls, they're predetermined and there's only a single city(Town walls) per province. You can't build any other buildings other than what you designate at these build slots. There's generally three cities per province which means you focus one city on income, one on military and the other on food/happiness. It's as basic as it gets i'm afraid.
For military you're stuck to only raising forces under a general and you only have a specific number of generals at a time which means you start with 2 generals then 4 and so forth. I don't know what the cap is or the determining factors for how many generals you can have and how to rank up but it seems to be tied to a separate level within the campaign as in you gain enough cities you gain experience which allows you to raise a general and thus raise an army. You can't build units to defend or garrison a city, town or village, all of that is done with a general which means you have to waste one of your armies by having them sit in a province to keep happiness up and act as defence against invaders for the entire province. This is problematic as you have one army to defend three cities spread across a province. This means an enemy can simply walk into a city without any resistence save for the default garrison and take it with minimal losses.
What this means is you can't actively defend your territory without being at a significant disadvantage and you can't go on the offensive unless taking it painfully slow. To make matters worse gold is balanced in a way to deter you from raising large armies and maxing out each general. This means most of the time you'll only have a single active army on the map at any given time making the pace of the game extremely slow and lack luster.
It was clearly made to serve as a simplified title to get more people into the franchise but it utterly failed to raise the bar and do anything but damage the brand. Rome 2 was supposed to be a great game and it would have been if they kept everything from ROME: Total War and added quality of life features from successful titles such as Shogun 2 to it and kept the much larger map(It's a very big map! Very impressive for Total War as a series) but instead they removed a lot of features that made the game series great in order to gamble at a chance of introducing new customers to the series... It failed and it's evident by how bland and sterile the game feels. There's absolutely no dept to it.
If you play this prepare to restart entire campaigns over and over due to poor AI, overly simplified gameplay and silly mechanics that make very little sense other to condense the game and make it more accessible. If I could give you a tip it would be to take over any allies you're given at the start as soon as possible before they're capable of defending themselves. They'll either get in the way, start wars for you and spam you with joint war requests.

I am a veteran Total War fan.  I've played the games since the very first Shogun Total War came out, which is when I was just a little history/video game nerd.  I love the series, there really isn't anything quite like it.
Rome Total War is one of my all time favorite games, and I'm not just talking about the RTS genre.  I was very excited when Rome II was announced.  LIke many gamers who don't have money to throw away on full priced games,  I said to myself: "I sure as hell ain't paying $60 for this."  So I waited and got the game on sale for $15 as a Valentine's day present for myself because I deserved it.  Who doesn't like a little self love?
After spending a good amount of time with Rome II, I can say that I really did enjoy the game.  That may have something to do with the fact that I am a longtime fan, but I'd like to think I've evaluated it fairly.  The game did a lot of things right, and a few things wrong.
The Good:
The real time battles are still amazing.  Loved the variety of formations for each faction.
Naval battles are excellent as well.
Personally, I liked how recruitng units was done within the context of armies.  I found it to be much more efficient than recruting units from a settlement.  I also like that some buildings provided garrison troops for your settlement.  It gave me a much better shot in siege battles since I prefer to fight defensively.
Public order is much more easy to manage and it gives a better breakdown of what the problems were in a given settlement.
I also liked how cities were contained within provinces.  Its much more efficient to manage them in a group as opposed to individually.  Often times in the original Rome Total War I found myself saying: "Oh yeah, I do have territory there.  Oh, they're losing money and revolting.  Damn."
You can manage the skills of your generals and admirals to build them to function as you like.  Specific armies also have traditions that give them bonuses in combat and on the campaign map.  Its a great way to customize your troops.  In some cases, you can have the enemy's morale so low they immediatly flee the field of battle!
The Bad:
The game does not run well at times.  For me, it has trouble transitioing from the campaign to real time and vice versa.  I've also had the sound cut out on multiple occasions.  I will admit I am a mac user and my computer is not as powerul as a gaming pc by a mile and then some.  If you have a powerful computer, take the above with a grain of salt.  However, I still think it should be noted.  It has improved after a rather disastrous launch though.
The campaign interface is kind of a mess.  Everything is crammed to the bottom of the screen.  This allows you to see the pretty campaign map, but I don't think its a worthwhile tradeoff.  As a veteran player, I expected to come into the campaign and be able to pick it up and play immediatly.  That is not what happened.  I guess I can summarize the above by saying: "Play the effin tutorial ya dingus!"
Politics make no sense, so I ignore it.  Probably not a good thing.
All the DLC.  The game comes with two campaigns built in.  However, there are three campaign packs and a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of unit packs.  I shouldn't really be complaining about it in this day and age, but it still is an issue.
With all that said, I do believe the game is an excellent continuation of the series.  I'm not sure its worth the full price, considering what one actually gets for just buying the game.  However, I look forward to spending more time with it and Total War Attila when it goes on sale.

Journey to the West is one of those folktales I've always meant to get around to, specially being a fan of Dragon Ball and having seen the founding members of Gorillaz work on music and art for a stage show version of the fable.  I remember ENSLAVED being hyped up and on shelves back during the early days of the 360/PS3 era, but having no consoles of my own at that stage in the game, I never got around to playing this one.
Fast forward a few years and BAM, the whole game plus all the DLC in one package on Steam for a good sale price, I could finally see what the deal was.  The cast is at least semi-star studded, with the whole thing being the brainchild of Andy Serkis (Gollum, Snoke, Caesar, like a ton of other roles in sci-fi and fantasy movies you might have seen) and Ninja Theory (Heavenly Sword).  The sidekick is voiced by Lindsey Shaw, who played Moze in Ned's Declassified on Nick back a few years ago.  So the game at least has star appeal if you're a fan of their past performances.
The game apparently had poor sales, and while plans were laid out for expanding with sequels, etc., the whole initiative was scrapped because money.  After having given the game the attention needed to see it through to the end, I'm kind of bummed I won't see anymore of this world the developers and Andy built together.  Enslaved takes place in a post-apocalyptic America (the fallout of some sort of robot revolution...maybe?), and the majority of its competition in the late 00's, is really, really vibrant and full of color throughout its various locales.  From the rocky cliffs, deserts, and crumbling New York City, everything is just so vivid.  This is a future that mother nature is in the process of successfully reclaiming.
I think part of Enslaved's problem is that it marketed itself as a third person combat/platformer, but in practice, the combat is not a major highlight or feature of the game (but still manages to look cool, albeit repetitive in some spurts).  Enemy types are changed up with different combinations of foes with varying weak points coming at you in different situations, forcing you to adapt your combat tactics as some sort of puzzle mechanic.  The platforming especially is not the free-world climbing of Assassin's Creed, nor is it the anything-goes hopping-to-your-doom of 90's platformers like Mario 64.  You have to try really hard to find a way to die in the climbing sections of the game, as many times it keeps you from making a suicide leap.  Instead, the puzzle nature comes out in full force, and you as the player are looking for the correct way to navigate the space Monkey is in, while still collecting ammo, power ups, collectibles, etc.  If the game had been marketed more as a puzzle of "where do I jump to next?" then maybe early reviewers in the 00's would have known what they were getting into instead of being disappointed by the (at first) seemingly restrictive controls.
The area where Enslaved really shines is the cut scenes and character interactions.  Performances were motion captured, and these nearly decade old characters do a better job at emoting than many AAA NPC's I've seen even in 2016 titles.  There is so much chemistry, subtlety and character interaction going on just in the main trio's body language alone, and these are elements of human communication that games tend to leave on the cutting room floor in favor of more polished gameplay.  That's fine in practice, but it was just so refreshing to see, and the uncanny valley never even became an issue!
I mentioned this package includes the console DLC, you also get access to a several hour long campaign starring a different character, with totally different movement and combat mechanics.  This is a nice way to fill in some of the gaps for this character's backstory and habits, and a refreshing change of pace from Monkey's acrobatics and staff abilities.  Plus, hey, extra story content for free!
Enslaved is just such a curiosity of its time, and even then only console cycle into the past.  I'm disappointed the plans to take the franchise further didn't pan out, but I still think this game is worth diving into for the things it tried to be different at.  It may not have succeeded on all fronts, but when it does get it right, it really shines through, and you can tell the people behind it put everything they had into making something unique.

If you just want something fun to play through and be left satisfied, Enslaved is likely a great choice.

Disclaimer: I played this during a free weekend, and so may have been in a rush to complete it.
I was very interested in ESO because it was an MMORPG that did away with my arch-nemesis - subscription fees. But, you could be easily mistaken for thinking that ESO already runs on a free to play basis.
Distances are long, and mounts are not free. Gold is fleeting, and essential, because inventory upgrade costs are steep. Merchants will give you barely anything for what you collect in your adventures, but trading items with other players in guild stores will see you paying literally thousands of gold for a flower, let alone some sort of weapon.
In my free weekend and many hours, I reached level 19. Some players I saw had reached 600+. Perhaps they could afford flowers more easily. On the topic of other players, it is hard to see how they add much to the experience. In ESV: Skyrim (which I thoroughly enjoyed, and highly recommend), I wanted a friend or two to come adventuring with me. In ESO, you will be surrounded by players at every turn. They will crowd crafting stations, and be sprinting and jumping over every obstacle as they run, like you, from objective to objective. It was not immersive in the least, and the only respite was that you can clip through other players, but not NPCs - so if you find yourself stuck bumping into something in the dense crowd of the busy cities, you have found an NPC. Players are useful in defeating dungeon bosses, who can and will one-hit you, regardless of how powerful you think you are. Cooperation in some areas is, no doubt, crucial to success - but by design.
On the positives, this game is big, there is a lot to do, and explore, and the "campaigns", which see you waging war and capturing castles over the period of a week, or month, should have good replay value. Not to mention how much talking and reading there is to be had. Some amazing voice actors, but some quite awful scripting at points.
Overall, I give the game a solid "eh", because I wouldn't mind playing more of it, but could see myself quite quickly becoming frustrated with the intense grind if you're not paying for progress. I will likely not purchase the game, but I wouldn't be surprised if the base model becomes free to play shortly, perhaps with a few more limitations on content.

Great game with an interesting concept, very fun to play every now and then. It's a low poly first person shooter with plenty of weapon and vehicular options with interesting and engaging maps.
PROS:
-MODS!! yes, this is perhaps the best part of the game, the community is amazing providing with plenty of mods and weapon packs to fully flesh out the game. There is a mod for anything and everything, from WW1 to WW2 to modern weapons and maps, even Star Wars! Lots available and lots more to come!!
-Regular Updates: SteelRaven7, the developer, is always engaged with the community listening and responding to feedback, and updating the game every other week adding new content and mechanics. To get into this it's best to join the Discord server
-Sandbox style game: You can pretty much set up games how you want, how many bots, how many on each team, what weapons they carry, how they attack/defend etc... it gives you great control on how the battle plays out
-Well optimised: The game runs very well, even on my potato PC (Some maps may be laggy, just lower the res)
-Quick and fun: A great plus for me. You don't need to put hours into the game, as you can simply start the game play a match and exit, Maps load fast (Modded maps may take time to load) making it great to just chill out in a 30 minute break.
-Vehicles and weapons: Really great selection of all sorts of vehicles and weapons, with SteelRaven adding more every now and then. It really make it feel like a Battlefield style game with tanks, helicopters and planes all zooming by.
CONS:
-MULTIPLAYER!: Yes this game is SINGLE PLAYER and will remain so, as SteelRaven7 has expresed his desire for this game to be purely single player. It's not a big deal for me and I don't mind it, but I am aware that a lot of people are very disappointed in this factor, and it turns them away from the game
-Lacking AI: Sometimes the AI can be rather lacking in the brains department, but it is improving with each update. Some bots may ignore orders and run into the slaughter or simply just do stupid AI things
-Bugs and glitches: Yes the game is still in Early Access, so do expect some unusual stuff to happen, there are a couple of known bugs and glitches which the dev is working on, some are new and fun to point out in the Discord
Incredibly fun. Well worth the price. I have supported it since it was in its free beta stage and I'm really happy with how it turned out. With some mods it did D-Day better than CoD WW2 ;)

Smite
Smite is my most played game, and trust me there is a reason for that. I will add a TL; DR at the end.
Gameplay
Smite is a MOBA that has been around for a couple years and has gained some nice popularity. The main thing that people like about smite, that it offers different than other MOBA games such as Dota or League of Legends is that it is in third person. This means you actually have to aim your basic attacks and abilities and you much more control utilized the WASD keys for movement.
The game itself offers a total of 7 different gamemodes, not including ranked, that you can play. The gamemodes include a 5v5 Arena, 3v3 Joust, 5v5 Conquest, 5v5 Clash, 4v4 Siege, 5v5 Assault and a gamemode of the day that always offers something different. The matchmaking is on a decent timer usually taking anywhere from 20 seconds to 3 or 4 minutes to find a match (usually, ranked can easily take longer).
In smite there are gods from a handful of pantheons actually to be exact 76 gods in the game as of now, each with varying usefulness depending on the situation. An amazing thing which personally all MOBA games *cough* League *cough* should do is have an ultimate pack like Smite. This ultimate packs includes every single god in Smite, present and future, for one purchase and it is honestly one of the greatest things available. Smite also offers its premium currency as a daily reward and has a good community. By a good community I mean that this game has a good community, not a perfect community, don't get me wrong you WILL run into toxic individuals. I personally play joust and the people I find are kind and helpful and usually understanding, but what people need to understand is the every single MOBA is toxic and smite, for me, seems to be toxic mostly within arena and conquest although you will run into horrible people in other gamemodes as well.
Graphics/Sounds
The environment in smite is highly detailed and the maps such as joust also have the perk of being quite colorful and interesting in their design. The game also contains music packs which you can gain along with announcer packs which change the default ones given and are able to make your experience quite better if you get the right pack.
Pros/Cons
Pros
+ Third Person MOBA
+ Good tutorials
+ 7 different normal gamemodes
+ Ultimate god pack
+ Game events
+ Actual god lore (I mean I could read up on it, but it's a nice thing to look at when in que for a match)
+ Fun to play
+ Much better community than Dota or League (in my opinion)
Cons
- Certain toxic gamemodes (gamemodes where you will almost definitely run into someone who worsens your experience)
- Achievement Glitch (if you already had a smite account and got a major portion of achievements, those achievements will NOT unlock on steam)
Final Thoughts
I love smite, I won't hide the fact that this game has caught me perfectly. I have 420 hours on record of the time of this review being written and I don't regret a single second. I've met great people who I still regularly play with and I've also met people who simply stunned me (NOT in a good way). I usually play Joust and Assault like crazy because those are the two gamemodes I started with. Now I'm trying to get into conquest, but it's a completely different way of playing when you compare Joust and Conquest. I tried League and I hated it, simply hated it. I tried Dota for awhile, but once Russians and others started yelling at me in different languages because of their own mistakes I dropped Dota too. Then finally Smite was released on steam and I bought the god pack within the first 2-3 weeks of playing and I played with some of my close friends. I left smite for a while just before season 3, but now I've come back and nearly doubled my hours since I took my extended break.
For someone to be able to write an in-depth review for this game you need around 100 hours in my personal opinion before you've actually started to truly experience the game, but for a funny and quick review a lower time is perfectly alright. You can't go in-depth, truly in-depth with a review for this game with little hours. If you have under 30 then you simply don't know practically anything about this game! Anyway, I do love this game and am glad I found a MOBA which I actually like.
TL; DR
As the funny review which made me try this game said "Smite is the MOBA for people who hate MOBA's". This is a MOBA in third person where you aim all of your abilities and basic attacks, not just click and wait. The game contains 76 gods and 7 different normal gamemodes (not including custom/bot/ranked) at this time so there is a lot of variety for players to try things out. You will run into toxic people, don't get me wrong, but you will also most likely be able to meet good people in different gamemodes as you continue to play who will help you out, be supportive, and compliment you.

Ludicrously good.
Factorio allows you to build the biggest, most complex systems I've ever seen in a game.  Combines some of the best elements of Infinifactory, Spacechem, The Incredible Machine, Minecraft's industrial mods, and Open Transport Tycoon.
It features seriously addictive gameplay, while allowing for a variety of playstyles.  Compact, efficient factories?   Long-range rail infrastructure joining specialized sites?  Decentralized drone-driven production?  Safe, low-pollution sites built on expensive solar power?  Smog-belching, self-supplying defense outposts under constant threat?  All can work.
The graphics are sharp and well suited, the game performs extremely well on even large scales, and the interface, while requiring a bit of learning, is very powerful.
The main criticism is lack of content at or after the endgame, (though this is a matter of continuing development).  Once you've exhausted the research tree and completed production for the rocket, most everything shuts down, as there's no consumption to drive production.  What is the point of expanding to more distant, dangerous lands when there's no demand for the resources there?  You can try to create your own, by just continuing to produce unused, high cost items, but the feeling of progression is easily lost.
Or you can install one of the excellent mods.  Problem solved.

I'm a bit divided on my opinion of this game.  On the one hand, yes, it is an excellent gaming experience, provided you play it: a) on the hardest difficulty and b)you keep moving and don't doddle.  Doing both a) and b) will keep the game exciting and fast-paced, and you will be able to overlook (or not notice) the sometimes goofy things the AI Alien does as it stomps around the Nostromo.
Gameplay is simple and subtle, which is rare for a big-budget game these days.  It boils down to really getting comfortable to how the alien reacts (or doesn't react) to your movements and positioning, and capitalizing on brief windows of opportunity to distract or flee the monster. If you can overlook the rather loud stomping noise the Alien makes (or the insane amount of noise the creature makes while running through the vents), it makes for an exciting cat-and-mouse experience. Some extra human and android encounters are thrown in to add a bit of variety, but the Xenomorph is far and away the star of the game.  I think the very simple gameplay is probably why the game might have benefited from being just a couple of hours shorter, but, having said such, it's nice to get a nice long adventure for your money.
Unfortunately, the simple concept stretched over 20+ hours does make this game divisive. The inane mini-games and "press button to do thing" (ie. cutting open doors or using the wrench) elements are utterly stupid and as unengaging as most quick-time gameplay gets (think "Press F to pay respects). I assume they're really only useful as a time-wasting device to make you panic about completing them before you're spotted by an enemy.  I also found that the only really useful item was the noise-maker.
The game's graphics and style are absolutely gorgeous in every respect, and kudos to having a functioning SLI profile from the start.  It really feels like being in the first Alien movie, with all the hilarious and cool 1980's tech dressed up as futuristic (including CRT monitors and gas-generators strewn everywhere).
Ultimately, I got this game on green man gaming for 30$, and thought it was extraordinary.  For 60$, though, I think from a purely psychological standpoint, I would have felt a bit letdown.  It's dumb to put it like that, but I don't think I'm the only one who thinks the same way.  Give it a play when it's on sale!

This is what I experienced in the game and what my opinions are of it right now with about 2 hours of play (at the time of this review):
Pro's -
Clones - I can compare this game all day long to a bunch of different survival games, sci-fi games, etc. Not only is that not fair to do, it's impossible to find an exact clone. This game has elements from many different games, crammed into one. I'd say this game is more like Rift than anything else in that regard. They found what works, what was unique, and great and compiled it into their game.
Graphics - I'm a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥... I like looking at things on my computer that don't bore me or damage my eyes. But, I also can find ways to disregard graphics with gameplay mechanics. This game solved that problem for me, because it has game mechanics I like, and looks amazing at the same time. This is top tier graphics and I was stuck on a low resolution. I streamed the game, it still looked absolutely amazing where others would look terrible.
AI - I liked the way the AI functioned and responded to you, even if there was only one type. The one creature still managed to do a number of my "base" and was fun to hunt down. I enjoyed grabbing them and slamming them into trees, or better yet... throwing them up into the air and shooting them mid-fall. Like some sadistic skeet shooting. :P
Freebuilding - This reminded me of Rusts style of building, without the whole naked man junk in my face. It's quirky and needs some work, but overall I could sit all day and build a massive base for myself. If only saves worked. :P
Performance - I have a solid rig and I'm glad this game treated me right. I usually get penalized for having a decent computer where my GPU or CPU is either not used enough, not balanced, or just flat out not compatible. Not only did it work great out of the shoot, it performed perfectly. I had a few instances of lag, but then I was also streaming too. I could see frames dropping on me, but not frequent enough to be a major issue. That's the sign of a good solid foundation of a game.
Con's -
Saves - I mention this first so it's out of the way. You can't save. So, everytime to jump in, don't get attached to anything. This is supposed to be fixed and the rumor was in a patch by 02-06-15. We'll see if that happens because that will be HUGE for people.
Crashes - I list this, and not sure why I use the plural sense... because I had only one. I didn't get too far into the game (about 30 or 40 minutes) but because of the saves I lost everything. The crash may have been a collision issue that I'll forward to the devs. But, another hour or so of gaming... and not another crash.
Multiplayer - Or in the case of this, lack thereof. I am a HUGE multiplayer guy and usually pass these games up if they don't have it. I took a gamble on this game and am satisfied with it, but I would be a fool not to mention that this game is IDEAL for multiplayer. The devs say it's a likely future addition... but until then, I'll be disappointed without it.
Content - There's not much to do once you have a huge base and killed most of the creatures nearby. You can't explore and find anything else (besides resources for crafting). No additional AI, lairs, ship crashes, survivors, etc. I think once the base game gets finished more content will be added, but if you're hoping for this right off the bat you will be disappointed.
All in all... worth the price of admission. I'll be playing it when I can and enjoying what the game has to offer in the meantime. Keep up the solid work and I look forward to seeing what you can add.

Notice: Played a lot more before Steam release.
I checked out Eden Star way back when it was a tech demo, it had its ups and downs, and seeing it still alive and kicking is always awesome. It was using the Unreal Engine 3, and now they're using the Unreal Engine 4, but did it change much in terms of how it plays out? only a tiny bit.
This is their very first release of the game to the public (aside from that tech demo), which is really early, where you go and build an 'Eden' which protects you from the night damaging atmosphere, and it's also your main point of where you can construct structures, weapons, tools, and powers. And you have to protect it from the creatures it lures in the night, by constructing defenses (walls), turrets to shoot them, guns for you to shoot them, and new powers to destroy them, OR use your telekinetic melee powers to hold them, and then smash them in the direction of you choosing, to the closest hard object that will deal massive damage.
That's the game at the moment, gather resources, build stuff, protect and attack, but how good is it? well to me, it has the good looks, although a higher field of vision would help in making the world feel bigger, it's relatively easy to get into and have a good game going with how simple you get the resources, and then craft the structures you want, but all that is low in performance to what I think the game does extremely well, and that is its melee combat system with how amazing awesome it plays out, and that's what lured me to the game in the first place.

I write this review for the demanding buyer of the 21st century - who eschews the Twitter-sphere and read lengthy reviews longer than 150 characters. For those not matching this profile, here's my review:
Stole bathing salts. Leap-frogged like Deus Ex steampunk assasin, then crawled and skidded better than Adam whats-his-name Deus Ex sexy.  Played an empress to intrigue my wife and played it right - the stealthy, non-violent way to feel like a "real" man.  Not done yet, but story made me laugh while drinking wine and re-loading a badjizillion times.  18/20 thumbs up.
OK, it's a few more than 150 characters. A lot more.  But I suck at Tweet faux-reviews, and this game deserves a little more than that.
Storyline: 8/10
It's great and all, pulls at the heart strings, and I'm not too jaded to appreciate that, but I can't say that there are many personal stories beyond the main character's choices and the cut-scenes.  What more do I need? Well...Witcher 3 and Vampire Bloodlines and a number of other games provide a world of stories, in which characters each have their own perspective and their own aching tale to tell. Not only do they communicate this through letters left on desks but they plead with you, they engage in witty reparte with you, their secrets are discovered through hard choices, not just an (albeit interesting) ephemeral heart of magic.  That said, it would be unfair to rate this lower than an 8.  The fact that people's dark secrets are revealed through a magic device you can listen to is a very interesting concept. And choices do matter- and that's important.  Even if I do wish for a more open world with interesting side quests.
Character design, narration: 8/10
This, like above, is quite good but limited. Voice acting is superb and reaches the highest levels ...for the notable characters.  But I wish I could have some longer conversations about rumors and side quests with more characters. There are a few, and I won't give away where those are, but there are basically 1-2 per level.  For the price tag, it's comparatively little.  But I suppose Dishonored isn't really marketed as an rpg. It's an action-stealth game with rpg elements.
Stealth, action: 9/10
In this Disohonored 2 shines quite well.  It's a hair better than the recent Deus Ex games which are quite good (especially HR).  It provides arguably more avenues for exploration and stealth than Deus Ex: HR, and that's saying something since that has all the options of a cyberpunk world.  I really enjoy my different weapon options - sometimes using the grenades for spectacular but non-lethal ends.  The same goes for the gun.  The fact that I can destroy and distract with explosive and non-lethal force is very satisfying.  I have it on nearly the highest difficulty, short of Iron Man mode, and this requires I reload constantly.  Still, I find it incredibly satisfying to figure out the puzzle of the scenarios they give me - and often I discover odd ways to do them because of their innovative design.
Graphics: 9/10
I don't really feel qualified to rate this since my fairly new computer and graphics card (2.5 years old, don't laugh) only runs this on very low settings.  It's still beautiful. It still runs well.  It holds up to Deus Ex HR and whatever that newer version is, and almost as pretty as Witcher 3. Almost.  Optimization isn't as good, so maybe it's as pretty at the highest settings.  Anywho, I can't complain.
Other: 9/10
If you get it on sale, like I did during the Summer Sale for something like 50% off, then it's well worth it. I still wouldn't  recommend purchasing this at full price, but at that kind of deal it was money well worth it.  What else to say?  Oh!  It
surprisingly creepy as all get-up with headphones on if you don't like insects...  Mmmm, I'm only half way through and there's a really fresh level in there that requires a lens to see things in alternate ways.  I enjoy seeing the effects of my choices in newspapers or journals or planning boards.  Nice touches. Makes it all feel realistic.

I really wanted to like this game. But I found myself not wanting to spend the money on this.
First off, this isn't an elder scrolls multiplayer game. It's an MMO with ES trimmings, as other reviews have said. Random exploration isn't really a big part of the game, more of a sidebar "look, you can go explore this part - checkbox marked". It's definitely more "on rails" than any ES game, even with the "One Tamriel" aspects, it feels zoned and the quests feel go-for.
The story is "okay" for an MMO, and mediocre for an ES game. Granted, I didn't get far, about level 12 or so, but while a few of the story lines were decent, many seemed like filler more than actual meat. Getting into the questline at level 10 seemed to improve things a bit, some decent questing in the rescue storyline.
The leveling design was really well done. The mechanics (as an archer) felt well-designed. I wanted to continue leveling my character, and the side-quest of "collect Skyshards" didn't feel as tacked on as, say, DA:I. The skill powers felt meaty and their improvement seemed pretty organic, While there is a huge number of skills/feats opened up by joining different guilds, taking different professions, training with different weapons - it didn't seem as confusing as it did at first glance. Synergies were pretty easy to figure out, and while I did waste a few skill points I could have better spent elsewhere, but it wasn't devastating to the experience.
Combat was very fluid, defintiely one of the better action combat games (as an archer). You could switch between closers and ranged attacks, and even CC with the abilities you get pretty early on. It felt very satisfying in a fight. Death happens pretty swiftly if you don't play smart with a medium armor build, but the starting areas mitigate this pretty heavily for you (you have to really be bad to die).
I didn't explore social and grouping much, but the basics seemed to be there in the party and guild functions. I'll leave off on that. Inventory and money came pretty easily, I didn't get into crafting (I've never been a crafter in MMOs, but it seemed like a pretty decent crafting system).
The beginning areas suffer from being some of the worst in a game that I've experienced. At one point, I simply had no more quests and was around level 5. I learned later I was supposed to talk to the same guy I ended the last quest with, even though the dialog indicated we were through for a bit. No quest marker, so this was poorly designed. Getting items to suit your playstyle is also a chore, with too much RNG going on (for example, I was using a two-handed sword all through the intro; it was a waste of rank ups - if there had been a bow lying about, or some option, that would be better).
While I'm labeling this game "not for me", there are some good design elements present. Sadly, it wasn't enough to keep me playing past the free weekend. For those seeking more "elder scrolls" experience: save your money and use modded Skyrim to fill the void. Or wait for TES VI.
For those looking for a good MMO, I think you'll enjoy it (depending on your playstyle). Sadly, it would have to be an exceptional MMO to keep me - and this, while excellent, wasn't exceptional.

Wube software has a real gem on their hands.
Factorio might be the ultimate sandbox game; a creative tool allowing for truly intricate machines. Named for the tendency for these creations to resemble factories, many other unrelated things are absolutely possible. And that’s not including the (extensive) library of user-created mods for the game already available.
Like Don’t Starve, Terraria and Minecraft before it, there is a survival element to the creative process that adds a sense of urgency. It comes to this game in the form of a sprawling, infinite alien horde which objects to the pollution your factories generate. On your quest to launch a spaceworthy rocket, you will encounter them frequently.
One pleasant surprise for me though was the overall quality. Despite still being in alpha, the game is already heavily optimized, and fully supports online multiplayer play, with optional mods. I have seen 100+ player servers online at times. The quality shows though, and actually the way I discovered the game was via its Steam Reviews. For a time it was the highest reviewed game on Steam of all time. That is a significant and well-earned achievement.
If you are a sandbox gamer, this one should be a top pick. Get it.

I'm a bit divided on my opinion of this game.  On the one hand, yes, it is an excellent gaming experience, provided you play it: a) on the hardest difficulty and b)you keep moving and don't doddle.  Doing both a) and b) will keep the game exciting and fast-paced, and you will be able to overlook (or not notice) the sometimes goofy things the AI Alien does as it stomps around the Nostromo.
Gameplay is simple and subtle, which is rare for a big-budget game these days.  It boils down to really getting comfortable to how the alien reacts (or doesn't react) to your movements and positioning, and capitalizing on brief windows of opportunity to distract or flee the monster. If you can overlook the rather loud stomping noise the Alien makes (or the insane amount of noise the creature makes while running through the vents), it makes for an exciting cat-and-mouse experience. Some extra human and android encounters are thrown in to add a bit of variety, but the Xenomorph is far and away the star of the game.  I think the very simple gameplay is probably why the game might have benefited from being just a couple of hours shorter, but, having said such, it's nice to get a nice long adventure for your money.
Unfortunately, the simple concept stretched over 20+ hours does make this game divisive. The inane mini-games and "press button to do thing" (ie. cutting open doors or using the wrench) elements are utterly stupid and as unengaging as most quick-time gameplay gets (think "Press F to pay respects). I assume they're really only useful as a time-wasting device to make you panic about completing them before you're spotted by an enemy.  I also found that the only really useful item was the noise-maker.
The game's graphics and style are absolutely gorgeous in every respect, and kudos to having a functioning SLI profile from the start.  It really feels like being in the first Alien movie, with all the hilarious and cool 1980's tech dressed up as futuristic (including CRT monitors and gas-generators strewn everywhere).
Ultimately, I got this game on green man gaming for 30$, and thought it was extraordinary.  For 60$, though, I think from a purely psychological standpoint, I would have felt a bit letdown.  It's dumb to put it like that, but I don't think I'm the only one who thinks the same way.  Give it a play when it's on sale!

The game has save stations, which adds to the terror of dying, and genuinly does a good job of adding suspense, however, you can only load 'current save', 'previous save', and 'restart mission'. Which normally wouldn't be a problem, but if your game bugs out, and an NPC refuses to speak with you, then you're hosed, and you are playing that chapter over.
The animations when characters speak are a throwback to previous generation consoles, where you just see flappy jaws as dialogue goes on.
You'll see graphical glitches, such as the alien's head cutting through locker doors to join you inside the locker.
I'm still enjoying this game, but unholy hell am I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that I have to restart my chapter, and I have no idea what caused the glitch in the first place, so there is a good chance I'll cause the glitch again.
If this game wasn't so unique in a sea of sandbox crap, I wouldn't suggest it, but because it's unique, i'm willing to overlook some of it's glaring flaws.

What can I say about the greatest game ever? This game stands at the top of a list of extremely amazing game.
- Story is top notch. Pick whatever term you want. Classic. Epic. Gripping. They all apply.
- Gameplay was/is unrivaled. If side scroller would be 1 plane of movement. Other greats like Age of Empires and Command and Conquer would be 2 planes of movement, but Homeworld offers a true space RTS experience with 3 planes of movement. Swarm from the front, back, left, right, above him, under him, and everything in between. Limited resources per map mean that you need to manage your ships with some level of care (or get big on swarming enemy units with salvage corvettes).
- Soundtrack is a cut above all others. Few experiences can top being hit with shocking revelations followed by insurmountable odds all to the timeless masterpiece of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings, vocal arrangement, Agnus Dei. More recent music-in-games titles that I would compare this level of excellent soundtrack to would be the Mass Effect Soundtracks and the Witcher 3 Soundtracks, as an example of 'Damn quality game music'.
- Modding is somewhat alive. There are quite a few very solid mods for the game. Most notably the Star Wars mods, Mass Effect mods, Star Trek Mods, and all other SciFi reimaginings.
- There was/is multilayer capability, but only in skirmish mode.
I highly recommend this game for everyone. I wouldn't suggest that its multiplayer experience will grip your gaming attention for months or years, but the single player campaign here is something that can stick with you for a lifetime.

I write this review for the demanding buyer of the 21st century - who eschews the Twitter-sphere and read lengthy reviews longer than 150 characters. For those not matching this profile, here's my review:
Stole bathing salts. Leap-frogged like Deus Ex steampunk assasin, then crawled and skidded better than Adam whats-his-name Deus Ex sexy.  Played an empress to intrigue my wife and played it right - the stealthy, non-violent way to feel like a "real" man.  Not done yet, but story made me laugh while drinking wine and re-loading a badjizillion times.  18/20 thumbs up.
OK, it's a few more than 150 characters. A lot more.  But I suck at Tweet faux-reviews, and this game deserves a little more than that.
Storyline: 8/10
It's great and all, pulls at the heart strings, and I'm not too jaded to appreciate that, but I can't say that there are many personal stories beyond the main character's choices and the cut-scenes.  What more do I need? Well...Witcher 3 and Vampire Bloodlines and a number of other games provide a world of stories, in which characters each have their own perspective and their own aching tale to tell. Not only do they communicate this through letters left on desks but they plead with you, they engage in witty reparte with you, their secrets are discovered through hard choices, not just an (albeit interesting) ephemeral heart of magic.  That said, it would be unfair to rate this lower than an 8.  The fact that people's dark secrets are revealed through a magic device you can listen to is a very interesting concept. And choices do matter- and that's important.  Even if I do wish for a more open world with interesting side quests.
Character design, narration: 8/10
This, like above, is quite good but limited. Voice acting is superb and reaches the highest levels ...for the notable characters.  But I wish I could have some longer conversations about rumors and side quests with more characters. There are a few, and I won't give away where those are, but there are basically 1-2 per level.  For the price tag, it's comparatively little.  But I suppose Dishonored isn't really marketed as an rpg. It's an action-stealth game with rpg elements.
Stealth, action: 9/10
In this Disohonored 2 shines quite well.  It's a hair better than the recent Deus Ex games which are quite good (especially HR).  It provides arguably more avenues for exploration and stealth than Deus Ex: HR, and that's saying something since that has all the options of a cyberpunk world.  I really enjoy my different weapon options - sometimes using the grenades for spectacular but non-lethal ends.  The same goes for the gun.  The fact that I can destroy and distract with explosive and non-lethal force is very satisfying.  I have it on nearly the highest difficulty, short of Iron Man mode, and this requires I reload constantly.  Still, I find it incredibly satisfying to figure out the puzzle of the scenarios they give me - and often I discover odd ways to do them because of their innovative design.
Graphics: 9/10
I don't really feel qualified to rate this since my fairly new computer and graphics card (2.5 years old, don't laugh) only runs this on very low settings.  It's still beautiful. It still runs well.  It holds up to Deus Ex HR and whatever that newer version is, and almost as pretty as Witcher 3. Almost.  Optimization isn't as good, so maybe it's as pretty at the highest settings.  Anywho, I can't complain.
Other: 9/10
If you get it on sale, like I did during the Summer Sale for something like 50% off, then it's well worth it. I still wouldn't  recommend purchasing this at full price, but at that kind of deal it was money well worth it.  What else to say?  Oh!  It
surprisingly creepy as all get-up with headphones on if you don't like insects...  Mmmm, I'm only half way through and there's a really fresh level in there that requires a lens to see things in alternate ways.  I enjoy seeing the effects of my choices in newspapers or journals or planning boards.  Nice touches. Makes it all feel realistic.

A bare bones and flawed game on a solid concept and design foundation.
I've only spent on hour in the game so far on the day of initial E.A. release.  The controls are great as are the graphics.  But, right now, it doesn't really feel like a game per se.  You have about 6 minutes of daylight to run around and zap trees and rocks, then about 6 minutes of night to zap bugs.  The bugs seem to just warp in under my feet as well.  The daytime doesn't seem to be long enough to really dig into any kind of building or exploring and nighttime is a tower defense mini game.
Some suggestions to what's currently in game (not additional features):
Harvesting trees makes visual sense.  I can see the tree fall and break into pieces.  And they take a comfortable amount of time to do so.  Harvesting rocks is a visual mess and takes far longer.  Perhaps tightening up the visual clues of what's left in a rock to harvest or something to clue me into the progress would be helpful.  Also, since I only have abou 6 solid minutes of daylight, spending 2 of them on a rock is extremely limiting.
The bug alien critters seem to just pop out of nowhere.  I'm not sure if that's a bug (no pun intended) or that's how they work.  It was odd to be turning around looking for these things and they just pop in under my feet.  Perhaps if they originated from their little dens or mounds and skittered toward me.
They day/night cycle time is very rushed.  Right now, I feel like the game can't decide if it wants to be a exploration/construction game or a tower defense.  It has aspects of both, but they are hampered.  And one major way is the short time windows.  Let me explore and harvest a little longer and actually have some time to build something and maybe have some kind of build up at night, the pacing and number of bugs attacking increases or comes in waves instead of the static two pop in at a time in exact intervals.
Overall, I think the presentation of the game is solid.  The help pop ups are clear and understandable.  The graphics are nice and the art direction has its own identity.  I think there's more foundation in this game than many E.A. games in terms of setting, design, and concept.  It certainly has a long way to go, and I'm excited to follow it as it develops.

Borderlands 2 is an amazing game. I've only played for around 70 hours so I can't exactly give as much opinion and input as possible, but I'll review what I can.
This game is fantastic. It's engaging, fun, intense and fast-paced. The characters are absolutely hilarious, and as the game progresses the love towards them grows and they become more amusing. The storyline is great as well and all the events can often catch you by surprise. This is one of the few games where I almost feel like I grow a connection to the characters and treat them as if it were reality. This often influences different decisions throughout the game.
The mechanics of this game are great as well. From the action skill to the different types and abilities of guns makes this the kind of game where you can spend hours trying to find the perfect weapon set and build. The fighting is fun, fast-paced and intense, while also very rewarding.
The game also doesn't feel very grindy. Despite there being some points where you struggle to get from one level to the next, it is more fun as you're often doing missions to get experience, not constantly killing enemies or farming through dungeons to get experience, making it a lot more fun and less boring.
The skill tree mechanic is fantastic. It allows different combinations to be made, that change the way your character can be played, from causing Phaselock to completely obliterate enemies nearby with elements to allowing the Commando's Turret to have a protective shield. Different skill trees can be invested in for each character, allowing a lot of flexibility to change how the character can be played. Different builds can be easily made as well as doing a skill respec doesn't cost much. Different items in the game, such as relics and classmods can also change the way skill trees can be made, often by adding extra levels in a certain skill.
The level of weaponry in this game is the best I've seen in any video game. There are so many guns it's impossible to even get close to obtaining even half of them. There are also many shields, class mods, grenades and relics too, allowing for a serious amount of different builds to be made for each class.
If you're going to get this game, I'd recommend buying the Game of The Year edition, whether it is on sale or not, as this provides so much more gameplay, storyline and fun from the base game.

I expected a generic Action/Adventure game and the game delivered... With something extra.
Going through the first few chapters, ENSLAVED: Odyssey to the West felt like a normal action-platforming game with an interesting story, but it became better.
Even with a not-so-special battlesystem, the action in this game is still something fun. You'll find yourself battling enemies quite some time between the usual platforming. So if the battlesystem doesn't suit you (it takes some time getting used to, the game getting far more easy if you get into it), you might not have a lot of fun.
The platforming itself is not much of a big deal. Sure, the game has decent graphics and pleasing sceneries but the controls can be a bit annoying when you're hurrying. For example, your character not jumping because your aim was slightly off, not correctly pushing the analog stick the right way.
Now we're talking about controls, yes I did play the game with a controller and overall it was fine, besides the camera working against me sometimes. Can't say much about the keyboard and mouse controls 'cause I haven't tried it myself, but lots say that a controller is recommended since this game is a (pretty good) console port.
That game at normal difficulty is actually quite easy. First you'll have some problems learning how to defeat enemies efficiently making the game quite hard first but after a few chapters it does get really easy, especially if you get the (health) upgrades. Regeneration makes surviving a whole lot easier, and never actually found myself in need of the health syringes you can get from your companion Trip, who I forgot to mention. (Yes, part of the game is basically an escort mission, but no, Trip won't get in your way at all.)
Also want to give a quick shoutout to the voice actors! They did a really great job.
TLDR: The game might not look like anything special at first sight, but doesn't fail to deliver. The gameplay isn't anything new yet is still fun. The story (based on an old Chinese novel) is great and makes up for the few cons this game has. Definetely worth a buy.

My first Steam review and unconditional recommendation goes to this game.  Amazing first person action; definitely the smoothest and probably the most immersive first person game I have played in recent years, even on my aging GTX570.  Great atmosphere and amazing stealth mechanics, too.  Plus, I love the way it riffs on the Alien lore.  Go for it.

My enduring thanks to the Creative Assembly team that crafted this diamond!
Beautiful, horrific, tense, atmospheric, these are but a few of the qualities that fail to fully realise what Alien: Isolation truly is. Based on Ridley Scott's 1979 sci-fi/horror masterpiece Alien, never before has a film translated into a video game so well. Capturing the low-fi dystopian future of Alien perfectly, Alien: Isolation is all at once a terrifying and enthralling descent into the unknown, slow burning but measured in its pacing. If you are a fan of sci-fi, horror, or well made games in general do not hesitate to pick this up, because once you board Sevastapol station you will regret and love your decision.

Even though it sh!ts the bed in few places, Isolation is one of those rarities that makes 90% of other games look incredibly bland. It's also the most accurate movie-to-videogame adaptation, which nails both the visuals and the feel of the first movie. Who would have thought that Xenomorph could ever be scary again? I swear this f*cker has a mind of his own - when he cautiously approaches me as I aim my flamethrower at him, or when he's searching the room while I'm sitting in a locker, trying not to poo myself.

Very few movie-based games capture the feel of the film they are emulating quite as well as Alien: Isolation.
Sort of a sequel to Ridley Scott's original movie "Alien", the game's designers clearly made a huge effort in capturing the sort of retro scifi feel of that the movie has.  It is also one of the few legitimately suspenseful games I've played. With no weapons powerful enough to destroy the Alien, the player instead has to relay on the use of cover, hiding places, and improvised weapons that can drive the creature off... for a time.  I've never before played a game that made me actually sweat in chair with nervous energy as I crept through a level hoping not to get caught, and while there are a few "jumpscares" in the game, they are effectively used and fit the atmosphere of the game rather that feeling like a cheap contrivance.

theHunter is a very detailed, beautiful, and somewhat immersive hunting game. And it's free. The actual tracking mechanics are very easy to grasp and they work well for a game that seems to focus on patience and careful, calculated movements. The small GPS-like tool you use to track and use as a map is a good addition and it works perfectly with the concepts. The shooting mechanics in the game are basic from my experience, but it works well.
The game itself is absolutely stunning looking, the graphics and the sound work on it are almost unmatched by any other game, especially other hunting games. The feeling of the world is very immersive and it is almost perfect. But it is very difficult to run on a lower end computer.
Me, being someone who has gone out to many forests and reserves to hike and take pictures, was astonished by how easily the game immersed me into it. The sounds, as I said, are fantastic. The graphics are fantastic also, being one of the best looking games I have played in a long time.
As the hunting part goes, it works very nicely. The tracking system is great, the animal AI is fair, and the movements of your character and the controls are great also.
The biggest problem is the subscription system. You can only hunt Mule Deer unless you pay for either a 3 month, 6 month or 12 month subscription to access the other licenses. Also, you can't host your own multiplayer games without a subscription.
Pros: Beautiful looking and sounding, great hunting mechanics, immersive
Cons: Difficult to run on a low end PC, Sometimes lengthy and boring hunts, you need to pay real money to get licenses to hunt any other animal than the Mule Deer.
Overall, if you are a hunting fan or love good looking games. I think this is perfectly enjoyable.

Simply put if you liked old total war games you probably wont like this one.
deal breakers (for me)
AI that cheats even on normal settings making it impossible to truly be strategic and draw armies apart so you can lets say flank or attack while they are distracted
useless agents (for you) that the AI just spams at you endlessly
cities no longer exist they are replaced by "provinces" where 2-4 cities make up a super city. while it sounds nice in theory in game play it means 2-3 of your cities will always be dedicated to agro/happiness and end up 99% identical. there is no way to make a "warpath" civilization or a "im loaded with money and i just buy everything". there is an exact certain way you must build your cities and if you deviate from this you will be punished with rebellions and provinces that are simply ineffectual IE gimped.
confusing unit cards that don't really explain units at a glance
units in general have been so over-engineered that any semblance of rock-paper-scissors is out the window. and in the end most units just end up feeling bland and reduces tactics to just using the best units in class vs a varied and balanced army.
no more blitzkrieging cities get unhappy way to easily with no way to fix imbalances except to simply raze buildings and start rebuilding from scratch with the aforementioned formula.
your armies are limited by generals, while i do like the idea that every army has a general i don't like that you have a finite number of them and it always seems like you simply have to few to go around forcing you to make big stomper armies instead of smaller armies to cover your empire.
because of this it also forces you to almost exclusively fight on one front. while i know it isn't realistic to fight a war on two opposing fronts it really forces you to fight in only bottleneck situations because you often end up outnumbered even against one opponent. again the AI cheats and not to make up the difference between programmed skill and human tactics but simply because the AI is♥♥♥♥♥♥and cant compete unless it hordes you endlessly.
battle AI is still buggy with sieges and the game is over a year old. things like armies just standing still on battles with no timer limit, armies refusing to attack during a siege or just sieges in general being very buggy like siege equipment getting confused or simply not attacking the gate/wall you directed it too.
really I cannot even list all the crazy %#$(*# that happens in battles and most of the time its breaks realism and will completely throw the outcome of a battle whether its the enemy refusing to attack you when they are the provocateur or your armies simply not responding to commands.
even tho i got this game as a gift i wouldn't recommend it at all if you were hoping for a real Rome II. this game is an arcade game with a total war look.

Angry ape child wonders why frightened intelligent girl puts a slave band on his head to keep him from hurting her.  Despite her position of control, he still ends up ordering her around.
I didn't know much of anything about the game, but I had some suspicions about its story when the ape child pulled out a staff as his main weapon. Move like an ape and swing a staff, there's really only one character he could be based on. When the names are revealed, yup, that explains the whole "Odyssey to the West" bit.
This game shows promise. Its got decent graphics. The story its based on is classic. When you have no idea what world you're in and suddenly you pass a ruined Statue of Liberty, you get one of those rare "woah, cool" moments in gaming. However, it is deeply marred by its controls, especially the janky camera work. Sometimes you are moving fast. Sometimes slow. Sometimes the camera seems to follow you. Then it takes agency away. You think a jump join is a certain direction only to find out its the opposite. It creates frustration, but not quite enough to kick the game to the rubbish bin.

This is the first time I've felt strongly enough about a game to write a review and it's based on only about 20 minutes of gameplay: the story is horrible.  The only way I would play this is if I found out that at some point in the game, I get to gruesomely murder the female for what she does to you in the first 20 minutes of the game.  An "uneasy partnership", says the game's description; I've never heard enslavement referred to as an "uneasy partnership".  I could have excepted that, though, but within half a second of being told that he is now her slave, the protagonist basically says, "Cool; let's go."  After spending 20 minutes fighting to escape a slave ship, with this woman actively trying to leave him for dead in her wake, he's suddenly cool with having a slave headband put on that will torture him if he disobeys her or kill him if she dies.  "I guess I have no choice," were his words when she wants him to help her...you always have a choice: fight.  He should have killed her and died free instead of suddenly becoming cool with the idea of being a slave.  With writing like this, I wouldn't have been surprised if they had started having sex before the first hour was done.  I won't be finding out, though, as I've uninstalled the game.  If you don't care at all about the story, you might enjoy this, but if you're a fan of good storytelling, skip this game.

Completed the game on hard with 100% achievements.
Dislikes:
Controls are very clunky. Playing with mouse and keyboard would be a pain. I played with the Xbox 360 controller, but it still felt like it could use some polishing. Probably because it was ported from console platform.
Gameplay was bland at the best. Fighting sequences were too easy and repetitive: your run-of-the-mill press X to attack, Y to attack stronger, A to evade and b to block.
Platforming was simple yet messy. It takes a long time to get used to it because it doesn’t move smoothly. Don’t expect Assassin’s Creed’s smooth climbing in this game. No matter how properly you are lined up to jump to the next platform, you find yourself doing flips at the edge instead of jumping over.
Boss fights were generic yet frustrating (although I did play on hard).
I got the game mostly because I was interested in the story. It didn’t turn out to be the best plotline, the voice acting seemed forced and unnatural, and character development was cheesy.
Visuals are bit outdated, Even for its time. Textures are blurry, and it is really hard to believe they used motion capture for the actors, because the character movement and model seemed really shabby.
Likes:
This game is definitely not for everyone. If you get impatient with the things I mentioned above, you won’t likely last through the first two chapters.  Nevertheless, if you are tired of playing hard-core games and are looking for a break in a casual platformer with interesting world setting and a story driven adventure, it’s not a terrible game. I am guessing you could finish the game in 10 hours through a casual run. Grab it when it’s on 75%+ sale.
Other:
I spent so much time on the game because I like completing games with 100% achievements. This game was especially tough, because there are these collectables called orbs (in-game currency for upgrades) that are nearly impossible to find all 100%, and they aren’t even that rewarding for in-game content (there is plenty of extra orbs from fights). But if you don’t care about achievements, moot point.

I have to say in terms of beauty, characters and overall acting this game is one hell of an awesome trip. The scenery is awesome, the characters believable and well written. The overall story is gripping and entertaining. However, this game also has some serious issues. First the combat is so-so, but the wonky mouse/keyboard controls, and the weird camera angles and shifts make the combat outright horrible. Secondly, the cutscenes cannot be skipped. If you struggle a bit - like me - you might have to watch some scenes a couple of times, without having a way to abort them. Come on folks, it's 2016. I have to give the game credit for the take down animations without quick time events. The climbing parts are fun and fluid, with only a few places suffering from the dreadful camera movement. Overall I'd recommend the game, just be prepared to be frustrated by the controls and the camera.
Overall I rate 8/10, the nature of this game is irrepressable!

This game is a suprisingly addicting, good, and fun game that exceeds all my expectations for a single developer.

The game is not a "the player is the god of the game and will dominate the entire enemy team" like most games of this style are. You, yourself, are not any better than the bots on your team and the other (unless you get mods that give you OP weapons). This kind of difficulty is not reppelling, but neither is it too easy, its the goldilocks of game difficulty.
The game has infinite playability, as the game has great mod support, so you can never truly "Be the best at every map".
LIke what I was saying about the overall difficulty, your not invincible or a god in this game, you are a mere soldier on the battlefield, and vunerable to the same death as any other bot near you. It makes the game more immersive, as your constantly trying to not die (which will happen, a lot), and it makes you more aware of your surroundings.
The AI exceeds expectations for a single developer. Two problems I have with the AI at its current state: squads are irritating to control. In other words, Forming a squad with more than 1 ground vehicle controled by AI turns into micromanaging mayhem. Another is that when bots form their own mini squads (which is just 1-2 vehicles controlled by 2-3 bots each) it tends to be ineffective and pointless, and I would rather see larger waves of bots attacking a point rather than at most 6 bots (I'm leaving groups of soldiers w/o vehicles out of this as they are map exclusive)
Recommendations:
1) A mode where you dominate the entire map by capturing all the points.
2) Multiplayer, which would be rather pointless to add at the game's current lack of a playerbase.

One of the most repetitive and frustrating games I think I've ever experienced. By the time you've played it for an hour you've genuinely seen virtually everything it has to offer. There's nothing new in any of the later levels and I wish I'd just stopped playing instead of slogging through to the end.
The alien makes things quite tense at first, but it rapidly becomes ridiculous as you realise it must be virtually omniscient to be able to follow you all over this huge space station - lifts and rapid transit systems apparently don't cause it any trouble for example. It and later the other aliens seem capable of tracking you flawlessly wherever you go, employing what must be the most extensive system of overly large air vents in human history. Having to crawl slowly around the vast majority of the time just so an alien doesn't pop out of a vent and grab you every 7 seconds really helps to artificially increase the play time of the game. Similarly the EVA sections are extremely tedious because you move so slowly and are given long distances to walk for no apparent reason. Once you get hold of a flamethrower, it's a waste of time trying to hide from the alien if you do encounter it - a couple of bursts of flame and it'll scurry off into a vent (there's always a vent within a few metres), removing most of the intended suspense and threat.
Aside from the boring "stealth" parts, the game is just a constant stream of "Go to place X and pull lever Y" missions. You can explore a bit if you want sometimes, but there's not much incentive to do so when you have a checkpoint save system and the chance of dying almost anywhere and at any time depending on where the alien decides to pop out next.
The game also features some of my least favourite FPS cliches, such as forcing you to give up all your weapons at one point, scripted scenes where you're just a passenger being told to press a key occasionally, multiple instances of dangling from a ladder over a long drop of some sort, taking you back to levels you've already seen earlier, and your character surviving all kinds of falls and explosions and other hazards that would have killed a normal person. One section towards the end I remember as being an example of the worst type of level design went something like this: 1) sneak through a series of rooms to find a keycard 2) sneak back through the same rooms to another set of rooms and use the keycard to unlock a door 3) try to open the door, but a generator stops working 4) sneak back through all the same rooms once again to restart the generator 5) sneak back through all the rooms one final time to get to the door again. It's so so so boring.
I can't think of any reason why I'd ever want to play this game again. For all its flaws, I'd rather play Colonial Marines.

Just Cause 3 feels more like an iteration on Just Cause 2. More toys, bigger open world, event more types of vehicles are made obsolete. If you liked JC2 and "just more toys" is enough for you to justify a purchase -- go for it, you probably won't be disappointed. Probably.
The story, as always, serves as a nice bonus on top of the usual destruction sandbox. It's a light, not intrusive, but quite simplistic and repetative set of missions. It's OK. Not that bad, but nothing special either. And final boss is a helicopter. Helicopter. That's a... really appropriate ending, i guess? Just destroy yet another helicopter. Oh well.
It also sounds and looks great. Soundtrack is way cooler than I expected.
But the main treat is a sandbox, and that's where JC3 lacks compared to JC2. Bases and towns are more interesting, but there are way less of them. Like, the handful of really intersting and big military bases, and only one small city. Installing DLCs helps a bit, but still, that's not enough. And the final island feels empty. Also, there are no big civilian airport, so there is no Boeings. That was a bit disappointing for me. And islands don't have a certain themes anymore. In JC2 there were a very distinct "the desert bit", "snowy bit", "more populated city bit" and "the foresty bit". That added some lovely diversity to environment. And even your vehicles got snowy in snowy areas and dusty in the deserty areas, that was a cute touch. But now "the foresty bit" is preety much all there is. Yes, you still can find some snow and some desert, but there isn't enough of those, and they look a bit dull.
And don't get we wrong, destroying bases are really fun, and that's where this game shines. There is just not enough of them.
And a wingsuit. It's the most fun I ever had freeroaming is an open world game. You can buy the game just for that. And you can get one with rocket, if you buy Sky DLC (which is, to be honest is a must-buy).
So, in conclusion. It's a perfect game, for those of you, who really enjoys sandboxes with a lot of toys in them and a fans of JC2, but a cautious recommendation for everyone else.

I'm going to preface this with: I have only really played two MMO's before this, TERA and World at Warcraft and Runescape if that counts? I've also Only played 3 Elder Scrolls games Skyrim, Oblivion and Morrowind all on console.
So far I have only played because of the free weekend and wouldn't of bought this game otherwise. I am 15 hours in and enjoying it. I haven't felt the need to just 'buy' stuff to progress and there is tons too do. It's like and Elder Scrolls game with the hundreads of things dotted around the map, so much stuff to do it can be abit too much. I have purposely stayed away from guides and 'build guides' because its fun being a noob and experiencing a game with no prior kowledge of it. In those 15 hours I am level 15, done a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of quests, crafting and general exploring as the world is very open and interesting kinda like skyrim/oblivion in that regards.
Gathering materials can be a pain and sometimes hard to find, however I find the best way to get materials is just quest and you will often see Iron ore, Plants or anything else on your way. I can see why someone wouldn't like this but I would not say it is pay to win. It is however grindy, but not to the extent of Tera or Runescape.
I will say when you start you are awarded 500 Crown currency or whatever it's called, use that to buy the Starter Pack, you get a Horse, Dog and some other items. I only found this out when I hit level 15 and probbaly could of progressed a little faster If I knew about this earlier.
The game runs fine for me, My specs are AMD Fx6100, GTX 660, 16GB 1600mhz Ram and 1tb HDD. I can run this game on Ultra at a healthy frame rate and the Loading times are often very quick.
TLDR: Really Enjoying it and lots of stuff to do, can be abit grindy but I am still buying it.

The best remaster to be utterly destroyed by bad marketing, rushed release, and poor multiplayer support. Has lost 84% of it's player base in the 3 months since launch, and incredibly the multiplayer is still in 'beta'. While some work has been done in the way of fixing glaring issues with said multiplayer, and one hopes efforts continue to be made, I fear that it is already too little, too late, and the game has quickly been rendered utterly irrelevant after holding so much promise at launch.
Definitely recommend the game in general, but given the state of the multiplayer and overall lack of player base, I cannot recommend this for anyone but the most devout RTS and space simulator fans at the $35 price point. Definitely keep an eye out for this one to go on sale!

I bought Homeworld Remastered because I loved and still play the original.  I thought the new version was an upgrade from the original, that would take advantage of the newer more powerful computers today.  The only real improvement I found was the graphics.  They are great!!  The senerios  are the same as the original, but the controls have been changed  in ways that make play a pain.
The ship count is limited in the original and even more limited in the remastered version. The more powerful computers  of today should be able to handle larger fleets and the ship count should only be limited by the number of berths.  Building or capturing carriers should allow for an increased ship count. The ship count limit placed on ships within a class ( like only 14 salvage corvettes ) limits stratagies and tactics.
The salvage corvette was my most useful ship, but the limit and the inability to band box multiple targets makes it less useful.
I am both disappointed and happy with my purchase.  The remastered versions controls are to complex and the pull down menus are going to take some getting used to.  I'm glad the original versions were included as I no longer have put the installation disks in the drive to play.
This game is worth the price as you get 4 games instead of just 1.  I hope they add Homeworld Cataclysm to the package in the future.
