theHunter is a very detailed, beautiful, and somewhat immersive hunting game. And it's free. The actual tracking mechanics are very easy to grasp and they work well for a game that seems to focus on patience and careful, calculated movements. The small GPS-like tool you use to track and use as a map is a good addition and it works perfectly with the concepts. The shooting mechanics in the game are basic from my experience, but it works well.
The game itself is absolutely stunning looking, the graphics and the sound work on it are almost unmatched by any other game, especially other hunting games. The feeling of the world is very immersive and it is almost perfect. But it is very difficult to run on a lower end computer.
Me, being someone who has gone out to many forests and reserves to hike and take pictures, was astonished by how easily the game immersed me into it. The sounds, as I said, are fantastic. The graphics are fantastic also, being one of the best looking games I have played in a long time.
As the hunting part goes, it works very nicely. The tracking system is great, the animal AI is fair, and the movements of your character and the controls are great also.
The biggest problem is the subscription system. You can only hunt Mule Deer unless you pay for either a 3 month, 6 month or 12 month subscription to access the other licenses. Also, you can't host your own multiplayer games without a subscription.
Pros: Beautiful looking and sounding, great hunting mechanics, immersive
Cons: Difficult to run on a low end PC, Sometimes lengthy and boring hunts, you need to pay real money to get licenses to hunt any other animal than the Mule Deer.
Overall, if you are a hunting fan or love good looking games. I think this is perfectly enjoyable.

Insanely addictive strategic building game, nostalgic C&C like graphics. Would reccomend for anyone who likes old-school strategy games and logistic-building games (Starcraft merged with TransportTycoon) as it marries the best of both together in a unique title.
Addictive - High gameplay hours and replayability.
Macro - Havent yet found any sort of build limit, map limit or enemy limit. Its all as endless as you would like it to be.
Research and Character Progression - Upgrades for buildings armor and weapons.
Building - Intuitive, easy to build logistics systems allowing for practically limitless creative solutions.
PvE - Constantly respawning, multiplying and evolving enemy alien colonies keep the game challenging.
Pollution - The more you pollute the local atmosphere, the more it upsets the locals.
Vehicles - Go cruising the infinite world in cars or tanks after creating your stronghold.
Multiplayer - Can connect over 60000 players to a single multiplayer game.
If you are interested enough to like what you saw of the gameplay and graphics style in the preview video, just buy it, you probably will not regret it!

This game is very enjoyable and the battles are a lot more diverse (ambush is really usefull and unlike most people I don't think sieges are that catastrophic) and more difficult to manage than some other total war games, such as Napoleon or Empire, where all you have to do is use your artillery (grapeshot is op) to destroy enemy armies.
The new polititical system can be quite a distraction and really annoying when you want to stop civil wars from breaking out, but generally is a nice addition to the game.
The best changes that were made in Rome Total War II are the Diplomacy with other countries, breaking treaties doesn't haunt you for the rest of the game, and military alliances actually have a purpose since your allies will help you in war. Also, almost everything that has to do with the campaign map has been changed and in my opinion for the best, armies now have several types of mouvements, also the new system with regions, capitals and settlements is a great change from the previous games and the management of food, public order and income have to be balanced in order to keep things running smoothly, where before you just built to get a bigger income and lowered taxes from time to time.
The only bad things in the game would be the squalor and political penalties that can be quite exasperating, the AI is often pretty stupid sometimes, but somehow can be really good with agents ?
Anyway, Rome total war II is probably the best total war i've played so far, and I don't understand all the hate it gets, because after the last patches to the game, it's really worth trying (after the price drops a bit, I wouldn't pay 60$ for it)

Play "Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition" first.
No, it isn't a REQUIREMENT by any means...
But you will appreciate much more of the Dark Souls world.
Dark Souls II.
An amazing game that gives little direction, and a lot of challenge to those who don't pay close attention.
A must buy..especially for gamers who are sick and tired of games lasting ~ 10 hours and TELLING them where to go and what to do and how to beat such and such..
The on-line features tie into the world's lore very well, and can be quite fun.
For example; Bloodstains.
They are left when a player dies. And any other player can click on the stain and view the last 10 seconds of the 'phantom' who just died.
Now, when you walk into a room and see blood-stains EVERYWHERE....you get anxious...and very alert.
The enemies are challenging.
The play-style options are numerous.
Want to be a heavy armoured sorcerer?
A cleric/samurai?
A gladiator wielding nothing but 2 caestus (fist weapons) and his loincloth...go for it.
There are options and weapons to make whatever kind of character you want.
..just don't expect the whole game to be easy for every specific character-build.
The game is unforgiving.
Accidentally attack that NPC in town who sold that item you need?
Well..deal with the consequences until New Game Plus or you remake a character.
Boss fights are pretty damn hard. (Hell, many of the basic enemies can be).
Traps. You will fall for them.
Combat feels very fluid and intuitive.
You actually feel the weight and impact of your (or the enemies) actions.
Other players invading...it happens.
But it's all part of the fun.
In a desolate world where you do feel quite isolated, the on-line play still makes you feel connected.
Although, even offline (which a great many people prefer) is still quite fun.
A "Must own" game.
For those who enjoy pain

In Factorio, you make machines that make machines to make machines.
10/10 would break my brain again figuring it out.

Ludicrously good.
Factorio allows you to build the biggest, most complex systems I've ever seen in a game.  Combines some of the best elements of Infinifactory, Spacechem, The Incredible Machine, Minecraft's industrial mods, and Open Transport Tycoon.
It features seriously addictive gameplay, while allowing for a variety of playstyles.  Compact, efficient factories?   Long-range rail infrastructure joining specialized sites?  Decentralized drone-driven production?  Safe, low-pollution sites built on expensive solar power?  Smog-belching, self-supplying defense outposts under constant threat?  All can work.
The graphics are sharp and well suited, the game performs extremely well on even large scales, and the interface, while requiring a bit of learning, is very powerful.
The main criticism is lack of content at or after the endgame, (though this is a matter of continuing development).  Once you've exhausted the research tree and completed production for the rocket, most everything shuts down, as there's no consumption to drive production.  What is the point of expanding to more distant, dangerous lands when there's no demand for the resources there?  You can try to create your own, by just continuing to produce unused, high cost items, but the feeling of progression is easily lost.
Or you can install one of the excellent mods.  Problem solved.

Factorio is a game that sneaks up on you. You start out so simple, harvesting some coal and iron, chopping down a tree or two. Then you plonk down a machine that starts mining iron ore for you, and you feed the result into a furnace. You build more machines, then some inserters. More machines, and it becomes easier to link up a few things with conveyor belts.
Four hours later you look down on a factory system so complex you couldn't have designed it; and yet it grew so gradually, so organically, that at no point you felt overwhelmed.
You look at the time - maybe ten more minutes; you want to quickly redesign this bit around your assemblers to fit in another conveyor belt. It would speed up the production of green electronic circuits.
Three hours later you realize that you should have been in bed for hours, but you can't stop now - you just build a tank and you really want to try it out on that alien base that has been growing way too much.
Factorio is fun. As simple as that.
Factorio has taught me how to love again. This is my life now.

In 2014, when this game was released I gave it a skip. I thought that the futuristic setting wasn't very interesting and kind of spoiled the whole Call of Duty-series. How wrong was I!
I bought this game very recently, and played the campaign through in just a couple of days. And when the credits started to roll, I immediately started to play it again just to play it through again in just couple of days. The game mechanics were excellent with all the weaponry, exo-skeletons and everything futuristic I thought was boring turned out to be just the opposite. Everything was well made, balanced and easy to grasp. The characters in the game were well written and all of them had a good depth of personality, which is very important in a story-driven game.
I played it through on the hardest difficulty and it seemed okay. At some points it could have been harder, but I have to admit having experience on FPS games since the original DooM, so that is the case with many games though... Overall it gave a good challenge and never felt too easy.
The plot was very well written and dragged me into it fully. No big twists maybe (like Black Ops-series, especially third) but it made reason and felt actually pretty realistic setting in the future world. For me, the plot is maybe the most important thing in single player games and this one hit the spot better than most of games ever.
Overall the game for me was 10/10. For everyone seeking for good gameplay without too much hazzle, a good storytelling and plot and something new in the game industry, I can only recommend this fully. Best entertainment regarding gaming for a long time.

So I went into this with all the bad stuff I've ever heard about this game, stuff like its♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring, cash grab etc...
I'm going to preface this with: I have only really played two MMO's before this, TERA and World at Warcraft and Runescape if that counts? I've also Only played 3 Elder Scrolls games Skyrim, Oblivion and Morrowind all on console.
So far I have only played because of the free weekend and wouldn't of bought this game otherwise. I am 15 hours in and enjoying it. I haven't felt the need to just 'buy' stuff to progress and there is tons too do. It's like and Elder Scrolls game with the hundreads of things dotted around the map, so much stuff to do it can be abit too much. I have purposely stayed away from guides and 'build guides' because its fun being a noob and experiencing a game with no prior kowledge of it. In those 15 hours I am level 15, done a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of quests, crafting and general exploring as the world is very open and interesting kinda like skyrim/oblivion in that regards.
Gathering materials can be a pain and sometimes hard to find, however I find the best way to get materials is just quest and you will often see Iron ore, Plants or anything else on your way. I can see why someone wouldn't like this but I would not say it is pay to win. It is however grindy, but not to the extent of Tera or Runescape.
I will say when you start you are awarded 500 Crown currency or whatever it's called, use that to buy the Starter Pack, you get a Horse, Dog and some other items. I only found this out when I hit level 15 and probbaly could of progressed a little faster If I knew about this earlier.
The game runs fine for me, My specs are AMD Fx6100, GTX 660, 16GB 1600mhz Ram and 1tb HDD. I can run this game on Ultra at a healthy frame rate and the Loading times are often very quick.
TLDR: Really Enjoying it and lots of stuff to do, can be abit grindy but I am still buying it.

Dark Souls II is my personal game of the year.
I know, I'm late to say that, but not one other game had me being focussed on nothing but food and itself.
For someone who did not play the first part, it might be a bit overwhelming to have so many ways to go right from the start,
but I personally love trying it out to see if I could make it or not.
So in my opinion, this game offers the best open world experience there is.
But still, I'm not sure if I just got better by playing the first part of Dark Souls or if it is the game that got a lot easier.
It still is challenging and thus, rewarding you with a lot of positive feelings for beating a hard boss or area,
but even for the worst bosses I needed five to six tries max.
(While in its first part, needing up to twenty tries were on regular basis.)
Which is not a negative aspect at all, but I'm just not used to killing some bosses on first try.
(For those seeking for more difficulty, there is an option right at the start to make the whole game more... challenging.)
The coop system is way cooler than it was before.
You can do complete areas together, or just some hard enemies you just can't beat yourself, or whatever it is that brings you to tears.
All in all, this is my clear recommendation for you to play this game.

Just Cause 3 feels more like an iteration on Just Cause 2. More toys, bigger open world, event more types of vehicles are made obsolete. If you liked JC2 and "just more toys" is enough for you to justify a purchase -- go for it, you probably won't be disappointed. Probably.
The story, as always, serves as a nice bonus on top of the usual destruction sandbox. It's a light, not intrusive, but quite simplistic and repetative set of missions. It's OK. Not that bad, but nothing special either. And final boss is a helicopter. Helicopter. That's a... really appropriate ending, i guess? Just destroy yet another helicopter. Oh well.
It also sounds and looks great. Soundtrack is way cooler than I expected.
But the main treat is a sandbox, and that's where JC3 lacks compared to JC2. Bases and towns are more interesting, but there are way less of them. Like, the handful of really intersting and big military bases, and only one small city. Installing DLCs helps a bit, but still, that's not enough. And the final island feels empty. Also, there are no big civilian airport, so there is no Boeings. That was a bit disappointing for me. And islands don't have a certain themes anymore. In JC2 there were a very distinct "the desert bit", "snowy bit", "more populated city bit" and "the foresty bit". That added some lovely diversity to environment. And even your vehicles got snowy in snowy areas and dusty in the deserty areas, that was a cute touch. But now "the foresty bit" is preety much all there is. Yes, you still can find some snow and some desert, but there isn't enough of those, and they look a bit dull.
And don't get we wrong, destroying bases are really fun, and that's where this game shines. There is just not enough of them.
And a wingsuit. It's the most fun I ever had freeroaming is an open world game. You can buy the game just for that. And you can get one with rocket, if you buy Sky DLC (which is, to be honest is a must-buy).
So, in conclusion. It's a perfect game, for those of you, who really enjoys sandboxes with a lot of toys in them and a fans of JC2, but a cautious recommendation for everyone else.

Dear Developer
After playing ravenfield for about 40 hours, i feel that you have created a fun game with potential to be really great. It is a nice break from conventional hitscan shooters. There are however, a few problems with it. This is quite long and specific so there are titles that outline the basic factors.
Stalemates:
This is by far the most pressing problem. It is almost impossible to win a game by capturing all the points and feel a sense of accomplishment. This is because it is so hard to take all the points as even if you give your team a numerical advantage, you may push back your enemy back to one point, but then they just respawn so quickly that you cannot take it. If you set a high respawn time then there is just a single fierce fight and then the surviving team takes all the other points. It is also a pain if you get killed and then either have to wait or restart the game. The winning that is in place seems very insignificant as the game continues and you can come back. This means there is no pressure to try your hardest to win.
Suggestion - Add an attack/defend system where a defending team cannot take back a point that they lost. Adding a timer would also fix this problem, as it would make a defending team only have to defend for a certain amount of time, whilst also adding a sense of urgency to an attacking team. This may not be where you want to take the game, but it is just a suggestion. Also, put the spawn point away from the capture point, meaning that you if you were taking a point, enemies would not.
Maps:
Although community custom maps are great, many are very unbalanced and not very fun. The official maps are the best. Some more would be really nice.
Weapons:
Some weapons (patriot, Signal DMR)  are overpowered and others (greaser) are almost useless. Pistols are also completely worthless, even as a weapon to finish someone off, as your primary weapons usually kill quickly and will reload fast enough. Weapons like the shotgun are very powerful in some situations, but getting yourself into those situations in the open maps that are available is very difficult.
Pointlessness:
This is another major problem. Quite often (especially with bigger teams) I feel that whatever I do, it will have no effect on the outcome of the battle. Although this is better than it was, it is still a problem. It is also very annoying to try and get a large squad together to take a flag and have to wander around and find all the scattered teammates who are defending points that are not under threat. Also, potentially seperate the order your squad and the recruit more squad members, meaning that your squad does not move back andd forth as you miss you recruitments.
Suggestion - Make it so that it is a lot easier to order your entire team to attack a point and the bots actually follow the plan that you suggest. Also, change spawning to mass respawning, where all the dead enemies respawn every few seconds. Although this does sort of happen, making it more extreme would mean that you would not have a steady stream of bots getting cut down by a machine gun.
AI:
Although it is improving, the AI is still slightly off. Quite often either your bots will not shoot, or the enemy will just walk straight past you and not do anything. Also, on many maps (especially mod ones) the bots may take one point and then just stay there and not do anything. Also, if a bot is in your 'squad' quite often they will not obey, and when they do, they will walk in a straight line and it only take one rocket to completely destroy your push. The AI is slowly being improved with each update though.
Controls:
Planes and helicopters are quite difficult to control and quite unforgiving if you make a mistake, and changing the sensitivity makes them slow and sluggish. Cars and quadbikes flip very easily and therefore are quite annoying.
Conquest:
This would just be really nice to have.
Machine guns:
The mounted machine guns are very powerful and can become a great obstacle. This is good but I would like to be able to turn them off (like you can turn off the vehicles). This is because some of the things I love to do are 'melee wars' or 'musket wars' where you just have select (and often impractical weapons). This is a lot of fun but machine guns break it and I am force to go to custom maps without machine guns (of which there are not very many). This is a very specific and less important than some of the other things that I have mentioned.
Vehicles:
Other than the aformentioned control problems, there are a few problems with vehicles. It is not all that fun to have a helicopter take you out when there was nothing you can do, or to have a tank come into your base and having no ability to take it out. Grenades are almost useless against tanks and so you really need a rocket launcher, which takes up two slots that could be filled by med kits or something else useful. Bots are not at all reliable in taking out tanks so often they just sit there until you die and equip a rocket launcer. The bombers are also confusing to use and I am not sure how to aim at the ground for a bombing run. Therefore they are very unreliable and not fun to use.
Suggestion - make tanks have a weak spot to regular bullets, increase grenade damage to tanks, make rocket launchers only take up 1 slot, or make it possible to equip other things in the pistol slot.
Friendly fire:
Although it is sometimes enjoyable to shoot your own team, it is annoying to be randomly shot in the back or run over by a friendly car. Just a small point.
I understand that this is an early access game and that many of the problems will be fixed in the future.
Thank you for reading this long list of things you are probably already considering.
Regards

Alien: Isolation is an excellent video game.
Admittedly, it's more likely to strike a chord with pre-existing fans of the Alien Series, but that's not to say it wont provide for newcomers too.
Here's my breakdown.
PROS:
+ A faithful homage to the original '79 film.
+ A spellbinding atmosphere.
+ Gorgeous visuals, complemented by a masterful sound mix.
+ Amazing attention to detail creates a truly immersive experience.
+ A unique and genuinely scary extraterrestrial antagonist, that keeps you guessing.
+ An easy to utilize crafting system.
+ Great character performances.
+ An interesting plot with loads of fan-service.
+ High-stakes. Think before you act.
+ A real sense of vulnerability and isolation.
+ DLC enables you to revisit the original '79 film, The USCSS Nostromo and her crew. The original cast reprise their respective roles in these cool add-ons.
CONS:
- Some minor graphical glitches (eg. floating props, clipping). These only occur rarely and are easy to overlook.
- Pacing issues. The game is arguably, a little too lengthily. A [roughly] 15 hour campaign that could have been condensed into a more concise experience.
- Somewhat repetitious. (Though, contextually - this makes sense.)
- An abrupt, perhaps dissatisfying, conclusion.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
Creative Assembly has really done justice with the license - making this game a 'must-play' for Alien fans and a truly worthwhile endeavour for those players seeking some legitimate thrills and chills!

Nostalgia drove me to buy this, the original Homeworld ranks up there with Half Life in terms of legendary PC games.
The upside
- Looks amazing, alongside Black Mesa this is visually the best remake I have ever seen
- Original, untouched versions of both games are included (thank god)
The downside
- Gearbox have put massive effort into making HW look pretty, and in that respect they have succeeded. This comes at a cost, the core mechanics of HW1 have been completely subverted. The biggest issues are broken formations, a poor UI, and ship AI ripped straight from HW2 without a thought if it applies to ships from HW1 (it doesn't).  Where the challenge should come from tactics, formations and resourcing, the challenge actually comes from fighting a fiddly UI and ships that refuse to hold formation the moment they enter combat.
After two missions I switched to vanilla HW1, and although it looks dated, it is so much more... fun. I guess after porting the game into the HW2 engine there was not a lot of time for what really matters, the game itself.  I find it telling that so many reviewers have neglected to mention how such core parts of HW1 are either missing or broken from this game.  Or maybe I am just a demanding (and ageing) grouch who misses the golden age of PC gaming :)
Hopefully a hail mary patch from Gearbox or some talented modders can rescue this missed opportunity. I would encourage everyone who feels the same to post in the Gearbox support forum.

Sledgehammer's debut in the Call of Duty series is both a hit and a miss.
Let's start of with the great: Sledgehammer really pulled off putting some variety in the tried and true COD franchise. There are some cool new weapons, you got exo abilities like double jump, strafe boost,  climbing on walls, and there is even a fun to use grapling hook.
It's just a shame that many of these cool gadgets are restricted to using only when the game wants you to use them. So this doesn't allow for a lot of freedom on the player side. Meaning that you are still stuck with a linear COD campaign.
But this is one of the best COD campaigns I've played. The missions offer a lot of variety, and like I said there are some cool weapons like a laser gun and a grenade that homes in on targets. The stealth missions on offer are also of a very high quality.
The graphics in the game are pretty great, lighting and texture work are top notch. And last but not least: the sound design in this game is absolutely fantastic and truly the high point of this game: Walking in debris and broken glass, the gun sounds, the explosions, ... All of it is shown and heard realisticly in this game.
Where this game drops the ball however is in performance. This is Sledgehammers first COD game, but it also shows it is their first PC game. Sometimes the FPS will just tank for some reason. And loading times are also pretty long.
But if you can bite throuh some of these mistakes, you'll find a very enjoyable COD campaign.

Wube software has a real gem on their hands.
Factorio might be the ultimate sandbox game; a creative tool allowing for truly intricate machines. Named for the tendency for these creations to resemble factories, many other unrelated things are absolutely possible. And that’s not including the (extensive) library of user-created mods for the game already available.
Like Don’t Starve, Terraria and Minecraft before it, there is a survival element to the creative process that adds a sense of urgency. It comes to this game in the form of a sprawling, infinite alien horde which objects to the pollution your factories generate. On your quest to launch a spaceworthy rocket, you will encounter them frequently.
One pleasant surprise for me though was the overall quality. Despite still being in alpha, the game is already heavily optimized, and fully supports online multiplayer play, with optional mods. I have seen 100+ player servers online at times. The quality shows though, and actually the way I discovered the game was via its Steam Reviews. For a time it was the highest reviewed game on Steam of all time. That is a significant and well-earned achievement.
If you are a sandbox gamer, this one should be a top pick. Get it.

TW: Rome 2 is not a bad game by any stretch. It's not so dissimilar from TW: Rome that I think it was worth revisiting, but it does have enough changes to it so as to make it a somewhat different and streamlined experience.
It's not a perfect game, and certainly not the most polished of the TW series. Even now, the AI pathfinding is at best clumsy, and at worst atrocious. Particularly when trying to cross water or engage cities your units will sometimes just head off in the complete opposite direction for no reason. Units on the battle map will STILL take the shortest route to their destination, regardless of whether that means walking into a friendly unit and slowing to a crawl, or into an enemy unit and getting slaughtered. The waypoint system is somewhat effective, but I feel that a drastic and long-overdue  overhaul is needed in the movement mechanics.
Also the 'Prologue' tutorial campaign fails to cover the diplomacy in any great depth and the politics at all, meaning that half of the game mechanics are hidden away behind a couple of tiny buttons and you have to accidentally discover them yourself, even though their effects are in place from the beginning. It's too in-depth a system not to be explained to the player and a major oversight in terms of design.
But other than those two gripes (which are glaringly obvious, but not game-breaking) the game is fun and I've been playing it like a full-time job lately so it's certainly addictive. Controlling your cities is streamlined in that buildings have local and provincial effects, of which you can change and view at the click of a button, and taxation is globally controlled so much of the nit-picking has been removed - which is a boon as your empire expands. However, it makes it difficult to make the most out of your happiest and most lucrative cities when you can't edit your taxation for fear of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your more restless populations. So the newer features have some good and bad points.
It's no-ones pick for GOTY, but it's still a TW game, and once you get your head around everything it's hard to put down.

I highly recommend playing this game if -
- You want a fun, seamless and non-complicated - though stylish - story-telling, platforming and hack and slash (more like smashing and wacking - since the protagonists weapon of choice is an extendable staff/pole)  experience.
-  You want a break from long-winding rpgs and you just want to play a fast-paced action game that plays out like a movie, with a decent story.
-  You want to play a hack-and-slash that's inventive, provides decent platforming and repitition-breaking alternative means for character movement. In other games while this comes in the form of flying a beast, or riding a horse, in this game you get a futuristic hover board (which is super fast, fun and very exciting)
The Story & Characters - Few but Memorable

The game is heavil inspired by:
- The Matrix: post-apocalyptic world ruled by machines, enslaving humans minds or killing the free ones)
- The legend of the Monkey King: for its protagonist (voiced by Andy Serkis) who wields an extendable pole-like weapon in combat which Sun-Wukong (the monkey king) is known to use, and apes the movements of a monkey whilst platforming. He's also called monkey.
- The Prince of Persia: for the significant side-kick, who in this game is a survivalist called Trip (short for Tripitaka). She's escaped the clutches of the world-ruling machines like "Monkey", and somehow manages to tie a mechanical death-collar around his neck, promising to disable it only if he gets her to safety (one of the unique elements of the game's plot). A lot of the game's platforming includes Monkey and Trip collaborating to get past obstacles, like P.O.P
An interesting character to watch out for - PIGSY (very well-designed and very likeable, despite being a fat pervy slob )
What's not so cool about the game -
... Is also that which is one of its coolest factors, i.e. the game just has a bare handful of human characters (all the other characters being machines you have to kill) and it still manages to make these principal characters memorable
- Not So Memorable - is the world the game is based in. It didn't draw me in or intrigue me as much as the characters, because it felt like it was a very simple world to conquer. The machines which are supposed to be the rulers of the earth, don't seem intimidating or very intelligent, and although the environment design of the game is as great as the character design, you don't feel like this is a place you'd want to conquer, live in or go back to.
Concluding Comments - I really really loved the character design of this game the most, whether it's Monkey's headband alluding to the Monkey King's crown perhaps, or Pigsy's huge belly sticking out of his ragged singlet. The combat of the game is engaging and for a hack and slash - it's important for the game mechanics to provide a good-looking and smooth-flowing evasion ability. This games provides just that and the camera movement coupled with Monkey's simple to execute acrobatic evasions, make the combat feel more dynamic and cinematic. All in all, the game looks great and plays really great, and even has some fun combat upgrades - which adds to the game's smooth sense of progression.

(writing this about halfway through the game, I think. Completed through chapter 7.)
There's a few glitches, but most of them aren't gamebreaking. I've had to restart a checkpoint a few times.
The sparsity of checkpoints is actually my main complaint. When hunting for all of the tech orbs, sometimes I have to go back several minutes to try a segment again. I believe the game saves what you've picked up when you restart such a checkpoint, but it's not consistent for me - I kept having to pick up the same orb behind me during the final shootout in chapter 7.
Auto-targeting is another problem. I can't seem to keep focused on one enemy to finish them off. Luckily, a stun lasts for a set period of time and isn't broken when I use a regular attack, but it's aggravating in some of those frantic multi fights.
Graphics: eh. I played a lot of DmC, so the colors/aesthetics feel kinda samey. If you *haven't* played DmC, it's lush, and beautiful. Sometimes it's too bright and colorful for me to find the next platforming segment. Trip's pants make no sense, but whatever.
Also: not very good with alt-tabbing. There's no windows/no border option in the graphics, so it's crashed a few times. Beware!
The story is great so far. I think I've really become a fan of how Ninja Theory does their character relationships. Even though Monkey is the controlled character, is more experienced, and does all of the fighting, Trip is treated as an equal.
I picked this up because of a passing interest in Journey to the West, and the story is roughly paralleling what I know about the original plot, but in futurepunk ways. It's neat to guess what's coming next!
The platforming works. Wonky platforming controls aren't too bad, because the game will only let you jump to valid locations. So that's nice.
This feels like it's mostly detailing my complaints, but I'm always eager to continue to the next chapter, to see what happens next.

This game. This game lets you experience a wide variety of feelings from "what the f*ck is this sh*t?" to "wow, this is so f*cking awesome!"
The most confusing part was the very first dozen of minutes, where you experience the harsh reality of a console port:

This game is like your real life simulator. The one where you live with a woman. You experience the things like:

-You have to toss her around.

-She gets you in trouble all the time.
-She is like the characters from the horror movies, Always trying to be brave at the wrong time.
-She talks a lot. Especially when she shouldn't.

-She lies.
Women. ^^

From the team that made DmC Reboot (which I wasn't a fan of) comes Enslaved, a super charming, beautiful game. I first played this on the PS3 when it launched but its poor frame rate turned me off the game. Fast forward a few years, I bought this on a Steam sale, just an impulse purchase and didnt play it for a long time. This year I finally wanted to go through my Steam backlog and gave it another chance and I'm so happy I did. Enslaved gives me a lot of Beyond Good & Evil vibes (it even has a pig character!), the game has stunning environments, good narative driven cut scenes and a great atmosphere. It runs super smooth on my PC and is a joy to play. You collect orbs to upgrade your character, there's a good amount of Prince of Persia style platforming, some stealth and adventure sections and combat sprinkled in between. The game has good mechanics and has impressed me so much that I feel like replaying DmC again. I went in with super low expectations and I'm pleasantly surprised how good Enslaved is and how it managed to keep me hooked. Going forth, I'm a fan of Ninja Theory and looking forward to their next game.

All things considered i feel this game had big boots to fill and unfortunately didnt meet up to expectations in my opinion. This game could have been so much better and im dissapointed it isnt therefore i cant recommend it unless it is on sale. Get just cause 2 anyway its amazing.

This this would eat up all of it at first and after I finally got it running with "windowed mode" command in Steam and trying to go over some resolution settings as the window would be out of place with display glitches, it will eat abouut 12 GB of RAM apart from the 2GB that the other resoourse take on my computer. The bad thing is that the RAM should clear up after closing the game, but it doesn't and the task manage just doesn't show what's eating up the RAM. It only happens when the came has run and even closing it, that RAM is just taken up space. One has to reboot the comptuer to clear that RAM.
I would also add that the sign in option when the game starts would be when the screen would jump out to way out resolutions. What I did to fix it was also to put steam in offline mode so it doesn't try to log in when starting. Once that was done, I put steam in online mode and ran it again to get working.
I hear some pretty bad things from the developers from other people that bougth this game where developers are still releasing DLC for this game, but it clearly needs to be fixed first. I can agree to that as well.
The RAM requirements don't say 16 GB, but if you don't have 16 GB, you are in for a bad time.
Once you have the game running, you will be encountered with cheesy and bad voice acting with fluctuating volumes that get drowned out by music on defaults. (recommend to have subtitles).

Another thing that I see happening is that the game will stutter or freeze for a few seconds or less until it catches back with itself. I'm not sure if it's releated to the RAM getting eaten up with memory leaks, but it could be.
The game over all is mindless fun and just gives you a bunch of filler for a lot of things to do as well.

Borderlands 2 is another romp through the hectic world of Pandora. With more improvements to gameplay, and environment over its predessor and with its interesting cast of eccentric characters, this game is quite enjoyable, with multiple playthroughs the world keeps getting more crazy as enemies get more buffs and scale in level. Multiplayer and being able to play locally is where this game thrives as it increases the difficulty. A good game to run through if you just feel like shooting things.
Rank A-
The gameplay is great though not enough to hold interest for long periods, but shorter bursts. You can knock a lot of quests out in a solid hour and feel satisfied. The gunplay is smooth whether you play keyboard/mouse or on controller. Though they boast about the bazillion guns, most are just cashed in for currency and you tend to stick to a set, or ones earned from specific missions. Enemies tend to just run in mobs and are preditable, but the number of them and variety keep it fresh. A plus is that the more people playing, the more enjoyable the killing.
Rank A+
Though it is an unreal game, the overall asthetic aged very well with its styleized cel-shading. The game also runs well on low-end and looks spectacular on high-end machines.
Rank C
The overall story arc through the game is ok at best. The villian has no presence besides quips over audio logs, and backstory. The small bits you do find create a backstory is great and well defining. Though the last bit of DLC shows how well the main plot could have played out, and its sad that I have to give it an average overall score.
Rank B
The game features a wide cast of characters eahc with thier own quirks, giving a great identity overall but somewhat lacking when it comes to the characters you play as. Thier lines make them feel empty, and repetitive compared to the people you meet. They fixed this in Borderlands Presequal but it would have nice to build upon the characters as the world building was already great from the first game.
Though the gameplay does get tiring over time, bringing new friends, or switching up characters tends to keep it fresh and me wanting more. If they kept releasing small DLC (not cosmetics) and character packs over the years this game would be my ultimate choice.

I don't typically write reviews for games, yet I feel the urge to for this game. (Despite how hard this game triggered me.)
Emily is Away is actually a very well designed game in it's style and in it's ability to suck you in. It's immersion is through the roof. Too much so, in fact, if you lived in the era of AOL or MSN. This will bring back extreme nostalgia and may or may not make you want to drink a bottle of alcohol to drown out the memories it will stur up in you.
This is not a game to be enjoyed, might I add. I love the idea of making a choice driven game in this style, but I'm almost certain this game has no happy ending to be had or even an ending to be enjoyed slightly. You will leave it feeling like an awkward teenager, regardless of the fact that you're supposed to be in your last year of college at the end.
I don't exactly get where the creator was going with this. The characters don't exactly mature and still give off the same vibes they did at the start. It just seems like the awkward exchanges of early teenagers through and through.
Would I still recommend this game?
I'm a masochistic idiot, so yes.
It's interesting for a change and I'd like to see more games in this style pop up. Not to mention that it's free, so it's not like you've got anything to lose...
You'll just be regaining awkward memories and probably come to hate the creator for making this game.
You've been warned.

I really, really desire to like this game. I can't.
I loved Homeworld classic. Everything about it worked. The gameplay was fantastic, the epic expansiveness of it, the spirit of adventure, sweeping vistas, a sense of us against the galaxy. I liked playing to keep my ships alive and capture significant ones of the enemy. If I wanted to capture a specific set of enemy ships, I could reasonably expect my fleet wouldn't kill them while I was off handling something else.
I never could get into Homeworld 2. It seemed to be a game of spam-ships-at-the-enemy. I don't find a lot of joy in fighting a battle where my ships have a 25-50% survival rate, and just get repenished with fresh yokels who have no clue they're in the space version of a Sherman tank. Simple things like "stay docked" to keep your strike fighters in the bays don't work between missions, so they're vulnerable to ambush early on. Ships set to "Passive" attack the group of enemy support frigates I'd planned on capturing (they're not going anywhere, and I can't build any more).  And they melt at any sign of reasonable opposition. Everything melts when its breathed on. There is no defense; only who can kill the fastest. Formations are a joke. You kind of get the impression that the whole fleet is crewed with wet-behind-the-ears teenagers so eager to shoot the enemy they can't hold a formation. Or obey any order that dosen't include who to shoot. Including the Captians. Any nuance short of mass assault is lost on these guys. And nuance is how epic battles are won, particularly when outnumbered and outgunned.
If you liked HW2, you'll be fine with the remastered version. If you liked the gameplay of HW1, importing it into HW2 engine, however beautiful, completely wrecks the origional gameplay. From a fleet operations standpoint, the HW2 engine is a complete fail, and remains so here.
I filed several bugs against what I thought were the most egregarious transgressions. Even relatively simple fixes like "stay docked dosen't work between missions" remain unfixed.
I can't explain how utterly heartbroken I am over this.  I loved HW classic; it easily makes my "favorite games of all time" list. While pretty, to be sure, this... dosen't even make honorable mention.

Gearbox did an amazing job with this and I would highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys sci-fi and strategy games.
Pros:  Great story, awesome ship designs, beautiful scenery, fun multiplayer, solid voice acting, and being able to maneuver one's fleet in 3D space instead of on a 2D plane.
Cons:  I have noticed one or two glitches thus far, but not anything overly bad or game breaking and I have to believe that they will be patching/updating the game in the future.  I also remember the original being slightly more of a challenge, but maybe it's just because I remembered enough of the original to know what to do during each level.
I'd give this game a solid 9/10.  New players will find a deep, immersive strategy game with a solid story and players of the original game will be delighted top have a chance to re-experience the game with updated graphics and remastered audio.  It's well woth the money.

Hi everyone! I hope you're all doing well today. So I gave this "f2p" a try and found it's simply "f2t" which means it isn't really free to play at all. It's free-2-try. The pricing is ridiculous. If I'm going to spend this kind of money, I'll be doing some real hunting. If you have tons of money and think you might give this a try anyway, I suppose it might be fun practice for some folks. Anyway, let me tell you how my hour in the game went, and you can judge for yourself if you want to try.
I play on three monitor Nvidia Surround. Some games have built in limitations to make it fair, but I don't think that's the case with this game. The resolutions given in the options appear to support my setup, so I made the switch and bam! I get what looks like a normal widescreen view squashed flat and stretched across three monitors. Needless to say, I don't think the game looks very good that way.
So I see a cabin and decide to walk up to it, but can't get up on the porch even though it looks like I should be able to step up. Maybe the front of the porch looks lower to me because of the stretching effect, so I walk around to the steps on the side and get up on the porch... only to find I can't open the door anyway--or at least I couldn't figure out how.
So I look around and see a shooting range. I head over, pick a spot, lay down, and cannot clearly see all targets because they are obscured partly by the targets in front of them. I don't feel like creeping over to another spot because this one is clearly marked as viable and the movement mechanics are so slow and clunky, so I do some practice shooting with the one free weapon you start with by default. Wow! My persona must be a complete jitterbug because I can't seem to hold the weapon even moderately still. I open options and look for a key to let me either empy my lungs or hold my breath, find it, and... heh... not much help at all.
After practice, I get up and just start wandering around the woods. I see a lot of bugs and a few birds. The sounds are great, and I think I might like this game for meditation if the view wasn't squashed flat and looking so completely odd. I do glimpse one deer off in the distance, but if I'm supposed to be able to track it I'll never know because I can't seem to find the spot where I spotted it. So I wander. And wander. I find a nice peaceful spot and sit down. And I wait. And I wait. And then I leave.
If they fix the resolution, I might come back and try my luck again. If walking around and waiting seem like a good game to you, give it a try. I know this is supposed to be realistic hunting, and I'm okay with that. Really I am. But when the view is squashy, the shooting mechanics are clunky, and the movement is so darn slow and irritatingly stupid, it gets tedious to say the least. If I could at least enjoy the scenery, it might not have been such a terrible experience for me. As it is, I can't even do that. I read that if you keep practicing, your ability to hold the weapon still gets better, but I'm not sure the rest of my experience rates a keep-trying approach.
No, I can't recommend this game. You might try it and like it, but for me, it just doesn't work. I'd rather be out in the real woods hunting real animals for practice. At least then, if I see a porch I want to hop up on, I can do that without having to creep slowly around to the steps on the side. Talk about silly.

Smite definitely dosen't follow the formula for your traditional MOBA, but it pulls it off nonetheless.
For fans of third person shooters or other third person genres, you'll be right at home.  Unlike most MOBAs, the camera angle is adjusted to be more central to you, and you use the WASD keys to move, along with using your number keys to cast abilties.
I found the wide selection of gods to be both visually appealing, and fun to play, with each having voiced lines, unique skins, and attributes.  While not having as many options as larger MOBAs such as League and DOTA, there's certainly no shortage, with the folks at Hi-Rez adding new gods frequently.
The free-to-play system is, I believe, quite balanced.  However, not quite as balanced as games such as Warframe for instance.  Just about everything can be attained with enough play time, with only minor paywalls on things like cosmetics.  The only complaint I have in this department would be that the grind can be a little long without EXP boosts or a premium account.
While I've not yet progressed into the higher tiers of the game, I can say that the community does not seem to be the same sort of toxic filth that plagues League and DOTA.  MOST games tend to be very friendly, however, as with any game, this can change dramatically.
Being several years old, the graphics are starting to somewhat show their age, but it still looks quite good, and I give props to Hi-Rez for doing an excellent job optimizing the game.  You could almost run this game on a potato.
So, in conclusion, Smite is an awesome game to play with friends, if you're looking to get your feet wet in a MOBA, or if you just wanna try something new.   I have a blast playing this game with my Skype group, and I think you will too!

Someone strongly gender conscious might take issue with the male-female/masculine-feminine dynamic going on, since there's some clear definition in the game; The two characters are strong and weak, protector and protected, etc... The story telling is done

My standards for judging an action adventure game aren't exactly tough, however, there have been annoying design elements/styles in this genre through recent gens that will make my opinion of a game plummet when I encounter them, and this game doesn't have any such serious cons.

Oh, what a beautiful and tranquile game of exploration belies within after the first minutes and stages of confusion, when you've blasted few times in the space engines full running and crashed into something very lethal and thus spectacularily died. After realizing that the key to success is in subtle, slow and considerate boost use and the receipt for survival is stealth and evasion, since you do not have the luxury of blasting the dangers away with lasers or missiles, you start to feel the poetic power of empty space. You will start to appreciate te success in survivalism, since the space is vasta nd hostile. You're not going to dominate this environment. It will dominate you. Still, life in the void feels pretty easy once you get the knack of it.
And then it all changes once again. In stages 1 and 2 things were pretty peaceful, with enough consideration I was able to float past scorching suns and deadly debris pretty easily, nice and slow. Now it's stage 3 and it's getting hectic again. There' s mines. There's tons of scrap flying around. There are hostile aliens, some content with blasting past and cracking few potshots at me, some trying to follow me and bombarding me with their missiles. The quests are getting longer, the environment increasingly hostile every step. And I'm just a peaceful guy, trying to scrape by, unable to shoot back!
As frustrating as it can be to experience once again being blown away in cold space, it is also highly rewarding when you manage to haul one enormous cargo of materials to your mothership, to find something useful in spcae, to upgrade your pilot or ship one small notch to survive just a bit longer next time... These are the moments that keep me playing on. That, and the constant unending feel of exploration, the gift of finding, the beautifully desolate and dryly nihilistic but poetic blurts of machine voiced astronaut that is me speaking out his feelings once every year I have drifed in space.
In its own way RymdResa is merciless as any roguelite. On the other hand, it gives you much leanway by not stripping you of your labour's fruits (namely levels and items you've found) after your death - unless you want it to by activating difficulty levels above "normal". Most of all it is nearly zen-like in its nature of slow and tranquile space exploration, and I love it for what it is. For me this is some kind of equivalent for meditation, the way to escape the hectic real life into something slower, but not dull. I give this little big game my heartliest recommendation.

EDIT: The review below was written a few years ago after playing for only 3 hours. I gave it another try with a different mentality and am enjoying the game a lot more. Review changed to Thumbs Up. Don't think Dark Souls 2 as an RPG where you're trying to build up your character (at least in the beginning). Think of it instead like one of those old Nintendo games where your goal is just to progress to the next area/save point. If you happen to pick up some power-ups along the way, bonus. As others have told me, this game can be beaten without leveling up very much.
I haven’t played Dark Souls 1 or its predecessor Demon Souls so I can’t speak to how similar Dark Souls II (DS2) is to either of them. I can say however that if the previous games are as hard as DS2, I probably don’t want to play those either. I only played this game for a few hours so keep that in mind when weighing my opinion.
In DS2 you start the game as some sort of undead being. You are warned about the dangers of becoming “Hollow” which I guess is a kind of damned spirit. The game’s narration has the feel of a dream where you’re not entirely sure what’s going on but you have a general idea of what you’re supposed to do. The game follows your progress towards reaching “The King” (and probably fighting him). Obviously I didn’t get far enough to see how that works out. There are a number of neutral people that you meet on your quest that you can talk to or interact with, but large portions of the game world seem uninhabited. By the way, some of the people can be hard to see since they blend into the environment very well (NPCs kind of sit around in random places). I’m used to games where objects and people have some sort of highlight around them to let you know someone/something is important.
I was a little disappointed in the game’s graphics to be honest. I thought that being a modern game DS2 would have slick high definition gameplay, but actually the textures are similar to older games such as Darksiders 2 but without the cartoony feel. I’m not saying it’s bad (it’s still pretty good), just that I expected a 2014 AAA title to be amazing. One bright side to this is that my 3 year old computer didn’t have any problems running the game. Dark Souls 2 is clearly a console port so playing on a game controller is strongly recommended. Since I have very little experience using controllers (I don’t own any consoles) I first tried Keyboard + Mouse. This didn’t work out so well since performing even basic actions would require combinations of keys. For example, the “action” button would be shift+left click. And when using keyboard + mouse, the on-screen prompts would be for controller keys (Press A button to pick up item). After a few hours play I still haven’t figured out how to put items on the “quick use” belt. There is basically no tutorial for gameplay mechanics.
When people describe the Dark Souls games probably the first thing mentioned is usually the difficulty. The game is very hard because you have no “advantage” over many of your enemies. It takes them only a few hits to kill you just as it takes you a few hits to kill them. You also have a stamina bar which limits how often you can swing your weapon. This means you can’t just dive into a battle chopping with your sword and hope that you make the first strike. There are no “weak” enemies; everyone can all kill you in seconds if you’re not paying attention. And if you die, you lose ALL your money/experience and respawn with lower max health. The money/experience of the game is counted in “souls” which are used as both currency and experience for leveling up. You have an opportunity to retrieve the souls you drop on death, but if you die again before picking them up (happens a lot because enemies respawn), they’re lost permanently. I can only imagine what some of the later boss battles must be like.
Pros:
+The game can be immersive and is actually fair. Every time you die you’ll kick yourself because you know that if you had done it “right” you wouldn’t have died.
+I like how the money and experience is combined into “souls” which are automatically gained on killing an enemy. I get easily tired of looting corpses in RPGs.
+The game is challenging and I’m sure you’d feel like a god if you actually beat it.
Cons:
-Dark Souls 2 is too hard for me. If you didn’t have your life bar shrunk with every death I wouldn’t mind doing some grinding, but as it is the game just gets harder and harder as you die.
-The controls (even with a controller) can be hard to master if you’re not experienced with this kind of game. The platform jumping was especially annoying for me since it takes a combination of buttons to accomplish a simple jump. And if you fall, you die.
-The level up system is not very well explained. You start at around level 12 depending on what class you chose and the game does not explain the level up process. Every time you increase a stat by 1 it counts as a level up. I’m sure I could read up on it online before playing the game, but I don’t like having to research a game before playing.
-The game has no “objective clues” or game map. You’re just given this huge world to explore, seemingly at random.
Overall I’m not going to recommend the game unless you’ve played the previous ones. All of the cons I mentioned would probably melt away after you’ve played through the game at least once. I thought the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games were weak too but I enjoyed them after playing through at least one time. Then you’d know where to go and what you need to do (including what order you should explore areas in). If you’ve never played the previous Dark Souls games and don’t like super challenging games, stay away from Dark Souls II until the price drops. The game has a meta rating over 90% so most people must love it. If you really must try it, gather your patience and do a lot of pre-game research.

Alien Isolation is a terrifying game. The scare factor is present 24/7 as you never ever feel as if you are safe. This intensity becomes so frustrating in a good way that I was very glad to finally finish the game; my horrors would finally end. The Alien is not scripted making it even more fearful as you can never predict when you are about to die.  The sound department was also a huge plus as the game's sounds were perfect for instilling a fear that will long remain within me. Despite these great sounding factors, the game is plagued with redundant moments, a horrible storyline, and bad stealth. I often found myself walking through corridors wondering if  I had been there already and it is ture; A:I gets extremely repetetive very fast yet it preserves its creepy and terrifying experience
Sound: 9.5/10 - The game's impeccable sounds and voice acting make it a dreadful experience from start to finish.
Fear: 10/10 - I have never wanted to quit a game more than I wanted to quit Alien Isolation. Its a constant rollercoaster of fear and horror as the Alien simply cannot be harmed. It truly made the movies proud.
Campaign: 4/10 - The story was probably one of the worst stories I've ever played-through. It's filled with repetetive go there, do this, turn that on, moments, making for a very terrible experience. There are a few good moments but they are very rare and the last few hours are just absolute crap, followed by what could be the worst ending ever.
Gameplay: 8/10 - A:I has very solid shooting and gameplay mechanics but the stealth could be a lot better. The other enemies besides the Alien are very forgettable and annoying.
Overall: 78/100 - Alien Isolation is a must-buy for horror fans however, if you are expecting a good story and amazing stealth gameplay you should probably look elsewhere. I repeat, Alien Isolation is an amazing and very scary game but the campaign hurts it far too much.

I rarely check out games that are less than a dollar because most of the time it is a copy and paste of another game or it required minimal effort. The actual game portion of Tank Destroyer was a very pleasant surprise, launched the game and you're met with the launcher, change your settings and you're good to go. 20 levels, starting from easy and progressing to challenging and then on to difficult. The only gripe I really had about the game was that the camera angle was awkward. Getting rekt out of nowhere from down south was fairly annoying but getting used to it was easy,

Takes me back to the glorious days of building huge fleets and battling it out in the endless void. The visual advances are stunning and it's great seeing the previously boxy ships of the original Homeworld given a complete make over with new textures and lighting.
However, playing Hoeworld 1 with Homeworld 2 mechanics just doesn't feel quite right. Having some of the formations missing and none of the original tactics options is a bit of a disappointment.
In the end this doesn't detract from the overall experience and it is still a joy to play, especially with a friend or two.

If you have never played any of the other Home World games you are in for a treat, jaw dropping graphics, beautiful visuals, astonishing audio. If you have, leave your memories at the door, they will be shattered.
This is definitely not a remastered collection. This is little more than a re-imaging of HW2 with HW1 ships added in. If you have fond memories of the multiplayer lobby experience, don't come here expecting to make new ones, that key feature is totally absent and no plans are in the works currently to add one. This is definitely NOT a remastering of the originals.
If you can live with those differences more power to you, me, I give it the following scores:
Visuals: 5 out of 5
Audio: 4.5 out of 5
Controls: 2.5 out of 5
Game play Single play: 3.5 out of 5
Game play Multiplay: 2 out of 5*
*IMHO lack of a lobby seriously drops the score for multiplay, game play can be really fun, but no chance to talk with your team mates after a game or to discuss games in a lobby while waiting for games to start, really drops the longevity of the title.
UPDATE:
Since this original review was posted the developers surprized the community with a functioning lobby. It isn't the lobby system we had in either of the originals but it does raise the fun factor and multi-playability a tremendous amount. Now you can talk with anyone  in the main lobby or in the game lobby while waiting to get enough people to join. That alone is enough to raise the score I put for multiplay to 4 out of 5.
The developers also released a major patch that fixed a lot of issues but there is still a load of work needing completion. The game is better now than it was at release and hopefully we will see the final polish put on the game in 2017.

What a load of crap.
It does some things right... the writing is actually pretty good, what little atmosphere is there is very nostalgic if you were alive during the early 2000's, and the game is free.
It's also manipulative and deceptive.
The game's description reads, and I quote: "Emily is Away is an interactive story. Create a screenname and choose your path through the branching narrative."
This is bullcrap.
The narrative does NOT branch.  The ending is the same no matter what you do.  The game only gives you an ILLUSION of choice.  It flat out LIES to you that your choices matter.  They don't.  Remember in some of Telltale's games like The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, how the game would tell you that people would remember your actions and words, and actually react accordingly?  That doesn't happen in this game.  No matter what you do, no matter what the game tells you, your choices do not matter.
And that's why it fails.  The story would be good in a linear format.  Maybe a youtube video?  Or a short story/novella?  But this just isn't the right format for it.  Video games allow choice to affect narrative, and this game uses the illusion of said freedom of choice, only to sting you in the end no matter what you do.
Heck, maybe even as a video game it could've worked if it at least was honest, and didn't lie to you about your choices having any impact whatsoever, or didn't give you any choices in the first place.
I get the message the game is trying to relay, I really do.  And in another format, it could've worked.
But BECAUSE of the format, BECAUSE it tried to be a video game, because it flat out lies and deceives the player about their interactions with the game, the message was lost on me.  Instead of getting it's actual intended message across, I really felt more like "Wow, why did I have to waste my energy typing all this when I can't affect anything in this game?" and I'm pretty sure that wasn't the point.
If you want an interactive visual novel where every action you take DOES matter, that actually USES the medium and the message effectively, get Analogue: A Hate Story.  That game actually allows you to role-play while simulating a PC, and you get all the more invested in it because it feels like what you do MATTERS.  Or if you haven't played those Telltale games yet, play those.
Don't play this.  It's not free.  It may not cost money, but it will cost you time.  Time you could be spending playing a less deceptive game.

To get the cons out of the way:  Occasionally you find yourself stuck on a random bit of scenery.  This isn't game breaking, it's not forever stuck, sometimes you just hit it at the wrong angle and you roll instead of jumping, which is only really frustating in the timed sections in which you die you don't make that jump.
Also, the camera occasionally just decides that you should definately be looking in THIS direction, right now -- which is maddening when you're trying to aim, or find the next hand hold, or whatever.
All that said, the game is fantastic.  The Graphics aren't bleeding edge or anything, but it's colorful, well drawn, well animated,  I'd call it decidedly pretty, and a huge relief after years of gritty brown "realism."
Combat is intuitive and easy to pick up, some of the mechanics are great fun, and as someone who is not a fighting game junkie, that means a lot.
The climbing and jumping around bits are fluid and entertaining.  The characters are likeable, even though the escortee does do the occasional annoying reminding you of the objective every two minutes shtick that escortees do, you still find yourself rooting for them.
There's a romance, bit it doesn't feel awkward, or forced or slapped on in post production, it's actually a bit of a slow burn and quite enjoyable.  No sudden but inevitable declarations, no because-the-back-story-said-so -- there's actual chemistry and lingering glances.
This game sucks you in, and rarely lets you up for air, so try not to start it an hour before you have to be somewhere -- you are going to be late.

You can also just ram their Bubbles with your Rocket, but it's risky since at that point freaking blank range, they're practically guaranteed to hit you unless you perfectly time your Shield, which makes you invulnerable for a couple seconds.
The game is very fast pace, colorful, with great music. Music that actually makes me want to purchase its soundtrack, which is saying something since it's $8. There is a fine line between being pretentious in a way that's endearing, and being pretentious in a way that's insufferable.
RymdResa is the former; somehow, floating through an endless void of clip-art, ambient music, and pseudo-poetic snippets whilst being pelted with rocks and occasionally read bits of free-verse by someone who clearly had too much fun with a ring modulator just... works.
I can't say WHY it works.  By all rights, it shouldn't.  And yet, somehow, it just does.
Definitely not for everyone; if the phrase "floating through an endless void of clip art, ambient music, and pseudo-poetic snippets" made you roll your eyes, RymdResa probably isn't for you.  Otherwise it's definitely worth a look if you want a meditative, artsy take on space exploration.

A hopeless mission: a lone man sent out into the abyss looking for salvation. The longing for a new place to call home drives him deeper into the void. Hints of life still remain, yet nothing in this empty universe can replace the utopia he was forced to leave behind.
That isn't the plot of the game...its how I feel everytime I think I've stumbled across a spiritual successor to FTL. Rogue-like space exploration, ship customization, an original concept, and choices that matter, all of these promises convinced me to give RymdResa a chance.
I give credit to what seems like a genuine artistic attempt. Slow safe travel emulates the solitude of a long solo space mission, while rocketing forward into the unknown represents the urge to discover, to explore, to hope. The art style fits, as do some of the game mechanics, all of these shades of blue and grey traveling through spaces on their own axis make your lonely little ship seem like an afterthought. On the surface I see endless potential...the existenial trappings of films like 2001: A Space Oddyssey or Moon.
Too bad the game is as empty as its space theme. Gameplay is more or less Asteroids minus a gun. Motivation to explore dissipates as soon as you realize choices dont matter. At all. Fly til you die, every experience feels the same.
Then there's the poetry! I get it, poetry is hard, and while RymdResa delivers decent (albeit rather brooding) prose, it also rambles. Endless. Pointlessly. Shut up, spaceman! Get out of my head! I know these are ment to be the musings of madness from a man who has spent years in solitude, but I don't need it sprung on me every 3 minutes. Just make these into "logs" available from the main menu; I'll read them if I'm curious. Supplement my gameplay, dont interrupt it.
Upgrades ultimately mean next to nothing, a meaningless point in a stat that barely matters. Fly slightly faster to nothing in particular! The deeper I try to go, the more shallow this pool seems to be. You, RymdResa, are no contemporary to my dear Faster Than Light. You are simply a pretty face with an empty soul.
And so for a brief moment, I thought I had found a new flame, but alas, she is cold and superficial. The spark fades, we drift apart, and once again I begin my hopeless mission. The next FTL is out there. It has to be. But not here. Not like this. Prehaps I will find it in my next life. For now though, I press on into the unknown. Godspeed. *mic drop*
Nevermind. I'll just smash into the sun again. I hate you, Poetry Slam Spaceman.

Ludicrously good.
Factorio allows you to build the biggest, most complex systems I've ever seen in a game.  Combines some of the best elements of Infinifactory, Spacechem, The Incredible Machine, Minecraft's industrial mods, and Open Transport Tycoon.
It features seriously addictive gameplay, while allowing for a variety of playstyles.  Compact, efficient factories?   Long-range rail infrastructure joining specialized sites?  Decentralized drone-driven production?  Safe, low-pollution sites built on expensive solar power?  Smog-belching, self-supplying defense outposts under constant threat?  All can work.
The graphics are sharp and well suited, the game performs extremely well on even large scales, and the interface, while requiring a bit of learning, is very powerful.
The main criticism is lack of content at or after the endgame, (though this is a matter of continuing development).  Once you've exhausted the research tree and completed production for the rocket, most everything shuts down, as there's no consumption to drive production.  What is the point of expanding to more distant, dangerous lands when there's no demand for the resources there?  You can try to create your own, by just continuing to produce unused, high cost items, but the feeling of progression is easily lost.
Or you can install one of the excellent mods.  Problem solved.

Factorio is a game that sneaks up on you. You start out so simple, harvesting some coal and iron, chopping down a tree or two. Then you plonk down a machine that starts mining iron ore for you, and you feed the result into a furnace. You build more machines, then some inserters. More machines, and it becomes easier to link up a few things with conveyor belts.
Four hours later you look down on a factory system so complex you couldn't have designed it; and yet it grew so gradually, so organically, that at no point you felt overwhelmed.
You look at the time - maybe ten more minutes; you want to quickly redesign this bit around your assemblers to fit in another conveyor belt. It would speed up the production of green electronic circuits.
Three hours later you realize that you should have been in bed for hours, but you can't stop now - you just build a tank and you really want to try it out on that alien base that has been growing way too much.
Factorio is fun. As simple as that.
Factorio has taught me how to love again. This is my life now.

A wonderful platformer in the same vein as Super Meat Boy or IWBtG, Fly'N is a difficult platformer that comes with a surprising amount of content and fun. It's well worth the price, and there's plenty to enjoy.
Fly'N is a challenging platformer that relies on reaction time, problem solving skills, and a lot of resets. Unlike it's Super Meat Boy or I Wanna Be the Guy counterparts, Fly'N is easier from a mechanical standpoint. The levels are long, and feature multiple checkpoints, so small mistakes aren't punished by sending you back to the start, but just to the last checkpoint. Instead, a lot of the difficulty of Fly'N comes from trying to find the glowing seeds and orbs scattered throughout the level. Even though the gameplay is linear, the level encourages a lot of exploration through objectives set in each stage.
And on the topic of the stages, we can't ignore how well designed most of the levels are. The levels rarely rely on creating "unfair" (unavoidable unless you know it's there) traps. Furthermore, each subsequent "world" after the first introduces the player to a new Bird with brand new powers and stages to complement and challenge the player to master those new powers. This keeps the game fresh, both in the introduction of new features and allowing the levels to have new obstacles that would otherwise be impossible to tackle.
Furthermore, old powers aren't a one-and-done deal, they consistently make a reappearance during all latter stages and the scaffolding between stages ensures that the player is adequately prepared for each rise in the difficultly curve. The game features 5 "worlds", which offers
more content playtime than one would expect. Couple that with an exciting soundtrack, excellent animation, and obvious attention to detail, Fly'N is an experience one should not miss.
: 9.8/10 - An amazing quality work from an indie studio; Bravo.

What a load of crap.
It does some things right... the writing is actually pretty good, what little atmosphere is there is very nostalgic if you were alive during the early 2000's, and the game is free.
It's also manipulative and deceptive.
The game's description reads, and I quote: "Emily is Away is an interactive story. Create a screenname and choose your path through the branching narrative."
This is bullcrap.
The narrative does NOT branch.  The ending is the same no matter what you do.  The game only gives you an ILLUSION of choice.  It flat out LIES to you that your choices matter.  They don't.  Remember in some of Telltale's games like The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, how the game would tell you that people would remember your actions and words, and actually react accordingly?  That doesn't happen in this game.  No matter what you do, no matter what the game tells you, your choices do not matter.
And that's why it fails.  The story would be good in a linear format.  Maybe a youtube video?  Or a short story/novella?  But this just isn't the right format for it.  Video games allow choice to affect narrative, and this game uses the illusion of said freedom of choice, only to sting you in the end no matter what you do.
Heck, maybe even as a video game it could've worked if it at least was honest, and didn't lie to you about your choices having any impact whatsoever, or didn't give you any choices in the first place.
I get the message the game is trying to relay, I really do.  And in another format, it could've worked.
But BECAUSE of the format, BECAUSE it tried to be a video game, because it flat out lies and deceives the player about their interactions with the game, the message was lost on me.  Instead of getting it's actual intended message across, I really felt more like "Wow, why did I have to waste my energy typing all this when I can't affect anything in this game?" and I'm pretty sure that wasn't the point.
If you want an interactive visual novel where every action you take DOES matter, that actually USES the medium and the message effectively, get Analogue: A Hate Story.  That game actually allows you to role-play while simulating a PC, and you get all the more invested in it because it feels like what you do MATTERS.  Or if you haven't played those Telltale games yet, play those.
Don't play this.  It's not free.  It may not cost money, but it will cost you time.  Time you could be spending playing a less deceptive game.
