“Hello guys, so, I have this wonderful concept for a game, a really depressing and poetic space exploration game, but I have no idea what to make in the gameplay department, any Ideas?” Said the Lead Designer.
“How about a rogue-like, asteroid-dodging-on-ice skates simulator? The frustrating mechanics won't totally ruin the atmosphere and the lonely experience.” Said a stupid yet influential employer.
That kind of gives away what I think about this game, but read me out, I don't hate this game, nor do I find it bad, it's just that the gameplay is trying to be a rogue-lite in an atmospheric setting, but you can't deepen yourself in it because you've got to dodge the damn asteroids, so it kind of works against itself, but it also makes some sense, depression and loneliness are quite frustrating, but you can always turn off the game, you can't turn off life (well, you can, but it's a touchy subject), so if you feel frustrated with the rather backwards gameplay design, you can just turn it off and go relax playing Dark Souls or something.
But let's get into it, shall we?
Earth exploded, and now you, alone, must find us a new home, and so you wander through the infinity of space searching for the perfect planet to welcome us, while having some loneliness induced depression along the ways, and that is really well done, you read these pieces of poetry scattered around space, in clutters of stars, planets, debris, and old vessels; and it really conveys the feeling of depression this game goes for, sometimes you even have hallucinations and hear voices, even furthering the feelings of sadness and loneliness.
Nothing to complain in that department. It's actually really well done.
The gameplay is simple, it's a rogue-lite, so when you die you re-start, but your progress is saved, and it's very easy to die, because, you know, YOU HAVE NO WAY TO DEFEND YOURSELF. That is so backwards, why is there no way to destroy the asteroids without spending a rare consumable? The only thing you can do is dodge, and it gets old and irritating fast! Kind of like an old man with Alzh… Know what? I won't make that joke.
You basically point somewhere in the screen with your mouse and your ship boosts into that direction, keeping the momentum from your boost indefinitely, but beware, if you want to change directions and avoid certain doom, you also have to work against that momentum, and you will probably have that PTSD from the ice levels in the old Mario games triggered. And trust me, there are so many irritating hazards.
There's also an really unintuitive level-up and upgrades system, not once explaining the mechanics in-depth. You also have different ships to choose from, and they all have a price tag, but when you pay for one, it's for that run only, when you start the next one, you won't have the ship anymore, I figured that out the hard way.
There's also a FTL-like decision system, but unlike FTL, it gives you two choices, and when it's the wrong one the message is basically “U don goofed, pick the other one next time” even though it's all RNG, where in FTL there's story and possibilities and is generally well done.
In the end is all really mysterious and hard to grasp at first, but after sometime it grows on you. But that isn't necessarily good, tumours also grow on you, and you want rid of them quick!
The graphics look rather good, all the explorable locations are nice, and the ship designs are also cool, and the music is incredibly soothing and relaxing, but the game is so boring, you probably will put on music on your headphones as you play it.
And that's the game's biggest fault, it is boring! Really boring, even though you sometimes still want to play it, you can't stand it after some time. Sure, it's supposed to simulate loneliness and nothingness, but this is a game, you better gimme something to do, or is out the drain with you.
Overall, I neither recommend nor I don't recommend this game, I got no real feelings from it, ironic isn't it? The game is extremely boring and repetitive, so if you're into that, whatever really. Me, if I wanted to feel depressed, I'd watch Melancholia, with the late John Hurt, may he rest in peace.

RymdResa tries to be two things that can't ever work well together.
One the one hand it's supposed to be a relaxing, atmospheric experience with a touch of poetry. In that regard the success is partial - while the music sets the tone during your lonesome treks through space masterfully and the artstyle complements the whole, the slivers of poetry you arrive at during your travels are as if a teenager's first venture into creative writing.
On the other hand, the roguelite mechanics the actual gameplay revolves around are needlessly frustrating, without any feeling of catharsis. Especially the third level is an exercise in patience I'm not willing to undergo, as death and loss of progress is sometimes so sudden you hardly have time to comprehend what's happening. It's not a game you can get better at, the winning strategy is to move at a snail's pace and hope for the best.
It's just not fun to play.

'..is a poetic, roguelike space odyssey in a procedually generated world' - full of grave dangers & fine bonuses, without real aim & feel of progression, except for pure manchkin drive to collect the bestest stuff in the Universe.. and of course not to die & lose everything (if you have chosen to play on harder difficulties with permadeath).
But the main difference here which makes the experience so poetic is certainly the totally pacifistic gameplay where you only control your ship's motion in the tricky 2d gravity space, trying to dodge the asteroids, space garbage & soulless machinery leftovers, continuing to serve its lethal duty while their civilisation is long gone & there's no one to defend.
I play it with Xbox controller & the flight feels really satisfying when in a long swing trajectory I use full drive against a massive sun to escape its mighty gravity field & still manage to pick up some goodies off its orbit. I doubt you can have nice time in here without an analogue joystick, the physics model rules.
You have to be very patient, for the bonuses seem totally random, & I generally suggest playing RymdResa only if you have plenty of free time ahead & you totally don't rush anywhere, for it was clearly made up as a dedicated meditative space (pun intended) for relaxed gamepad gravity dancing accompanied by quality ambient music & vague spiritual sayings.

RymdResa (Space Travel) is one of the most interesting titles I have ever come upon.
This game could be described as a mixture between "Out There" and that old space game from back in 70's.
You have a space ship that you must navigate through space to get to your destinations all the while exploring debris of space techs from the past and space anomalies and planets that you come across.
This game some how manages to be one of the most atmospheric games out there with its way of presenting the game and expressing itself.
All in all the gameplay system is simple yet difficult to master, the story is deep but easy to grasp, the sound design is a mixture of 8bit sound effects and some very soothing soundtracks that help the game's atmosphere and presentation to reach an even higher level of greatness and the graphics are simple, very simple and yet some how enough to help the game to get to a point that you can easily consider this game a work of art, a true master piece!
This game might seem simple and empty at the first glance but give it more than 10 minutes time and it will surprise you.
If you are a fan of space and space travel this game is for you.

You navigate a spaceship through a fairly simple gravity-based physics system in space. Don't hit bad stuff. Collect a 'star-like' currency. Upgrade your ship. Unlock better ships meta-game style with the currency. Collect weird poems and just figure the whole thing out.
+Fun little zen-like space game that will have you playing in short, yet still engaging play sessions.
+The artwork is certainly original and is very nice, in my opinion.
+The universe all has a ambience and feel to it.
+Metagame unlocks.
-Yeah, it's a bit pricey.

Enslaved is an action-plateformer with some combat where you play as Monkey, a really agile and really strong guy "enslaved" by Trip, a really intelligent girl who needs him to get back to her tribe. It's set in a post-post-apocalyptic world, apparently centuries after a war against machines. Cities have been deserted and plants have grown everywhere, but in the ruins of civilizations, ancient mechs still lurk and do what they have been programmed for : kill all humans.
Halfway through the game, after a not-so-surpising plot twist, a third character is added to the duo, Pigsy, a fat, smelly guy kinda obsessed with pigs. He will help Monkey and Trip finding and destroying the Pyramid, a place where all humans captured by mechs are enslaved... or are they ?
It's a fun and rather short little game ( maybe don't buy it full price ) combining a lot of easy climbing ( you generally can't die and there is only one path ) and some dynamic fighting, with a bit of shooting and puzzle solving. Monkey has some kind of daibo he uses to kick mech's @sses with, with a light attack, a strong attack, a wide attack and a charged electrical attack. You can also unlock a "fury" attack available after the daibo is fully charged by hitting enemies with normal attacks, and you can protect yourself with a shield, well, two shields in fact : one protects you from bullets, the other one you can activate it when attacked in melee.
The daibo can also shoot plasma and stun rays, used to deactivate enemies shields and kill them from a distance.
In addition, there is one under-used mechanic that only serves a few times in the game : the hoverboard. Called the Cloud ( like the Magical Cloud in Dragon Ball ), it's a really fast disc that Monkey can use at very specific locations to get accross water for example, or fight fast bosses.
And then there is Trip. You can't control her directly, but you can give her orders, she can generate a decoy to attract enemy fire, heal you, and she'll mostly be used to open locked doors, hack stuff and put ladders down. She has an EMP to defend herself in case she gets attacked in melee, and overall she's not really a burden ( unlike most games where you have to escort an NPC, I'm looking at you, Ashely from RE4 ), except when she glitches through the floor and you have to restart the whole chapter/zone.
PROS :
- nice story loosely inspired by the 16th century Chinese novel "Journey to the West" ( Dragon Ball was inspired by that too, you might find some similarities ).
- nice characters, voice over and facial animations during cutscenes. Monkey is voiced by Andy Serkis, mostly known for Gollum in LOTR.
- easy and effective climbing mechanics, it's quick, responsive, and you can't fall to your death
- upgradable hero and gear
- nice graphics for a 2010 game
- light humor after Pigsy joins the group
- unlockable costumes for Monkey and Trip when you finish the game
- unlockable mini adventure where you play as Pigsy, with its own gameplay mechanics.
- nice cutscenes
CONS :
- the camera sucks most of the time, but especially during combats
- some bugs and glitches, Trip disappearing into the environment, scene becoming black when you alt-tab, game crashing when you alt-tab
- no real save system. There is a checkpoint system when you die, but if you quit the game or if it crashes/glitches, there is a big chance you'll have to start the whole chapter over
- characters are a bit cliché : you have the strong hero, the naive cute girl and the funny sidekick. I'd like to have seen some more "extreme" personalities to get more tension between the characters. especially between Trip and Monkey.
- not a big variety of enemies : normal mechs, gun mechs, shielded mechs, stun mechs, some stronger versions of mechs and variants and combinations of the above.

The game left me feeling pretty good, like I had enjoyed myself through the journey.
That's ultimately where my recommendation stems from.
As I look back and wonder what makes it feel so good, there's really only one big reason: the actor Andy Serkis and his performance. Serkis plays the player character, lending both his voice and motions, and that really is what carries the game.
Serkis made his character likable and got me engaged and invested, interested in what will happen to the character next. After my initial infatuation over the game's colourful appearance, clever premise and certain small, wonderful gameplay decisions, my feelings settled to be all about doing whatever busywork the game wanted me to do as fast as possible so I would get to the next good bit. Thankfully it's less tedious that it sounds. My experience boiled down to constantly looking forward to whatever event would be happening or encounter coming accross just around the corner. Anything that triggered dialogue, made the characters interact and Serkis do something entertaining was a joy. The story mostly progressed at a brisk enough pace to not let the cycle of anticipation, excitement and satisfaction completely settle down. Gameplay segments were - with a notable exception or two - short enough to not form a frustrating obstacle between the player and progression, even if a number of retries might have been required at times. They're largely just an inconvenient speedbumb.
The game's not bad, it's well crafted and mostly has a ring of quality to it, but it's also not very bold. It's got the groundwork, but it does nothing with it. The premise of the player character being enslaved, after being set up as a cornerstone of the game in an initial cutscene, is left unused. The game starts soon feel monotonous and flavourless, spreading its content too thin for too long, but the small juicy bits of Serkis are sprinkled densely enough that I didn't feel like quitting before the end.
In the end, the game's enjoyable but also forgettable. I had good time with it for a while, but after it was over and it was time to put it down, it didn't really leave me longing or thinking about it much afterwards.
If you are in a position to pick between different platforms, a console version of this game might be a better bet. The PC port smells like it was done in a hurry with no budget. First i'd like to say that... as of writing this, the game is still in "early access" and.. this means that the game isn't done yet, obviously. More content is to come.
And there's a demo, which you can download here:
<- official site.
Anyways!
What's the game about.. well, there's the gameplay trailer, which basically shows how the game could look after having played several hours. but you start off, like in the demo, with nothing. you can craft basic coal-fueled drills, stone furnaces and coal fueled inserters (robot arms that move an object between 2 spots)
When you got that stuff going, you can further your tech by building a steam engine, which makes electricity, then you can get electric drills and so on, which are faster.. then later you can get robots, tanks, solar power, oil drilling, a car, various weapons ect. incl. a flamethrower.
there's enemies in the game, that attack you based on your pollution (hence the weapons, and also defensive buildings, such as gun turrets, and walls)
The good things about the game:
Graphics remind me a lot of Red Alert's "3D" models on a 2D surface, But you can easily see what's what. And the game runs smoothly at 60 fps even with large factories that span the entire screen (many many many moving objects!)
You can zoom out pretty far, or zoom in pretty close to see what's what.
Supports mods, and there's many out there already.
Overall there's always something to do in the game.
negative things about this game, which can be fixed down the road - it's still early access, remember this!
- The early game is, imo. too short, but if you spent too much time there, you'll get attacked and die, because there's no access to additional types of guns, proper ammo or turrets at the start, you need to develop tech, which requires electricity among other things.
- there's basically only 1 way to progress. having difference ways to go would be more interesting. (like, should i focus on defense/offense against the aliens, get some resources from fighting them, or should i just be defensive, hide behind my walls and develop my tech.. i'd like to see different ways to reach the end goal (or get multiple end goals) instead of the current one, which is basically, reach the highest level of tech and build a space ship - launch it to win.
- the aliens are non interesting. You cannot "negotiate" with them, you don't know at what point you're at risk of being attacked (they supposedly attack you based on the amount of pollution you cause, but there's no "pollution meter" or anything - even though item tooltips show that items level of pollution. Being able to build stuff FOR them, to make peace with them, would be kinda cool. Though they seem very primity (sorta "Zerg" from starcraft-like) so i guess that's not an option.
alternatively, they could add multiple types of aliens, that life in different types of environment. nomads in the desert, zerg-like things on the plains, tribal folk in the forest and so on. so that you can have more reason to explore, except the current reason which is, looking for new resources or "i need alien artifacts for tech development". that's the only 2 reasons you have to explore, right now. that's a shame, since the world is a proceeduraly generated world, that's completely limitless in size.
Anyways!
overall the game is good, if you like to build and plan stuff.
but if you want a deeper meaning with the game, then you should wait a while, because it will most likely get added to the game later - so add the game to your wish list, follow the development and return later!
If you just wanna see how ♥♥♥♥ing smart you can be, by building the most complex factory, in the smallest amount of space then this is the game for you.
also, it has multiplayer co-op, which i have yet to try.

Aliens were always used in shooters and finally they made an actual, pure survival horror game about the Alien. My personal expectations were sky high and oh boy this game lived up to them.
[Tut, tut]
The graphics in Alien: isolation are not the prettiest out there but definitely are to my taste. The Sevastopol is designed with such high attention to detail, it's simply ridiculous. You can tell developers love the alien franchise because they nailed it perfectly. I've explored each corner of that huge space station and trust me I'll do it again in my next playthrough.
[You're becoming hysterical]
Fear. It's present throughout the entire game thanks to amazing atmosphere, lighting effects, sound and of course the main star of this show - the Alien. This creature is unpredictable, it can go anywhere, it can randomly start running in any direction, it can hear you miles away and it will punish you for every single mistake you'll make. The Good the Bad and the Ugly
TheHunter is a game that most people will either hate or love. I myself have developed a love-hate relationship with theHunter over the years. My first impression of theHunter was very skeptical and has grown to an absolute distrust of Expansive Worlds, the current developers. The game itself can be very addicting and enjoyable.
It took me some time before I even thought it was safe to install theHunter. That's not a good first impression. TheHunter is partnered with shady marketing scams and distance themselves from all issues that arise from their use. Why would any developer tarnish their reputation before a potential customer has even been sold on a product? The reason is simple, revenue.
Recently Expansive Worlds announced that they now had over 3 million accounts. To say that is a gross misrepresentation of the current status of theHunter is an understatement. If I would have to guess, I would say that active paying membership is probably in the 50,000's range. Most of the accounts are phony, not created for the intention of playing the game.
So who does play this game? At its core are some long-term hunters who have invested thousands of hours and hundreds of dollars in this game. TheHunter forums are basically run by the die-hard fanatics who refuse to see the problems with Expansive World's current business practices. If you were to post this kind of feedback about the developers, you would most likely be lynched if not outright banned. Don't get me wrong, the forums are a generally mature crowd but ignorance does abound. What would you expect from humans who think it's ok to kill other animals for fun and call it a sport? Fortunately this is just a video game and we are not killing real animals. A recent poll also showed that about 50% of theHunter members are not hunters in real life.
This is most definitely not a Free-to-Play  game. It is a Subscription based membership with a Micro-transaction shop. It does have a non-expiring "Demo" version which you can hunt one animal, with one weapon, in one reserve or zone, for free. Upon completion of in-game Missions you can earn enough gm$ currency to purchase one more weapon and hunt one more animal, but the ammo will run out. Though in general the gm$ earned are mostly useless without investing more real money into the game. You can potentially just play the full game  by purchasing a relatively inexpensive membership subscription and using the above mentioned "Marketing Partners" to earn enough em$, the other in-game currency, to purchase all the items in the Micro-transaction store. Again, buyer beware. At the least you may not receive the em$ and at the worse you may be infected with Spyware, Mal-ware or other potentially harmful software. And you will get no help from the developers. It should also be mentioned that you can earn em$ game currency buy winning "Competitions" but do not expect them to fund all of your desired store items. The Competitions are mainly won by having the most amount of time to spend gaming and just plain luck with a very small amount of actual skill involved, although knowledge of game mechanics are still needed.
TheHunter is not a true Multi-player game in the sense of what gamers expect from today's Multi-player games. It was originally designed as a Single-player game that kept track of player statistics online, but not the game data. All of the game data resides on your local computer, there are no Multi-player servers that run the game. Because all the game data resides on the local computer you can imagine the hacking and cheating that have to be dealt with. About a year ago they decided to alter the programming to basically create a 8 player Co-op based LAN game that is hosted on the computer that starts the game. Running a Single-player game over a WAN, with no dedicated server, has introduced even more problems.
So, what about the game itself? TheHunter has a beautiful environment with amazing details that can give you the feeling of actually being there. The playable areas are enormous, allowing you to spend hours at a time playing. There are 7 reserves or "zones", 18 different hunt-able animals and 33 weapons. Quite frankly there is nothing else like it.  It is a very niche game that some will find quite immersive, complex and addictive. Others will be bored stiff after a few hours. This is a very slow paced game that requires a lot of patience. Patience not only because the game play is so slow but because of poor performance and  software bugs.
After many years playing, testing and reviewing video games , I have to say theHunter is one of the most enjoyed, longest running Betas (by game performance) I have ever been involved in. To be fair, the current developers at Expansive Worlds were not responsible for the original core problems implemented when the game was designed. That's not to excuse the current incompetence in management, but some of the existing problems just can't be fixed. One thing for sure is that anyone playing the game for a certain length of time will encounter serious bugs. Whether you can live with those bugs or not is an individual choice but do not expect them to be fixed. The development team is basically a Monday to Friday crew that is focused on graphical design and cosmetic items for the store. Though I am quite impressed with the single Support Staff (in the US) that handles all of the Support Requests in a professional, courteous and timely manner.
I could imagine the potential of this game if it was redesigned from the ground up. Dedicated servers running multiple versions...Realistic, Arcade, Adventuring. More to do than just shoot animals. Like Botany, Camping, Hiking, Cooking, Fishing, Survival, Crafting, Etc. There are so many areas that could turn into skill based activities with achievements and accomplishments. It could be marketed to more than the niche hunter crowd. There would be no need for shady marketing and deceptive business practices. The game could be better programmed to get rid of core problems like the blinding glare of the sunlight, or the inability to cross a stream without needing an engineering degree, or  independent volume controls for things like the headache-causing-pounding-chronic rain, or not being able to look straight up or straight down and the list goes on and on. But more importantly it could fund a professional staff of developers that could provide an enjoyable game and make a profit.
Alas, we have what we have. I would give theHunter a "C" rating and that's only after accepting the game for what it is, a poorly developed, perpetual Beta with a small market. Yet addictive and enjoyable. I would encourage anyone interested to try out the "Demo" and see if the game is for you.
PROS:
•	unique game
•	vast beautiful zones
•	amazing details
•	endless game-play
•	addictive
•	worldwide player-base
•	can try for free
CONS:
•	poor development
•	perpetual beta
•	aging game
•	poor performance
•	lacking "gaming" features
•	requires a lot of patience
•	small player-base
•	can be expensive

I recently finished Alien: Isolation after almost a year of off-and-on play, and I really felt the need to review it.
First off, if you're a fan of the Alien movie franchise (hopefully not 3 and Ressurection), then you have no excuse to not already own this. If, of course, you're not a fan or familiar with the movies, I'd still recommend this game. It's that good at what it does, and what it does is freakin' awesome.
This game has everything a good horror game should: a tense and foreboding atmosphere, great scares that don't rely on someone jumping out at you (most of the time), a very relatable main character who properly reacts to what's happening around her, incredibly tense stealth gameplay that keeps you on your toes and forces you to think before you act, and even a minimalistic UI that keeps you invested in the game and doesn't get in the way at all.
Honestly, all I have to say about this game is positive. I never noticed a single thing I didn't like throughout the entire experience and this is honestly somewhere up in my top 10 games of all time.
Also, did I mention that beating this game makes you feel like you just fought your way through an actual space station where their was an actual risk of death? It really does, it gets that adrenaline going. Also also, there are a lot of fun nods to the movies and everything resembles exactly what you'd expect these space stations to look like in real life.
Basically, this game is awesome in every way and you won't regret the purchase, no matter what.

Fly'N is one of my favorite games, not just because of the cute graphics, but the difficulty increases at a fun level as you go along. At least in my opinion (I've cleared Super Meat Boy and that was $#$#@#^% tough).
The graphics themselves are top notch, but there is an FPS bug that will likely never get fixed. Play it in windowed instead of full screen and you'll likely have no issues, otherwise you'll get FPS drags/spikes randomly. Though it seems this bug doesn't affect some older PCs. Anyway, the backgrounds, characters, and creatures are so colorful and vibrant. You'd swear an artist came in and beautifully painted each area.
The characters are really cute and well animated, not to mention the main antagonist is a....hair dryer named Dyer. You play as the four buds of the world trees- Flyn (blue), Lyft (green), Ywok (black), and Nyls (orange). Each has a different ability that will come in handy as you progress through the stages. There will also be "chase" stages where you have to make it to the end without dying once, so that you can save some of the various creatures of the world trees. If you want to know a little more about them, check out the commuity guide about them.
Gameplay goes fairly quick, even if you end up dying a lot. You have unlimited lives and if you get stuck, you can just "pop" yourself back to the respawn point. This game can be quite difficult, but it helps you get used to the pace and characters. Each level is more difficult than the previous, but also challenges you to think of new ways to use the buds. Like Ywok for instance can turn into a ball, so in the earlier stages you'll see guidelines of collectables on how to bounce at the right angle, but later on the angles get more specific and require good timing. There are also a bunch of bonus levels (tied to rescuing of creatures in chase stages) that are much, much harder than the normal ones. I would suggest tackling those after completing the game. Oh, and of course, there are boss levels at the end of each tree, which challenge you to use the buds to the best of their abilities. You may die a lot and you will get frusterated, but the music and sights help take the edge off.
The music is beautiful and if you enjoy it, definitely grab the soundtrack. It's soothing and appropriate to each area. In the beginning of each level it starts out softly, but as you progress through the level more beats are added. I feel like it adds some fun to progressing through.
There isn't any dialogue to the story. It's told mostly through cutscenes and it's pretty clear about what is going on. I feel there is also some story related visuals in some of the levels, but generally it's the cute cutscenes.
To me, the only real complaint is the bug I mentioned previously, but thankfully has a simple workaround. It only took me about 10 hours total to complete the game, so it's short and sweet. If you want to see some gameplay or check out the design, feel free to check out my Let's Play

Very fun game, and even maintains replayability beyond just the first playthrough. The comedy is fantastic and truly sets it aside from similar rpg shooter games. The only issue I have with this game is the later playthroughs become much more difficult, causing players to specialize and because of the steep difficulty increas, prevents casual players from enjoying the game. Furthermore, much of the skills you unlock only accumulate with time, but if you only play the first or second playthrough for a character, you only get to ever experience a third or two thirds (about) of the characters skills/potential (at one given time, since you can always realocate skills, but you only have a set amount of skills based on level). So again, if you stop enjoying the game or it becomes too difficult, you will never get to experience the full extent of the characters. Absolutely phenomenal level design, and great mechanics with a nice balance between stealth and combat.

The game is pretty, no doubt about it. There's some lighting magic that generates glints of color that made me stop my game for a few minutes just to play with them. The levels are inventive, well laid-out, and beautifully decorated. Every map has multiple ways through it, and the story rewards those who have to search every nook and cranny. The audio is fairly good, aside from a somewhat limited collection of things for the NPCs to say and a disturbingly notchy positional system.
But did I like it? Eh...
Dishonored sits in that genre of enforced sneakiness that you also see on display in the Deus Ex franchise. The game gives you all kind of tools of mayhem, but brutally punishes you if you dare to use them. It turns the game frustrating and slow.  Maybe that's a good thing, though, since the levels might have induced a bit of claustrophobia, if not for the fact that it takes the better part of a half hour to traverse it.
There's a quick-save system that you're going to end up leaning on pretty heavily for two major reasons: First, there's very little prior indication if a person on the street in an enemy or not. At least one of the gangs -- the hatters -- can be identified because they're wearing hats. Secondly, the previously mentioned punishment incentivizes completing the entire map without being seen... and when you've just spent a half hour crossing the city, only to get spotted at the last minute, it becomes pretty easy to convince yourself that save-spamming has merit.
Then there's the tools that you never get to use.  I never did find whatever was needed to craft the whalebone charms. I ended the game with the better part of a whale skeleton, and never used a single piece.  I collected all my bone charms from the environment. I'm not sure why I bothered, since it is hard to spot any evidence that they had any effect.
In the end, I got my 40 hours of play time out of it, and there's even the promise that I could come back and maybe get a different game out of playing the other story fork with the other character.  But, right now... eh... I don't want to have to spend another 40 hours on a game that just doesn't make me *happy*. I'll come back to it if I'm desperate for a game, but I can think of a bunch of other games I'd rather replay, first.

I have really mixed feelings about Dishonored 2.
From a pure gameplay perspective, it has more of what I liked about the first game - and more of what I didn't like, like the stupid morality system designed to stop you from killing people even though most of your abilities and equipment turns you into God's perfect killing machine.
So, whatever, I killed almost every person with a sword I saw. I knew I'd get the bad ending, and I didn't care - the game just isn't all that much fun in my opinion when you play totally non-lethally. I'll probably replay for the good ending, but I don't see myself playing this one more than twice, and I've played the original Dishonored probably 6 or 7 times.
Pros:
* More maps for Dishonored, basically
* Bigger maps
* New powers, tools, enemies to outsmart
* More of a thing I liked, so I guess I like it.
* (some) excellent architecture.
Cons:
* Villains feel 1-dimensional, with the emotional maturity of very small children.
* Everyone else does too.
* Corvo is Emily's dad because _why exactly? and why is everyone just OK with that??_
* Serious ludonarrative dissonance - how are the Overseers still around and in a position of power if Corvo, a known heretic, is in a position of such high office? What? How?
* "instead of expanding on Dunwall, rats, whale oil, and powerful political dynasties as core gameplay and story elements, let's come up with ENTIRELY NEW stuff that sucks instead!"
* Bloodflies are less interesting than rats
* No new powered devices, because this story is about m a g i c
* No interesting political alliances, because this story is about m a g i c
I liked it, and I recommend it on sale to people who liked the first one, but I'm falling out of love with the franchise.

I originally plus voted this game, I had joined a clan (TAW) for it and found the game amazing fun, but now I look back upon that, having not played the game in literally months and finding myself utterly reluctant to play I decided a Plus vote was wrong.
The game is a HD remake with a few bonus goodies thrown in, but with terribly done systems which are currently being overhauled by the 3 guys who've been assigned to this. IT does feel like Gearbox has dug this one up because a few of the nerd guys kept ♥♥♥♥♥ing on at them to do it, so they did, only to abandon it for them to do with literally no resources. Updates are still in dire need for problems which have been around since day 1, the SDK >STILL< hasn't been released limiting the modding community and holding off the HUGE mods everyone loved and adored on the original game, despite having this beautiful steam workshop support.
The community for the game is basically dead, with the peak online players being 30, at one stage it was still only roughly 100 people and it only goes up to this magical 30 during the sales, after that it goes straight down to 3/4 people, if you're lucky.
Online play is hardly a matter of tactics anymore, it's a case of either people rush you, or they rush you. It becomes less about master tactics and more a matter of who can speed their sorry♥♥♥♥♥to the end-game ships in under 10 minutes. Making even large 8-player games really short and unfullfilling, plus it ends up being a game where poeple just write out build queues and stick religeously to them and even trying to counter said attempt doesn't work outside of a 1v1 situation (As they will likely have someone else with them doing counter-tactics).
The sheer lack of playable races only enforces the above, having an RTS game where you can only play as 4 factions makes the game pretty stale, pretty quick, as there is nothing in the way of fun and variety, you quickly find out what's useless and what's not within about 3 games and then find yourself re-repeating the same tactics in every game.
The campaign is marginally better than the online, as you do often have to think about tactics and such. Although the AI is pretty easy to outfox and out-manuever (as they don't seem to use this brand new vertical plane as much as you'd imagine they would).
Pros:

The addition of the Vertical axis makes the game more intense and brings a greater need for tactics
Units and upgrading are all fairly simple to pick up.
Cons:
In Multiplayer you only get 4 factions and the Hiigarans are the one with the best units, Vaygr are okay but only a really decent player can use them effectively and the Kushan / Taiidan are rushing races which have paper-units compared to the other two.
Cannot play as the other introduced races w/o mods which are often filled with unbalanced units. (Would like to see the others come in officially at a later update or expansion pack with more campaign).

The incredibly inept porting of Homeworld into its sequel's engine has the upside of me rediscovering the original game's brilliance.  Downside is it doesn't look nearly as pretty as the remaster, but at least it's not broken.

Let's just make this clear:  both of these games are absolute classics.  However, even for the skeptic, Remastered should be played if even just for Homeworld 1's campaign, which is perhaps the best campaign of any RTS I've ever played, which has aged more gracefully than the vast majority of games held dear to my childhood.  Beautiful artwork and music, with brilliant writing and voice acting compliment a fun, unique and challenging experience.
Gearbox has treated the material with genuine care, restoring garbled audio, vastly overhauling the graphics, applying the superior Homeworld 2 UI to Homeworld 1, and combining all four factions of both games into one multiplayer experience.  A few tweaks have been made, namely the removal of fighter fuel and stances, as well as breaking fleet formations.  The latter two are a bit of a disappointment, but as a whole, barring the most anal of purist, these changes should not hinder anyone's experience.
An exodus story to rival Battlestar Galactica, with a foreboding and interesting universe to explore, this is an absolute must for any sci-fi or RTS aficionado.

ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS is hands down the most entertaining way to get carpal tunnel playing couch co-op. It has beautiful aesthetics and is quite enjoyable to play with a friend, against the AI, or even in the more pacifist Zen mode flying around and making art with rocket trails. The combat is simple, intuitive, and amazing, with three projectiles and a dash maneuver which allow for diverse gameplay. You can shoot missles, leave nasty mines, and drop bombs to cause beautiful, beautiful havoc. I'm not kidding. It's quite beautiful watching the brightly colored projectiles and stages blossom with bright, cheerful explosions as your enemies spin, hit by your barrage of missles and bombs or blasted by a mine. There is a lot of potential for skill, but even beginners can play without too much barrier.
Pros:
Fun gameplay
Beautiful (minimalist) graphics
Great game modes
Couch versus, co-op vs bots, and Zen mode
Cons:
High risk of intense button mashing, play at your own risk.
No online multiplayer (and, given the intense speed of matches, it makes sense, though it would be amazing if it existed)
Basically requires a controller- playable on keyboard and mouse, but much less fun.
I highly recommend this game if you have a friend nearby or just want to relax and unwind against a bot or in Zen mode.

A pedantic asteroid-smashing simulation.
Pros:
+ Different difficulty levels
+ An overall consistent and efficient aesthetics
+ Space atmosphere
+ There is probably a lot of stuff to dig out further in the game
+ Rogue-lite progression (at least in some difficulty levels)
Cons:
- Pedantic (chunks of poetry appear among disperse stardust; why is there poetry characters floating in space?)
- No sense of real exploration (everything looks the same)
- Inertia controls the ship more than you do
- You can die instantly by crashing into an asteroid
- Very slow pacing; nothing happens until suddenly a field of asteroids pops up and by the time you wake up you're dead
- Hard to dive into the story (if there really is one)
- When you purchase a new ship with rogue-lited money, you keep it only for one try (specifically annoying if you have saved for a few games and then smash into an asteroid after one minute)
- Almost nothing to do (at least in early game) apart floating in space from place to place (this is your main objective in Chapter One). No fight, no quest, nothing.
Verdict: Chapters 2 and 3 are probably a lot better than the first one. Yet it's the one we begin with, and it's boring. Permadeath has no use save from being frustrating. Without any real sense of control, it just feels meaningless. As the said chapter one requires a lot of trials to complete, it's a repelling barrier hard to overcome.
The most boring and useless software purchase of 2016. I'm glad that year is already a past.

I never thought there would be much overlap between the roguelike and chill-in-space-and-look-at-things genres, and yet here we are. Rymd Resa is by far one of the most relaxing roguelike-things I've played, with a lot of drifting through the cosmos and collecting star stuff. That's not to say there's no death, or frustrating ends to promising runs, but it doesn't take much to get past that and into the soothing embrace of eternity.
Rymd Resa starts pleasantly enough, with a rogue asteroid annihilating your homeworld. Stuck on your dinky starship in the vastness of space, it's up to you to find a new home for yourself and maybe unlock a few secrets of the cosmos while you're at it. The gameplay is very familiar Asteroids-style jetting about but with several extra layers of resources, stats, and items to keep you busy. Most of what you'll be doing at any given time is seeking out and exploring objects in space, while avoiding dangers like rocks, mines, and angry suns.
There are three chapters to the game, each with very different goals to tackle. The first chapter has you following a trail of signals across the universe, while the second tasks you with finding resources and returning them to your base. The third is a mix of both, with objectives to locate in deep space while also bringing back materials for upgrades. A helpful coordinate system and objective marker (which is actually a small companion ship) keep you from getting too terribly lost in the void as you putter about.
You're still going to get lost, though, because space is vast and ever-changing. The heavenly bodies of Rymd Resa move quite a bit, with some drifting lazily in the sea of stars and others streaking off into eternity. They're a lot of planets and nebulae and asteroids but also derelict satellites and stations and stranger things like kittens in F-14s. I should say now that this isn't a terribly immersive game, and it gets a lot more mileage out of its chill atmosphere than simulating any sort of actual space.
Getting near a safe object prompts you to explore it, at which point several different things can happen. You could get Resources, which serve as both your hit points and fuel. You could get Spacepoints, which are spent on unlocking new ships and abilities via research. You could get a bit of poetic dialog that presents you a choice. Or your exploration could fail. Any of those outcomes can also produce a random item, either a consumable that helps you in your journey or a piece of equipment for your ship. There's a pretty broad spread of items to find and equip, which helps give the game a bit more longevity after you complete other upgrades.
There are also levels to gain and skillpoints to assign and audio logs to find, and these are all welcome additions to keep you exploring space. You'll have plenty of reasons to putter around the stars, exploring and collecting to your heart's content... and then a bit of space junk will come out of nowhere and annihilate you. Rymd Resa has one big flaw, and that's how easy it is to die, at least at first. I mentioned your Resources are your life and your thrust, and the base ship can hold up to 300 points. Well, a rogue asteroid is going to do well over 100 points, so if you've been out exploring for awhile and drift too far the wrong way, or just happen to be in the way of a comet, that run is over. You can even bite it from a particularly unlucky exploration that saps your Resources with no recourse.
I had a few moments of intense frustration as lovely space journeys ended abruptly and unfairly, and it's all due to how weak your starter ship is. You can unlock better ships with 600 or even 1000 Resources to run with, but this costs Spacepoints and it's NOT a one-time unlock. You're buying that ship for your next run, so you'd better hope it's a good enough run to earn all those Spacepoints and more back. Items and research upgrades can also mitigate these issues, so by the end of the game you should be back to drifting happily through the void. It's just that first hour or so that threatens to disappoint.
Hopefully you can get past that hurdle because Rymd Resa is an excellent chillout roguelike full of wonders to discover. The simple, high-contrast graphics and the synth soundtrack are perfect for your treks into the unknown, building upon the strange and solitary atmosphere of your quests. There are some pretty poetic audio logs and text that might annoy you if you often find yourself deriding things as pretentious, but I found they added pleasantly to the offbeat presentation. In the end it's a relaxing journey in a colorful, creative galaxy that I find myself just as strangely drawn to.

I'm a wimp when it comes to horror games, so I put this one off a long time. What I've found is that it's not actually a horror game. It's a tense, sometimes creepy stealth game.
And it's a great stealth game. In most circumstances, you need to traverse the world and get to some other point, and enemies prevent direct travel. You distract, blind, wound, or sneak your way around them in the usual fashions. That makes it sound bland, but the level design is exquisite; you move up/down staircases, ladders, vents, and hallways. You hide behind the smallest cover, peeking and desperately checking your motion detector to see what's going on. At many points you feel suffocated, as if there's nowhere safe to go. But the game has lots of ways to make it work - you just have to keep alert. It feels a lot like Sir, You Are Being Hunted (a weird comparison, I know) because of the feeling of constantly being hunted and hedged in. Sometimes you have to sprint away, in full view of an enemy, just to dive into safety and scramble to safety.
But let's talk about the alien. People say it's "heavily scripted", but it's really not. It's largely unpredictable, you really don't know when it's going to pop out. There are things which make it more _likely_ to pop out, but they're non-deterministic. It sometimes scrapes its way out of the ceiling when you're not even doing anything. That adds to the sense that you're not at all in control of the game, and you're really surviving, making you paranoid and constantly looking for exits and hiding spots.
And is ♥♥♥♥ing
. I've never been a fan of '70s aesthetic, but this game absolutely elevates it. Old clicking analog computers, wavering CRT screens embedded in every wall, beige and cream white lounges, soft yellow lighting, all surrounded by oddly dirty (but never filthy) floors and girders. It's hands-down the most beautiful game I've ever seen, and I'd recommend buying it just to experience the art. The screenshots (for once) don't do it justice.
The downsides is, as everyone else has mentioned, the sheer length of the game. I played seven hours (at time of writing), and felt as if I'd pretty much seen everything there was to see. It didn't feel like i was really making any progress, or being given a reason to continue. The story presented itself in obvious terms almost immediately, so there was no mystery to solve. I felt no attachment to characters, so I didn't really care when they were in danger. And everything else boiled down to "we need to flip switches in different parts of the world in order to survive", which is as fine a goal as any, but doesn't inherently make me want to play.
But really, if you've ever enjoyed stealth games, you must play this. It's not perfect, but it's sure great.

Fly'N is a gorgeous 2D platformer with puzzle elements and fast paced gameplay. Fly'N progresses through 5 worlds, each with a different and gorgeous art theme.
As you play FLy'N you will acquire additional playable characters (for a total of 4), each of which has its own unique skills. The skills include singing, wall-climbing, bouncing, and darting through the air rapidly. These skills are necessary for navigating levels, opening new pathways, and avoiding damage. Each character can also double jump or glide. In my experience playing the game, I felt that character controls were responsive and smooth and I did not experience any bugs.
The aspect that really drew me into the Fly'N was the art style. Fly'N art themes range from a botanical/floral theme to a mechanical/industrial theme. Each world has a unique look and every world is very colorful. The characters themselves are also very unique, colorful, and well animated. I also felt the sound design and music are well above average in quality.
Fly'N also stands out in level design. While the levels can be very challenging, they never seemed frustrating. Out of my (many) deaths, I never felt I had anyone to blame but myself. The levels typically involve using your different skills to get past obstacles, avoid touching deadly surfaces, navigate moving platforms, and outrunning a rising layer of gears, bolts, and screws which kill you if you touch them. For lack of a better description, I will refer to this as the "ocean of doom" from here on. In addition, there are three types of levels throughout the game. The first, which makes up most of the levels, involves navigating obstacles and finding the way to the end of the level. The second, more challenging level type is similar to the first but adds the additional challenge of the "ocean of doom" gradually rises through the map, forcing you to move quickly. The last level type is the two-stage boss battles where you must first fight a mechanical boss which usually involves avoiding projectiles and a significant amount of platforming. The second-stage of the boss battles involves you traveling inside the boss to dismantle it by collecting glowing orbs and using them to break down the machinery.
If you are interested in a story, Fly'N has one but don't expect much. It is very minimal and its not why I would choose to play the game. The story is very basic and is essentially just there to provide a context to play. There is a bad guy, he is messing up your world, and you are trying to stop him and repair the damage he does. However, I don't consider the minimal story a drawback because that really is all this game needs to make it fun.
I have seen some reviews critique the difficulty of Fly'N . However, though Fly'N was challenging, I was able to complete the game without too much trouble and I would not say that my skills are above average when it comes to platformers. Fly'N also gives you the option of decreasing the difficulty of the "ocean of doom" levels if you die too many times by stopping the "ocean of doom" from rising. On the other hand, if you are a completionist, the "ocean of doom" levels have optional bonus objectives that require you to complete levels quickly and without dying. The game also offers many collectables and secrets to discover. I was content with just completing the levels and finishing the game. In my opinion, trying to collect all items, find all secrets, and getting through the levels without dying would take a great deal of skill and dedication.
As you can see from my recorded hours in game, I was able to complete the game in just over 7 hours. I imagine that this would be in the ballpark of how long it would take the average gamer. If your platforming skills are better than mine you could probably shave that time down by a pretty good margin as I died pretty frequently. If, on the other hand, you are a completionist....expect much longer since I imagine you will be replaying and restarting levels a ton. I would also say that Fly'N has a pretty decent margin of replayability. Overall, I felt that the game was definitely worth the price tag.
TL;DR: Fly'N is a great little platformer with excellent art and sound design, exceptional level design, and provides a good challenge that any fan of platformers can enjoy. I highly recommend this game and I also tip my hat to the developers who clearly put in a lot of effort to make a high quality and very fun game.

I havent played Dark Souls 1 or Demon Souls. But the label of the "Hardcore experience" thats promised if you should buy these games always kept me eyeballing with them. So when DS2 came out i gave it a try and boy, what did i miss. I consider myself a casual AND a hardcore gamer but the thing is, once you gave in to the fact that Dark Souls 2 is a difficult and punishing game, you dont want to play anything similiar which provides a more easy experience. Why ? Because; If you sucessfully mastered all the difficult fights, overpowered bosses and mean traps, you are rewarded with the best "I finally did it !!" experience a game has to offer. You get souls, which are basically used for everything in the game. Be it leveling up, buying weapons and improving them or forging unique weapons from boss souls, you'll always want more of them. This is why you continue
You play as one of the many so-called
that strife the land of Drangleic in search of worthy challenges. Basically that means defeating your regular run-of-the-mill zombie as well as unique and very strong bosses which always can be defeated in several ways. This is one of the strong points of the game. No matter how you distribute your skillpoints that you have to buy with your souls, many combinations will work for you if you know the mechanics behind every attribute. Which leads to one of the weakest points to the game: It explains less than nothing. Item info on spells dont clearly explains what the spells are doing. Same with most items you'll find. Its trial and error if you dont want to consult one of the many Wikis that exist for this game. But fear not; If you think your build is weak and ineffective, you can always use one of several souls vessels to reskill your character.
Dark Souls 2 is a console port and one can clearly see that. Objects buffer slowly and sometimes you can see the textures loading. Some textures have a very low resolution and look kinda "muddy". Also the game feels slower than 60 FPS. Specially in object cluttered enviroments such as Majula or Aldias Keep you can see tearing and a decrease in FPS. But what it lacks in technical conversion, it compensates in atmosphere. Majula for example is always shrouded in the beautiful light of a setting sun. The lightrays of the grafics engine add drastically to this nice scenery.
The sounds are well done and weapon impacts have a good acoustic feedback. What is worth mentioning is that you can hear the elemental infusion of a weapon on impact. A weapon that has lightning damage sounds differenet than a weapon with dark magic infusion. Thats a neat detail. The music is well done and adds a lot to the boss battled which always have been a strong point in the series. On the other hand, the game is a bit silent at times. Maybe to put the well done music in perspective.
I'll make a bold move and be straightforward: This game plays horrible with keyboard and mouse. As mentioned earlier, DS2 is a console port and as a passionate gamer myself i own many devices i can use with games. So of course i own a XboX 360 pad and imho this game really should be played with a gamepad. Only thing i have problems with are game mechanics like guard breaking and parrying because its hard to accomplish with the analogue sticks of the XboX pad. Maybe a PS3 gamepad would be better with that. Anyway, in my opinion, a gamepad is mandatory to enjoy this game.
Like in every other Souls game, DS2 includes a so called Invasion System. This means that players can invade each others game sessions in attempt to co-op with the host or to stop him from progressing by defeating him which gives the victorious players souls and covenant specific items as reward. Unfortunately its a bit tricky to summon friends. There are obstacles such as Soul Memory, which has to be very close to each other so one can summon another. Also, you need items you get while progressing in the game. You kinda unlock multiplayer that way. Playing together from the get go is not possible because of that.
Then theres other phantoms, that try to defeat you as a host to rank up in their covenant. While it adds tension to the game and its hostile enviroment, it can be a bit annoying if you are on your way to the boss, cleared the area all alone and get invaded just before you can enter the fog gate. On the other hand, the game gives you several methods to prevent that situation. Burning the item Human Effigy prevents being invaded for about one hour. Also, theres is the item Black Crystal that sends an invader back into his own world.
My opinion is that the invading system is as fun as it is frustrating. PvP is a bit like playing the lottery; Sometimes you are lucky and have a good fight. And sometimes you invade a guy and his two friends that stomp you. Or you get invaded buy someone who does nothing else than PvP and he finishes you off before you are ready for a fight.
All in all, i give this game 8 out of 10 points. This game is very well executed, its addicting and offers a dense atmosphere in a enviroment that encourages exploring.
(Review based on 200+ hours of gameplay)

"Emily is away" is a free game about you, the player, talking to a friend of yours called Emerly35.
You go through a period from 2002-2006 with each year being a chapter of your story.
The game takes place in a chatroom where you and Emerly talk.
With each year you find out more about her and to be honest, more about yourself (not in a deep emotional way, more like your character)
Graphics:
The graphics are a nice callback to that timeperiod online. It really does bring back memories.
Story:
I'd just like to say that the story is great. No spoilers here. The game is free and takes about 30 mins to complete.
Gameplay:
They implemented more than I'd expect to here. Every time you choose a dialogue option, you need to press your keys to write it out (random keys, not the actual text) which makes you feel like a part of the story. Also, you can check you friends list, where you can see everyone's bio, which is a cool way of reminding us how stupid we sounded with them. Also, every year you can choose a new icon for your profile, which is a cool remider of what happened in that year.
Overall:
8/10 - They could've tied up some loose ends, but it kind of feels that they meant to present it that way.
An extra tip to make you feel more immersed:
Open up you Steam Overlay and go to Youtube, in there write in "Top Hits (insert the chapter year here)"
While it may sound dumb, trust me, it'll make the experience even better.

Ninja Theory is one of my liked studios. They have made good games but nothing that has pushed them into that great level it seems. Enslaved is one such game. You play as Monkey and from his posture to his climbing acrobatics the name fits. In a dystopian future you break free on an air ship and do battle with the machine guards. The combat is simple but can be fun nontheless. Getting enslaved by a computer hacking beauty once on the ground for the purpose of safely seeing her home begins your journey. Traveling through destroyed cities the game is a fun trek with your budding love interest. Meeting Piggy another character is fun as well. It's not a great game by any means. But it is a fun one with a nice little story that will be good for a play through.

You play as Monkey and will spend 90% of the time tirelessly hopping from pipe to pipe, jumping across walkways and climbing buildings while all Tripp needs to do is walk a couple of steps to get to the exact same destination.
What's a little annoying is the limitations on what you can do and go for. You can't jump down edges or leap in a different direction when the game doesnt want you to. You can't even fall from ledges unless you're supposed to. The game insists on holding your hand throughout the game. Despite this, I sometimes found myself in situations of not knowing what to do next, only because the objectives weren't mapped out clearly.
These invisible barriers for a game isnt new or that bad actually... In fact, it's a good thing since I won't ever find myself accidentally jumping in the wrong directions and falling into a pool of acid or something but it also means no sense of danger, freedom or thought needed for the player.
The gameplay mechanics are pretty interesting the first few times, then starts getting rather repetitive when you realize this is what you'll have to go through for the rest of the game. Climb this, climb that, deal with conveniently placed turrets, pull some lever and fight mostly the same robot enemies over and over again that you'll encounter throughout the whole game. Unlike what it seems, this is mostly a platformer-puzzle game than it is an action-adventure game.
Not to say I hate platformer games. I've played games like the Prince of Persia series and enjoyed them, but for a game like Enslaved, all the climbing segments are all too similiar and with all the protective invisible walls in place, there's no challenge to be found in any of it.
There are thankfully several instances of more fun action such as running from a giant robot dog or fighting a big robot that shoots his balls at you, but these are few and far in between.
Levels are mostly linear and despite the changes in environment for each chapter, the map designs never really of changes and soon starts to feel way too repetitive.
There's little reason to roam in the maps apart from collecting bright shiny red floating orbs that you can use for upgrades which are pointless anyway. Because with such shoddy controls for this PC port, I couldn't even be bothered to use half of new movesets I unlock. One particuarly useful attack of Monkey swinging his long pole at multiple enemies (space+left mouse) can't even performed with the keyboard, with Monkey jumping up and down like an hapless dolt more times than when he actually performs the attack successfully. This is the biggest problem I had with the game and I never found a solution to it.
Mouse sensitivity is all over place and it took me multiple attempts at tweaking the .ini file and in-game settings to finally settle things down. Even then, I had problems with the aiming controls, trying to aim with projectiles feels like trying to aim with WASD than with my own mouse. People who play on the controller probably wont be affected by all this crap porting issues, but hey, this is a effin' PC game. If they want to port it to PC, then port it right.
The story of Enslaved starts off with a half-naked dude, Monkey, being enslaved by a girl called Tripp, thus the title "Enslaved". Many elements are borrowed from Journey to the West, but mostly it's just the characters. Not sure if they were even travelling to the 'West'. The relationship is between Tripp and Monkey is interesting but never fully explored. Their journey spans across a few different unique locations but I honestly couldn't get that feeling of a refresh. Structures and paths are largely the same and having to battle the exact same robot enemies for all these levels made this adventure a tiring slog through.
I can't give a proper conclusion to the story since I've not reached the last chapter, and it's pretty much the main reason why I, and most people I guess, play the game for. But with the kind of gameplay I have to put up with, I don't think I can be bothered to.
Graphics is pretty okay for 2010 standards, but far too bright and vibrant for my tastes. The excessive bloom washes away texture definition and environment details and the brightness can sometimes be too distracting instead.
Enslaved Odyssey to the West has a potentially good premise in its world that leaves much to be answered but as much as I hate to say this, it just squanders too much repetitiveness, linear level design and gameplay mechanics that makes the game more boring to play than enjoy.
If you're fine with a very mediocre gameplay experience and prefer playing the game for a story or adventure you might enjoy this game. But personally, as much as I wanted to, I couldn't.

I also love that Axel is basically the tutorial guy and he is subliminally teaching you how to play the game and that at the last time you see him, he shows you what NOT to do: make a lot of noise.

When I first delved into Dark Souls 2 I promised not to make the mistake of comparing it to Dark Souls during my time in it aside from lore connections (( wich are relativly few and far between)) the game I found to be relativly challenging at first and the bosses where all well thought out with different move sets depending on your position when facing them, unfortunatly many bosses can be simply sidestepped via holding your joystick right, wait for their attack to miss, and then unload your stamina bar depending on how big your attack window was. Rinse repeat. This occured for several bosses in the game who would have been more engaging if they had simply a side swipe. Luckily this isnt the case for most bosses, several of them will react accordingly via a 360 attack or a side swipe (( DLC bosses especially, they thought of this and improved their boss designs substantially in the new content)) The game is certainly intense, having to manage your stamina bar and time your attacks and defence puts alot of depth and stratagy into the combat, some bosses are very difficult requiring perfect timing to avoid being combod to death. There is a severe lack of personality to alot of the bosses though, some are re-used by having to fight 2 of them instead at once although usually they have some different abilitys. a keen exsample is the Dragon Riders mid game. they have the same skillset and armor but one has dark armor and starts on a ledge, pelting you with arrows. Then we have bosses like Mirror Knight who re-define boss battles, adding a pvp element to the table by being able to summon another player as a phantom to assist it and fight you! these kind of things you simply NEVER see in video games and are very thought provoking designs. The game has an increadible amount of character building customization as well, after spamming PVP for nearly 4 hours one day I seldom ever ran into another player with the same build. From Hexers blasting you to sorcerers playing Prop hunt with Chameleon to a visit from the Monarch weilding duel avelyns to simulate his wrist darts (( There is a butterfly costume so he was certainly cosplaying)) there is increadible fun to have building different characters and doing multiple playthroughs with tons of weapons and 4 schools of magic to combine into your own personal playstyle. This game is a must for all hardcore gamers and maybe that casual player ready to enjoy a challenging yet increadibly rewarding experience. If your new to the series do not be afraid to try Dark Souls, its also a challenging and extremely rewarding game.

An exceptional, beautiful platformer. It piles on the cute factor by the bucketload as I found myself going "awww!" on far too many occasions as the adorable buds repair the damage of the inhabitants of stunning worlds ruined by electrical garbage
Don't be fooled though... this isn't for the light hearted. The difficulty becomes fantastically challenging to the point that I was breaking a sweat on many occasions. It's tough, but you get infinite lives and feel like a complete boss when you execute it perfectly. I'd definitely recommend a controller for this one, as the keyboard might be a bit awkward at times
The only thing where this game really fails... the ending. It grudgingly just felt very rushed. Maybe I've played too much Sonic and want to enjoy utterly wrecking a big, evil machine in the final level - but it weirdly switched from the fun boss fights it had throughout to basically dying repeatedly whilst you learn the sequence to basically avoid dying. After the anti-climatic level; the end doesn't seem to conclude much too. Without spoiling it, you kinda get a "yay! It's all sorted"... without anything really being sorted. There's still 4 tree worlds completely wrecked with garbage. It just really sucked considering how well the game had been executed up to that point
In the grand scheme of things - it's a small gripe, as I got 10+ fantastic and gripping hours out of this game (just the basic game too... I've still to find all the goodies on the levels and complete the bonus ones) - but I found the end leaves you with a bit of an "oh... that's it?"
It is okay. I played for a bit. However, it didn't grab me and make me want to play more. Regardless I would still recommend it, but there are other platformers out there that are better.

Fly'N is a puzzle platformer game in which you rotate between different creatures with various abilities. The emphasis of this game is on the platforming but the levels are laid out in a way that makes it more puzzley, having to backtrack and figure out where you are headed.
The game starts out simple enough, and seems very casual friendly, but as you unlock more characters, the levels get harder and the difficulty becomes very steep towards the end of the game.
I love the visuals in this game. It has a cute art style that is completely unique. You begin to appreciate the world you're involved in.
The gameplay itself revolves around trying get through basic levels, but between all the collectables, and the different characters you use, it doesn't feel very linear. This can be frustrating or enjoyable, depending on the level and depending on the type of player you are. The mechanics are very solid, the game controls well and the mechanics that each creature has lends itself to creative play. The Black creature, which uses a bouncing mechanic was difficult for me to get the hang of, but once you understand it, it can become quite fun to play around with.
The game took me about 6 hours to completion, without collecting much and without doing the bonus levels. I was very satisifed and felt very challenged towards the end. This game might become too challenging for a more casual audience, as I'm use to playing more hardcore platformers.
The boss fights were also interesting as they were focused on the platforming itself, which I feel is the right call instead of a typical "jump on the bad guy" playstyle you might see in platformers
The story is hit or miss, I wasn't 100% sure what was going on but the cutscenes were still enjoyable to watch.
-Great length for the price, good value
-Solid and Unique Mechanics
-Lot of extras in levels and beyond
-Interesting Boss Fights
-Awesome Art Style
-Challenging, bit steep on difficulty curve
-Saw Minor Frame Rate Drops at some portions
-Might be too challenging for casual play
-Nonlinear level layout may confuse players
-Some players might feel overburdened by the large amount of mechanics
I really enjoyed Fly'N and I highly recommend it. Even a casual player will enjoy the early portions of the game. This is another must have platformer on steam if you love this genre. The collectables, unique mechanics, and pretty art style is just icing on the cake

TL;DR - This game is a f_ucking masterpiece. The sound design has stepped up from the last game. The graphic design has stepped up from the last game. The level design has stepped up from the last game. The replayability has stepped up from the last game. The storyline and characters have stepped up from the last game. The game is a step up from the last game, and that got a 9 from me. 10/10!!
The sound design of this game is immense. Many people don't really pay attention to this, in fact it's often lost to the main premise of the game, however you take away music and sound effect from any game, especially this one, it just isn't the same. The sound design keeps you on edge, the music reflecting the mood of each scene, the SFX really adding to the horror, suspense and fear the game wants to portray. The game isn't intended to be a horror game but it has a moderately scary vibe at time down to the sound design. Once again like I did in the last game, I would accidentally knock things off of tables and creat a loud noise amongst the silence and s_hit myself up. The sound design really helps immerse the player in the game, giving you the feeling of being part of it despite it being a game.
The graphic design naturally has taken a massive improvement, obviously. The game was released only last year, in 2016 (2017 is the year at the time of writing this). In 4 years, a lot has happened for graphic design and graphics in games in general. The game looks stunning and the art style of the game has progressed even further, and has matured into an even better product than in the first Dishonored. The team has clearly got even more comfortable and got a better grip on what they are going for with this graphic style. I can't commend the graphic design enough - the game looks how it feels, the rich areas look lavish and luxurious, the bad areas of each part of the map look dingy, dark and neglected. Really the graphics suit the game so much, not going for hyper realism, but also not going for an overly cartoony design style.
The level design is awesome too. The level of thought that has gone into level design alone is truly amazing, with multiple different routes to the same place, the map takes intuition and imagination to use, however provides a rewarding feeling when conquered and used to the players advantage. Having played through non-lethally, the map has to be used a lot more than if you kill everyone. The map is like a playground and when combined with the powers the players is granted, it is such an exciting thing to travel in. Some of my favourite moments in the game have been simply looking for ways to avoid conflict and violence to complete the game non-lethally through the map design. It truly is an awesome rewarding experience.
VOICE ACTING! Finally the character you play has character. One of the FEW shortcomings of the first game was the fact Corvo was silent. This happens in many games and I doubt the first Dishonored did it stylisticly but because they didn't want to give a voice to their character much like many other games. This changed in Dishonored now Corvo has a voice actor. Corvo talks to other NPCs when you interact with them and will talk to himself when something notable happens, hinting to the player what to do but also adding substance to the senseless killing or hours sneaking. To many people this may be a small and insignificant thing but little things like this really polish a game and give it a gleam other great games don't quite have.
On top of Corvo and Emily having voice actors while you play them, the voice acting is just as filled with emotion as before - it feels real to listen to. Often in games, voiced characters have little to no emotion but this is not true of Dishonored 2. Dishonored 2 has some great voice actors who put their all into the performances they give for the game and it adds so much to the game.
The gameplay has the same awesome feel to it it had in the first game, not much room for improvement in this category really. Despite this, some parts have got worse. One of the few minor shortcomings of this god-tier game is how clunky the extended jump feels compared to the first game. This does seem rather picky but it was a noticeable thing to me. The other mechanics feel great, in fact ever so slightly more refined. With that in mind, there are new gameplay mechanics added this time - further upgrades for the previous mechanics and all new mechanics through being able to play as Emily. The tutorial at the start introduces Emily to you as a playable character, and works as a tutorial that actually has some value and adds to the story - this is great. Other new mechanics include the addition of bloodflies to make up for the dissapearance of violent rats which came with the plague of the first game. These are good as they make it more difficult to access certain places. In general, gameplay has improved the most it possibly could have really from its almost perfect standard before.
The amount of time that can be put into the game is immense too. I played a non-lethal playthrough and it took just over 10 hours for me to complete. I am by no means incredible at the game however I didn't take as long as I could doing everything. I didn't collect all runes, bonecharms and paintings. To say I got over 10 hours in one playthhrough is awesome.
All in all the game is a masterpiece and a graceful evolution of the first game, furthering the story, furthering the attachment to Emily and Corvo, providing an awesome game. In truth I could have wrote even more for this game as it has really done so much for my interest in singleplayer story-driven games again. Yes, I do reccomend this game, buy the f_uck out of it.
