The Alien franchise hasn't had very much luck in gaming lately, between Aliens vs Predator and Aliens: Colonial Marines both turning out pretty lackluster to say the least. Alien: Isolation barely had to do much more than exist in order to be the best game the franchise has had for several years, and in that regard it accomplished its goal. But it also has its own fair share of problems, unfortunately.
The biggest issue is that while the game is called "Alien: Isolation", you're not really isolated, and the alien isn't really there that often. When I went back and replayed the game game a second time I used a stopwatch to keep track of just how often the alien was actually hunting me, and it came out to be 1 hour, 36 minutes, and 34 seconds. Now, this number was only tracking the amount of time that the alien is forcefully encountered, and there are at least a few hours of areas where if you make too much noise it's possible to summon him, but I didn't count those because as long as you crouch instead of running around banging on everything you see he'll never show up in those areas. If this were a 4 hour indie game that would be a fair number, and I'd even accept it if the game had puzzles or something to fill the rest of the game. But even knowing where to go, the game still took me around 15 hours to replay, and most of the rest of that time is filled with stealth segments with humans and androids.
Let's start by describing the androids. The androids are used pretty frequently throughout the later parts of the game, and at one point take up 3 chapters in a row where the alien is nowhere to be seen. It's hard to even consider them a threat, though, because all they do is slowly walk towards you, and if they manage to catch you you can just do a QTE button mash to escape their grasp up to two times times before actually dying on the third (this is on Nightmare difficulty, so it might be even easier on lesser difficulties). But the "if" is a big "if" there, because while they were presumably trying to capture the feeling of an unstoppable robot slowly but relentlessly pursuing you like you might see in a movie like The Terminator, they left out the whole "relentlessly" part, and all you have to do to evade them is just run past them and go around a corner until they lose you. The only way I could see someone dying to one of them is if they panic and run so far that they end up looping around and running back into the same android they were running from.
Secondly, we move on to the humans. The humans have guns, and aren't afraid to use them - the loading screens try to convince you that they won't mess with you if you don't mess with them, implying that maybe at one point the game had a mechanic like in I Am Alive where you can negotiate with survivors and interact with them, but it's a lie; all the humans know how to do is walk and shoot. The thing is, the humans aren't very bright, and don't have very good survival instincts, so you can do things like this.
. Flares are essentially the only item you need to get past any group of humans, because once they see one they all bunch up and run towards it like a bunch of moths. But later on you don't even need any flares, because you can just do this.
(for the record, this doesn't count as killing them yourself either, which is why I have the achievement for completing the game without killing any humans). Even though everyone knows there's an alien on board, they have no qualms opening fire the moment they get the chance to, and then you can just hide until the alien kills them all and leaves. They also have infinite ammo, and it's a good thing, because they don't really know how to conserve it well.

But what about the Alien itself? Surely that one hour and 36 minutes must be great, right? Well, usually, but not always. Once again, I'll let the webms do some of the talking. The big problem is that the alien isn't necessarily stupid so much as completely schizophrenic, so you'll see things like this pretty commonly
where the alien will start walking into a room and then immediately remember he left the oven on in another area and turn around, or this
where the alien just seems like he's lost, or someone less commonly things like this
or this
. The alien could be controlled by Twitch Plays Pokemon and I wouldn't be able to tell any difference, because its movements are just completely random. Instead of feeling like a deadly predator it just feels like an old man looking for his car keys, and the only way he'll ever catch you is by pure chance, such as him deciding to do a 180 turn for no reason when you're trying to sneak past him. Thankfully the craftable noisemakers have the same effect with him as the flares do with humans, so he isn't much of a threat either.
It's really a shame, because you can tell the developers really put a lot of effort into the rest of the game. The visual and sound design is fantastic, and everything looks and sounds like you're straight in an Alien movie. The graphics are fantastic, and the game is equally well optimized. The story is pretty much just a typical Alien story, but it's still fun to see, at least the first time. And the game even has rough Oculus Rift support, which even I have to admit is pretty terrifying compared to playing the game normally. But even though the game does a great job of building tension and atmosphere when you're alone, it all goes to hell when you're around any enemy because of just how stupid everything is. The game plays like a stealth game with half the game code missing, and while I think a hardcore Alien fan might be able to appreciate the rest of the game enough to enjoy the game anyways, if you're just looking for a survival horror game there are way too many better options that don't cost $50 for me to recommend this one. I'd love to see them make a second game using the same groundwork but with improved pacing and AI, but I just didn't enjoy this game very much. It might make a good Holiday Sale purchase, though.
If you do choose to buy the game at some point, I would strongly recommend playing on either Hard or Nightmare (the game warns you before starting Nightmare, but it's still pretty easy). I played through it the first time on Hard and found myself flooded with so many crafting resources that I constantly found myself crafting useless trash like flashbombs that I knew I would never use just to make room in my inventory for more crafting ingredients, which doesn't really strike me as "survival horror". Nightmare fixes that by veering off to the opposite end and making 99% of the containers in the game empty, which at least makes it feel like the items you do manage to find are special even if you probably won't use them since all you ever need are flares and noisemakers. Nightmare also breaks your motion detector and makes it give false readings sometimes, making it less slightly more challenging to sneak past the enemies (which is a much needed addition, in my opinion).
Halfway through the game it gets pretty slow, but its perfect recreation of the original Alien movie makes this purchase worh the money. It's also very hard, good luck (but still worh it).

I grew up with the original Homeworld back in 1999 (I was 9 then) and I remembered playing the crap out of Homeworld back then. Homeworld 2, when it came out in 2003 was meh. Shinier but too difficult and had several gameplay mechanics I didn't like.
The Remaster is essentially Homeworld 1 & 2 in the Homeworld 2 engine only shiner. There is the combined multiplayer which is probably what you want since you can play as Kushan, Taiidan, Hiigaran, and Vagyr all on the same map. I don't recommend the HW1R Campaign since, even though it's in the HW2 engine, there are some gameplay mechanics that don't transition properly. For instance HW2 had a dynamic difficulty system where the difficulty of the AI in the Campaign was determined by how many ships you had at the end of the previous mission (i.e. went into hyperspace with). So having a fully functional fleet at the beginning of a mission was not in your best interests unless you wanted to get swarmed by the AI. This mechanic was transferred over to the HW1R Campaign.
In HW1 Classic it's advisable that you have 6 salvage corvettes built and ready to go before the end of mission 2 to make capturing the three assault frigates in mission 3 easier (and for getting you two free Assault frigates...the third is always retired and converted into RUs) as well as shortening the amount of time it takes to salvage the cryo trays. HW1R screws that strategy up by adding additional Assault Frigates depending on your fleet size so instead of three, you're facing six and they will ignore your fighters and corvettes in favor of obliteratig the trays which can lead to a quick mission failed screen.
But fortunately they do offer HW1 & 2 in their classic form which is highly recommended. I only use the remastered form to play offline skirmishes against the AI. There are a few bugs with the Remastered version though. Salvage Corvettes/Marine Frigates/Infiltrator Frigates have to be ordered to capture each individual target instead of group targeting a group of targets. However salvage corvettes can now capture enemy fighters and corvettes much easier now. Formations are a joke since in HW1 the ships stayed in formation and fought in formation. HW2 they break formation the minute they enter combat and the sphere formation, the formation meant to be the best defensive option availible, is useless as they don't form a spherical barrier around the target they're protecting.
There is some saving grace in that the modding community is very active here. Many of the popular mods from Homeworld 2 Classic that were around prior to the release of the Remastered version have been uploaded here on the Steam Workshops. Even better, you don't have to go through a complicated installation process. The Remastered Version has a built in mod launcher on the main launcher. All you have to do is subscribe to the mods you want, download them (which begins automatically upon subscribing), go to the launcher, click mods on the bottom right of the launcher screen, select the mod you want to run, click select on the mod menu and then click run. It's very easy. No having to go into the game files and put files into specific folders, no having to worry about damaging the game's basic files. It's a wonderful additon that I'm very much enjoying.
I highly recommend the Star Trek Continuum Mod for HW2C. It's very well done and a Remastered release is reportedly on its way.

In a word: Tedious.
For a roguelike, it's both too hard and too easy. Death can come quickly for a while, but then after a while you may want to die rather than play the tediousness any more, as you have enough equipment to survive. Once you see that you can make the camera stay centered, much of the artifical difficulty of no forward view disappears. There's no way to zoom out your view, so that sucks, especially when you run right into a sun just offscreen. The designers did this, though, because half the time the game "procedurally" generates stuff as it's coming into view. Really poor design.
Want spacepoints? Grind. Can't afford a higher-level ship? Too bad. Get research? Oh, that's random, so early level stuff might not appear for you until chapter 3. You also buy research with the same spacepoints you get ships with. See a planet? Press a single key and hope the RNG gods favor you. Even when you have choices, 95% of the time comes down to luck. Want achievements? Well, congrats, because the "beginner" achivement requires that you get level 25. Out of 40. You'll hit halfway through chapter 3 before you get level 25. Want to access those science events? You get to pour 25 points into a skill that has no use until chapter 2, so you'll neglect it until you realize those events are the only way to survive.
There's no save and leave feature, so I have hours and hours of "play time" when I left the computer for work or sleep. And since I didn't want to lose an expensive ship for no gain of spacepoints or "legacy" (which sucks), I idled the game for easily 85% of my "play time".
The poetry sucks, so I turned it off. After playing for a while longer, I realized that reading (or at least clicking past) the sucky diaries gives you points. So, back on it went. And I grew more annoyed at the "depth" of a teenager's lamentations of loneliness. The voice was just as annoying, so that left as well. The music was decent, but tied to a game wholly undeserving of it.
Don't buy this. Go find something else.

TL:DR pretty good game with a decent story and likeable characters in Trip and Monkey. The gameplay revolves around climbing and close combat that isnt too bad itself but gets a bit boring towards the end of the game.
Enslaved is loosely based on the Chinese story Journey to the West. Its set in the future where most of humanity has been wiped out and the survivors live in fear of mechs who capture or kill people. The main character Monkey finds himself imprisoned on a slave ship at the beginning of the game when the games other main character Trip, attempts an escape. The ensuing chaos allows Monkey to also attempt to escape as the ship crashes. Monkey awakens to find Trip has fitted a slave headband that will kill him if he doesnt do what she says. Her only order for Monkey is to get her back to her home.
The game has you playing as Monkey with Trip as an AI controlled companion. Most of the game revolves around climbing structures and platforms, quite similar to the climbing in the Uncharted series, with a bit of combat against the mechs where Monkey uses a retractable staff. I quite liked the story and Trip and Monkey are also both likeable characters as their initial uneasy alliance blossoms into a friendship.
This game was overlooked a bit (a bit undeservedly) on its initial console release but it is a pretty good game even though the gameplay gets a bit stale towards the end though. This edition also features the DLC Pigsy's Perfect 10 which is also a decent add on where you play another character from the main game Pigsy with a more stealth focused type of gameplay.
Good points:
- Enjoyable story and Trip and Monkey are both likeable characters.
- the companion AI for Trip is actually quite good. Games with an AI companion can be hit or miss but they get it right here.
- I loved the level design particularly the earlier levels in the ruins of New York. Rather than go for the grim dark crumbling ruins of other post-apocalyptic games the ruins in Enslaved are full of colourful plant life as nature reclaims the city and it does lookreally nice.
-The Pigsys Perfect 10 dlc story is quite a good add on which mixes up the gameplay from the main game with a bigger focus on stealth.
Bad points:
- There is very little variety of enemies particularly bosses. Most of the bosses are the same couple of mechs which you'll fight a few times throughout the game.
- Combat mostly boils down to button bashing with the fast and heavy attacks. You can unlock other attacks but theres never much cause to use them.
- The camera is a bit finicky at times as it will suddenly snap to a new angle as you move around a level and it can be a bit disorientating.

This is a really really good game. If you like a game with a brilliantly crafted story (a la Mass Effect, To The Moon etc.) you will love this.
So, the strongest aspects of Enslaved are the story and acting. Andy Serkis and Lindsey Shaw do a fantastic job making their characters believable and interesting. The "screenplay" by Andy Garland is excellent and I thought it ended in a very original and interesting fashion. The motion capture is done very well so facial expression really come through to convey emotion. Truly first class work.
The graphics and ambience are utterly superb too and I loved just spending time looking around at the amazing world Ninja Theory created. I had been playing this concurrently with Dark Souls 2 and it was such a delight to escape into this colourful world having been stuck in the rather miserable (though attractive in its own way) world of Hidetaka Miyazaki.
The only niggles I have with Enslaved are the camera, which behaves in a wild and frustrating fashion, and the combat which, whilst fun to begin with, becomes somewhat repetitive by the end. Luckily the story was so good that I was more than happy to carry on through even if the gameplay was not quite to my tastes.
I would really love to see this story continue following the intriguing ending but I understand sales were not great. That is a  real shame because It is massively evident this game was made with a lot of love, attention and professionalism, and excels in areas most games are incredibly weak.

"Crunch-wise": 8/10
-Graphics: 9/10, the game is gorgeous. Most vistas are worthwhile, the characters' looks have much improved since the last game. When ran with the Ultra settings, the graphics are close to perfect at that point in time.
-Sound/music: 7/10. The sound effects are decent, but the music feels uninspired. Most of it doesn't feel that different from Dishonored 1 in general. Special mention for the Addermire Institute though, that level had excellent sound design (and ambiance in general).
-Gameplay: 8/10. Emily's new powers are refreshing and innovative but feel somewhat superfluous; there are always more boring and efficient ways to do pretty much anything in this game. Corvo's powers are the same from the old game (or so I'm told, I haven't played him yet). There are many new ways to visit violence upon your enemies, that being said, including non-lethal jump-in takedowns and Emily's Shadow Walk power. That means High Chaos playthroughs (or very combative non-lethal playthroughs) allow for a lot of entertaining combat.
"Fluff-wise": 6/10
-Story: 7/10 As far as the story goes, it isn't very imaginative. Delilah carries out a coup to oust Emily. Either she or Corvo escape with their lives and work à la Dishonored to eliminate Delilah's allies and uncover how she organized the plot to take over. You carry out missions to that effect and that's pretty much it. There is a (relatively forseeable) minor plot twist involving a character in the game, but it's overall unexciting, but still tolerable and above passable.
-Game world: 5/10 Unlike the first game, in which one of the prime features was the exploration and discovery of the Empire of the Isles, its inner workings, its culture etc etc, there is very little to sink a lorehound's teeth into. You're given one interesting piece of information in regards to the Void, but the rest is already known to players who already went through Dishonored 1. Karnaca is devoid of any interesting history or details outside of a few key elements. Maybe there isn't much to say about the world at all, after all.
Overall: 7/10. It's a good game, it has good value overall. Your initial playthrough should take inbetween 20 to maybe 30 hours depending on whether you're rushing through or looking around a lot. Then there's New Game+ if you're craving for more. It features excellent gameplay and superb graphics, but lacks a bit of soul in terms of storytelling, in general. It's a bit pricey outside of a sale, but it's a decent premium for easily up to 50 hours of game play. Absolutely grab it during a sale or just do buy it if you can spare the money and are a avid fan of the first Dishonored.

HW1 Remastered is still Homeworld and still a great game.  It's even more beautiful than it was back in 1999--and it really was beautiful then (and the Classic version still has its charm).  ...but it's got a bunch of problems.
Some minor spoilers below.  If you haven't played at all, I'm just going to say I think the Classic campaign is better and Classic actually seems better-polished, even if the Remastered has better graphics and the advantage of some more modern RTS UI conventions.  I *really* recommend Classic.
Special ship abilities are plagued--gravwell generators don't turn off reliably.  Support frigates tend to just kind of wander off, and guard mode no longer causes them to repair guarded ships.  Proximity sensors don't even *get* guard mode anymore, and require some kind of micro to use them (I rapidly stopped caring).  Salvage corvettes can't get their salvage orders assigned to a group of ships, meaning salvaging is micro--but ships seem extra-distractable in this new version, so despite the UI difficulties and a hard cap of 14 salvage corvettes, salvaging is still ridiculously easy.  Mostly I just felt discouraged from using the special abilities in general, which is too bad, because Homeworld put a lot of special unit abilities in and it's one of the things that makes the game as good as it is.
Mission breaking-bugs are available in force.  I hadn't even put on my alpha-tester hat.  I just fired up the sensor manager in, for example, the Cathedral of Kadesh, noticed I could see something I didn't expect to, focused on it, and script broke the mission so badly that I had to restart it once I realized enemies weren't spawning in anymore.  Mission 14 just kind of crashed on load the first time.  Blowing up a hyperspace gate in the Junkyard made it seem impossible to get one of my units back at one point, though it showed up none the worse for wear in the next mission.
The single player campaign also feels watered down.  I was actually looking forward to auto-resourcing, but it looks like all the maps have way more resources in them now, because within a handful of missions I had tens of thousands of RU and didn't really have anything to spend them on.  I stopped sending the harvesters out at all except to occasionally spite the enemy, which took most of the difficulty out of a particular mission near-ish a star.  The unit cap and salvaging difficulties (more micro to pick up a bunch of ion frigates at once) meant I really never built up a big fleet despite the RUs.  It mostly didn't matter, either.  The AI kept on blowing up my frigates but mostly couldn't deal with destroyers or bigger, so I just stuck with those, eventually started building huge clouds of multiguns and bombers because I may as well spend RUs on something.  I don't think I blew up a single enemy cruiser prior to the last mission--just salvaged them instead--and expected to get punished by adaptive difficulty or something, but never was.  The frigateball was only intimidating by memory of the Classic game--I finally murdered the whole thing out of spite, and hardly lost any ships doing it--and the last mission was way tamer than the chaotic final-knife-fight that I had to replay like five times a couple of months ago when I reinstalled the 1999 Homeworld from disc.
UI changes are a mixed bag.  The right-click-to-do-anything RTS convention works really well for the most part:  you usually get what you want out of it, and it makes directing your forces dirt simple.  Right click on an enemy, and you'll attack or salvage.  Right click on empty space and the movement lines get brought up, letting you fiddle with them a bit before confirming them.  Right click on a friendly and, depending on the unit, you might just move to them, or you might dock with them (docking with the ship you wanted to was a terribly difficult process sometimes in HW Classic).  It's also now easy to see what your ships are doing, with a convention I think was borrowed from HW2 but it's been so long since I played that I forget:  lines goin places.  If you've directed a group of ships to attack another group, the lines will tell you who they're going to shoot at.  Handy.  Though sometimes it's sitting right on top of the ion cannon lines.  The build/research/launch interfaces are now sidebars instead of separate screens, which is nice sometimes, except mouse scroll acts both on their lists and on the map at large.  Also, the default single-key bindings (B, L) bring them up but don't dismiss them--CTRL+B CTRL+L do that--except for Research, why is it different?--and if you change them, which I did, the game doesn't remember them properly if you exit and return, and you actually have to reset the keys first then reinstate your change because some bug links the toggle and non-toggle versions of the keystroke.  Remain docked/auto-launch is no longer stored between missions, leading to some frustrating moments.  And the launch manager is just generally worse than classic's--I can either click on every ship I want to launch, individually, then launch them, or just launch everything.  Usually what I want to do is launch all my interceptors, or launch all my salvage corvettes.  Classic lets you make that choice--though it doesn't let you choose to just launch a handful of interceptors, say, which the new interface does.  I don't care about that, but maybe someone does.
The launch thing is doubly frustrating because a group UI change allows you to select groups that are currently hangared.  If I could give that group orders and they would launch and execute them, that'd be totally rad.  But the orders just don't really do anything.  Focusing on a hangared group seems to just...take you somewhere on the map.  Oh well.
Speaking of hangared ships, ship recovery is worse now.  In Classic, the ships would bundle up near the bay then queue in from there.  Now they form a gigantic line stretching away from the mothership.  At least once, my huge queue of fighters has accidentally stumbled across the enemy.  Not sure if that's just another thing from using the HW2 engine or a Remastered change.
Perhaps worst of all is the new hyperspace button.  It's alright in some parts of the campaign--you get the option to hyperspace and you're usually ready to go.  That's not always the case though, and you have to turn off a lot of UI to get the gigantic "hyperspace" button out of the top-center of the screen.  Worse, I clicked it by mistake once and cancelled the jump, and the sensor manager was disabled until the next mission.  Just...c'mon.
Some of the voice acting also seems to have been re-recorded.  It warms my hear to think of some of these folks working together again, even minus Campbell Lane, but I don't think the new recordings improved anything.  Fleet Command in particular feels different.  You might hear her voice a lot, too, because "Group X is under attack" can apparently play once every couple of seconds now...really don't remember that from before.  Particularly a problem if you send cap ships through the Junkyard.
My Steam codes came with the Remastered Boxed edition, which included a Hiigaran insignia keychain (bigger than the one that came with the old game), a registration card to unlock the game (from a website that then gives you a Steam code--seems redundant), and a 4"x6"-ish booklet that contains the EXCELLENTLY WRITTEN histories and fluff from the Homeworld 1 manual and some art.  I was really looking forward to the artbook and the art definitely doesn't disappoint, but I expected something bigger.  I still have the original homeworld manual, which I think is 5"x7", and just as thick since it contains extra tutorial stuff and some things about units and the tech tree--things you'd read as a kid during the car ride home from the store.  The box also contained a really quite large model of the Pride of Hiigara from HW2, probably about a foot long, with light up bits.  Rad.

Story premise of RymdResa is a bit of a cliche as you see the Earth explodes leaving our astronaut avatar only one hope – to find a habitable place in the neverending vastness of space. Soon you start to realize that your are probably the only human left alive, and that there is a little chance that you will find a new home in the ‘Big empty’. As years go by and your resources run low, so does your psyche, burdening you with moral doubts and at times deep poetic conclusions.
Separated in a three unique chapters, each having a different premise, Rymdresa feels and acts like a true space odyssey. As space you travel through is procedurally generated by means of y and x axis there are literally no bounds to where and how far you can go, and for how long you can try to survive.
As in any rogue-like game, the basics are difficult to master and take a bit of time to get used to. You gather resources scavenging through celestial bodies and abandoned spacecrafts or picking up particles of astral dust. Well, it’s not exploration as it first comes to mind, as you just need to get close to the objects and click the explore button.
There are many different upgrades that you can apply to your spacecrafts; maybe you want your shields to be of a higher capacity so you can take a more rigorous punch from space debris or hostile UFOs, or maybe you want more powerful engine to cover more distance faster, or, maybe you just want a whole new ship with different preferences altogether. The RPG-ish style of your inventory immediately lets you know that there is huge amount of upgrades available.
Weapons are permanently offline as there is no combat in RymdResa, and i’m really glad there isn’t any, because the omnipresent melancholic atmosphere is just as perfect as it is. Actually that’s the thing that stroke me the most from the very start of my adventure. That strange, even bizarre feeling of loneliness and complete separation from some kind of a illusionary safe-zone.
RymdResa is the most tranquil space rogue-like you will ever play, but so unforgiving at times. With it's unique twist on space exploration and rogue-like features it somehow manages to separate itself from other space exploring titles.

This is a
for any plaforming fan.
Don't let the cute art style fool you. This is a
challenging and very rewarding precision platformer. The best part about it though, is you don't
to collect anything. If you want to grab all the orbs and seeds, and sing to all the creatures that's great, but if you don't, that's ok too. The game gives
the power to decide when you want a bigger challenge. Even on the boss levels with rising "lava," every 10 deaths the game will ask you--in a patronizing way--if you want to disable said "lava" (except on the final boss).
The controls are tight, thank goodness. You will be jumping, floating, phasing, and sticking/bouncing/dashing constantly. The level design encourages speed and will challenge your muscle memory and reflexes. You will have to plan a small route, then execute these abilities within fractions of a second of each other, and then adapt and react on the fly to whatever you couldn't see. These levels are quite large and varied, and there are 5 worlds with 8 levels in the cute main story. Despite their size, I never felt lost, and there are checkpoints strewn all over them that let you change characters. The camera pans and zooms by itself, so it kind of suggests what you should do (along with the seeds). The automatic camera was a necessary feature as most of the time you will be too busy doing something to look around.
While the art style is great and the game is beautiful, there are practically no graphics options, and the menus are too minimalistic. I hope you have the recommended specs. On the other hand, the game has great sound design with happy, upbeat music during puzzle oriented levels and intense music whenever the villain is involved. The music also gets muffled and changes when you phase kind of like Giana Sisters.
Overall this Is an amazing platformer with beautiful art and sound, amazing level design, and tight controls.
P.S.
Random observation: I swear the final level was inspired by the final level of Earthworm Jim. Luckily you float way slower than Jim and can double jump while floating.

Neon Shadow is a first-person-shooter originally developed for mobile platforms. The game attempts to emulate oldschool shooters like DOOM and Quake with a modern and simplified twist.
As a $5.00 Steam release you can't really complain about the game too much, especially if you bought it on sale for a single dollar like I did. It's fairly polished, especially for a mobile port. However, as an "FPS inspired by classic shooters" I think it misses the mark in a couple ways.
First of all, this game has some incredibly uninspired and cookie-cutter level design. Classic shooters like DOOM and Quake wouldn't be as fun without their creative and memorable level design; a statement which Neon Shadow proves true. Sure the weapons work and the game movement is smooth, but when the few levels this game has blur together into an indistinguishable blob of steel interiors and neon lights, it starts to lose its fun-factor after less than an hour.
Secondly, this game has a really bizarre weapon load-out; both in weapon-choice and balancing. Your starting shotgun sucks, the rifle is the ace weapon that'll do you no wrong, the grenade launcher doesn't do nearly as much damage as it should but it can kill you by accident without a moments notice, and the not-BFG has the same issues as the launcher while being a bit more reliable. The weapons function but they don't feel like they've been fine-tuned enough, and as such they make the gun-play feel weird and unsatisfying.
As for the multiplayer: its uh... there I guess. Expect everyone to spam the not-BFG.
Like I said though, as a $5.00 game, Neon Shadow doesn't feel like a rip-off. It's a humble little game with a small price. As a mobile port it held up fairly well outside of some optimization issues, but in terms of gameplay it works quite well on PC. I recommend this game on the grounds that you're a die-hard classic-FPS fan, you have a little cash left on Steam, and you want to blow a couple hours on something.
PROS:
- Clear and concise visuals, if a bit generic.
- Controls are responsive.
- Mostly glitch-free.
MIDDLE-GROUND:
- Extremely short.
CONS:
- Repetitive level design.
- Odd weapon-balancing.
- Enemies can get a bit annoying.
- Lackluster multiplayer.
- Spotty optimization.
- Frustrating and anti-climatic final boss.
SCORE: 6/10
Grab it on sale if you can.

TLDR: Great game, fun to play, fans of JC2 will love JC3. But bugs get in the way, and after nearly a year the developer still hasn't fixed them.
I almost hate to write this review, because it's mostly just echoing what many other people have written. At the same time, I'm hoping that with enough consistent feedback from players, the developers might actually do something to fix what is very nearly an amazing game.
So here it is.
In terms of the gameplay, Just Cause 3 Feels like an enhanced version of Just Cause 2. This is a good thing. JC2 was endlessly entertaining, and JC3 builds on that by adding things like the wingsuit, an unlimited supply of C4 (though you can only place a few at a time), the ability to attach multiple grapple lines to objects, and then have the lines retract and launch the objects at each other. The map is enormous, and every part of it feels handcrafted, no two towns or military bases feel quite the same. It's a good-looking game as well, I'm on a laptop with a GTX970M, and I can run it on high graphics at 60fps with no problem.
But then there are the goddamn bugs. The flies on top of what would otherwise be a perfectly delicious slice of gaming cake. In my 8 hrs of play I have encountered at least half a dozen bugs, ranging in severity from irritating to potentially game-breaking.
For example:
\
Bottom line is that this is a great game that needs some touching up. If it weren't for the embarassing number of bugs and glitches, I would give this game a positive recommendation. The fact is that they have had nearly a year to fix these glaring problems, but instead have chosen to release three DLC packs. To me, that smacks of pure greed, and even though I bought the game at a massive discount, I'm still a bit disappoined in the quality of the product.
I've been looking forward to the game, but sadly my computer and most computers can not run it, so I recommend you get it on the Xbox 360 or something. All in all this game is quiet fun.

Oh my god.... I might have actually found something nice. This was the first though that went through my head when starting this game, but quickly that though got stabbed by the extremely jagged edges of this unpolished gemstone.
What do I mean? I mean that this game is actually nice, but it suffers from some rather crippling problems.
Allow me to elaborate..
I will not talk about the story, but I can surely spoil it for you with the following phrase:
. Now with that ruinous spoiler out of the way I can get to the real problem, the slackjob effort of an free-running system.
Something that has a great emphasis on one way of moving around, should try to avoid from making it annoying, but sometimes it manages to do more than that and that is to occasionally bug out completely stopping all momentum of movement when speed is of the essence. Spoilers: This thing happens a lot.
Oh and the climbing sections are within the same framework.
Now the annoying movement aside, we could have a jab at the second major mechanic of the game and that is combat and spoilers again, it's completely underwhelming.
The combat is pretty much the same as the Batman/Arkham games, but janky as all f*ck. Combat animations are Mo-capped, actually every character animation is Mo-capped.
I guess that was a given with Andy Serkis as your lead actor, who does a f*cking great job to be totally honest.
However back to combat, I'm not sure if this is really the case, but the animations that run during combat feel disjointed to say the least. Secondly the combat is made more annoying by the fact that our main character doesn't close the distance between enemies when he starts swinging. Causing him to swing thin air how many times you pressed the button. You are required  close the distance manually, which although makes sense, but makes the tense moments a bit annoying, when you just stand there doing your best windmill-impersonation when the enemies wait to shank you.
Tertiary point I can summarize with one phrase: F*ck that camera, it's a monster of it's own...
Anyway those wide and pointy serrated edges aside, the story that this game tells is pretty nice. I honestly can't say much besides that lest I spoil the whole thing. But I feel that it is a pretty good combination of a generic adventure-film plot with some light comedy towards the end and a rather anticlimactic ending..
So If you enjoy those generic martial-arts/adventure-film and have the patience to sit through some minor annoyances with it. I really could recommend this..
But only if you can keep an open mind and can stop yourself from throwing a controller in the first half-an-hour.

The combat is as you'd expect from this sort of title, mildly frenetic, not particularly deep, can be achieved mostly through button mashing, but more control yields better results.
The voice work was fantastic in my opinion. Really believable characterisation with little nuances here and there that make each one unique.
Storywise, it drops you right in with little explanation but that's not really an issue as things are explained fully as you progress.
Oh, and the version I got (possibly all versions) came with what was for me an extra 4.5 hours of gameplay in the form of an extended mission set with a different protagonist to the main game. The extra missions were the same playstyle, but with different tactics, which was very refreshing. In fact, I played the extra missions through in one sitting, often thinking "Cor, I'd have thought this would be over by now given it's an added extra, but it's still going..."
All in all, highly recommended for anyone who enjoys third person combat and platforming of the roughly Prince of Persia vein.

I was hesitant to pick this up at launch due to the reports of technical issues, but finally decided to give it a try during the 2017 Steam Summer Sale. I cannot comment on the full extent of the issues at launch, but as it plays now, I highly recommend the game if you’re running a fairly modern PC.
Using an i7 6700K and a GTX 1070 I managed to max the game at 2560x1440 (with resolution scaling enabled), with performance that was basically locked 60fps. Given the minimal amount of tweaking that was necessary to achieve this performance, I would imagine people with cards similar to the GTX 1060 / RX 480 will have no trouble running this game at 60fps using the right balance of visual settings, or by simply playing at 1080p.
The game plays a lot like the original but with a drastically improved rendering engine and more sophisiticated animations. Melee combat as a result looks much sleeker and more natural, so if you’re a fan of playing the game “high chaos” style, you will quickly notice the improvements over its predecessor. The levels are generally large, complex, and with multiple ways to complete your goal. The game also has a New Game+ feature, something I have not yet tried myself.
As far as I know the game does still utilize Denuvo which is a dealbreaker for some people. The only thing resembling an issue I noticed that might be Denuvo related is the length of the intial load screen before getting to the game menu. I use an SSD and it’s a pretty substantial initial load screen. Once that is done however, load times are not unreasonably long. It would be nice if Arkane decided to remove Denuvo given the fact that it was cracked months ago, but it did not prevent me from enjoying the game.

This is the Bioshock 2 of the Dishonored Universe.
It's not a bad game, but it doesn't do much that is new. Playing as a new character with a completely different power set is interesting and I do like the ability to craft bone charms, however it's basically the same game as Dishonored 1. In a way it feels more like a gigantic full game DLC than a sequel. Even the story is a rehash of the first game. I would only play this if you want more Dishonored, but don't expect anything radically different from the first and don't expect a story as compelling as the first either.
What's sad is that the random pieces of literature littered around the environments is more compelling than the main story. The world of Dishonored is gigantic and rich and yet the only thing the creators could come up with is another revenge story with you reclaiming the throne? The potential stories in Dishonored are undless. Even Sokolov's adventures you read about in the game are more interesting. I think Dishonored 2 should have been a vastly different game, with an entirely new character, exploring the far reaches of the world of Dishonored, or at least doing something that is different. How about a mission to rob a bank or find some legendary whale or locate a mysterious unknown civilization? Instead the creatores clearly took the safe route and created a very very safe uninteresting game.
A good analogy are the blood flies in Dishonored 2. They are just like the rat plague in Dishonored 1 except they fly and aren't really threatening.
Also the game is super easy even on the hardest difficully. Granted I have been playing a heavy chaos style but I imagine I'll do fine even during my 100% stealth playthrough. Still my biggest issue with the original game was how easy the game was if you played a chaos playthrough. Ironically to make the game hard you have to try not to kill people. I would prefer a more metal gear solid approach where the game gets brutal if you're not stealthy.
BTW the keyboard controls are terrible just like the first game but you can fix them. Thankfully you can assign all of your weapons to various keys on the keyboard. Instead of assigning everything to the standard 0-9 keys I recommend the following:
G - Grenades
F1 to F4 Powers
1-6 Guns, Crossbow Bolts, etc.
TAB Heart Item
You get the idea. It it so much easier.
Anyway I would recommend this game for anybody who wants more Dishonored and more powers to combine and screw around with. If you are looking for something fresh don't buy this. It's just a rehash.

I had a dream last night.
In this dream, I sat around and realized that my life would be so much easier if I could just automate everything.  I could automate cooking and cleaning if only I had the ability to build a grabber which could grab dirty dishes and insert them into the dish washer while a grabber also reached in and removed clean dishes, or grab food from the fridge and then place it on a plate once cooked.
I became frustrated because I realized that I didn't have the knowledge of how to simply... automate.  I didn't know HOW to build these devices.  I knew that I need copper wiring or steel or iron gadgets but... but how?  How could I do it? My life was so inefficient.  What am I even doing?
Then I woke up. I woke up and I realized that all of this came from playing Factorio - a game of automation.
I played Factorio well before it came onto Steam and I felt proud to offer more cash toward the developer.  The game is, quite frankly, one of the best crafting-esque games to exist.  The game also teaches some interesting problems and challenges when it comes to automating "things" - a problem that exists in anyone who programs or for engineers who build cars.
But beyond all that, it's just fun.  Especially multiplayer.
You will be inefficfient for a long time when playing this game.  Yet it's those inefficiencies that really make the game fun and make the game shine.
You'll build treadmills that go under treadmills which go into factories which produce goods that go onto more treadmills which get put onto other treadmills just to build more treadmills.  And if that's not enough, if you play this game for more than a few hours in a given week you will absolutely have a game dream about automating your life.
And you will be frustrated by it. But not by the game.

I've watched all Alien films and this is the first time i can say i watched (played) a true sequel to the original Alien movie (and it's not even a movie, it's a game!!).
Truly , Alien Isolation is the first real Alien game that i've played, and the best one. It is, surely one of the best games of 2014 and possibly the best horror game i've played in a long time.
The story is simple, but very functional and even interesting at times, because it involves the story and cast of the original one (just a little of, mind you) because this a story about Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, of the Nostromo crew in the original Alien movie. It is a sequel to the first alien, and you can play it like that, but its more an homage, a love letter to the horror, the atmosphere, and the classic design by HR Giger of the original creature, the unknown terror that lurks in the guts of this gigantic space station, the Sevastopol. And like it's name, all the game reeks of industrial futuristic design, lots of metal, steam, dark passages, strange noises, and a few surprises along the way...
Many people had praised the game for it's quality, graphics, sound, artificial intelligence for the creature, the game itself, the excellent design of all things and objects in game, the horror, the intensity of the experience, even playing on easier modes...but i think they are overlooking something else. There is something else to this game i think... something that's resonating with many people of different ages, different backgrounds and tastes in gaming...
I've played games, consoles and pc, for many many years (since the 90s) and alltough it has been said already about video games as an art form, and being the new medium for telling stories, there was (there is) still some kind of stigma of video games being not at all a serious medium, like movies and cinema, a stigma of being...well, mostly for kids, and teens, maybe young adults MAYBE but not really for adults.... You know , like, if you have 40 years or more and you play games it is kind of inmature... (And i think that kind of thinking is completely wrong)
Well, playing this game, i've been scared to death (many times) and the game was difficult, the game was scary, not at all like any game i've played...and yes..it's not for every one...it is not for people that don't like this genre, it is more for adults that wants to play (And experience) an alien story, but more than that, a Sci Fi Horror story, real sci fi, real horror, and it doesn't make any apologies for that.. i think it is one of the first of its kind , and more importantly, it shows that YOU CAN HAVE many different genres in gaming, many different kinds of stories, and public, for different kinds of games (not just the 4 or 5 types of games that are going around these days)
Even more, this game has raised the bar so high in terms of what to expect of a horror game, true horror, that i think, this is one of those few games, that believe or not, will change all the games (of it's genre) that come after it, because, just simply because, every other horror game from now one will be compared to this one... maybe it is not so clear at this point still, but i think time will show more and more what i mean...for better and for worse also (many space horror games will follow, that try to copy/emulate the success of alien isolation with silly results. But also, i think..i hope, this will show that you can make good quality games, with focus placed in story, atmosphere, design, all in service to tell different kinds of stories, experiment and reach for the different ways of expression in this art form that we love.

I'm a great sci-fi/horror and especially Alien fan. I have all the movies and can't count anymore how many times I've watched them. This appeared to be the first really good Alien game. And it definitely could be. The first few hours I loved it. But then the game slipped extremely close past perfection right into my "games, I will never finish"-corner.
-Spoiler-
How the game should be imo:
The Alien appears. You manage to not get noticed. You hide for some time. After a while the Alien goes away to search other areas of the space station. You have some time to do your stuff. After a while it comes back (maybe sooner, maybe later, maybe much later) and you need to hide again.
How it actually is:
The Alien appears. You manage to not get noticed. You hide for some time. The Alien will lurk around the same, small area, making its rounds forever. When you leave your hiding place, you need to rush to the next one, as the Alien will walk by just a few seconds later. If you stay in the hideout, it will find you eventually. Every time it walks by, you have a random chance that it inspects the hideout. Then you need to hold your breath and lean back, where you have another random chance to not get caugt.
It's all about exact timing and luck. It's much too random and there is not enough room to make this whole thing interesting.
The worst thing is that the game never gives you a hint what the "proper way" is. I often had no idea what i'm supposed to do. When I managed to escapte the Alien, it felt mostly like mere luck, or that the ai had some glitch.
The game builds up a solid atmosphere in the first hours. But as soon as you encounter the Alien for the first time, it will never leave your side ever again. There are many survivors on the station, yet it's focused only on you. It attacks other people only if it's part of the story or if they stay directly in its line towards you.
It seems that it can smell or hear you from miles away somehow. But when it has found the general area where you are, it suddenly can't smell or hear you anymore, even from a few feet away. Yet it seems to know for sure that you are somewhere around. No matter how silent you were before. And it won't leave the area until you leave.
It's completely scripted. The Alien never freely walks around the station. It's always where you are.
There are 2 states.
First you can only hear it. (it never comes out, no matter how long you wait)
Then it comes out at a specific point. (and never goes away).
It could be one of my favourite games. It's extremely close to the first movie. The graphics are great. The atmosphere is intense. The sound effects are one of the best i've heard. I like the Idea that there are also other dangers, such as desperate survivors or malfunctioning androids.
But the Alien is way over the top.
It suddenly changes - what has started as an exciting horror/surival-Adventure - into an annoying hide & seek orgy.
-Spoiler end-
Having to repeat 5, 10 and 20 minute parts over and over (even if you use the save points as much as possible) is no fun anymore at some point. A game should be a challenge. You need to fail sometimes to keep a game interesting. But there is a thin line between fun and frustration. For me it has exceeded this line greatly.
Just my point of view. It could be a 10/10 game for you.

Story premise of RymdResa is a bit of a cliche as you see the Earth explodes leaving our astronaut avatar only one hope – to find a habitable place in the neverending vastness of space. Soon you start to realize that your are probably the only human left alive, and that there is a little chance that you will find a new home in the ‘Big empty’. As years go by and your resources run low, so does your psyche, burdening you with moral doubts and at times deep poetic conclusions.
Separated in a three unique chapters, each having a different premise, Rymdresa feels and acts like a true space odyssey. As space you travel through is procedurally generated by means of y and x axis there are literally no bounds to where and how far you can go, and for how long you can try to survive.
As in any rogue-like game, the basics are difficult to master and take a bit of time to get used to. You gather resources scavenging through celestial bodies and abandoned spacecrafts or picking up particles of astral dust. Well, it’s not exploration as it first comes to mind, as you just need to get close to the objects and click the explore button.
There are many different upgrades that you can apply to your spacecrafts; maybe you want your shields to be of a higher capacity so you can take a more rigorous punch from space debris or hostile UFOs, or maybe you want more powerful engine to cover more distance faster, or, maybe you just want a whole new ship with different preferences altogether. The RPG-ish style of your inventory immediately lets you know that there is huge amount of upgrades available.
Weapons are permanently offline as there is no combat in RymdResa, and i’m really glad there isn’t any, because the omnipresent melancholic atmosphere is just as perfect as it is. Actually that’s the thing that stroke me the most from the very start of my adventure. That strange, even bizarre feeling of loneliness and complete separation from some kind of a illusionary safe-zone.
RymdResa is the most tranquil space rogue-like you will ever play, but so unforgiving at times. With it's unique twist on space exploration and rogue-like features it somehow manages to separate itself from other space exploring titles.

While a bit complicated to get into at first (like any roguelite) this game really got me interested after I spent about 20 minutes to get my bearings. It took me another hour or so to really understand, but this game is a very relaxing, slightly eerie game of exploration.
There's lots of persistent progress (equipment and levels) that make failed runs much less painful, and generally if runs are going to fail it seems to happen pretty early on. There's lots of ships for different play styles (I love the turtle ship) and the graphics and music really add to the haunting yet peaceful atmosphere.
My two major complaints are yes, starting is a bit rough, and the game has some near-instakill events at random that can discourage exploration. Especially in the starting ship, exploring a planet can mean certain doom even when not at particularly low health. I should say before I post this review that I've only made it to the second stage (out of three) on this game. I'll mainly be reviewing the gameplay. As far as other parts of this game go, I will say that I find the soundtrack particularly calming, and the audio cues convey their meaning quite well.
The gameplay to this game is rather simple. First, you get in your Embla Colonizer (or a better ship if you've saved up points), and you engage your thrusters. One important thing to note is that your ship will continue to travel in whatever direction you push it unless something is close enough to exert gravitational force on your ship; usually this will be either a star (deadly), or an interactable object.
Your fuel/health are the same "resource", so generally you try to achieve a desired speed, and then only use thrusters to avoid trouble. You will feel the pull of gravity from objects along the way, until you interact with them. You can gain and/or lose either points or resources from doing so, and earn xp. Some things you interact with will drop items afterwards; if you're particularly lucky, you may even find items adrift in space. Use these items to upgrade your ship, or scrap several of them to make new items.
The only things I can think of that hinder the gameplay are a lack of interface options, such as being able to zoom out (while reducing the saturation or hue of objects further away so as not to give away danger zones), and having a map that has last seen locations/headings of interactable objects.
Overall, I've enjoyed this game, and at a little over $10, it's not too expensive. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone that's a fan of space and roguelikes.

RymdResa is an attempt of making a "poetic game". So in place of conflict and challenge as in most other games, it's trying to bring the player inner peace and mindfulness.
The devs have been working hard in that direction, obviously. The artworks, visual style, music and poems are well fitting together, and the mood is well set. However, the game design fell short and ruined the whole experience.
So the biggest problem is, the game is not really calming.
You have to be on high alert almost all the time against sudden and deadly annoyances, it's like a bizzare marrage between poems and cheap jump scare flicks.
The gameplay elements are not nicely tuned either, e.g. I see no point in taking anything else other than the "tough" ships. The items seem pretty useless most of the time too.
So in all, it's a nice concept lacking proper game design, which ruined the day eventually.

This game is a very unique and refreshing experience. I assumed it was going to be a "roguelike" in the same vein as Rogue Legacy, and it's not far off from that from a gameplay perspective. You make progress with each game which goes towards future playthroughs, in short. However, what makes this game worthwhile is the setting contrasted with interwoven poetry and ambience that attempts to capture what it would be like alone in space. It's kind of a unique mix of fast-paced, almost twitch gameplay with a slow ambient artful experience musically, visually, and in story.
I thoroughly enjoy seeking out unique games regardless of genre, and this is definitely unique. I haven't made it very far yet and I can't speak on behalf of the long-term gameplay, but for now I'm very much enjoying myself. I can see others who are tired of rehashes of the same game over and over doing so as well, especially those big into video games as an artform.
This is a good example of what a game can be like when artistic vision is followed through to completion without seeking input from crowd-sourced game design, like how many early access titles seem to be doing. It's like people vote on what they want to see next and the majority wins. That's not art, that's just attempting to appeal to the masses, and you can't make everyone happy. Just look at the forums for Darkest Dungeon after an update. It also loses that something that makes each game special when developed that way too.
TL;DR: This game is delightfully melancholy.

To keep this short and sweet I'll focus on the part of the game I care about most: PvP.
But first, let's get something out of the way. On your first run-through, the vanilla game is enjoyable even if you run PvE only. It's not too onerous in difficulty, and the gameplay and UI changes over Dark Souls 1 make this a viable starting point for newcomers. The two DLCs currently out are also vast improvements on level design and content over the base game.
On to PvP. In short, it's a mess. The Souls games have always had problems on this end but the biggest sticking point is lag, given that it is entirely possible to fight your way out of any situation. I also have not experienced any practical problems with Soul Memory as a matchmaking method despite my opinion that the idea on paper sounds pants-on-head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ - you can always farm souls and upgrades offline and build a viable character. There's no avoiding lag in online gaming, but I have never had as inconsistent and frustrating an experience as in this game. PvP in Dark Souls 2 amps lag and lag compensation up to the point where the vast majority of encounters are insane guessing game rollfests. By this I mean that in order to hit and not be hit, you have to constantly be guessing where your opponent actually is instead of where they are on your screen. When 80% or more of your hits on enemies turn out to be latency-related whiffs, you can really only rely on luck in what is a battle of attrition.
The lag is also extreme to a point where there are players who can hit you from about 30 metres away. Throw backstabs into the mix and at worst you'll not have stood a chance and at best you'll start off the fight at a disadvantage as you get hit figuring out your opponent's actual distance.
Throw magic spam into the mix and this gets even more ridiculous. I don't mind non-homing projectiles that much, but when they're fast, huge and autotrack (my issue with some of the DLC spells, especially when paired up with the one that slows your movement), you often get hit and killed in one hit despite having clearly and visibly dodged the spell.
I should note that I play from Australia and while our connections and general location from the rest of the world isn't the best, no other game I've played does lag and lag compensation this badly. It's also insulting that of all the places in the world to matchmake Oceanic players with, FROMSOFT chose Europe. Maybe 1 in 60 matches will pair me with an Australian player. Those matches are the few that feel entirely fair and in those times it's a pleasure to get a taste of how the game is really meant to play: fast, fun, versatile and based on tight timing.

Broforce is a side-scrolling high-intensity shooter with an emphasis on big explosions, absurd weaponry, and shout outs to an era of action films rife with stereotypical alpha male behavior. The mechanics are simple enough to grasp and the actual number of buttons required to play could be thrown on an SNES controller with buttons to spare.
You and a number of friends will zip across short to somewhat long Bionic Commando-like levels as you decimate enemies within stages before the the inevitable boss battle takes place.
There's a great deal going on visually and the smooth pixelated look goes well with the theme of the game. Sound is pretty solid and captures the gnarliness of Arnold swinging a Conan sized greatsword whilst lamentations continue in the background. The controls can be a bit twitchy and the deadzone for certain controllers may cause some players to fall to their death a few times before getting the hang of things.
I found myself surprised and disappointed by the one-hit kill system in place for your character as there is often so much flying across the screen that it's easy to not realize one pixel is a bullet about to take you down. Constant and erratic movement does help somewhat but you'll likely need to memorize and play through tougher levels via trial and error before nailing the more difficult missions. It's a fun local and online shooter with decent online community so give it a shot.

I almost hate to write this review, because it's mostly just echoing what many other people have written. At the same time, I'm hoping that with enough consistent feedback from players, the developers might actually do something to fix what is very nearly an amazing game.
So here it is.
In terms of the gameplay, Just Cause 3 Feels like an enhanced version of Just Cause 2. This is a good thing. JC2 was endlessly entertaining, and JC3 builds on that by adding things like the wingsuit, an unlimited supply of C4 (though you can only place a few at a time), the ability to attach multiple grapple lines to objects, and then have the lines retract and launch the objects at each other. The map is enormous, and every part of it feels handcrafted, no two towns or military bases feel quite the same. It's a good-looking game as well, I'm on a laptop with a GTX970M, and I can run it on high graphics at 60fps with no problem.
But then there are the goddamn bugs. The flies on top of what would otherwise be a perfectly delicious slice of gaming cake. In my 8 hrs of play I have encountered at least half a dozen bugs, ranging in severity from irritating to potentially game-breaking.
For example:
\
Bottom line is that this is a great game that needs some touching up. If it weren't for the embarassing number of bugs and glitches, I would give this game a positive recommendation. The fact is that they have had nearly a year to fix these glaring problems, but instead have chosen to release three DLC packs. To me, that smacks of pure greed, and even though I bought the game at a massive discount, I'm still a bit disappoined in the quality of the product.
I've been looking forward to the game, but sadly my computer and most computers can not run it, so I recommend you get it on the Xbox 360 or something. All in all this game is quiet fun.

As an older gamer with 20+ years of experience in video gaming, lately I have been jaded by the whole "get a quest, complete the quest, turn in, rinse repeat" process.  Let's be honest: I'm sick of pretty much all games these days as they are not much more than several game elements from other games mashed together, and improved graphics.  Some do this well such as Path of Exile.  Others are more obvious about taking ideas from other successes, and mashing them together regardless of whether it actually fits.  Elder Scrolls Online seems to repeat this ubiquitous gaming industry practice, but a slight improvement in terms of freeform gameplay.
As usual when starting a new game, I mindlessly went through the tutorial scene, and yet again popped up in "who gives a crap" central mission hub with all the other new players.  As is so familiar throughout the decades, I had zero skills and gear along with the jaded, "oh look, let's kill mudcrabs for the next thirty minutes" attitude.  Fun.  But instead I just started killing NPCs.  Whatever.  Then I noticed something different.
In the decades past I would have been met by prompt judicial punishment.  Countless guards would come swarming from all over.  The NPCs themselves would be fighting back with a one shot that would invariably put me in my place.  But not in ESO.  No, strangely, no one came to the aid of the poor defenseless NPC that I had just murdered in plain sight.  I tried it again, and this time a guard responded, but I ran away easily.  A bounty was issued, and yet, no one cared.  The guards were easy enough to avoid, so I just sneaked around them, and continued my assault.  I didn't care, and the game didn't seem to stop me.  What was this?!  I felt more free in ESO than countless games before it.  It was nice for a change.
Of course it♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the guards, but they were easily evaded, and I actually started stalking NPCs for the fun of it.  And I was actually getting levels for not following the "goody two shoes" path laid out before me as has been the case for so many years.  I was being rewarded for beating my own path.  I accumulate a bounty, but no one has given a crap about it so far.  I ignored other players; didn't want to grief actual people.
Now, I'm not going to comment on graphics or sound or anything since others have already done so, but I will say that this murderous "honey badger" playstyle is not typically available in other games, as far as I know.  The fact that it is possibly available in ESO means there is a unique place for players like me who have become so bored with traditional gameplay that something like this is a breath of fresh air.  So, I recommend it.
If you, too, are gamer who is sick and tired of being hand-held to quest around as someone's personal errand boy, then maybe Elder Scrolls Online will sate your appetite until the next distraction comes around.  Recommended (for now).

A few years ago I was searching the Internet for hunting games and I stumbled upon theHunter. I played the game for a fairly long time, since it was a one of a kind hunting simulation. First I started as a guest (it's a kind of trial membership) but I became bored pretty fast, since you only can hunt one species (mule deer) and only have one gun. If you're willing to pay for a real membership, you can hunt all the species in the game and also get a couple weapons and unlimited ammunition for them.
Eventually the company behind theHunter became kinda greedy and that changed the whole game literally. If you want to enjoy the whole game and want to take part in all competitions, you have to invest a good amount of money. For example, you don't have to buy every single weapon but then you'll have a limited selection of competitions you can participate in. You don't have to buy every lure or whatever but then you have a disadvantage against other players, who bought all the stuff you're not willing to buy and use.
Long story short: The "free" version of the game is just a playable demo in my opinion. If you really want to have fun in theHunter, you'll have to invest a good amount of real money. Other reviews already mentioned the prices, so I won't go into that in my review. If you're willing to do so, you'll get the best hunting simulation you can get at the moment. It's nothing like any other hunting game out there. Here you'll get a simulation for your money and not just another Cabe*** arcade type of game.

“A poetic, roguelike space odyssey in a procedurally generated world! RymdResa is a challenging and evolving adventure where abstract poetry and art are expressed throughout a lonely and and calm journey in space.”
This game.
Well it’s pretty amazing. It’s atmospheric, entrancing and adorable in a borderline creepy way. With your character (or is it the ships AI?) telling you stories, while sometimes even managing to make me laugh.
It has you piloting a ship and attempting to fulfill various missions. The graphics are almost a Risk of Rain style – Minimalist, but it works withthe title. Less is more and such.
On one hand it is a relaxing game, on the other it is a nerve wracking drift through the unknown. Too often I would find myself coasting along looking for something and then out of nowhere a space rock would smack into my ship, or a sun would appear in front of me. The game is difficult, it is hard, but you will probably enjoy it.
It’s a great serving of “In small doses” gaming. I’ve got a few minutes to kill, so I’m going to zip around in space.
It’s a somber journey of melancholy proportions with a fascinating soundtrack (I immediately purchased the soundtrack from
, since I purchased it, the soundtrack is now available via Steam, oh well) to go with the gameplay and help carry it.
There were a few issues for me, but nothing that kept me from wanting more.
The biggest issues I encountered were due to the Steam overlay. Anytime I attempted to screenshot the game, it wouldn’t work. When I attempted to reply to a message by hitting Shift+Tab the game would immediately crash. After some time in the game I figured my friends could wait for my reply, because I’d be damned if I started from zero again.
The game is rogue-like, you have a ship, you pick up things, equip the ship and carry on. When you die / lose your ship you can restart, which allows you to have the same items equipped. There is a leveling system that also carries into your next game and things called Starpoints that you collect, that are essentially currency. To bring it all home the game has various ships to use and unlock, each with their own pros and cons, adding to the re-playability.
Would I recommend this game, without a doubt. The game mixes a surreal space adventure with poetry that is far better than any I could write and a unique visual style that works. With that all that being said, the price point of 12 dollars and the type of gameplay nearly guarantees you get your money out of the game. Even if it’s only 5 minutes at a time.

I could see what the developers wanted from RymdResa, even with the underwhelming controls and the frustrating first hour of the game. It really is a poetic treaty on loneliness and exploration, which is very well underlined by the soundtrack and the whole art direction. But the main thing with a game like this is to keep you interested, and I was ready to quit after 30 minutes...but I had to do this review. The game picks up as soon as you get your second ship and it might have been a fluke, but after I got enough money to get the third ship, it became a by the numbers game, with absolutely no danger for me to die. Except in the boss battles, which are a trial and error, “what did the author mean” dialogue. With a bit more balancing between the countless deaths at the beginning and the lack of deaths after that, it could’ve been an enjoying ride. But as it is, I cannot recommend it.

Broforce is a side-scrolling high-intensity shooter with an emphasis on big explosions, absurd weaponry, and shout outs to an era of action films rife with stereotypical alpha male behavior. The mechanics are simple enough to grasp and the actual number of buttons required to play could be thrown on an SNES controller with buttons to spare.
You and a number of friends will zip across short to somewhat long Bionic Commando-like levels as you decimate enemies within stages before the the inevitable boss battle takes place.
There's a great deal going on visually and the smooth pixelated look goes well with the theme of the game. Sound is pretty solid and captures the gnarliness of Arnold swinging a Conan sized greatsword whilst lamentations continue in the background. The controls can be a bit twitchy and the deadzone for certain controllers may cause some players to fall to their death a few times before getting the hang of things.
I found myself surprised and disappointed by the one-hit kill system in place for your character as there is often so much flying across the screen that it's easy to not realize one pixel is a bullet about to take you down. Constant and erratic movement does help somewhat but you'll likely need to memorize and play through tougher levels via trial and error before nailing the more difficult missions. It's a fun local and online shooter with decent online community so give it a shot.

Alright.. first off, I'm not finished with the game. I'm about a third of the way through, I believe, and I have to say.. I hated this game the very first time I played it. Not because of the difficulty, but because I entered the game with its predecessor firmly rooted in my mind, thinking to myself, "Dark Souls 2, huh? I'll bet I can conquer this game in a week like I did the first!"
Hindsight is often 20/20, and I realize that thinking this way was a mistake--and a disservice to a well-made game. The first thing you have to know about this game, is that despite being a veteran of the previous title, you're still going to have to learn. Some things take little time to adapt to--weapon degradation, teleportation, only able to level at the home fire--but figuring out the delay in the dodge-roll, when exactly the best time to parry is, and whether or not it's worth risking those 50k souls on a single jump for an item that probably won't be worth it.
However.. that was when the game first came out. So, I looked up some basic strategies, and recently started a new game--as a caster (yes, yes; op, I know, but hadoukens are fun). And, having done so, I have to say.. despite the numerous deaths I've had, they've always been due to myself and not thinking a situation through properly. Like dodge-rolling on a two-inch bridge, like an idiot, even though if I got hit by that lazer-sword, it'd take the last sliver of HP I had--so, damned if you do, damned if you don't. But these scenarios have helped me to grow as a gamer, and have helped me to learn more about this game. The combat is very tight, the story is.. well.. kind of there? I haven't been as involved with the lore as I was with Dark Souls, but I'm still enjoying trekking throughout the land, vanquishing foes, finding new equipment, then missing the jump back and falling to my death.
Overall.. I truly enjoy this game. The visuals are superb (probably not as good as the previous title, but, who cares?), the audio design is haunting and memorable (especially the lack of music throughout most of the game--it adds to the ambience and actually works in this game), the controls are tighter than its predecessor (which already had very tight controls), and the challenge--while seeming impossible at first, gradually evens out. I recommend this title to those who enjoy well-designed combat engines, fairly entertaining character customization (come on, we all did it, fess up), and a decent challenge.
While the difficulty level is high, it is nowhere near as insurmountable as many people would have you believe--beating the game will take a lot of patience, and the ability to tell yourself after dying five times in a row on the same boss because you missed the bloody windmill yet still got her to about 1/4 hp, "Okay.. I'm taking a break for a while."
In closing.. yeah, give 'er a shot. But be prepared to die. Again, and again, and again.. and again...... and..... once more.
