Dishonored 2 is, firstly, an excellent sequel to an excellent game. It does what it should as a sequel, the way I see it. It improves upon the mechanical complexity of the original, while not robbing it of what made it fun and unique in the first place, and gives an excellent continuation of the story. The game is graphically bounds better than the original's muddy textures and basic effects. This is a modern game, built on a modified IdTech engine, the one that ran DOOM 2016 so it does look great. If you liked the original Dishonored, I would describe its sequel as a must-play.
Of course, it's not perfect and before I get into the larger reasons of why I think Dishonored 2 is an excellent game, I'm going to describe what could turn you off. Firstly, it's a technical mess. I mean, it's much more technically impressive than the original Dishonored, but in contrast to the original, this game runs terribly. I've got a decent setup (FX-8370, RX 480, 16GB of RAM) but even at the lowest settings the game loved to dip to 30 FPS or so. That said, at high settings, it was maintaining near or at 60 the majority of the time, but framerate fluctuation at all is a problem because of the way mouse sensitivity is bound to framerate. Luckily, the game's relatively slow pace when playing stealthily, as you should, means it's not unplayable when it dips.
To add to the game's technical woes, I witnessed visual bugs all the time, some z-fighting here, some shadow pop-in there, lighting applying incorrectly at times, a bad texture seam, etc. It's not like every level is riddled with these but on my two seperate playthroughs I noticed them in the same places so it's clearly an issue with the game. As for other bugs, there are thankfully few. Sure, the AI can be wonky at times, and when that happens it can be quite distracting, but I personally wasn't that bothered with it.
Truthfully, those were my main gripes with the game. It looks great, it plays great, the level design is amazing, the story is genuinely intriguing. It's just a great game.
As for the gameplay, if you've played the original Dishonored, you likely know exactly what to expect. You're given a box of toys and are told you can use them however you like to accomplish a fairly clear goal. If you'd like to go in sneakily, sparing everyone you see, that's a fairly easy thing to do. The non-lethal options for your targets are mostly interesting and inventive, often you could consider what's being done to these people as worse than death, just like in the original game. Good, wholesome fun. Your toybox is expanded from the original game and I would suggest two playthroughs, as you're given a choice in the beginning of the game to play as either Corvo or Emily, with no context provided as to the differences between them. Both have very cool abilities available to them, and both provide a satisfying campaign.
Level design in this game is pretty spot-on. Sure I've gotten frustrated at some of these levels, and the first couple are just sort of rote. But there is a point, maybe two or three hours in where I was genuinely blown away. Every level in this game is designed cleverly at the least, and frankly I love it. Sure, some of the gimmicks aren't fully realized, but for a linear singleplayer experience, this is one of the coolest series of levels in any game ever.
The story in this game I think fully delivers on the promise a sequel implies. It gives us answers, and leaves us with more, which is what at least I want from a Dishonored game. There's no fun in knowing everything. We see the return of some cool characters from the original and its DLC, and we find some more characters, fun and charming, if few. Without spoiling anything, I will say that this game features a lot more of the Outsider (whose voice actor isn't great, just a warning) and the story behind him, as well as fleshes out the characters Corvo and Emily.
TL;DR - Play the first game, if you like it, play this one. If you didn't, and it was because of level design rather than anything else, still play this game.

I never had a chance to play the original Homeworld so the Remastered Collection was my first experience with this genre. The quick thing I noticed was the high quality sounds of combat and explosions that accompanied all of my battles. Coupled with updated graphics this made the experience so much more enjoyable. Every battle I engaged in was like a high quality lightshow filled with laser beams, flak turrets, missile explosions and jet streams trailing my fighter and corvette class units. Homeworld is definitely worthy of its praise and my money.

Visually, this game is an amazing update of the original. There are some minor mesh issues with salvage; single sided faces and the like can appear to disappear but this is a minor thing and does not interfere with gameplay.  I find it hard to play at a strategic level since you want to be as close up to the individual ships as possible and admire the work put into them.  Since modding has been part of the design, I can't wait to see what the community develops.
Because Homeworld 1 is utilizing an updated version of the HM2 engine there are some changes to gameplay in HM1.  Exampes: hyperspacing in matches does not maintain the tactical formation of your ships.  Repair frigates no longer repair multiple ships, it must be selected and directed to one ship at a time.  Certainly nothing that breaks the game but does modify strategy if you're familiar with the original.
Sound is great, it's just as wonderful and immersive as it was when it first came out.
I do wish i could run the game full screen. I currently run Nvidia Surround (5760x1080).  The game does support that resolution and there is no real performance hit for doing so.  However, several parts of the HUD are elongated horizontally and cutscenes are resized to fill the screen width.   Also turns into a lot of screen to cover in order to get from one side of the UI to the other.  In a 1920x1080 environment there is absolutely zero issues.  I do very much like the ability to scale the UI.
The Remastered Edition is a wonderful update for those seeking nostalgia.  For those new to Homeworld, I think you'll find a beautiful RTS with an interface that's easy to use and a very modest learning curve.

An exceptional survival horror game, perhaps the best title in its genre to be released so far. A truly harrowing, nerve-breaking and extremely tense experience, which manages to keep your fear alive all throughout and constantly feeds it with new catalysts. Perhaps its strongest point is that you are never actually safe in the game. Whether you are under a desk or hiding in locker, you're still very vulnerable. Its impressive gameplay and extremely realistic (note the paradox) environment make up for its rather shallow storyline and characters.
Since I thoroughly enjoyed this game, you will notice I will try to explain the cons more than I do the pros, since the latter are more obvious.
Pros:
+excellent and extremely realistic atmosphere. Having all those buttons around with fancy names really makes you feel like a brainless monkey, as you would expect a good Sci-fi game to do. But, in the same time, it also manages to be pretty intuitive most of the time.
+very serious scares and tension
+intelligent and perceptive AI
+smart crafting system, which is often the key to survival
+intelligent and intuitive gameplay overall: motion tracker, lots of places to hide, terminals to check, systems to reboot, vent system etc
+a very well-made sound system, which makes up a lot of the game's atmosphere
+lovely graphics, especially in the moments you're looking out into space
Cons:
-the story isn't very original or complex. Even though it is tense and interesting most of the time, it's mostly just for the action.
-character models are very similar. For a game with such excellent graphics, it's really disappointing to see the lack of detail the characters are condemned to.
-a lot of technical objectives, which sometimes require you to go from one place to another without revealing anything significant for the story. At some point, I even forgot what I was there to do. But, as I mentioned previously, the story isn't exactly the game's focus.
-some repetitive level design. You may or may not see this as a problem, since, as I said before, Sevastopol station does manage to be very realistic. But most places are pretty hard to tell apart from others and, without the map and the indicators, you'd probably be lost completely.
Overall, I'd say it deserves a 9/10. It is actually one of the best survival horror games I ever got to play.

This is a game that looks and sounds like an alien movie.
The dedication of the creators to the style of the franchise was- in my opinion - as great as
humanly possible.
So we have a game now, that looks and sounds like an alien movie, but is it fun to play?
I pondered that question many times during work.
It was stessful to play the game, I would say it's a special kind of entertainment, not the
relaxing sort. I wouldn't fire up this game just to play something a little. In fact I think I've
only played it on weekends, never after work, after work I wouldn't want to handle it.
The xenomorph is scary, indestructible by your weapons, and it's faster than you. Here is a
little something from the game. When you hide in a locker the xenomorph sometimes suspects that
you are there and leans closer to the slats on the door. You are offered by the game to pull back
from the door, as far back as the locker allows. Then it offers you to hold your breath,
with the right mouse button...
That's what kind of a game this is. And if you release the button too early that locker door will
snap open.
It was frustrating at times, I died often (Hard difficulty) and had to replay certain parts over
and over again because, you can only save at save stations.
I would like to address here a complaint I've read in a Steam review about the game, namely that
the xenomorph follows you wherever you go. It's true, you can never leave it too far behind if
it's part of the map (some maps are safe), even if you sneak away somewhere undetected, you'll
soon hear it clambering in the vents and it will drop down somewhere near you. It's indeed
unrealistic, but it was necessary for the game to work, otherwise the xenomorph would just stay
around the area where it had last seen the player and the player would just roam around in the
rest of the map, entirely unhindered.
But back to the game. It has a technology fetish, the depiction of technology and machinery is
done with a flourish and with intricate detail. Cutting doors open with a blowtorch (1st gas,
than upgraded to plasma and eventually ion), hacking doors (mini games), using computer terminals
and rewire terminals, restarting generators, even pulling switches is done in the spirit of
techno-fetishism. And not just the interactive bits, simply walking down a corridor I often
wondered how could they design something fictitious to look so seriously purposeful.
The sounds are not inferior to the graphics, they are top quality. I probably haven't spent this much
time in a game just listening and waiting since the Thief series.
I believe that sounds affect the brain more directly than visual data, it's harder to resist
their effects. So for a good horror game, sounds are important, I guess Creative Assembly
understood this very well.
The xenomorph has quite the repertoire and the sounds it makes are important clues as well to
it's current state and position.
It's kind of smart too. If it's running towards you it's enough to just point the flamethrower at
it and it will stop, but that doesn't make it less menacing. And then it just starts walking towards
you. On Hard difficulty I've found this useful, because I didn't have enough ammo to scare it
away enough times to get to my objective, but this way, I was ablo to just walk there, facing
mostly backwards, keeping the creature at bay and when I reached my destination, I scared it back to the vents
and got about to restart a pesky generator.
Due to the stomach cramping gameplay I found myself wanting it to end 4-5 hours before it did.
It still baffles me how ambivalent I feel about this game, It's beauty and accurate recreation of the
familiar Alien-movie feel is stunning, but thinking about going back there isn't exactly tempting, although I still want to do the Crew Expendable DLC.
So is it fun to play? The question is, do you want to be with a xenomorph on an abandoned space station?
This game is the closest thing to that, at the moment.

Turner, despite what the description says, is not a puzzle platformer. It is an action/precision platformer with few puzzles that appear later on the story.
You assume the role of a man named 'Turner', a man with a troubled past and an unstable state of mind that is held in an asylum. Your goal is to escape through a variety of levels that as weird as they look, from simple to complex fulfill their purpose, to make you feel that you see the games world through the eyes of an insane person with a guilty past! The music is entirely on spot to complement the game and the sketch art, both in the various levels and in the story comics, along with the abstract background of each room give a feel of unstable-ness.
The mechanics of the game, besides the basic movement of Turner, is that you can rotate parts or the entire level. Walls can become platforms and vice versa, and while it may not sound much, it will become as you unlock wall jump and later on, slide and double jump. The game is not hard at start and it does an excellent job at introducing new elements at a good pace, such as various switches or non-rotatable platforms, without the need of you having to read a single word, by putting some easy levels as tutorials along your journey to escape. There will be hard levels and few almost impossible ones, however the majority of the game is quite fast, especially once you get the hang of it and while that may sound discouraging there are over 400 levels for you to beat! Additionally there will be some 'cut-scenes' that either introduce a new ability or explain a little bit of the story, which I found to be quite interesting, especially on the way it was delivered! I strongly recommend that you collect the 20 pages that can be found throughout the levels as they add to the story and some can be quite a challenge to obtain! After you finish the game you unlock the hard mode that is exactly what it's name say and additionally, to my surprise, is part of the story! So I strongly recommend that you give this game some time and let it tell you Turners story, but even if you are not into that, the game is indeed a good challenge for platforming fans as there are times where it requires good hand to eye coordination skills.
While it supports controller and obviously keyboard, it offers zero customization for the controls. Thankfully the controls are relative simple both on keyboard and the controller, thus it's a small issue that you must get used to them. However the main menu greatly favors keyboard (and mouse) because on the controller the highlighted option is barely noticeable and the selection of a button can become awkward. While the game has over 400 levels it has really poor level selection menu with the only 3 options, 'previous/next level' and 'input of levels number to jump to that one', so unless you remember the number of the level you are looking for, you'll have to search it manually, one by one. Additionally while the game does have quite many good and interesting mechanics, I felt that there are few levels that combined them. Finally the menu felt greatly unoptimized, as I've noticed quite many freezes when I mouseover or clicked an option and sometimes the entire game crashed on Alt+Tab.
On a grey spot is the fact that there are no sound effects, mostly because there are actions, such as jumping, sliding or dying to electricity, that could use them. But on the other hand the music and the atmosphere are so good, that their absence wasn't noticeable.
Besides all the negatives about the game as a program, I enjoyed myself a lot while playing Turner! I believe its price is definitely worth it, since it can keep you occupied for quite some time. Additionally with a recent update a much fitting feature, for the precision platformers genre, was added, speed run mode! Lastly, I hope to allow players to create their own levels, as the game has already quite many mechanics to support players creativity!

In Turner Bean Boy Games don't really attempt anything that hasn't been done before. However, the results of their game are a well executed gem has a price that screams bargain.
Turner is a 2D puzzle platformer. The game is set in an an asylum with the player being inserted into the role of Turner. Turner  has led a troubled past and an unstable mind. Why else would he be in an asylum? There are two movement mechanics in the game. The first is your basic set of left, right and jump. The second is a rotating/turning system. This second system rotates or turns the entire level in either clockwise or anti-clockwise direction - it's your call. You will need to quickly learn and become skillful with both mechanics as they are equally essential to complete the game. They have been well designed and work as expected.
Even the toughest of levels are generally completed within a matter of seconds. This would normally be a problem because players like to have a lot of content within their games. However, to encapsulate the 'bargain' feeling of the game there are over 400 of them within the game. The games range in difficulty from very easy - those that introduce new gameplay mechanics (such as collapsing platforms, activation pads, etc.) and ridiculously challenging. This is a fantastic mix that will have you rage quitting often. But the key thing to note is that the game is very fair. For every level that I've felt was designed poorly (unfairly) I've returned to it later to realize that it is fair and that it was me.
I've played my fair share of puzzle games this year. Many of them offer nothing more than that, a puzzle game. Turner is different. The comic book style cutscenes tie together a well structured story. This was one of my favorite aspects of the game. It shows that the developers pay attention to details in their game development. This is something that I can appreciate as I continue to study a tertiary level game development course (on top of my multiple degrees). I wish this was something that I could see from more developers. However, I understand that if you fail at this aspect of your game that the response is "Why bother?" or "That was pointless."
As an added bonus the game's soundtrack has been added as a free downloadable DLC. The soundtrack includes all but one of the 17 songs that are played throughout the game as well as 3 bonus tracks. The soundtrack is created and performed by Kevin Thomas. Unfortunately, the game's main menu song was unable to be included in the soundtrack as it was performed by a different musician. While this is unfortunate it's impossible to not appreciate the addition of the soundtrack.
Turner features both a set of trading cards and Steam achievements. Therefore, it is most certifiably Steamified. As a result that means that the asking price is really even lower for trading card sellers as you can do just that.
Not only is Turner a finely made puzzle game but it's a downright bargain. The game can be challenging to a point of rage quitting in a good way. As a result, I wholeheartedly endorse your purchase of the game.

Ok. Here's the deal. The baseline for a game could be realism. Then there's pseudorealism. Then there's chaos. This game has found a nice spot in between, so that you can experience "how it is" to run a factory. At least that's what the game's premises are: provide you with plenty of ways to automate and produce.
What would be hardcore realism then? For example: The conveyors move "for free". That's not realistic, but it works for a game. Why would you want anything other than realism? That's where this game excels. This game is "gamey". It does what it can to make you feel comfortable while completing puzzles and making things work.
So. The game lets you run around and mine, craft, research, defend, offend(kill aliens, animal cruelty), drive vehicles (a car as far as I know), order trains around and the occasional other thing that I have not yet seen. The crafting can be automated for any task, which demands your attention and puzzle solving capabilities.
A lot of fun. I recommend this game.
Post Scriptum: There's plenty left for me to explore. I have merely scraped the surface of Factorio.
PPS: Make science! Make it with your bare hands! ahaha
Addendum (a week after, approximately): I visited a friend whom I showed this game, and he pointed out the following: It's weird how you can use your pickaxe since the game is about building circuits. I do still believe that the game makes a point in that it lends some feeling of empowerment to the player. The avatar is good to make the progress noticable, rather than non-existant. Something like the science station from starcraft, or some other graphical object" The line of reasoning was that the game was "not logical". Good:
The action is fast, gory, and satisfying. The slow motion takedowns have a real cinematic quality to them that I have yet to tire of. The abilities are  varied and allow for some very creative sequencing. The maps are quite handsome with multiple approaches, tons of hidden blueprints, bonecharms, coins, runes, etc to be collected. Mission Plus allows you to create a new save with the benefit of previously collected runes/blue prints and the full availability of both characters abilities.
Bad:
Story
Dishonored 2 has truly awful story telling, featuring a forgetable supporting cast and weak central villain. The cutscenes and character interactions rarely go beyond exposition, often serving as little more than direct summary of events that have just transpired or clumsy, explicit statements of character motivation. The dictum, 'show, don't tell' was clearly lost on the game's writers.
I much prefer the Corvo of the first game; a human cipher, a mute psychopath in a skull mask running around a rotting city seeking revenge. D1 was a pure, barebones tale of revenge in which you by and large filled in who Corvo was while the game provided action in spades. In my playthrough of Dishonored 2, the character that emerged via dialogue and cut scenes was often incongruous with my in game decision making. For instance, minutes into the game and only moments after choosing to KILL rather than incapacitate 3 guards, I got this gem:
'what do I have to do to get Emily back? Who do I have to become?'
(Dishonored 1 spoilers below)

Evidently, the canon position on Corvo's deeds in the first game is a rather sunny one. Unfortunately, this comes at the cost of immersion if you want to play the game through on high chaos. The only thing that eventually happens is that your chosen hero will utter a few 'cynical' lines to reflect your increasingly murderous tendencies and you'll get a slightly nastier, more stern cutscene summary ending. Corvo and Emily are still pretty much represented as decent, sane people even after wading through an interminable number of their own citizens corpses in an effort to resecure the reins of power.
Optimization:
Even with a system that pretty far exceeds  the minimum specs and running everything on the lowest possible settings, I still experienced consistent drops in framerate.

I want to recommend this game desperately. Unfortunately, I find myself unable to do so. I'm sure if your reading this review you already have a basic idea of what SMITE is: A moba with various play modes; viewed from a 3rd person perspective with an emphasis on skill-shot play.
The gameplay is fast paced and exciting. It really keeps you hooked and you'll find yourself so absorbed in the game you become oblivious to real life around you. There are a ton of different gods to choose from and most of them feel unique and interesting. The community is ok'ish; meaning: you'll get your fair share of toxic players but you also come across some really awesome individuals who enjoying helping out less experienced players. Better then the the LoL community at any rate imo.
So why in the world have I chosen to not recommend this game, you might ask? Well, Hi-Rez has always had less then stellar server performance since the release of SMITE. Yet, for the most part, I had found it tolerable (though plenty of others did not). The odd DC here and there, the occasional lag warp of characters, delayed responses on skills, ect. I found it tolerable because I didn't feel it happened frequently enough to cause me to stop enjoying the game.
This has changed to my disappointment. The frequency with which server-caused issues occur seems to increased over time. Lag warp and delayed skill activations have become more common. DC's occur on a pretty regular basis (if not you, then someone else on your team). Not to mention all the odd UI issues; like being unable to buy items while hearing the clinking coins of the "transaction complete" sound, being stuck in the character select screen but everyone can still chat, being unable to click the "Accept" button when match found window pops...the list goes on.
The game is solid. The servers that the game depends on leaves a lot to be desired. If Hi-Rez can fix that, I will give my recommendation without hesitation. Until that time, the game lacks the responsivness and reliability that any faced-paced competitive moba requires.
*I have many more hours then STEAM indicates. I have always used the SMITE launcher until I began using STEAM recently.

RymdResa is a relaxed roguelike that is divided into three chapters. Each has different goals but all involving trekking across space looking for things and not crashing into a sun. It's full of random items to find and is procedurally generated afresh each time you play.
It begins in chapter 1 as a laid-back, lonely search for a home planet. Your spaceship follows a compass sentry around the galaxy while raiding derelicts to keep your resources stocked.
You pass through different biomes in space, each colour-themed, and each spawning different kinds of dangers (and rewards). You can't shoot, but you can dodge enemies and hyperspace away.
Raiding derelicts is mostly just a button press that may lead to gaining stuff, losing stuff or a mixture of both. Sometimes there's a choice to make.
As a roguelike it does have permadeath. If you die, you'll need to spend money to buy a decent new ship, although a lot of stuff does carry over: You keep money, XP and any ship upgrades you found. In chapter one, death also means losing your mission progress.
[Mild spoilers ahead]
Once you've completed chapter 1, things get more complex. Chapter 2 forces you to explore the galaxy unguided - you need to locate raw material and take it back to your home planet to push the story on and earn ship bonuses. Not being led around by the nose makes this for a satisfying contrast to the first chapter - and if you die, you're allowed to keep all the progress you've made with your home planet. But you still need a new ship.
Once you finish upgrading that planet, you unlock chapter 3, where the difficulty increases and you have several types of missions to complete instead of one. This chapter introduces different, harder biomes mostly full of things that can hurt you. There are also boss fights!
I won't spoil the boss fights, but be prepared to have to outthink the bosses without being able to directly attack them.
Gameplay video:
Good & bad stuff:
* The story, atmosphere and graphic style are excellent. It all fits together perfectly. Just be prepared to fiddle with the gfx settings, the scanlines etc aren't for everyone.
* Be prepared for gnomic poetry floating in space and pop-up ship logs about loneliness. If you find this sort of thing annoying, you're out of luck.
* You do have a choice of up to 8 different ships to start out in, but you have to pay for most of them. New players may find a vicious circle that when they're doing badly, they'll only have a weak ship to use and will find it hard to grind to get money.
* Most ship upgrades you find in space only fit to one type of ship, so you can end up with an inventory full of stuff mostly useless to your current game. Luckily, you can earn new items by scrapping a lot of old ones.
* It's not always clear why the choice you made in some dialogue boxes result in a "good" or "bad" outcome, which can lead to the occasional death that feels unfair.
* It's a great game for lore hunters and collectible finders. There are legendary items and unique randomly generated items to find, lots of achievements, collectible logs, and items that increase your luck and make hunting easier. You can even personalise your ship with styles, once you've found them.
Fantastic!

Story:
RymdResa (Rimmed-ray-sah - Swedish for Space Travel) is described as a procedurally generated space odyssey.  This is absolutely true... but it is actually so much more.  It's pixilated poetry.  It's 2015: A Space Awesomity.  It's the game I didn't know I had been waiting for and I get sad when I think about the possibility that I'd have missed it.
It's a tale of a destroyed Earth and mankind's last hope to colonize a new world.  It won't be an easy journey, and like all epic journeys, there is a heavy price that is paid by our lone cosmonaut. Its told in a simple and effective way via space diaries and it builds an intricate background narrative as you play the game.  Nothing is jammed down your throat in RymdResa.
Like Asteroids without the lasers; this game is an excellent example that not every game needs violence/combat to be fun and meaningful. That isn't to say that you are totally defenseless; sharp reflexes and some fun items will go a long way in increasing your survivability.
Gameplay:
Procedural World - Exploration is the name of the game and each run is going to be a little different.  Not just in the position of the neat things you'll discover in the vastness of space but each for the 3 Chapters has a different approach to exploration that helps mix things up.
8 Different Ships - After you beat Chapter 1 with your first ship you'll get many options of new vessels to buy for your next run.  They use starpoints but you'll have plenty to spend on the craft that best suits your playstyle.  You want a tanky Vanadis or maybe a speedy Skadi Cruiser? Or spend a ton of points for the dominating Ragnarok you just unlocked? It's up to your play style; they all have pros and cons and it's a lot of fun taking them all out for a spin.  Some items you collect are ship-specific so putting new gear on your new ride is just gravy.
Getting Around - Finding a new world to inhabit will not be easy.  Numerous obstacles will keep your ship from good happy success: Asteroids and debris will try to damage your ship, red mines litter the galaxy, huge gravity-rich suns will pull you towards a fiery & instant death, and, just like a true rogue-like, if you interact with a random planet and it penalizes you too many resources you are going to have to start over.  Luckily your ship comes equipped with a sentry that points you in the direction of my main objective keeping you in the action instead of needing to use a map.  There are also scattered stars you will come across that give you star points & XP that you can spend on new ships and such.
Resource Management - Resources are scarce and essential to your success.  They also act as your life bar and your fuel; you run out and your journey is over.  A lot of the game is stumbling across a moon or derelict spaceship and interacting with it to have an outcome.  Usually your get star points XP) and resources but a bad roll of the RNG and you may lose resources instead.  You also may fail to explore altogether!  This process is all done with a single key press and is a seamless, quick way to try your luck and keep the action moving forward.
Leveling Up and Skills - Pilot level as you fly through space, survive each year, find random spacedust and complete objectives you'll be gaining Pilot XP to advance your four basic skills;  Exploration (more positive outcomes), Scouring (more items), Technology (allows you to tap into alien technology found randomly in space) and Survival (more found resources)
These skills, your level and your ship's inventory carry over to new playthroughs so it gives you a feeling that even a bad run is contributing to a better playthrough next time making this a great game for rogue like fans who are less brutal (perma-death may be available in future updates).
Death -  Dying isn't the end on RymdResa.  So you flew directly into a huge sun on accident, your run will be over and you'll need to purchase a new ship next time but you'll usually be in a better position to win next time around as you keep your levels, skills, inventory and star points.  Still, the fun is playing to win!
Graphics:
RymdResa is a fantastic looking pixel game.  While your ships are fairly simple in shape it helps keep you focused on the amazing style of space exploration.  While space feels as vast and empty as you'd expect that makes the various satellites, moons and spaceships you encounter all the more interesting.  I was always admiring how cool some new thing I stumbled upon looked.  Everything is in a muted bluish color (except those friggin' suns) that just makes perfect sense. Really beautiful stuff, all around.
But your spaceships being simple in shape doesn't mean that there aren't a sizable number of fun customization/styles you can find and equip to tweak your look slightly. Its not overwhelming but nice to have as it make you feel like your ship gets better visually as well as stat-wise.
Sound:
FX: The sound effects are just fine, the sounds of thrusters, alerts and taking damage all work well.
Music:  By Tom Croke and Pat Jacobs, the music in RymdResa is an excellent fit for the atmosphere.  Spacey, industrial, everything you ever would want without being too abrasive and getting on your nerves.  The music does a fantastic job of setting the mood.  Space is haunting, lonely and dangerous.
Voice Acting: The poetic parts of this story are other voice acted and done so in such a way that it really makes you feel the helplessness and solitude of space travel.  I love hearing the cosmonaut speak they really speak from the heart.
Levels/Maps:
Space is huge. I found this out this the hard way when I jumped in a teleporter and ended up an insurmountable distance from my next objective.  It became a zen coasting back to the main playable area while trying to minimize my resource usage so I didn't end up floating forever in the void.
Closer to home the game is much more active and dangerous.  Its meant to be played in proximity to your missions and this is where it is really fun; but I was surprised the game didn't automatically fill the dead space with more random stuff when I was on my accidental journey.
Final Verdict:
RymdResa is a fantastic game.  Overall it hit all the right spots with a great universe, wonderful visuals and moving music.  Personally it was a perfect game for me as a fan of pixels and sci-fi games; and the fact it could grow into a bigger game in the future is a welcome bit of hope. The only negative to this game is sometimes the space travel goes on for awhile without anything cool spawning; but these zen moments make the activity all the more interesting.  I hope you get a chance to play it, it's a great experience!

*Some spoilers perhaps*
Interesting short-story game. Sort of like a visual novel, but interactive in a different (slightly annoying) way. You play a guy who is friends with Emily, a girl you clearly have feelings for in your senior year of high school, and you get to view some slices of life through their college years via a recreated AIM interface.
The sounds are incredibly nostalgic, hearing the door opening/closing sounds made me feel like I was really on AIM again for the first time in many years. Viewing your friends profiles and seeing the various song lyrics and typical things you'd find there is a nice touch too. The creator of the game certainly spent plenty of time on AIM back in the day.
I am not a fan of the fake-typing input that is used here. You pick one of 3 options to converse with, but then you must input the keys yourself. However, since you don't know what exactly is going to be typed, and you are just forwarding the script with random inputs, it essentially feels like you're playing HackerTyper or something. It would have been totally fine if they had just automatically typed in the responses for you once you picked your choice.
Watching the protagonist type in responses, erase them, and then reconsider his words is probably the most compelling part of the story. At first he is just correcting typos, but as you go into the story more, he starts completely rephrasing his words, and in the final chapter, you watch as he completely freezes up and stops writing what he means.
If you've ever talked to someone you had a crush on over AIM, MSN, or any other kind of chat program, this story may hit close to home for you. I wish there were some different endings, as you get a ton of different answer prompts throughout the game and it even notifies you that Emily will remember certain things you say, but it doesn't seem to make a difference at all.
Overall, it's free, it's short, and it's an interesting approach on telling a story of online-based (or at least, online-oriented) romance. Along with Cibele, I think this is an interesting trend of storytelling. It does have some flaws with the way it is played, but it's a neat game and one that I will remember.

Endgame sorceries in PVE deals less damage than an unupgraded dagger. (300 damage soul spears with the best staff in the game, 800 damage dagger+0 backstabs) So I had to abandon my pure sorcerer character.
Miracles do now also suck. Spell charges were nerfed by about 75% (e.g. Lightning Spear 11->3) So sorceries are now more of a pulling tool than actual combat magic.
Hexes are somewhere in the middle, but also pretty mediocre as it stands now.
Pyromancies are decent as usual since they don't require any stat investment to be effective. However all enemies in this DLC are super fire resistant, and the ones in the last are super magic resistant in general.
Regarding the new areas: They look and feel decently designed. Lots of secrets and hidden details. However you'll soon notice that there are once again only very few new enemies and the level designers once again just put DOUBLEAXESKELETTON x5 in pretty much all rooms (with slight variation on whether the enemy is burning or using a sword. Still the same things over and over and over until you are at the last boss).
Speaking of the last boss. I don't want to spoiler anything, but he has EXCESSIVE amounts of health (at least he doesn't corrode your weapons this time..) and damage. Playing anything but a dodge centered build is pure lunacy. Blocking nearly always (and certainly always in phase two) drains your whole stamina, leading to a short stun, leading to a follow up oneshot.
So basically this DLC comes down to: Play a quality STR/DEX build or go home. All my characters are useless and I really can't be bothered to level a new one for another 20 or so hours.
2/10 for effort.

When I first started playing the original Dark Souls I was a bushy tailed, fresh faced scamp with a bright outlook on life. The sun was shining and birds were chirping happily that particular day, and I was in need of a new game. Having what I thought was more than sufficent gaming experience I fancied myself quite the gamer. I ran into my local Gamestop with the friendly clerk greeting me as per usual and began perusing the shelfs...then I saw it. The game sat alone on the shelf, the other games seemed to want to get as far away from it as possible, even resorting to fall to the ground in order to escape its dark aura. I found myself enthralled by this title, why was it alone? Why did I feel this chill run up my spine, and why did I feel like it didnt think I was worthy? Well I picked it up and immediately felt the anguish of thousand swell in my hand, but I couldn't put it down. I found myself walking to the clerk, his face twisted in pain as he rung me up. Walking outside I found the sky had darkened and the birds had either fleed in terror or began foaming at the mouth...the nightmare had begun. Upon returning home I inserted the disc and my playstation seemed to screech in pain...the title screen showed up and from there it all went to hell. I figured out in the first few hours that I was nothing...never had been anything, but a filthy casual. This game brought out the devil in me, the sheer evil that had been waiting for something to release it. My eyes grew dull, my friends left me, and my hair slowly fell out. I found myself yelling more and more at the screen, hating my existence, hating everythings existence...loathing the very air I breathed. Days passed in the darkness that consumed me, then it was over. The final boss fell and for a brief moment I felt happiness...then nothing. My soul was empty, as I searched frantically for something to fill the void that Dark Souls had left me with. Nothing compared, nothing gave me the abuse I writhed after, nothing filled me with emotions anymore. I was truly dead...to the gaming world. Years went by, and I thought I had finally broken my addiction to the abuse. I found myself getting the old gleam I used to have, and my hair had filled back in nicely. The game sat untouched for sometime, and I was back to normal...and then this came out. I saw it while browsing through steam for something to play, but more percise it saw me. My heart stopped, I felt the dread return and my soul shout at me for its return to the darkness. Without thinking I purchased the game, turned off all the lights and found myself laughing maniacally while drifting off into the bosom of insanity that I so missed. So in closing 10/10 for losing ones life alllll over again. Praise the Sun fellas.

Full disclosure: I know those who make the game and took part in early beta testing.
Turner is an interesting little puzzle platformer in which you utilize a power of turning the world around you to reach a goal. As the game progresses, you unlock new abilities in order to reach the end of the level.
I enjoyed my time playing, and recommend it, especially at this low pricetag.
However, here are my pros and cons for this game:
PROS:
- Art style. The hand drawn aesthetic works well with the theme of the asylum.
- Soundtrack is decent.
- Good General puzzle design (for the most part)
- To add, the best puzzle are the slower-paced ones, in which the rotating mechanic is at the forefront
- Some of the puzzles utilize the rotating mechanic in a really interesting manner.
- Fun to play for most levels
- Game introduces mechanics, old mechanics are not made obsolete.
CONS:
- Control. Note that this is for keyboard, have not tested with a gamepad. There is a slight delay from pressing the keys to the actual movement of the character, which can make for some frustrating moments. In addition, the jump feels slightly floaty. You won't find the crispness of platforming found in games such as Super Meat Boy and Spelunky.
- The wall jump mechanic is simply not satisfying to play. The levels that focus on the double jump are some of the least fun.
- Some levels are simply not fun. There is a series of levels early on in which the worlds moves automatically, and you have to traverse the whole circle to reach the exit. Due to the nature of the controls, the precise timings lead to a very frustrating experience.
- Very limited options menu.
- No sound effects besides the soundtrack
While not without its problems, I recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun little puzzle game for a low price.

Turner is a simple puzzle-platformer with mysterious exposition.  Although it isn't a terribly long game, it does feature challenge versions of every level once you complete the game. Turner does a great job at leading the player level to level, slowly teaching them how to play.  By the end of the game you will find yourself using every ability and skill you have learned along the way, none of which become obsolete.
This game is fun, challenging, and intriguing, but there are a few features I would have liked to see. I really would have loved to see a "Reset Level" feature, as I had to go back to the main menu on level 182(?) as it is possible to get stuck. Also, since this game is ripe for speedrunning, in-game timers would have been nice. Or at least an individual level mode to try to get the best IL times.
For the ridiculously low price tag, you really can't go wrong.

I'll summarize the flaws of this game first so you see all it's weaknesses before you invest too much time into reading.
The mix of Action-Fights with Climbing Levels is done well, but there are new games that do this exact genre noticably better- for example Tomb Raider (which does not focus on melee fights, though), Prince of Persia, or Assassins Creed.
The camera is not chosen optimal in several locations, using forced perspective quite often in climbing scenarios. The combat control is not "hyper-precise" when it comes to blocking, but then again, that's not what this game is about. A gamepad is recommended (but many people play Assassins Creed on Keyboard as well, so it's not that big of a deal).
Considering the price, though, those imperfections seem justified to me.
- Mechanics -
The fight mechanics are satisfying- this is your typical action/platformer with a focus on melee, suited for relaxed evening sessions. The game is a straightforward Port from the console version. I already described the mechanics in the introduction by comparison.
- Story -
Not brilliant, but solid and enjoyable. It's not a killer feature- I wish the story had a bit more time for depth- but then, most of the AAA games out there don't have an outstanding story either. Maybe I have too high standards. Why could you want more story? Because of...
- Characters -
a light dressed redhead and a muscular man might seem awfully clichee, and the cover page can leave you with an impression of shallow, onesided characters- which is simply inaccurate and a case of bad presentation. The (through most of the game, subtly executed) addition of depth to the characters happens almost instantly in the story.
The clichee of "damsel in distress" characters already gets abandoned in the very first cutscene. Every character has emotion, and thereof resulting progress. The whole story is framed by the interaction between very few characters, and those are crafted with care. Two particular aspects seem worth a notice here:
a) The character's style of expression changes with the progress of the story. Once you pick up the subtle differences in HOW things are told, you notice the adapting manner of speak through the whole game. This sounds obvious, but is rarely found in games when it comes to simple expressions thrown around like "hey, do this", "maybe we should try that", or "help me"- mostly, games contain only a single "mood" for those messages, replayed over and over through the whole campaign, sometimes ruining tense atmosphere by shallow talk. Not in this game!
b) There's cutscenes which prove: One sentence can carry enough weight for a whole conflicted situation. This is how visual art can work! You don't tell emotional progress. You simply show. And sometimes, a sad smile is all there's needed.
-SUMMARY-
Lush, warm graphics quite different from common cold, hard postapocalypse environment designs.
Decent Action Fight gameplay. Add exploding robots, and minor flaws with the climbing design.
Characters "with soul": Credible lines, subtle changes in communication.
The developers commitment to their way of storytelling distinguish this game from others in the genre of Action/Platformer games.
Judging from quality and content, it's worth the price- even more when it's on sale. You got a gamepad and/or don't hate Action/Platformer games? This is for you, then!

Grand strategy is where Rome II truly shines. The management of armies, provinces, trade, diplomacy, faction politics, spies (& champions & dignitaries), all combine to make the experience the closest imperial simulation I've yet played.  If you think you would've made a better Caesar than Ceasar, this is the game to prove or refute your claim.  There is no other contender.
The tactical experience is above par, and I found it entirely satisfying, when I've had the time and inclination to spend on tactical command of a battle.  The nice thing about that is every battle can be resolved by the AI.  You will almost inevitably do better if you choose to command your armies yourself, but when the odds are 3:1 in your favor, it's usually carrying coals to... well, to Nero's Rome, at that point.  Granted, my most recent tactical command gaming experiences involve mostly games where the tactical experience is the equivalent of rock, paper, scissors on a pretty backdrop (ahem, looking at you Endless Space... so disappointing...) so YMMV.
The tactical (and strategic) user interface is simplistic (in a good way) and relatively easy to navigate for how complex this game becomes.  tactical combat management is very similar to my remembered experiences playing Sid Meier's Gettysburg!  It would help if the controls for fine-grained unit management were outlined more clearly in the tutorial, but a few moments searching the in-game encyclopedia's table of contents led me to the right section.  I wish the tactical management system were a bit more refined, but the dizzying array of formations covers most out-in-the-open situations when battle does not occur in a settlement.  It becomes more difficult to accurately place and orient units in closer spaces, but having served in the National Guard, I can assure you that real life isn't all that far from art in this case.  All-in-all, having played the tutorial campaign and secured the entirety of the Italian peninsula as the Junii party in the Roman faction main campaign, I have no significant complaints regarding the tactical management.
If you like strategy gaming, love playing any CIV game (or Endless Space, Endless Legend, GalCiv, etc...) on a massive map, and like the ability to play a different game every time, this game is for you.  The main campaign alone allows (even without DLC) you to play as widely ranged factions as the Iceni or the Seleucids and many more.  The DLC nearly doubles the amount of playable factions, each having their own tailored victory conditions and inherent starting difficulty ratings.  (Because of the complex nature of the game, it is difficult to estimate from one game to the next how the difficulty will vary, and I suspect my first game has become rather more difficult than it needed to be due to some early diplomatic blunders.  Must remember to fire my foreign minister.  Oh, wait, that's me...)  In short, the designers of the game were clearly well aware of the Butterfly Effect, so don't make the mistake of assuming that the diplomatic game is as simple as bribing the people you like.  Even that small action makes others change their views of you.  This is no Civ diplomatic engine.
TL;DR - if you like grand strategy with decent but not overwhelming complexity, this is well worth your time.

This game has a really good atmosphere. You care about the two protagonists from the beginning, for no real reason outside of that they're good people in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation, and eventually they begin to care about each other, and it shows. While you play as the fighter, monkey, who protects the "damnsel in distress", trip, you most certainly gather that they are a team. They couldnt progress through their trials without each other, and that idea is developed well. Combat is fun, and just challenging enough in some places, but the forgiving checkpoint system makes toughing through even the hardest sections pretty easy. I will say, this game is almost 100% atmosphere and combat, as there is no real story to speak of. It starts as "I need to get from point A, to point B, and youre going to be the one to get me there", and doesnt develop past that single concept until maybe the last 30 minutes of the game. There are a few hints of intrigue here and there about what happened to make this interesting setting what it is, but just a few. There are literally 0 story developments besides the midway point where you get to the aforementioned "point B", and the veeeerry end after you beat the "final boss" (which is nothing more than a set piece with a few waves of basic enemies, and shooting what totals out to maybe 10 weak points). My biggest gripe with the story, is that they set it up for a sequel, which never happened. You dont leave a cliffhanger ending, when there was no story to be intrigued about until the cliffhanger itself. Overall, its a good enough game, with great atmosphere, protagonists who you really care about almost on an emotional level(the games strongest two points), fun, but repetitive combat and a solid score. The repitition and lack of combat depth and story hold back what could have easily been a classic action adventure title. I'd rate it a 6.5/10. Worth picking up on sale. Low replay value. Not enough challenge, enemy variety, combat depth or collectables to warrant playing again. Took me a month and a half to beat because it has 0 addictive qualities. Can be finished in a day if focused.

I just spent some time with the Emperor's Edition for this free weekend, and came away fairly unimpressed with Rome 2. I was a huge fan of Rome 1, and I feel this game is inferior to it in almost every way.
1. Graphics: Rome 2 looks very good at high settings. The units on the battle map are fairly detailed, the terrain looks decent and the effects are nice. The campaign map also looks gorgeous.
2. The AI does a fairly good job on the battle maps. They attack in unison, send in their infantry to charge while their light/missile infantry support from behind, they actively send their cavalry around your main force and try to flank you. Overall, well done.
That's about all the good I have to say about Rome 2 though.
3. The UI during battles. It is completely useless. The game needs a simple, organized UI that lets you easily distinguish between units. The pictures on the unit cards are such that it makes it farily difficult to tell apart different units when clicking on their cards. Also, the current status(es) of the unit flash at the centre of each card in 1-2 second intervals. This means I need to wait up to 5-6 seconds just looking at a specific unit's card to see if they are under enemy missile fire, routing, or whatever. This is competely useless and unacceptable when previous TW games dealt with this much more efficiently.
Also, the lack of walls and siege equipment. WTF happenned there? One of the most fun battles you could have in Rome 1 was assaulting a huge city with a full army of light/heavy infantry, archers, cavalry, and most importantly, trebuchets. The onagers available in Rome 2 are fairly weak and just not as satisfying to use to wreak havoc in an enemy's city.
Another big issue is the campaign map province system, which makes it so that only the provincial capitals have large walls. All other settlements are minor, with to walls defending them. This makes it very easy to steamroll the majority of enemy settlements you encounter, and makes the overall campaign much too easy.
Speaking of the campaign map.... although it does look gorgeous now, much of its openness from previous TW games is gone. Italy especially feels just like a highway connecting 1 settlement to another. This is a problem because the game forces you on a linear path between settlements, rather than letting you do whatever you want.
Diplomacy is still an issue. The AI will propose stupid deals on a regular basis. For example, I would propose a mutually beneficial trade agreement and have it rejected. 5 turns later, I get an offer from that faction for a trade agreement, but they also want 4000 gold. Or I will almost destroy an enemy, and when they have 1 city left they request peace, but also want me to pay 10 000 gold to them for that peace... when I have a full army beside their last city and they have 5 units defending it.
The AI has some issues on the campaign map as well. There have been numerous times on the campaign map when I am holding a city wih a garrison of 20 units, and I am attacked by armies of 4-8 units, which are of course massacred by my forces. Thankfully, the AI works well on the battle maps.
Naval battles are an exercise in frustration and poorly implemented. You have little incentive to build actual navies, since when you order an army on water, they magically transform into transports. This is very frustrating when you have several enemy ports blockaded, only for them to send a random small force to attack one of your settlement behind the front lines... ♥♥♥♥ing seriously? Those transports will usually be a match for actual navy ships... making navies completely useless in the game.
Unit collision was a big problem in Empire/Napoleon, although I did not find it to be a big issue in Rome 2, despite it using the same engine. The formations are nowhere near as clear/fluid as in Rome 1, but unit-on-unit combat works fairly well. A unit of 60 cavalry charging into a unit of 80-120 light/missile infantry will make short work of them in a few seconds. However, combat between heavy infantry units is a bit of an issue. The units tend to lose formation and congregate into a blob, which kills the immersion and makes it frustrating to try to command units.
Lastly, the price. The game is a complete rip-off for $66.50 CAD, especially given the almost $100 of DLCs. The greek states should have been included in the base game, as should have blood/gore. Charging additional money for blood and gore is completely ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (yes, it was for the rating. Well, ♥♥♥♥ your rating). Some DLCs are cool and worth it on their own, but it feels like there was basic content cut from the game just to be sold as DLC, which is unacceptable.
I held off buying Rome 2 for a long time, and after spending a weekend playing it, I refuse to pay CA for this game. Yes, it is quite a fun game, but it could have been so much more, and as a sequel, it ultimately just makes me want to go back and play Rome 1.
Well.... maybe I will buy it, but once it gets to under $15 CAD with all the DLCs. Otherwise, the game is simply not worth it, even at $16.50 + $20 for DLCs.
Edit: I purchased Rome: Total War Gold Edition and started a campaign in the original and in the Barbarian Invasion expansion. Comparing vanilla to vanilla, Rome 1 feels a lot more polished/better done and a lot more immersive. Very happy with the RTW Gold purchase.

A great game. An upgrade from many previous games in the series in some ways, more in technical ways.
I think that the game has improved a lot since the release. One of my most favorite features is the Imperator Augustus campaign.
Some things could have been better. Some lack, but if you are a history buff, or a strategic, patient gamer and you don't mind having a few issues, then this game is for you. Some may prefer Rome: Total War, but some may prefer Rome II because of its massive scale, superior graphics and modern feel.
- There are a lot... and I mean a LOT of factions and cultures. The Gallic tribes are all split up, as well as the Germanic tribes, the Greeks, etc. There are no bunched together factions(ex. "Gallic Tribe", "Africans", etc), which I really appreciate. There are always factions that are rising and leaving, not always historically, but they add some spirit to the game. Carthage is split into Nova Carthago and Carthage to balance Carthages power right off the bat. The Greek city states are all split up and wage war with eachother. Each faction has realistic starting positions and bonuses.
- I think the army sizes are great, but I do not like the unit limit. You should be allowed to set the unit limit from 20 to 40 according to what you think your PC can handle. Besides the unit limit, the rest is fine. The Heroes of Sparta limit is dumb and unrealistic, but whatever. The player has a lot of units to choose from for each army aswell.
There are some great strategy games out there and this is one of them. I loved Rome II and continue to play it.
The only big problem I have is the amount of DLC's and the prices. They are a little expensive altogether. I have them all, but I wish some of the content simply came with the game, specifically the Greek States and the Blood and Gore DLC's. Other than that, the DLC's were worth it, but could've been a tad bit cheaper.

Alien: Isolation is now one of my favorite horror games. While I don't necessarily think it's the scariest game out there, it's very atmospheric and is a very enjoyable experience.
The game's character is the daughter of Ripley from the movie Alien 1. While on a mission to find the whereabouts of her mother, she finds herself stranded on a decaying space station filled with the horrors caused by the murderous alien on board.
The atmosphere in this game is gorgeous. You are put in a first person perspective which makes the experience very immersive. The graphics, music, and sound effects give it the feel as if it is part of the original movie. There are even sound clips from the movie that I recognize, intermingled with the new voice acting. There are tons of small details in the environment to be appreciated and it's the small details that really give it a great look.
The story is quite well-developed. There are a few cut scenes but it's not overbearing. There are numerous voice recordings scattered around that leave tidbits of story.
Apart from the look and feel of the game, the game mechanics are great and they make the game challenging. Simply put, this game has done a lot of things right that other horror games did wrong. Let me try to list a few things:
While there are weapons, ammo is limited and they seem very ineffective on hard mode. This keeps the game's spirit as a survival horror game and not another action game with horror elements like half-life or bioshock. The stealth mechanics are essential and you will simply get killed if you make too much noise. This includes running and even using your motion detector!
The alien is pretty unpredictable and its very sensitive to noise. In games such as outlast or amnesia, you could eventually figure out the path the AI is taking and avoid it quite easily. This game is harder in difficulty, which really adds to the experience. Not to mention, the alien can open up lockers!
The maps are not linear and there's many spots to explore. The game forces you to scavenge for parts, since items such as medkits and smoke grenades must be crafted. You also have a limited battery on your flashlight. This is a great game mechanic that was neglected in games like Amnesia 2.
There are other little interesting mechanics that add to the experience. You can only save the game at save points which adds to the danger when you are trying to sneak around an enemy. When hacking the security systems, you must solve a simple puzzle but time is not paused. It's possible for enemies to sneak up on you while you are interacting with the simple puzzles.
Alien: Isolation has just about everything I expect in a horror game. Great immersive atmosphere, detailed story, solid and challenging gameplay elements add to the experience.

This game actually starts out like a lot of other crafting/building games: Mine resources manually and build a pickaxe to mine faster, just like you've probably done a hundred different times in dozens of different games. Boring, right? Why not build a machine to mine for you? That makes things easier, although you still need to transport coal over to keep it going. That's pretty tedious, so let's build a conveyor belt and an inserter to transport the coal automatically! Pretty neat, although building all of these conveyor belts is a lot of work. Hey, let's get an assembler to automatically build conveyor belts for me! That works great, except now there's conveyor belts everywhere and it's all a bit confusing. Why not build flying robots that replace the belts.... you get the idea.
This game basically gives you tasks to do, and as soon as those tasks get boring, it gives you an easier way to do it. It is insanely addicting, in a way that I haven't experienced from a game in a long time. Sure, it is early access, but the game is very stable and already has a lot of content. Plus, the devs give weekly updates on their website, so you always know what's been going on. This is as well done for an early access game as Kerbal Space Program and Prison Architect.
Also, as of this review, the current count on Steam is 1,778 positive reviews to 6 (SIX!!) negative reviews.

This is the game I wanted when Treyarch first announced Black Ops II and said that it would be a series overhaul, moving Call Of Duty into a future setting with sci-fi weapons & combat gadgets. I was severely let down by that game as I felt it didn't deliver what it promised (at least in the campaign), but Advanced Warfare fills that void for me. The weapons & gadgets used in the game are creative, futuristic (but plausible), and not only fun to use but have numerous tactical aspects that add to the gunplay. The global settings and massive amounts of detail in them also provide a strong sense of place and period. The game uses some elements from Crysis, Titanfall, and even Splinter Cell, though at its core, it is a true next-gen Call Of Duty experience with some amazing combat technology and set-pieces grander than anything the series has accomplished to date. The production values are so good that this is one of a small handful games I use as an example when someone is curious about my new PC and wants to see how good its graphics capabilities are. While the single player campaign is on the short side, clocking in at around 6-8 hours, I think of it as an interactive big budget action flick. Call Of Duty has always been a corridor shooter, and though Advanced Warfare is no different in this regard, I had more fun playing its campaign than I've had with any COD since the Modern Warfare series. It is one of the best looking games of this generation with sound design of equally high caliber. Performance-wise, this is well optimized but not free of hitches (primarily frame rate drops during cinematic sequences), though nothing bad enough that it detracts from the overall experience for me (your mileage may vary; I'm playing this on an i7-5930k @ 4.2GHz with a GTX 1070 and 144hz monitor, and it is glorious to behold; the Filmic SMAA T2x anti-aliasing sets a new bar for the series, but make sure you disable shader caching as that takes such a heavy toll on your GPU that the game is practically unplayable unless all settings are dialed down.
Unfortunately, I cannot comment on the multiplayer portion of the game as I am late to the party - the servers are like ghost towns at this point, though I found the single player campaign well worth the $15 price tag I paid during a sale. Yes, the story is predictable and does not live up to its excellent premise, leaving many unanswered questions in an ending that feels rushed, though it's passable and far better than a lot of Call Of Duty plots. Kevin Spacey in particular turns in an excellent performance as an antagonist (almost an anti-hero in some respects). The missions have tons of replay value - this is one of my go-to FPSs when I simply want to kick back and shoot some people (and drones) and be taken for a ride, and I highly recommend it to anyone who is looking for a shooter or action game for similar reasons. Multiplayer enthusiasts should look elsewhere, though, due to the lack of an online community at this point (in a half hour, I ran into only two other players).
Based solely on the presentation and performance of the single player campaign (which is the main reason I play Call Of Duty games), I give Advanced Warfare a solid
(8.5/10). Yes, it is another formulaic, annual COD offering, but it adds some strong elements to the gameplay and is better than Black Ops I and II (III is similarly high-quality and features more extra modes) and as good as the Modern Warfare trilogy.

is a beautiful game and in this context beautiful is referring to the visuals of the game. No matter how you look at the game and even if you don't like platformers you have to admit that the complete game is looking fantastic.
The story is told fast: A hairdryer called Dyer is attacking the world trees in order to rob their energy the "Helys". To prevent this, the world trees have created the buds to stop Dyer  polluting the trees even more.
is a platformer. You are trying to reach the top of the different trees and fight the specific world boss there. Every world consist of 7 levels plus one boss level and three bonus level (exception is the last world with only one bonus level) so there is a lot to do and the game is gradually getting harder. You have four different buds and every bud has its own special ability. Fly'n can sing and activate the Helys and revive the inhibitants of Helica, Lyft can stick to any (unpolluted) surface and crawl on them, Ywok can transform to a ball and bounce around and Nyls can propel himself (up to three times). And all Buds can jump, double-jump and glide. You can not change the buds freely everywhere, only in the specific checkpoints which is a good thing because you don't have to think too much with whom you have to solve a specific part of the level. Additional to all the abilites the buds can also change between two visions which may make different parts of the level solid and/or accessible.
As for the difficulty: If you only try to reach the exit it should only need patience since you may die as often as you "wish" and you will restart from the last checkpoint. But you should notice that the game has been tagged as "hard" so keep that in mind. It may look cute but you need to know what you are doing. For those looking for a higher challenge there are different options: You may try to "complete" the levels which means you explore more and collect all the Helys and pollen which are hidden. If you are still not satisfied you can try to play the levels without dying. And for the motivated there are the Leaderboards where you can compare your points to the rest of the playership.
All in all I think I can't recommand this game enough. I bought the game on release day and never regretted it. I put more than 100 hours into this game which says a lot. The buds are lovable and each world has a different beautiful design. If you like platformers you have little to no reason to not buy and play
. All this is rounded up with a beautiful soundtrack which you can and should buy aswell.

Really fun platformer that should probably have gotten more attention. The art and animation are gorgeous! The audio is pretty nice too.
You control 4 different characters that all have double jump/float and a special power. 1 crawls on walls, 1 can bounce on deadly surfaces, 1 can dash any direction for long distances, and the last is the least maneuverable but sort of a key. In each area you're trying to use the available characters to explore and open up areas for the other bugs (or locate spawn areas for a different character).
The movement feels really tight with just the right amount of skill and finesse. You can also swap between light/dark words at any time to toggle certain platforms, walls, and deadly areas. So often you'll do something like: double jump and stick to a wall, detach, toggle off a dangerous platform above, air jump through it, toggle a platform above off, double jump through it, toggle the platform back on, and land. The trick jumps get much crazier from there... the difficulty is somewhere between Sonic and Super Meat Boy, but it never feels unfair.
Anyway, if you ever miss challenging old school platformers or want to see where the evolution of platforms has gone, check this one out. I finished in about 8 hours, but missed most of the secrets which unlock bonus levels.

*SPOILER ALERT* (Play the game before reading this review. If you are wondering if this game is worth your time, the answer is yes)
I stumbled across this game by pure accident while complaining about how similar most games on Steam. I was instantly sold on the premise and downloaded it immediately. Emily is Missing is a very interesting game, that is able to subtly portray the emotions of the two characters in without the need for exposition or facial expressions. The game masterfully constructs immersion through believable interactions between the two characters which change drastically  depending on where the characters are in there lives. For example, In the first chapter Emily and the protagonist (who I will call Kyle) speak to each other as if they are best friends and the characters take turns in asking each other questions. However, in the last chapter Emily asks very few questions and leave the Kyle to keep the conversation going. This is definitely the games strongest points and is the main selling point of the game.
Unfortunately, there are a two features in the game that I personally feel shatter the immersion at times. First of all, for to send a message you first have to select the message and press buttons on your keyboard which will cause Kyle to type them. This gets a little tedious at times and swiftly breaks the suspension of disbelief as a I don't actually have to press the right keys to type the messages, which resulted in me repeatedly tapping the space bar to proceed. Having the character type out the messages automatically would have been a quick and effective solution. The second inclusion is the messages that read "Emily will remember that" or "I chose to talk to Emily about ...". These shatter the immersion a little more than the previously discussed feature, however I do realise that this feature was implemented to allow players to easily identify which decisions made affect later event in the game.
At times, when reading the options it felt like some situations were only designed to have two options, but a third option was included for the sake of consistency. Speaking of options, there seemed to be little dialouge choice that affect the overall plot of the game, only choices that affect some minor events. For example, in chapter 4 you can make a choice of whether to have Emily visit and when she does you can choose to hang out in your dorm room, do activities around campus or go to a party. Her reaction to each event is the same in chapter 5. Granted I have only played through this game twice and I have currently not found a way to change the final chapter in the game.
Despite the minor gripes I have with the game, it is written beautifully and does a very good job of encapsulating you in the story of two faceless charaters. The writing and characters and great and resorts to the fantastic strategy of revealing the personalities and feelings of the two characters in veru subtle ways. This game is definitely worth having in your Steam Library.
*DISCLAIMER* I critique because I care. Kyle Seeley has a lot of talent as a developer and a writer and I want to see that grow and develop. I hope I see more of your work in the future.

Other users have pointed out in the review's comments that they could play the game without any issue with only 8GB RAM. By my assumption, only people running a Radeon GPU will have this problem while Nvidia users tend to be running the game smoothly.
