Instead, do a bit of research first to determine whether or not Just Cause 3 will run on your current system.
Below is the original review I wrote before it was mentioned to me that the issue wasn't present for all users with 8GB of memory or less.
- - -
This is the first and last thing you should know about Just Cause 3. The optimization is the worse.
Do you know why Just Cause 3 wasn't delayed? Because the optimization was so bad that the game had to be launched on the same year as the infamous Batman: Arkham Knight so that the optimization would seem comparably good.
All jokes aside, how. the. ♥♥♥♥. do you screw up the optimization a sequel to one of my favorite game of all times (Just Cause 2) so ♥♥♥♥ing badly. How. Where did you go wrong, Avalanche? Just Cause 2 was amazing. Sleeping Dogs is considered one of the best open world games out there, and I recently finished playing Mad Max which has beat any of my expectations by a long shot, and hyped me for the release of Just Cause 3. All three of these games had excellent optimizing and great graphics. Then what happened for Just Cause 3? Who was in charge of optimization for Just Cause 3, if anyone?
I know that the developers are constantly working on improving the performance and fix issues with the game, but so far these attempts haven't been very convincing at all, with updates after updates doing a whole lot of nothing as far as I can tell, and as I try to deal with the constant freezing, crashing and frame drops, the game is still, unfortunately, unplayable. Why? Because you WILL have memory issue if you have 8GB of RAM or less installed in you computer. You WILL have poor framerate, you WILL be forced to reduce the graphics (which really aren't that elaborated, let's be honest here, I can play most games some of which have better graphics, on highest settings without problem except for Just Cause 3 – don't get me wrong, the game is gorgeous, or it would be if it actually ran properly on medium graphics settings).
---
"Crashing – Lack of RAM"
So far, I have
left the game on my own even once. The game will kill itself eventually, usually after around 0.5 to 1 hour of gameplay. Hooray for modern technology, insuring that quitting a game is never necessary for PC gamers around the world.
---
"Freezing – Lack of RAM"
Again; apparently 8GB of RAM will not be enough, because as soon as you attempt to open the Steam overlay in-game, your game will freeze. Your desktop will freeze
you manage to exit to desktop. Your computer will freeze. Your mouse cursor's speed will be reduced to 1FPS, and you will not be able to do anything at all, except force a shutdown of your entire system.
Yes, I did try Ctrl+Alt+Del, and no. Even that didn't work, because my memory usage was at ~35% in use and 65% modified (or at least, if I can trust AMD System Monitor (which I do). That's what happens when you don't have any free memory.
---
"You have been disconnected... again"
I can't explain that one, neither why it happens nor if it just happens to me, but I keep being disconnected from the servers and requested to re-attempt login. And no, I don't want to play offline. Why? Because the online part of the game is a feature of the game which I expect to function correctly. I shouldn't have to disable a feature because it just doesn't work. It
work.
“Is the game good?” I hear you ask. Well, I honestly can't say. Is it good? I couldn't really get a chance to try it thoroughly due to the awful optimization. From what I've seen so far, it is an amazing game, or should I say, it
be an amazing game. However, unless you have a monster rig of a computer to play the game on, forget about this game ever running properly. Unless you have 16GB of RAM or more, forget about Just Cause 3, it won't run, you will have wasted you hard-earned money. Get Mad Max instead. Same developers team, godly optimization. It may not have parachutes, wingsuits, grappling hooks and machine guns, but at least it's playable.
I really hate to give this game a bad review, but as I've already repeatedly mentioned in this review, the game is simply too poorly optimized, and until the developers fix it (which I doubt they will), I will most likely not change my review. Sorry Avalanche.
PS: The game is fun though. If you have a very good computer, it's probably worth it.

Alien: Isolation is now one of my favorite horror games. While I don't necessarily think it's the scariest game out there, it's very atmospheric and is a very enjoyable experience.
The game's character is the daughter of Ripley from the movie Alien 1. While on a mission to find the whereabouts of her mother, she finds herself stranded on a decaying space station filled with the horrors caused by the murderous alien on board.
The atmosphere in this game is gorgeous. You are put in a first person perspective which makes the experience very immersive. The graphics, music, and sound effects give it the feel as if it is part of the original movie. There are even sound clips from the movie that I recognize, intermingled with the new voice acting. There are tons of small details in the environment to be appreciated and it's the small details that really give it a great look.
The story is quite well-developed. There are a few cut scenes but it's not overbearing. There are numerous voice recordings scattered around that leave tidbits of story.
Apart from the look and feel of the game, the game mechanics are great and they make the game challenging. Simply put, this game has done a lot of things right that other horror games did wrong. Let me try to list a few things:
While there are weapons, ammo is limited and they seem very ineffective on hard mode. This keeps the game's spirit as a survival horror game and not another action game with horror elements like half-life or bioshock. The stealth mechanics are essential and you will simply get killed if you make too much noise. This includes running and even using your motion detector!
The alien is pretty unpredictable and its very sensitive to noise. In games such as outlast or amnesia, you could eventually figure out the path the AI is taking and avoid it quite easily. This game is harder in difficulty, which really adds to the experience. Not to mention, the alien can open up lockers!
The maps are not linear and there's many spots to explore. The game forces you to scavenge for parts, since items such as medkits and smoke grenades must be crafted. You also have a limited battery on your flashlight. This is a great game mechanic that was neglected in games like Amnesia 2.
There are other little interesting mechanics that add to the experience. You can only save the game at save points which adds to the danger when you are trying to sneak around an enemy. When hacking the security systems, you must solve a simple puzzle but time is not paused. It's possible for enemies to sneak up on you while you are interacting with the simple puzzles.
Alien: Isolation has just about everything I expect in a horror game. Great immersive atmosphere, detailed story, solid and challenging gameplay elements add to the experience.

I picked up this game for free over the "free weekend" event, and let me tell you: it was not anything like advertised.
First off, it is not anything like Skyrim as many people (and the title) would trick you to believe. This game has no dragons, snow, draugr, or perks. The first person mode is wonky at best, and you are pretty much forced to just go 3rd person and hack and slash away. Enemies take about 10 x more time to kill than Skyrim.
Remember hitting enemies and leveling up your weapon skills? This time you just get flat exp that levels up your skills. Boring and unimaginative - if I wanted to level up in such a 2-dimensional way, I would go back to World of Warcraft and just level my Warlock.
Worst of all, they took away what really made Skyrim such a great series. Dragons flying above you, shouting the mystical teachings of the Highborne. Snowy adventures in ice-caves that lead to a murder mystery and ice lions clawing at you. The adventure in this game is lacklustre compared to Skyrim because nothing can ever kill you; the danger has been removed by a scaling system that scales your attributes to match the enemies.
I was really hoping this was the new best Skyrim and I think Zenimax has some thinking to do. We moved away from a great game, and into a multi-player experience that just isn't all that Skyrim was hyped up to be. Skyrim was great because it offered an experience the whole family could enjoy in the comfortable couches of their homes, and live the life of a dragon warrior who shouts unspeakable things at enemies in cold, harsh tundras. Tamriel has a new gatekeeper, and he is no dragonborn.
Fus-Ro-Dah, true fans of the Skyrim series.

30 Hour Review:
I saw a lot of reviews that said that this is not like Skyrim but dont really saw how.  A few things are different. I play this using my xbox 360 controller so my review will be using it for examples. You do not use left trigger to control your left hand and right trigger to control your right hand. You use right triger to attack and left trigger to defend and you can defend with any weapon. Small difference but it is quick to get used to. The way you assign skills is completely diferent. You get to assign three skills to X, Y and B as well as 2 skills to left bumper and right bumper. You also get an ultimate skill that you assign to Left Bumper + Right Bumper (you have to hit both at the same time to activate it). So the aspects of gameplay controls are pretty different compared to skyrim. We also have a somewhat different way to go through your items. But it isn't too different. It just looks a bit different and you can not go overweight like in Skyrim. You have an item limit cap that can eventually reach 200 from what I read.
The next session will talk about ESO+ (premuim subscription) and the crown store (premium currency store). ESO is not pay to win. Surprisingly enough the only eye catching thing about ESO+ is the craft bag. This bag lefts you hold unlimited crafting materials. Seeing as crafting isn't required at all in the first 30 hours this bag seems like it is only useful for gathering materials for later (I recommend if you get ESO+ to turn auto loot on and check everything). As for the crown store. Nothing in there is required to make you better in the game. Most of the stuff in the crown store has an equivilent item in game. The only thing you can't buy in game is the dlc stuff, cosmetics, mounts, pets. Seeing as the pets are non combat they are just cosmetic and the mounts are all just skins and do not affect any stat they are cosmetic as well. The only advantage it could possibly give you is repairing armor for $$ and healing for $$ with a little boost to exp for $$$. All in all though the prices in the store seem very fair for everything (except maybe the 2500 crown mounts).
As far as the story goes. I rolled altmer (high elf). I will not be spoiling it but I really do like the story. It engaged me quite a bit and I cant wait to get to the next area to keep hearing more and helping more but these darn skyshards are everywhere!
Also dont forget to get an addon for a minimap and a skyshard locator (if you do not want to follow the riddles).

A hidden gem. There are many games that are somewhat similar, there are also many platformers on this site that are more expensive and more well-known.... it shouldn't be that way. Fly'N is an amazing game in terms of content ~ the gameplay, and especially the music. The music is AMAZING.
So if you ever think of whether you should buy "They Bleed Pixels" or "Fly'N" with your money, then this is the game you want for a charming, yet challenging platformer.
This game is absolutely charming.

Fly'N is a fantastic, brutal and beautiful 2D platformer. The gamepad controls, platforming and level design are solid and the game provides a challenge even for players experienced with platformers. There's enough incentive to 100% levels for the unlockable concept art, puzzle rooms and easter eggs in the home areas and, on rising lava levels, solely for the satisfaction you'll feel if you manage to pull off a perfect run. Having no reason to replay levels or improve my skill to perfect them is an area where I'm let down by quite a few indie platformers, so it's nice to see another one doing it right.
Acquiring new forms, each with unique platforming abilities, and being required to shift between them adds to the fun, and they're introduced at a rate that revives the learning curve just when you think you're getting comfortable and keeps things from getting too repetitive.  Regardless of which form you're in, you'll also be required to shift between two dimensions where platforms, collectibles, obstacles and hazards appear and disappear—adding another element of timing and skill to the formula, similar to the new Giana Sisters.
You'll die a lot trying to perform well on the timed levels; fortunately, there are plenty of stages you can explore at your own pace in between these skill checks and boss battles.  Watch the Steam trailer if you're considering picking this up; in this case, it accurately showcases how the game plays and whether it's something you're likely to enjoy.

I want to see more games do to the post-apocalyptic genre that ENSLAVED has done here. There's no cold, drab, desaturated colour-palette; instead, everything from the environments to the characters are beautifully vibrant. If there was a single word to describe this game it would have to be "lush".
There's not much to the story, there's almost no exposition, but that's okay. I enjoy how the very, very few characters interact with each other. The humour and insults exchanged throughout the dialogue are quirky at first, and there were a few words said that I wasn't expecting to hear from a game such as this, but I found it hilarious and strangely comforting. Maybe because I'd grown attached to what appears to be the only humans left in existence.
There are a number of issues, though. Firstly, the battle camera is horrendous, it makes fighting a lot more difficult than it needs to be as there is no lock-on camera. The field of view is so close to your character it's hard to tell when to block or evade an incoming attack. The battle system is also quite clunky, fighting numbers of enemies at once with melee attacks is sometimes frustrating and tactics such as countering and evading attacks aren't accurate. I found that maximising your ranged weapon's upgrades makes it a lot easier in order to manage groups of enemies from a distance.
The story also seemed to come to an abrupt end. I feel as though an additional one or two chapters would have improved how the last portion of the game unfolded but that's not to say it was a poor ending, it just seemed to be over sooner than I'd have liked. It's a shame too, because the ending raised more questions than had been answered; it was a huge contrast to what I'd previously experienced through my journey and not at all something that I expected to happen.
I also hugely appreciate that the optional collectibles throughout the map actually add to the significance of the story. It's not clear at first what meaning is behind them but it all comes together quite neatly in the end.

Very quick review here.
I'm super impressed. One of those games I just purchased on a whim after hearing or reading good reviews, didn't know much about it, so when it came up in a steam sale, just grabbed it and let it sit in my backlog.
Nice, short and sweet. Supurb character development and a great story to go with it. I remember watching Monkey as a kid and it didn't click until the names of the characters started to ring a bell and did a bit of research on the story this game is based on.
Anyways, graphically, pretty ok, considering the Unreal 3 engine is starting to look old. I had to tweak the .ini file to no ends to get this running above 20 fps on my decent pc. Problems with some ATI cards apparently, even though it runs games like Witcher 3 above 40fps on higher settings. Just beware, anything in the graphics options arent final, turning on some settings won't do the trick, you'll need to delve a bit deeper to get it running and looking nicer.
Soundwise, meh, a lot of bangs and crashes which sound like people smacking trashcan lids together but I guess that's what beating up mechs is supposed to sound like. Music is actually half decent though.
Gameplay. Well, it's good, I mean it's not God of war or Darksiders, heck the combat is nowhere near the fun of the Batman games but it seems to work enough to keep you going through to the end. Use a controller! Though I found the keyboard mouse setup worked well enough for me, some of the button combinations when you upgrade your skills arent exactly clear.
What keeps you going through this game? To see what's at the end. This game is all about story. I wouldn't put it on the level of Mass effect epic but it's good.
I didn't play through the Pigsy's perfect 10 DLC, I got the gist of it from watching the Letsplay cutscenes.
One gripe. The other DLC, Monkey's ninja suit, classic monkey and Sexy trip robot, you can't use them until you complete the game....and you can't use one of monkeys appearances alongside trips sexy robot costume. Which, in my opinion look pretty darn good.
Overall, get it on sale, even the current price tag is pretty good.

Grand strategy is where Rome II truly shines. The management of armies, provinces, trade, diplomacy, faction politics, spies (& champions & dignitaries), all combine to make the experience the closest imperial simulation I've yet played.  If you think you would've made a better Caesar than Ceasar, this is the game to prove or refute your claim.  There is no other contender.
The tactical experience is above par, and I found it entirely satisfying, when I've had the time and inclination to spend on tactical command of a battle.  The nice thing about that is every battle can be resolved by the AI.  You will almost inevitably do better if you choose to command your armies yourself, but when the odds are 3:1 in your favor, it's usually carrying coals to... well, to Nero's Rome, at that point.  Granted, my most recent tactical command gaming experiences involve mostly games where the tactical experience is the equivalent of rock, paper, scissors on a pretty backdrop (ahem, looking at you Endless Space... so disappointing...) so YMMV.
The tactical (and strategic) user interface is simplistic (in a good way) and relatively easy to navigate for how complex this game becomes.  tactical combat management is very similar to my remembered experiences playing Sid Meier's Gettysburg!  It would help if the controls for fine-grained unit management were outlined more clearly in the tutorial, but a few moments searching the in-game encyclopedia's table of contents led me to the right section.  I wish the tactical management system were a bit more refined, but the dizzying array of formations covers most out-in-the-open situations when battle does not occur in a settlement.  It becomes more difficult to accurately place and orient units in closer spaces, but having served in the National Guard, I can assure you that real life isn't all that far from art in this case.  All-in-all, having played the tutorial campaign and secured the entirety of the Italian peninsula as the Junii party in the Roman faction main campaign, I have no significant complaints regarding the tactical management.
If you like strategy gaming, love playing any CIV game (or Endless Space, Endless Legend, GalCiv, etc...) on a massive map, and like the ability to play a different game every time, this game is for you.  The main campaign alone allows (even without DLC) you to play as widely ranged factions as the Iceni or the Seleucids and many more.  The DLC nearly doubles the amount of playable factions, each having their own tailored victory conditions and inherent starting difficulty ratings.  (Because of the complex nature of the game, it is difficult to estimate from one game to the next how the difficulty will vary, and I suspect my first game has become rather more difficult than it needed to be due to some early diplomatic blunders.  Must remember to fire my foreign minister.  Oh, wait, that's me...)  In short, the designers of the game were clearly well aware of the Butterfly Effect, so don't make the mistake of assuming that the diplomatic game is as simple as bribing the people you like.  Even that small action makes others change their views of you.  This is no Civ diplomatic engine.
TL;DR - if you like grand strategy with decent but not overwhelming complexity, this is well worth your time.

I just spent some time with the Emperor's Edition for this free weekend, and came away fairly unimpressed with Rome 2. I was a huge fan of Rome 1, and I feel this game is inferior to it in almost every way.
1. Graphics: Rome 2 looks very good at high settings. The units on the battle map are fairly detailed, the terrain looks decent and the effects are nice. The campaign map also looks gorgeous.
2. The AI does a fairly good job on the battle maps. They attack in unison, send in their infantry to charge while their light/missile infantry support from behind, they actively send their cavalry around your main force and try to flank you. Overall, well done.
That's about all the good I have to say about Rome 2 though.
3. The UI during battles. It is completely useless. The game needs a simple, organized UI that lets you easily distinguish between units. The pictures on the unit cards are such that it makes it farily difficult to tell apart different units when clicking on their cards. Also, the current status(es) of the unit flash at the centre of each card in 1-2 second intervals. This means I need to wait up to 5-6 seconds just looking at a specific unit's card to see if they are under enemy missile fire, routing, or whatever. This is competely useless and unacceptable when previous TW games dealt with this much more efficiently.
Also, the lack of walls and siege equipment. WTF happenned there? One of the most fun battles you could have in Rome 1 was assaulting a huge city with a full army of light/heavy infantry, archers, cavalry, and most importantly, trebuchets. The onagers available in Rome 2 are fairly weak and just not as satisfying to use to wreak havoc in an enemy's city.
Another big issue is the campaign map province system, which makes it so that only the provincial capitals have large walls. All other settlements are minor, with to walls defending them. This makes it very easy to steamroll the majority of enemy settlements you encounter, and makes the overall campaign much too easy.
Speaking of the campaign map.... although it does look gorgeous now, much of its openness from previous TW games is gone. Italy especially feels just like a highway connecting 1 settlement to another. This is a problem because the game forces you on a linear path between settlements, rather than letting you do whatever you want.
Diplomacy is still an issue. The AI will propose stupid deals on a regular basis. For example, I would propose a mutually beneficial trade agreement and have it rejected. 5 turns later, I get an offer from that faction for a trade agreement, but they also want 4000 gold. Or I will almost destroy an enemy, and when they have 1 city left they request peace, but also want me to pay 10 000 gold to them for that peace... when I have a full army beside their last city and they have 5 units defending it.
The AI has some issues on the campaign map as well. There have been numerous times on the campaign map when I am holding a city wih a garrison of 20 units, and I am attacked by armies of 4-8 units, which are of course massacred by my forces. Thankfully, the AI works well on the battle maps.
Naval battles are an exercise in frustration and poorly implemented. You have little incentive to build actual navies, since when you order an army on water, they magically transform into transports. This is very frustrating when you have several enemy ports blockaded, only for them to send a random small force to attack one of your settlement behind the front lines... ♥♥♥♥ing seriously? Those transports will usually be a match for actual navy ships... making navies completely useless in the game.
Unit collision was a big problem in Empire/Napoleon, although I did not find it to be a big issue in Rome 2, despite it using the same engine. The formations are nowhere near as clear/fluid as in Rome 1, but unit-on-unit combat works fairly well. A unit of 60 cavalry charging into a unit of 80-120 light/missile infantry will make short work of them in a few seconds. However, combat between heavy infantry units is a bit of an issue. The units tend to lose formation and congregate into a blob, which kills the immersion and makes it frustrating to try to command units.
Lastly, the price. The game is a complete rip-off for $66.50 CAD, especially given the almost $100 of DLCs. The greek states should have been included in the base game, as should have blood/gore. Charging additional money for blood and gore is completely ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (yes, it was for the rating. Well, ♥♥♥♥ your rating). Some DLCs are cool and worth it on their own, but it feels like there was basic content cut from the game just to be sold as DLC, which is unacceptable.
I held off buying Rome 2 for a long time, and after spending a weekend playing it, I refuse to pay CA for this game. Yes, it is quite a fun game, but it could have been so much more, and as a sequel, it ultimately just makes me want to go back and play Rome 1.
Well.... maybe I will buy it, but once it gets to under $15 CAD with all the DLCs. Otherwise, the game is simply not worth it, even at $16.50 + $20 for DLCs.
Edit: I purchased Rome: Total War Gold Edition and started a campaign in the original and in the Barbarian Invasion expansion. Comparing vanilla to vanilla, Rome 1 feels a lot more polished/better done and a lot more immersive. Very happy with the RTW Gold purchase.

A great game. An upgrade from many previous games in the series in some ways, more in technical ways.
I think that the game has improved a lot since the release. One of my most favorite features is the Imperator Augustus campaign.
Some things could have been better. Some lack, but if you are a history buff, or a strategic, patient gamer and you don't mind having a few issues, then this game is for you. Some may prefer Rome: Total War, but some may prefer Rome II because of its massive scale, superior graphics and modern feel.
- There are a lot... and I mean a LOT of factions and cultures. The Gallic tribes are all split up, as well as the Germanic tribes, the Greeks, etc. There are no bunched together factions(ex. "Gallic Tribe", "Africans", etc), which I really appreciate. There are always factions that are rising and leaving, not always historically, but they add some spirit to the game. Carthage is split into Nova Carthago and Carthage to balance Carthages power right off the bat. The Greek city states are all split up and wage war with eachother. Each faction has realistic starting positions and bonuses.
- I think the army sizes are great, but I do not like the unit limit. You should be allowed to set the unit limit from 20 to 40 according to what you think your PC can handle. Besides the unit limit, the rest is fine. The Heroes of Sparta limit is dumb and unrealistic, but whatever. The player has a lot of units to choose from for each army aswell.
There are some great strategy games out there and this is one of them. I loved Rome II and continue to play it.
The only big problem I have is the amount of DLC's and the prices. They are a little expensive altogether. I have them all, but I wish some of the content simply came with the game, specifically the Greek States and the Blood and Gore DLC's. Other than that, the DLC's were worth it, but could've been a tad bit cheaper.
General - 8/10
Performance - 7/10
Graphics - 9.5/10
Diplomacy - 9/10
Battlefield - 8.5/10
Armies - 9.5/10
Campaign Map - 10/10
Unit Variety - 9.5/10
Historical Battles - 6/10(great but not much variety)
Are the DLC's worth it?: Yes.
Are the amount of DLC's too much?: A little bit.
Overall?: Completely worth it, although the price should be lowered by now. 8.5/10

I played the original Homeworld, mostly multiplayer, and it was one of my first online gaming addictions.  It was awesome.  When I heard it was being updated to play on modern machines with better graphics, I was really excited.  Then, I read that the game was going to use the HW2 engine ... red flag.
First, the graphics are gorgeous.
If you have never played any of the Homeworld games or were a fan of HW2, the Homeworld Remastered Collection will likely be very impressive and, for those folks, I can actually recommend it.
If you are like me, and played the original Homeworld game (particularly multiplayer), I think you'll be disappointed.  Many of the game play mechanics from the original Homeworld are gone.  Remember corvette wall, supported by support frigates? Not happening.  Formations don't work right.  Support frigates do some odd latching thing rather than trailing behind.
Multiplayer has all 4 HW races from both games and balance is proving to be a major challenge.  Again, if you loved HW2, it'll be familiar.  If you preferred the original, you're pretty much going to have to learn a new game (and one that you most likely won't like as well).
Multiplayer stabilty is improved over HW2, but still has some issues.  Gearbox has released 2 patches to date and they seem to be trying to address bugs, stability and balance issues.  They've done a lot a good stuff, but it isn't the game I knew and loved.
If you're an original Homeworld vet and haven't bought the game, you might want to wait a bit and keep tabs on the Gearbox forums to see what direction the game is headed.

To start, this game has flaws. It crashes more than you would expect for a game with this budget, and there are sections that lack the polish that the rest of the game has. That said, most of the game is well polished, the sound work is excellent, and while sometimes the animation is a little clunky, once you're engrossed in the game it's easy to overlook. It starts a little slow, but once it picks up it becomes an engaging experience that added up to a thoroughly enjoyable game. Despite the game's AI driven nature, it never felt completely predictable.
It's does expect some patience out of the player, and sometimes the character AI happens to generate frustrating loops of behaviour that can take a couple minutes to break. I was able to get out of all of them, so it's not like the game was broken. I even escaped a clearly glitched section, where I crawled under a desk that should have completely blocked the line of sight of a motion camera, but it went off as though it could see through the desk, causing the alien to be alerted, which kept the alien more or less locked in front of me. I eventually figured out that the camera had to be seeing my head clip through the desk, and got out by looking directly at the ground.

As a huge fan of the first Dishonored game, I feel like this one falls short on enough things to make me give it a negative review.
- Graphics. They look too "real" to be dishonored. Compare D1's art style to D2's. D2's is more of a real and sort of saturated approach while D1's style is washed out colours with an oil-pastel-esque look to it all. Faces especially.
- Voiced protagonists. It really took me out of the mood of "this is personal revenge" and made me feel like I was helping Emily/Corvo get revenge. In D1's DLC, it made sense as Daud was already a character with a voice. Maybe they just speak too often in D2.
- Fairness. Compared to Dishonored 1, the game feels less fair toward the player. Remember the leaning mechanic? The thing that made it so you could peak out of cover without being spotted? You now get spotted while doing it. Wanna move forward while holding the lean? Nup. That makes you peak upward and get spotted.
It's definitely a good game but I just didn't have the same amount of fun with it as I did with Dishonored 1.

Very good game. It's the first game in a long while that made me wanna play through it twice. It's also the first game that actually does let me legitimately play stealthy assassin, or roided berserker and the levels are just right in terms of size and detail. The campaign is the perfect length for the game to be enjoyable, (~12 hours) but the story is a little on the meh side. In short, if you want tight exciting gameplay with excellent level design and replayability, then this game is a godsend.
A bit of advice. For Far Reach, get the ability that lets you pull enemies asap. It's always fun to pull them towards you and kick their teeth in to knock them out.

WOW, I am having a blast!! Emily is a badass!
I finished D1 at 5PM on high chaos and dove into D2 at 9 PM (All German download servers were slow as heck...)
And, I fell in love already in the main menu! This game has improved on EVERYTHING but still sticks to its roots. You feel home yet every press of a button does a thing more than before. This is the best sequel without disappointments since SONIC 2 on the MegaDrive when Tails has been introduced.
Dishonored 2 has been beefed-up and is even cooler than the first game without trying to be cool - it just is! The menu and HUD is clear, and we finally get a real options menu, statistics, a tutorial and such. As if the designers and developers were not so sure with D1 but got their well-deserved accolades. The result is that D2 is a game in a long time that I really enjoy playing by turning off all other things like TV and radio, close the window, get me a drink and focus on the game.
~PERFORMANCE~
I am still running my old Acer Predator. Built in 2012, its i7-3770, 16 GByte RAM and later added GTX970 are struggling hard at medium settings and 1080p. I heard it's a general problem, but the amount of random stutters are weird. I am about to upgrade to a 1080 anyways, and the game is playable indeed, but the hardware hunger is evident. Even though, the game looks very great on medium settings already.
~STORY~
Well, I am pretty fresh into the game, and to be honest, I don't care about the story. It has the same formula of "I want revenge/justice" and that's all I need. Whatever has to be done.
~PLAYER CHARACTER~
I did not care for a sequel of D1 until I finished it. When I first saw that young lady at the artworks, I was like "is it really her?" And yes, it's Emily. And THANK GOD, I CAN PLAY AS HER! I expected it to be some stupid BS like in Tomb Raider AoD where you are forced to switch between Lara and Curtis, but no, when the selection screen popped up and it would let me select Emily, I literally screamed in joy. After finishing D1 on High Chaos and saving Emily, I think it's time to take her path.
This is a highly subjective topic, but I really love Emily. Her design, her attitude, her look and general visuals. She is smart and very attractive unlike the generic, overdrawn, big-titted bimbos you see in other games. Fighting for herself instead of letting her father Corvo do the job feels good and brings - yet again - this "you all deserve your death" feeling to it.
~COMBAT~
The combat has been improved a lot, mostly the different (read in: better) weapon feel and a more stylish, fast-paced combat. Instead of just swinging the blade like in D1, there is much more "martial arts"-like fighting going on. Emily kicks men in the nuts, does judo chops to the chest to overwhelm people and has some more nasty finisher ready.
Firing the pistol now feals like actually firing a projectile; in D1 it was more like an uncontrolled discharge of gunpowder, often missing point blank (!). You can also throw now people by grabbing them in a headlock but use the right trigger. Throwing a guard into a bunch of attackers is more fun than it sounds. In general, the game game became faster.
Also, the damage behaviour changed a bit; dying is easier now, but health regernates quickly to 50% after a while. This makes it more intense and realistic, but also enemies do not survive that many hits anymore.
~MOVEMENT~
As "THIEF(4)" player I missed a fast-paced movement. In D2, it's there: Dashing over obstacles, banisters and such is finally possible, climbing and jumping works very well in a first-person view. Also: A bit faster than in D1.
~ENEMIES/NPC~
What I also enjoy much is the behaviour of the NPC, might they be hostile or civilians. The panic you can cause is funny and something D1 lacked in. In D1, enemies are like "Huh?", "Heh?", "Uh?". Here they are like "What was that?!" - "A shot?" -"Maybe, let's look" and such stuff, the more guys alerted, the more chaos is going on. It's maybe just me, but I love to cause chaos like that, I did so in 2005 (Splinter Cell 3) and still like it. If the enemies are stoic as in D1, that does not work, here it's funny. Sometimes, the enemy also run away from you in panic, not sure yet whats the trigger for that. I once chased a screaming guard down as he ran just to shoot him in the back, that was refreshing compared to the over-confident machos in other games. Sniping down from a balcony and missing the shot will cause people to chase and other to throw rocks at me. It feels in general a bit more clever to fight than in the first game where a cluster♥♥♥♥ of guys just dance around you while letting you stab them.
Civilians react fearful when you pose a threat (or steal money from their cash register) and will also regocnize you later on, causing guards to assault you. So it's up to you if you behave friendly or walk over dead bodies. Finally, they fear a spree killer assassin, which is human and makes the NPC less 2-dimensional.
~GRAPHICS~
The graphics and level design are top notch again, too bad many of the eye candy can't be turned off. E.g., glass looks great now with the light reflecting on the shards and the glass-like surface, but the sum of all this causes a high load for the GPU. Older systems, like mine, struggle. I wish I could turn off the lesser important things, but even on low, the game eats up ressources. For those who have the power, the game looks fantastic. I get already a glimpse on that on MEDIUM, can't wait to try in HIGH later after upgrading my rig.
~AUDIO~
The audio has much improved. I turn off music in all games (except for DooM and DooM II) but the ambient sound is great. Nothing super oustanding, but many improvements over the first game as well. E.g. a rock that has been thrown had just 1 sound effect on impact, now you can hear its knocking sounds when it's rolling behind you. Subtle details, but they add to the atmosphere. Weapon sounds are also improved.
Emily (and maybe Corvo) talk during gameplay, finally something that I hated in D1. I am a person, I am the Empress and I have my feelings and thoughts about this situation. A guard, my former guard, that was about to kill me now is "not worth the uniform he wears" upon killing him. So she basically stated disgust; in D1, Corvo was all like "whatever". Screams in pain are now really audible which enhances the "fight for life and death" theme much better now. I often go like "ouch, that hurt", that includes the enemies but also Emilies own screams. As said, it feels much more like I am the actual player, not as passive anymore as in D1.
There is a "Headphone" setting in the menu, I think it changes the stereo panning to maximum (e.g. reloading the pistol plays the sound not "a bit left of the center" anymore like in D1, but "really to the left" now, where the weapon is also displayed on-screen).
~FIRST-PERSON IMMERSION~
In D1, as I wrote in the review to that game, the first person view was super lackluster. The gameplay was stiff and unpleasent. Corvo's hands did not really move, nor his head, it felt like there are two plastic zombie hands on a stick in front of the camera, and said camera just hovered trough the levels. I can also still not see my feet in this game, what sucks, but the whole animations of the hands have improved much - thank god! I already talked about the fast-paced combat, and now I really see and feel that Emily is really fighting with power and passion, there is a reasonable head movement now, when kicking I can see my legs (yay!) and my sleeves when tossing people (or their bodies) around. Due to the better audio, the immersion is way, way better. With the fast gameplay and such, D2 finally has found the right balance of first person view and motion sickness :-)
I could go on a lot more, but barely anyone nowadays reads more than a couple of lines, so, I make it short:
Very, very well-spent money!! Emily is a baddass and the game is outstanding!

I love this game.  If you're a fan of 2D platformers like me, and you don't mind using different abilities to traverse levels, then this is the game for you.  This game is a lot of fun, but it's also quite punishing when you die.  There's a lot of replay value...you can replay levels to get a better score and save more creatures.  Creative use of each character's abilities is present in this game.
It can definitely get difficult at some points.  I'm on world 4 right now and it's defintely a lot harder than the previous worlds.  There are essentially 3 types of levels: casual levels (where you can take your time and collect all the little dittys), rush/timed levels (these levels are intense...an unstoppable rising pool of lava is out to destroy you), and boss levels.
Boss levels are well designed.  Each of them is a mechanical machine that you need to traverse using the abilities that you are given.  Then once you beat the boss, you make your way inside the machine and disable it from the inside.
The rush/timed levels are the only gripe I have about this game.  I think there are too many of them.  If you die, you don't save the creature at the top.  If you die too many times, the game pretty much tells you "You suck" and a dialog appears that gives you the option of turning off the rising pool of lava.  These levels are designed to be hardcore, and it's pretty much impossible to NOT die your first time through.
All in all I would definitely recommend this game.  If your feverishly addicted to platformers like I am, this is not one to miss.  I rate this game an 8/10 with a BADASS seal of approval.  I love the art style and the music is amazing.  Definitely a complete package no doubt.

Don't get me wrong, this game as the right idea, but it just doesn't cut it, as it feels very lazy and non-player friendly the further you dive into it.
I played the game on Normal Difficulty and wow was it a challenge, this is coming from a guy who plays lots of shooters and has played previous Half Life titles. One of the main problems is that the "challenge" does not come from design, but of flawed game mechanics. I'll list them for ya:
*--* Every enemy, (with a gun), in the game is insanely accurate. I'm talking like 200M full auto burst with an inch clearing of your head showing and 5 bullets will hit. It almost feels like your playing against aim-botters. In the open with no cover and about 3 marines, you're dead within 3 - 4 seconds.
*--* Ambushes or "Boss" areas where you fight a lot of enemies are a complete mess. Not only are they a struggle to survive in because of the swarm tactics of the AI, but they are just not thought out. Events happen without leaving any time for the player to react and you're left reloading a save multiple times going "What just happened?"
*--* AI is pretty darn buggy, as they will sometimes not even be able to follow you through a door. Some enemies will spawn and T Pose or just remain still as you light them up.
*--* Gun balance. So please tell me why the cross bow and laser gun are the best weapons in the game for ... everything? Everything feels useless the further you go. About mid way, your pistol is useless as enemies kill you quickly but take 12 -15 shots to kill. You obtain a rocket launcher AFTER the laser, but it's complete crap. Why shoot multiple, slow moving, weak missiles at a helicopter when you can just charge your lazer gun for two shots and it's down instantly? And a Cross bow kills pretty much anything in one shot, but multiple shotgun shells to the face do nothing?
I wanted to like the game, but it's very hard because of the poor execution.

Riptale is a roguelite action platformer with procedurally generated rooms you will have to traverse to get to the end of the in-game areas. In terms of story you play as a ronin-like samurai on his way to attack an opposing force mainly consisting of dragons of different sizes and abilities inside a dungeon while wielding nothing but his sword.
I have to say, this is the game with the most felt impact on each kill in a long time. And the simple graphics don't interfere with that at all. This was my first impression and it lasts until now. Because of that the combat feels very satisfying.
Mentioned feeling gets intensified by the immediate risk any attack on an enemy implies. There's no blocking or other dedicated defensive movement option to get out of harm's way - you'll have to do one of two things to try and dodge out of a foe's expected aggressive reaction: You can jump. This is only possible if you happen to stand on ground at the time you are in need of evasion and is - depending on the type of enemy you're facing - more or less high risk. To resort to this normally means that you have run out of attacks and therefore the other possibility of retreat: The slash. You can slash three times in a row and move quite a distance along the way. One one hand this is a much safer method of avoiding attacks and is usually the better way to do that. On the other hand it requires planning ahead and keeping your cool, containing the last attack for an emergency or slash-dash in a triangle to return to your safe position in the end. Depending on the complexity of the room and the visibility of it's parts (if it's very high you might not see what's upwards or worse down below in case of a fall) this is not always easy and you will have to take risks now and again. Sometimes it's also important that your attacks are spot on, which brings me to the central gameplay element of Riptale: The slashes.
They can be best described as a kind of running / jumping straight forward attack with a sword strike at the end which both play out in lightning speed. This slash hits not only straight forward (or the exact direction of the attack), but a little later also registers some way behind the fighter. Aside from bosses I haven't met any foe that didn't die instantly from one hit. On the other hand your fighter takes four hits to die on normal difficulty (one on hard). Standing on flat ground you can attack forward and even when you slash partly down (but still also left or right) the samurai will rush exactly horizontally, even when he runs over a gap or into thin air, but the following slash will 'fire' in the exact direction your analog stick was facing, enabling a few strong tactics against lower placed foes. But you can also aim into the air or / and attack subsequently while not touching ground. From jumping, while falling, in all directions, even downward - until your three actions (represented as gems) run out. Then you'll have to wait shortly for them to replenish - long enough to get you in serious danger if you are in the wrong spot. Many reviewers describe the handling as lacking in precision. I think this feeling comes from two things: Firstly, the distance covered with one slash is enormous and it's quite difficult to predict where exactly your fighter will stop. Secondly, as soon as you hit some enemies or other obstacles you stop, even if the slash hits one or more targets behind it. Combined with the fast pace of movements (also some enemies') the struggle against the layout of the rooms sometimes amounts to quite a challenge. When adding the roguelike element of luck when in need of healing hearts this can quite often seem unfair. I had my best runs while keeping calm without focusing too much on achieving anything.
Concerning the possibilities of healing you sometimes get hearts from killed foes and crates or urns which replenish one hit on your fighter. But you can also find money. It can be spent in randomly occurring shops. These (randomly) offer attack gems different from the straight slash. Since the fighter has three slots representing the chainable attacks you get to choose when the bought variant activates. I had much fun playing around with different combinations, because other than in some roguelites I ran into an opportunity without having nearly the amount of needed money only once thus far. And that might have come from clumsily missing lots of coins in the rooms before.
Which brings me to a point I like and dislike at the same time: While you can go back to previous rooms to your left and right and even take the contents there indefinitely (meaning neither coins nor hearts dissolve - kudos to you, developers !), once you fall down into a room you're cut off. You can't go back up, not even using your slashes. Since you can't pan down while standing on safe ground you'll often need to do a 'leap of fate' (no misspelling) which might draw you into a slashing fight with dangerously positioned foes while driving you into spending all your attacks. If you end up floating over a downward exit at that time you will simply fall down, because there is no double jump, forcing you to abandon all (possible) coins and hearts. While I can live with that, this may concern some players who struggle a little with roguelike elements, because this might make some runs much harder - especially luckless ones.
All in all, I recommend you watch some short reviews or Let's Plays of the game and at the same time keep my description of the combat flow in mind. That way you might be able to figure out if Riptale is for you or not. I won't try to explain graphics or music to others, because that's easily solved nowadays - with all that media out there.
While sceptical at first I got a gem out of a sale that I'd have paid more than the full price for had I known what awaited me beforehand.

Riptale is an excellent platform/fighting game where you have three gems that represent your attack combo and they do massive, high mobility attacks that chain together and let you dash around like an absolute madman and kill any non-boss that you hit - but with the catch that they take a bit of time to regenerate. The attacks are extremely satisfying; the sound, the hit slow-motion, the mobility, the way blood sprays out, it's great. It's also pleasingly tactical; you have to consider how the enemies will move as you approach and where your attacks will carry you so you can get in, land your hits and then end somewhere safe to pause for a second to get ready to attack again. That approach feels original and interesting. The graphics are simple but the animations are good and the high contrast style is striking.
It's great, original and cheap, so I would highly reccommend it.

It is very fun, easy to pick up and difficult to master. The difficulty comes from some design flaws, like the fact that enemies can cheap shot you with a clairvoyance that is utteraly ridiculous, right as you enter a room... or that controls are in fact
precise.
You do have to aim at your target before striking, and while it may seem like the controls are a little off - they are in fact incredibly pinpoint, almost to a fault. The angle and timing really matter, even more so given that you only have up to 3 consecutive attacks. If you have good spatial awareness, you'll get used to having to adjust your angle by literally a fraction of a degree. This could mean the difference between executing a sweet combo... or just getting executed.
The biggest issue I have with the game is the BG Music for the main levels. It's the exact same looped track and it does not really vibe well with the music in the Menu, Shops and "secret" Lore Rooms. It's way too fast-paced, and bass drum heavy to be the song that you're hearing throughout most of your playtime. The 16-bit Midi feel is great, but every other song in the game is much better than the main track imo. It wouldn't be so bad if it switched every 3 or so stages after you find the lore room.
Would also be nice if you had the ability to switch the locations of your abilities at will, but maybe in a future update?  Anyway, it's a great game and I Highly Recommend it. Cheers!

If you are new to homeworld, you will find immense pleasure at the depth of the story, the quality of the music and voice acting and the sheer scope of this remaster. Homeworld 1 and 2 was far ahead of its time when it released back in 1999 and 2003 respectively in terms of gameplay mechanics, ship design, UI and story.
One thing that it did lack back in 2003 was support after launch, even compared to what was the norm back then. This seems to have been rectified with Gearbox having already released two huge patches within a month of release. These patches have fixed a ton of techncal issues players have been having and they have now started on focussing on the balacning as well. They have also taken a lot of player feedback and implemented them already and this bodes very, very well for future support. The devs seem comitted to improving the game.
Pros:
- Epic storyline from both HW1 and HW2.
- Includes both HW1 and HW2 classic, now made so they will run on Windows 7 and 8.
- Combined MP with both HW1 and HW2 races able to fight against each other.
- Amazing Graphics, Voice and music remastering. Every model has been updated and retextured.
- EPIC Mod support with developers publishing multiple mod tools and helping players getting their mods up off the ground.
- Extensive graphical options to make the most use of whatever hardware you have.
- Very good patch and technical support.
- 20h-30h of single player gameplay with 3 different skirmish/multiplayer modes and all maps from both HW1 and HW2.
Cons:
- HW1 veteran players who did not like HW2 will be dissapointed that they used the HW2 engine.
- The HW1 end theme song is missing due to liscensing issues.
- Multiplayer balance still in Beta.
- Some audio scripts are still a bit buggy (Last mission of HW2 is missing a song and Mission 3 of HW1 is missing an audio line)
If you have never played Homeworld and like RTS games you are doing youself a disservice with not grabbing this game.

Dark Souls 2 is a game that is good but suffers from several small fundamental flaws that makes it feel inferior to it's predecessors, Dark Souls and Demon's Souls. On a techincal feat, the game has been a much improved port from the first, has new combat additions that are a nice touch (shield breaking / dark magic being hexes instead / poise balancing / weapon balance / improved network code) but lacks some of the charm, such as more meaningful covenants (no dire consequences for leaving covenants), casualization of the game (dying is a joke with the new rings that are repairable instead of outright destroyed, flasks can heal much faster with the new stat ADP, gems are abundant), poor enemy variety/placement (majority of enemies have absurd amounts of ambush locations in unreasonable places, some enemies are outright unfair or not fun to fight [those fire breathing frogs spamming Forbidden Sun fireballs in particular], and Shrine of Armana pre-nerf), and level design is a huge step back in the series (Demon's Souls was linear but pleasing and very atmospheric, Dark Souls had a interweaven world connected individually by several linked locations, and Dark Souls 2 has some of this but in absurd design ideas, the biggest offender being the Iron Keep being reached by an elevator to the sky above a harvest field).  I won't be discussing the PvP, but I can say the Soul Memory concept is a travesty by preventing twinking in exchange for no incentive to not over-level and steam roll other players with the best of everything or maxed stats, as well as separating with many complications friends that would like to simply co-op or play with other people reasonably around their Soul Level.
To be fair, Dark Souls has it's own fair share of flaws, yet many are because of the rushed publishing date and the terrible port that required mods to be enjoyable, whereas Dark Souls 2 had a much larger budget, development team, and more production time, so there is really no excuse for the drop in quality.
Having played hundreds of hours of it's predecessors and only around 120 or so of the console version of Dark Souls 2, I cannot say I can feel like dragging myself once more through the game.
Is it an awful game? Not at all.
Is it a bad Souls game? Somewhat.
I think I've said my share, and that is all.

WOW, I am having a blast!! Emily is a badass!
I finished D1 at 5PM on high chaos and dove into D2 at 9 PM (All German download servers were slow as heck...)
And, I fell in love already in the main menu! This game has improved on EVERYTHING but still sticks to its roots. You feel home yet every press of a button does a thing more than before. This is the best sequel without disappointments since SONIC 2 on the MegaDrive when Tails has been introduced.
Dishonored 2 has been beefed-up and is even cooler than the first game without trying to be cool - it just is! The menu and HUD is clear, and we finally get a real options menu, statistics, a tutorial and such. As if the designers and developers were not so sure with D1 but got their well-deserved accolades. The result is that D2 is a game in a long time that I really enjoy playing by turning off all other things like TV and radio, close the window, get me a drink and focus on the game.
~PERFORMANCE~
I am still running my old Acer Predator. Built in 2012, its i7-3770, 16 GByte RAM and later added GTX970 are struggling hard at medium settings and 1080p. I heard it's a general problem, but the amount of random stutters are weird. I am about to upgrade to a 1080 anyways, and the game is playable indeed, but the hardware hunger is evident. Even though, the game looks very great on medium settings already.
~STORY~
Well, I am pretty fresh into the game, and to be honest, I don't care about the story. It has the same formula of "I want revenge/justice" and that's all I need. Whatever has to be done.
~PLAYER CHARACTER~
I did not care for a sequel of D1 until I finished it. When I first saw that young lady at the artworks, I was like "is it really her?" And yes, it's Emily. And THANK GOD, I CAN PLAY AS HER! I expected it to be some stupid BS like in Tomb Raider AoD where you are forced to switch between Lara and Curtis, but no, when the selection screen popped up and it would let me select Emily, I literally screamed in joy. After finishing D1 on High Chaos and saving Emily, I think it's time to take her path.
This is a highly subjective topic, but I really love Emily. Her design, her attitude, her look and general visuals. She is smart and very attractive unlike the generic, overdrawn, big-titted bimbos you see in other games. Fighting for herself instead of letting her father Corvo do the job feels good and brings - yet again - this "you all deserve your death" feeling to it.
~COMBAT~
The combat has been improved a lot, mostly the different (read in: better) weapon feel and a more stylish, fast-paced combat. Instead of just swinging the blade like in D1, there is much more "martial arts"-like fighting going on. Emily kicks men in the nuts, does judo chops to the chest to overwhelm people and has some more nasty finisher ready.
Firing the pistol now feals like actually firing a projectile; in D1 it was more like an uncontrolled discharge of gunpowder, often missing point blank (!). You can also throw now people by grabbing them in a headlock but use the right trigger. Throwing a guard into a bunch of attackers is more fun than it sounds. In general, the game game became faster.
Also, the damage behaviour changed a bit; dying is easier now, but health regernates quickly to 50% after a while. This makes it more intense and realistic, but also enemies do not survive that many hits anymore.
~MOVEMENT~
As "THIEF(4)" player I missed a fast-paced movement. In D2, it's there: Dashing over obstacles, banisters and such is finally possible, climbing and jumping works very well in a first-person view. Also: A bit faster than in D1.
~ENEMIES/NPC~
What I also enjoy much is the behaviour of the NPC, might they be hostile or civilians. The panic you can cause is funny and something D1 lacked in. In D1, enemies are like "Huh?", "Heh?", "Uh?". Here they are like "What was that?!" - "A shot?" -"Maybe, let's look" and such stuff, the more guys alerted, the more chaos is going on. It's maybe just me, but I love to cause chaos like that, I did so in 2005 (Splinter Cell 3) and still like it. If the enemies are stoic as in D1, that does not work, here it's funny. Sometimes, the enemy also run away from you in panic, not sure yet whats the trigger for that. I once chased a screaming guard down as he ran just to shoot him in the back, that was refreshing compared to the over-confident machos in other games. Sniping down from a balcony and missing the shot will cause people to chase and other to throw rocks at me. It feels in general a bit more clever to fight than in the first game where a cluster♥♥♥♥ of guys just dance around you while letting you stab them.
Civilians react fearful when you pose a threat (or steal money from their cash register) and will also regocnize you later on, causing guards to assault you. So it's up to you if you behave friendly or walk over dead bodies. Finally, they fear a spree killer assassin, which is human and makes the NPC less 2-dimensional.
~GRAPHICS~
The graphics and level design are top notch again, too bad many of the eye candy can't be turned off. E.g., glass looks great now with the light reflecting on the shards and the glass-like surface, but the sum of all this causes a high load for the GPU. Older systems, like mine, struggle. I wish I could turn off the lesser important things, but even on low, the game eats up ressources. For those who have the power, the game looks fantastic. I get already a glimpse on that on MEDIUM, can't wait to try in HIGH later after upgrading my rig.
~AUDIO~
The audio has much improved. I turn off music in all games (except for DooM and DooM II) but the ambient sound is great. Nothing super oustanding, but many improvements over the first game as well. E.g. a rock that has been thrown had just 1 sound effect on impact, now you can hear its knocking sounds when it's rolling behind you. Subtle details, but they add to the atmosphere. Weapon sounds are also improved.
Emily (and maybe Corvo) talk during gameplay, finally something that I hated in D1. I am a person, I am the Empress and I have my feelings and thoughts about this situation. A guard, my former guard, that was about to kill me now is "not worth the uniform he wears" upon killing him. So she basically stated disgust; in D1, Corvo was all like "whatever". Screams in pain are now really audible which enhances the "fight for life and death" theme much better now. I often go like "ouch, that hurt", that includes the enemies but also Emilies own screams. As said, it feels much more like I am the actual player, not as passive anymore as in D1.
There is a "Headphone" setting in the menu, I think it changes the stereo panning to maximum (e.g. reloading the pistol plays the sound not "a bit left of the center" anymore like in D1, but "really to the left" now, where the weapon is also displayed on-screen).
~FIRST-PERSON IMMERSION~
In D1, as I wrote in the review to that game, the first person view was super lackluster. The gameplay was stiff and unpleasent. Corvo's hands did not really move, nor his head, it felt like there are two plastic zombie hands on a stick in front of the camera, and said camera just hovered trough the levels. I can also still not see my feet in this game, what sucks, but the whole animations of the hands have improved much - thank god! I already talked about the fast-paced combat, and now I really see and feel that Emily is really fighting with power and passion, there is a reasonable head movement now, when kicking I can see my legs (yay!) and my sleeves when tossing people (or their bodies) around. Due to the better audio, the immersion is way, way better. With the fast gameplay and such, D2 finally has found the right balance of first person view and motion sickness :-)
I could go on a lot more, but barely anyone nowadays reads more than a couple of lines, so, I make it short:
Very, very well-spent money!! Emily is a baddass and the game is outstanding!

Black Mesa is an incredible remake of the original Half-Life that I reccomend any Half-Life fan should pick up and give a go. Keep in mind some areas are changed slightly and XEN is still currently in development (as of 1/4/2018). Overall you will still get the feeling of playing a valve quality remake of the original Half-Life.

Despite the effort in recreating Half-Life in the source engine, the Black Mesa project isn't very good in my opinion.
The first 2 ish hours are very very solid. It feels that most of the time was spent in the early complexes of the HL story. The rest of the ~5 hours are a mess. The final straw is that after so so many years of this game earning sales money in 'Early Access', there is still no Xen, and this the last levels and ending of Half-Life.
At the midpoint, when you progress outside, things get hairy. Soldiers have pin-point accuracy and know where you are at all times. Some of the art direction is great, but the technicalities of the game  let everything down.
The controls feel like slippery water and other times like mud, be prepared to load a lot because of the horrible controls. You can get stuck into scenery a lot of the time as well. Half-Life 2 was a lot better, I can't understand what this team have done here with the movement.
Then there are the bugs, so many of them. AI freezes up sometimes and soldiers or aliens just stand there. Sometimes they just run at you guns blazing until they are right on in your face. They don't really take cover properly, and you have no real chance to at all. If you circle around they already know where you are and shoot.
Oh and my oh my the aim-punch when you are hit is absolutely nauseating. Not to forget to mention that the guns reload way too slow and sometimes have a delay when you fire. All of this adds to the frustrations of playing this amateur endeavour. Despite the sentiments of the development team, the execution is incredibly sloppy.

The difficulty is spot on: never too easy or too hard, unless you are trying to get 100% completion. The way collectibles work is also similar to Rayman Origins, but the gameplay similarities stop there. The pace in Fly'n is slower and there is an emphasis in using the abilities of each of the 4 characters to overcome obstacles and transverse the levels, which are not simple left to right affairs: they are big and sprawling and you move both horizontally and vertically, free to go back and forth. To start, this game has flaws. It crashes more than you would expect for a game with this budget, and there are sections that lack the polish that the rest of the game has. I was able to get out of all of them, so it's not like the game was broken. I even escaped a clearly glitched section, where I crawled under a desk that should have completely blocked the line of sight of a motion camera, but it went off as though it could see through the desk, causing the alien to be alerted, which kept the alien more or less locked in front of me. I eventually figured out that the camera had to be seeing my head clip through the desk, and got out by looking directly at the ground.
It might sound like all I've said is negative, but compared to how engaging the game felt after the first section ended these are minor complaints. It's certainly worth a buy when on sale.

Ravenfield is a fun little game that will keep you occupied (depending on your age and geographical location) for a few hours to a few days. In its current state, you can expect no more.
It's early access, which depending on your experience with Steam and the modern gaming industry at large, can mean many things. It could mean that after the initial cash injection the dev has recieved by monetising an unfinished project, his interest in progressing Ravenfield might decrease along with the cash flow. It could mean that despite the dev's best efforts, being a team of 1 (or so I think I understand) means that the game will make limited progress over an extended period of time, and already we're seeing the workshop overtake the dev's role in providing the game with a consistent stream of workable content. This is nothing special, and many EA games enter this modder-reliant state, but it's a telltale sign of things to come in my opinion.
So it's going to crash and burn, or slowly progress and become reliant on the community to introduce fresh and exciting content whilst the dev chips in a few core improvements over the months. That's my take. It's one of those two scenarios.
I could be wrong of course, and hope I am... buuuuuuuut Steam has made be a cynical old ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and I have come to expect the worst when it comes to EA titles.
So what does this game offer? As others have said, it's a low-tech Battlefield style singleplayer experience focused around capturing flags, killing hordes of bots, watching your own hordes repeatedly underperform, and of course getting bored to death by the inevitable stalemate after you've taken two thirds of the map's capture points. There's like, 3 or 4 official maps, and about as many good ones in the workshop (from a functional perspective). So choice is limited there, but this is bound to change as the modders begin to relieve the dev of that responsibility.
It says bot count can be set depending on the might of your rig, but I'll tell you right now it's very CPU dependant. Doesn't matter what your RAM or GPU are upto, if you ain't bringing that processing power to the gun fight, then you're not going to have 60 FPS on anything over 50 bots. My desktop has an AMD 4300, and I get around 30 FPS at 100 bots, so I guess you could use that as a kind of guide post? I unno, I don't really understand jack about the internal workings of computers anymore. I just pay obscene amounts of money for pre-built ones, and use them until I can afford the next model in 3 or 4 years.
But I digress.
The dev has thrown in a few token game modes, such as "spec ops" and haunted, and whilst these hold promise they're not something that are really worth playing beyond a few minutes in their current state.
Unfortunately, though it is a solid game, it is a small game and you will tire of it quick (unless you are forced to play it by either your lack of access to modern technology ($$$) or if you live beyond Germany's eastern borders), leaving you wondering if you couldn't have spent that money better on your car's fuel tank.
At this point, if you're having to choose between seeing what this is about, or putting more fuel in your car, go for the latter.
BUT, despite all that, I will still recomend it for the following reasons.
1) It has a ton of potential. If the dev doesn't leave it to die in a ditch, and is able to work to a reasonable deadline, Ravenfield might well blossom into one of the greatest singleplayer experiences of our time. Patience is key here, and so is faith in the developer to follow through with everything. As it stands, I have faith, and I have patience. And my car's got half a tank of petrol so I'm good for now.
2) It can run on a Russian toaster. I don't just mean Western toasters where you put in bread, and get out toast. I mean Communist-era, Buk radar toting, bear wrestling, genocide loving toasters. The kind that was once used to beat Nazis to death way back in the Great Patriotic Dance Contest. If you're like me, who carries around a sub-par laptop about the house and away for casual entertainment, Ravenfield should be able to help you out here.
3) It is mindless fun. At least, in small doses. The bots don't tea bag you, they don't use their pre-pubescent voices to deafen you, they don't play music because they think trolling the mic is fun. There's nothing to really get angry about. Just a plug'n'play kinda deal. So it's easy to start up, easy to get into the action, and really easy to get blown up by the bazooka happy A.I who only seem able to use either a sniper rifle or an RPG. I'm joking, their weapon choices do vary a fair deal (and you can dictate what weapons are available to them). What I'm saying is, you can just boot this up and massacre a bunch of barely-sentient beings for a few minutes whilst your porn downloads.
And er, I guess that's all I got to say about that.
In short, if you're looking for a solid single player experience, then you'll want to look into this. Just bear in mind that it is fairly bare bones at the moment, and so holding off until the dev delivers meaningful progress might be the act of a wise man/woman.

Riptale as a casual experience is short, fun and challenging hack and slash platformer.
You start in one out of 3 randomly selected zones, go through random premade rooms with randomly placed enemies in them.
It's pretty straight forward - keep advancing until you reach the next stage (3 per zone), which will also increase the difficulty by placing more enemies / spikes to deal with. Once you made it past 3 stages, you will fight a boss, and advance to the next zone.
You're offered to mix 'n match your combo system to create a verity of attack patterns - these greatly change the gameplay so I advise trying them all out.

As someone who has indeed played the original (albeit never beat it since I was still quite young, stuck on the supernova research station level hahaha), I have to say that this collection is a MUST have and a MUST play for any and all fans of RTS games and great stories, not to mention it having an amazing middle-eastern influenced soundtrack, and really cool space ship designs. Yes, the HW1 remaster does have issues with it's strike craft AI being really stupid at times because of issues with remaking HW1 with the HW2 engine but that won't hurt your overall enjoyment of the game; it was still quite the enjoyable experience (the HW2 remaster works just fine). And in addition, if you're a veteran and are stubborn to accept crappy HW1 strike craft AI, they've even bundled the original HW1 and 2 with this deal! It CAN be quite challenging to newcomers but you can easily learn from initial mistakes and adapt.
A few tips for new players:
general:
-remember that resources and your fleet are persistent, meaning they carry through each level in both HW 1 and 2's campaigns; try not to loose too many ships or waste too many resources or else you could be setting yourself up to being forced to restart from the very beginning
-in the remaster, any resources you have not yet harvested in a level by the end of the level will automatically be added to your resource unit count once you hyperspace to the next level, so no need waiting for your collectors, if you've developed that habit as veteran HW player.
HW1:
-USE SALVAGE CORVETTES; I cannot stress how important capturing ships is. Capture as often as possible and in this priority order: Heavy cruisers>destroyers(any type)>ion cannon frigates>assault or support frigates. Heck, capture a few turanic raider corvettes in the earlier levels. Early in the game when you're really strapped for resources, capturing is the best way to acquire a powerful fleet.
-stop using fighters all together other than bombers when you're at late/end game in the campaign: as I have stated, fighter AI in HW 1 remastered is quite dumb, and I've literally had an entire wing of 30-40 defenders wiped out in seconds. Bombers are still somewhat useful for adding additional damage when attacking capital ships however. For all strike craft vs. strike craft engagements in late/endgame, you should be using purely multigun corvettes.
-take advantage of the time the game gives you when you've cleared the level and rebuild any lost ships before you hyperspace to the next level. Many levels in this game pits you against massive forces right from the start of the level and you will want to be very prepared for anything. You will not have this luxury for the most part in HW2, btw.
HW2:
-Flak frigates, marine frigates, defense field frigates, proximity sensor probes, and sensor distortion probes are completely useless; do NOT invest/use them. Capturing in HW2 is pretty much useless, since anything and everything can and will shoot down marine frigates in time while they are boarding an enemy ship, but unfortunately some levels require you to use one to fulfill mission objectives, in which you should build them for that and then retire immediately afterwards and use that space for an ion or torpedo frigate instead. Same goes for that defense field frigate which has a virtually useless shield ability that lasts like 5 seconds, but you will need 2 of them for this one mission objective in this one level, so likewise, retire them when you're done with them.
-Use carriers more: HW2 does not have support frigates nor effective salvaging ships, so you'll have to approach this game a bit differently in general. I highly recommend sending out a carrier behind your main fleet to act as a repair station/support frigate to repair strike craft wings and to also keep building/supplying fresh new ships to your main fighting groups because unlike in HW1, you will be building most of your fleet on  your own instead of capturing.
-delay mission objectives whenever possible to rebuild your fleet: having your fleet at full maxed out fighting power is important more than ever now with how much salvaging sucks in this compared to HW1. You do gain alot more resources alot more quickly so you should almost always have the full 14 fighter squadrons, 12 corvette squadrons, 21 frigates, and later on 5 destroyers and 2 battlecruisers cap, or at least keep it that way whenever possible (and before the final mission at least, have the cap of 4 carriers, trust me, you'll be thanking me in the final mission).
-strike craft are actually VERY good this time, so DO NOT hesistate to use interceptors and bombers. Use the pulsar gunships in conjunction with bombers to attack frigates and capital ships but also against corvettes whenever needed.
-always pick torpedo frigates over flak frigates, like, ALWAYS; flak frigates suck.
anyways, tl;dr,  I LOVE homeworld and I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I really hope gearbox decides to do HW cataclysm in the future even if they lost source code and would have to rebuild the assets from scratch; the beast and kiith somtaw were badass.
