It is a pretty great game, really it is, but it isn't for me.  I recommend this to OTHER people however because I really did enjoy this game, I just wasn't able to play it to its full potential.  The combat system is pretty complex... like... i failed the prologue (basically the tutorial)... Granted, I was mainly focusing on having fun rather than winning and that is why I died, I still feel like this game isn't for me.
If you play strategy games like Civilization or pretty much any other domination/conquer battle game, and feel like you want a more realistic combat system, one that is not turn-based and one where battles are not always determined by who has the most or the strongest units (I mean that definitely plays a role in this, but you CAN win with smaller, weaker units if done right) but rather, is based on strategy like flanking and group formations, then this is the game for you...
For me however, I feel like this game has almost TOO complex of a strategic system... I mean, I could probably figure it out, but i feel like the learning curve would take longer than most games I have played, like usually I can either charge right in and play without tutorial, or spend a couple minutes learning controls and basic format of the game, but I feel like this game would require between 10-30 minutes to truly understand what you are doing (and by that I mean being able to understand what all the strategic buttons on the interface do, it would probably be much longer before you could figure out how to EFFECTIVELY use them)
All in all, I recommend for either dedicated (not necessarily skilled, just dedicated) or Pro Strategy players who are looking for a challenge/more realistic experience
Casuals/Medium/people without patience should probably stick to Civilization or other games..
(people with medium skills could probably play this if they are willing to put in time)

I've never heard of this game before a friend on Steam recommended it to me. At the first glance, the game is absolutely gorgeous, despite its age. But our first meeting was marred by a s-hitty camera and bad controls (keyboard and mouse). I was told it'd be better with a controller but I don't have one to test it with. But anyway, I managed to complete the game with only keyboard + mouse.
The Chinese story (or legend) that it was based on, Journey to the West, is a personal favourite of mine; and so, I persevered and boy, was I glad I did. I got used to the control somehow (though it did still gave me problems, especially during fights), and I fell in love with the game. I didn't even take to Trip initially because she was very needy and all, but she grew on me. There was never a dull moment in the game and even though it's a face-paced game, the dialogues gave us valuable snippets and insights into the characters' personalities and helped the players' immersion into the story.
+ Loved the graphics; for a post-apocalyptic world, it was vibrant and stunning
+ Loved the characters, yes, even Trip, the damsel in distress ("Save me, Monkey!" ~ *sigh*).
+ Loved the dialogues, especially the light and funny banter between the characters.
+ Good melee system, though simple.
+ Great story.
+ Superb voice acting.
+ Very forgiving check points.
- S-hitty non-flexible camera, sometimes made me dizzy
- Average controls (keyboard + mouse)
- Easy and short final boss fight.
- Unskippable cut scenes
- Linear; path is marked.
It was sad to say goodbye to the characters;
. *sigh* I wish there'll be a sequel.
Anyway, yes, I was glad I gave it a second chance. It was definitely a fun ride. Would absolutely recommend this at its original price, and it's a no-brainer if it's on sale.

First, let me address the elephant in the room - story and writing. I will conceed that both are rather ham-fisted and low quality. I'll also conceed to being a little dissapointed by this - the original suffered from the same problem, and I was under the impression that this would be improved. Next, the graphics. The texture resolution can often be quite low, but it's only really noticible if you focus on an object. Otherwise, this game looks great. The definitive art style from the first game is present and better than ever. The increase in saturation compared to the first accentuates the painting-like style.
The world is, again, simply fantastic. If anything, Arkane hits home with truly amazing level design and worldbuilding. The world of the game feels real and lived-in, with cluttered streets and narrow roads. The contrast between Dunwall and Karnaca is immediately noticable. It truly feels like traveling from the dreary, oppressive weather of the British Isles to the sunbleached Mediteranian.
My initial concern with the game was the selectable players. It's a problem present in MOBAs as well - how do you ensure the different characters are unique yet balanced? After spending way too many hours playing as both Corvo and Emily, I can assure you that Arkane hit the nail on the head. Every power in the game is viable in its own way, and many are interchangable in certain circumstances. Even playing as Corvo, the last game's protagonist, the game felt fresh. Every power has niche uses to explore accross your playthrough, and when used properly, you become a force to be reckoned with.
The play-your-way feature of the first game is stronger than ever. There are many changes to the ending depending on how you play, as opposed to the first, in which there were only really three distinct endings. In this game, your playthrough can end in a myriad of different ways depending on who you killed, who you spared, what you did, how you did it, etc. For replayablility, Dishonored 2 is even better than its predecessor.
The game retains its intense violence and gore factor from the previous entry. Killmoves often involve bloody, Mortal Kombat-esque decapitations and severings. The various gadgets, like the infamous Springrazor, evicirate anyone who stands in your way. There's a definite feeling of power as you take foes to pieces with only your sword.
While the writing is sub-par, the voice acting is superb. Stephen Russel lends a rugged, experienced edge to Corvo, while Erica Luttrell delivers her lines with the commanding voice of an empress. Erin Cottrell returns as Delilah, lending the character a haughty, infuriating tone. The only complaint I have is Robin Lord Taylor as the Outsider. Taylor is a great actor, but he's more suited to characters like Gotham's Penguin than the eldritch god of the void. Even the side characters are well-acted, with a good deal of inflection to their lines. It's easy to see everyone gave their all.
Overall, this game is a modern masterpiece of level design and artistic vision. After reaching new heights with both entries in the Dishonored series, I have complete faith in Arkane's ability to deliver masterful games.

As a final note, I have to say this: if you like adventures, you have to try this game out. It will surprise you from the beggining and keep you wanting to know more.

Platforming Action Adventure
Medium-Hard
In the world of Riptale, Dragons threaten to take over the world. You have acquired three arcane gems that allows you to perform attacks on the dragons with your sword. You venture forth on a mission to kill as many dragons and their servants as possible.
In your journeys you collect gold from slain enemies and destructible items on the levels. You can use that gold in sparsely, scattered shops to by different and arcane gems that alters the way your attacks work, such as a quick-draw dash attacks, double and triple attacks,  homing attacks. You can chose in which order those appear and thusly create new combos.
In your journeys you may also come across magic rune stones that alter how you play, such as making you bunny jump, move faster or having more gems but not regenerating health.
You start with 4 hearts and getting hit by an enemy or their projectiles removes a heart - at zero hearts you die. But luckily enemies and destructible items on the levels can drop hearts. There is also one heart at the end of every lelve.
Some levels may also have challenges that range from navigating a maze in darkness on time, not taking damage or killing all enemies in the room. Completing a challenge awards you with a trinket - a collectible item in the game.
Each stage has 3 regular levels and then a boss level. Defeating a boss grants a bonus such as more gems and more hearts. All the levels, except the boss levels, are procedurally generated.
The narrative is delivered through the intro and books found in library on some levels and books between levels. Those are entirely optional to read, but gives a nice insight into why the ruin you just traversed became a ruin or why the garden you just got through was abandoned.
The game uses a minimalist 2D art-style. The base game is black, white and red, but as you progress in the game you can unlock different screen filters, such as the "classic" filter, which is green and reminds me of a nintendo gameboy or a red one which reminds me of the virtual boy. The screen filters does not affect the gameplay and is purely cosmetic. The game is well optimized and will run smoothly on most machines.
The soundtrack is uptempo and upbeat and will have your adrenaline pumping as you slay the dragons and their minions and strive for survival. The sound effects are top quality and helps you immerse yourself in the slaughtering.
Riptale has near-infinite replayability as the levels are procedurally generated and there are plenty of different gem / attack combos for you to discover, not to mention that the difficulty is high, so even just defeating a boss will be challenging by itself. You will easily find yourself telling yourself "just until I die next time, just one more try".

I used to play Homeworld: Cataclysm and Homeworld 2 back in the day.  This is a very impressive remaster!  I been having a lot of fun playing this and the remastered graphics just look beautiful!  It's a great 3D RTS and I'd recommend it to anyone that likes playing RTS games.  The single player has a great story line.  The multiplayer has a lot of gameplay options that really make the skirmishes fun.

As someone who has indeed played the original (albeit never beat it since I was still quite young, stuck on the supernova research station level hahaha), I have to say that this collection is a MUST have and a MUST play for any and all fans of RTS games and great stories, not to mention it having an amazing middle-eastern influenced soundtrack, and really cool space ship designs. Yes, the HW1 remaster does have issues with it's strike craft AI being really stupid at times because of issues with remaking HW1 with the HW2 engine but that won't hurt your overall enjoyment of the game; it was still quite the enjoyable experience (the HW2 remaster works just fine). And in addition, if you're a veteran and are stubborn to accept crappy HW1 strike craft AI, they've even bundled the original HW1 and 2 with this deal! It CAN be quite challenging to newcomers but you can easily learn from initial mistakes and adapt.
A few tips for new players:
general:
-remember that resources and your fleet are persistent, meaning they carry through each level in both HW 1 and 2's campaigns; try not to loose too many ships or waste too many resources or else you could be setting yourself up to being forced to restart from the very beginning
-in the remaster, any resources you have not yet harvested in a level by the end of the level will automatically be added to your resource unit count once you hyperspace to the next level, so no need waiting for your collectors, if you've developed that habit as veteran HW player.
HW1:
-USE SALVAGE CORVETTES; I cannot stress how important capturing ships is. Capture as often as possible and in this priority order: Heavy cruisers>destroyers(any type)>ion cannon frigates>assault or support frigates. Heck, capture a few turanic raider corvettes in the earlier levels. Early in the game when you're really strapped for resources, capturing is the best way to acquire a powerful fleet.
-stop using fighters all together other than bombers when you're at late/end game in the campaign: as I have stated, fighter AI in HW 1 remastered is quite dumb, and I've literally had an entire wing of 30-40 defenders wiped out in seconds. Bombers are still somewhat useful for adding additional damage when attacking capital ships however. For all strike craft vs. strike craft engagements in late/endgame, you should be using purely multigun corvettes.
-take advantage of the time the game gives you when you've cleared the level and rebuild any lost ships before you hyperspace to the next level. Many levels in this game pits you against massive forces right from the start of the level and you will want to be very prepared for anything. You will not have this luxury for the most part in HW2, btw.
HW2:
-Flak frigates, marine frigates, defense field frigates, proximity sensor probes, and sensor distortion probes are completely useless; do NOT invest/use them. Capturing in HW2 is pretty much useless, since anything and everything can and will shoot down marine frigates in time while they are boarding an enemy ship, but unfortunately some levels require you to use one to fulfill mission objectives, in which you should build them for that and then retire immediately afterwards and use that space for an ion or torpedo frigate instead. Same goes for that defense field frigate which has a virtually useless shield ability that lasts like 5 seconds, but you will need 2 of them for this one mission objective in this one level, so likewise, retire them when you're done with them.
-Use carriers more: HW2 does not have support frigates nor effective salvaging ships, so you'll have to approach this game a bit differently in general. I highly recommend sending out a carrier behind your main fleet to act as a repair station/support frigate to repair strike craft wings and to also keep building/supplying fresh new ships to your main fighting groups because unlike in HW1, you will be building most of your fleet on  your own instead of capturing.
-delay mission objectives whenever possible to rebuild your fleet: having your fleet at full maxed out fighting power is important more than ever now with how much salvaging sucks in this compared to HW1. You do gain alot more resources alot more quickly so you should almost always have the full 14 fighter squadrons, 12 corvette squadrons, 21 frigates, and later on 5 destroyers and 2 battlecruisers cap, or at least keep it that way whenever possible (and before the final mission at least, have the cap of 4 carriers, trust me, you'll be thanking me in the final mission).
-strike craft are actually VERY good this time, so DO NOT hesistate to use interceptors and bombers. Use the pulsar gunships in conjunction with bombers to attack frigates and capital ships but also against corvettes whenever needed.
-always pick torpedo frigates over flak frigates, like, ALWAYS; flak frigates suck.
anyways, tl;dr,  I LOVE homeworld and I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I really hope gearbox decides to do HW cataclysm in the future even if they lost source code and would have to rebuild the assets from scratch; the beast and kiith somtaw were badass.

Amazing action adventure game, although not without some flaws. Its most compelling aspects are the story, voice acting and world design. The game is set in post-apocalyptic USA and looks amazing. The destroyed remnants of modern civilization are overrun by vibrant plant life and the world looks absolutely gorgeous. The story was written by Alex Garland (author of The Beach and screenwriter of 28 Days Later, Sunshine, Dredd) and the player character is voiced by Andy Serkis (who did a great job and should totally be in more games). If you're the kind of person who plays games for the story, give this game a try, it's really great. There's quite a lot of platforming, frequently involving puzzles which are mostly not very difficult to solve. The combat is pretty decent: your weapon is a staff that serves both as a melee weapon and a long-range weapon, providing a variety of options for dealing with enemies. In the DLC you can play as a different character with a completely different combat style and powers.
The less great aspects of the game are the rather linear nature of the levels and the stupid checkpoint system which will put you before the cutscene (some of which are completely unskippable) if you reload the game, but if you die the game will restart from the point after the cutscene. Makes no sense. Another thing that makes no sense is the forced camera in many situations where it's not needed to highlight an important area or path (since it's hard to get lost in the levels anyway), so it's just mildly annoying for no reason. But other than that, the game is a very enjoyable experience and a must for fans of good storytelling in games.

This game cannot be praised well enough by a pesant like myself but I will atempt to give a decent review of the game.
When it comes to telling an engrosing story, very few games come close as this, the environments are breathtaking, the characters are flawed and are portraid as real and emotional. There are moments early on that make you feel resentful for being forced into a caretaker roll on an "escort mission," but that is an important part of the story telling.
As the game progresses you start to forget that you are a slave, you become attached to the one who holds your life in their hands, you are afraid of harm beffaling the one person who has taken your freedom, and you choose to be the guardian. This is organic story telling that to some gamers not having choises or playing a linier game takes away the feeling of exploration and freedom.
While being a linear game, it does lead one event to another in a fluid and imersive progression.  I would place this game high on a pedastal for the concept alone, and the concept came together in a perfectly voice acted, immersive engrosing story with some of the most mature content in any game I have ever played. This game tells a story of genocide, slavery, the cost of freedome, the fear of isolation, and Stockholm syndrom.
It is by far the most original game that has come out in a very long time, and that made so many gamers over look a game that should be in every gamers library.

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is the 2010 action-adventure game developed by Ninja Theory (noted for Heavenly Sword and infamous for DmC: Devil May Cry) and published by Namco Bandai, recently re-released for the PC with all the DLC included.
Important to note: use a gamepad. Most are compatible with PC and easy to set up, it's a worthwhile investment, especially for games like these.
The majority of the time spent ingame is on a functional if barebones hack n slash combat system and "Uncharted-like" platforming system.
Combat itself is very responsive - the counter will always work, the evade has a nice amount of i-frames, and you never feel like you're working against the game, just with it. It is, predictably, marred heavily by its sheer lack of variation - you will be working with the same moves from beginning to end, bar a few bought "enhancements" that won't affect your actual combos, and enemy variation caps out at 4 with three minibosses.
Combined with the platforming that's completely braindead and nigh automated, and while the game never gets boring it's never in danger of challenging you or demanding anything resembling skill, even starting on Hard. The upgrade system ingame exacerbates this, simply making an already easy affair easier.
Despite the odd novelty shooting segment or "Cloud" platforming section, where you impersonate Tony Hawk in a post-apocalyptic setting (the most fun sections of the game), and the aforementioned minibosses, the game never has any "real" boss battles or sense of climactic moments. The game eventually blends into a continuous slurry, pacing-wise.
A gorgeous slurry at that. Every single environment in Enslaved is eye-candy, with even the more robotic-leaning levels managing to impress and becoming absolutely stunning during the Village levels. Animations are fluid and the camera supports it, with the game taking advantage of its limits. While the story goes from interesting to dull to absolutely stupid, the voice-acting throughout all of it is top-notch.
Worth mentioning is that the included DLC, "Pigsy's Perfect 10", is more than just weirdly good: it's almost as fun as the base game, a 3-hour or so romp playing as "Pigsy" with four gadgets, an unlimited amount of bullets, and more stealth-oriented gameplay. You can access it in "Extras", which is a bit out-of-the-way.
Unfortunately the OST - outside of the DLC's banjo-infested romps which never fail to get old - is boring orchestrated filler and completely forgettable, with a lot of seeming SFX issues on top of it; actions triggering with no sound attached. The game as a whole is almost hilariously glitchy - nothing game-breaking, but I've had to restart at Checkpoints several times with Trip falling through the game world or Monkey doing the monkey dance midair. Forever.
Enslaved, at its best, plays like the likes of "Jak and Daxter" with fast-paced combat and platforming, and at its worst, plays like a dry, dull AAA affair with railroaded platforming, forced cover-based shooting segments and blatant technological problems. Ultimately, it's worth playing and then some, but not without keeping the caveats in mind.
It's not a game you should be buying for the mechanics, but to look at idly while you skim through it once then forget about it. It doesn't have the depth or the variety to support multiple playthroughs and ultimately ends up a bit of a chore (take it from me). Absolutely no incentive to 100% it either, not so much as a congratulations message. Still a bit sore about that.
Keep it in mind when you see it in a sale, is what Enslaved: Odyssey to the West deserves. It deserves something.

Well, overall this game was okay. It is very much a console port and because of that, it suffered from a poor control scheme, and delayed control reactions. Also, that said -- they didn't update the lettering for the PC, so when you learned some more of the combat moves, you had to fumble around through trial and error to figure out how to use some of them. Also, you cannot remap the controls.
Jumping, climbing and combat all suffered greatly due to the odd camera angles you get for the entire game. Often running one direction until you round a corner and then your camera angle changes, making you go in a another direction you didn't want to go. Jumping and climbing also suffered because you had to really point the character exactly in the right direction or you would not make the jump from one flashy hook point to another.
Also, being tethered to your sidekick was immense pain because you really didn't get to explore your surroundings as much. This was really irritating because you need to collect little orbs to upgrade your character. Also, there will be times you need to save your sidekick, but if you don't really realize you need to, she dies and then so do you.
This is also very much a check point style game, and you'll often repeat sections over and over because of one reason or another. Not usually a big deal unless there is a cut scene, which you CANNOT skip.
On the other side of things, combat wasn't too bad in general aside from not being able to use all the moves. The shooting mechanic was also okay, but was only really useful more toward the end of them game.
The story line was interesting and the environments were kind of neat. Overgrown New York City was an interesting idea, would have been better if they could have done more with it. Also, another section of the game they could have done more with would be when you get to ride the "cloud" hover  device, the control for that was well done and enjoyable.
The game itself is kind of short, finished in less than eight(8) hours according to steam. I got this game way back on the summer sale at a pretty steep price cut. Would I buy this game at it's current price of $20USD -- no, I wouldn't.

I remember being intrigued by Enslaved way back in the day of it's original release on PS3 and X360 (I owned Sony's console at the time). Having heard positive things aobut it made me try the demo out, and it, in turn, wetted my appetite for the full game. But somehow I only managed to play this game now, years later, and on PC. It started great, but slowly got more and more disappointing almost in every aspect.
The beginnings are strong - quite unique concept of interaction between two characters with active and passive roles, great location design and interesting world, seasoned with a bit of character development (through upgrades). Sadly, none of this ever develops past what you see in the first 30% of the game. Combat quickly becomes repetetive and feels stiff, platforming is straight up brain-dead, enemies lack diversity (and there are only two unique boss fights throughout the campaign) and character development never really manages to get interesting story-wise. The ending feels glued on, and while it attempts to round off the game while also introducing a twist, it falls flat on it's face by feeling really, really out of context.
The game manages to present the player with reasonably diverse environments throughout the campaign, though I couldn't shake the feeling that the further I got, the less inspired they were. Game's visuals are also compromised by some gnarly texturework at various spots, shadowing glitches and one of the poorest motion blur implementations I've seen (it's luckily possible to turn it off) and 30fps, highly compressed FMV's that litter the campaign. Dialogue is well done, but it's coupled with awkward lip sync and character animations - I don't really know where all that motion capture Ninja Theory bragged about is utilised. And finally - the camera has really narrow FOV, which sometimes caused confiusion for me (it tends to get stuck and perform rapid rotations on it's own), and there is no way to adjust all that.
All in all - I am very disappointed by Enslaved. I've finished the campaign once, didn't even touch Pigsy's Perfect 10 that is included because I really don't see a reason. As a non-interactive story this possibly could have worked, but all the "game-y" aspects of Enslaved feel half-baked way too often. With so-so quality of PC port, I really can't recommend this game. A real shame.

I had missed out on this game when it first came out, and picked it up as part of a humble bundle a few months ago. I finally got around to playing it this week, and I'm glad I did.
Gameplay-wise it's similar to Uncharted (or games of that ilk) - climbing/platform-y sections interspersed with fights with enemies and the occasional puzzle. The key differences in gameplay are a focus on melee attacks (which I prefer) and your constant escort/partner, Trip. She has a few abilities she can use to help you out (distract enemies, EMP) and she's also the one who can upgrade your abilities (which means if she's not around then you're not upgrading♥♥♥♥♥♥. The gameplay is solid, though not very challenging. The platforming doesn't even let you fail; there are some jumps you have to time correctly, but you can never accidentally jump to your death. The combat, on normal difficulty, never made me feel like I was going to die.
The setting is pretty cool - it's a post-apocalyptic world not unlike what the previews for Horizon: Zero Dawn look like. Things are reverting back to nature, there are antagonistic mech animals and humanoids, but some technology is still around and kicking. The story is decent, though I didn't quite feel like the concept was explored enough - the story was also written by Alex Garland (28 Days Later, Sunshine, Dredd) which was a pleasant surprise.
The protagonist, Monkey (not actually a monkey, it's just his name, but he has some monkey-like characteristics) is pretty great. I like his character design (if I were twice as big as I currently am and all muscle I would probably want to cosplay him), and he's performed perfectly by Andy Serkis. Monkey's partner, Trip, is also pretty great. She's a little damsel-y at times, but I like that they just establish that you each have your own skill sets, and beating up mechs is Monkey's. The chemistry between Trip and Monkey makes the first half of the game fantastic.
Then, halfway through, they introduce a third wheel named Pigsy. He is the worst ♥♥♥♥ing character. He's needlessly crude, hits on Trip in a creepy way, and kind of kills the dynamic. Everything else about the game I love, but Pigsy is an attempt at comedy relief that fell horribly flat.
In spite of that, I still definitely recommend this game. The third act doesn't quite come together (the presence of Pigsy and an underwhelming plot resolution combine to bring it down a notch or two), but even that isn't enough to put a damper on the overall game (and it only took me 7 hours to get through).

Factorio is a fine example of a well developed early access indie game. The game combines aspects of resource collection and management, base construction, research, puzzles, survival, and simple combat mechanics into one neat package. Factorio uses a unique concept of creating automated production lines linked by mechanical arms and conveyer belts to deliver produced resources to factories, and developed items to their player-designated destinations. This simultaneously gives players a goal to research and expand their production while also challenging them to make their production as efficient as it can be. The game gives players a variety of tools from simple conveyors and mechanical arms to wiring and drones to allow players of all skill levels to refine their Factorio efficiency as they see fit. Factorio uses procedural world generation that can be tailored to the desires of the player, allowing them to control the difficulty of the game as they see fit.
Factorio's development team has expanded the game at a decent pace for years, but has always delivered the game in a playable and enjoyable state for all players that are enticed by what it has to offer.

I really wanted to love this, and thought it would be a blast to go through: I liked the mod back when it was free and innovative. Sadly crowbar collective decided to "polish" the game.
The original decided to capitalise on the advances in Game engine design: interactive physics, environmental hazards, improved AI. It wasn't a remaster or a retread, it was a game that told the same story as the original Half Life, but had a distinct feel. Where Half Life was limited by Technology - BMS uses the state of the art. Where Half life has given us memorable moments, BMS had unmatched, meticulous fidelity.
The original mod, (back when it was free) made a few tasteful changes: Levels were redesigned, no doubt to accommodate the new and advanced AI, the assets and graphics got a facelift, and the gameplay had many more interesting puzzles. It was what Half life would have been if it were made in 2007. It lacked the Xen chapters so people were stoked about the new release. We thought the game would be even better and would come out in 2009-ish.
This version is meant to be that, but in many ways its a leap backwards. The FIrst few chapters play almost identically to the old version. The only differences are cosmetic: more detailed artwork, better animations - welcome changes.
However some time later you'll notice a general lack of polish. Occasionally you won't be able to shoot, for no particular reason - hardly game-breaking, but certainly annoying. A while later you'll notice that the game is poorly balanced. Vortigaunts miss more times than they should, even on hard, I wasn't hit once during my playthrough. HECU marines are even smarter, which would have been a good thing if they were not able to simultaneously survive three headshots from mp5 and snipe you from across the map. THe biggest disappointment is the blast radius, rendering grenades completely useless. Worse still the level layout hasn't changed a bit to reflect those shifts, nor were there complementary mechanics introduced.
With the way enemies behave in this game, and the weapons they're given, the tools of Half Life 1 don't work. If you have clever hitscan AI, at least have the decency to give the player original run'n'gun attributes. The game is either too easy, or too hard, and unless you go to the options to change the mode as frequently as you're in a fight, you won't enjoy the experience.
Making matters worse, the late game is overflowing with annoying bugs: missing textures, dynamic shadows that don't render properly. Even the most singnificant improvement - the meticulously crafted high resolution models are a big step backwards. They don't look good-enough to justify the time investment and the performance drop. And believe me I won't notice the fact that the Marines' outfits have actual 3d objects and not textures for their equipment if the helmet is glowing purple.
The sound design is a mixed bag, much in the same way this whole game is. The environmental sounds do a good job of remastering the old feel, but being very different. Gunshots - some are good, like the glock, 357, mp5, the Shotgun (personal favourite), some are abysmal - like the explosives, snarks, the hivehand, and the two energy weapons. This is quite a problem, since the most popular mods for BMS are actually gun sounds. Music itself is great, but the developers couldn't be bothered to adjust the volume. The monsters aren't that good either. The houndeyes look the part, but they're awfully quiet and their sound design is just dull. Bullsquids which used to make this odd "Meow" now barely make any discernible noise.
Volume levels are an entire chapter of terrible. The explosions are extremely quiet, the soundtrack is extremely loud and everything seems to have little to no dynamic range. If all of the energy that was spent on creating consoles we won't even look at, was instead channeled into making sounds more tolerable the game would be way better.
All in all this game was a disappointment. Fair is fair, it's in Early access. My above review should be then treated as constructive criticism and not like a rant. I must say the the game deserves its pricetag and is probably the best remaster of any game I've ever seen. However its a boring jagged experience, and as of now, its difficult to recommend.

Much has been written about the improved graphics in the game. The screenshots speak for themselves. But, unfortunately, apart from enchanced graphics there are few positive moments to notice.
The in-game speech seems to be recorded anew. I liked Makaan's voice. Fleet Command and Cpt. Soban are good, too. Karan is a bit… not like herself. But you won't probably notice that.
theme from the last HW2 mission I've been anticipating the most is just absent. All the other aspects of sound and music are ok.
Cutscenes are renedered in 1080p and look just awesome. But the in-game video player is implemented poorly: horrifying lags are obvious, while Media Player Classic plays the same smoothly even at x4 speed, let alone at normal.
That is all for the good part. Now the bad part.
First, despite nice textures, all the animations and VFx are left as it was. No new interesting additions (such as docking bays holding grip of resource collectors while unloading resource units or a destroyer losing a part of hull being heavily damaged). The repair beams and welding flashes stay as they were, while the soul craves for something more spectacular and immersive. Some of capital ships just don't fit the Mothership docking bay, going through textures.
. Hiigaran miners dock "through" Vaygr refineries, piercing the solid metal with antennas. Damage model is exactly as it was in Homeworld 2 — weird and unimpressive. And so on. Nothing positive has been done here since the Classics.
Procedure of taking a "clean" screenshot is spectacular. To do that, you must manually disable all the HUD elements and deselect all ships, and having taken a screenshot set everything back as it was. All in all, nearly 10 key presses are necesarry to make a screenshot.
As the game is about playing, not watching, and the Homeworld series is a thrilling experience to play through, in 20-30 minutes you will completely forget about graphics and concentrate all efforts and attention on gameplay.
Hotkeys map seems to remain at the initial state. Most keystrokes are 2 or 3 keys combinations, scattered all over the keyboard without pretty much structuring. Learning and using those is a piano challenge. Nothing has been done to improve the keyboard controls.
The campaign felt hopelessly easy. Closer to the end of the game (each one) the resource pool grows to 6-digit magnitude. That causes "why don't I build a full fleet of these and try them on something hopelessly well defended" thoughts. The overall state of the campaing indicates that by the time of release no one of the developers had taken a notepad and made a full playthrough of the campaign, marking bugs.
. I have spotted a swarm of such mistakes during the playthrough.
Enemy AI can make a grown man cry. No cooperation between ships is observed, and any signs of intellectual activity within the enemy ranks seem absent. Sending frigates wave after wave into the same minefield is just an example of a typical AI routine. The multiplayer AI seemed a bit better to me. In campaign there is none.
Ship behavior is untouched (or even wasted a little). Single corvettes are ineffective (due to special placement of their turrets). That concerns all other ship types as well, so the ships with high coverage ratio are the most powerful ones.  Optimal attack patterns or any means to assign them manually are absent: a bomber can grind a resource collector just standing in one place, but instead it will move at max speed, and on the second run won't shot a single round because of asteroids blocking the shot. So, fighters and corvettes are a pity to watch at (especially single ones, with no squads and poor coverage). Whenever a ship escapes to safety through Hyperspace, rest assured: all your forces will target the enemy base to avenge the humiliation. Repair corvettes and minelayers will go in the lead, as the most agressive and eager to fight.
There are worse things. Sometimes resource collectors just get stuck in place cutely blinking the engines instead of mining. Sometimes one of the ships boosts to 4000 speed or so and goes darting to the enemy lines or making enormous circles. My opponent once said his collecors are stuck inside one another and unable to move. Sometimes two corvettes try to repair each other, so they can't dock and go waltzing up to the uppermost boung of the map.
, and Assault fighters had the kamikaze damage compared to a full-sized frigate each (has been corrected on 05-03-2015)
The user interface. The only thing I did not expect of it is to get
worse. The largest button on the screen is "Menu" — the button to be used 5-10 times in total. The next one in size toggles sensor view and is
used, as it is bound to the Space key (which is extremely convenient). Right under it is an enormous control group panel that does nothing. Fleet build queue reacts poorly (especially the pause button) and takes 3 keystrokes to open (3 more whenever a build-capable ship is built or lost). The lower right corner is occupied by never-used basic action commands, such as Attack or Move.  Everything listed above and to be listed below is to be scaled manually: extremely small on dtfault and clumsy and self-intersected on larger scales. Build and Research queues provide as few useful information as possible, and have to be scrolled due to the command panel below. Selection and commands do not work near UI objects, selection mechanism is suboptimal, so in combat situations the UI is bound to fail you constantly. Building 50 fighters take 50 clicks. 50 more whenever you change your mind. Overall element placement inUI and credits sequence indicate it has probably been done by a secondary school boy in exchange for a day off school. There is (maybe was corrected on 19-03-2015) a place where one of the names was covered with the white frame around a picture. I haven't even started a talk about possible improvements of the original: robust and fast probe deployment, fast access to compact build options, advanced formation and beharior tweaks (must be implemented in "real life", not only on the GUI.
Balancing factions is a great work. Great work yet to be done, as the task seems untouched by the developers. This task is in tight relations with ship behavior, so I don't even know where to start.
to be straight and honest — this is an alpha. Totally raw; loads of aspects haven't received due attention. Multiplayer platform is good and priceless for seasoned players. Textures and models are great. Everything else has been neglected with or spoiled. And it is not the graphics what makes a really good game.

Let's get this straight: Homeworld is a fun game.  It's a space RTS about commanding large fleets and obliterating the enemy.  What's interesting is that unlike most RTS games, it doesn't take place on a flat 2D plane, rather taking place in all 3 dimensions.  This enables (and requires) quite a bit more tought into your attacks and movements.  Another game called O.R.B also does this, but in my opinion, it's not quite as fun as Homeworld.
Now, let's be honest, Homeworld is HARD.  Even on easy the A.I is difficult to beat (or maybe I just suck).  Also, the tutorials don't quite teach everything that is nessesary to have a good time, you have to play a match to really get into it.
Speaking of a good time, if you want the best good time, look no further than mods.  The workshop is full of them, and I can recommend a few, like Star Trek: Continuum and Homefront.  There are also a few very funny things you can do to get a good laugh.  Try telling a few Salvage Corvettes to steal a powerful ship, and just feel great about yourself and feel not guilty at all about doing what you are doing, you monster.
Overall, I recommend this game.  Or at least I say "this game" when really I should be saying "these games".  This is because you get not one, not two, but FOUR games in one when you buy this.  This means you can play the remastered or classic versions of Homeworld and Homeworld 2 whenever you want.  Just beware of the long installation time...
Overall Rating: 95/100
So yeah.  Why are you still reading this?  Buy Homeworld Remastered Collection!

ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS probably has the most rockets of any game on Steam. The mechanics are simple but solid. The only officially supported game mode in this early Early Access build is one-on-one against the AI, but there's plenty more planned along the way. There's also
to tweak how the game is played, which is pretty neat. The graphics are basic, but are beautifully stylized and suit the game well. Flying your rocket just feels
which is a pretty crucial thing to nail.
I was initially drawn by the similarities to Gimbal, another top-down space shooter. That's about where the similarities end though. Gimbal has a variety of different parts and lets you build your own ships, all with a unique way of handling. ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS puts everyone on an equal playing field with only a few tools, focusing on individual skill. Gimbal is a very serious take on the genre, whereas ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS is as crazy and flamboyant as its art style. Both have their appeal, but ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS is infinitely easier to pick up and play, especially on the couch for local multiplayer.
It should also be noted that you should have a controller to play this game. Keyboard controls are included, but the game is designed around the analog capabilities of the thumbstick. It's also far easier to hammer on the buttons of a gamepad to fire rapidly than on your keyboard, though you can make use of the aforementioned config file to up the fire rate of your weapons when you hold down the button.
Lastly, it's important for any Early Access game to have devs that respond to user feedback and actually work on building the game rather than using the Early Access tag as an excuse to sell something that normally would be decried for being incomplete. From my observation of the devs thus far they seem trustworthy, so nothing to worry about on that front. If the concept interests you at all, I'd definitely recommend picking this game up sooner rather than later to get in on it while it's still cheap ($5 at time of writing, $1.25 if you can snag a 75% off coupon).

username: Jet to the Stream to the Sam
text: Loved it.

Combat: I think the combat is best described as solid. It offers enough attacks and enemy-types to keep you entertained, but it is a bit simplistic. There is really not much more to say about it.
Climbing: On the positive side the climbing is very well animated and the sceneries look good. Unfortunately, it is impossible to die. This somehow takes the tension out of the climbing-sections and more than ones i caught myself just mashing the jump button until I hid the correct direction. So climbing is basically a distraction from the action-based combats.
Camera: Maybe you wonder why the camera is its own bulletpoint. The reason is: the camera control/movement is awful.
The camera is way too close behind the character, there is no lock-on mechanism and most of the time it feels like the camera is delibarately moving away from the enemy you are attacking. In the sum it is near impossible to have an overview of the battlefield or even to aim for one specific enemy. Even most games in the late 90's (when 3D-gaming was something new) had better camera movement than this. Seriously, who ever decided the game can be published with this camera should never be involved in game developement ever again. Yes, it's that bad.
Graphics/Presentation: I like that instead of modeling a brownish desert-like wasteland the developers were going for an overgrown-by-plants like wasteland. So everthing looks really nice and colorful. Another thing that has to be mentioned is that the animations are very well done. Especially, the faces of the characters show an impressive amount of emotions.
Story: For me it is a mixed back. The overall story is interesting enough and its presentation is, as mentioned before, really good. Unfortunately, the story shifts its tone half way through the story and trys to introduce some goofy/cheesy humour, which imho doesn't work out very well. Another problem is that there are to many cut-scenes in-between the battles. For me it just broke the game-flow if fights are constantly interrupted.
Summary: Enslaved is a casual game with a good presentation. Casual here is ment without any negative connotation. So if you are looking for a nice distraction and can live with the atrocious camera behaviour I think I can give a recommendation. Just don't expect too much.

It's over. I have finally completed this game with around 28 hours under my belt.. I've been so anxious to review this game because I simply love it. The graphics and visuals are simply stunning. Great fog display and color detail. The game's appearance is both tedious yet beautiful. Also the Alien itself looks intimidating and I've never experienced such a intelligent AI before. The Alien is unpredictable, there is no pattern, no pace, no rhythm. This make's the game more horrid, stressful and enjoyable. Every walkthrough has a different turn of event's and you never know what you will encounter. The Alien isn't the only threat on the ship, the Androids have a great dose of gameplay as well. This game is designed to put you in difficult situations and the outcome is usually a fright fest... for example: Android's walk at a slow pace, so you might assume you could easily escape their grasp.. but you can't run away since the sound will attract the Alien, so you're simply walking as the Android's are stepping on your heel's. Every decision you commit to has a consequence, either startling the Alien or you killing innocent people trying to survive. The hacking and crafting are creative and add their own special spark in the gameplay. Music was genius in it's attempts to fool you if the Alien was making an appearance or not. Of course Alien Isolation had some minor negative touches, the game was repetitive and I thought they could've added more to it's story. The ending wasn't as satsifying as I was hoping but this is just minor flaws and the majority of the game is executed nicely. Alien Isolation is a great experience with a mixture of emotion, fear and innovative gameplay. This game deserves a 9.1/10 and I HIGHLY recommend it.

Here lies the dilemma, (spoiler alert) being that this is an isloated area of space, and this is such a large space station, wouldn't it have been more meaningful to have military class hardware ?? The military would rely on such a station to be able to replenish much needed hardware if needed at such a time ..
As the player advanced to the last of the missions maps of the which it is found that there are more than just one Alien, military hardware should have been made available at this point in the game, because nothing would have been lost in keeping stealth because the Alien would still respawn regardless, perhaps even more because of the gun fire ..
This aspect of common sense was overlooked in this series, that an area could have been made availble to get the hardware to finish the job, and would have not made the rest of the game play or ending any different being that the military class weapon could have been lost in some arbitrary way (ie: no more ammo to be found, weapon lost in video preview after dawning space suit for final time, in some unforeseen explosion .. etc.. ) ..
This in itself is what was missing from the earlier Aliens series, and should have been enlisted in this one as well, (in other words the ability to actually be able to kill an Alien) .. the game play is basically centered on stealth, through out the entire game ..
Also a second play through should allow player to keep all said hardware, except military class weapons, the first here can be added the second (military hardware) for the game can not ..

text:
This game does an incredible job of creating the atmosphere of the Alien movies with stellar graphics, but that's where the incredible and WOW! factor of the game ends for me.
The first encounter with the Alien was pretty frightening and action packed, but after seeing the ♥♥♥♥ing thing the next 10-20 times running around it becomes stupid. What's even more stupid is that you can't damage the Alien at all besides scaring him away with molotov cocktails, a flamethrower, or pipe bomb; but only for a short while. I thought maybe blasting him in the leg with a .357 magnum would cripple it by making it slower, NOPE! Bullets just bounce off it.
After multiple encounters with the alien, and some being straight up dumb, I shudder at thinking how the game is at the higher difficulties.
The level design is hit and miss, some areas have a good area to move around in and hide while other areas are scant. There is a TON of backtracking in the game, this is somewhat annoying.
The story I didn't pay attention to at all, but basically the missions involve finding item XYZ, activating system XYZ, then leaving area XYZ. All this happens while evading the alien that will walk around the station impervious to damage.
-
If the developers made a sequel, I would recommend to them that the Alien be damaged by weapons, and have encounters be more rare to keep the fright factor up.

The game has a lot going for it visually, and does a very competent job of setting tension through details. However I was only able to get 4 or 5 chapters in before I was annoyed into quitting. The game had devolved into one long stealth mission. Which can be good when done right, I loved the Thief and Hitman franchises and the accomplishment of working through your surroundings to accomplish your goals. But in Alien there really wasn't much to DO other than creep from one side of the room to the other to go to the next macguffin. By the time I quit, the opponents were cyborgs and the namesake Alien.
Cyborgs are slow and slow-witted, more an annoyance than a proper enemy. I spent a lot of time sneaking past them, but realized it's just more effective to run past them and get to your objective. They have very uneven levels of intelligence, sometimes you can duck under an open table and they can't find you sitting right in front of them, sometimes you can hide inside of a closet after losing them around several turns and they just b-line straight to your closet, open it up then beat you. Just... so annoying and dumb. So maybe I'll try and take one out? Oh, I unloaded all six shots of this revolver into your face and it didn't matter? That's great. Why do they even give you the pretence of holding a weapon?
Then there's the Alien. Once he joins in, the never-ending stealth mission now has frequent random losses where he appears from nothing and stabs you for instant death. So you end up creeping along very slowly to make less noise which helps a small amount, except now you're moving so slowly he'll just wander over you and kill you because apparently he wants to kill you more than everyone else combined. So it's a slower, more boring death that takes way more time to get to. Despite the hugeness of the station there's never a moment where this #*(@ is more than a room or two away from you. Why is he camping my character specifically? How is he able to always be around me even if he can't find me while sitting under a desk the same room? Do I have some sort of Ripley connection to the monster that makes him so much more interested in me than everyone else? What was I supposed to know to avoid these obnoxious instant lose surprises? Riptale is a fast paced rogue-like action game where the emphasis is on quick movement and chaining combos. Fluid and simple controls make the game easy to learn and the fast fighting means it remains an intense experience throughout. The game is not without problems though.
Sometimes the enemies can hit you just as you're falling down to new room, and the black and white color palette - while aesthetically strong - can sometimes make it hard for the player to see what part of the scenery is background and what is a stationary snake ready to kill you. Also while the soundtrack is well made, a lack of variation meant that I turn the volume down a little more each time I start playing the game.
Ultimately whether you should buy the game or not can be summarized in two questions:
1) Is the game fun, and
2) Is it worth the asked price
I can quite safely say "yes" to both questions. In the grand scale many of my issues with the game are nitpicks, and despite sometimes being ruthlessly difficult the game never feels truly obnoxiously annoying. Plus everytime you strike an enemy down the sword makes a pleasing slashing sound, the game stops for a moment and you see the enemy get cut  in half with all the pixelated blood spraying around. And really that alone is quite enough for me.

This is a really cool minimal hack-and-slash roguelite. The combat is probably the most satisfying of any game ever, which is great. My complaints about the game don't even begin to overshadow how fun this is. For $5, it's a must buy.
However, I have some complaints with the game, and I think my biggest complaint is that there's no sense of area progression. Areas are randomized as far as I can tell, so your first level could be any of the game's levels. The red and white theme also makes sure that all of the levels really blend together. I played for over an hour and at all times I could never really tell you which level I was on or how long my run had been. None of the areas ever say "Level 2" or anything, so there's no way to know how long your run has even lasted. The fact that there's no sense of progression really hurts this game in my opinion.
The artstyle is a bit difficult to get past for me. Although it definitely looks cool, restricting the whole palette to three colors gives serious limitations which hinder the game's enjoyment. Having different areas be different colors would be a great way to differentiate them, which would solve some of the progression issue. However, I'm sure the developer is married to the style they created, so the most I can ask is to PLEASE make non-interactive scenery pieces a light gray rather than a white. It would be so much easier to interpret everything going on on screen if there was at least a little bit of differentiation between the important objects and the scenery.
There's a few other improvements I'd really like to see patched in. First of all, the D-pad doesn't work on controllers, which I'm sure would be simple to code in. Secondly, the antialiasing on the homing attack looks INCREDIBLY out of place compared to the rest of the tricolor graphics. There's also no way to see your health unless you get hurt, which I think is a mistake. I understand that this game is trying to stay minimal, but you can even see your gold at all time. Your gold count only matters when you're in a shop, but health matters *always*. So, that would be a good improvement.
The mechanic of switching out your gems is cool, but there's a few ways it could be made better. First of all, there's no way to rearrange your gems unless you're in a shop. This seems like something that would give the player more choices without affecting balance, so I'd really like to see it added. Next, there isn't much of an explanation as to what each gem does. I'd love to see a menu when you press select that lets you rearrange your gem and see a more detailed description of their mechanics. I admire the simplicity of "show, don't tell", but I honestly can't tell what some of the gems do compared to normal gems, even after playing with them for a while.
I really hope the developer(s) keep working to improve this game. The combat is so cathardic that I'll probably play this all the time, and I'd love to have some improvements to the rest of the game to top it all off!

Not a bad game by any means, but due to the flaws and not that much variety in gameplay I suggest waiting for 50% discount.
In Riptale you take the role of the swordsman, a dragon hunter of sorts. You go through randomly generated levels and hack/slash through the enemies. Literally. There’s lots of blood and when you strike an enemy, you really go through him. Non-boss enemies die from one hit, but you must plan your attacks carefully, because it’s pretty easy for them to hit you too.
-	Hitting enemies feels great. The blood, the slow-down of time at the moment of impact that allows you to start another combo.
-	Challenging Difficulty: the game is really hard and unforgiving, although if you mess up - you know it was your fault most of the time
-	Good selection of music and sounds. The music can get repetitive after a while, but it never felt annoying. The hit sounds are very satisfying: it’s exactly as you would imagine when you think about something alive that got hit by a sword.
-	Customizable attack combos: you don’t have a traditional attack cooldown. Instead, you have three attacks (gems). Each attack costs one gem, so you can do three rapid attacks at once. Gems replenish over time though, so you can’t combo immediately. The interesting thing is you encounter shops as you progress in the game, and those sell special gems that can alter your attack pattern and make you stronger. This is the main way to change your strategy and playstyle. For example, as you play, you discover that placing some gems in first position makes charging harder, so you put them in second attack position (i.e. your first attack remains normal, but second attack becomes homing, allowing to kill the enemy quickly if he dodged).
-	Collisions could be better. Occasionally you go through flying enemies without damaging them.
-	Gems are not recharged when you enter new room. If the game expects to have a fast gameplay, it’s a bit counter-intuitive to have player stand in one place and wait till the gems are refilled.
-	Aiming controls felt subpar quite a while: the 45-degree directions are fine, but enemies that are located at a different angle from you are frustrating to hit.
-	Slow-mo during falls could be useful. From time to time you get into situation when you jump down a platform and collide with a monster below (but there was no way to see it).
-	The levels are randomly generated. Traversing some rooms is not very pleasant due to a huge number of obstacles or maybe randomly placed stuff. The level compositions seems to be a bit broken and the gameplay speed gets hindered because of that.
What game excels at is the feel when you kill something: once your character cuts an enemy, you know this was for real. The time slows down for a split second and you just know that you’ve delivered a crushing blow of unstoppable force to something. That feeling of speed, action and being in the center of the events is something. Due to the other flaws and pretty simple graphics – I suggest waiting for 50% discount before grabbing the game; It gave me ~2 hours of good gameplay, but I doubt I’d return to it later.
If you love games such as original Ninja Gaidens on NES chances are you'll find Riptale a good bargain.

We all like to watch action movies. Well, maybe not all, but there must be a decent amount who have to like them. There are really two types of action movies that are made; smart and dumb. Smart ones are the ones that usually put a story behind the glorified explosions, and while they usually vary in affectiveness, you can look to movies like the James Bond movies and the Dark Knight movies just to name a few. Dumb action movies, the ones that have no story or just throw one in gratis, are a dying breed at best. Movies like The Expendables are some of the last ones to come out nowadays, and while yes, a lot of the time people want meaning and knowledge, most people just want to watch heads explode and♥♥♥♥♥♥blow up. I bring this up because Broforce is the second brought up into a game definitively. Yes, Call of Duty is kind of the posterchild, but this game has it beat. The question is, is that a good thing or not? Let's take a look.
STORY: You're a group of Bros, who head out to fight terrorists for Muricah and
liberating the poor and helpless and give them freedom! You go around the world, liberating people, killing terrorists
to save the free world from them goddamn communist terrorist scum! The story is the most shallow thing ever, if it was written seriously it would be credited to Rush Limbaugh or Bill O'Reiley when they were five, though don't take it too seriously and anyone with a brain could tell this. It's stupid and practically nonexistant, yea, but what do you expect from a goofy platformer named Broforce?
GAMEPLAY: Platformer. At the beginning of the level you deploy with a bro. You have to go through the whole level without dying or else you have to start over, either at the beginning or at a checkpoint. However, along the way there are other bros held hostage, and if you rescue them, you get their help as well as an extra life. While at first this is fair enough and it is fine, it get a bit insane near the end and honestly feels a bit unfair. That might be the point, but not sure, and this isn't exactly Dark Souls difficulty. Still, it is fun to play and when you beat the hard parts it is satisfying, so at least that. There are a decent variety of characters here, and while a few are just crap, for the most part they've designed them pretty well.
GRAPHICS AND PERFORMANCE: 8-bit style graphics. The pixel work on the characters is nice and the environments look decent, but they have kind of repetetive designs. There are a couple cave levels, a couple forest level, maybe a few more types that I'm forgetting, and thats it, other than a cool level for the end. Performance is fine, it stays at a steady 60FPS. One thing that does suck, though, is that there are some annoying glitches that end up forcing you to restart the level you're on or even have to use Alt+F4 to exit the game. The game is mostly stable but it still sucks when it does happen.
MULTIPLAYER: Up to four player co-op, honestly the only way to play this game. Played with one friend for the length of the game and a few randoms on and off for the second half, and it probably would have been a good idea to see if we could have gotten the random slots filled by friends, but that's just how things go with multiplayer games generally. It's fun, so don't sweat it.
FINAL VERDICT: If you want to play the equivelant of the American foreign policy for the last couple years, this is it. 7/10, if you got friends, pick it up. It's worth playing with friends only pretty much, so if you have nobody to play with, might want to pass, because the rating goes down a point or two. Find a friend or three and buy this game, you should have a decent amount of fun with it.

Homeworld Remastered is a literal blast from the past. When the original Homeworld was released, there was no other game like it. You'd think combat on a 3D plane would be complicated, but through some kind of magic the people at Relic somehow perfected it. Combat is swift, heart-racing and tactical. Nothing's more satisfying than hyperspacing cloaked ships right onto an enemy, only for them to find out too late.
Though, I feel combat isn't Homeworld's strongest point. It's the story. From the first cutscene, there's are waves of emotions. Fighting through the entire galaxy to reclaim your homeworld is a true struggle, and losing any ship along the way is heartwrenching.
The remastered Homeworld 1 is slightly different though. Being made in the Homeworld 2 engine has removed fuel from ships and classic formations aren't quite the same. Enemy waves during the final mission (of HW1RM) have a lot of down time, either due to different damage rates, large time between waves themselves, or both. The final mission is still as epic, but I remember it being more intense in classic Homeworld 1.
This collection is well worth your money. Four games for less than price of one modern game? C'mon... there's no question.

As much reverence as I have for Homeworld, this game feels like it's in beta.
Broken damage from ion cannons and capital ships, pitifully low salvage corvette cap, fighter pathing issues that will make you throw your monitor, dumbed down missions, dumbed down resource collection (rendered moot after misison five due to auto collect), dumbed down AI (refusing to use capital ships to defend primary missions objectives, not using gravity well generators, not using cloak generators), and most importantly, the game RANDOMLY HAVING MISSION OBJECTIVES GO BLANK, which renders your current mission unable to be completed.
That was fun, after I took three hours to capture the entire enemy fleet on mission 14, Bridge of Sighs, and my objectives went blank, refusing to let me finish the mission despite destroying the inhibitor array.
The game feels watered down and panders to the "can't be bothered to figure it out" type of gamer. Much as I dislike badmouthing studios, this is the reason gearbox is sketchy. It honestly feels like an EA product: well intentioned but relentlessly frustrating. If steam had better customer support I'd try to get my money back.
The pretty skins and good memories of creepy space don't outweigh the absolute frustration of trying to bumble my way through this trainwreck.
This is a very fun, low-polly game. The community is great, and the dev makes things fun even when he's the only one working on it. I would recommend it, and the gameplay is good.

Homeworld Remastered is quite possibly one of the best RTS games I've ever played (this is coming from someone that has put MANY days worth of time into the starcraft series among many others). I adore this game from top to bottom, the learning cruve can be a little high if you've never played a RTS game before, but after you get around to move ships and such this game really starts to shine. The amount of time you will put into each planning units movements and the sheer amount of room you have plan your next attack or searching for resources can be outright daunting but joyful all at the same time. This game takes it's time with unit speed just flying around can take a good while to just get from one side of the map where you located to the side where the enemy fleet is located if you use large ships as your main force.
Now onto the combat which to me is the bread and butter of this game besides the atomosphere. During dogfights the ships behave like you would expect but they also make for some very interesting plans in the future with the way you can come below or from above with smaller units or larger ships if you prefer and wipe out a enemy force.
The story is solid and I found myself wondering how I was going to overcome certain challenges that were presented to me. I really hope they start to make more games like this in the future, This is how to make a RTS game, fun and challenging all that the same time.
I highly recommend this game to anybody that is a lover of the RTS genre, please make more games like this in the future!

A:I is a terrifying experience that beautifully captures the horrific masterpiece that is Alien, while simultaneously creating a thrilling and anxiety-driven game that outmatches most modern stealth and horror games. The gameplay is encapsulating, simple, and challenging; the story and mood are focused, tense, and nostalgic; just the audio alone has done incredible things to immerse the players senses. A:I is the most deserving horror game out today simply for its ingenuity and reinvigoration of a rather predictable genre, but even more notably for its feats in outstanding Artificial Intelligence. The Alien, aka Xenomorph, is smart, unpredictable, savage, and seemingly organic, and the programmers who directly contributed to its success should be recognized.
A:I builds off of the success of the original movie to create the ultimate Alien simulator, and is worth buying for $25 - $50. In the best way possible, I absolutely never want to face off against the Alien again, or for that matter, any other predatory beast in real life. My poor heart just couldn't take it.

Is Alien: Isolation for everyone? Perhaps not. If you demand reassurance, telegraphed threats, predictable solutions, and an inherent, hand-holding sense of "fairness", you might find the experience too much to handle. But those of you brave enough, those of you tired of existing video game approximations of survival and horror, and craving a real test of your skills, instincts and nerves - will find a bounty of thrilling, engrossing, profoundly fulfilling rewards. If you truly embrace it, then during its most powerful moments, Alien: Isolation will probably make you feel more alive than a video game has in years.

After playing for a bit, I realize I should have waited until this game went on sale.
I'll start with one of the best things this game does. It does not punish you for jumping ahead or finding your own way to do something. The completely open environment and grappling hook means you can find just about any way to complete an objective, there is no guiding you a certain way (however, stealth is basically out of the question.)
Now the not so good things. The game is fun, but repetative and not polished. The control mapping for the PC has to be completely redone when you start the game. Things like Control being the back button in menus, why? And shift is handbrake, instead of Spacebar like every other driving game on PC. Instead, Space is the "jump out of your car and watch it explode" button. A minor annoyance, but remapping controls gets tiresome when there are about 4 different keys that will make you jump out of a vehicle.
The grappling hook is cool and very helpful, however, it seems like it fights you at the most inoppurtune times. Sometimes when you hook to the top of a building, he will automatically jump up on top of it, sometimes he will jump, not make it, and just fall, and sometimes he won't jump and you have to shoot over to somewhere else.
Finally, the worst part of this game and many like it, the artifical difficulty. Things like enemies calling in reinforcements. An enemy can be on fire, ragdolling through the air after you shoot him with a tank but he can still finish calling them in. There is also the impossible spawning enemies. You can walk down an alley, look around and make sure no one is there, turn around and be shot from behind. An enemy will magically appear. These things don't make the game more challenging, they just make it more tedious.

Total war: Rome II started out in rough condition, but after a year of solid patching culminating into the Rome II: Emperor Edition it has become one of my favorite games ever. If you are new to Total War, Rome II is a massive scope historical strategy game centered around the birth of the Roman Empire starting at 272 BC. At this time, there are massive amounts of cultures and conflicts with different people vying for power and for survival. Even Rome starts the game with humble amounts of land and power. It will be up to you to recreate the glory of the empire OR extinguish the dream of power for the Romans and have your own people dominate the world.
Rome II has a massive amount of factions (around 120) with 32 being playable! not only are there so many factions, but there is considerable diversity between factions, especially between different cultures. Greek factions (including Sparta and Athens) boast powerful hoplites, spear infantry with very heavy armor who have the ability to form a hoplites wall which boosts there defensive capabilities significantly. Rome has it's famous legionairies who can form testudo formation where they lock their shields in a dense formation making them resistant to incoming archer fire. Eastern factions field powerful cavalry such as heavy armored cataphracts who devastate anything on the charge. Nomadic factions have entirely horse armies fielding mostly a giant horde of horse archers showing their preferred way of combat. There are so many unique units and armies to face depending on where in the world you are fighting.
The campaign map is extremely large which is pretty typical for Total War games and has a "province" system where there can be anywhere from 2 - 4 cities within a province. There are many types of buildings  each colored coated ranging from city center(orange), military(red), industrial(brown), agriculture(green), sanitation(cyan), ports/docks(blue), temples(purple), and city commons(yellow). City center buildings are the main building and is present in every single city but can be upgraded to provide various bonuses (including more resources if that region has a strategic resource). Military provides the ability to recruit powerful units into your armies and provide garrison soldiers if the city is attached. Industrial provides mostly large amounts of wealth at the costs of food and public order. Agricultural building provide mostly food (in which your empire and armies would starve without) with a bit of wealth. Sanitation provides public order, some wealth, some culture, and many of bonuses depending on the faction. Ports are only available if the city is a port but can be branched to form military ports where you can train powerful fleets or trading ports where you can make more money. Temples are largely used for improving culture (culture problems can lead to large public order problems) and flat out public order bonuses at the cost of food. City commons are highly branched ranging from libraries (improving reseach time), gladiator games, wine traders, slave markets, and many more.
The battles in total war are the hallmark of the game. Battles are massive in scale and provide a large range of tactics to defeat your enemy. Your armies are divided into units, comprising of 80-160 soldiers in a unit (depending on the unit size selection). You can have 20 units in an armies and up to four armies can be present for both the attacher and defender each. Do the math and you can see battles with over 10,000 individual units that you can zoom in and look at fighting for their lives. After the fighting occurs you can see the carnage wrought by your generals or your enemies as thousands lay dead. Truly awe inspiring and glorious.
As far as tactics, there are stratagems available on both the grand campaign map and the battle maps. On the campaign map, you can move your armies into various stances such as raiding, defensive (where the army forms a fort), ambush stance (where you can make your army invisible to other forces and can ambush them if they fail to detect you), and forced marched which allows armies to move twice the distance BUT are guarenteed to be ambushed if caught in this stance! There are also bridges, forests, mountains, rivers, and other choke points on the grand campaign map that you can use to give yourself an advantage.
On the battle map, there are large differences in terrain including dense forest, hillls, desert, rivers, bridges, and snow to utilize to help your armies achieve victory. Bridge can hold off massive amounts of troops using only 1 unit, forests can hide units allowing you spring quick ambushes, hills provide bonuses to those at a higher elevation and also you can hide units behind a hill if the enemy does not have line of sight. Snow and rain make units tire faster and have trouble recovering, fog makes ranged units' accuracy lower, etc. You can always use the terrain to your advantage!
In summary, this game has incredible replay falue fielding so many factions where most are very diverse in terms of units, buildings, culture, events, and starting location. The province system forces you to spread your own culture, take strategic resources, and specialize/synergize your cities into maximizing your economy. The campaign map is highly detailed with many terrain factions to use when facing enemies. The battles are unrivaled and are extremely addicting fielding thousands of soldiers. Excellent DLC content with other campaign maps.
As for negatives, there are no faction intro videos like other total war games. The game had a bad release due to various bugs and glitches and blatant oversights (though almost everything is fixed in my opinon). End game is too easy even on the highest difficulties. Lots of DLC that is enjoyable but you have to pay extra money for.

The only thing you need to be wary of, is that you will have the best experience using a controller.
