TL;DR: Black Mesa is a flawed but good game, but Half-Life's BMRF is infinitely cooler in my personal opinion.
Black Mesa is...odd.
Personally, I think it does a lot of things better then the original Half-Life - the world is more believable, the weapons feel better, and the AI actually is (or at least seems) better. Sometimes it breaks though, like an HECU soldier will just forget you exist or the Lambda codes guy will just stare at the ♥♥♥♥ing wall until the end of time. On one REALLY bad occasion, if you load a save on a particular map, the AI will just break. (This is way in Lambda Core, so be careful down there.) Aside from that, however, there are a few intentional turnoffs.
First is the amount of ammo the player gets for their guns. 30 rounds in an MP5 magazine? Fine. 12 spare rounds for the .357? No, ♥♥♥♥ off, get out of here. 10 spare rounds for the crossbow? The Resonance Cascade wasn't worth this. Thankfully this is just one skill.cfg modification away, but that kind of blocks you from playing on (public) multiplayer servers from what I can tell, so...do that at your own discretion.
Second is the accuracy of the HECU. This seems like a minor thing. It's not. It's not a minor thing. They are going to kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Headshots are your friend in this game, and the magnum is the word of GOD. Too bad the game only gives you a maximum of 18 rounds total for it. That's 18 soldiers if you have the reflexes of a cat stocked up on all the mephamphetimine in the United States. That's a lot of meth. Personally, I think what offsets this is that the game is fairly liberal with health supplies, and soldiers tend to call out if they've spotted you a bit before they start shooting, which helps. Another thing that helps is turning "Always Run" on so that you can be that magnum cat I described earlier, meth and all. Personally, I hate myself, so I keep this off. Besides, even when it's off, you can shoot while sprinting. You'll just be holding down your sprint key while you do so.
The third thing that might turn people off is the voice acting for the HECU. It's admittedly pretty generic. It doesn't have that radio filter or "hoo-ah" attitude from Half-Life, or even the mod. Outside of that however, it's pretty good. The voice actor displays a lot of emotion and kind of makes you empathize with the soldiers, especially throughout Surface Tension. That being said, while I think Half-Life beats both the retail and mod versions of Black Mesa in one scene in particular, and that's the ending to Apprehension. The mod has the sort of Half-Life vibe, but it's way too overexaggerated, even for Half-Life. Retail has the subtlety, but it's a bit too subtle, and again, it could be seen as generic. Half-Life's Apprehension scene is subtle, but at the same time it's exaggerated just enough, plus it has the Half-Life vibe. Valve knew what the ♥♥♥♥ they were doing, I can tell you that.
Okay I'm gonna stop nerding out over Apprehension and start nerding out over something I've never seen a single person seriously consider at all. It also happens to be the last thing that might (but honestly probably won't) turn ANYONE off of Black Mesa.
The facility itself. Hear me out, this'll get weird.
Why this would turn someone off is twofold: the first is probably the most noticeable, and that's puzzles. Most puzzles in Black Mesa remain in tact, such as Questionable Ethics' surgery unit thing, or the Unforeseen Consequences box platforming charade. But there's a few puzzles that are severely dumbed down simply due to making the levels more logical, and I think the best example of this is in Residue Processing. In the original Half-Life, in the area where you regain the revolver, there's a puzzle involving a punch of conveyor belts and crushers where you need to have good timing and jumping skills in order to do it properly. In Black Mesa...all the timing is gone. You turn on the belts, you turn off the grinder (which has replaced the crushers), and...that's it. Personally, I don't mind this particular example. I hated this puzzle in the original Half-Life. It felt stupid and needlessly punishing. It's still the best example I can think of, however.
The second reason why this might turn someone off is because - this is the weird part -
In Black Mesa, everything mostly makes sense. Why are there a bunch of crates suspended over a canal? It's just a transitioning area for the crates to get to other areas. What's this area with a big door and a bunch of cars? That's a parking lot. What are these giant crushers? They're exposed generator pistons. You look at every part of the facility and you think to yourself, "Yeah, okay, that's fair."
Half-Life is...different. Why are all these crates suspended over a pit of nothingness? I don't know. How did they get here? I don't know. Where are they supposed to go? I don't know. Okay, what's this place with a bunch of now-dead aliens and a bouncy cancer tumour? Nothing's here, I don't know. What about these giant crushers? What do they do? I don't know.
I'll admit that Half-Life may be this way for gameplay purposes or because it was 1998 and technical limitations or something. I don't think that matters. Because either way, Half-Life paints a MUCH more interesting picture of the BMRF then Black Mesa does.
Black Mesa's interpretation of the facility is a regular, if very big, research facility, with perhaps a few strange areas (take the sector from Questionable Ethics [I don't know which sector it is, sue me] for example), with mostly normal staff. Half-Life's interpretation is a bit...stranger. It's normal at a
, sure, but when you start looking closely it quickly becomes a surreal fever dream. The staff seem totally out of it, even in the face of what amounts to an alien invasion. Like for god's sake, ALIENS are invading and all you care about is where the ♥♥♥♥ing DONUTS are?! The facility itself has so many strange quirks and confusing design decisions. Black Mesa paints a picture of a team of regular scientists who got in over their heads. Half-Life paints a picture of a team of genius-level psychotic druglords (with some regular folks mixed in) who ♥♥♥♥ed with TIME-SPACE GOD, and got their asses obliterated as a result. This, in my opinion, is what Half-Life will ALWAYS have over Black Mesa. I don't care how pretty your game is or how seamlessly you can transition between maps. Half-Life's team of maniacal psychos with a god complex will ALWAYS be more interesting then your regular pack of nerds.
That being said, do I recommend Black Mesa? Yes. Yes I do. It's really quite enjoyable, and it's interesting to compare it to the original Half-Life.

Hey! I am a member of TEAM ROCKETS so my review would be biased and terrible for you. But we would like to hear your feedback; we check the steam forums many times a day!
But if you want to know what I really think about ROCKETSROCKETSROCKETS, let's get *serious* for a moment.
I've been a game developer for many years. A lot of times you work on an exciting idea that seems like it might work, and a lot of times you work on things just out of momentum, and sometimes you wake up and discover you're working on something you should have cancelled months ago. It's sorta the way life goes, as a developer; it's hard to objectively see what you are working on as anything but "good." A lot of the time it's hard to even find playtesters to help you out.
Sometimes, though - rarely - an idea comes along that hits you like falling in love does. You jump out of bed every day to work on it. You can't stop thinking about it. The whole world gets more vibrant, and you see your idea everywhere. Everyone you show the early prototypes to instantly get it and also fall in love. You start gaining fans and all you have is a title screen or a doodle on a napkin... And they aren't friends or family. This kind of experience is incredibly rare, and I am stupendously honoured to be feeling it for ROCKETS right now.
I know I'm in the thick of it right now, and I still have those rose-colored glasses on, but I think I will fondly look back on ROCKETS for the rest of my life. It may not be my best technical work, it may be unfinished right now, and it may not become a commercial success (I'm writing this before the Early Access launch!), but by golly does this game feel right in every way.
It feels incredible to build, it feels incredible to play, and it feels incredible to be a part of this talented team.
I hope you'll fall in love with the game like I did.

OK, let's get this clear right from the start: I am awful at this game. I haven't completed it. I haven't even gotten close. I even died on the way to Majula, the game's hub zone, after absent-mindedly rolling off a cliff. Nevertheless, I love Dark Souls 2 and I'm going to try and explain why.
For more reviews, visit:
First of all, this game is hard. Hard with a capital fist-through-your-screen.* There is no quicksave feature, no regenerating health. The closest the game comes to helping you is through the strategic deployment of bonfires throughout levels and which act as checkpoints.They also play a pretty important role in the game's subtle and gradually revealed lore. They're worth looking into, and as the game's respawn points, you'll be seeing a lot of them. Oh yeah, also each time you die, as well as your character looking increasingly disheveled and zombie-like, your overall health is gradually reduced (thankfully, though, this process is capped at 50%) and can only be restored through the use of certain relatively rare items, aaaaand all the zone's enemes all respawn, but any health-restoring items wont. The game's one concession to ease is that if you kill an npc 15 times, it will stop respawning. 15 times. 15. Like I said: get used to seeing those bonfires. All this being said, the game is rarely if ever actually unfair; the npcs don't cheat or have dubious hitboxes, and although there are plenty of lethal traps, most of these can be avoided with a little caution. In short, if the game suddenly feels easier, you should be worried, its luring you into a trap.
*OK, so it's not THAT hard (I managed to take down a boss on my first attempt the other night), and most enemies can be countered by a well timed combat-roll, but it is definitely tougher than nearly every other game currently in the charts. If you completed the first Dark Souls, you won't have any problems with this. However, according to early reports, the new DLC ('Crown of the Sunken King') is likely to offer even veteran players a challenge.
As you venture around the kingdom of Drangleic in a bid to acquire the four 'great souls' (obtained by killing some particularly tricky demons) and defeat the game's mysterious end boss, you'll go through a variety of environments, ranging from beautiful coastal villages, like Majula, to crumbling castles, forests, grimy tunnels and desert settlements. The game is beautiful and more than makes up for its predecessor's shortcomings in the graphics department, which suffered at the hands of an appalling PC port devoid of even the most basic graphics options. Dark Souls 2 comes with the full set of graphical options that you'd expect of any modern PC game, and puts them to great effect.
However, you'll rarely have the opportunity to spend time gazing at the beautifully rendered sunsets, as the game will pit you against a whole host of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, err, enemies. These range from undead soldiers, to fire-breathing basilisks, to iron-clad monstrosities, dwarfs (of a sort) and even greatsword-wielding elephants. They will all kill you. Many times. Then there are the bosses, drawn from a cast of demonic freaks, giants, and powerful warriors. These will also, with the possible exceptions of the Last Giant and Dragon Rider (who were fairly feeble even by my inept standards), kill you many, many times. Yet despite this, Dark Souls 2 is still thoroughly addictive. The exhilaration of killing a boss or surviving a level is unmatched by anything else I've played in years. In an era where games are generally so dumbed-down and tutorial-laden that they feel the need to include special hardmodes (see Bioshock Infinite's 1995 mode for reference), it's genuinely refreshing to encounter something specifically designed to present a challenge. And the challenge is addictive. Bosses have to be learned - you can't just run in a hold down the attack button. Mastering a boss provides such a powerful sense of achievement that it more than makes up for the repetitive deaths.
As well as the challenge, the other huge draw that Dark Souls 2 and its predecessor have is the overwhelming sense of place and atmosphere. Unlike many games which try to constantly bombard you with lore or background, Dark Souls puts you on a drip feed, barely giving you enough to know what's going on. The game is like a drug dealer, handing out a few grams of uncut story, leaving you hankering for more - it becomes a kind of meta game in itself just to work out the plot. The game's npcs say just enough to provide a hint about where to go or what to do, sentences short and curt or meandering to distraction. They are, without exception, excellently voiced - it's almost a shame they don't say more. These characters, often forelorn or morose, add to the sense of decay that fills the game's atmosphere with their references to futility - they help make Drangleic feel like a beautifully rendered version of purgatory.
It's also worth remembering that Dark Souls 2 is a multiplayer game. You can summon in allies to help you beat bosses (although this does also have the effect of increasing the boss's health), and by taking up the banner of one of the game's various enigmatic factions, other players can be summoned into your realm for pvp. This is honestly one area of the game that I've left largely unexplored for now, not least because I have enough trouble playing it without real people running in and killing me. The most noticeable aspect of the multiplayer system is the ability to leave messages etched into the floor. Players can create these messages using a set pool of words, presumably to prevent spam. Still, this doesn't stop players from leaving innuendo-laden comments around every female NPC, 'Hooray for hole!' is one message I've seen scrawled into the floor repeatedly...
Dark Souls 2 is definitely a game worth getting, provided you have something of a masochistic streak. Players of the original game will notice a lot that's familiar and that may detract from the challenge, but it certainly doesn't detract from the game overall. Buy it. And I mean this in the nicest possible way: I hope you die.

The gameplay is that of an MMO taking heavy influence from the classic Elder Scrolls. Once you get past that you got a good game that the developers have worked hard on since its release. Most of the problems from its release have been fixed by now and a lot of base gameplay mechanics has changed.
I was never a big fan of MMO's and their very static gameplay, lack of movement in combat, cooldowns, being able to phase right through enemies. Classic things like that. ESO was the first MMO I've played that really wasn't like that. Using the classic Elder Scrolls resource system of being able to use your spells or attacks as fast as you can, only limited by the speed of the animation etc.
That on top of a world full of fully voiced NPCs and varied quests makes for a good MMO in my opinion.
The base game at its price is by far worth it if you like these type of games and the added "DLC" adding large expanses of land or even new gameplay mechanics that can change the way you play the game if you want it to.
I've spent a decent amount of time in the PVP part of the game as well and my experience has varied a lot so take that as you want.
The game does have cosmetic things available to buy and a few convenience items but nothing that will make you stronger than other players in any direct way. When I say this I mean things like consumables that raise the number of experience points you get for a limited amount of time or lets you access your bank from any location. But nothing that I would consider pay to win.
All in all, it's a good game, it has its flaws but your money won't be wasted if you know what you are paying for.

This game is visually stunning, tense (although a couple hours too long), and is Alien done for today's horror standards. The sound in this game is great, definitely play with either a decent pair of headphones or a good surround sound system. I'm really split between loving and hating this game. The setting is beautiful, the characters are interesting and loads of ideas went into it. Alas, some design decisions annoy me pretty often.
For once the game is littered with invisible walls. While the scenario would lend itself perfectly for a more open-world approach (and the game clearly flirts with it), the levels themselves are pretty restrictive. The game takes you by the hand and makes sure you don't fall off a cliff. Monkeyboy magnetically jumps to safe ledges and everything generally feels a little overprotective. It's hard to make a "wrong" decision and as such the stakes aren't very high. This gets especially annoying when you want to explore the level: Due to all the player-security going on you often cannot take a shortcut like jumping down a wall. Nah, you gotta take all the way back you came from.
And the other big annoyance are the plentiful cutscenes, which constantly interrupt the gameflow. There is no reason to introduce EVERY enemy with its own cutscene! You don't need a cutscene to move the player from one level area to the next! This leads to quite a stop-and-go flow, that i really hate in games. Maybe Ninja Theory just has too many animators...
It's a good game, but be prepared to be lead through like an 8-year-old.

(Note that I have spent most of my time playing the non-steam version of Factorio hence the low play hours)
This game is like the best of Infinifactory, Minecraft, Terraria and Trevor Chan's Capitalism all thrown into one intoxicating mix. Somehow this game is more than the sum of all it's parts too, the systems gel very well together into a cycle of driving your production forward which causes more pollution which causes more alien agro which forces you to up your military game which forces you to up your infrastructure and production chains and so-forth.
The multiplayer code seems to be very stable and robust, super-easy for a friend or two to drop in and play and no crashes or synchronization issues even after a full day of hard play.
It starts off extremely simple and familiar with an axe, some trees and a nearby iron patch and then about 15 minutes in you think, "Hey woudn't this be easier if I just built a conveyer belt to take that ore to my furnance, what could possibly be complicated about that. Oh I just need to build one of these arm things to feed the ore off the belt into the furnace. Oh the arm needs fuel... I'll just build another conveyer over here..." and next thing you know you are the proud architect of a budding Rube Goldberg creation that you need to defend from aliens, who have caught the first wiff of the fumes of your glorious machinery and have decided the planet was better off without you and your machines on it.
I can't recommend this game highly enough. Once you get a feel for the vanilla version, go check out the modding community. I recommend "Bob's Mods" in particular, they take the game to an entirely new level.

I started playing this game 2 days ago. Look at my hours. Look at them.
And this is my first playthrough. To be fair though, I'm doing my low chaos / clean hands / ghost run and it is usually the longest (save and load a lot). However, assuming that this one takes around 30 hours, we're looking at around 10 hours of each run.
Now if you're like me and planning on doing this in multiple ways, here is what we're looking at:
and twice for both characters. On top of that, there are two ways of playing for each of these items in the list:
Again, for both characters. So by the time I'll be done with this, its gonna be at least 100 hours of gameplay. And I got this game when it was on sale. Mind you, this game isn't a rogue-like or randomly generated in any way (well, exluding bone charms). I don't really see a lot of FPS games with a rich content like this. I spent around 100 hours on Dishonored 1 too, and I'm not done with it yet so do the math.
Right now, I have a higher-level rig for video games so I'm not experiencing those issues anymore. Maybe this is the reason why I was super happy with this game. Not only I've never experienced any spikes, crashes or gameplay issues but also I'm playing this game around 100 FPS.
For those who are wondering about my system:
Even though I'm playing this on a HDD, it isn't causing any stuttering or performance issues for me so I'm assuming those who do experience these are either running this on a bad HDD or not using intel processor. Otherwise, the game shouldn't cause any problem just because your graphics card isn't GTX 1080 but GTX 980 (at least you shouldn't run the game in 30 fps max.
Again, for all PC games, performance depends on various factors so there isn't one specific answer. My experience was great though.
Story wise, this game is way weaker than the first Dishonored game. I still haven't completed the story but I'm on the last mission and so far, the story isn't that interesting. Lore wise, though, it is better than Dishonored, mainly because it does a better job at explaining what exactly the Void is or what or who the Outsider is.
However, there is one level with a certain gimmick to it that involves time. The mechanic was originally from a DigiPen game called "The Void" (you can play it for free from DigiPen archive) that uses it the exact same way. I've been waiting for a sequel to that DigiPen game and this was a delight for me for fulfilling it to a degree. It is very smart, fun and very different from other Dishonored levels. I'd honestly play it just for that level.
I'm not gonna talk about the gameplay because its very similar to the first game, albeit more difficult and makes more sense (for example, leaning actually has visibility now).
Level design is both better and worse. It has more vertical movement now, which gives you a vibe of a more intricate city but I felt like we have less rooftops - which personally is my favorite aspect of Dishonored 1- as well as less routes to take. First Dishonored truly felt like there are multiple ways you can take, however I don't have the same feeling for this game. There ARE different paths sure, but they don't FEEL as varies as the first game.
Another addition to the first game is the variety of bone charms and bone charm crafting. Seriously, there are 50+ bone charms in the game and you can combine charm effects to extend their uses. I'm faster than normal walking when I'm crouching and carrying a corpse right now. I wish I had a third person camera to see the monstrosity :)
I still hope they make a thief-like game with breaking into homes and stealing♥♥♥♥♥♥though. My ultimate dream is Arkane meeting up wtih Eidos to make the best Thief game ever made.
I wrote a serious review for this game so it should count for my personal feelings toward it. I LOVE Arkane Studios and I played all their games since Arx Fatalis multiple times and to be honest, they're one of my dream places to work at as a newly-graduated developer. However, I'm not a fan boy and this game is very good in my opinion.
The major thing I didn't like about the game is the way levels feel as I mentioned above and the new Dark Vision mechanic (the pulse mechanic is abysmal). Other than that though, it is a worthy heir to the first game and I'm loving it.
In conclusion, this game doesn't deserve to be called a failure. Maybe the launch wasn't as successful however, the current state of the game is great.

I just want the few keys I'll be needing around the WASD and then skills/magic from 1-9.  I don't want t, y, u, i, o, p, [, ], \, g, h, j, k, l, ;, ', b, n, m, ,, .. / to all have their own useful function!
Being a completionist/pack rat, my bag was full after wading through the intro area They only give you 60 slots unless you buy the upgraded version (surprise.. surprise...).  When I get to a shop and try to sell the junk/crafting items, most of it sold for a whopping ZERO gold.  Well,I thought, maybe I can combine some of these mats to craft something.  That would open up a few slots. Nope. Don't have all the mats nor the recipe.  Enchanting is vastly different from Skyrim and provisioning (why not just call it cooking?) requires a recipe at every single turn.  The crafting system seems like it's geared more for mid to late game.  Too many variables in the crafting system different from Skyrim, and different means more new things I have to get use to.  I'm not going to do that when I'm still learning a new game.
I was like,"OK, as long as there's an auction house, I can still unload these without waste."  Nope.  No auction houses.  How is that possible?  I went digging around online and it seems you need to join a trading guild to sell your items in their guild bank.  Why, Bethesda? I'm trying to enjoy the game. but it seems like they're slamming a wall into my face at every turn.
By this time, I've had enough.  I just uninstalled the game.  Like I said, It's not the worst MMO, but it's not really "polished" either.  Maybe give it another year or so before trying again.

Homeworld Remastered is a remake of two classic and very popular games, Homeworld 1 and 2. It's a real-time strategy space game that is basically the best one to this date with no game to overcome it, in most peoples eyes.
This is going to be a thoughts on the game, my thoughts, as a person who never played the originals, and a friend who did play them and now playing the remake. Also, neither that friend or I have finished the game, just to note.
Both of us thought that the graphics are, for how old this game is, compared to the classics, it's beautifully remade.The ship models are a lot more pleasing and awesome, same with the background (space), and the UI is adjustable which is neat, but for me that UI could have been better.
The story, for my friend has always been great, and to me it is just great. The only complaint so far for the game is that me and my friend thought that moving the camera around can be a pain, not hard, just annoying, and most of the other issues for the game are coming from the fact this is a remastered game, of an old game, that didn't get a makeup of modern technicalities and controls that we get in most new games nowadays, which isn't necessarily a negative thing, but it would have been great if it were tweaked to have them.
So overall the game is great, for new players and for the fans, and for the price it has, for two remade games in one, with the mixed multiplayer, it's a great purchase, and a cleaned up superb old/new game/s.

ENSLAVED presents us with quite a conundrum.  It entertains us very well.  The characters, environments, animation and voice acting are excellent.  The plot is sparse and cliche, but it's no worse than many movie plots.  But that's the conundrum: it isn't really a game.  It's more of an interactive movie.  You move the thumbstick and hit button A over and over again to make the movie continue, but at no point is there any decision to make.  The only part that is a game is the combat, but this is mostly so simple that it would never stand up as its own game without the rest of the movie-parts.
I'm not sure how I feel about this new form of entertainment.  Yes it's good while you're experiencing the content, but the development cost must have been equivalent to a blockbuster movie.  I'm not sure if that is worthwhile given it has no replayability.  There are many games with low budgets and little content that manage to provides hundreds of hours of entertainment by virtue of the gameplay.  For games, fun is almost like an emergent property, not directly proportional to how much effort the developers took.  I wonder if this would have been as good or better as a movie or mini-series.

Well, this is a very linear story-based game. I very much liked playing through it.
On the downside, the game sometimes likes to force a camera angle on you that you don't want, and it also likes to quickly block off the way back or dropping you into a cutscene and when you get out of it you're somewhere else. This makes exploration for collectibles unnecessarily annoying at times, or outright impossible until you replay the chapter.
On the positive side, the bosses are not particularly frustrating (I've seen far worse), although the end-fight seems to drag on forever. The story plays along nicely, although the midgame surprise wasn't much of a surprise. And even though your companion isn't doing much she requires no babysitting, and the game generally pulls off a good feeling of cooperation between the two, at least until the third character joins the team.
Didn't like him very much, and I think that it might have been a better idea to either provide some control over him as well, or not add him at all. Basically, the game looses the coop-feeling at this stage.
In terms of controls, don't expect any platform puzzling. The game doesn't let you make jumps or climbs that aren't meant to happen, Which is probably a good thing, as the checkpoints are spread out rather thin (and, more annoyingly, you don't really know when the last one was. The game tells you with a little icon when it saves, but I generally didn't notice that.

This game is technically speaking one of the worst console ports I've played:
- Impossible to Alt-Tab
- Impossible to use the mouse pointer in the menu
- Impossible to change settings in-game
- Ugly graphical glitches with the shadows in the cutscenes
- I didn't even manage to change the keyboard settings with the help of ini-file modifications, which wouldn't be so bad if you didn't need to use WASD, the Mouse AND the arrow keys almost simultaneously
- When you unlock new moves, you have to look up on forums what keys you need to press in order to execute them as they only show the Xbox buttons in the game.
The second main weak point of the game is, as many others point out, the gameplay.
Platforming is a joke, you can only die if the wall is crumbling and it takes you longer than 2 seconds to press space and vaguely point in the right direction. Other than that, just mash the space button and WASD and you'll eventually get there. There's some parts where the idea was that you have to time your jumps to avoid fire shooting out of the walls, but at this point in the game you should be maxed on health and health regeneration so you can simply jump straight through the fire as it really is not that taxing on your health.
Aside from combat, the game is just way too easy:
- Puzzles are not really complicated so much as lengthy to solve.
- The camera most of the time points in the direction of where you should be going
- If not, figuring out where to go next boils down to "spot the glowing thingy closest to the ground"
What is infuriating about walking from place to place is that they've placed pretty much all of the experience orbs just a little out of the way, so you can easily spot them but collecting them is terribly annoying as you have to take a longer route every time.
The combat is somewhat challenging, but very repetitive and doesn't offer enough variety, neither in the range of moves Monkey has nor in the enemies he faces.
The story to me wasn't really as compelling as many say it is, I found it rather thin for my 8 hours of gameplay. It's mainly conveyed in cutscenes. Pigsy was the cringiest character of all time and Trip was little more than a sex object. I like Monkey mainly because I like Andy Serkis.

Absolutely recommended for those with nerves of steel looking for a unique first person challenge. Sitting at your computer, EVERYONE can hear you scream.

Normally I ignore Early Access titles, and normally I wait until I've finished the game before reviewing it, but oh.my.god. this game is amazing. Screenshots on the Steam page don't do it justice, the team behind this remake has made Black Mesa feel alive like never before, particularly the attention to detail in the level design (watching the game world slowly infected/taken over by Xen life is great). I'm just completely blown away by the level of quality in this title, I can emphatically say that Crowbar Collective has done the original title justice. If you love the original Half-Life, this will hook you start to finish. If you've never played Half-Life 1, but want to know what you're missing, and are perhaps put off by the 1998 graphics, this is the way to play the original campaign.

I was skeptical based on how long this title has been in development, but I've gotta say as a long time Half-Life nut, this is a very well built, refreshing take on a familiar game with some beautiful visuals, and solid presentation.
The team has done a great job recreating a classic using modern resources, and thanks to the physics and graphics upgrades, this is basically Half-Life 2 with better lighting parading through Half-Life 1...and it's awesome.
The Xen levels are not complete yet, but I'm happy to support the devs to facilitate completion.
If you loved Half-Life 1 and 2, you owe it to yourself to play Black Mesa.
9/10

It's been a really long time since I had that gaming experience that makes my jaw drop and makes me cry because of a deep storyline paired with beautiful scenery and music. Go figure something as adorably cutesy as Slime Rancher would manage to do this. I can't go into details without spoiling things but yeah, definitely a deeper game than it appears to be.

Slime Rancher is a clear example of a game where there needs to be a 'Mixed' review option. This is true of a ton of games, and the reason I suspect Steam doesn't include such an option is because most people, on average, will defend a game purchase they made (after all, they wanted it) and decide for a 'positive' overall between two choices. This is how so many games on Steam are rated as 'Overwhelmingly Positive' as if they are masterpieces when, really, they're just solid games with more things to praise than complain about.
That latter sentiment is precisely the case with Slime Rancher, but the complaints cannot be ignored. While the game is no doubt cute and very appropriate if you are a parent who wants to share in a gaming experience with your kid(s) -- given that the overall presentation, music, and so on is infectious and the definiton of unoffensive -- the game experience itself, if you are looking for something to really dig into, is going to come up lacking and even quite tedious. There are a number of examples to look at here:
1) Exploration. While Stardew Valley's exploration was fraught with secrets and dangers, Slime Rancher really doesn't have much of either. What few dangers there are remain easily avoidable with just a few dallops of water or some liberal sprinting, the greatest risk most likely just falling into the ocean somewhere. This is a little curious because the game offers a mode where the danger of Tar Slimes is removed as if they present a huge risk in the standard 'Adventure' mode -- a distinction which caused me to assume that something out in Slime Rancher's world was indeed dangerous -- but those Tar Slimes really aren't a credible threat so long as you understand the basic principle of not letting Largos near a third type of plort (which really just relates to your ranch rather than exploration). Also, though the game at one point warns you against going out at night for certain dangers, there is nothing dangerous about being out at night when any of the proposed threats are not at all threatening. In other words, what I'm describing here is a tension between the way the game presents itself -- as an exploration game with dangers to avoid -- and the way it actually is, a largely risk and consequence-free jaunt through a colorful world. Additionally, Slime Rancher's secrets aren't much for secrets. Gordo Slimes (the big ones you feed to nab further progression and shortcuts) are about the only thing you really have to find, with most of the secret treasures locked off to you without buying the unlock abilities (the latter of which aren't particularly easy to acquire in natural play as they require you craft a fairly large number of gadgets -- which many players aren't going to do before doing pretty much everything else anyway -- and in any case, whatever they contain can only be so useful as I have a thriving ranch without their help). The map, while appearing large, really isn't (particularly when you can sprint so quickly), and the 'puzzles' which involve shooting certain plorts into statues to unlock progression are less any form of satisfaction at 'solving' them than they often are the tedious process of running to your ranch, getting the plorts, and running back. Really, these 'puzzles' seemed designed more often than not to just take up your time, and that leads into the next issue:
2) The game wastes your time because it knows it only has so much content. There are two major ways it does this: 1) teleportation is limited. While there are some shortcuts, their placement isn't particularly useful. The more useful shortcuts take you back to your ranch, but not vice versa. While you can set up your own portals, the materials are very rare and most players, whether playing casually or just children, are not going to set up access to them without having already spent a lot of time in the game and, most likely, uncovering the whole map anyway. 2) You can spend in-game days just collecting crops/chickens and feeding your slimes, then tediously collecting the plorts and depositing them. This speeds up a bit once you can afford to make a portable market depositor, but there is no way to link farms and pens so that you don't have to keep doing this. There really is no reason why there cannot be an automated system for feeding, collecting, and depositing plorts in a single process when those systems are so simple to begin with, and when you've seen what the game offers in terms of exploration the reason for this becomes obvious: if the game wasn't forcing you to keep completing tedious, repetitive tasks, it would be over in a few hours (and while, yes, Stardew Valley is full of repetitive tasks, it also offers so much customization and additional activities that it redeems this, as is the repetitive nature of work integrated into the game's ethos). It doesn't help that the gun itself is much, much too slow to collect and dispense plorts when consideirng just how much time you waste on these repetitive tasks. I understand the speed for most functions, but there should be a way to upgrade the speed it collects small things like plorts at and there just isn't.
Other complains are more minor, like the 'story' being much less impactful than it thinks it is (no 'Stardew Valley' here, but still a cute little story and not that important to the overall experience) and the 'missions' very quickly offering rewards which aren't worth the effort. Again, many of these issues end up being mid-to-late game, but, again, that mid-to-late game is going to come quick. My play time is representative of two people playing, though most of the time (about 20ish hours) is my own. I can confidently say that at more than *half* of that time was just those repetitive tasks which I should have had the means and resources to automate early on. Also, for a game out of Early Access, the final point of exploration you come to (where the story of the ex-rancher ends) is very clearly meant to lead somewhere else, but doesn't. I don't know if everyone else might consider this a complaint, but they might as well have put up a sign that says 'Come Back Later for More Content!'. As it currently stands, it is a pretty dissapointing end to a fairly long series of mostly tedious tasks required to get there.
So why am I giving the game a positive review? Refer again to the first paragraph. For the price, it offers the charming entertainment it promises and is simply excellent for kids and adults looking for something relaxing and simple. It doesn't promise being this deep experience, and I know that. All the same, the tedious tasks, the time-wasters, and the inconveniences which do exist clearly do because their lack would make the game shorter than the developers want. A game not respecting your time when it so easily could is, ultimately, a pretty damning criticism, especially when the reason for it is to simply artificially lengthen the experience.
tl:dr - Do not get this game looking for a deep experience. Do not get it at all if you are wanting a deep farm-building experience like Stardew Valley, or any similar social features. Be aware that it is unnecessarily tedious and often doesn't respect your time. Do not get this game if you want even somewhat deep exploration which offers highly rewarding secrets, or for that matter, competent dangers. Get this game if you have kids or want a relaxing, 'cute' casual game, and though at least half of your time will be repetitive tasks, it is just long enough to justify the asking price for most people. Slime Rancher is a 'good' game which yet shows much potential but would need about twice the development time to achieve (something which at least leaves room for a sequel).

TL;DR: If you want an otome game that is all about the romance and exploring the idea of falling in love with the different characters... you're not really going to get that. It's a card battling game with a bit of princessy fluff surrounding it. The card game itself is fun and not super challenging, so if you want something you can come back to and play from time to time even after you 100% the game, you should pick this one up!
---
: Generally positive. It's a bit rough around the edges in places, but certainly is a game I'd recommend for younger players or those who are quite sensitive to more mature content. It might also be a good way to get a friend into otome games if they wouldn't normally play them but might play a card game.
: I can't think of any content warnings that might be necessary. It's rather G-rated. About the only "questionable" content I can think of is if you fail a particular battle you'll be [SPOILER - locked in a cage and kept as 'pet']. Neither the art nor the text implies anything sexual or violent about it. Rather, the princess is just bored out of her mind.
: N/A (?) As far as I'm aware, the creators speak English as a first language.
: A few typos here and there, but nothing glaring.
: Pretty decent. It's a cute anime style. A few odd CGs here and there, but effort was clearly made. If you like what you see in the screenshots; etc, you should be fine.
: It was a little amusing to see how they'd incorporate strawberries into each of the outfits the princess collected throughout the game. Some of them are positively outlandish. (Not necessarily negatively - just out there.) Some of the outfits are pretty nice.
: A spoiled and disinterested princess feels her position as heir to the throne threatened by an upstanding citizen named Olivia. (Olivia is herself an hommage to raising sim games, particularly Princess Maker.) She enlists the help of friends to become accomplished in about the only thing Olivia hasn't mastered yet - Prima, a card-battling game for (generally upperclass) ladies.
Along the way, she can fall in love with one of three gentlemen - her tutor (honestly, he's useless at his job), a thief/shady card trader (you can only trade cards with him in Freeplay Mode), and the prince her family wants her to marry. There is also a fourth "unlockable" love interest, a demon. [SPOILER: You win him over in the game proper, don't end up with one of the other three love interests when you end the game, and then in FreePlay, spam "Trade Cards" until he shows up instead of the thief.] The gentlemen suffer a bit because they're not given enough time to show off their personalities. The two characters I liked most got the least amount of "on screen" time. The other two felt bland, just because they were of a similar character type and, again, didn't have much of a chance to develop, even though they had the most screen time out of the guys. Even side characters like Lina, Olivia, and the demon princess were more fleshed out and distinct in spite of having less time on screen.
Don't expect much more story than, "I'm not letting Olivia take my place! I'll learn Prima and get good! (Maybe I'll fall in love too?) Oh hey, here I am at the huge Prima tournament and once that's over, that's The End."
Honestly, as a "story", the game suffers a little for being just that. There's nothing in-depth about the romances. No real "falling in love" stage for any of them and even the bonus stories don't do that great a job of bridging the gap. It all seems quite abrupt. I'm also a little bummed that there was no ending where you and Olivia decided to get along.
: On the positive side, she has a personality of her own. She's quite distinct as a character. Unfortunately, I find her terribly rude (sometimes even in her "good" answers) and self-centered. She improves only very slightly throughout the story. Fortunately, she does have her moments, but I honestly thought for all her faults, Olivia really was a better heir for the kingdom. I'm not entirely sure whether I was supposed to admire the princess or not.
: I sound quite negative about the game overall, but I'm really not. It's a cute game that's very light and fluffy. The Prima card game is the shining feature and clearly a ton of work went into making it run well and polishing the game flow. The fact that it's a game that I could let my nieces play when they're a little older is even better.
I know I'll be returning to Princess Battles from time to time just to futz around in Free Play mode. Prima's good fun!

Princess Battles is a charming, quirky, totally enjoyable little card battle/visual novel hybrid that despite a silly story and simple game play stands as a shining example of how creativity and humor can make a smaller title more fun than flashier games in the genre.
Life as a princess isn't all it's cracked up to be.  Between unwanted marriage proposals and commoners aiming to dethrone you through popular opinion, it's a tough life.  What's a princess to do when even her royal parents find her rival more praiseworthy than herself?  Card battling, that's what!  The premise is preposterous, but that's why I love it so much.  Princess Battles knows exactly what it is and plays to its silliness with perfection.   In this world, a lady's parlor game is no laughing matter. Tournaments, black market card trading, demonic overlords, card battle schools, all ridiculous ideas that click together and work mostly because the story never takes itself too seriously.
I love Lillian.  She's a spoiled, lazy and entitled brat, but that is precisely what makes her so endearing.  We're given a caricature who acts more realistic than most other "perfect" protagonists.  Even though she's far from the ideal princess, through the challenges she faces in her rise to
champion, she grows and matures, but never entirely loses that impudent attitude.  Oddly enough, her love interests make more sense for it.  Perfection is boring, guys want a girl with character and spunk, and Lillian has it in spades.
Speaking of love interests, the boys are appealing, too, in their own ways, though we're not given nearly as much time with them as I would have liked.  Perhaps another scene or two of dialogue and a little more development of their characters would have fleshed out their stories a bit more.  But I admit, outside of satisfying my own desire for experiencing the "feels" of romance, it probably wouldn't have benefited the game much as it works so well simply because it's not as deep or complicated as it could be.  That goes for the game play as well.
The game consists of visiting various areas and selecting dialogue choices between characters to further the plot with card battles sprinkled in.  The battle system itself is simple enough to enjoy casually, but allows for a bit of strategy to keep the player engaged.  A race to max stats against your opponent, you play princess themed cards to either increase your stats or decrease your opponent's, all while juggling your gold and energy.  As with other card games, success often comes down to the luck of the draw which at times can be frustrating, but the battles are usually short enough to not feel like a total waste of time if you lose.  My sole complaint with the system is a bug that does not allow your opponent's attack cards to affect your stats.  While this makes the game easier (although success is by no means guaranteed), it removes some of the strategy from play and makes Free Play mode less attractive.  I certainly hope the bug is fixed as I'd love to build and play around with my own free play deck, but it's only worth it if the card battles are working the way they should.
Which brings me to game length.  Free Play mode would add several hours of game play if only the battle bug were fixed.  The main game itself is rather short taking only about 3 hours to complete.  There is plenty of replayability, however, with over two dozen achievements leading through most of the branching dialogue paths and in-game events.  It took me a good 12 hours to make 27/28 with that last one eluding me, but I'll get it yet!
Despite a few shortcomings, I enjoyed Princess Battles immensely.  It's not often I am this impressed by a title that looked much less adventurous and entertaining than it proved to be.  The price may be daunting for some due to the short play time, but I feel I've gotten my money's worth given how much I enjoyed what's here.  If you're looking for silly fun with a dash of romance tossed in, pick up Princess Battles.  On sale, off sale - it's worth it either way.  I know I'll be supporting Nekomura Games in the future, especially if they continue to bring the same creativeness and humor to their other titles.
Bottom Line - Worth it for the humor alone, Princess Battles deserves a spot in any visual novel lover's library.  Recommended.

However, there is one level with a certain gimmick to it that involves time. The mechanic was originally from a DigiPen game called "The Void" (you can play it for free from DigiPen archive) that uses it the exact same way. I've been waiting for a sequel to that DigiPen game and this was a delight for me for fulfilling it to a degree. It is very smart, fun and very different from other Dishonored levels. Just for clarity's sake, I'd like to point out I played this on Hard mode and my review reflects my own personal experience. I was also not planning to write a review of this game until the Xen update was released, but considering it's delay (again) I'm not sure if I'd ever end up publishing one.
The initial sell of Black Mesa is really quite solid, and if all you ever saw was the first 2 or 3 hours you'd be impressed. It neatly captures the aesthetic and tone of the original Half-Life and polishes it up using the Source engine; whilst this means it looks a little dated in some parts, it looks a lot less dated than the '97 classic and perfectly captures the horror rampant in the facility. The sheer devotion to creating something that's faithful and evocative of the original game, yet memorable in its own way is something that shines right throughout the game, even in the later parts of the game. The tweaks to level vary from the subtle to the more obvious, but they feel appropriate when done, and even the more drastic changes made to a level's design never feel truly egregious or poorly executed. The soundtrack is also wonderfully done by Joel Nielsen, and even though this review doesn't recommend the game, I would highly recommend you go get the soundtrack (which is free to download too.)
However, once you scratch the surface of Black Mesa, the flaws become more apparent. The improvement in engine means that a lot of tweaks and enhancements were made to AI and level scale, without fully thinking through the implications from a game design standpoint. The HECU (Marines) could hit a flea from a country over, they're tediously accurate and have done 30 lines of cocaine before going on duty. Firefights are often reduced to cowering behind cover, and praying that leaning your head out doesn't result in it being turned into Swiss cheese. This problem even extends to the humble Alien Slave, the use of the Source engine's squad tactics and the Slave's quicker Half-Life 2 attack animation means that some early sections of the 4th chapter (Office Complex) can become an outright chore, with 2 or 3 Alien Slaves posing as big a threat as a squad of late-game Alien Grunts.
Whilst there is some design merit in having Gordon hopelessly outclassed by trained soldiers, the fact that the game's maps are now on a grander scale than the originals actually discourages a more cowering, Call of Duty-esque play. The spacing between objects of cover has dramatically increased and the game can be quite stingy with medkits, indicating that the developers desire a more aggressive, arena-shooter based playstyle. However, because the game uses Half-Life 2's slower movement system, the ability to freely weave through combat zones is heavily diminished and the aggressive AI will punish you for your foolishness. The cumulative nadir happens towards the end of the Early Access experience, in chapters such as Surface Tension and Forget About Freeman, where wide open desert spaces and hordes of stupid strong Marines will shoot your bum to Mars and back as you don't possess the speed to quickly evade their fire and move around the map, nor the appropriate cover to play patient.
I'm really torn on my further investment in Black Mesa, I want to like it because of the sheer devotion that has been put into this game by passionate fans who clearly care about the franchise and want to see it blossom again. However, this blind optimism comes with its problems, as the pure novelty of playing Half-Life 1 maps experience in the modern Source engine seems to be the only appeal. The core gameplay itself is woefully and aggravatingly unbalanced, the game is plagued with mostly minor yet cumulative technical issues and with the delay of the Xen maps yet again, I struggle to recommend the game in its current Early Access state.
Unless you're a curious HL fan or someone who is abhorrently disgusted by low-polygon-count graphics, go play the original Half-Life instead.

Graphics 6/10 - Story 6/10 - Gameplay 5/10 - Controls 6/10 - Overall 6/10
This game fell under my radar until it was ultimately forgotten by pretty much everyone. I generally like to play games once they've sort of fizzled out their popularity, but I'm not sure this one was ever received well enough to be defined as popular.
My first impression, prior to playing, was that this would be a post-apocalyptic, linear exploration game. I wasn't too far off from my expectations, which would be a good thing if the game was any fun. It ends up being a poorly scripted, hack-n-slash, with bad fighting controls and an anticlimactic ending.
The graphics were decent, for the time it was released, but the cartoony and oddly shaped character designs make the realistic set pieces feel odd and out-of-place.
I should mention that Andy Serkis makes a physical appearace throughout the game, and by physical, I mean "non-computer-generated", which also feels weird and out-of-place. He also does the voice of the main protagonist, "Monkey", although you'd never know it unless you check IMDb like I did. But, overall, the voice talent is pretty good, and to be honest, was enough to keep me playing.
Story:
The story starts with some sort of large ship transporting slave-filled pods in the sky. Then the main supporting character, and love interest, breaks out of one of the pods and begins wreaking havok all over the ship by pushing buttons on computer consoles and whatnot. Then Monkey breaks out, and we have some pretty fun gameplay of him working his way through the ship in an attempt to catch up with her. The slave ship crashes into New York City and our two heroes make a narrow escape. I enjoyed this first 10-15 mins of the game. Then it gets boring and repetitive. The story takes a few odd twists that don't make sense, but for the most part is kinda straight forward. The only issues I had with the story, was that the character motivations often made no sense, and the ending was pretty lame.
Gameplay:
Like I said before, the first few mins of the game are pretty fun. But overall, the gameplay turns into a weird combination of stealth & hack-n-slash, and becomes incredibly repetitive and boring.
Controls:
The controls weren't terrible. The game is definitely playable. But the issue I had with controls was 2 things: fighting and navigating (whch is the whole game).
The fighting controls were so simplistic. They didn't even bother to include some sort of combo system. There're upgrades you can purchase, but they don't improve anything noticible, and I ended up using all of mine to make my health last longer.
The navigating would get pretty frustrating, especially when trying to move quickly. There's a weird "sweet-spot" you have to find when approaching ladders, and ledges, for some reason.
Overall:
So overall, I would not recommend this game, simply because it's not very much fun. I suppose if you were to play it over long stretches of time, for example: you play for an hour and then come back to it a week later and play another hour (rinse, repeat), I suppose it wouldn't feel so monotonous. But if one were to do that, they'd have a hard time remembering what their characters were doing, and why, when they return to the game. So, unfortunately, this game falls short in the fun catagory. But, it might be worth checking out if you're an Andy Serkis fan or something, because the acting is decent.

There are numerous bugs in the PC version unless you set the graphical settings to maximum, including one where you can't actually leave a boss battle because the game uses high graphics settings for object destruction; and on low settings the wall doesn't break.

The only nitpick i have is that the vast majority of character models' eyes are all super space apart, like a bunch of ♥♥♥♥ing r****ded people, and that upsets me.

It's  difficult to recommend or not not recommend this game. I did play both Homeworld games, and i think that HW2 lost something of what made HW1 great : tactics, formations, and most importantly 3d manouering. If you played HW1 you probably noticed that in HW2 ships manouver only on a 2d plane first, and when moving vertically they stay aligned to the horizontal plane, while in HW1 they actually turn towards their destination (e.g. if they move up, they move nose up) and hw2 they only turn in one plane, and move up or down without changing their orientation (they stay parallel to a virtual ground). In other words, its not really 3D anymore.
Also, formations next to useless : they dont fight in formations. Annoyance is that ships has a tendency just do whatever they want - like you are capturing a ship they will quite happily shoot it into pieces despite giving them the stand down order.
On the other hand, there is a lot of eye candy. If you preferred the simplified HW2 over HW1, this is a game for you.  I wanted to say I dont recommend, but this is still not a bad game to play and i can't say i did regret the purchase. I wish they would remastered HW1 instead of HW2 as the main game. But have the classics to play :)

If you were a huge fan like myself you may be dissappointed with the First homeworld remastered game. As that was the main one I was looking forward to. It makes a great first impression till you start to realize that the hotkeys are now more complicated then they were in the past. So it feels like you are trying to dance with the keyboard. Having units autotarget friendlies and enemies is a tedieous task. The worst example is with repair vessels. Before you could tell them to fix any damaged ships you selected. Now they only focus on a single ship till you tell them to change. Sphere formations guarding a vunerable ship was a great startegy in the past. Not anymore. If you tell a ship to guard another. It would be distracted by something as a single probe and forget about its target you told to guard. Because of this I have the odd feeling that is why they decreased the number of enemy ships you have to fight on some missions. Because they must have been like  "Oh crap we made this game harder then the orignial to play. Maybe we should give them a tiny bit of slack if we want them to micromanaged every single ship. Also you know how you could easily select formation of ships in the orignal as well? not anymore. Now you select every single ship of that type on screen when you double click. That is all I found so far before I gave up and replayed the orignal to make sure my memory of how it controlled and played was the same. Sure enough the orignal plays as great as it always has but this remastered edition feels like 1 step forward and 2 steps back.
Wait a month or two before buying and maybe gearbox might patch some of the old gameplay features back in. If not we will have to rely on the mod community to help fix the remastered versions. Well 16 hours through and campaign complete.
Admittedly without formations things were a little more difficult, but not so much that it's unpassable (I just passed it!)  I played the original when it came out, and pre-ordered here. I can't say that without these features that this game isn't HomeWorld.  The story, the voice acting, the music, the gameplay, it's still all top notch.   This is what really made Homeworld.
So I have to naysay the naysayers.   You still get the originals if you need to be that purist.  Maybe they'll patch it, but the game was very releasable at the point it is today.  It's still a fun game that can invoke emotion in you.
For folks who have never played...
Homeworld was created during a time 3D on a computer was still in its infancy.  There was a lot of games made at the time that were duds, and a few greats like Homeworld.    The game did well enough to warrant 2 sequels and a port to Mac.
You play the part of a exiled race who discovers warp technology.  As soon as you fire up your engines, those that exiled you come and destroy the only home you had, the desert world they left you stranded on 4000 years earlier.   As the fleet, you are responsible for the last remaining survivors of your planet.  There is no turning back.
As you progress through the game, you research new ships, each with unique abilities.  Levels are laid out in a way where you have to put every newly learned ability to use, almost like a Puzzle.
If you've ever watched The Angry Video Game Nerd talk about how perfect Mega Man X is for teaching you how to play, through gameplay, Homeworlds puzzles are a bit like that.
One peice of advice I can give... Save.. Save often.  It sucks to have spent an hour trying to get through a level, only to die right before the end.

Although a number of bugs plague this game (pretty much all in the remastered campaign for the first Homeworld), I love this series. It is great to come back and see it revived with better graphics. If you are a fan of 3-dimensional strategy, science-fiction, and space battles, seek no further than the Homeworld series. Here's homeing that a third installment is in the works!

I see a few reviews about this game being buggy, and apparently I lucked out. The only bug I encountered was one that caused graphocs to appear transparent if I had something that could overlay my game screen running alongside - in my case it was Trillian, my chat client.
I guess I got lucky and didn't encounter any bugs other than that, save two random crashes during HW1 campaign, and they were both within moments of a save, so I wasn't even that mad.
As to an actual review, well, let's get started.
Graphics: Okay, so it's a remaster. The original game was pretty, and this is essentially the HD remake of it. Of course it's pretty. It's VERY pretty.  Not only is it very pretty, it's also not that system-heavy. My box is comfortably mid-range with a decent GPU, and I can run things pretty much full tilt with no frame drops or hiccups of any kind on an intel/NVIDIA setup. Space is beautiful, and I don't mind sometimes losing a couple of ships for idly spinning the camera around and admiring the view. Ship detail is excellent, and the combat scarring is a nice touch, though I'm rarely zoomed in enough to truly admire it.
Sound: Faithfully reproduced sounds and bringing back the original voice actress for Karan S'Jet from HW1 to reprise her role for the HW2 campaign both made me happy in special places. The sound of ion cannons blaring away at a target, my collectors telling me to expect delays, the pilots calling out a little too calmly/matter-of-factly that there's a breach in the starboard fusion chamber, or just that awesome warble of entering/exiting hyperspace... Ah, the memories that came rushing back. Sound is excellent, crisp, and nothing is too repetitive unless you're like me and reload saves a bunch of times if things go a little too far south/you secretly suck at video games like I do.
UI: Yes, the UI is getting it's own section here. Wonderfully redesigned based on HW2, however my biggest grips with the game is also here. Considering it's a startegy game, you will spend a considerable amount of time interacting with menus. These menus are all tucked nicely to one side of the screen, and stay until dismissed. Which means for me, they pretty much just stay there. And that's fine, because they aren't obtrusive in any way. Except that the selected ship list is too small at scale 1. Yes, you can scale the UI in game. A very nice touch. Except that, even at 1080p (since my monitor goes no higher) anything above 1 makes other parts of the UI waaay too big. I really don't need the menu button in the top left of my screen to take up a THIRD of my real estate. And that's at scale 3! Fortunately, there's a mod on the workshop right now that remedies this issue, but having to pause the sampaign to change my UI scale so I could properly select a ship just to pause again to scale back down so I can see things got annoying. If you're running at 1080, I suggest you download the UI resize mod.
Gameplay: Ah, the meat of the review. The gameplay is solid. Super solid. Like, really effing good. So you know how most RTS games give you units and you move them around on the ground? And you know how even in most space RTS games, you're still given a 2D plane? As if you were still dealing with the ground? Well not here. You have a full 360 degrees to move your ships through. That's three axes. That's forward/back, left/right, UP/DOWN. There's really little practical use for it in a tactical sense, since your sensors also cover 360 dgerees, and the direction of an attack won't matter so much as everything has the same freedom of movement, but it does allow for some very good strategic moves. For example, I played a friend who had never played homeworld before. His first game ever was versus me. I took it easy on a seasoned RTS veteran. I was only half surprised, then, when he showed up at my mothership with the fleet I SHOULD have had at that moment. I then grinned as my hyperspace module finished construction. I jumped to a nowhere bottom corner of the map and survived on mobile refineries and a carrier while building my fleet in secret, jumping to another random corner any time his scouts got near. By the time he managed to find me with probes, I had amassed enough of a fleet to jump eveything I had, including my mothership, directly in the engines of his mothership. His fault for not building a gravity well generator. His fleet, which had moved to engage mine where it was being staged, didn't return in time to save him.
The gameplay isn't all awesome, though. As others have pointed out, there are issues that are irritating to old fans like myself. Ship stances - aggressive, defensive, and passive tactics - used to divert power to weapons, engines, or keep it balanced, respectively. This made ships behave very differently. With aggressive tactics, nobody really flew around much back in the day. They just parked at optimal firing range and unloaded. This was a great way to take out isolated capital ships. Sphere up on a target and go aggressive. Reinforcements arrive? Fighter screen and defensive, watch your fleet suddenly scatter, cap ships line up and start orbiting, and fighters swarm incessantly. No longer. Now it is simply a visual difference in how the HW2 squads fly in their individual formations - which used to be a visual clue for what tactics fighters/corvettes were using. Also, group/fleet formations, as mentioned by others also fall apart in combat. The moment anybody is in weapons range, the formation is over. Every man for himself. Tactics don't change anything, and the only thing the formation changes is who gets to shoot first. After that, it just becomes a really pretty furball.
Targeting subsystems used to be hugely important. I can't tell you how many ships I saved because I sent bombers after the missile batteries/ion cannons on BCs as soon as I could. Gave my cap ships a fighting chance, and made me feel like a badass commander. Now it's basically  "1-A" (Select your ball of death with 1, press A to attack) game for victory with a few exceptions - mostly the last couple of missions/moments where you need to do something specific for victory that isn't "Kill everything that isn't yours."
Even with these issues, I would still pay $35 for this game. AAA games today don't grab me quite like Homeworld did. When the original launched, I put many hundreds of hours in to it. Ditto the sequel. I also know the modding community is very strong, and the developers are actually working WITH the mod community to make sure the game can do things THEY expect it to do. And considering there are mods like Complex, which makes things like weapon placement and individualk ship placement/positioning REALLY matter, not to mention adding so many new ships that it may as well be a different game... Yeah, this game is worth the price of admission. And it's technically 4 games, considering you're getting the original HW1&2 as part of the deal, though playing those is pretty painful by comparison. There's a reason I mentioned the overhauled UI, and the original IS 15 years old. Pretty for 15, but still definitely outdated.
Nutshell: If you want the hands down best 3D space RTS you will play this year and likely ever, look no further. Story, graphics, gameplay are all excellent, a lively and talented modding scene, and just a damn good experience. If you want my advice, buy the game, smoke some pot, dim the lights, turn up the volume, and go on a journey across the Galaxy like nothing you've experienced yet.

(Note that I have spent most of my time playing the non-steam version of Factorio hence the low play hours)
This game is like the best of Infinifactory, Minecraft, Terraria and Trevor Chan's Capitalism all thrown into one intoxicating mix. Somehow this game is more than the sum of all it's parts too, the systems gel very well together into a cycle of driving your production forward which causes more pollution which causes more alien agro which forces you to up your military game which forces you to up your infrastructure and production chains and so-forth.
The multiplayer code seems to be very stable and robust, super-easy for a friend or two to drop in and play and no crashes or synchronization issues even after a full day of hard play.
It starts off extremely simple and familiar with an axe, some trees and a nearby iron patch and then about 15 minutes in you think, "Hey woudn't this be easier if I just built a conveyer belt to take that ore to my furnance, what could possibly be complicated about that. Oh I just need to build one of these arm things to feed the ore off the belt into the furnace. Oh the arm needs fuel... I'll just build another conveyer over here..." and next thing you know you are the proud architect of a budding Rube Goldberg creation that you need to defend from aliens, who have caught the first wiff of the fumes of your glorious machinery and have decided the planet was better off without you and your machines on it.
I can't recommend this game highly enough. Once you get a feel for the vanilla version, go check out the modding community. I recommend "Bob's Mods" in particular, they take the game to an entirely new level.

Disclaimer: I'm assuming a long-standing familiarity with the Homeworld series here, for anyone who reads this.
I'm very torn on this game. On one hand, I am a long-time fan of the Homeworld series of games. From the moment I'd played the original HW demo prior to the game's release, I was in love with the game. So much that over the years I've wound up with several copies of it so I could play with friends who didn't have their own at the time.
Fast forward past Homeworld: Cataclysm (since it's not in this collection), to Homeworld 2. I was still quite happy with the game, although I was not so impressed with the new game engine. Also, I was quite confused with some of the continuity errors introduced into the units. Why were capital ships no longer capable of jumping themselves, with the exception of ships that could build the hyperspace module? In HW 1, all frigates and up were jump-capable without support. Why were formations and tactics effectively non-existant? They played such a huge role in carrying out a successful combat action in the original. The list goes on.
So, here we are today, with the Homeworld Remastered Collection. As a lover of the series, I'm thrilled with its existence. From a collector's standpoint, this is a wonderful addition to the Homeworld Universe. It preserves the story and music from the original versions, and does indeed do a very nice job of updating the appearance of the setting.
Now, the gripes...
First off, they made subtle modifications to the classic version of Homeworld included in the collection. There is a queue-limit, restricting how many active build queues per mothership and carrier. Want to queue a whole mixed corvette wing at once? Nope, you can only build 2 types at once, regardless of how many of each. This continues on through to capitals ships. Also, they removed all capablity for multiplayer. There isn't even a LAN option. If LAN was still an option, through some network trickery people could still play multiplayer, even if there was no ability to just find and hop into a game like before the multiplayer lobby finally was shut down.
Regarding the multiplayer side of things in general, I've only tried one game over the beta system (well, beta as of this writing, anyway), and I was unimpressed. About 15 minutes in, just as my teammate and I finished fending off an initial assault from the other players (6 went in via lobby, 4 of us wound up in game), the game just up&closes on me. No error, no crash message, nothing. Just back to my desktop.
Now, onto my gripes with the "Remastered" version of Homeworld 1. In short, it's just a mod for the original Homeworld 2 engine (as "improved" for the remastered version of HW2). Unit caps, insanely-decreased hangar capacity on the mothership, a queue that can only build 2 or 3 different things at a time per production ship, RUs required for research (and no parallel researching anymore, just one tech at a time no matter how many sections you build for the research ship), and otherwise the same failings of the Homeworld 2 engine that the original HW2 suffered from. Namely the joke they called tactics and formations. And the same, clunky&screen cluttering interface (I loved the simplicity of the original HW's interface, it let me spend more time dealing with events in the gameplay, rather than trying to wrestle with which panel or convoluted "shortcut" I needed).
As it stands now (and any patches/updates aside, will ultimately probably remain so), I really can't recommend the game collection. I really only bought it for the inclusion of "Homeworld Classic," and while mostly happy with that part of the collection, I still have some complaints about the changes made to the game.
Only get this if you have a similar love of the franchise as I do, otherwise you should save your money and look for something else to scratch your space RTS itch.

Dark Souls II is a really good game, but it does not live up to the lofty standards of the Souls series. My main gripe with it is that the enemy placement feels very lazy. Instead of crafting a level with enemies placed to create memorable fights and interesting challenges, the devs often throw far too many enemies (all of the same or similar type) into a long hallway just before a boss in attempt to seemingly make that section of the game "harder". It's tedious, frustrating, and just not very much fun. I also think the world itself feels like it's lacking a lot of the polish and depth that previous games had. The way areas are connected together often doesn't make any sense at all. There are some very beautiful looking areas, however, so I guess it's forgivable to some extent.
One other problem I have with the game is that the boss fights are just... brutally unfair at times, just for the sake, again, of feeling "hard". Demon Souls had two boss fights that incorporated multiple enemies (three if you want to count the Storm King I guess). Dark Souls had five (if I remember correctly). Dark Souls II has like... twelve multiple enemy boss fights. It's freaking ridiculous. All it does is drive players to do more co-op rather than grind it out and learn how to take the bosses out themselves. If there is any word I could use to describe Demon's Souls and Dark Souls 1 it would be "Fair". Despite being challenging those games were, for the most part, very balanced and fair. If you died it was on you. Dark Souls II feels very unfair a lot of the time.
I'm not much of a PVP player, but to those who play the Souls games for the PVP I would warn you about Soul Memory. It is a system meant to stop experienced players from grabbing late game weapons with a low level build, spending all the souls on leveling up the weapons, and invading new players to kill them over and over again. I guess it works for that purpose, but once you reach Soul Memory 1,000,000 you're basically free game to be invaded by anyone of any level. This means if you want to stick to a SL150 build and play with others who adhere to that SL limit, you can still be invaded by a SL450 player. This can make match making really unfair and frustrating.
Aside from those problems though, which are admittedly big flaws, the game is a lot of fun. I really enjoyed it for the most part. Also, the first DLC showcases some of the best level design in the whole series. Definitely grab the DLC if you can, it's awesome... even if the boss fights are still brutally unfair.
