Black Mesa is one of the rare games that managed to sadden me. But in a positive way. The context is so dark, humanity's future is unsure in front of the disaster of the Black Mesa Research Facility. The experiment that went wrong, the facility personnel getting slaughtered by the conscious-less invaders, even the US army special detachment, the HECU, can't handle the invasion. It really makes you think of how humans are weak, even with all of our means. Well I may be a person that thinks way too much, but I love this game.
Let's talk about the game experience.
First of all, the soundtrack is INCREDIBLY AWESOME. It's just PERFECT. It really plunge you into the deep atmosphere.
Graphics are decent too, the full potential of the source engine is being used. Corpses bleeding, realistic looking explosions, even muzzle flashs of weapons, reminds me somehow of GTA V. In comparison of Half-Life 1, Black Mesa really immerse you in the dark atmosphere of an incident that will bring apocalypse to Earth.
Enemies are quite smart (except for the headcrabs lul) human soldiers will throw grenades at you if you hide behind cover, snipers will shoot explosive barrels if you, again, hide behind cover.
The most annoying enemies are probably alien soldiers, -or alien grunts, whatever- who are heavily armored and well armed. They will most of the time rush you and try to crush you.
Weapons that you use are well-balanced, from a simple crowbar useful to open sewers to an unstable uranium-powered canon capable of tearing bodies apart.
Quite a long review, just go watch the trailer and hit that add to cart button. You won't regret it.

That pretty much sums up this review. Continue reading for more specifics.
Let's start with the good. Definitely get this game on sale, the story is definitely worth 5 bucks and once you get the hang on the controls and the annoying camera, you'll have a great time with it :)
I just ended my first session after 1,5 hours, because it's 2AM and I need to get some sleep. I planned to play this for half an hour, just to check it out, but the story and characters grabbed me and didn't let go. Even now, I actually want to go back and continue to find out what's going on...
The gameplay, however, is rather lazy. But I'm pretty sure you want this game for the story, not for the brawler combat, not for the "Baby-Prince-of-Persia"-esque platforming (you can't miss a jump, you can't fall - I'm still wondering if you can even die in this game), not for the (not really) explorable post-apocalyptic New York.
Bandai Namco is definitely a lazy company when it comes to ports. So far every game of theirs that I have tried, has the same issues that all come down to the developers being lazy c*nts wanting to make more money with as little effort as possible.

It's Meant For Console Gaming:
Honestly, this game is not meant for PC. When I started playing and the camera started going all over the place, I quit, plugged in my controller, and resumed. It does have an option to turn down the mouse sensitivity, but I didn't try it. It's much better with a controller, so I stuck with that. Since it is, it makes me feel this game was really meant for console.
The Good:
-The graphics are great, and I was playing on all low. I liked the idea of the plot of being a captive slave and escaping. The main character guy cracks me up because he reminds me of a monkey and a big cat cross-breed.
-The combat is action-packed, something I normally don't like, but it was so similar to fighting games that I felt right at home. The main character feels a lot like playing Kilik or Seung-Mina from Soul Caliber IV, so if you're good at playing them, the main character will feel very familiar.
-The characters look amazing and cool.
-I really liked the main character guy's personality. He seems like a very likable guy, and is caring despite his rough look.
The Bad:
-Like other reviews, the linear gameplay is very noticeable.
-The hand-holding and inability to fail while maneuvering makes it feel like a game for beginners despite the edgy and shiny look (and being on normal difficulty).
-The game's save system is based on checkpoints and autosaves without the ability to save at your leisure - and it's game-breaking. As I saw the girl run while escaping, I tried going after her to have my game clunk around and skip-ahead like a skipping DVD when the little autosave icon showed up. I thought it was because it was loading the background and effects since the game is quite detailed, but I was wrong. It does this at every autosave checkpoint, and I have to sudenly stop what I'm doing and wait for it to pass like nausea.
-Even with switching to a controller, the camera does as it pleases. You can move around the camera yourself to get a better view, but it still doesn't seem possible to get the angle right without running away from where you want to go, then make a circle, and come back. And it's still facing the wrong direction from where you're trying to go.
-The lady companion is annoying. She's always scared,
. Yeah, screw her. :P

{TL;DR} An amazingly fun game that sets the role model of what kind of indie games Steam should allow on its platform, and what Triple A companies should be more like.
This game is literally a breath of fresh air from what games have become these days. A look into what games used to be like, before triple A companies became greedy and ruined them.
The idea of a game that has no dlc and gives free updates without expecting anyone to pay for it would be madness to most devs. The idea of being able to unlock skins in game without buying dlc or loot crates? If you pitched this idea to any company these days they would fire you straight away. I mean, some companies would even scoff at the idea of making a single player game that had no multiplayer aspect to manipulate you to buy more. What i’m trying to get at is I have to give this game my full blown respect for being a fun, long, well made game that doesn’t try to milk you dry like the triple A companies that refer to people as ‘Whales’ and other fish to describe how much money we give them. Season passes, dlc, dlc not included in the season pass, loot crates, regular/silver/gold editions, pre order bonuses, and so on. This game has none of that and is a great representation of what video games used to be like. I would even be fine with this game adding dlc if it is actually content that was actually added after the game was actually completed, and not made with the game but walled off as DLC to force you to pay more for what should have came with the base game. Oh… and DLC skins of course.
Now onto the actual game. In a world where it becomes harder and harder to get your game noticed on Steam when 30 other garbage Unity games come out on a daily basis, Slime Rancher got noticed as a great representation of what indie games Steam should be allowing on their platform. The Slime floated out of the sea of garbage and quickly became a role model of what games should look like these days. The casual gameplay and cute styles of the slimes make it very fun and relaxing, to the point where even your kid can sit down and enjoy this great game. Breeding the slimes and taking care of them is incredibly fun. By breeding them into bigger slimes you get more payment out of them but also they become more of a risk, since you have to leave them to explore and hunt newer slimes that are worth more. As your journeys take longer and longer, you need to make sure you have everything prepared for your slimes on your trips so they don’t run out of food and break out to destroy your ranch.
I will list a few problems I had, the first being the controller support. Pressing start rapidly flickers the pause menu on and off. Pressing B is supposed to back you out of maps and info books but is also bound to an upgrade that uses stored energy to fire a weak blast that barely pushes slimes away. Upon going to the controller config in the options that brings me to the steam chord page, it would completely freeze my computer and I would have to restart my PC.
While I do understand this game is casual, I was still hoping for a bit more of a challenge. I only died once through my whole playthrough, and that was because I couldn’t make a jump from one cliff to another because I didn’t have a jetpack yet. The hostile slimes that are supposed to pose the biggest threat never killed me. The frame rate on the final boss also has a bad habit of dying off.  Some levels have pretty long load times.

Can some people have fun with this game? Yes. Can I, personally, recommend this? No, sorry. You licked my lollipop, rewrapped it, and then sold it back to me; what did you expect.
Full disclosure: I own the original disc versions of HW1, HWC, and HW2, and have been a big fan of at least the first two.
I played the crap out of Homeworld 1 and Cataclysm for years, both the campaigns and multiplayer. I rediscovered them all over again several times, when unpacking boxes or reinstalling a new PC. They are at the top of my all-time favourite games.
HW2: I think I finished the campaign once, and not in one go. It just felt like a step back from the previous ones, for several reasons. Still, it entertained me for a good while and in some way stilled my hunger for a continuation of the HW1/HWC line.
Was I excited about a remaster? Absolutely; I like shiny new graphics and better sounds, and I looked forward to having the games install and work 'out of the box' on current day OS. But for me, that was literally all they needed to do. Because functionally, HW1/HWC already worked exactly as they were.
For me, they could not have done this remaster any more wrong if they'd tried:
*
. If it was at all true that they could not do a remaster of both with each their own engine, I would've picked HW1 over HW2 every day and twice on sunday, From my perspective, it would've made their job easier: just dumb down the HW2 races/campaign to ignore the superior HW1 formations and strafing and ballistics, et voilá, HW2 on HW1 engine. Besides, this argument reeks: they went to the trouble of completely redoing/reinventing the HW1 campaign and ships and balance on a HW2 engine... and that was somehow less effort than simply keeping those parts of the
source code unchanged? Hogwash.
*
. Yes, it took a few moments and maybe a peek at the manual to figure out how to call up the HW1 UI, but the almost entire absence of it made Space(tm) feel Real(tm). I agree that the research/build/launch dialogs would have benefited from an overlay implementation, but functionally they worked much better than HW2.
*
. In HW1, when rotating the camera with right mouse click, the pivot point is the ship or object you focused on. This feels utterly natural, because that is what focus means: maintain your view on your point of interest while rotating to get an overview of all that surrounds it. In HW2, the camera instead pivots
. Aside from breaking immersion (wait a minute, am I part of this story, or am I filming it?), it does not maintain focus on what you told it to. Homeworld is not an FPS!
*
. Strikegroups break formation the moment they start moving, or never form up the way it was intended in the first place (sphere guard, anyone?), broken pathing makes ships get stuck in places, ships forget halfway what they were ordered to do and need to be reissued so they don't either stop in the middle of nowhere or decide to do some suicide move on their own.
* The remastered graphics and sounds, while pretty and certainly a significant step up from the originals, end up being underwhelming when compared to community mods like Complex which have been available for years.
And as if messing up the Remastered versions wasn't enough:
*
. Yes, they included a 'Classic' version that supposedly kept the original experience intact for those who may not like all the changes in Remastered. Which I would've been happy with, except... they kept the bugs/shortcomings intact (no widescreen/high resolution support unless hacked through registry), but they messed with things that should and could have been left alone (load/save no longer compatible with original savegames; LAN multiplayer removed; D3D/sw rendering removed).
Why? Especially that last one: it was already becoming difficult to make the originals work on current hardware and OS... and they go and remove compatibility options that existed in the originals! What exactly is the point of including HW2C then? It's not as pretty as HW2R, *and* it's now almost as bad about backwards compatibility. Pointless. If you need a lighter version to run on somewhat lesser hardware, just run HW2R with all graphics options turned to minimum. (except now, since they removed the other pre-existing rendering options, it's OpenGL 3.3 or nothing. Sucks to be you if you don't have updated compatible drivers).
I played a few missions into HW1R before I got too irritated and went back to HW1C. Two missions short of the end of that campaign, they then published a patch for the Remastered version that somehow managed to break load/save in HW1C, making it freeze and crash on loading savegames created just days/hours before.  So I ended up playing halfway through the campaign on my original disc versions before even feeling like trying again.
Did I miss the remastered resources while playing HW1C / HW1 original? Quite honestly, not in the least. They are a shiny bonus, indisputably, but simply have no bearing on the masterpiece that was and still is HW1.
In the end, I just feel duped for letting my nostalgia win and buying into the pre-order. This collection does not deliver: it removed what was good and added new gripes, in exchange of some shiny graphics and rerecorded sounds. On top of things, where my original dics versions came with the soundtracks included, now they want additional cash just for the soundtracks (which are not even complete btw, something about licensing quarrels).
I noticed some people keep arguing that it's 'only' been days/weeks since release, that we cannot expect everything to work right yet, that we should allow them to get feedback and patch things. I regard this a non-argument.
Under normal circumstances, with a production from scratch, that argument already makes me grit my teeth. Software/gaming has to be the only industry where consumers not just accept, but even *defend* incomplete and bugged-to-hell product releases. This should not be acceptable, and if consumer rights were anywhere near any other industry, we'd all be eligible for a refund.
BUT THIS IS NOT A NEW RELEASE!! They had full access to the original sources. Again: they started with
. They even had the original developers assist them! And even with all that, their release is broken through bugs or intention. They do not get to claim 'needing time to fix inevitable issues' when those issues are in most cases clearly caused by meddling with code that did not need to be touched to begin with.
Whether some people may like HW1/HW2 Remastered the way they are is frankly irrelevant to me. I'm sure there's plenty of people that feel Mona Lisa's smile could use a little retouching. It still does not make it right to put a marker to the master piece. If the original developers felt like they didn't get to make their 'definitive' version of Homeworld before, they could've saved that for Homeworld 3, or more likely, a future DLC for Homeworld Remastered.
End verdict: A lot of money for shiny graphics and rerecorded sounds packaged with broken functionality, which makes at least this vet go back to the originals.
P.S.: for the ones asking about Steam showing my play time increasing - that is me trying out the dozens of mods already coming out trying to restore what Classic/Remastered changed from the originals. Just let that sink in: the community, with limited tools and gimped access to game data, making right what the developers couldn't do with full access to everything.

One of the most moving RPG games I've played in a long time. It just sad that it didn't find it's way to the spotlight, and therefor a sequel seems an impossibility. I'm so glad it made it's way to PC.
With brilliant motion capture from actors like Andy Serkis (Gollum - Lord of the Rings/The Hobbit Trilogies), the emotions from the characters are very believable, and make your actions that much more meaningful. Great visuals and a fantastic soundtrack add to the story even moreso. The gameplay is great fun, with acrobatic elements and teamwork between Monkey and Trip, meaning a good blend between action and environmental puzzles, which can also come into play during combat, which is a great stress reliever with epic finishing moves and great sound engineering to enhance those "smashy" sounds.
The only place that the game fell short for me was the staff's "aim and fire" feature, although this is only required in a few points of the game, so you won't have to rely on it. That, and sometimes the game would have trouble realising which object to whilst making use of acrobatics; although almost every game with this kind of "play" has this issue, so it's quick to learn how to minimalise it with certain camera angling and/or stick pushing.
A unique and moving game I strongly recommend to those who love a good story, but still like to smash some robots in the face.
Still the best in the series, IMHO.  Highly recommend playing with friends. Also, writing this review will help me get a Steam badge.

Dishonoured 2 is a reasonably deep game with the same brilliant and free flowing fighting mechanics from the first game, its a good successor.
The story material is good, I thought, with some actions which I think do affect your play throughout:  from your killing habits to your actual actions in dialogue.
The skills required for the stealth and beserker roles do matter and I found it quite hard to upgrade half of my skills on my first playthrough, this isn't made easy like it's Saints Row.
The game has not watered down any of it's orignal components, thankfully! Levels are designed with multiple routes and areas are worth exploring. Items collected range-from simple loot, to collectables, to actual upgrades that can upgrade your character. What reduced my oppinon of the new Deus Ex(Mankind divided) has not done so with Dishonoured 2.
Alot of it seems very polished, if not over-polished, with visuals in the world looking very pretty and the musical and audio bits being very good. I hear some people have had difficulty with performnace, I have had no such issues.
A really solid and good game which maintains the integrity of the original and extends with worth while content. There is not alot to complain about with it.
It's worth comparing with the new Doom actually, where Doom is addictive mindless violence - mostly, Dishonoured can be far more ponderous and elegant.

Some of my favourite games of all time are the Thief series and "Dark Messiah of Might and Magic", the latter being quite unknown for no reason (give it a try). And if you mix those two, you get Dishonored. It is only surpassed by the brilliant second part which offers the best singleplayer experience I had for several years.
The gameplay is a delightful sandbox full of stealth, combat and powers to experiment with. The environments are stunning and multifaceted. They are fun to explore and hide many secrets. The game offers different approaches which can be overwhelming for some. Its like the Mount and Blade of stealth games. Lore and characters are top notch, the main story does its job (but is a bit shallow to be honest). For stealth fans there are lots of options to make the game truely hardcore. The AI can be really "realistic" and is the best I ever encountered in a stealth game (not talking about Hitman, which is different). Its a huge step compared to Thief/Splinter Cell/First Dishonored.
On top of that it runs PERFECTLY on my old crappy laptop :D No bugs, no performance issues, nothing. I guess the performance issues can occur on high-end PCs where users want high-end results. If you just want to play the game and can live with low settings (still looks ok), go get this masterpiece.

Pros:
1. 3rd person MOBA

Cons:

3. Some of the gods look great but others are very poorly designed (visually). The menu is unintuitive, poorly made – as if the designer’s only goal was to have a working version, just throw in the options as they come to mind.

---

As interesting as it may be, you can only dangle a carrot for so long before people lose interest.

Homeworld Remastered is genuinely a breath of fresh air in the RTS genre all over again. Gearbox have done a fantastic job of reviving this classic series of 3DRTS action, with a beta multiplayer to boot. At the time of writing this, the multiplayer needs severe balancing and bug fixing, but it shows great potential. All four races (kush, taiidan, hiigaran, vaygr) are now all available in the multiplayer, however the homeworld 1 races need the most adjustments.
The remastered collection runs in the Homeworld 2 engine, with revamped graphics and the formations of homeworld 1 are now implemented into the game (however I don't think they function as gearbox intended, most likely will need fixing).
The collection also comes with the classic editions of both games if you feel like a trip down nostalgia lane, or if you just want to see the difference between the original games and the remastered editions.
If you enjoyed the original games, or have just come across this for the first time, I highly recommend purchasing it.

Let me start off by saying I haven't encountered a single glitch, bug or hic-cup in my 53 hours of gameplay. Stability of the game may have been an issue at release but it's all good now.
Quick Summary:
I'd rate it a 7.5/10 without the DLC and an 8.5/10 with the DLC.
If you liked JC2 you will love JC3. If you haven't played JC2 and want to pick up JC3, don't play it for the story but play it to go live you're life as a "professional badass"(quote from the game, not trying to be corny :).
Pros:
Cons:
Some more details:
I played JC2 a lot and really enjoyed being able to grapple hook everywhere and just be a professional badass. JC3 takes it to the extreme, a lot of new mechanics added into the game. Nothing that was fun in JC2 was removed, simply improved upon with additional features added such as the wingsuit.
However completing missions felt like a drag, with a total of 25 missions the game could be finished pretty quickly. As some missions can take a few minutes at most. The cutscenes that would accompany the missions were not that great, which is weird because you can make better and bigger explosions ingame.
Vehicles were a really big part of the game and made it a lot of fun. All the vehicles are pretty easy to pick up and when used properly are a lot of fun. With the addition of the DLC you get to use a mech, completley wrecking an entire brigade of soliders with a mech is so much fun.
There is also a lot of emphasis on the grapple hook and the wingsuit. The wingsuit is pretty easy to get the hang off and with the grapple hook now allowing you to hook multiple hooks there are a lot of fun and creative ways to play the game. With the additon of the DLC the wingsuit gets a pretty nice upgrade.
There are a bunch of collectibles micro achievements in the game you can just ignore. Collecting them all is not necessary for the story at all and finding all the collectibles is a pain. So I would recommend just ignoring them all.
The characters in the game are very one dimensional, the antagonist of the game General Di Revello is the typical evil madman hungry for power. Nothing he does is smart or catches you off gaurd, which is strange because you get to know how he manipulated his way into power, yet he acts as smart as a potato when confronting you.
There are also these things called mods in the game. You can activate a mod to enchance a feature in the game such as nitros, more grappling hooks, more explosives, stronger vehicles etc... To unlock the mods you need to complete small challenges placed around the map. The challenges are fun, but once you unlock the first few mods the rest of them seem pretty useless as just the first few are already a lot of fun.
One major drawback of the game stopping me from rating the game higher is that it really is too easy. If you die while trying to take over a settlement, you respawn next to it... with full ammo... 0 heat so no one is chasing you... and no progress lost. So there is really 0 consequence from dying. If you die during a mission you reset back to a predefined checkpoint, and these checkpoints are pretty common. The game's difficulty would have been perfect if dying actuall mattered, as the enemies are pretty well balanced.
Overall the game is a lot of fun even though the story and difficulty is lack luster. Definitely worth the price and definitely worth getting the DLC.

Rome 2 had numerous bugs and lacked many features at the start, but after countless patches and the re-release as the Emperor Edition it did deliver what was promised since before launch. Not the "best" of the Total War franchise, but it is somewhere in the top.
The Grand Campaign map is rather huge, although it is not that challenging once you get a hang of it.. And the AI is still almost the same as in any other Total War game, though a little bit improved in terms of seige and pathfinding. Once a few turns into a campaign, it will turn into "How many cities should I take this turn?".
All in all, Rome 2 has stunning graphics compared to its predecessors, a larger map, immersive Ancient Antiquity era, a moderate AI, good online battles, co-op Campaigns. Yet it lacks in every other aspect compared to the rest of Total War games, especially with the removal of the Family Tree, and countless other features that should have made it into the game not counting the new ones we were promised..
I'd recommend waiting for Attila, and hopefully Attila will be a complete game on launch.

Mixed feelings, honestly. I narrowly recommend.
Pros:
The visuals are pretty neat. It blends the nostalgic 8 bit appearance of 2004 AOL with a bright color scheme and neat icons to pick for yourself that make it easy on the eyes.
Story. For what you get, it's interesting. The method of seperating each chapter by years and only highlighting single conversations in between said years was a unique way to tell this story.
Feels. There are moments when I played that reminded me almost word for word of my troubles with the ladies. It's very relatable in a neat way.
Cons:
My mouse had difficulties alligning with this, so clicking things was pretty difficult. This was offset by the fact that you only really have to click something with the mouse like 4 times total.
Manually typing is super tedious. I get that it's meant to make you see more of the protagnists inner thoughts from when he types something out but decides to delete it before he sends it, which is cool but still offset by the fact that it makes each message take too long to send.
The game eventually feels pointless. While there ARE several different choices that affect bits of the story, the end result is almost exactly the same. Which I suppose isn't bad considering what the game really is and means to reflect but once you see the different endings, you realize that it doesn't even take into account whatever personality/attitude you used.
Overall, this game is far from perfect. I feel like there's a lot of potential for it's idea and what it is. A sequel, spiritual successor or just remake that extended on these premises would be cool. That being said, it's free and a fun way to spend around an hour.

Frustrating game to review. This game has so much going for it-- stunning art direction, great learning curve and solid combat upgrade system, and decent to good acting and story (a little weak, forced, and abrupt ending imo)-- but the thumbs down (one of my first on Steam) comes from the quality of the PC port. The flaws aren't terribly obvious at first, but the boss battles really expose INCREDIBLY frustrating problems with camera angles,  hit detection and timing.  It's less about skill and timing than it is about "will the AI cooperate this time (finally)?" The frustration reaches an apex with the rhino boss chase following its defeat. What should be a simple and fast pod-racer style pursuit is dampened by the seemingly arbitrary environment effects that don't give you a clear reason of why you've slowed down. I haven't played this game on consoles, but I strongly suspect the problem is in the quality of the port, and that many of these problems would go away in those versions.

Let me start off by saying I haven't encountered a single glitch, bug or hic-cup in my 53 hours of gameplay. Stability of the game may have been an issue at release but it's all good now.
Quick Summary:
I'd rate it a 7.5/10 without the DLC and an 8.5/10 with the DLC.
If you liked JC2 you will love JC3. If you haven't played JC2 and want to pick up JC3, don't play it for the story but play it to go live you're life as a "professional badass"(quote from the game, not trying to be corny :).
Pros:
Cons:
Some more details:
I played JC2 a lot and really enjoyed being able to grapple hook everywhere and just be a professional badass. JC3 takes it to the extreme, a lot of new mechanics added into the game. Nothing that was fun in JC2 was removed, simply improved upon with additional features added such as the wingsuit.
However completing missions felt like a drag, with a total of 25 missions the game could be finished pretty quickly. As some missions can take a few minutes at most. The cutscenes that would accompany the missions were not that great, which is weird because you can make better and bigger explosions ingame.
Vehicles were a really big part of the game and made it a lot of fun. All the vehicles are pretty easy to pick up and when used properly are a lot of fun. With the addition of the DLC you get to use a mech, completley wrecking an entire brigade of soliders with a mech is so much fun.
There is also a lot of emphasis on the grapple hook and the wingsuit. The wingsuit is pretty easy to get the hang off and with the grapple hook now allowing you to hook multiple hooks there are a lot of fun and creative ways to play the game. With the additon of the DLC the wingsuit gets a pretty nice upgrade.
There are a bunch of collectibles micro achievements in the game you can just ignore. Collecting them all is not necessary for the story at all and finding all the collectibles is a pain. So I would recommend just ignoring them all.
The characters in the game are very one dimensional, the antagonist of the game General Di Revello is the typical evil madman hungry for power. Nothing he does is smart or catches you off gaurd, which is strange because you get to know how he manipulated his way into power, yet he acts as smart as a potato when confronting you.
There are also these things called mods in the game. You can activate a mod to enchance a feature in the game such as nitros, more grappling hooks, more explosives, stronger vehicles etc... To unlock the mods you need to complete small challenges placed around the map. The challenges are fun, but once you unlock the first few mods the rest of them seem pretty useless as just the first few are already a lot of fun.
One major drawback of the game stopping me from rating the game higher is that it really is too easy. If you die while trying to take over a settlement, you respawn next to it... with full ammo... 0 heat so no one is chasing you... and no progress lost. So there is really 0 consequence from dying. If you die during a mission you reset back to a predefined checkpoint, and these checkpoints are pretty common. The game's difficulty would have been perfect if dying actuall mattered, as the enemies are pretty well balanced.
Overall the game is a lot of fun even though the story and difficulty is lack luster. Definitely worth the price and definitely worth getting the DLC.

I recommend this game to both people new to the Souls series, and people who aren't new to the Souls series.  Let me explain why.
For people new to the Souls Series:
This game is a great RPG, and it's much easier to get in to and get used to than the other Souls games. It introduces you to the game well, and the enemies start off at the perfect difficulty to understand how combat works. This game is basically the gateway drug of the Souls games, especially on PC, because in Dark Souls you're faced with a giant boss that 2hits you in the tutorial with 1 tip on how to defeat him, which is just a drop attack. It's a fun game to play, and it's accessible enough to get in to, but it doesn't compare to Dark Souls or Demons Souls in level design and immersion.
For veterans of the Souls Series:
This game is not the best Souls game by any means, having played through Dark Souls 1 8 times I can tell this game has a different director. This game's maps are linear, straight forward, and not quite as intimidating and dark as any maps in Dark Souls 1. The bosses sometimes become bland with boring movesets, but then I think we've all gotten bored of Nito and Four Kings at some point. This game is entertaining and fun to play, and it is a great game, however it does not hold up to Souls games standard. The storyline and plot are lackluster, not nearly as immersive as Demons Souls or Dark Souls. The plot is there, it's just not amazing. Why do I recommend it then? It makes you appreciate just how amazing and spectacular the other Souls games are. It shows you that they're not fun just because they're difficult, because in reality they're not that difficult, it's because of the universe it creates for you to explore. Souls veterans all remember getting stuck on Taurus Demon for hours, and wondering where the hell am I supposed to go next after beating the Gargoyles. Dark Souls 2 just doesn't have those experiences.
Overall, it's a fun game to play, and you can get a lot of hours out of it. It's a good first Souls game, but it doesn't hold up well to the standards of the other Souls games. Worse, but not bad.

Not quite as good as the first, Dark Souls 2 is still a great game.  It has some great additions to the series but a couple negatives also.
The addition of bonfire ascetics is an excellent one, allowing you to reset bosses, enemies and loot off corpses in the area along with upping the difficulty, adding tons of replayability to the game - easily the best addition.
Resetting enemies by resting at a bonfire has changed as well, enemies can now go "extinct" if you reset them after a certain number of clears making the game easier to explore farmed areas but preventing you from farming "easier" areas for levels for extended periods making the difficulty of the game a bit double edged.
The bosses in this game also felt much easier than the first game, possibly because I'm used to the mechanics but I didn't feel like there were really any standout fights in this game like Orenstein and Smough or Artorias from the first game as far as challenge.  The fights that are feel more annoying than difficult - DLC gank squad and chariot to name a couple.  Most boss fights play out like they are holding signs over their heads saying "I'M ABOUT TO ATTACK NOW"  "YOU BETTER ROLL DUDE"  *SMASH*  "dang you rolled".
There are still 2 DLCs unreleased so we'll see about the boss fights in those, so far the DLC is enjoyable with the only issue being where the last 2 bosses are located.

Let me get the obvious out of the way: the game isn't as good as Dark Souls. However, it's still a high quality, and fun game with much strategy and exploration involved.
Graphic wise, the game has certain aspects, such as animations and textures, that are better than Dark Souls. However, on the whole, it's quite clear that the graphics were ruined to account for the low power of the PS3 and Xbox 360. The lighting engine was totally scrapped and the game looks washed out and boring. Torches and sconces have been rendered useless for the most part when they used to be essential. I didn't play it with any post processing, but anyone starting out might want to.
Gameplay-wise, the game also exceeds Dark Souls in many ways. The single player game is more balanced so that you can't just roll through with a melee weapon like in Dark Souls. You have to use ranged attacks effectively to succeed, as well. Different weapon damage types are more pronounced in their effectiveness. Unfortunately, the bosses are much less interesting and original, many of them are simply mobs of regular enemies and others are variations on a knight wielding a shield. Some areas of the game had a lot more potential for interesting enemies and could've been more expansive. The bonfire placement is just too lenient, as is the ability to warp to any bonfire from the start. It makes the game into more of an arcade style one and ruins the atmosphere.
In addition, weapon durability in the game is glitched and depletes twice as fast, which still hasn't been patched. And the multiplayer suffers from issues such as the ill concieved Soul Memory mechanic which decreases the replay value in co-op.
The plot of the game is minimalistic... maybe a little too minimalistic in comparison to the previous games. While there is an overarching story, I found Dark Souls to be a little more interesting in its backstory.
Overall, Dark Souls II is the weakest of the Souls games yet, but that doesn't mean that it's a bad game, it's still better than most action RPGs on the market.

"...the sole purpose of human existence is to kindle a light of meaning in the darkness of mere being."
-Carl Gustav Jung
Dark Souls encourages us to find our own meaning by keeping its storytelling subtle and open ended. As the protagonist searches for meaning, we search for meaning in his endeavors. To me, the Dark Souls series is very much about our desire for purpose, to grasp and cling to the light of meaning we construct for ourselves, fearing that without meaning and desire we'll fall prey to nihilism, alive in body but dead in spirit, a kind of undead limbo.
The game is a huge success in terms of storytelling, but also has very clever level design, challenging and engaging combat, and appropriate music and atmosphere. Dark Souls 2 even attaches meaning to its rules and mechanics, such as its hollowing mechanic, and all of these elements in Dark Souls 2 converge to enhance its narrative. The end result is deep, mysterious, and intriguing. Though there are some frustrating flaws within the game, such as unrealistic hitboxes and a very irritating degree of lag in pvp, it is still an extraordinary video game that anyone interested in the artful side of video games should consider playing.

I really don't see what the big fuss is. I only see minor issues with the game. I would recommend this a a fellow Total War fan who played the first Rome Total War. Why? Because there are a lot of improvments in this game.
The graphics have improved and NO they don't look bad from a distance if you have a computer that can actually run it properly. The amount units has vastly grown. The amount of space for units per army is now colossal. There is now an ability to actually play the boat battles. You can even depart your units from your boat and onto land during a battle. You also have a lot more DLC and multiplayer features to use. There's more than one campaign. The battles are even more intense than the original Rome Total War! The A.I have been improved and there are a few more difficulties. There are way more options. They have a better Encyclopedia.
These are all fantastic additions to the game and only a few of them I've mentioned. I have not yet got this game but I will get it on the next sale. This game does occasionaly go up on sale too. Although I probably wouldn't want to buy it at it's normal price though as it seems a bit too costly since it came out just over 1 year ago.
The only bad things that I see with this game are (these were copied from Chief WH's review);
- Generals -I simply don't care for them, why should I? They have no connections, no background, the traits come along all too easily that you can stockpile them and they have no 'wow' value.
- Armies - you cannot have an army without a general. Previous TW games enabled you to have small groups of units led by a non-detailed 'Captain'. The lack of captains prevents you from moving units from one area to another to join up with a different army without taking the whole army or designating a general as a taxi driver. Often not possible if you have multiple fronts. Armies also always tend to be huge, (perhaps as a result of no captains), this means there are no small skirmish engagements, always large battles.
This game is by far the one of the best Real Time Strategy games ever made in my opinion. I would recommend this to all ages as this is fun, addicting and teaches you some famous historical battles and units.

Pre Xen: I am no stranger to the Half-Life series as evident by my profile and gametimes on all 6 of the currently released games. I love this series, and it holds a dear place in my heart as
game I have ever played. With that being said, let's get into this review.
The beginning tram ride brought back waves of nostalgia and wonder that I haven't felt since my original time on Half Life over 12 years ago. As your character rides a large tram throughout the Black Mesa complex, you can see how much the new game engine complements these environments. The lighting, textures, and dust particles all fit in seamlessly to make the experience both daunting, but inviting.
The layout for this complex remains relatively the same, with a few added corridors and the occasional room. Getting the HEV suit for the first time is still an awesome experience along with the added Easter eggs/achievements that line the locker room and the dining area. We are even introduced to some characters who have appeared in the older installments of Half Life (2, Episode 1 and 2) who are welcome additions to the game. The main test chamber is expansive and reacher high into the air, the large "lazer" that stands in the middle of the room made me stand in  awe. The new lighting affects (Especially ones from the beta) compliment this room, especially when we finally push the large crystal into the machine, triggering some Unforeseen Consequences....
Seeing the Black Mesa complex in ruins after the resonance cascade is great, and it captures the original chaos and helplessness of the original.
. This section is also where we receive our firsts weapons, our trusty crowbar and pistol. The both, work as they did in the original game, with newer models/textures/animations that compliment them greatly.
The office sections got a much needed graphical overhaul, making the game look as if it was used by a group of scientists, it looks lived in, and the chaos caused by the invading Xen creatures  is done extremely well. Unfortunately, this environment gets much worse, as a new foe steps in.
The military in this game are done great! Gone is the annoying scratchy voice of soldiers and welcomed is the human, non gravely, voices of soldiers coming to clean up the science crew. This section is also the first point where we are introduced to the outdoors, with its luscious red rocky environment and large attack ships which quickly usure us underground to safety from the onslaught of bullets, mortar, and explosives.
THE TENTACLES ARE AWESOME! This was always a tedious section in my eyes but the new models and sounds made by these large Japanese fetish like beasts is amazing. The clanking as they slam their large battleaxe like noses on the metal flooring and the groans and moans they made as the rocket was test fired, eventually melting them into a fine nothing was great. The section with the radiation is also very well done, the large fan churning this goop around is really nice looking and the “white noise”  on the screen as you get closer and closer to this goop is cool.
This remains the same as its HL1 counterpart aside from some graphical enhancements and a few differently designed environments.
This section makes the
Blast Pit chapter look like the best thing since sliced bread. On a Rail has always been a boring chapter in my eyes, luckily the developers realized this too and kept this chapter extremely short, getting us onto the more interesting sections like shooting off the rocket and killing the Ichthyosaur with the crossbow.
Again, this section is much like its HL1 counterpart. Aside from the Black Ops Spies (Which are extremely annoying haha), the level plays like the original.
Seeing a pattern? This map plays the same to its HL1 counterpart, aside from some of the puzzles being slightly different, along with certain mine traps being really hard to disarm.
\
This is most likely my favorite chapter so far. The tests are really enjoyable to do, and the new Tau Cannon is beautiful.
FINALLY! The outside! The outside areas are beautiful, and it really captures the feeling of being in a hot, dry, mountainous mesa. The helicopter is also present here and it’s a fun little boss battle.
More time in the outdoors. More environments created around the outer Black Mesa complex. The Xen invasion is in full force and both the military, scientists, security guards, and you; Gordon Freeman are in danger from these alien menaces.
The final chapter currently in the game. It plays like the original, except in the last segment which really beefs up the teleporter, making it look like a behemoth of technology. After fighting off the creatures of the Nihilanth, the portal opens, and your character jumps into it.
I can definitely recommend this game for the experience it has given me so far. This is OUR Half-Life 3.

Saw this game when it came out, I had no idea it was actually good.
It plays out kind of like a cross between "The Last Of Us" and "Uncharted"
The game features only 3 characters for the most part, the rest of the game taken up by the thousands of "mechs" that need to be disposed of. My only personal qualms with the game were that the acrobatic puzzles got to be a little exhausting after awhile (Jump here, climb that, pull that lever, etc.) but these are parts of the game that seemed to be most enjoyed by others.
The voice acting in the game was phenomenal with a leading performance by Andy Serkis (Gollum from Lord Of The Rings, you won't realize it's him) as the tough perpetually angry 'Monkey' and Lindsey Shaw holding her own as his reluctant captor. Watching the voices from the trailor for the first time is what convinced me to buy the game and it's what made me play all the way through. I recommend the game just for the voice acting.
My biggest grip with this game and one I felt could have improved on the game A LOT, was that there was simply not ENOUGH of the voice acting. The game is chalk full of dialogue and banter, but games like Mass Effect and The Last Of Us have shown us that if you think you have enough dialogue during the "gameplay" sections of the game, you should probably just quadrouple it. After playing the game through to the end, I was happy with where the character development ended up at, but more dialogue throughout the game would have improved the plot significantly especially during puzzle sequences... and probably more during the combat ones as well.
All in all a great game that I believe only suffered because of the way it looks. The cover art for the game, while appropriate and well put together doesn't do it very much justice in the advertising department as it gives the game a very "generic" look and feel when it's far from that. If you like games like Uncharted or The Last Of Us and value excellent voice acting and story paired with "pretty good" combat and game mechanics, play this game.

Pros -
-Sweet animations

*[with the exception of the turrets, and no raw mouse input though I used 360 controller]

Cons -
-Almost ZERO visual options

That's basically it, other than that it's a really fun game with an intriguing story line and dynamic environments.

Slime Rancher was one of the first games on Steam I felt truly compelled to buy from having just seen a handful of screenshots.
In a vast sea of gritty macho violence and realism, Slime Rancher stands out as a fun and creative farming simulator / platformer / exploration masterpiece.
I love bright colors, cute cartoonish characters and rewards for a sense of exploration and curiosity - BUT I hate the gross objectification and oversexualisation of women in many cute japanese titles. That's why this title is so perfect. It's all about the gameplay, which feels smooth, intuitive and varied.
This game feels a lot like a mix between Stardew Valley, Luigi's Mansion and Metroid Prime - with the best parts of each game blended into one.
This is a great game for anyone who loves farming sims and exploration. It has MANY features that keep the game feeling fresh and interesting for a long time. Amazing game. Updates keep coming. Well worth the 20$ I spent on it.

Ravenfield is built for people that like the large-scale, objective-based skirmishes of the Battlefield games, but also don't like playing with other people in general. Ravenfield is botmatch heaven in a lightweight package, designed for those of us that enjoy those silly and frantic moments that only subpar AI can deliver.
The game has super low system requirements, due to its lack of things like dynamic lighting, high-poly models, or fancy post-processing. This is definitely an intentional move, however; Ravenfield features large sprawling maps and a potentially huge number of combatants (you can set this number to whatever you want; one-on-one or literally hundreds of soldiers on the battlefield). You'll find your traditional Battlefield gameplay here; the main gametypes see you capturing spawn points or reducing your enemy's respawn tickets to 0. Weapons are loosely categorized into classes, but on the loadout screen you are free to mix and match as you see fit. The game features a health system, Battlefield-style vehicles, and a rudimentary squad system. All of this comes together with you as the sole human player in a sea of friendly and hostile AI soldiers that boast the perfect amount of pure stupidity. In smaller matches, you're usually going to win because your actions so strongly influence the tide of battle, but the game really shines when there's 100 people on each side and you're frantically battling over a new spawn point while your stupid teammates hand another one over to the enemy. These kinds of botmatches are fun in their own right...they're certainly not for everybody, but if botmatches are your thing, there's plenty of fun to be had here. While the game's official content is a little limited right now, more maps will certainly be added as development continues. And with Steam Workshop being introduced to the game, there's plenty of user-created maps and weapons to fill that void. This whole game is being developed by just one guy, and for being a one-man show it's a really impressive piece of work.
If you're more of a multiplayer person, you'll probably be disappointed here. But if you like botmatches and you just like killing time by shooting at things in a nice little sandbox-y package, you'll probably end up sinking a decent amount of time into Ravenfield. Pick it up if you're someone like me, looking for a multiplayer experience in a singleplayer package.

Written from the point of view of someone who has played 123 hours of Just Cause 2 and would probably rank it in my top 5 games.
JC3 is pretty fun. Pretty all as expected. It looks fantastic. I really like the better implemented destruction. Driving is feels a lot better than JC2. Being able to see on the map the things you need to destroy to complete a settlement is a life saver. Having unlimited plantable bombs makes a long session of destruction easier and means you don't mind using your rocket launcher or similar weapon more. The progression is more interesting than JC3 with you getting more abilities rather than just weapon hits harder. Couldn't imagine life without the wing suit now.
But the main missions are dull af, very few highlights. Its mostly just 'escort' missions where you have to protect something, so its just adding a rule holding back your destructions. Just Cause 2's location feels more interesting than Medici; it has as snow, desert, forests, mountains and huge cities where medici only has forests, mountains, coastline (very pretty) and quarry areas. The challenges are pretty dull; Wing suit ones are alright but the destruction ones are again just adding rules to limit how you want to play. It feels like its missing one extra variable to really vary things up. And I'm not just talking about co op, but that would have been a great addition.
JC3 is more of the same with a few improvements. If you found JC2 repetitive you probably won't get a lot out of JC3. For some reason I don't think I'll keep coming back like I did for JC2. So overall I did have a fair amount of fun with JC3, but it didn't blow my socks off as I was hoping.

Really, it's a disappointment.
Nothing awful. It isn't eye-schorchingly bad, it isn't going to offend you, but it also just isn't fun. Avalanch Studios found a way to make blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up not fun.
See, in Just Cause 2, this wasn't a problem. The game was a lot more open, and bases were smaller and designed better. If it was red, you were supposed to shoot it, and it would explode. Do this abot 5 times, and the base was liberated. Add in some combat as a natural obstacle and make traversal generally fun, and you've got a good little set up. Everything in Just Cause 2 just worked.
Just Cause 3 is a different story entirely. Vehicles are sluggish, the wingsuit is thrilling at first but you'll tire of it quickly. The combat is fine, nothing more, nothing less. The base liberation is outright boring as hell. You have a laundry list of small doodads you have to destroy, and the base isn't liberated until you've gotten them all. This wasn't a problem in JC2 with the crates you had to collect, because it had indicators and a minimap. Here? No such luck. If you want to know where stuff is, you need to open the menu which just trashes the pacing. Destroy a thing, check the map. Walk across town and have some boring combat. Destroy a thing. Check the map. Finally, you finish off the town by flying over the walls of a base, pressing two buttons, then going to the center of town and pressing another button to raise the flag. Repeat with slight variations (like in the powerplant, where it adds time limits to press the buttons for added pain) for every base so far.
This really stings because the game has a lot of good stuff in it! The combat is close to being good, I love what you can do with the wires now, the graphics are just gorgeous and so is Medichi. With another year in development, this would have blown Just Cause 2 out of the water. Sadly, it's a bunch of super cool mechanics (and a few not-quite-finished ones, like the driving, the combat) floating in an awful framework. I couldn't even make my own fun. My helicoptor raids ended in me getting quickly shot down by the F-YOU SAM sights, and my planned assault on a city with a tank ended with the tank bugging out of existance and me rage-quitting.
Oh, bad PC port too. Not terrible, just bad. You can't re-bind F without it still doing something else, it doesn't like to be in fullscreen, and you literally can't skip the opening FOV with the company logos unless you have a controller. This might be a good game to play with the Steam Controller honestly.
Hey, maybe it gets better. Maybe the missions later are really good, or the chalenges that I didn't try were fun, or something. But the fact that I have literally no desire to keep playing the sequel to just cause 2 says a lot. Give it a miss, play JC2 instead.

I really don't see what the big fuss is. I only see minor issues with the game. I would recommend this a a fellow Total War fan who played the first Rome Total War. Why? Because there are a lot of improvments in this game.
The graphics have improved and NO they don't look bad from a distance if you have a computer that can actually run it properly. The amount units has vastly grown. The amount of space for units per army is now colossal. There is now an ability to actually play the boat battles. You can even depart your units from your boat and onto land during a battle. You also have a lot more DLC and multiplayer features to use. There's more than one campaign. The battles are even more intense than the original Rome Total War! The A.I have been improved and there are a few more difficulties. There are way more options. They have a better Encyclopedia.
These are all fantastic additions to the game and only a few of them I've mentioned. I have not yet got this game but I will get it on the next sale. This game does occasionaly go up on sale too. Although I probably wouldn't want to buy it at it's normal price though as it seems a bit too costly since it came out just over 1 year ago.
The only bad things that I see with this game are (these were copied from Chief WH's review);
- Generals -I simply don't care for them, why should I? They have no connections, no background, the traits come along all too easily that you can stockpile them and they have no 'wow' value.
- Armies - you cannot have an army without a general. Previous TW games enabled you to have small groups of units led by a non-detailed 'Captain'. The lack of captains prevents you from moving units from one area to another to join up with a different army without taking the whole army or designating a general as a taxi driver. Often not possible if you have multiple fronts. Armies also always tend to be huge, (perhaps as a result of no captains), this means there are no small skirmish engagements, always large battles.
This game is by far the one of the best Real Time Strategy games ever made in my opinion. I would recommend this to all ages as this is fun, addicting and teaches you some famous historical battles and units.

The original Rome was among my favorite games of all time. As a result, I rushed to buy this game at release. The broken start is well known to everyone, but no amount of patches can fix some fundamental problems. At the surface, the game looks expansive and pretty. When you play it for a few hours, you realize how limited the game really is. The depth of previous TW games is long gone, and you will find yourself performing the same combo of buildings and soldiers in every single city. The process has been dumb-downed and streamlined into a hollow shell of its former self. The same can be said of the tech system. I loved its addition in Empire Total War, but the tech system has become simplier and simplier with each new game until you find yourself following the same linear path in RTWII.
Also, what the hell CE with your playable factions? You have how many Greek factions now? You have Greeks, Greeks on horses, Greeks on Elephants, Greeks in Ukraine, and Greeks in Africa, yet there is not a single ethnically African or Arabian faction. This is one of the worst cases of CE's Euro-centric racism. According to CE, Africa and Arabia do not matter historically. If you want to play something other than a variation of Greeks or Barbarians, this isn't the game for you.

For all of those who care for a weighted review or whatever, I'd like to point it out: this is basically a love-letter, from a fan-boy (who's not a boy for a long time now).
This is the game that brought all the beauty of the space before my eyes, when I was younger. This is the game I waited for oh so long to be either continued or be remastered. And when the news came in, I was happy that I could once again meet the Hiigarans and listen to that incredible soundtrack and command fleets and... oh so much more.
Even though so many years have passed it still gives me that incredible sense of... adventure, that I somehow miss in modern games. And even though I know all the story from A to Z, it is still incredibly fun and exciting to go through it. The gameplay is not at all weaker, and the enhanced graphics only make it more immersive.
There are some people who give the game 'thumbs down' either because they think it's wrong to use the name of the older version (or its score on the Metacritics). There are some, who think little bugs are... well, it seems they think those are kind of sin.
But I disagree. This is one of the best remastered games I have ever played, And I know for a fact that I will enjoy playing it. Again... and, then, again =)
Now, the policy requires to me give pros and cons:
Pros:
- Excellent graphics
- Incredible OST (I wonder why do they not sell it separately?)
- Involving story
- God, it's Homeworld, how can it not be a pro? )
Cons:
- Little bugs
- Some balancing problems
But after all, who cares? ) It is only up to you to decide whether you want it or not. But I would strongly recommend to play it, because, who knows, we may have a HW3 someday... perhaps even sooner than HL3 =)

I'm not entirely sure what they were thinking with Homeworld 1 remastered, especially putting the original in there beside it. Strikecraft, tactics and formations feel incredibly neutered and pointless in the remastered game. All it does is just confuse a fight more times than it helps, unlike the original where it was an important part of small unit tactics. Still, the story and pacing are mostly the same and it feels right.
Homeworld 2 remastered... Where do I start? The story they give you is strange and vaguely nonsensical that wrecks some of the plot points from the first one for absolutely no reason that is apparent to me. It lacks the relaxed pace of the first game with crisis' piling up in your lap before you have a chance to deal with previous ones. Your opponents, the Vaygr, not only vastly outnumber you in each mission, but you quickly notice the quality of their craft also outstrip your own in most instances, this leaves every single engagement an attempt to overwhelm them and the fact that the mission automatically ends (also unlike the first one) means you have no chance to rebuild or reinforce your fleet before heading to the next mission.
The game looks pretty, but I feel that was Gearboxes ONLY concern when they remastered this game.

Fun overhaul of one of my favorite 90s games. Sadly, as of this writing there are some significant bugs that prevents level completion, unless you do some levels in a very specific way (like on the Galactic Core level's "destroy source of gravity field" not being obtainable if you kill the gravity wells "too quickly".)
There are a number of other smaller bugs, such as ships (especially destroyers) failing to stand down when set to passive mode, thus blowing up things your salvage corvettes are tugboating back to the mothership. The asteroid level oddly kills all your fighters (because they apparently don't know to fly around big rock things?) Fighter class ships now seem to be almost completely useless in general. Your squads also seem to suck at maintaining formations now. I get the impression that the cloaked fighters are also bugged / not cloaking when you toggle cloak mode. In general, this feels like a beta that was rushed out the door.
If you can live with the bugs, it's worth a shot. The game was classic for a reason: good soundtrack, good voice acting, pretty good play mechanics, and a relatable and fairly interesting story.
I wish they added an "auto repair" function to the repair ships, but oh well. An auto-loot all the resources button after clearing a stage of enemies would have also been welcomed. As of now, you still have to stick around (or go make a sandwhich or five) while your resource gatherers putz around rounding up the last few rock chunks on most levels.
I like that I can still salvage the hell out of enemy ships to build my fleet.

No More Room in Hell (NMRiH) is a free-to-play zombie game that offers a suprising amount of content.
The game is split into two modes: objectives, and survival. In my experience, I hosted and played in my server with my friends and we finished all the official objective and survival maps, and had a blast doing it. This game, in both modes, emphasizes the scarcity of resources. If you pick up a nice, powerful shotgun, good luck getting enough loads to make it last long. As a result, you have to make due with what you have, and use weapons you wouldn't usually use. With that said, the objective maps can be very difficult, even though the zombies have a rather limited variety.
I'm so suprised that this game is free and yet offers a tough game with solid mechanics. I'd say that soloing this game is not a good idea though, because most of the maps are just too hard. Also, I've heard that on some public servers you can get infinite ammo / gun choices, which I would AVOID. Those features completely fracture the core mechanic of the game that separates it from others like Left for Dead. If you opt for those servers you'll probably get tired of NMRiH rather quickly. It would be like the aftermath of hacking a game.
So I'm going to definitely recommend it. I think that the devs could take this release in different directions, and add other mechanics, but as it stands it's still a solid game.

Slime rancher is a... well.. the name speaks for itself. You collect slimes in a huge world, take them back to your farm, feed em, and you get these diamond things called "Plorts"; Sell those and get profit. But that's not all though. There are different slimes with different attributes and quirks for each type of slime AND you can combine 2 different types of slime into 1 largo slime that poops out (yes, they poop the plorts out when you feed em) the plorts of those 2 slimes that you combined! In this way, you could double your profit in no time. Well, enough of me rambling on about the game, its time for the pros and cons.
Pros/Cons (+/-):
+Huge open world (Biomes!)
+A wide variety of slimes to keep in captivity for your profits
+Adorable slimes
+Farming! (you can grow fruits and vegetables to keep your slimes fed and happy while in captivity)
+Your character's tools and farm can be upgraded (also, color customization)
+LOTS of lore! (slimes, tools, unlockables, character story, etc.)
-Can get a little tedious, needs more automization.
-Not much to do after you've gotten all the upgrades and stuff.
-Needs more optimization (the game slows down when you've played for a while)
Overall: 7/10

From the narrative structure, to the personality of each character, we come to began to know Monkey and Tripitaka (Trip for the folks) in a very emotional adventure (that is inspired obviously in an ''journey to the west'' by Wu Cheng'en) in which every step you take in this devastated world is a risky one.
The game visuals are astonishing, a nice character modelling (i have to admit that i fell in love with Trip xD, and i liked the tough looks of Monkey) good music, and a brand new way to tell a story, by reimagining it.

First of all I'm gonna say this is not going to be an in-depth review of the game but rather a point by point review of what really stood out to me in this game.
-GRAPHICS:
This is a port of a game that originally came out on the Xbox 360 and PS3 in 2010 (I believe) but later made it's way to steam.  I make that point because the graphics are beautiful - they really are! The face animations for the lead characters are humanly accurate and the textures for the world are stunning. You won't be let down.
-STORY
The story was good, but I'm not talking about the actual plot here. I'm talking about the character development between the two lead characters progress very well as the frustrated yet powerful 'Slave' and the vulnerable yet dominating 'Slave owner' grow a bond that I won't spoil, but will say it was welcomed.
As for the main plot; well, it is what it is. It's good! But if you've watched most of the major sci-fi filmes of the last 20 years you'll recognise what book this page is ripped right out of.
-PIGSY'S REVENGE
I played the Premium Edition of the game that comes with all the extra costumes and a nice expansion pack called 'Pigsys Revenge' which is pleasantly long, and surprisingly good! You are not the physically powerful 'Monkey' of the main story but a grotesquely obese gadget god of the wastes; meaning you have to rely on gadgets in every room you enter. Which is great, because it's a nice change of pace compared to the main story. You have to stop and think in EVERY situation you enter.
Overall this game gets a 9.5/10. I'm taking .05 off because the story is just not original enough. The rest of the game however, is a professionally polished joy ride.

But for someone that doesn't understand the concept of the original game, it's mundane and boring! Combine that with difficult movement and aiming, and ridiculous weapon damage (seriously, is that all the damage that the BMG-50 can do?), I lost interest in it rather quickly. I'm just thankful that I bought it at the "sale" price of $4.99. If I'd have paid full-price for this I would likely have raised holy-hell with Steam!
So if you're looking to waste a few bucks on something that will give you a couple hours of enjoyment, before you get bored, then this is for you. For everyone else, it might be advisable to look elsewhere.

While it's not what Dark Souls I (or Demons Souls for that matter) was, it's still a brilliant game in its own right. I prefer the action in this one to DS1 and I much prefer the crafting system here as well. The weapons are just a lot more interesting this time around for me and thats a big plus in its favour.
What really sucks is the disconnect you feel from the world thanks to bonfire warping from the get-go. A nice timesaver, sure, but you no longer feel the size of the world like you did in DS1. Tha's really a major issue I have, but it's really secondary to the games biggest flaw for me: the boss fights. There's almost none of the fear and/or awe you felt when meeting the bosses of the previous games. They're bland, on the easy size and not very rewarding as a result. Souls games are built upon their impressive and frustrating boss battles and this game lacks "soul" for this ommission.
Overall it's an absolute must play and the first DLC helped rectify a number of issues the game had. The level design is much better in the Crown of the Sunken King and the three boss battles are not bad either.

Fantastic
Is it a perfect remake? No. Some of the mechanics in HW1 in particular have been removed, and make certain missions that were monstrously difficult (at least when I was young) rather easy - like Gardens of Kadesh. The removal of strike craft fuel and the change in formation tactics makes it a very different level. There are also some bugs here and there like you'd expect from any new release. None of them I encountered were game-breaking.
What surprised me is that nostalgia didn't cloud my recollection of this series. These games are truly incredible, and unlike any other game you'll experience. They require patience and deliberation that many games now have done away with, but it is every bit as rewarding as I recall. A millenia-spanning story, gorgeous visuals done the justice they deserve, and demanding, yet oddly relaxing gameplay married to one of the most unique UI's in all of gaming. Thank you Gearbox. I had considered this series lost in IP limbo until the THQ auction, and now a new generation can appreciate a flawed, astounding masterpiece along with its excellent sequel.
TLDR: If you haven't played Homeworld and you like the RTS genre, buy it. You're in for something truly special. These remakes are awesome, and if you don't like the changes made, enjoy the originals in all their glory.

TL;DR The game is an INCREDIBLE entry into the Dishonored ethos. But after seven and  ahalf months it's still DEFINITELY not fixed.
Now. I am giving this game a positive review. But that doesn't mean I've had a very positive experience in terms of how the game runs.
What's positive about it is the fact that it does so well AS a Dishonored game. With more incredible level design, character design, sound design and gameplay mechanics, it does TRUELY fit in the ethos AS a Dishonored game. And for that the game is FUNDAMENTALLY GOOD and worth recommending. Just not on PC.
(Despite not having had played as Corvo Attano yet. My experience is purely from the Emily Kaldwin side of the fence for gameplay. And she's executed well, although her dialogue can be annoyingly long winded for no good reason other than re iterating on the scenario she just perfect encapsulated not 2 and a half seconds before that in the same sentance. But I digress.)
As a huge Dishonored Stan, I'm bitterly disappointed in the IMMEDIATE FLUIDITY of the game's performance.
I've been wanting this game since before release, and I have been waiting out for awhile and decided to pick it up cause summer sale.
From what I've read. performance was horrid on day one. And from how my 4.8 hours have felt in the game that I've put in in a single sitting. It's still pretty horrid. (Although I will admit the further I get into the game the less abbraisive the FPS drops become. But that might be due to conditioning and not the game's performance actually improving.)
Frame drops reguardless of what my settings are and what resolution im running at. Hell I even got drops at 800x600 of about 12-25FPS below my V-Sync of 60 and they weren't just occasional. They where persistent. Constant crashes reguardless of settings as well. Feels very RNG'd in terms of the crashes too. Sometimes it's 30 seconds, others 10 minutes, others an hour. But it always eventually happens.
I'm loving the game for the game that it is. The combat is as good as I remembered in D1, the game is stupendously beautiful with some of the best environments and concepts I've ever seen. But it's a technological quagmire still. Almost eight months later, and it's apparently "fixed."
I've jumped through every fix hoop on the forums and on YouTube (mainly the same stuff. Max pre redered frames to 1, maximum performance, borderless fullscreen with an FPS cap at your refresh rate, same old.) and I can't tell if anything's improved or not honestly.
I'm just saddened that such an incredible ethos and IP, one of my favorites of all time in gaming as a whole, has been dashed so horrendously.
I have also seen that people have been and can run the game locked at their desired framerate. And I wish I was one of those people and that the performance of this game wasn't such a mishmashed quagmire of mixed results from people on both lesser and better hardware than I'm on.
GeForce GTX 1070
R7 1700 @3.7GHz (I've seen people with Intel chips still suffering the same problems too, and recently)
16GB G.Skill Trident Z @ 2933MHz
It's not like my hardware isn't up to spec. The only thing I can fisibly point the finger at the devs on for this game's performance is their attempt to create their own nonsensicle branded engine out of the idTech5 Engine. If they had of just picked the idTech5 Engine and had at it, this game would probably run flawlessly.Hell they could of gone with Unreal Engine 4. From what I've seen it looks just as good, if not better in some areas. But for whatever reason, they muddled limes that didn't need to be muddled, and now the consequences have been laid bare.
I give them props for trying and to a very large extent having succeeded in fixing A LOT of the performance problems from day one. But it's still got a long way to go.

It’s a prime example of making a boring, run-of-the-mill, uninspired game with the intentions of using a popular brand or name to make it somewhat successful rather than making a game that could stand up on its own merits as an objectively fun, innovative, or good game.
If this hadn’t been labeled or tied to TES then it would have crashed, burned, and been forgotten even harder.
I legitimately feel bad for those people who paid money for this, but moreso I feel bad for those poor souls who used time, effort, and their skills to develop this.
Please stay away from this game and don’t support the industry that shovels this tripe onto your plate. It’s not worth your time. Go play Skyrim if you like TES and if you like MMO’s then go play one of the other successful ones that do everything better than this.

Finished my first playthrough, taking 27 hours on low chaos, as I took my time and enjoyed the scenery and the world. It's some of the best level design I've seen in a game. Every nook and cranny is filled with detail and there isn't an item placed that doesn't seem like there is a purpose. The city of Karnaca truly feels lived in. I don't know how to explain it, but you can see the history of this city with just the level design alone.
Graphics are good, sound is good, and mechanics are good. There are the occasional texture poppins, and I did get stuck in a hole you can normally crawl through (though blink/far reach can still pull you through).
I ran the game on Ultra settings. My card is a GTX1060 3 gb VRAM, 16 gb memory and an i7 6700HQ at 2.6 Ghz. I know that a lot of people with better specs than I have complained about framerate issues - my advice is kill all background processes and update your drivers. This game is a resource hog so having internet or other backlground processes have a noticeable impact on the game's performance

Dishonored 2 is a wonderful expansion on the first game, but with all its pros, it does have a few downsides compared to the first, and for me, mainly the atmosphere is what bothered me. Standalone, Dishonored 2 has an excellent setting and feel to it, but if you came for the same feel of the first game, you might be a bit dissappointed like I was.  In the first, It's as if you are exploring a dying city, with the threat of the rat plague being common, and real, because you're surrounded by it and you see the effects of it. The game is depressing, but in a really intriguing way. Dishonored 2 on the otherhand, is much more bright, the location is livelier, and the plague that replaces the rat plague feels like it's hardly there, just being in a few secluded houses, like quarantines. I would 100% recommend playing the first, then moving to this one.
The level I enjoyed the most (with one exception) is the last one, because it feels like the first game.
TL;DR: I enjoyed the first game more because of the gloomy and dark atmosphere of it, rather than the brighter and livelier feel of the second. I recommend playing the first, then the second (Do not skip the first!!!)
