A wonderful side scrolling shooter that demands strategy, timing and thought. To truly do this game justice, I will break it down to its base components and review them
Story
The story, even though it might as well not exist, was very fun to see. It has one of those very satisfying endings, with an insanely hard boss battle. I beat it with a friend by my side and it was just a cluster ♥♥♥♥ of "Dude get an extra life!" and "Dude shoot him! Use your special!" The ending actually gives you an option, and my friend unfortunately picked the bad ending. Either way, it's a blast of a campaign
Gameplay
The game, though the gameplay is very simple, is a good kind of simple. It's not simple to the point where it's annoying. It's fun to try and tackle new enemy types and try out the different bros, which are all played with differently. That being said, some of the bros are flat out useless, the most useless of the bunch being Ellen Ripley and Indiana Jones. And, some bros were brutally over powered, like Commando. As well, sometimes there was a ridiculous spike in difficulty, and some less than legitimate deaths. But all in all, these problems are negligible, since the game does more right than it does wrong.
Graphics
This games retro style of graphics works perfectly with the gameplay. It's just a high enough resolution to make out what's going on. The cute little sprites running around the map make the game stick with you, and keep you comming back. The cinematics are also nice to look at, because the pixel art is pretty amusing, with the ripped bros doing their manly poses in front of epic backgrounds.
Music
The music, though not very varied, is quite an epic conclusion to each screen. It's somewhat similar to SOAD without the lyrics, in my opinion, though some might not think so. The music, overall, is solid
Overall, this game is definitely a buy. This game will give you tons of hours of fun, due to its replayability and mindless fun style of gameplay. Perhaps the full price is a bit steep, but if you've got the disposable income, buy it now!

But what you should play this game for is the story. It's very rare I've found a game that is so expansive (for a linear game, at any rate). The environments are varied and the game never gets stale from the opening chapter to the very end. Some deadly boss battles too, which is a great plus and keeps it engaging. But, the story is just breathtaking. There are few games that've left me speechless and fewer still that've left me thinking about whether or not I did the right thing at the end. For those who don't know what a moba is, I will explain. Basically a moba (massive online battle arena) is a game type that features both strategy and skill. typically, you chose a character with 1 passive abilites, 3 regular abilities, and 1 ultimate ability. As the game goes on you gain xp and gold based on how well you have done, and you can use xp to level up and gold to buy items. Leveling up increases your stats and allows you to put an extra point into an ability. The objective is to push through you enemies defenses and destroy their base.

Ignoring that this game was an absolute joke on release day (yes, I'm still bitter about getting duped into pre-ordering so I could use one of the factions included in the game without having to pay for it), it's still a huge disappointment. The Emperor Edition is a massive improvement, but still falls way short of what was promised. Even with all the patches, the game is a big step back from Shogun 2.
Firstly, the game is lifeless and boring. I've yet to even get close to year 0 in a save and I've probably started about 20 of them. Just look at the hours I've spent playing this game. I've tried so hard since the day it was released to get into a save in this game, and it's never happened. All of the screenshots and promotional media for this game looked amazing and captivating, but that feeling never materalizes in the actual game. I never have the urge to expand my empire, or make my enemies pay for crossing me. It just feels like I'm engaging in a strategy (if you want to call it that) exercise against AI, nothing more.  CA have sucked the life out of this series by dumbing down things like politics and diplomacy, and removing things like family trees for no aparent reason. The best feeling I got from this game was when I finally accepted that I wasted my money on it and uninstalled it from my system.
The AI is still horrendously bad. It's a million times better than it was at release, but it's still terrible. It's so easy to learn AI tendencies, and it takes a huge amount of restraint to stop myself from exploiting them. Battle AI is really bad, but luckily there are a lot of mods that can fix this and actually make it enjoyable. At the same time, there's only so much modders can do to cover up CA's mistakes, and it's really sad that CA needs other people to fix their game for them to make it playable.
Campaign AI is atrocious and not even challenging. There's hardly any logic in the strategy of AI factions. They don't seem to care about defending their cities and they never create any type of organized, strategic attack. The only way to make the game challenging is to put the difficulty on very hard, so the AI can just churn out full stacks at will and send them at you one by one. Even then, it just turns into a game of fending off the armies, one or two at a time, until the AI does something inexplicably stupid to give you the advantage. It's extremely frustrating to have a back and forth war with an AI faction over one of its settlements, only to have that faction just randomly move all of its armies away from that settlement, basically allowing you to walk right in and take it. This type of thing happens ALL OF THE TIME and takes all of the intensity and excitment out of wars.
Some parts of the game are still broken, even in the Emperor Edition. Sieges are somehow even worse than Shogun 2. City gates are broken. Any unit can just burn down a gate by throwing flaming sticks at it, but then they are unable to walk through it. I'm not even sure if battering rams work at all. Ladders and siege towers kind of work though (at least with the overhaul mod that I've used), so there's that.
Obviously the game is still addicting in some way, as it's managed to get me to pour 200+ hours into it, but it feels more like I've wasted a massive part of my life trying to get this game to entertain me than anything else. People who have never played a Total War game before may find this game neat because of the setting and the battles (which are absolutely a standout feature for this series when compared to other strategy games), but those of us who have played TW games before know how much of a disappointment this was. For those who disagree with me: go back and look at the promotional videos that CA released prior to the game's launch and compare that to what we paid for. I've not experienced anything close to what was advertised, and I've yet to see anyone who has been able to make this game look anywhere near the way it did in the videos of the ♥♥♥♥in alpha (that CA said was still going to be further optimized). It still looks cool at times--some of the cities having unique features on the battle map is a really cool feature, and the campaign map looks by far the best it has in any game of the series.
Overall, Rome 2 was a huge failure and a waste of time for everyone involved. It actually compares really unfavorably to Rome 1 and Medeival 2 from 10 years ago. CA has already rushed into making another game, Atilla, which is really just a remake of one of Rome 1's expansions released as a full game. I will not even be touching that game unless it gets great reviews and goes on sale for <$20. You'd have to be a fool to preorder that game after the trainwreck that was Rome 2's launch. CA has used up all the good faith it built from its early games and deserves to be under heavy scrutiny going forward.
As for anyone thinking about buying this game, I would strongly recommend not to. Even if its heavily discounted, it's really not worth the time that you will pour into it before finally accepting that it's just not a good game. I would suggest waiting for Atilla's release and seeing what the community consensus is (let's not forget how many gaming websites gave Rome 2 highly favorable reviews at launch). Hopefully CA will get its act together and release what Rome 2 should have been.
TLDR:
Pros
+Campaign map looks really good compared to other games in the series
+Modding community is amazing and did CA a huge favor by saving this game before CA could make it playable on its own
Cons
-The AI is so bad that it's really hard to actually use strategy in a meaningful way
-No immersion due to features from previous games being streamlined or removed
-Game was released with numerous broken features and many of these features still remain broken despite all the patches
-Really disappoints graphically in a lot of areas (poorly optimized)

Alien: Isolation was one of 2014's most anticipated games and rightly so. This was Sega's shot at trying to revive the franchise after the failure that was Colonial Marines from Gearbox Software. Unlike Colonial Marines, Alien: Isolation is a story-driven first-person survival horror game with shooter and crafting elements. It is the first game to be set upon the actual film, taking place years after the events of Ridley Scotts Aliens film from 1986 i believe. You play as Ripleys daughter, Amanda as she tries to uncover the secrets to the dissapearance of the Nostromo, and her mother. The game itself is a breath of fresh air for the Aliens game franchise. For one, unlike the previous games, it is not primarily a first-person shooter, but it is not in any ways similar to Amnesia or Outlast for that matter. You have a vast variety of tools; from the pistol, stun baton, shotgun, flamethrower and a bolt gun. You can craft medical kits, molotovs, smoke bombs, emp, pipe bombs among all different variety of things. The maintenance jack is a tool and is the first main weapon you aquire in the game. Throughout the game, you encounter enemies, from 'working joe' seegson maintenance androids that are originally operated to be friendly but end up hunting and killing you to other survivers on the ship but like previous games theres one more, an Alien. Nope, not aliens, just one. A ruthless hunter that cannot be killed at any point in the game and its job is to hunt everyone down and kill them all. The game itself was very fun for me, i had no issues playing it and i think that Creative Assembly proved that Isolation is a huge step beyond what Colonial Marines was. I hope for the next installment Sega could let Creative work on it again, would love to see what they come up with next. Definetely a recommendation from me.

It all started with an offer for a free adventure and an hour or two of preparation doing the seemingly never-ending task of "downloading" we set off. Alas there were already challenges on the road but experienced as I am with previous adventures my mind told me to not give up. This was the first mini-boss, the little nasty bugger known as "Log-In Failed".
"You shall not pass!"
The battle was tough at first until I discovered its weakness known as "create account", a powerfull spell taught on the official page. This page must be part of the Elder Scrolls themselves. So as "Log-In Failed" was defeated I was tossed into a maelstrom of options. Twas here the real adventure began. Choices, are they good or are they bad? We shall see.
I saw a light and woke in a place never before seen yet so familiar... it was like walking through the past itself. Oblivion, yet not, nor was it Skyrim. No, this was different. I wondered - am I dead? I was led through darkness and smoke, forced to fight without my weapon of choice but alas I won but the adventure still hadn't ended. From the darkness I was once more sent away and woke in a land where there was no smoke or darkness around me. Tamriel, beautiful Tamriel.
"U r gay!!!!" a voice whispers and I'm reminded why I have avoided all adventures known as "MMO".
I look around and there are many people by my side. Who are these strangers? They start running like chickens who just had their heads cut off. Interesting. I start walking, finding a few mudcrabs along the beaches. My old nemesis, it's time for revenge! However I'm new to the world here, I need coin and the mudcrabs here have none as the almighty monocle-mudcrab in Skyrim took it all. I am forced to take on tasks from the people known as "NPC". Grinding, more dungeon trolls and a few strange symbols, it started to look bleak. Did I make a bad choice joining in on this adventure?
Six hours in there are no more whispers directed at me, people leave me to my adventure but my keen ears pick up new conversations. People helping one another, ignoring these dungeon trolls and here are there are some traders looking to sell. Tamriel seems calm and in one of the battles with bandits that occured I heard a gentle "thanks :)" whispered from a tall elven lass. I stop and look at her. Shiny armour, giant sword, 251 username hovered over her and a flying demon was by her side and she thanks me? Me... who was dressed in rags and with a crooked staff on my back? I smiled. Maybe it's not that bad... in fact, I think I will continue this adventure.
I pay my toll and wave as I log off.
"See you soon!"

In the first, It's as if you are exploring a dying city, with the threat of the rat plague being common, and real, because you're surrounded by it and you see the effects of it. The game is depressing, but in a really intriguing way. Dishonored 2 on the otherhand, is much more bright, the location is livelier, and the plague that replaces the rat plague feels like it's hardly there, just being in a few secluded houses, like quarantines. I would 100% recommend playing the first, then moving to this one.
The level I enjoyed the most (with one exception) is the last one, because it feels like the first game.

People really need to give this game a chance. I was on the ban wagon of 'its had bad reviews im not bothering' but since the free weekend its been so enjoyable and i love it. The combat is awesome. The amount of customisation you can do to you class is crazy and the amount of content is great. I have played this game for about 29 hours now and still haven't left the first area after you leave your starting area. With latest update you can explore all of Tamriel and do quests in the other factions zones which is pretty cool. Just give it a try. Don't assume its a bad game because it was in bad shape on release. Oh btw there is no pay to win on this game which is a huge + for me. I hate pay to win games they're the worst. You can sub to ESO for minor buffs such as small exp bonuses to crafting and lvling but that's it. You're not missing out on anything if you don't sub.
So after playing a fair bit i'd like to update my review on what i think of the game now.
Pros:
-Massive content.
I can't believe the amount of content in this game. It is crazy, i have put in 120ish hours into the game and i have only completed one zone. Mind you i do all side quests, guild quests etc. I don't plan on rushing story mode just yet but yes i have also been doing the story line bit by bit and so far the story line is great.
-Crafting.
Crafting on this game is amazing. You can craft your own gear with your choice of traits, enchants etc. The best thing about it is that you can choose what style of weapons or gear you want to craft (As long as you have learned different crafting styles). Crafting does not feel like a grind unless you want to go grind out materials you can find throughout Tamriel.
-Questing
Ok people can have different thoughts on this but for me i love the questing in this game. The best thing about the quests in ESO is that it feels like an Elder scrolls game. Most quests are unique. Unlike other mmos its not like EVERY quest is to go kill 20 Bandits and collect 10 pieces of cloth. Most of ESO quests gives you choices on what you want to do. For example save Jack or kill him which changes the outcome of the quest. I honestly wonder sometimes if i made the right choice which is awesome.
-Character Creation
With every mmo you select a 'race' 'class' and 'faction' then you can change a few things like skin colour, hair styles etc. ESO however allows you to change every detail on your character making you feel more connected to the character. I think i spent a good hour on my first toon constantly changing his appearance. Just like the other Elder Scrolls games there is plenty of customisation options.
-Class Customisation.
Whats that you want to be a mage that can wear heavy armour and duel wield? or do you prefer to use 2 handed weapons?. At first i was against this as i thought it would be stupid for a mage to duel wield or a night blade AKA assassin to use heavy armour but after playing around with the different weapons on classes its honestly amazing. You can go with your own personalised build and play around until you find something you really like. Unlike other mmo's prime example 'WoW' if you choose a class your locked into 1 set of weapon style you can use and everyone playing that class are using the same build. WoW is still a good game however unlike ESO you truly don't feel free to how you want to create your class. So if you want to be a mage and use a sword then the option is yours.
Cons:
-Laggy servers
If your like me and live far away from the NA or EU servers you're going to suffer from a bit of lag . I have good internet speed with 90 down and 45 up and i get about 230 ping. It doesn't really bother me because i'm not doing PvP. I mean i'd love to do PvP but i'm afraid the little bit of lag will make it a bad experience for me
-Multiplayer Experience
ESO definitely feels like more single player then multiplayer, WHICH is not really a bad thing. In fact some people might like that, i'm not really bothered by it as all the other Elder scrolls games are single player but if you truly want that group style of game play you're going to have to play with a friend. There is still group finder options and random dungeons ques etc but if your in a group and you like getting in to the quests you have to just click everything and ignore the dialogue other wise you get left behind unless the group your in also listens to the dialogue
-Editing your appearance
Ok this is not really problem but i like to be able to edit my characters appearance. Unfortunately the only way to do that is to spend real money on the crown store to edit your characters appearance which is a bit poor because with an mmo you're going to spend a lot of time on one character and eventually you're going to want to either change your hairstyle, facial hair etc. I was happy with my characters appearance but regretted my hairstyle so i had to buy crowns just so i can change my hair style, i know that sounds dumb as you can just wear your head gear and you cant see your hair but i honesty prefer the 'hide helmet' option on. Now someone did tell me that sometime next year they're implementing a npc where you can change and edit your characters appearance whether that is true or not i hope this becomes a thing.
Overall i highly recommend this game if you're either into mmo's or the Elder Scrolls franchise as this game give you the feeling of both. This game has huge potential for the future so i'd love to see where the developers take this game. Thank you for reading if you made it this far and i hope i can make your decision easier to make. :)

Emily is Away is an interactive messaging-SIM that tells the story of a highschool/college boy and his best friend: Emily. The game interface replicates a classic Windows feel, along with boot and message sounds. It took me 50 minutes to play through once; some people took a shorter or longer time.
I decided to play this game on a whim, and hey, it was free. I was actually pleasantly surprised that messaging wasn't the only thing you could do. Along with the messaging window, there is a "friend list" kind of thing, where you can check up on your contact's profiles. In every profile is a description written by the user, but most of the time, they are song lyrics.
The game spans over 5 chapters, with a 1 year interval between them. With each year, the relationship between the two characters will flow as smooth as rocks on an asphalt road can flow. For every year, you can choose a profile picture. This can affect what Emily will say at times. Every time your character will type, you are given three dialogue options, which dictate what he will say (not verbatim). You click/press enter, and then keyboard characters are either typed or deleted with each keystroke, so typing yourself will really have no effect. Choices seem to only affect the ending in miniscule ways, from what I've seen. Sometimes, the boy would type something, only to backspace and type something different. It is truly interesting to see what the main character is thinking but is hesistant to say.
As I stated before, each person using the messaging program has a profile, and you can use details on these profiles to help you choose what to say sometimes.
-------------------------------
As soon as I found out that typing didn't matter, I told myself that I would try to predict what the boy'd say and type along anyway. And you know what? A lot of times, what came up was exactly what I had inputted. Cool.
I had literally no expectations of this game, as I didn't even know it existed until a few hours ago. However, right in the middle of the first chapter, I began to let myself connect. I am just a highschool boy in a similar situation, so perhaps for this reason, the game had more of an impact on me.
Playing this game gave me a little insight on how a relationship like that could progress/retrogress after separation and attending different schools. Given my life experiences, it really spoke to me. It also didn't help that a lot of the musical lyrics in the messaging profiles were from songs that I know and love (especially those by Death Cab for Cutie).
Even if choices don't affect the ending much, it affected my experience throughout the game. I felt like I was stuck between a rock and a hard place sometimes, wondering to myself if it really was the right thing to say. The main character changing his mind occasionally hit me hard, seeing Emily's typing patterns evolve from barebone letters to sentences with capitals and punctuation reminded me of my situation, and
, as opposed to Emily, were all nice touches.
After beating the game, I felt insanely crushed. My fears had come true in some alternate video-game world. No, even throughout the whole game, I felt horrible, down, sad, depressed, angry even. Not only was I angry at the other characters like Brad, I was angry at myself for making someone else go through these things, even if it was a video-game character.
I'm still recovering from this game now.
Play it, please.

I've just finished Enslaved: Odyssey to the West on Steam, letting me mark off another game from my Steam "Backlog of Shame". It's a 2013 PC port of a game from 2010, originally on Xbox 360/PS3.
Being a port, it definitely had its issues. Crashes and lock-ups for some of the cut scenes, especially late in the game. But it was definitely worth the frustration to push past these and finish the game.
In the game, you play as Monkey, a loner surviving in a world set 150 years in the future and overrun with an army of killer robots. You quickly meet up with Trip: a young woman who traps Monkey with a slaver's headband in order to get what she needs. Her deal for Monkey: get her home and she'll set him free. Oh, and if she dies (or he tries to leave) he dies too. He'll have to help her cross 300+ miles through the wasteland, avoiding death at the hands of mechs and slavers along the way.
The story centers on the relationship between Monkey and Trip. She has complete control over what he does, but is completely dependent on him in order to survive. The power dynamic goes back and forth until they finally start to trust and care for each other.
The game play folds out in a series of platformer puzzles and combat set pieces in between scenes pushing the story forward. Monkey fights with a bo staff that doubles as a ranged energy weapon. Most of the time Trip is out of the way for combat, but she does support Monkey by providing upgrades for his equipment, scouting the way forward with a small drone, providing distractions for the ranged turrets and mechs and acting as a second person for some of the puzzles. She doesn't fight or climb and she can't jump quite as far as Monkey can, so more often than not the puzzles are you trying to find a way for her to move forward. The slave headband also lets Trip see and hear what Monkey does and allows her to overlay information as an augmented reality display in Monkey's vision, allowing him to see hidden mines and the detection range of powered down mechs.
Combat is mostly fun and not too difficult or frustrating (with a few exceptions). The camera is over-the-shoulder and sometimes makes it a bit hard to see what's going on, but that doesn't usually get too much in the way of a good brawl. You'll find yourself using a mixture of cover/stealth to get around enemies or to get into position, and Trip's support features help out with this a lot. The game will usually put a helpful "flaw" in some enemies, giving you an advantage if you care to exploit it, and making sure that the combat doesn't get stale and repetitive. The only real punishing fights are the boss battles, where a single mistake can mean starting the encounter over from the beginning. The puzzle aren't too challenging, and are kind of standard fare, in the line of games like Tomb Raider and the Uncharted games.
In addition to Monkey's bo staff, another item in Monkey's tool set is the Cloud. It is an energy based "hoverboard" that is only activated in a few areas of the game, allowing Monkey to hover over water, travel at high speeds and jump across gaps that he normally wouldn't be able to clear. I really wish that this was available for more of the game rather than just the few areas that you could activate it, but I was just happy to have it. The Cloud is a lot of fun to get around on, and always felt like something that I wanted to use rather than just another puzzle mechanic.
In addition to the puzzles and combat, the game encourages exploration (to the extent that Trip doesn't think that Monkey is abandoning her and kills him) in the form of Tech Orbs and strange floating Masks. The Tech Orbs unlock upgrades for Monkey and are well worth the effort of tracking down (aside from just achievement hunting). The Masks tie into the story and are related to Monkey's slave headband. Each shows a set of images from before the war, lasting only for a few seconds. They are interesting, but not necessary unless you are an achievement hunter.
Late into the game, you are introduced to a third character: Pigsy. He helps Trip and Monkey on the last stage of their journey together and he's ridiculous and crude and completely full of himself, all of which makes him an amazing character. Pigsy is also the focus of his own DLC (included in the Steam version of the game), set before he meets up with Trip and Monkey, which is definitely worth playing.
By the end of the game, I felt emotionally invested in the characters, They felt like fully fleshed out beings rather than two-dimensional fantasy archetypes that you usually get with games. They had depth and had grown. I understood their motivations and their actions made sense, and the ending wasn't one of those "and they lived happily ever after" endings. It made you think about what was next for the characters and the (spoilers) army of freed slaves released from the Pyramid, and if they did the right thing. It was very satisfying. I'd love to see Ninja Theory do another game set in this universe again.

A wonderful side scrolling shooter that demands strategy, timing and thought. To truly do this game justice, I will break it down to its base components and review them
Story
The story, even though it might as well not exist, was very fun to see. It has one of those very satisfying endings, with an insanely hard boss battle. I beat it with a friend by my side and it was just a cluster ♥♥♥♥ of "Dude get an extra life!" and "Dude shoot him! Use your special!" The ending actually gives you an option, and my friend unfortunately picked the bad ending. Either way, it's a blast of a campaign
Gameplay
The game, though the gameplay is very simple, is a good kind of simple. It's not simple to the point where it's annoying. It's fun to try and tackle new enemy types and try out the different bros, which are all played with differently. That being said, some of the bros are flat out useless, the most useless of the bunch being Ellen Ripley and Indiana Jones. And, some bros were brutally over powered, like Commando. As well, sometimes there was a ridiculous spike in difficulty, and some less than legitimate deaths. But all in all, these problems are negligible, since the game does more right than it does wrong.
Graphics
This games retro style of graphics works perfectly with the gameplay. It's just a high enough resolution to make out what's going on. The cute little sprites running around the map make the game stick with you, and keep you comming back. The cinematics are also nice to look at, because the pixel art is pretty amusing, with the ripped bros doing their manly poses in front of epic backgrounds.
Music
The music, though not very varied, is quite an epic conclusion to each screen. It's somewhat similar to SOAD without the lyrics, in my opinion, though some might not think so. The music, overall, is solid
Overall, this game is definitely a buy. This game will give you tons of hours of fun, due to its replayability and mindless fun style of gameplay. Perhaps the full price is a bit steep, but if you've got the disposable income, buy it now!

Ignoring that this game was an absolute joke on release day (yes, I'm still bitter about getting duped into pre-ordering so I could use one of the factions included in the game without having to pay for it), it's still a huge disappointment. The Emperor Edition is a massive improvement, but still falls way short of what was promised. Even with all the patches, the game is a big step back from Shogun 2.
Firstly, the game is lifeless and boring. I've yet to even get close to year 0 in a save and I've probably started about 20 of them. Just look at the hours I've spent playing this game. I've tried so hard since the day it was released to get into a save in this game, and it's never happened. All of the screenshots and promotional media for this game looked amazing and captivating, but that feeling never materalizes in the actual game. I never have the urge to expand my empire, or make my enemies pay for crossing me. It just feels like I'm engaging in a strategy (if you want to call it that) exercise against AI, nothing more.  CA have sucked the life out of this series by dumbing down things like politics and diplomacy, and removing things like family trees for no aparent reason. The best feeling I got from this game was when I finally accepted that I wasted my money on it and uninstalled it from my system.
The AI is still horrendously bad. It's a million times better than it was at release, but it's still terrible. It's so easy to learn AI tendencies, and it takes a huge amount of restraint to stop myself from exploiting them. Battle AI is really bad, but luckily there are a lot of mods that can fix this and actually make it enjoyable. At the same time, there's only so much modders can do to cover up CA's mistakes, and it's really sad that CA needs other people to fix their game for them to make it playable.
Campaign AI is atrocious and not even challenging. There's hardly any logic in the strategy of AI factions. They don't seem to care about defending their cities and they never create any type of organized, strategic attack. The only way to make the game challenging is to put the difficulty on very hard, so the AI can just churn out full stacks at will and send them at you one by one. Even then, it just turns into a game of fending off the armies, one or two at a time, until the AI does something inexplicably stupid to give you the advantage. It's extremely frustrating to have a back and forth war with an AI faction over one of its settlements, only to have that faction just randomly move all of its armies away from that settlement, basically allowing you to walk right in and take it. This type of thing happens ALL OF THE TIME and takes all of the intensity and excitment out of wars.
Some parts of the game are still broken, even in the Emperor Edition. Sieges are somehow even worse than Shogun 2. City gates are broken. Any unit can just burn down a gate by throwing flaming sticks at it, but then they are unable to walk through it. I'm not even sure if battering rams work at all. Ladders and siege towers kind of work though (at least with the overhaul mod that I've used), so there's that.
Obviously the game is still addicting in some way, as it's managed to get me to pour 200+ hours into it, but it feels more like I've wasted a massive part of my life trying to get this game to entertain me than anything else. People who have never played a Total War game before may find this game neat because of the setting and the battles (which are absolutely a standout feature for this series when compared to other strategy games), but those of us who have played TW games before know how much of a disappointment this was. For those who disagree with me: go back and look at the promotional videos that CA released prior to the game's launch and compare that to what we paid for. I've not experienced anything close to what was advertised, and I've yet to see anyone who has been able to make this game look anywhere near the way it did in the videos of the ♥♥♥♥in alpha (that CA said was still going to be further optimized). It still looks cool at times--some of the cities having unique features on the battle map is a really cool feature, and the campaign map looks by far the best it has in any game of the series.
Overall, Rome 2 was a huge failure and a waste of time for everyone involved. It actually compares really unfavorably to Rome 1 and Medeival 2 from 10 years ago. CA has already rushed into making another game, Atilla, which is really just a remake of one of Rome 1's expansions released as a full game. I will not even be touching that game unless it gets great reviews and goes on sale for <$20. You'd have to be a fool to preorder that game after the trainwreck that was Rome 2's launch. CA has used up all the good faith it built from its early games and deserves to be under heavy scrutiny going forward.
As for anyone thinking about buying this game, I would strongly recommend not to. Even if its heavily discounted, it's really not worth the time that you will pour into it before finally accepting that it's just not a good game. I would suggest waiting for Atilla's release and seeing what the community consensus is (let's not forget how many gaming websites gave Rome 2 highly favorable reviews at launch). Hopefully CA will get its act together and release what Rome 2 should have been.
TLDR:
Pros
+Campaign map looks really good compared to other games in the series
+Modding community is amazing and did CA a huge favor by saving this game before CA could make it playable on its own
Cons
-The AI is so bad that it's really hard to actually use strategy in a meaningful way
-No immersion due to features from previous games being streamlined or removed
-Game was released with numerous broken features and many of these features still remain broken despite all the patches
-Really disappoints graphically in a lot of areas (poorly optimized)

I've been a huge fan of the 1979 "ALIEN" film (and the original trilogy as a whole) ever since I first saw it on television growing up as a teenager. I became instantly mesmerized by the aesthetics and atmosphere of that retro-futuristic, industrial world imagined by Ridley Scott and of course, by the strikingly beautiful biomechanical look of the creature itself as designed by H.R. Giger. After having regrettably witnessed the "Alien" franchise being butchered, manhandled, vandalised and trivialised time and time again in recent times, it has been an absolute pleasure for me to finally enjoy an experience in which the heart and soul of the original film are preserved and treated with the respect, love and reverence they deserve in "Alien: Isolation".
One of the greatest achievements of this game, in my opinion, is having succeeded in making the Alien appealing and scary again. The Alien is unpredictable and unforgiving and, once the player accepts and embraces the fact that, at least for the first part of the game (until some limited means are provided to deal with the threat in a more aggressive way), he or she is nothing but meat ready for the taking by the creature (pretty much just like everybody else on board the ill-fated Sevastopol space station, where the action takes place), the true nature of the game (and how the game should be played) is revealed in the most honest possible way imaginable.
The world itself is unbelievably detailed and true to the aesthetics of the original film; the graphics are gorgeous and the lighting system is one of the best I have ever seen in any video game. There is, however, a slight problem with the way anti-aliasing is implemented and managed by the game engine, which admittedly isn't very good and runs the danger of breaking immersion. However, if you can let some occasional unwanted ‘jaggies’ here and there pass and concentrate on the many technical achievements of the graphics engine instead, the whole experience becomes a truly breathtaking one. Sound design is one of the highest plus points of this game, as well as the impeccable voice acting, character design and motion capture performance - actually, Kezia Burrows' portrayal of Amanda Ripley is one of the best I've ever encountered (she's basically the reason why I went ahead and picked up "Remember Me" earlier this week, after all), as well as Amanda's voice, played by Andrea Deck. Speaking of which... Sigourney Weaver also makes a more than welcome appearance in the form of recordings and audio messages throughout the campaign and most of the original cast members reprise their roles in a couple of the DLC missions - more on DLC below!
Some of the design choices might strike odd at first but once understood in context, they blend in just perfectly with everything else, I think, such as the infamous save system. Yes, it may appear frustrating at first, but once the player assumes finding and accessing save points as an indispensable survival skill to be mastered, it becomes a fun challenge trying to make it through a level looking for the welcoming 'beep' of a nearby save station and taking a deep breath of relief when finally stumbling upon one, inserting your card to save your precious progress. Backtracking actually does make sense in this game - since it's set on a space station and, well, 'space' is a limited resource, as expected - and the tool upgrades found as the game progresses actually allow for previously locked rooms or passages to be opened when revisiting those areas, thus rewarding exploration.
Whilst the game eventually does allow the player to adopt a more aggressive stance towards the many enemies populating the station - from cheap synthetic humanoids gone haywire to other survivors and of course, the Alien - it does heavily reward stealth and diligent conservation and managing of resources, which are pretty scarce and are used to craft all sorts of useful gadgets to either take out more powerful enemies (such as the resilient 'Working Joes' - with great satisfaction, I should add!) or create diversions and decoys to sneak past them. Most of the time, however, stealth is the only possible way to survive, as the Alien (which can kill the player with a single blow) cannot be killed or injured in any way - only momentarily pushed back or scared away later in the game. Please keep this in mind because although some weapons (i.e. firearms) eventually do become available, the game is most definitely not meant as a 'gun-and-run' shooter in any way, shape or form (actually, firing a weapon in close confinements usually ends up attracting the Alien, with devastating consequences).
Finally, about DLC: I find that, unless you are a hard-core fan of the “ALIEN” film and/or the original trilogy, DLC isn't really justified as a bonus to the experience, as the game itself already comes with loads of content that will keep you busy and entertained for a long period of time (I for one have put in more than 25 hours during my first run, exploring every possible corridor, vent shaft and crevasse I could find, ultimately finishing the game with a rewarding sense of satisfaction). If you are, I think IT IS A MUST that you get at least the two expansion missions featuring the original cast of "ALIEN": "Crew Expendable", in which you can choose to play as any other crew member of the 'Nostromo' and attempt to corner the Alien to blow it out of the airlock (I for one remained 'classic' and played as Dallas; having Lambert on my earpiece warning me about the Alien in the vents and urging me to move gave me absolute chills whilst recreating and reliving one of my favourite scenes in the movie), and "Last Survivor", where you play as Ellen Ripley and your objective is to escape the 'Nostromo' after setting the auto-destruct sequence on. Both of them are rather short, but the fact that they allow you to recreate some of the best moments in the film makes it worth getting them, IMHO.
Oh yes, I forgot to mention: 'Survival Mode' is amazing, really fun and adds a ton of replay value. Make sure to play it AFTER you complete the main campaign, though.
Overall, I found "Alien: Isolation" to be an AWESOME game, a thrilling ride and a fitting tribute to one of the finest science-fiction universes ever created (at least my particular favourite one). I highly recommend you picking up this game if you are a fan of the “Alien” universe or if you simply enjoy classic sci-fi and/or survival-horror games in general.

I know there are far more detailed reviews out there, and far more emotional, too. I'm not trying to compete with those, just expressing my personal feelings.
For those that haven't played HW1, just two words: go ahead. This won't disappoint, and you won't even notice the things us ♥♥♥♥♥♥s are unhappy about. For the likes of me, however, here's what to expect.
First off, this is not Homeworld 1. Close, much closer than expected, but still no. All those tiny details will make you feel something isn't quite right, no matter how well or poorly you remember the original. The UI, of course, is probably the worst offender, feeling too modern, too... I just don't know the right words. I guess the UI aesthetics have changed greatly over time, and I am sad to see Gearbox going the HW2 route when it came to styling (hopefully, it's not as clunky as HW2 was, but the overall UI art is on the same track). But this is a minor issue, and once you get over it, you will notice it is quite playable. Make no mistake, the old one wasn't perfect either, it was just much more "in theme".
Next thing you notice (unless, you crash on mission load as I did numerous times, in that case make sure you aren't overgenerous selecting texture quality), it looks gorgeous (albeit, a bit too "sleek" when compared to the first game. That is just a feeling, and it comes from the game defaulting to HW2 colour scheme, nothing else. Once you select original HW1 colours you're back with the old feel of "newbies to space". It is a great thing, really.
They did choose to port HW1 into HW2 engine, which made the game lose some of its original features, like simulated projectiles, and it fails miserably at holding formations, plus there are differences in resources available, ship costs, oh, and research now costs too. That all said, I am glad to say I didn't pick most of these things till I've been told about them. And, what's most important to me, the original feeling of being alone out there, a small island of life in the middle of cold indifferent space, it all has translated well into the remake.
Furthermore, most of these changes weren't there to "make the game better", rather because the new engine wasn't capable of supporting these things (although, research costs seem like a strange thing, it's not that difficult to set cost to 0, while timers are all there already). And, while it may be a minor thing to some, fighters SHOULD cost 55, not 100.And assault frigates were at 625, unless I'm mistaken.
Ok, enough, I'm just being too picky. This is a fine remake, none the less. It actually tries hard to be as close to the original as possible (although, heaven knows, we'd love to see nothing but new textures here). It is far more honest to the original than X-COM was to its grandfather, X-COM: Enemy Unknown, the latter I'd call a major disappointment - you don't make an excellent game better by screwing with it. This one isn't screwed nearly as much.
In the end, is it worth playing? It sure is for me - I did try to replay the original again, but that game has aged visually far too much. There are two space games for me that define the 90's. MOO II and HW1. Sadly, 3D does age faster. Playing this doesn't make me cringe as bad, as trying the original would. And yes, it is an enjoyment. Maybe there is this uncanny valley for remakes as well, when the original and the remake are just too close to be called a different game, yet are still not 100% the same, and this would fall into it. But, again, HW:Rem is almost where the original is. X-COM was right in the middle of that abyss.
Be a bit more open-minded about it, and you'll love it. Just don't forget you can't enter the same water twice.

I'll start with the obvious: yes, the remastered graphics and sound are absolutely beautiful. That alone almost makes this a worthy buy. HOWEVER...
This is Homeworld 1 re-created in the Homeworld 2 engine, which is actually a major downgrade. There are major differences that make this bad.
- They removed the ballistics system. Ship attacks are all random-number generator rolls now.
- They removed the ship tactics. You can't select aggressive or evasive tactics anymore.
- Formations still exist, but they don't actually work.
- Unit pathfinding is pathetic. Ships can get stuck easily.
Aside from the 3-dimensional game space, these were the things that made the game unique and exceptional. Without them, Homeworld 1 loses its most important elements, and you end up micromanaging your units instead of leveraging the brilliant ship formation and tactics system.

OK now that I have finished both campaigns, I am ready to leave my review.
I played both games back in the day SP and MP.
OK so for a few thoughts.
GRAPHICS:
The game looks great! First thoughts upon loading the game up was:  WOW THIS LOOKS AMAZING.
Yes the game is just stunning.   You have to be careful or you will forget to play and just end up zooming into one ship and watching lol.
AUDIO:
The audio in the game has all been redone and you can really hear the differemce.  I normally do not notice sound, but wow the new audio really helped.

THE INTERFACE:
The UI has been updated and is MUCH less intrusive.    In HW1, if you opened the built or research window it would take over your entire screen.     Now it opens in a pannel on the right side.    I really like the way they show what control groups you are using.    Overal the new UI is 10/10
THE CONTROLS:
The controls are well done in RM.  If you played the old games it will not take long to ajust to the slight changes.   It is mostly a verbatim copy of the HW2 controls.
For newbies:  do not let the 3D movement overwhelm you.   In the campaign, you will be playing on a 2D plane most of the time with a few exceptions.    Like in Mission 10 in the HW1 campaign.   But there is plenty of help to be had.  Just use the Wiki
.

PROBLEMS and BUGS!?!
Yes there are a few problems in the game.   Most of them are minor.   The first patch took care of a number of them.
The main thing to remember before you buy the game, make sure your computer can handle this game.    If you do not meet the minimum requirements, expect to have some problems.
The other thing to watch out for is your Antivirus.   Avast has been known to mess with the game so make sure you make the necessary exceptions before you launch the game.  If you have AV problems there is help to be had on the support forums.
ANNOYING GAMEPLAY  ISSUEs
For those of you that have played the first game.    Beware that at the moment, formations are not working as they should.    I have not found this game-breaking or anything but just annoying.   I am not to worried about it as it should be fixed soon.    IF you have never played the first game, this is not a issue for you.
The second issue is the support frigates and corvettes have to dock with the ship they are repairing.    I understand this is a problem caused by the port from HW1 to HW2.    Again not game-breaking, just annoying.
MULTIPLAYER:
Multiplayer is in BETA!   It is not yet balanced.   At first it had some stabilty issues, but the last patch did a lot to stabilize the MP game.  I have not had any issues getting into a MP game since that last patch.
Even in its current state, I have had a lot of fun with it.   There are few games more satisfying than homeworld in MP.   Nothing like watching your opponents mothership blow up!
FINNAL THOUGHTS:
I LOVE THIS GAME!!!!!   I give it 9/10.   If those 2 issues are fixed, I will give it 10/10.

It's not awful, but its many issues prevent it from being excellent. Overall ~7/10.
-The combat is dull, repetitive, and a lot of button mashing (but so are the majority of action games)
-The platforming is mindless and nearly impossible to mess up, aside from a few areas toward the end
-Music and sounds are alright, but nothing to write home about (I have no idea why people tagged this as having a "great soundtrack" when it was mostly forgettable background music)
-To call them puzzles would be insulting to actual puzzles (although to be fair most actions games nowadays do this too), but they were fast enough that they felt more like elements of the platforming rather than contrived timewasters
-Fairly short at ~10-13 hours (length felt about right to me, YMMV)
-If you're a completionist and you miss any of the collectibles/achievements you'll have to replay the entire chapter (no manual saving, points of no return occur every ~5-10 minutes)
-The colors and art really brought things to life, and are some of the game's stronger points
-Voice acting was excellent
-Repetitive level design with no real changes to mechanics (gaining the ability to shoot plasma out of your staff (no innuendo) hardly qualifies)
-Despite its predictability and lack of content the story was alright...until the last chapter. They decided to royally♥♥♥♥♥♥the bed there for god knows what reason; enough of a ♥♥♥♥-up to consider giving it a thumbs down. Without spoiling anything, the story's background became increasingly shaky and farfetched in the last third or so (but tolerable), and had a horrible, unsatisfying "conclusion" that made no sense in the story's setting. The presumed attempt to be dramatic and thought-provoking resembled an adolescent's fan fiction, or anything from M. Night Shyamalan. It didn't really give a proper conclusion, but left some room for a sequel, and wound up in a purgatory where it neither fully finished the story nor made a continuation necessary.
-Main character is the hellspawn of Superman and a gorilla, so his inhuman physical abilities can frequently give the false appeareance of Trip being a damsel in distress
-This type of game feels a lot like games made 10-15 years ago, and it would have been right at home amongst them. However, following an (outdated) cookie cutter action game design is not going to make you stand out.
It didn't really do anything unique, and with gameplay/story elements ranging from mediocre to slightly above average, it's hard to say that this game is underappreciated. Collecting magical orbs, jumping on platforms, and pressing x like a monkey whenever you're in combat just isn't that stimulating, or maybe I'm just too old. Despite everything wrong with it, I can't articulate why I still enjoyed it. It had a nebulous quality that made it fun to play and want to see through to the end; might have been my nostalgia for older action games. It wasn't bad, and I don't regret playing it, but if you're looking for something amazing, you can do better.

Wow, where do I begin to express my love that is Total War: Rome II - Emperor Edition?
For readers who have never played or heard of a Total War game before, let me summarize the gameplay.
1.  Upgrade your cities to increase your economic power.
2.  Use your growing treasury  to recruit and maintain armies.
3.  Use armies to conquer the cities of other factions, and maintain your growing frontier.
4.  Repeat steps 1-4.
a few weeks ago I went to  a electronics store and I was chatting with the salesman about Rome II.  I explained to him that the game was like crack and I could not stop playing.  Later that night, I decided to read some Rome II reviews on Steam, and to my enjoyment, I saw that another user also described his Rome II addiction like crack.
How can a game with such a simple overall mechanic be so addicting?
I think it has to do with the grand scope of the game The Creative Assembly has made.
First of all, I think a big reason I am so obsessed with Rome II, (an obsession that causes 99% of my other steam games to go unplayed and unloved), is the fact that this IS our history (more or less).  Rome II does not drop you in a fantasy world, asking you to fight off a goblin horde, or kill space mutants, it places you in a fairly historically accurate representation of our human ancient civilization.  The fact that you are leading armies that really existed, led by  generals who really influenced their countries, to fight factions that really existed on Earth at one point in time is so invigorating.
The game looks stunningly beautiful.  I recommend bumping all graphics settings to extreme if your PC can handle it.  The campaign map is highly detailed and a great way to move your "chess Pieces" around the board, until you actually engage in a combat.  Then the game turns into a traditional RTS.  The zoom ability is really well done.  You can observe your armies advancing from pretty high up, or you can zoom in close enough to see fine detail on each individual soldier.  You can even turn on a "cinematic mode" that brings your camera right into a unit that lets you see the battle from their point of view.  The terrain for battles is really detailed.  Again with high settings. you can see individual blades of grass, the vegetation on trees looks amazing, and water and sky details also add to the experience.  As your campaign progresses your battles will be fought in different seasons, such as a wintery battlefield complete with snow, and negative attributes from the cold.  Battlefield conditions can also vary, such as the super epic looking rainy battlefield, or the spooky foggy battlefield (Im so startled!).  The Creative Assembly also lets you change the size of your battalions, in an effort to help those who need to adjust for lack of processing power.  Your squads can have as few as 30 some men, to the extreme setting of 160 men per squad.  There is nothing quite like fighting a battle with the maxed out squads, and watching the brutal carnage that follows.
Gameplay is really well done.  Rome II blends strategy and RTS seamlessly and makes me appreciate both genres more.  As stated above, you start on the campaign board, which can be thought of like a game board.  Here you upgrade your cities which generously dot the HUGE game map, and move your armies around.  Once you enter a battle, the game drops you into the traditional RTS format.  Both parts are equally fun.  I was surprised at how addicting it is to upgrade your cities, negotiate diplomacy with other factions, and strategically move your armies on the board, in addition to actually getting the "boots on the ground" and fighting the battles.
Battles typically take the form of two full-sized armies dueling, but occasionally you can outnumber, or be outnumbered, depending on your choices on the campaign map.  A feature I really like is catching an enemy army in an ambush.  When the battle starts, you deploy your army however you like, but the enemy is forced to set his men up in a column, as if they were marching through and you knew they were coming.
The overall premise of a battle can also be broken down into a pretty simple formula.
1.  Line your men up in a big rectangular line.
2.  Bombard enemy lines with artillery and missile units.
3.  Await enemy line to charge into your line.
4.  Flank around with horses, or reserve infantry to win the day.
However, even though battles typically play out fairly the same, I rarely grow tired of playing them.  For those who might get battle fatigued, there are fast-forward buttons you can use during battles to speed up time, or you can choose to let the computer auto-resolve certain battles.  Be warned though, the computer typically calculates that you will lose or take heavy losses if you auto-resolve, but most of the time you can manually fight the battle and win with flying colors.
The AI is fairly smart in battles.  (I normally play on very hard or legendary).  Im always amazed when the enemy sees a gap in my lines and exploits it by charging calvary or men throught it.  (The AI is not afraid to exploit your shortcomings.  For example, leave your general's unit unguarded?  Get javelines thrown into his face over and over. The AI, although not perfect and some times just plain dumb, overall  presents a challenge on the campaign map and the battlefield, that keeps the game fresh.
A big plus in battles is Sieging cities.  When you attack large cities, you actually have to get ladders to the walls and storm the ramparts, and break down gates with battering rams or artillery.  It adds another twist that shakes up the normal battle formula.
Armies and generals gain veterancy as they survive and win battles.  Another plus.
Rome II features multiplayer as well.  I have only briefly explored this.  My favorite part is that you can CoOp campaign with a friend.
Replayability is HUGE.  There is so much content in Rome II.  It comes standard with the Grand Campaign, which lets you play over 20+ different factions  each with a unique starting position.  Factions are grouped by culture, and each culture has its own unique battle units.  There are atleast 7+ cultures.  Grand Campaign just dumps you in lets you try to take over Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and East Asia.  I was shocked at how big the play map is!  A campaign (again I play on hard-legendary) can take typically weeks to complete.  So prepared to invest tons of time into the game if you want to see victory.  A nice touch is that if you do end a campaign through victory, the game even gives you the option to continue.  Apart from Grand Campaign the game comes with A secondary Campaign, Imperator Augustus, sets up the Second Triumvirant, where Octavion (Augustus), Lepidus, and Antony all try to to gain control of Rome.  This  Campaign plays similar to Grand Campaign with the twist of this massive civil war taking place.  Besides Campaigns, there is also Battles.  Battles are set up after real historical battles, and lets you jump right into the fight to see if you can pull off a victory.
DLC is available.  Expand your game with DLC packs!  You can buy three additional campaign maps to play on, Caesar's conquests through Gaul,  Hannibal's conquest to Rome, and civil war of ancient Greece.  These packs give you new cmpaign maps to change up the gameplay.  I highly recommend these.  Besides "map packs" you can also buy culture packs, which give you brand new factions to play as in the Grand Campaign.  Blood and Gore add on is also recommended to increase the realism to the fact that when you stab guys, they bleed a lot.
Steam Workshop and Mods Available.  Mods for Rome II are abundant and awesome.  This game has a great modding community.
I look forward to, and have high hopes for Total War: Attila launching in a few days, but I know, no matter what, Rome II will be here to embrace me and show me a good time.

I found myself holding my breath, gasping in surprise and fright during many points in the game. Alien: Isolation is a prime example of survival horror done right. The alien AI is amazing.. and persistent. Don't expect to make it through the game without dying. If you can.. bravo! Probably took you ALOT of time creeping and hiding most of the game. Which is awesome. This game ISN'T about guns blazing and running into the fray. It's about subterfuge, misdirection and lots of sneaking and hiding.
That's all the good (and there is LOTS of it). Now for the "bad" (if you can call it that).
There are many tight spots that can be infuriating. I can see why there is an achievement for 100 deaths to the alien. But everyone plays differently and some may find better ways out of sticky situations. I ran into some spots where I went through each type of crafted item trying to find a way to avoid an alien to re-power up a generator. Tried different routes. Different tactics. Hiding in vents. Using distractions. Ballsy hide and seek. Lots of reloads. Eventually.. luck won out. That's not necessarily a bad thing at all... like I said.. infuriating. But I did get to see Amanda dying about 7 different ways :P
The only real "bad" complaint would be the ending. It just felt rushed. Abrupt. Incomplete almost. If you follow the Aliens universe, we know Amanda's outcome from the Aliens (#2) movie.. so I don't know if the ending was just a little bit of a disappointment due to all the stress I went through most of the game and feeling a little denied that sweet release of a conclusive ending. Here's hoping for Alien: Isolation 2!

As a Homeworld fan, I cannot help but recommend other people enjoy the spectacular visuals that Homeworld Remastered offers...
However I was extremely disappointed by the sheer number of bugs in Homeworld 1 Remasterd of which I have just completed my first play-through! (haven’t played HW 2 Remastered yet - intending to play through Cataclysm again before)
The sheer quantity of bugs in HW 1 Remastered is bewildering, and where as I didn’t encounter any truly game-breaking bugs I had to change my strategy to work around the problems in game.
Its fair to say, that HW 1 Remastered is NOT the same as the original HW in game play terms due to these bugs.
To name a few in no particular order:
* The removal of Evasive tactics and the way tactics affect the speed and attacking power of all ships (WHY??!!?)
* Ships set to passive tactics still aggressively attack other enemies they haven’t been instructed to attack, you have to Stop (S) or Move them to prevent them from continuing to attack (pressing passive tactics again does nothing)
* Formations do not work, ships to not keep in formation when given instructions...
* When sending some small ships to dock (with Mothership or Carriers) they fly off to the left or right and continue "into infinity and beyond!"
* Sometimes the move command just doesn’t work, press M nothing, symbol on cursor appears but it won’t do anything, same in Sensor Manager view
* Sphere formation no longer forms a sphere around ships being defended or attacked, ships just clump-up into a ball (and get Rickrolled)
* Credits roll, and there is some poor sod's name is blanked out due to a drawing of a ship dropped over his name
* Final mission has a seemingly impassable invisible wall preventing your advance (tip: go around the side)
* Cut scenes showing the Exiles on their epic journey from Hiigara to Kharak has my ships floating around with the Exile colony ships
* Repair ships now have to close to 0 range to perform a repair (same as capture range) - these ships also seem particularly susceptible to getting confused and doing nothing (Loved longer range repair in the original game.)
* Missile Destroyers cannot be told to bombard an area or mines for example
* Cloaking is broken, without any enemy sensor units on the field, enemies see and attack cloaked fighters and lone Cloaking Generators
* Capital navigation AI is abysmal, will refuse to move at all if another large ship blocking path, gets confused when assigning formations (takes forever to move into position, and not JUST due to the speed of large ships)
* Capital ships with multiple turrets (Heavy Cruiser in particular) does not focus fire correctly (with side cannon in particular)
* Bombers and light fighters seem far less effective against heavily shielded targets than in the original, I cite Mission 6 Diamond Shoals as evidence of this, don’t bother using bombers, defenders or any small ships in that mission is my advice (dock them or move off to the side).
* Another note on Mission 6, small ships love to suicide against the asteroids, funnily enough the large ships Frigates and above do a better job of avoiding the asteroids
There are probably other 'FEATURES' here I haven’t listed, the above are the main points that spoiled my enjoyment of HW 1 Remastered.
My advice to others would be to hold off on playing until the fix some of the fundamental flaws such as formations, tactics and movement bugs.
All in all a visually spectacular but disappointing game play experience.
What the heck were the QA department doing, they certainly weren’t testing the game... With Remastered having been announced so long ago I find it difficult to believe these bugs were due to release scheduling???

When I was a wee little lad, my first experience with Homeworld was Cataclysm. I enjoyed it immensely and to this day I wonder how could I beat it at the age of twelve. Of course when Homeworld 2 came out, I played it into bits. But I never played the original Homeworld.
Now, finally I got to experience it, well not in original form, but as remastered form, imported into Homeworld 2 engine and prettied up. And it was great. I played both campaigns of remastered games from start to finish and had a blast. While I understand that with the transition to the newer engine some of the original functionality of HW1 was lost but it never stopped me from enjoying the Homeworld 1 part of the remastered game. Everything functioned and it was a blast to play. Oh and how pretty it is. Really. I think I killed several hours just oogling at the pretty visuals and exploring every ship model inch by inch.
However, the Homeworld 2 part of the remastered collection is nigh perfect. While the ship models may not have gotten the same amount of attention as HW1 remaster got, they still look stellar and with the extra modern graphical options, I got even more oogling hours of it. Oh and the campaign of HW2R is just as hard as I remember it to be. When you finally beat a mission that was giving you a real hard time the feeling of accomplishment is real. I love it.
As for multiplayer, not all is well there but that's why it's still in beta. The combined HW1 vs HW2 multiplayer needs more work but if you strictly stick to playing Kuhsan vs Taiidan or Hiigaran vs Vaygr, you will have a good time. You also have a good time with playing the races of HW1 against HW2 but it can feel unfair at times, especially when HW2 ships are fully upgraded. But Gearbox is hard at work balancing the races out, so by the time it exits beta it hopefully will be as fun as the rest of the collection.
And if you really really want to get that Homeworld 1 feel back, it is included in the collection in it's original form.
Also, missing from the package is Cataclysm but... I don't personally miss it that much. If it's one day remastered, great, if not, meh.
Verdict:  Beautiful, plays well and has great value as a whole package. I definitely recommend it to anyone who has interest in experiencing the Homeworld universe and I really recommend it to Homeworld 2 veterans as for you there is nothing wrong with the remastered collection.
PS: You can find on community hubs that people have had issues with bugs, glitches and crashes but I personally never encountered any, except in multiplayer. Few crashes while joining a multiplayer game and one case of AI controlled opponents being forever idle in a players vs CPU match.

Enslaved is beautiful, interesting, well-acted, and highly polished.  Why no recommendation?  It's hardly a game at all.
I love the world, and the atmosphere they've created.  I like the characters, and wanted to see where their story went.  If it weren't for that, I would have quit after the first level.  This game is totally on rails.
Your character, appropriately named Monkey, does a LOT of platforming.  Most of it is climbing walls and jumping from perch to perch.  The problem?  You can't miss.  You hang from one pre-determined (and helpfully glowing) spot, hold the direction of the next one, and press A.  Then you get there, and repeat.  There aren't even any choices of where to go; you're simply following a path.  Even though you're jumping around like a monkey, it's effectively no different than walking down a hallway in FF13.
You can't even hop down from platforms in non-predetermined places.  The game LITERALLY won't let you die from jumping the wrong way.  Even in dramatic sections where the wall you're climbing on is crumbling away, you can rest assured that you will make it if you simply hold up and mash A.  Seriously.  As long as you push the button, you will never lose.  If you somehow DO manage to die, it only feels like the game's fault.
And that's the biggest problem: with 90% of the game so streamlined, whenever something isn't immediately obvious the game grinds to a halt.  More than once I found myself completely baffled by what to do next, simply because the game had never asked me to figure anything out before.
I beat this game back when it came out on 360, simply because I wanted to see how it ended (Answer?  Very strangely.)  Now that I'm REplaying it, all I want to do is fight the on-rails system in place here.  I find myself constantly grumbling about how Monkey won't do what I'm telling him to, because it's not exactly what the game WANTS me to do.
It's obvious that Ninja Theory really just wanted to tell a story and make some nice cinematics, only adding the gameplay to glue those elements together.  You are an actor in their movie, with lines and marks that you must follow, and that comes before actually PLAYING anything resembling a game.  If those elements appeal to you, and the game's on sale, you might ultimately enjoy it.
Just don't expect to PLAY it.
P.S. As far as the port goes, it ran well on my PC, but it doesn't support 2560x1440, and if you have both a controller and a joystick, you're gonna have to unplug one before it'll work.

Absolutely do not let how little I've played this game get you wrong. When I first saw Slime Rancher, I was convinced it could go either way - this could be really good, or really boring. I was, to say the least, pleasantly surprised by the amount of gooey, sticky content.
You play as Beatrix, a brand new slime ranchhand in this far off land. Chickens and slimes roam the area, along with semi familiar looking crops, like carrots and square strawberries. It's got a similar plot to other farming games, along the lines of titles like Stardew Valley or the Harvest Moon franchise. The difference is that you're not going to romance anybody. Sorry, slimes. Even with such a simple and basic story, you start discovering messages from a ranchhand before you, helping you delve a bit deeper into the world around you.
It's true - I'm a huge sucker for simplistic graphics. The slimes are simple blobs, Beatrix has a simplistic design, the graphics are all around very simple but retain this beauty that I see in games with similar graphics.
You farm slimes! You feed slimes. You feed them carrots, chickens, berries, beets, whatever you find. Sometimes you will see the evil Tarr and you'll fend them off from your produce. Very basic gameplay, but it remains fun to bounce around and explore. Did I mention this game encourages exploration? There's this huge amount of map I haven't explored yet - I'm so excited to do that.
I know my pitiful 2 hour play time can't help me accurately describe this, but I do know that with how much "work" I've been doing each "day" in game, I'll definitely be turning on this title for a good time.
I know what you're thinking - you ALWAYS give good reviews to games! Well, here's the trick - I only play games I like. I only review games I like. This game is a good one to pick up, especially right now during the Winter Sale. Adorable graphics, lots of playtime, interesting storylines and engaging world all add up to a really great game that's just about you raising pink and blue slimes.

I can't enjoy this game.
Back in May I purchased it and played for a bit. The lonely seeming world just depressed me. I refunded it.
This Christmas I tried it again. Unfortunately not much about the game had changed and for some odd reason I still could not get into it. I just requested my second and final refund.
These are personal faults of mine. Technically, this is a tight game. Gameplay is great and simple. The worlds are lovingly designed and everything is pretty charming! It's really hard to fault this game, it deserves it's reputation!
I will recommend this game as a whole. And while it's hard to pinpoint what I didn't like, I'll try and express that for anyone else that might end up feeling the same way.
-Maybe it was the open world with no sense of direction. Day one, you're told the controls and well... Go ranch some slimes! Ok, here I go... (Something I'd like: You're ranching slimes because of an outbreak or for a community or something)
-Maybe it was the objective not being rewarding enough. So you ranch slimes, farm their plorts and use those to upgrade your gear, your ranch and otherwise. But to what end? What after that? Is there a bigger reward? And if I'm not enjoying the act of ranching this early, why would I care what the eventual goal is? Maybe there isn't a goal? (Something I'd like: Maybe you're utilizing Slimes as your only means to get off the planet, or to get your boyfriend to this planet with the travel money?)
-Maybe it was the feeling of loneliness? On this planet The Far, Far Range, It's just you and the slimes. You'll get trading communications with about 3 other people. Plus text written letters from your love interest back on the home planet. Otherwise, it's just you and all those slimes. (Something I'd like: Insert NPC's hanging out. Other Slime Ranchers. A Rival. Some lore about the planet with Slime eating aliens.)
-Maybe it was the lack of control over the slimes? I kinda hated having a vac gun that lacked any accuracy whatsoever. You start out with only 4 inventory slots. You see some plorps over there you wanna gather for currency? Prepare to suck those up along with the slimes around them, several carrots and another fruit. Now your inventory slots are all full and you'll need to spit some of that out if you want to continue onward. (Something I'd like: A Vac Gun with attachments like real life vacuum cleaners. Gimme some nozzles!)
That said, I still recommend this game. It just does not click for me. I love this game and simultaneously am bored to death by it. I think it's because games like this deserve to exist and I can understand they don't need to appeal to everyone to be a great game.

So, you were expecting a glorified arcade mobile game on a PC? You know what?
It wasn't true at all! The game is very addicting. It's not actually an endless-runner (unless you were playing stream mode). There is endpoint on every levels, and every level increases its difficulty. Forget any endless-runner game you have played. This one is surely the best one out of them.
Let's take a deeper look on each sections.
1. Gameplay
There are A LOTS OF gimmicks in the game. I recommended re-binding the controls or playing with other controllers because those gimmicks are all squeezed into the left side of the keyboard, which cramped up my hand AF. The gameplay is similar to E-R game at its core. But the others, are different. Your character moves freely left to right on the running track instead of 3 lanes like other E-R. There are variety of moves you can perform to get through the obstacles such as jump, glide, grind, WALL RUN, tricks, drift, DISC attack and other stuffs. You might find the game easy at the very first levels, then it gets harder and harder. The great part of this game is no matter how much times you've failed a level, you'll never get mad or tantrum. It's just looks so easy that you could complete that level but somehow you couldn't. That's what makes you addicted to the game. There's also a game mode where you can ride the frickin' LIGHT CYCLE and derez enemies. Unfortunately, it's not actually a tron game where you race your light ribbon into enemy's face. Instead, guess what, it's a racing endless runner............... It sucked me up for a while. But the game mode is ACTUALLY enjoyable at least. If you have played Mario Karts or other racing games, this is a piece of cake at any level I'd say.
The game has 3 modes to play, (not included 1 from Outland DLC)
- Disc (Tron City)
You run through the obstacles to get to the end point.
- Whiteout
You ride a LIGHT CYCLE through the obstacles to get to the end point.
- Endless (Stream)
Combining 2 modes above and goes endlessly aka arcade.
2. Graphics
In my opinion, it looks great! REALLY VERY VERY STUNNINGLY PRETTY DARN GREAT! The colorful environment strained my eyes like a crazy. I love it! If you aren't into color madness, I don't recommend it. BUT HOLY USER, THE COLORS ARE SOOOOOO GOOOOOOD.
You might want to do some tweaks according to the guide in TRON Run/r Community. It really helps you out such as turning off blooming effects.
3. Controlling
Re-bind the control if you play it on a keyboard. The default setting will mess up your hand muscles.
4. Story
None of that.
5. Music
Giorgio Moroder = Perfection (Would have been even better if we have Daft Punk)
6. Value
I got the game when it was on 75% sales with the other DLC. I'd say it worth every penny.
-------------Final conclusion------------
Gameplay 9/10
Graphics 8/10
