I usually do a bit more research before I make a Steam purchase, as a result most of the games I own were either given to me or I bought because I knew I would love them.
I was a little wary of paying $35 dollars for a 15 year old game no matter how "remastered" it sounded, but I genuinely lovd the original Homeworld so much I decided to go ahead (I thought it would be great to be able to play online against friends for the first time in ages, as well!)
I was worried about that when I was still using the traditional definition of Remastered and not, "turned into complete trash." Between the bugs and the changes the game flounders near the area of unplayable. For examples of changes, fundamental tactical abilities like telling your fighters to be "evasive" has simply been ripped out of the game. Whether or not this was to foment HWI vs HWII multiplayer is as irrelevant as it is uncertain, it renders figher groups so much less meaningful or useful. Fighters instead seem to behave in a sort of constant half aassed evasive which means that their aggressive behavior has also been scuttled.
For examples of bugs, from mission to mission my groups would fail to properly select. If I hightlighted, say, all the ships in group one then they might all show they were in group one, but if I actually hit one, only a few respond to the hail. I have to reselect and reassaign them all to "rebuilld" between missions. But this is nothing compared to ships simply REFUSING TO OBEY ORDERS. I have tried playing The Wastelands three times now and in each instance a point was reached where some group of ships simply refused to move or engage no matter what they were instructed. I was especially impressed by my salvage frigates staring dumbly at me as I repeatedly tried to get them to capture a destroyer or, indeed, any ship as they slowly got picked off one by one.
I have never before felt compelled to write a negative review for Steam. It's one thing to simply make a bad game, that happens all the time. But this is a case of taking a masterpiece and destroying it. And I've been offered the chance to waste $35 dollars for the priviledge of watching one of my favorite games of old trashed in this manner.
Simply releasing the games for $5 apiece and rebuilding the multiplayer environment would have been the right move. As it stands, I regret this purchase without reservation and cannot recommend it, at least not until the myriad gameplay issues have been resolved. Even then, the graphis upgrades hardly justify $35. In my opinion, if you make this purcahse you are probably getting ripped off.

I have dumped an uncomfortable amount of hours into Factorio before it was on steam, and that was before even getting into playing with mods for it. It's a fantastically fun game focusing primarily on automation and secondarily on defending your base from the local (and very hostile) wildlife.
Pros:
+Has a significant amount of playtime with just the vanilla game, 20 hours is a 'fast' playthrough for a somewhat experienced player, wheras I spent nearly 100 on my first factory, then immediately jumped into another one so I could build it all better the second time.
+Large and active modding community, with modders that actually assist eachother in building better things.
+Developers actually support the modding community heavily
+The complexity and depth of the system allows you to spend a long time developing more optimal systems to produce each component in your factory, rather than being a simple "Ok I figured it out once and already found the optimal setup forever"
+The achievements provide quite interesting goals above and beyond the base 'objective' of the game.
+TRAINS, very fun and high-functioning rail network options, not quite on par with actual train simulators but more than sufficient for an automation focused game like this. You can easily build automated loading/unloading stations to feed your constant hunger for ores and oil.
+Has fully working multiplayer, with very few issues. The latency handling is just about flawless for a game of this style despite there being MILLIONS of active entities in large factories. (If playing with a friend on a poor connection or far away geographically, try increasing the latency slider in the hosting menu)
Cons: (this section may look long but it's mostly just me going into depths on the problems I do have with the game)
-It is very much a 'solved game' for the basic objective of launching the satellite, I don't recommend looking up walkthroughs or layout tips your first time through, puzzle it out, that's half the fun when completing the basic goal!
-The 'biters' (the enemies of the game) feel unfinished and overlooked, left in nearly their original state from earlier game versions. They still provide a significant threat early game or for massive factories, but are perhaps a bit too easy for even a newer player to uproot and exterminate with some amount of effort.
-The early game remains a bit of a 'restart wall', due to a lack of focus on the gameplay prior to significant automation, this would be fine, except the pre-major-automation phase actually lasts a fair bit of time.
-Trains are... not quite useful enough in an unmodded game in comparison for their effort and resource cost, yet remain almost necessary. It's not so much the trains themselves as the time it takes to deplete an ore deposit is fairly low compared to the effort required to set up a train line, the stations, the route, and the miners.
So, in summary:
There's areas the game could improve, especially in regards to the enemies and trains, but those are 100% definitely on the developer's radar right now. They're not just using early access as a 'cash in and get out' option and have been working non-stop on the game for years already, they actually deliberately waited on bringing it to steam until it was in a 'better quality' state. The automation aspect is amazingly fun and the achievements or even self-set goals you could come up with provide a tremendous amount of challenges to overcome.
Factorio is a wonderful simulation game. The game starts off slowly, and then builds quickly. Near the end game, you look back over your factory and it is amazing how much you have built.

This is an very underrated game.
Oddly enough, what first attracted me to this game was the music I had heard in trailers/demo of the game. I had filed it away as a game "I'd have to try someday" and it stayed there for years. I finally noticed it on a sale, and snagged it up. I can't believe what I had been missing!
To get the not-so-great stuff out of the way, the combat isn't that amazing or inventive. It works, and it's fun enough that I never got annoyed with it. The leveling system for skills is a nice touch, and adds some customization to the player to fit a play style.
The graphics are very nice, even for a game that came out quite a while ago. The art style fits the story perfectly, and the character models and animation are top-notch.
The main draw here though, is the story and voice acting. If these are big selling points to you, get this game now. I loved the story, really pulled me in, and the character interactions felt natural and believable. The incredible voice acting only adds to the wonderful story to help bring it to life. I'll have to add in here about the music again as well. The soundtrack is amazing, and helps to accentuate the rest of the game's high points.
TL;DR
If you want a game with a great story, amazing voice acting, wonderful music, interesting characters, decent combat and nice pacing, I'd recommend this in a heart beat. It's usually available for pretty cheap now, so it's really one to not miss!

This game is simply fantastic.
Dark Souls made itself a name, known as a game with a difficulty beyond the games of todays time.
I'm used to play many Retro Games, games which are old and used to be very difficult, but even those, were compared to Dark Souls, games for children.
This game made me laugh, smile, shout and cry, out of sadness and happiness both.
First of all the Story. I finished this game, and I am still unaware of the actual story, not knowing why I did all this, is a bit weird, but I think, it's simply because Dark Souls is mainly focused on the gameplay, not on the story.
For the story I can give a
Story 5/10
because the story is there, but its badly told.
The gameplay of Dark Souls is unique. You either be a damage dealer, rolling around everywhere and trying to evade all the attacks which mostly mean Death to you, the tank who slowly pokes the enemies to death, a assasin, using the shield to parry and his blades to critical hit or a mage to deal devastating anmount of damage with his limited spells.
This all explained like this sounds pretty simple and easy, but there is a reason the achievement "Welcome to Dark Souls" is acquired by dying. You can fight and fight dozens of enemies, and still get killed by just 2-3 of the enemies of the games beginning, just because they dont allow you to move, block or attack. Dark Souls makes every enemy a danger and the player will either learn seeing danger behind every corner, or wont finish this game.
Gameplay 10/10
is easily earned.
The Difficulty is what everyone knows about Dark souls, if you actually manage finishing this game without to summon anyone to help you, and are able to make it all by just yourself, you can proudly call yourself a good gamer. I saw myself frustrating, doubting if I could beat a boss on my own, yes, I look at you Ruin Sentinels and Demon of Song, but I tried, learned their behaviour and movings and beat them sometime. No game I ever played awarded me with such a good feeling as Dark Souls did. You feel undefeatable, strong, simply wonderful when defeating a difficult boss, yep, I mean you Vendrick RIP.
Difficulty 10/10
Also the fact that it ISNT POSSIBLE to set a easier difficulty is perfect, because there surely would be too many people, who just would evade to that when having problems.
The controlls of this game are sorta difficult, but fast learned. I'd definitly recommend to play this game with a gamepad, because I admit that the controlls with a keyboard and mouse are really bad, but compared rather easy to manage with a gamepad or on a console. When you're later into the game, have a little anmount of items in your inventory, it's very annoying clicking through them, till you find the one you need, because you can just scroll them into one direction (left to right, but not right to left). Also you wont be able to pause your game, so you'll often need to equip another armor, weapon, items but wont be able to do so, because there are enemies and dangers around, killing you when you're not fully concentrated.
8/10
Since at least a pause function could have been added, or a button set to scroll the items into the other direction.
Lastly the multiplayer. The multiplayer is something I mostly dislike about Dark Souls 2 and 1.
The help funcion is useful, since its always decided by yourself, whether you want to help or be helped.
But the Pvp is very annoying. When you're in a new area and suddenly get invaded by another player, getting killed, losing your souls and also your hard achieved humanity.
There is a function called "Soul Memory", it saves the anmount of overall souls you collected throughout the game, no matter if you lost of kept those souls. And this Soul memory determines who your opponent is, since opponents should have about the same soul memory.
Now the problem is that I have the soul memory of 3,6 Million, after finishing my first playthrough. I should be having a Soul memory of 1 Million, but I farmed a lot. So I get punished for farming to get all equipments, WHICH ARE MOST JUST FOR COLLECTION AND USELESS FOR MULTIPLAYER, with stronger enemies who invested their Souls into upgrading themselves with stronger armour, weapons and magics.
In my opinion MULTIPLAYER WOULD BE PERFECT, if you could turn off PvP invaders.
Also, very often people who started playing Multiplayer focused on magic, and before a fight starts just get themself a spell that flies at the first enemy encountered after casting, which is of course...YOU, then throwing spell after spell so you cant even get close. Fair when you play melee. Also some people lag around and even though they just stood directly in front of you, they suddenly are behind you and backstab you with their fire enchanted greatsword what is, of course, a one shot kill.
4/10 Multiplayer
since you can evade most of multiplayer (read following) and the help function is made very good.
For all people who play this game, and want to encounter as less as possible invaders this advice:
When you go to Majula, and see the gigantic obelisk, dont join the convenant of the guy sitting in front of it, because it will signigicantly multiply the number of invades you'll encounter. I didnt talk to him and had just 6 in my whole playthrough.
Overall this game is wonderful and I would recommend it to everyone who searches a challenge and thinks he can handle stress and happiness in rapid swappings.
Overall rating: 9/10

The game is a never ending stream of satisfaction, while still getting to use your brain to its fullest with gameplay never getting old, ever.
It's an endless pursuit of building, unlocking, crafting, improving, and always trying to make your productions more efficient/faster/bigger/higher yielding, all while having to constantly protect yourself and all your carefully crafted constructions and manufacturing lines from the Zerg whose numbers seem to keep increasing. You can never, ever forget to continue to keep up with defense and weapon tech or you'll slowly become overwhelmed over time.
You've played many games with systems that sound like this, but honestly nothing compares to this game. It's on another level and still manages to be extremely fun.
You'll always want to be more efficient with your building and manufacturing not for the sake of being efficient because who really cares honestly, but because you need MORE THINGS FASTER! EVERYTHING, MORE! NOW! When your inefficient hastily thrown together setup is becoming bottlenecked in various places and thus isn't making your flying robots nearly fast enough to satisfy your deep, angry hunger to see what the robots actually look like in action, it'll send you on a quest to improve each step of your manufacturing setup over several hours where you'll forget you were even making robots to begin with. From the outside you may see "tedious", but when you're on the inside, it's "adventure". You discover yourself what you need to do to fix one problem, one at a time without even meaning to. Endless discovery.
Highly recommend playing with a group of friends. After 15 hours or so you really start to get a real sense of what it must be like to run a company or manufacturing plant with so many moving parts. Get enough people together in a server and I'm sure you could simulate the insanity that is managing the LHC.
You make a server with 3-4 friends.
One friend decides to set up Iron Plate production and mining while everyone is off doing other things.
After 10 hours, you realize you've always had a steady supply of Iron Plates, Steel Plates, and Copper Plates coming in to help you build your chemical plants and batteries, but you really have no idea how the Plates are being made or are even getting to you. All you know is your friend would occasionally ask if you needed some, so he would bring you materials in the form of a conveyor belt whose path you would modify to fit into your automation you're working on, and it's working very well! You're well on your way to making robots..... But never mind how all these materials are getting to me from my friend.. How did I learn to make robots in the first place?
You realize your other friend has been unlocking new technology all this time with a lab setup, so you go to check it out and discover he has spent all this time setting up an automated lab researching process with 3 different products all being automatically manufactured and poured into the labs.. And guess what's being fed down there as well? Your other friends Plates, and your own Batteries and other things (since he needed some and you were like, oh I won't just give you some batteries, I'm going to give you an entire endless line of batteries). All while another friend has been managing a conveyor belt full of coal that circles every piece of equipment that uses coal, thus keeping all the machines operational, and loops back around for excess, where it is periodically stored into containers. And managing electricity grids. And turrets. Defenses. Exploring when you need more materials (stones, jfc). Killin Zerg any way you can... Or constantly trying to run away.
This is just the best. That's all it is. The best.

If the person joining has a very low download speed, this usually equates to a having enough time to make a sandwich and some coffee for the group. A smoke break if that's your thing. Not too much of a bad thing really, but it would be great if the game could continue to function while the new player downloaded the map.
We are.. 20 hours in or so into our map? And I still don't think we're anywhere near being able to build a rocketship. But we do finally have little flying robots repairing our base now!

Tron run is basically as the title says running with a little bit of bike riding which feels the same as the running but at least you get to jump in a light cycle. Sadly this game feels more like a mobile game then anything else, I do love the tron theme but it feels so lacking compared to other tron games before it. There is so much disney can do with the tron license but they seem to take small steps when it comes to gaming.
=======
The Good
=======
1. Character customization - Being able to pick some of the famous tron characters is rather cool. From the anime series to the classic. On top of that you can pick your favorite light cycle and color to go with it.
=======
The 50/50
=======
1. Game modes - The game modes are decent if they were a side game but as the core game experience they are extremely lacking and can get boring really fast. All the game modes are rather close to each other in sense of style, you run in the running mode, and drive in the light cycle however your on rails which kills the experience really fast.
2. Music - I found the music good but would of hoped for more Tron like music or the ability to add custom music while your running around in each game mode.
=======
The Bad
=======
1. Random Crashes - Sadly there are some times the game will randomly crash for no reason.
2. Very lacking on different game modes - There is so much that could of been done with Tron. Such as having more mini games or online mode where you battle with other players. Just think they could of added:
a) Light cycle battle - Like in the movies players would either pick free for all or teams and have to battle each other in a random arena which is based on both the classic and legacy (having the lower and upper levels with speed boosts and etc).
b) Disc battles - A free for all mode where players can battle each other on 1v1 or multi deck mode. The 1v1 would be based around the classic tron where the multi deck mode would be based around legacy having a dozen players randomly picked to go against another player at the same time. As players get elimated, the surviving players will continue to be randomly matched with the next until the last player is alive for the last 1 v1...if they win then they can even go against some random hard a.i boss..
c) Tank Battle - based on the old classic tron where players fight in tron like tanks.
============
Overall
============
I have nothing against tron run and do enjoy the modes but overall again felt lacking with what could of been done especially what has been done before on PC and consoles. Even if the game was meant for mini mode type games there are many game modes that could of been added with online support for players to challenge each other.
Either way if you enjoy playing simple running game modes where your on rails and simply just need to jump and dodge then this game will work for you. Other then that I can't really say much. I had my fun with it but I still go back to Tron 2.0 for my cravings.

I haven't played a whole hell of a lot of it, as I'm not quite in the mood, but from a gameplay aspect, playing through the game as Corvo is basically Dishonored 1.5. Playing as Emily is a much different game as her abilities are much, much different. Really, there's only one thing I'd like to talk on, and it'll contain many spoilers for the first game.
What really drew me in to the first game was just how subtle everything was. Was Emily Corvo's daughter? Your only clues were interactions between characteres, as well as a few well hidden notes that hinted that Corvo and the Empress were closer than they should have been. It was left to interpretation. In this game, from the very start Emily is Corvo's daughter. No reveal, no build-up, it's just flat out stated. It could have been an entire sub-plot with Emily's campaign, leading to a reveal or just a very strong clue. Either way, it's disappointing to say the least.
The Outsider is another one. Everything that had to do with him was a complete mystery. He was only in it because things interested him. He was almost like an Eldrich being that only ever spoke in riddles and never had a straight answer. In this game, he's a pretty straightforward god character that's more of a buddy to Corvo than anything. Not to mention the bloody heart. I loved the heart in the first game. It was only subtly hinted that it was the heart of the Empress, yet again, in this game it's just told to the audience.
I'm not far into the story at all, as you can see, but there was already one plot-point that I saw coming from a mile away. This change in writing is either a product of the game being rushed, or Bethesda meddling and attempting to make it more appealing to a casual crowd. These changes aren't necessary, and make it look like a betrayal of fans of the first game. For now, I'll leave a recommendation, but only because the gameplay and level design continues its great trend from the first game.

I bought this game on sale after it was patched and many bugs and errors were fixed. If you see negative reviews, then it is probably in relation to the issues which are no longer present.
As to the game itself. Dishonored 2 is a dynamic, non-linear steampunk stealth action game, and a worthy heir to the first Dishonored game (which I also played and enjoyed). In this installment you can choose which character to play, in addition to the style you prefer, which will shape the ending, also much like the first game. You have a wide range of tools at your disposal: weapons, items and magic. This comes along with a variety of ways you can reach your goal sneaking and evading enemies, or simply killing them.
Nearly everything is great about this game: gameplay, graphics, plot and even the soundtrack.
My only criticism would be voice-over, which is a bit 'cheesy' at times. But this does little to undermine the game's plot or a fun, challenging and engaging gameplay.
If you liked the first game, you will enjoy Dishonored 2 as well (maybe even more!), and if you are new to it, you will find it a nice introduction to Dishonored's universe.

This was a terrifying, suspenseful and amazing masterpiece true to the Alien franchise. So much detail went into the look and feel of this game to thrust you into the Alien universe. I found myself holding my breath, gasping in surprise and fright during many points in the game. Alien: Isolation is a prime example of survival horror done right. The alien AI is amazing.. and persistent. Don't expect to make it through the game without dying. If you can.. bravo! Probably took you ALOT of time creeping and hiding most of the game. Which is awesome. This game ISN'T about guns blazing and running into the fray. It's about subterfuge, misdirection and lots of sneaking and hiding.
That's all the good (and there is LOTS of it). Now for the "bad" (if you can call it that).
There are many tight spots that can be infuriating. I can see why there is an achievement for 100 deaths to the alien. But everyone plays differently and some may find better ways out of sticky situations. I ran into some spots where I went through each type of crafted item trying to find a way to avoid an alien to re-power up a generator. Tried different routes. Different tactics. Hiding in vents. Using distractions. Ballsy hide and seek. Lots of reloads. Eventually.. luck won out. That's not necessarily a bad thing at all... like I said.. infuriating. But I did get to see Amanda dying about 7 different ways :P
The only real "bad" complaint would be the ending. It just felt rushed. Abrupt. Incomplete almost. If you follow the Aliens universe, we know Amanda's outcome from the Aliens (#2) movie.. so I don't know if the ending was just a little bit of a disappointment due to all the stress I went through most of the game and feeling a little denied that sweet release of a conclusive ending. Here's hoping for Alien: Isolation 2!
================

There are many reviews for this game, some are simple, some are more complex and spacious.
Aside from that, i'm sure many heard about this game anyway, since the first Dark Souls made quite a name for itself as a popular, but not a forgiving, casual title, a title that makes you lose your sanity at some moments and brings immense satisfaction when you finally beat some boss you died to 20+ times. That's of course, not mentioning the fantastic atmosphere, overall design, interesting PvP and PvE gameplay and many more things. And... eventually another part of the Souls franchise was announced and came out, Dark Souls II.
Is it a worthy sequel to the original Dark Souls and Demon's Souls? Probably.
Is it the best game in the Souls trio? Not sure, in some places no, in some places yes.
Is it worth playing if you liked the previous games or you are a newcomer to the series? Yes, and yes.
There are improvements here and there, there are some flaws and mistakes too, but it's still a very good game and there are not many games like this at all.
The PC version is also pretty good, but a bit controversial. Sure, it has 60fps and superior graphics, but it also has some weird issues that are not present in the console version. For example, your equipment breaks faster because of the increased framerate and the A.I. of some enemies can work in a bit different way, compared to the console version of the games (although I'm not really sure about that, it doesn't break the game anyway). I still hope that all this will get patched someday, but it's rather unlikely.
EDIT:
Despite the fact that the DLC had a bit of reused content from the original Dark Souls II and Dark Souls in terms of boss attack patterns, and even a reused boss, it's still a great addition to the base game. I would even say that some parts of the DLC's are better and more interesting design-wise than a lot of parts of the original game. And overall, it's simply more content - more weapons, armor, spells, locations and enemies to defeat. For me, that's 100% worth the price tag.

I've played this game for a several amount of hours, and I want to review it because I think it is really good and it's a great early access game. It's the first review I've actually put time into, and I did it for this game because I think it's underrated.
This is a Battlefield type of game, expect it's singleplayer, and has more simple and goofier graphics. The gameplay of it works like any other shooter. Respawn, find bad guys, shoot, die, repeat. It's easy to pick up, and has a lot of fun to offer.
I'll go over some pros and cons over this game.
Pros:
+ Keeps a good framerate and offers a good amount of graphic options. I have a laggy laptop, and it can run this just fine.
+ This game has vehicles. It has tanks, quad bikes, jeeps, helicopters, and some others. I think it lacks in options just by a small tiny bit, but there are probably more to be added and the vehicles are fun to use.
+ You can customize the match with several options. You can choose how many bots you want in a game, balance the team sizes, decide if you can have vehicles, set the time to night or day, and a few other more. You can also choose what weapons the A.I are allowed to use. Have an incredibly OP weapon that only you want to use? Or are you sick of the A.I spamming 1-shot killing grenades or rockets? Well, you can disable the A.I from using them and you can dominate the field!
+ Workshop support. This is a HUGE plus for me, as this fixes the stuff that I think the game lacks, and adds a lot more fun to it. Right now you can only get weapons and custom maps, but they are a lot of them, and they're all cool.
+ Satisfying and silly ragdoll effects.
+ You can create a squad out of the soldiers and order them around, like making them follow you or making them hold a position. Doesn't sound worthy of a plus as it's a tiny bit lacking, but I liked this feature a lot.
+ You have the same stats as the A.I has, so you can't just run out like an immortal god shooting everywhere out in the middle of the battlefield without being shot to death by a whole squad.
+ The developer is cool imo, and updates are not rare.
+ The default maps are well designed, and so are the weapons.
+ There are also 3 gamemodes, but they aren't too different, as they all have holding control points in common. But it's still good to have them.
In between:
+/- The graphics. I personally really like these graphics as I find a charm in them, but I know some people who'd probably hate them.
+/- The A.I can be a bit buggy and stupid at times, but it's good enough and still fun to play with and against. It can be pretty smart sometimes too. My favorite thing about them is that they can use vehicles and hop on them at any time. Makes the game feel more alive.
+/- I found the options of weapons and maps to be pretty lacking, but it can be fixed with the workshop. It is also just an early access game, so I won't go too far with this.
+/- The cost may be a bit high, but I am poor so... Well, either way it's worth it.
Cons:
- I don't mind this as I love just playing it in singleplayer, but there is no multiplayer, and the creator has stated that there won't be any. If you came looking for a multiplayer game to play with friends, keep looking, but I still recommend trying this out.
- I found the swimming in this game to be very tedious to control. You should probably not go for a swim anyways, but it takes a pretty long time for me to get back up if I fall into a random river by accident.
This is a great game that I think deserves more attention. I'm surprised to see that it's early access, because it's amazing, and I'm really looking forward to new updates. There is also a campaign mode that's going to come out, and I'm curious to see what it is.

I sit here at my computer desk in the wee hours of the morning after just completing the first part of the Homeworld: Remastered games that were recently released on Steam, and as I type away I find it hard to come to the correct words for what I just experienced, so here’s me trying to sum it up for you with what to me is no longer a game, or a footnote on a sheet to check out and play sometime in the future without really ever getting to it, but an idea that was realised in it’s fullest potential and is now at the public’s door once again.
Let’s get one thing out the door right away, I never played the original Homeworld. I was too young at the time to really decide what I wanted to play, and what I did play was mostly Starcraft: Brood War (Still in my top games of all time) or rummage through the bucket of Lego in my corner.  So when the news that Homeworld was getting a remaster… I didn’t really celebrate at all and I certainly did not pre-order out the door like I do for way too many games.  Though as the ball kept turning and the time of it’s release drew nearer and nearer I grew infatuated with Homeworld, it’s lore and story that drew me instantly into it, and the sheer scale and effort being put into a game that was cracking on by now.  So this Monday, which is Monday the 2nd of March (I am writing this review on the 7th, in the early hours) I bought it as soon as I could, and here is the result.
Homeworld is now what I consider the best story told in gaming.
Or at least up there with the greats, of course.
The way it was told to me, and how it slowly started to show me this lore that spanned back millions of years in the games universe, the different races and characters I met along the way all felt amazing and diverse, each one beautifully voice acted and all done with space ships on a screen.  There’s no portraits, we aren’t given a face, it’s voices we go on in this experience, and holy hell it knocks it out of the park with that regard.
It’s game play (While frustrating at times) is brilliant fun to toy with, there’s nothing more satisfying then launching a full Missile Destroyer attack on the unsuspecting foe below as your attack bombers soar in to deal the final blow, it’s god damned addicting and the fun just comes from finding the ways to out manoeuvre your enemies in the slyest of ways.
And finally it’s the music, and how it complements each scene perfectly to the point I was left in awe at what was beset upon my eyes, to the point where this game brought me to tears with the myriad of feelings it produced.  Emotion is key with this tittle, and for the first time in a good long while I was feeling it while playing a game, the twinge of my heart as my favourite Frigate bit the dust, or the cut scenes I will not spoil.
Homeworld is an experience for everyone, RTS and non RTS fan alike need to play this game and make it through to the end for the most satisfying ending in gaming.  This game gets my rating of ‘Bury it with me so I can take it to hell’

A surprising gem of a game, and underappreciated.  I'm heartily impressed by the visuals, and the interplay between the characters and steady drip-drip of the story elements are fascinating.  The gameplay also is quite fun.  the mix between puzzle platformer and simplistic combat keeps the game entertaining without being frustrating.
I can see how the combat can become or feel repetitive, but I'm okay with that, since the work of getting to the enemies is really where the game shines.  The puzzle platformer side.
The cons to it, perhaps, is that you cannot fail a jump. Don't expect to fall tragically to your death, ala Assassin Creed franchise.  If the jump isn't possible, he won't try.  However, it makes up for it with certain sections requiring you to jump in rapid sucession to survive.
The secondary con is the camera.  The game itself rotates and moves it around, the idea being to help the player it appears and give the game a somewhat cinematic feel.  It didn't bother me most of the time, but a few times it was in an awkward spot.
Generally though, I'm heartily impressed. I'd recommend this game, and with it currently on sale in the steam store 75% off, a relatively cheap "risk" if you buy it.

For a long time I pondered, if I should buy this game for the PS3 or PC, as Heavenly Sword, a previous game by Ninja Theory, of which I adored, was PS3 exclusive, and the gameplay in Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is well suited for consoles (read: controllers).
But where Heavenly Sword could be renamed 'Goddess of War', could this game be called 'Uncharted: Beyond Arkham', or somthing like that, as the gameplay is mix of parkour stylish platforming from Uncharted and beat 'em up gameplay from Batman: Arkham series. And there's bit of Beyond Good & Evil in there also, consider it the BGE sequel we never had.
I noticed it on sale for five euros and went ahead and bought it. After playing it for some time I'm impressed enough to get it on PS3 as well some day.
This is one of those games, where the cover art itself is enough to buy for, just to get it in your collection, maybe hanging on your wall. The beauty doesn't stop there, as the graphics in this game are astounding. Where every other modern video game is just different shades of brown, Enslaved is vibrant and colorful. The art style reminds me little of Bulletstorm.
And unlike recent waifu-simulators, like Bioshock Infinite, The Last Of Us and Skyrim: Dawnguard add-on, Trip is actually an interesting companion.
However the game feels a bit rushed and unpolished.
The camera switches between fixed camera angle and free to move camera, which gets annoying.
There's little to no freedom in platforming. It's just pointing a direction and then pressing the jump button, everything else is automated. You can't fail.
And the Combat system from the Arkham games is a bit stripped down.
This is the only game in existence (that I know of), where I think a bit more quick time events wouldn't hurt.
I like that the game allows multiple playstyles. Aside from beating the crap out of everything, you can sneak past and avoid most battles. So there's a little of replay value (though only a little).

It might seem silly to praise this, but the acting, writing, and especially the direction in this game are the best I have ever seen. The gameplay is good too; the puzzles are clever, the fighting is balanced and fun, and the level designs are varied. Sometimes it's platforming, sometimes stealth, sometimes its a rail shooter, sometimes its a hoverboard obstacle course, but always with robots to destroy and glowy McGuffins to collect.
The adventure itself is not the reward however, it's the relationship between the two main characters. They are so well portrayed and realistic in their actions. It makes the emotion very palpable, and it makes the occasional laugh land a lot harder. I found out after I played this that the PC is played and motion captured by Andy Serkis, which makes sense. I certainly liked this better than any of the Hobbit movies.
The support character is really designed well, balancing her need-for and power-over the PC, making her both highly sympathetic and unbelievably selfish.
The Pigsy DLC finds clever ways to slighty adjust gameplay to vary it even further, but it loses almost all of the charm by losing the two main characters. Comic relief characters are usually made up of lazy and boring writing, and when the whole story is about them... but at least the level design is interesting.

First off, the story involves you escorting an NPC to her home village. Off the bat that sounds like it is going to be a bad game. Actually, Trip is a bit smarter than most AI characters and tends to not get in the way to often.
The graphics in this game are really well done. They took a good amount of time to show how the jungle toke over most locations. As you progress you slowly see the environment transition into the next area. As the wind blows you can see various objects flutter by just adding to the realism and desolace of where you currently are.
The music in this game is not anoying and compliments the gameplay quite well. The voice acting is great. Dialog however can be quite absurd at times.
The combat is your standard hack and slash with mini quicktime events for certain enemies. You have your standard attacks and your shooting atacks. The movement is very standard and quite responsive. The camera angles every so often will get in the way but for the most part allow you to see what you are doing.
To add to the storyline, there are items that show parts of the past. At the beginning these seam to be just jibberish. As you get towards the end, they start to make sence on what is going on. Which leads to the ending. Without spoiling it, the ending is quite different and a bit far fetched,
This is one of those good games that got overshadowed by to many titles coming out around its time. Definitely a game worth playing.

I waited until the game was on sale but was very interested in its bright, colorful graphics and thumping soundtrack. As I'm already a fan of Tron, I may be a bit biased in praising the game.
However, as far as runners go it offers some of the most variety beyond the simple platforming / dodging of the genre.
I am not a fan of the lightcycle / bike segments in the title, as they feel pretty clumsy with the driving. The on-foot segments shine though and have abilities you can equip before going into the levels to amplify your score or wipe out an entire section of obstructions at once.
The ability to customize your character / cycle, as well as Interesting platforming variety with rails to grind on, walls to run on, a double jump + glide, slide, and tank fire to dodge while taking out enemies invading the area.
The effects, fluidity, and soundtrack all go well together. If you're into the colorful effects and overall digital world of Tron, or just wanting to give the "Runner" genre a try, this is a title I'd recommend.

A very fun game to play, right off the bat.  Though, it may look like just another endless runner, it's really more than that.  It's more like an action/runner with a finish line.
The graphics are gorgeous... that part is obvious. The music is pretty awesome as well.  I highly recommend that you play this game with a good surround sound system.
The levels start out fairly simple and at boot, it teaches you how to use certain basic moves, to help you maneuver around the obstacles.  As you progress to each new level, things get more challenging, but it's nothing you can't possibly master. The controls are very sharp, so if you goof up, you'll know it was your fault and not the game itself (unless you experience a glitch, which I will discuss later in this review).
The later maps do seem to move slightly quicker, as you go along. Especially in the Outlands (DLC pack).
The cycle stages are pretty fun, once you get the hang of the turns and drift function. You'll be racing through obstacles as you try to tag each time loop, while collecting as many bits as you possibly can and destroy any enemy programs, who'll try to interefere with your mission.
The level designs for this mode, are different from the disc runner challenges, but just as pretty, with many cool elements flying by. (recognizers, etc)
I purchased the deluxe package, which in my opinion, is a must. You get all the DLC stuff, which includes the 16 Outlands maps, 9 extra disc levels, 9 extra cycle levels  and a bunch of characters and light cycles skins (from 1982, to the Uprising series).

NOTE: (If you're not amazing with a keyboard, I'd strongly recommend you grab yourself a Microsoft Xbox game pad to play this game).
YES, you can use a game pad with this game!  Someone had mention it wasn't possible. That is not true.  I am in fact, using a PS2 Dual Shock gamepad, with a usb adapter, to play this game.  All I had to do was, find the XBOX360 gamepad support files online, download them and place the 3 small input files in the binary folder. (so many tutorials online, to show you how to do it properly. It's very simple).
Or, better yet, just get a corded XBOX360 control pad and simply use the usb port to connect your pad and play. (make it extra fancy and find yourself a Tron edition XBox360 pad! :))
(Update) It seems I can now exit the game from the custom and map select menu as well as in the middle of a game, as opposed to having to go all the way back to the start screen. All you do is press the Esc key and press the Y button on your pad or as directed on the option menu you pulled up.
MICROTRANSACTIONS:
Yes, there are micro transactions available in this game, (called bit packages) but I'll be very honest with you, contrary to some reviews, I did not find thist to be an issue and I'll explain why below.
First and foremost, bits are very easily earned, just by playing the game.  The more bits you collect, per map, the more you'll have to aid you with obtaining the upgrades you'll need for some of the harder maps.  If you run out of bits, you can earn them back, by replaying any map you want, as many times you want.  Or, try your hand in the Stream mode, where it's possible to obtain a large amount of bits, depending on a how long you can keep up with the pace.
Buying bits, is only an optinon for those who do not want to grind through the maps.  But seriously...not necesarry at all.  My package came with 11k bits and I've still yet to use them, since I've accumulated many more on my own.  So, personally, imho, I don't think the microtransaction feature really damages any part of this game, like some believe.  I mean, whatever... The challenge is still there and even with upgrades at your disposal, you still have to master the game in order to climb up the leaderboards.  NOT easy, let me tell ya.
CONS: (Updated 9/18/16)
Yes, there are a few draw backs to this game, I'd like to see fixed.
Starting off with the little issues first. There are some innaccuracies to the character skins.  Sark for example, has his antennas pointing out the back of his head, when they should be lowered down to his neck area. It kills the look. Not sure who thought that was a good idea. It's just not accurate.  Beck's hair is exaggerated a bit much. Mara is missing the little neon green lights on her suit. I also would have loved to have seen the flesh tones changed to that of what it looks like in the films and animated show, rather than with actual flesh tones.  I would also love to have seen either Tron or Beck, with helmet on.  Maybe an option to switch one from the other.
Also, what is with the yellow recognizers on the start screen?? Looks like unfinished work guys...
At least if they were red, I wouldn't have mind it much.
Being able to skip through the beginning intro, (developer logos) would be nice.  It does get annoying, to have to wait nearly a minute, for the developer logos to fade out, before I can proceed to the game itself.
Now the big issues.
In the Stream mode, there's a problem (a serious one) where a game suddenly glitches and causes you to randomly derezz. It seems to happen at random points, where the maps would transition.
Also, there have been instances when I'd get hurt, or fall in a pit and actually continued to run!  This just happened to me recently when playing  the weekly challenge.  About 4 minutes in, and boom. Just derezzed, when I hit nothing. It happened 5 times now.  I'm assuming it's a problem with server lags, map loads etc. I don't know, but its needs work done, pronto. I think the developers should have considered a different way to handle the random map loads, like maybe have the game collect and prepare the maps before actually starting the run, rather than have it done, while running.
It can be a real pain when you're spending a lot of time running in Stream mode, only to be abruptly stopped, sometimes a few digits away from beating the time/score.
It doesn't happen all the time...but still. They need to look into this.
RECOMMENDATION:
With all that said, after spending over 30 plus hours on this game, I definitely can say with utmost confidence, that this game is worth the price,  if you're a Tron geek, like me and if you enjoy runner style games.
I'm having a lot of fun with it.
By the way. Important info.
I purchased this game in August.  There may have been lots of fixes made to this game since it's release, because I did not find half the issues some of the negative reviews have stated. Which many are dated as far back as February.  That's something to consider here.
There have been numerous negative reviews, stemming from their experience with the downloadable demo or the early access release.  Both of which are very incomplete and riddled with issues.  The full copy is much more stable with many bug fixes made.  It's not perfect by any means, but definitely much more enjoyable.
The Leaderboards do work although, once in a while, there's a server error that denies it to function properly.  Also, they can take a few seconds to load.
My game has never crashed on me yet and I am using Windows 7 64bit, not 10, on a very old machine with a Core 2 Duo 3.33ghz processor, with 8gbs of ram and a GTX 960 4gb video card. The game plays very smoothly with no noticeable frame drops.

TRON RUN/r is my first foray into any sort of temple runner style game. What drew me in was the fact that it's TRON. I'm a big fan of the asthetic and lore of the TRON universe, including both movies and the far too short-lived television series. I picked up the Ultimate Edition, so I suspect there are still modes coming my way via the Season Pass.
The game itself is all level based, which can be played over and over again to accumulate a higher score, as well as collecting 'bits' which are used to purchase one time use upgrades such as weapons and companion programs (think your classic Disney animal companion or in D&D terms - a PC's familiar). Both weapons and companions assist in racking up that score, or keeping you alive long enough to reach the end.
I've only scratched the surface in the Runner and Cycle modes. I lasted all but 30 seconds in the Stream mode, but I suspect I need more practice. This game is easy to pick up, but definitely hard to master. It'll humble you for sure and brings back some much needed challenge if you're up for it.
There are three main issues I want to see fixed by the devs at some point that I've found so far:
- I actually can't claim this one as multiple people in the Discussions forum have brought it up: the Recognizers in the menu screens are not solid! If the rest of the environment were wireframe, I'd have no issue, but even in the original TRON film, they were solid. Tired of seeing the yellow wireframe. I know this isn't a graphics issue as others have stated it and I even saw a Twitch stream with the same result.
- The opening title screen needs a way for it to be skipped! We shouldn't have to wait until the TRON RUN/r title starts to animate in to begin button mashing Start or A.
- In the screen where you select your upgrades, there seems to be no discernable way to quit the game. You must exit out to the main menu or mode selection. Seems to be an oversight.
Will update as the game progresses.
PRO's/
- TRON!
- Easy to learn
- Awesome soundtrack
- Disc throwing!
- Lightcycles!
- Sweet skin customization
CON's/
- Game development dead. Dev team refuses to discuss.
- Missing art for the Recognizers in the menus
- Needs a skippable title screen
- Lack of Game exit in the upgrades screen
- Lightcycle controls could feel a bit tighter
8/10 - Will keep rebooting
//END OF LINE.

Is it the best game in the Souls trio? Not sure, in some places no, in some places yes.
Is it worth playing if you liked the previous games or you are a newcomer to the series? Yes, and yes.
There are improvements here and there, there are some flaws and mistakes too, but it's still a very good game and there are not many games like this at all.
The PC version is also pretty good, but a bit controversial. Sure, it has 60fps and superior graphics, but it also has some weird issues that are not present in the console version. For example, your equipment breaks faster because of the increased framerate and the A.I. of some enemies can work in a bit different way, compared to the console version of the games (although I'm not really sure about that, it doesn't break the game anyway). I still hope that all this will get patched someday, but it's rather unlikely.
EDIT:
Despite the fact that the DLC had a bit of reused content from the original Dark Souls II and Dark Souls in terms of boss attack patterns, and even a reused boss, it's still a great addition to the base game. I would even say that some parts of the DLC's are better and more interesting design-wise than a lot of parts of the original game. And overall, it's simply more content - more weapons, armor, spells, locations and enemies to defeat. For me, that's 100% worth the price tag.

If you're looking for the old Half-Life with zero changes except updated graphics, I think you'll find Black Mesa to your liking. Even with  a few new areas in some (all?) of the chapters. Ever wanted to know what was inside some of the offices in Unforseen Consequences? Now, you know! Did you feel Office Complex was entirely too short? From what I remember of the original Half-Life (keep in mind, I played it when it came out in 1999), Office Complex featured a couple offices and then a giant stairwell with a sentry gun at the top. In Black Mesa's Office Complex chapter, you get to see more offices, cafeterias, and what I think may be "secret" areas with ammo, health packs, and batteries. Nothing overpowered. One of my most favourite chapters in Half-Life was On a Rail. Crowbar Collective definitely did an amazing job in vastly expanding On a Rail. I love it!
In a couple areas, I've noted little puzzles that make you have to run around a small area and look for something that'll let you continue. Nothing table-flipping, but I know I kept running around asking myself (aloud, no less) if I missed something somewhere. Turns out, I did. I feel it adds a little something extra, instead of just running around and shooting stuff.
One thing I absolutely love, though, is that not all scientists are one of 3 people. Not all guards are the same Barney Calhoun, and not all marines are one of two models. The updated graphics are pretty awesome, too! Another great advancement is ladder damage. Pressing E will mount/dismount ladders, so no worries about running off the side one one during a long climb and coming out with 20 HP.
For the AI, marines seem to try to flank you or shoot at you from several different vantage points, all at once. It can be challenging, but nothing a .357 magnum shot to the skull won't solve! Aliens and marines both can be a little derpy at times, though. I've noticed you can peek around a corner and shoot them in the arm, repeatedly, until they die.
One of two things I do dislike about Black Mesa, which may be a limit of the Source engine or my general derpy-ness, is that it's incredibly easy to get stuck on objects, like metal carts or boxes. The other is the achievements. One achievement has you "Help a barnacle and a headcrab find true love". You can save right before a headcrab jumps into a barnacle's tongue, and after it eats the headcrab you can load your save and do it again. You can do it 10 times in a row and get the achievement in 5 minutes. To me, achievements should be awarded for something great, not something you can do in 5 minutes.
The best thing about Black Mesa, by far, is all of your favourite chapters are there...and some chapters you may hate. *cough*Blast Pit*cough* And I feel none of the extra content was done in a way that's not in the spirit of the original. There's not a single added area I've seen, so far, that  looks like it was thrown in to add some fluffer to the total gameplay times. The music is amazing, but I miss the HEV charging music.
TL;DR: The added content in each chapters is amazing, the graphics and models are amazing, the puzzles are great and add to the story without being too anger-inducing. The AI could use some minor tuning, and the achievement system can feel cheaty.
In many ways I prefer Black Mesa to Half Life 2....and I love Half Life 2.

This is hands down my favorite adventure game
. It has absolutely everything you could want in a game, and in a world where games struggle to capture my attention for an extended period of time, this adventure had me engaged until the very end.
Enter Monkey, a man who wakes up on a slave ship in the distant future. Humanity has fallen to a war with machines, and our hero has been captured by a slave ship run by robots and the mysterious organization "Pyramid". Then Tripp, another girl captured on the ship, inadvertantly helps you escape. From this point on you need to help Tripp return to her home village in the West. That's the basic story, but the relationship that forms between these two characters through the course of the game is not only believable, but keeps you, the player, going. This is all attributed to the pitch perfect voice acting, and detailed facial animation system. And let me just say, it's been
since my first completion on the Xbox 360 and I still think about the ending to this game.
The gameplay boils down to combat with robots, traversing gigantic set pieces, and completing simple puzzles. Everything about this game is so incredibly smooth. Combat feels great as you unleash deadly combos on your enemies with a variety of abilities, and the finishing moves look amazing. Traversing is similar to Assassin's Creed, and many of these sequences involve climbing crumbling buildings, massive robots, and everything in between. The puzzles are an easy distraction and aren't too challenging, but probably the weakest aspect of the game.
My favorite part of the game is the world. The art direction is absolutely
. The world of Enslaved has been reclaimed by nature, and the first half of the game has you venturing through locations with lush green and vibrant reds. In the later stages the levels become more mechanical, and heavy hues of purple become a regular theme. Every once in a while I just had to stop and look around to admire the view, it's
amazing.
Other things I'd like to note are that the musical score is epic and really conveys a post-apocolyptic feel, and the game ran perfectly on my laptop with no issues to report.
Bottom line,
and get this game. It's beautiful, fun, and you will not soon forget it.

Enslaved Oddysey to the West PC review:
Enslaved : Odyssey to the West is best described as an adaptation of the novel and concept : Journey to the West. Despite never having read the novel Journey to the West I expected it to be a game with history about slaves and our history as a nation escaping slavery of the days of old. However, what I found was a game that has more on its plate then what is just under the surface of its base description.  It has parkour, a decently good story to follow along with at the start of every new chapter, collectibles for replayability and a world that seems as just a lonely and barren wasteland.
Story: At first the story I thought was rather lacking. However, once I made it past the first chapter this whole synopsis about this barren wasteland being the home of enslaved people really caught on to me. You play as a character named Monkey which later on finds one slave remaining that has survived and wants to return home to their family just like yourself. However later on we find out Monkey doesn't really have a home anywhere while Trip the female character you partner up with does have  a family and a home where she grew up.  Early on Monkey and Trip's friendship isn't that strong. However when later you need teamwork as you help Trip up to ledges she can't reach and more , the friendship between you and her get close and strong knit.
Appeal: Many people will be interested to try out this game because of the description of it being a game about companionship, emotions and the escape of being enslaved by your own world and order that controls your daily life. Many people's first question would be can you find freedom outside yourself and others through embracing a new life to claim your freedom. The answer is yes and the ending of the game's story concludes with a very emotional transversal of events. The thoughts that went through mine and I am sure others who have or want to play this game is , would it of made a difference if Namco Bandai Games added more history about slavery into this game?  I think history of enslavement and enslavement camps would of gave this game a more appealing and interesting story overall. That is not to say that the story was not good. I highly enjoyed the game's story and Pigsy this other character you meet along the way with his one liners that are somewhat humerous in tone.
Overall: 8.5/10.

When it comes to story, I was dissappointed first in the end of my first playthrough, but in my second I noticed more things that made it deeper. The story especially lends itself to those who played the DLCs to the first game, a nice addition. That being said, you don't need to play the DLCs to undertstand, though it makes the story even deeper. I highly recommend the DLCs, by the way.
The side-missions are also nice, though they are quite few.
The world and is truly amazing, and the city of Karnaca is very immersive. A massive selling-point of Dishonored is the openness and the amount of ways you can finish your objectives. Should you kill your target, or is there another way? There isn't any singular way of playing this game, which adds tons of replay-value. A testiment to this is the fact that I played the game twice in a row, under the time of a couple of days. Needless to say, I was and will not be bored for a long time.
All in all, I highly recommend the game, and if you've haven't played the first game, what the hell is wrong with you? Go to that first, or you will be left in the dark with a lot of elements of the game. While you're at it, get the DLCs aswell. They're dirt cheap, especially now during the Steam Summer Sales!

Dishonored 2 is a masterpiece. It's one of the best games of the past several years. Everyone knows it. Even the negative reviewers. So the question becomes, how important is optiminzation? As it turns out. Very.
Now, the developers went for somethings. Let's not just throw the umbrella term "optimization" out there any call it a day. The engine they used looks fantastic, what a lot of you might not know is that the void/idtech engines are very geared towards haldling unique textures. What do unique textures have to do with your playing experience might I hear you ask? Well, it's the same with wolfenstien and rage. These engines allow for the creation of an enviroment that is true to their vision. Most engines ask you to use tiling textures from a limited pool. Idtech 5 allows you to essentially paint whatever you want and bake textures into the enviroment at will. For the style of this game, that engine allowed for a open world that felt painted and unique. However because of the core engine about moving around extremely heavy assets of these unique assets baked at a high degree, it has to stream all of this around and swap it in and out. This creates a widly uneven presentation. Most of what i mentioned visually, may even go unobserved by many players.
They will simply go "meh, other games look just as good if not better so what's the big deal" - I am telling those people, the game you get here is actually 'premium" at least visually. The features and extent of each feature ranging from hbao+ to TXAA to very high end shadows are impressive because they are essentially grafted into an engine that's not about those features. Creating the very best of the high end shader style game (crysis 3 for instance) and the very best painted style vision (rage, doom, wolfenstein, have very organic textures).
What you get in return is a game that is.... a combination of two things. Demanding because of what i mentioned above, and also a little ahead of it's time. This is the kind of game you want as a minspec 1080ti for 2560x1440 and above and getting mostly 60fps. You also want an expensive cpu. So in a few years this game will probably be a little closer to smooth.
Which brings me to the least forgivable fault. The frame pacing.
Oh god. This is where the game really has issues. I can forgive it being ahead of it's time, I can understand how it's an advanced organic engine. What I really don't appreciate however is frame timings going all over the map. No doubt it's got something to do with the variable framerate, however this game is so demanding that the variable framerate is all you really have to work with on any "current" pc. And unfortunately in this rare exception gsync does not solve it, it just somewhat mitigates how terrible it is. God help those without it.
You can turn your viewpoint and there will always be a degree of microstutter, The lower the framerate you get the less noticable it is. So at 30fps it tends to feel like consistent enough judder that you can ignore it, however when your fps is 28-65fps constantly changing, that judder will drive you crazy if you're sensitive to microstutter.
Developers, I get it, you wanted to get your vision across. And it's probably not possible to fix the microstutter given the engine you are using. Variable fps on an evolved idtech engine was never going to be an easy task. It would have been better to aim for a easier to lock fps.
I still recommend this game to those that are not senstiive to it. The more sensitive to microstutter you are, the less I recommend it. It's a great game. But even great games are not worth headaches.

Many games are afraid to place effective tools in the hands of the player, and as a result suffer the curse of being mundane and linear. Dishonored 2 is not one of those games.
Player choice is, and always has been a very crucial part to the stealth-action genre, and Dishonored 2 merely gives a final destination to levels while leaving the journey entirely in the hands of the player. It has been a while since I had played a game that gave me so much freedom, and I cherished the opportunity at every turn utilizing the many interesting ways to dissect a level. As with the the first Dishonored, level design is the crux of this game, and it is mostly excellent.
The praise I give to the level design is matched to the amount of tools given to the player and the sheer power of those tools as well. The Blink ability was a staple in the first Dishonored, and I found myself once again relying on the extremely powerful ability to carry me through my first play-through. It's interesting to note that the hallmark void abilities from the first game are not a mandatory inclusion, in fact, the player can opt to not use the powers at all which may or may not have an impact on the game's story.
There aren't many games I can think of that give the player control of the difficulty in such a way as Dishonored 2 does. In most games, there are maybe 3-4 preset difficulty options each sporting a blurb about how difficult or easy that setting is, and Dishonored 2 does have these basic preset difficulties as well. The difference is that you can pick and choose how difficult and unforgiving a game experience you wish to partake in. I turned several of the options down to make myself more reliant on smart gameplay decisions, and not letting myself slip into a run and gun playstyle due to the brutal nature of combat that I was creating through the difficulty. It worked pretty well to keep me reigned in and made me think a lot more carefully about how I wanted to approach situations knowing that if I had to engage in open combat it wasn't going to be easy.
While I have done nothing but give praise to the developers for creating a great game, it is not without some major flaws accompanying it. Performance is quite awful even this far after launch which is disappointing to say the least. With my set-up, I shouldn't be forced to play at Medium graphics or take a giant FPS drop which is what I had to do. Many, many others have reported the same type of problems, so if you do not have a beefier rig, you may have some issues.
While I have praised level design, there are the rare occasions where the playground levels funnel into some linearity. This isn't awful for some things that should be that way such as a vault entrance, but there are a few times throughout the game where your options are walk into the open, or take the extremely annoying way around (usually through some bloatfly-ridden areas).
The story is quite predictable and linear, and leaves a lot to be desired in my opinion. The main antagonist has the typical angsty-edgy "my parents didn't acknowledge me" story, and then said antagonist comes across the powerful void which grants her great power. There are several points in time where I'm baffled as to why they don't try and stop the player from achieving their goals. There are some quirky characters that are met on the way, but they seem to fit the typical character tropes more than attempting to be unique.
The Bottom Line
A very enjoyable stealth-action game with a sandbox-style approach to traversing levels is exactly what you will get with Dishonored 2. That is, of course, assuming you have a powerful enough machine to run the game at a decent framerate.
I rate the game a solid 7.5/10. Good, but has a story that leaves you underwhelmed, and performance issues plague an otherwise great game.

I thoroughly enjoyed the first Dishonored due to my appreciation of playing games in a stealthy manner, I even play some first person shooters this way.

Dishonored 2 is an immense upgrade from the first one in the series.  The graphics improved (way more detail), the controls improved (can trigger powers and side weapons with the left trigger [I play with a controller] while still wielding the sword with the right trigger), powers and enhancements became more sophisticated (more options and more upgrade choices), NPCs became more intelligent and unforgiving, levels became less linear and included even more alternatives for movement based on approach you like to take, and there are now three gameplay slots each with their own save game slots.

I would recommend a small improvement in cutscene vocals, since it was hard to hear the Outsider and Delilah at times which made the story confusing briefly.  For some reason their voices were soft and far away sounding.

The Low Chaos ending was a bit confusing since there was no hint to head to the Overseers Chapel, and I regretfully had to look that up after a long confused time pondering what I had not accomplished yet.  So maybe there should be a small indication to complete that task.

I know I did not get anywhere near all the bone charms during my playthrough, but I was underwhelmed at the few Low Chaos bone charms available.

Far Reach would often fling me to places I did not choose such as the side of a building where I would fall down and die, I wonder if there is a better way to default the placements of this power or if that is just due to my poor aim.  But overall, the game was smooth and fresh.

The ending was rewarding given all the hard work to get Clean Hands for my first run through.  I will definitely enjoy playing through High Chaos and as Corvo to compare to my first run.  I look forward to the Death of the Outsider DLC and other future additions to this series.  Thanks Arkane Studios yet again.

Going into the game I had extremely high hopes that this was going to be an awesome remake of the game using Source as probably most people with interest in the game did. From the first hour or so you really do get that sense of a Source remake, but after that you start to notice flaws. The longer I played, the more and more I felt like the game was just a crappy mod in which they just did texture and model swaps. What made this more and more apparent was how sloppy it was.
Examples include:
-Guns look like real guns. (It didn't feel like Half-Life and was more like a Garry's Mod gun pack.)
-90% of the personnel have the same face. (They just have different colored skin and hair most of the time.)
-Player's model has colliding meshes on the wrist between the suit and the base of the glove. (Looks like plastic too.)
-Tons of textures are extremely low res and clash with the moderately good textures.
-Models don't work together. (The headcrabbed people look like their assets were pulled from somewhere else entirely.)
-Explosives are about 10% too big. (S.L.A.M. sections hurt you no matter how careful and far you get from them.)
-Quite a few physics, and game mechanics don't work like the original. (I thought barnacles die from being fed inedible objects 2x, unless that's a Half-Life 2 thing... Ladders are still derp.)
As for the Source engine. Nothing really stands out to make you realise it's there. All Valve games already run 250-500FPS so making it on a more optimized engine really doesn't effect FPS. Graphically speaking, they really could have done anything to make it look better than the originals and it still doesn't shine amongst modern games. The loading screens are just as long or even longer than the originals. (I'm using SSDs too.)
The final thing that bothered me is this isn't a line for line 100% accurate remake. A lot of the puzzles and contraptions to open doors and stuff have been dumbed down and streamlined to be more straightforward and easy to do. At first I didn't mind it and was kind of thankful, then I just realised how different it was. Some scenes are just totally different layout wise and it's kind of jarring if you know the original. The only good side to this was how they added so many more audio lines for NPCs who now comment on the specific situation which adds more immersion.
To finish up my review I'd just like to point out I picked this up just now. I haven't experienced the development cycle of this game but I know it's turtle slow and still not complete. I would definitely recommend just picking up the original Half-Life over this, especially because when it's on sale it's $0.99. If we're talking apples to apples $4.99 is fair for Black Mesa and purely because it's made on Source. Otherwise I don't recommend getting this, more so if you haven't played the original or Source versions. The old Source version works just as well if not better than Black Mesa. The reason I take such a big dump on this is because of Sven Co-Op, which literally did everything these devs did plus more, making the entire game co-op for free. (Except for writing it in Source which is where Black Mesa gets 90% of its value from, even if you don't notice it.)
All in all, if I had to give Black Mesa a rating I'd say 5/10. It's just not worth it when you compare it to the originals and Sven Co-Op... All you're getting with Black Mesa is a paid graphics mod for Half-Life 1 Source.

Unlike other Alien Predator games which employs the run 'n' gun, AI relies on stealth and survival skills.
I was wondering why are people always mentioning about the "Alien" until I played the game myself.
As Amanda Ripley, you're protrayed as a stereotypical weak female. Not a bad thing, but that's the point of keeping this game realistically difficult. Not because of the sheer amount of enemies swarming the motion tracker, but because you have to navigate from one checkpoint to another while avoiding the Alien and hostiles. And running makes enough noise to stop you dead in your tracks the moment the Alien storms towards your direction.
After playing it for a while, you'll understand that shooting doesn't make you invulnerable. And to top if off, you need loads of PATIENCE and TIME. Because, expect to die from the simplest mistakes such as attracting the Alien and failing to subdue enemies in time or a combination of both. Saving comes from save booths, not like "Press key to save progress". This adds to the difficulty. Mess a step and you'll have to start back from the last checkpoint.
Seriously, buy this game if you want to immerse yourself in a survival horror like no other. You'll "love" it in no time.

Sometimes I would just run around, knowing the noise would get me killed, but I wanted to find the objective, so on my next load I would at least know where I was going to spend my next 20 minutes sneaking to. Really sad to be writing this review because I was 100% sure I was going to LOVE this game, but in the end I really didn't. Mind you, I set it to Very Hard or whatever the max difficulty level is, but I found this game really repetitive. Its Dishonored 1 but with a woman and more dialogue. I miss Corvo's stealthiness, which really isn't translated well into Emily in my opinion. The guards were either really good at their job - and definetely require a raise - because in pitch black in stealth mode behind a column they found me, while others couldn't see me standing in front of their nose.
I'm really looking for an awesome stealth game and this one didn't deliver and I'm really hurt because I found Dishonored 1 to be amazing, having replayed it countless times. This one, meh.
I'd also like to say that the graphics are really unstable. My GPU is a top of the line AMD model and it just lagged and lagged, I was really dissappointed that max settings were so blocky.

Compared to the first game, Dishonored 2, feels much longer, more complicated and more difficult (although once you get a feel for things it gets easier). Personally I enjoyed those aspects of this game albeit it took me a couple of missions to get used to. The game looks and feels great but leans much heavier into the more mystical/magic side of things, very reminecent to D1's DLCs, and is a far throw from the orginal's main storyline, which in my opinion was a good balance of natural and void. The new characters are interesting and well-developed-"ish" but the story line didn't really "land" for me. The ending was strange to say the least and I felt much more detached than expected; and by detached I mean I felt like I had no real connection or emotional tie to anything really going on. Going back to the characters, the Outsider feels and sounds like Penguin from "Gotham," which I like this new change personally. Emily can be a bit wishy-washy at times but for the most part is a soild main character. Corvo is as brutal as ever and I feel like him actually having a voice makes him a lot better. There are aspects of a horror-esque game placed through various levels, some more obvious than others, I'm not a big fan of those styles of games but I felt like most of those genre additions were tasteful and useful to the plot points. Overall though, the missions are diverse, the levels are incredible, and the new mechanics, are all great upgrades from the previous. Music and art style still give you that steampunk vibe without effort and the variations of enemies and powers are a great dessert to this full course. If you liked Dishonored 1 you'll enjoy many parts of this new one, however, keeping out of spolier territory, you could feel indifferent about others aspects.
[Overall it is a solid 8.5/10 game]
