When the original Homeworld was released, there was never a strategy game like it.  Fifteen years later, the same truth still stands.  Homeworld is in a class all its own, thanks to revolutionary gameplay, a haunting and emotional story, awe-inspiring visuals, and a great story.  The Remastered Collection is a labor of love for the first two games, though I dare say most gamers are more interested in the first one.  Graphically, the Remastered Homeworld is an absolute delight.  It still plays the same as we all remember, but ship models are gorgeously detailed and crisp.  The game now runs natively in 1080p, which is just lovely, and all voices, music and cutscenes have either been given the HD treatment to make this the definitive edition of a timeless classic.  It's just a shame that the expansion title Homeworld: Cataclysm didn't make the cut.  Here's to hoping it comes along later in DLC format.
HW vets will notice that both HW1 and HW2 now share the same interface.  This makes it easy to jump from one game to the other.  I love the new HUD layout, but sometimes it's way too hard to see some details, like a group counter.  The HUD is scalable, but the other preset sizes are too large to be of any benefit.  A small quibble.
What DOES irritate me are bugs that have somehow survived 15 years worth of mothballs to sneak their way into this new edition.  If you've never played Homeworld before, then know that some missions can take well over an hour.  This is fine, but Homeworld has always had a problem with certain missions not ending due to something you've done during the course of your playthrough.  A prime example is Mission 10: Supernova Station, where you must carefully assemble a strike fleet to take out an enemy installation while avoiding pockets of intense and harmful radiation eminating from a nearby supernova.  It is possible to reach the installation, blow it up, then kill every single remaining enemy on the map without triggering the end of the mission.  Your only recourse is to load a previous quicksave (no guarantee) or start the mission all over again.  It's great to see developers giving so much love to such a beautiful game, but I wish they would take a bit more time to squash bugs that are already fit for a rocking chair.
Nevertheless, Homeworld isn't just a strategy game.  It's an experience!  No other game manages to capture a sense of isolation as much as this one does, and you truly do feel like you're "out there," sometimes.  It puts the vastness of space in jarring perspective, and offers up a challenging set of missions at the same time.  If you don't think fast in Homeworld, it can cost you a mission.  No two missions are entirely alike, so there's very little filler, here.  If you're not sweating it out to destroy incoming asteroids that threaten your mothership, you're being pulled out of hyperspace by an enemy gravity well to set up an ambush...and they have superior firepower!  It becomes a careful juggling of harvesting resources, building your fleet, and researching new technologies, all at the same time.  It's not for the faint of heart, and it's not forgiving, but it's rewarding in its own right.
I love this Remastered Edition, and it was certainly worth the wait.  Despite a few minor quibbles, it is *the* strategy game to buy this year.  Not bad for a 15 year old title!  Welcome back, Homeworld.  We missed you.

First off:
I never played the original Homeworld or Homeworld 2 but I wish I did.  I was too young at the time and it is a shame because I wish I had experienced these games when they first came out.  Now after playing them remastered I can easily say that these two games are on my favorite games of all time list.
So now on to the review.
Homeworld
Pros:
-The story of this game is amazing, I would say the best, surprisingly deep for an RTS game, hooks you immediately and keeps you going to the end.
-The missions are varied and entertaining also they get challenging and makes you think.
-The soundtrack is beautifuly awesome, forebodding opera music that sets the mood perfectly.

Cons:
-Some missions are buggy at release, if its not the AI then the mission glitches out where you can't finish it, requires a restart.
Homeworld 2
Pros:
-Pretty much the same as Homeworld only the story is not nearly as good, kinda B movie cheese crap but still entertaining.
Cons:
-The missions get insanely difficult towards the end, normally this isn't a problem but if you are not prepared you are toast, might have to reload a save to make sure you have a decent fleet with you when you start.
Homeworld Multiplayer
DISCLAIMER- As of this writing the multiplayer is in Beta so all of my criticisms will probably be addressed at some point
The mutiplayer is really buggy, random crashes, can't connect to games, etc.  Also some things are unbalanced like the way the Homeworld races play out against the Homeworld 2 races.  However with people that you know the game can be fun and if Gearbox stick with it the multiplayer can be awesome.  At the moment though just view the mutiplayer as a bonus to the singleplayer aspects to the game.
SIDE NOTE - You get the original two games with the remastered versions and full mod support so if you want nostalgia or endless hours of fun with mods there are those options.
I woudl recommend this to anyone just based off the story of Homeworld alone.  Absolutely amazing, beautiful visuals, just an absolute amazing package deal this game is a must play if you enjoy RTS games.  10/10 would put 30 hours into this game in 1 week again.

I'm writing this review mere minutes after beating the remastered Homeworld campaigns. Bear in mind that this review talks about the remastered games ONLY.
I cannot overstate how much I looked forward to something like this, since Homeworld never had a digital release (good luck getting those old CDs to run).
The remaster is done well, but not perfectly. My biggest gripe being ship squads. In multiplayer, the Homeworld 1 races simply don't stand a chance in the fighter/corvetter categories. Of course that could change with future patches (as I'm sure it will).
Campaign wise, the Homeworld 2 campaign feels nigh-on identical to how it was before. The Homeworld 1 campaign though definitely felt different. It seemed a bit easier, maybe because of the rock-paper-scissors combat system associated with the Homeworld 2 engine. Either way, it was fun and a great trip down memory lane... except it looked a hellova lot better!
But there are some issues, almost all being Homeworld 1 related. Formations need work, simple as that. If I put my ships into a sphere I expect them to hug around a guarded ship, not sit next to it in a ball. Fuel is gone, but TBH, to me (!) that was a positive change overall. The UI is neat and better to me than the old one. This one (like Homeworld 2's original UI) allows you to monitor the action while issueing build and research orders.
Most of the other changes are minor, such as Kadeshi Multibeam frigates not doing a barrel roll when firing or research ships not spinning anymore. All of that could be patched in later though, or modded.
If you can live with the above differences and consider the amazing visual upgrade, then this is absolutely a good buy!

About 20 hours of gameplay. Not including the sequel nor multiplayer.
I have some good things to say about this game, including the soundtrack which is by far the best thing (I believe) about this game. The soundtrack absolutely steals the show for me, and like many have said before 'it's like a space opera'.
For years on end I was wondering what was so great about homeworld, and really couldn't understand why so many people loved the game. I wasn't able to get my hands on it until now, and instantly fell in love with it. An RTS space game? Count me in!
First off, the games included are well worth the price. $35 bucks for TWO games? Including a beta Multiplayer.
A space RTS that has probably gone where no other space RTS games have gone before, and it included 3D movement which allows a wide variety of ship maneuvering and freedom most space games don't allow. Ships also have weaknesses on the top bottom and rear, ships take an extra 50% damage if attacked from behind. I like this mechanic, it does something a lot of RTS games haven't explored, which is the flanking damage.
I thoroughly enjoyed Sword of the Stars mainly because it felt like a 'total war' in space. But I was disappointed in the lack of a 3 dimensional movement system. I think the best part of my time playing was having two fleets of capital ships and flanking from the top and bottom of enemy ships and engulfing them from all sides. I feel like 3 dimensional movement is not used too much in games and being able to outsmart opponents by descending down upon their ships feels awesome. The game is also very pretty as well, which is important, because battles in this game are absolutely gorgeous and wonderful to watch!
The best part of a Space Strategy game is looking at what kinds of ships you could get, there are:
Fighters - Basic unit, self explanatory
Corvettes - A heavier ship class, can take more punishment but is slower.
Frigates - Capital class ships
Destroyers - Super-Capital class ships that destroy capital ships but are a little less effective vs. strikecraft.
Battlecruisers - A Homeworld 2 unit, I think only the Vagyr and Hiigarans can build these.
in multiplayer there are four races that play completely differently, and there are a wide variety of units. But I have not played MP much at all.
Campaign
Missions are very lengthy, depending on how you play and there is a dynamic difficulty that changes the enemy fleet's size depending on your own fleet size. So the better you are at the game, the harder it gets, but the game also has a fleet cap for the enemy fleet in every mission. So if you spent a lot of time salvaging ships over your fleet cap the game might become too easy. The game wasn't that easy for me though, I had to reload several saves.
The campaign works a bit like this. Whatever ships you build move on to the next mission. You are the last of the Kushan who were nearly wiped out and are hunted by the Taiidan. From there you must assimilate ships, and reverse engineer them to fight for your claim and survival against the Taiidan Empire. The thing I love the most about the game is how the ships you build move on to the next mission. This is your fleet, and it is shaped by how you play the game, whether you assimilate ships into your fleet or if you build them from scratch, it will show. Is your fleet big? Did you build them from scratch? Or did you assimilate the ships of the Taiidan Empire? At the end of every mission, your fleet will look slightly or more different depending on how you played. You can customize your ship colors as well, through the skirmish match, and the same colors you used in that match will show up in campaign as well.
The last few missions I had a tiny bit more ships than the actual fleet cap, and on those missions it spawned fleets nearly twice my size! On some missions I could count over 50 or so capital ships (one of the campaign missions has about over 100 ion cannon frigates I think, didn't have much time to count them all) and on the last mission it spawned about 40 ion cannon and assault frigates backed by destroyers and Heavy Cruisers. Insane!
Combined with a challenging difficulty, a steep learning curve, 3D movement, and gorgeous graphics battles can become very hectic and cinematic. I loved every bit and battle I had with the game.
I think the best thing about the campaign is seeing the new ships and trying to salvage the Destroyers and Heavy Cruisers in the missions. This game can get very hard if you don't know what you're doing or if you make too many mistakes or don't pay attention to the map. So for you newbies, there's a pause button :D
Fleet formations work, until you engage the enemy, hopefully it will be patched!

It may not be more TRON UPRISING or TRON 3, but it's a holdover until Disney gets over its Star Wars fixation.
(Don't fret, we ended up with the comics and TRON 2.0 when the last one took ages.)
ANYWAY, this is a Runner title, but seen from behind instead of side on.
Various typical moves come into play (jump, slide, move around obstacles) but others add to the genre (fly/glide, wall run, etc.). Adding to this is a few power ups and "Companions" (a neat little homage to Bit from the first movie) that have certain special abilities to assist you.
The power ups and Companions cost "bits", which you can earn running, or pay for them with REAL MONEY if you're daft.
Power ups activate for a limited time, and if you're hit once, you lose your Companion.
You also have a three-hit life bar before failing the level's run.
(Cleverly visible on the back of the avatar - blue bars while doing okay, last one goes RED.)
As you get further into Tron City, the harder it gets, more opponents added to the typical disc throwers and tanks.
The other two game modes allow for a race using Lightcycles, but sadly no actual Lightcycle challenge like in the movies.
(Rather bland bike too. It's like a poor racer with a Tron theme and a slight barrier behind the bikes. Seen better on unofficial dev ANDROID STORE titles.)
The final mode is a challenge mode, a randomly generated neverending level called "Stream", using ALL the challenges in Tron City and Cycle modes.
It's not perfect, but it's okay.
And hell, at least this game is keeping TRON on life support!

TRON RUN/r is an endless runner game similar to BIT.TRIP RUNNER, but in 3D. You'll jump, slide, glide, wallride and grind your way to the exit while also battling viruses and enemy soldiers who can also throw identity disks at you. Unlike BTR where you're send backwards at hitting something, you get 3 hits, but you can keep going, until you're gone. There is also a light cycle mode where you have to race the clock to get to the exit while passing through arches that add time and battling other light cyclers. Aside from a generic male or female program, you can play as most of the characters from TRON, TRON: Legacy, and TRON: Uprising, use many different models of light cycles, and have a variety of colors. After completing a level, you are awarded currency which you can spend on identity disk modifiers and buffs. You also have point goals that can result in 1-3 stars for a level.
The game does have its problems.
1. You cannot play as Sam Flynn, Old Kevin Flynn, or Zuse.
2. There's a decent amount of colors, but you can't be orange, despite being able to be red, as well as 3 shades of blue.
3. There should be a marker indicating that you've completed a level without having to go to the leaderboards.
The soundtrack isn't Daft Punk, but it's a decent electronic set.

I'm honestly uncertain if I want to recommend this game or not.
Pros:
-Pretty graphics
-Interesting world, characters and story.
-Good voice acting
Cons:
-Extremely linear gameplay, almost boringly so. I've been on actual train rides that have been less railroaded. I get that it is for console gamers originally, but please, they cannot be that weakminded. Not a single place in the game can you figure stuff out for yourself, which pathway to take, or which way to solve a problem. You're basically just following instructions the whole game.
-A lot of the gameplay involves jumping, but you can't jump wrong and there is only one path, so most of the time you don't need to see or aim where you're jumping. Just hit whatever direction you're going and jump, jump, jump. Ta-da, you're there.
-Occasional annoyances due to camera angles
-Some sections are impossible to succeed at unless you're very lucky or you know where the next obstacle is going to be.
-The port from console is not flawless, sometimes when selecting menus with the mouse the cursor is not where it is supposed to be.
-Unskipable cut-scenes. That you have to watch again and again if you die at a difficult section. Seriously, this is not acceptable!
Main gripe:
This could have been an awesome game. But the way it has been designed, it should have been an animation movie instead. There's just not enough actual game in it. The player has no agency. I still finished the game, because I wanted to see where it was going and I was marginally pleased. No spoilers, but a waste-disposal related question popped into my mind when I saw the end cutscene, which is the kind of thing that annoys me. Aside from that anal-retentive (pun may be intended) technicality, the game as a whole just doesn't do it for me. There were times in the early game when I thought, this is going to be neat once all the hand-holding and easy linear paths become more complex, but that never happened. As such, I would not recommend this game if you're looking for a good game. If on the other hand you're looking for a cute interactive animated series, then, heck, it's all right for that purpose.

A journey through a desperate mind.
Enslaved is an adventure game overlooked by a majority and (rightfully) loved by most who played it. It follows the story of the great classical Chinese novel, although is set in a post apocalyptic future where seemingly armed robots are enslaving people.
Armed with a staff and some sweet climbing skills, you play the enslaved warrior Monkey. Tasked with helping your captor, Trip, get home to her father. Throughout most of the game, you will be jumping, climbing over obstacles and mowing down mecs in either brawling close combat or shooting plasma bolts long rage style.The game is designed in such a way to keep this recipe fresh and not feel repetitive. Smart enemy placements contribute to this as mixing ranged and melee enemies in fights makes you think before you act. Boss fights are a sweet bonus.
Weapons, shields, health and combat techniques are all upgradable and a must to get past the later chapters.
Contrary to what you may believe, the post apocalyptic setting in Enslaved really does its art justice as the environment and visuals are just gorgeous. The greenest of trees, bluest of skies and warmest colors of explosions are visually pleasing. The art is well complemented by the ambient sounds and music.
After about half of the game, you are joined by Pigsy who is, although a disgusting pig, easily the most exotic and colorful of characters. He livens up the game to a high degree and counters the somewhat reserved character of Monkey.
Pigsy is playable in the included DLC and offers a different kind of play style by scrapping the melee combat in favor of a rifle and four kinds of cooldown-based items (distraction device, EMP, ally bomb and damage based bomb). Accompanied with the joyful Truffles, Pigsy goes on his own little adventure. The extra content is a must play and Is just as good if not even stronger in some parts than the main game.
The only weaknesses I found in the game was the overly scripted camera that takes camera controls away from you to show objects of interest in an overly obvious way. Sometimes the camera becomes fixed in a static position for portions of the pacing through the level. This can sometimes become a bit distracting. I was also annoyed with how some animations take to long to complete. While fighting (bosses especially) I found it very difficult to evade after attacking due to the attack animations not completing yet. Similarly when climbing pipes jumps to other objects would not register.
So, linear post apocalyptic action adventure brawler with ravishing visuals and interesting characters. Action, drama and humor packed into an adventure with a deeper meaning. It has completionist potential and took me 12 hours to beat with the must play extra Pigsy campaign. Sit back, plug in that controller and go on a fun adventure.

Mind you, I set it to Very Hard or whatever the max difficulty level is, but I found this game really repetitive. Its Dishonored 1 but with a woman and more dialogue. Compared to the first game, Dishonored 2, feels much longer, more complicated and more difficult (although once you get a feel for things it gets easier). Personally I enjoyed those aspects of this game albeit it took me a couple of missions to get used to. The game looks and feels great but leans much heavier into the more mystical/magic side of things, very reminecent to D1's DLCs, and is a far throw from the orginal's main storyline, which in my opinion was a good balance of natural and void. The new characters are interesting and well-developed-"ish" but the story line didn't really "land" for me. The ending was strange to say the least and I felt much more detached than expected; and by detached I mean I felt like I had no real connection or emotional tie to anything really going on. Going back to the characters, the Outsider feels and sounds like Penguin from "Gotham," which I like this new change personally. Emily can be a bit wishy-washy at times but for the most part is a soild main character. Corvo is as brutal as ever and I feel like him actually having a voice makes him a lot better. There are aspects of a horror-esque game placed through various levels, some more obvious than others, I'm not a big fan of those styles of games but I felt like most of those genre additions were tasteful and useful to the plot points. Overall though, the missions are diverse, the levels are incredible, and the new mechanics, are all great upgrades from the previous. Music and art style still give you that steampunk vibe without effort and the variations of enemies and powers are a great dessert to this full course. If you liked Dishonored 1 you'll enjoy many parts of this new one, however, keeping out of spolier territory, you could feel indifferent about others aspects.
[Overall it is a solid 8.5/10 game]

I've seen the horrors of war unfold in the game:
-Was with my squad that I randomly selected out of my 100 teamates
-6 People, all good men. Charlie, Winston, Garry, Sulivan, Mark, And Max
-Since I was the squad leader, I took point.
-It was dark, I couldnt see a thing. These Piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥Night vision goggles barely illuminated our path.
-I took the squad into a jeep. I was rolling with Charlie, Max and Garry. The others were right on our tail. In a jeep as
well.
-We took the first objective with ease. I remember thinking that it was way too quiet.
-As we were advancing to the second objective, I heard a rocket. I turned to see half my squad explode in thier jeep.
-We opened fire on the hilltops. I saw Winston, what a goddamn trooper he was, attempt to get up. His attemps were
futile as a stray bullet lodged in the side of his head. I remember thinking about his wife back home, and if I was ever
going to get out of this alive.
-Max, completely ignoring the hailstorm of bullets took down at least 6 with the .50 on the jeep before the entire
jeep exploded and rolled on its side. I didn't even look back. I couldn't. No-one could of survived a hit like that.
-Through the storm of bullets I saw a friendly tank, I don't even know thier names, drive straight into the pile of
enemies, trying to save what little squad I had left.
-Me, Charlie and Garry were cowered behind the burning remainder of the jeep, the stench I still remember to this
day. I Saw many of my teamates fall, thier blood sprayed across the road. I Instantly knew what I had to do. I Told
Charlie and Garry to fall back to our first objective.
-While they ran, I loaded my gun and I just started spraying the hilltop, giving the best chance to my brave
front-line soliders that I possibly could. As I looked back to reload, I saw Garry fall. He never got back up.
-As I looked into the fire and war, I knew I was surrounded. I took my gun in hand. Thinking this was the last
thing I'd ever hold.
-I broke cover, I swear everthing seemed to slow down. I took down 4 guys before they even turned to face me.
-As they started shooting, I took a bullet to the shoulder and fell on my back. Looking up to the sky I said my
final goodbyes to this war filled world.
-The enemies approched, still shooting, possibly thinking I was more then one. I smiled through the dirt and
dust the bullets were kicking up.
-They approched, as I thought that this was the way I'd go out.
-Then I heard twin .50 caliber weapons spray. It was the airforce. I had never seen the pilot in my life. And I
never got the chance too. His shooting was extremely accurate. I watched the enimies rip apart in front of
my very eyes.
-I took my chance and ran. I rejoined with Charlie on objective A.

I still yet have time to play with AW Survivle Mode! (Will Update)

I loved Just cause 2 and Just cause 3 has so many many many many more better things tha 2 in astronomical ways, but that doesn't mean there are cons. So here is my review of it.
The gameplay and the gameplay mechanics are make make this game, the story isn't there so the gameplay makes it, and it is incredibly fun to ♥♥♥♥ around for hours. you have your standard arsenal of guns, shotguns, pistols and assault rifles, you also have a mortar, multiple rocket launchers, even a thermonuke and a airstrike,. In the Land Mech DLC you get an EMP gun that is amazing fun to disable cars and helicopters with while going at high speeds. You have your parachute and your grappling hook as usual, except you will barely use your parachute because you got a new toy, a wingsuit. It is significantly faster and better in every aspect except for one, it is fast and you can't use your weapons while on it (Though the Air DLC gives you rocket boosters, machine guns and a rocket launcher on it). The grappling hook is also amazing fun, because now you can retract double tethers, crash things into other things or rip things appart.Also because the Remote Explosives were the only gear you used in 2, you now have an infinite ammount of them, up to a cap per time. You can also turn these into rockets to make anything fly.
So there are bad things and good things. So let's start with the bads, so you don't have to wait until the end to see something you consider a dealbreaker.
LOADING SCREEN THAT TAKES FOREVER:
There is this loading screen that does not add anything and takes way too long, it starts with Rico (the rambo you play) sitting at a beach in a chair. For about 20 seconds, only 3 things happen; he wipes his head with a towel and a far off explosion, Rico lifts his glass. This vast majority of this intro screen is nothing happening other than smoke coming off the ground far away. But this is not loading screen, after that it takes you to the loading screen, then to the obligatory login screen.
FORCED ONLINE:
The game will automatically connect to your steam account and be logged in, why you ask? Only for a♥♥♥♥♥♥measuring contenst of the higest killstreaks and the longest powerslides, nothing else, if you ever get as much as a hickup in your connectivity the game will pop up a screen and pause your game, telling you to log back in or play in offline mode, but if you play in offline mode the game might randomly pop up the screen again in a unconvienent time to let you know again.
STORY IS COMPLETE♥♥♥♥♥♥
I can tell you the whole entire story in only 5 words. You. Overthrow. An. Evil. Dictator. That is it. You do not give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about the story because that is literally all that happens. Along with no real sense of progression, the quests get harder but it is still the same, destroy this, kill that, get here, go there. You unlock new missions by destroying bases and strongholds, destroying vital parts of it suchs as antennas and fuel depos, unlike the last game there are no collectables to unlock the story, rather collectables and finadables that unlock special weapons and perks.
VEHICLES COMPLETELY SUCK:
With one exection but that is in a DLC so i will get to it later. You never have any real sense of speed in the game while in a car, the car is flow and limited to the road while you can scale mountains and cross oceans while parachuting or wingsuiting. With vehicles blow up at the slightest bump, is something taps you on the side you blow up instantly, though jumping off a cliff and landing on your side doesn't blow you up. A car going 30 crashing into your side will make you blow up and cause a game over, also if you going upside down, you blow up. The only exception to this are the Mechs from the Land DLC, they have OP wepaons and gravity manipulation fields that can pick up enemies and cars or even shoot a gravity pulse to shoot everything away (though be careful, if you see a pile of stuff and think "this will be fun" it might crash your computer due to all of the collision meshes the game isn't used ot)
So after all of this negativity, lets get to the postitive side provided that some of the cons haven't driven you away.
EXPLOSIONS ARE BEAUTIFUL:
The explosions in this game are amazing, you can even blow up bridges to make cars fall down. There is even a thermonuke launcher that makes a giant cloud with blue lignitng spread out from the initial explosion which you never get tired off.
COMBAT IS FUN:
Well combat can be fun, you you play this like a standard third person shooter the combat is♥♥♥♥♥♥ but have you ever bound two enemies (more more) together then put rockets on the first one, then watch the guy fly away and dragging everyone with them? The Dual Tethers open up all kinds of fun shenanigans, you can fire multiple teathers to one guy and tether him to 6 of his friends, then retract the tether into a giant moshpit before throwing one grenade at the mess. You can fire your tether at an enemy and reel yourself in to him because the third law of newton doesn't exist and kick him off a cliff face and watch him fly down.
CHALLENGES:
Challenges can be awesomely fun, can range from anything form a shooting range to races to gathering as much as you can and depositing it in a single spot. You are awarded with 0-5 "Cogs" whichs are like stars, rating from 0-5 points. You can use your cogs to equip upgrades which you can disable and switch between at any time, sometimes you want proxmity grenades and sometimes you want them exploding on impact, sometimes you want explosives to act as rockets and sometimes you just want to blow things up. However it should be noticed that you don't have to perfect every challenge in order to unlock everything, i thought it was so i didn't leave a challenge until i had 5 cogs in everything, then when i had unlocked every single upgrade in that field i still had 1 mission with 3 cogs and one misison i hadn't played at all.
I still return to this game for fun just for the gameplay, the story is not good and never will be, the DLC story sucks even more, not even having animated cutscenes, just a bunch of still that switch every 5 seconds along with the same voice acting, but they are still worth getting for the sake or the gameplay it adds.

This game is by far one of the BEST Rpg games I've played. Prepare to Die, Prepare to know your skill, Prepare to Improve. I cannot stress enough on how fun this game is. The mechanics of the game are made to counter the Hack-and-Slash point of view. (That means slashing like crazy with no bad side-effects) Where as this game if you don't plan your attacks right, if you don't try to out-think your opponents you will die, or be punished harshly. When I started playing this it made me realize that there is a MAJOR SKILL-CAP to this game. Of course there are multi-player functions, but you'll be soloing more often on mobs.
And
The PvP in the game is FORCED! This means that you'll have some really good npc's that are very player-like that will hand you your head on a platter if you don't think through what you're doing, and players will INVADE your game. This makes the game much more fun and adding a sense of "OMG I DID IT!" When you get your first player kill.
Although there are some really bad sides to the game. Such as the Bell Tower. If you go in there prepared to be invaded by 3 people. So it's best to get a squad of your own before you enter the area to fight the gargoyle (optional boss).
Worried about hackers? - Most of the main areas before bosses have been developed to knock off hackers with infinite hp, but they're a very small portion of the community and it isn't likely that you'll encounter one. Over all the time I've played I fought 1 hacker in the undead crypt. He ran at me with infinite hp and I shot him off the cliff using a giant arrow.
This is a 100% purchase for people who want to be tested on their ability. When you start a quick suggestion is to think "Hey what type of class do I want my person to be?" Look up some guides for things like that. I also suggest a PARRY GUIDE. Especially for those people who love dual wield. Becoming good at parrying helps a lot (not for bosses though).
Notes: Take your time. And there is one difficulty : DIFFICULT  But you'll get use to it quite fast.
and in the words of Illidan, if you are not ready to experience a skill-check as well as having a fullfilling satisfaction then...
"YOU ARE NOT PREPARED!"  And prepare to die... and have fun!

I love this game. It was a huge breath of fresh air in a market of dusty, gritty post apocalypses, and while the main cast is only 3 characters, never have they felt so real. It's some of the best of the best, a delicious mix of quality voice acting, design, and animation/motion capture. Watching Pigsy waddle makes my day every time I see him. And that's where the heart of the game is, to me. The characters take the spotlight here. That said, the game is very linear, and the climbing sequences, while often breathtaking, have very clear quided paths. It's also a relatively short playthrough, somewhere around 8 hours, and it definitely feels like there were some missing scenes that got cut out (maybe it's just me, but don't worry, the story still holds up well). Despite this, I still loved every second of it. I can't fully explain how much I loved watching Monkey and Trip traverse their world, and it contains some of my favorite settings of all the games I've played. This is coming from someone who just stops and stares at wonders both virtual and natural, no matter my schedule. I found the combat to be fun, though simple, and moves can be unlocked/upgraded by finding orbs throughout the game.
It's fine as far as ports go, but like many, it suffers from unclear controls. You'll probably have to look online to figure out how to counter, for example, which is something you'd think developers would have learned to deal with by now. Perhaps most sadening is that this game was clearly designed with sequels in mind. The ending is solid, so it's not a debilitating cliffhanger, but it's a crying shame this game didn't get the attention it so deserved. Hopefully we can send a big enough message of support via Steam that they'll pick up where the left off. Hey, naive hope for sequels is like, half of what being a gamer's about, right?

Like many others I overlooked this game when it was released on consoles several years ago. I simply love anything with a post-apocalyptic theme so it is somewhat odd that it has taken until now for me to get stuck into this. The storyline is based very loosely on the novel 'Journey to the West' written by Wu Cheng'en. But unlike the original story that is set in a fantasy version of ancient China, Enslaved is set 150 years into the future following a global war, with only the remnants of humanity left along with mechs left over from the conflict.
What is refreshing though is that coupled with the damsel in distress angel, the world after the war is actually beautiful to look at. The usual reliance on a grey and brown colour pallete is not here, instead Ninja Theory have taken a different approach and the world hums with light and colour. The ruined city of New York, now decayed and destroyed has been taken back by nature (think of the documentary 'Life After People' and you've got the idea). The games great art style is not restricted to the scenery, as the characters are also pleasing to the eye, especially during the cutscence sequences.
The game is a mostly linear experience that is heavily narrative driven, but this is combined with good action/adventure and platforming mechanics. If you're familiar with console games like Uncharted, you'll be familiar with the formula here. Get from A to B, fight a few monsters, climb on some buildings/structures along your way and deal with the occasional boss.
So go on and buy it! It's worth the asking price.

Key word: Frustrating.
I tried so hard to like this game. I really did. However, I've never come across a port which makes a game so frustratingly unplayable.
At first it had everything I'd normally love in a game - Breaktaking visuals, a gripping plot from the beginning and a feeling of freedom and fluidity in the movement and combat which is great (despite linear pathing and encounters). Also some of the best voice acting I've come across from a game in a while. The thing that lets it down is the actual 'game' part of it.
As many people here have mentioned, this is a port from the xbox. After half an hour of playing around with the mouse sensitivity controls, I accepted that it didn't have a setting which made it usable. A slight twitch and you're aiming the other side of the area, but somehow the mechs still run faster than your deaccelerated aim mode, making the turret sections frustratingly difficult. Further than this, the camera controls have a life of their own and you'll be fighting for control the entire time while being ripped apart by the enemies. Combine this with long checkpoint respawns and having to run around to the ends of the map every time to collect the tech orbs for an ultimate grind.
On top of this the port has a number of unpatched bugs, which left me stranded on a pole on the side of the building, unable to jump around a corner no matter what I try or how many times I reloaded (still not sure how I made it past after 30 minutes). The developers didn't even update the control guidelines for the PC, so every time I learned I new move, I had to minimise the game to google the equivilent PC controls.
Conclusion:
Seems like it could be a great game on the xbox. However, worst port of any game I've ever come across onto PC, making the game unplayable, frustrating and hindered by gamebreaking bugs. DO NOT buy for PC.

There are some games that are breathtaking from the moment you open them up. They are visually stunning and they engage with you mechanically in a way that is visceral and immediate. Journey, Transistor and Bastion are all games like that for me. Then there are games that excite you conceptually. They are minimal offerings but what they lay bare is so creatively exciting that it brings a smile to your face. This smile persists even while the narrative unfolds in melancholic tones. The experience is one of beauty and sadness as so intrinsically related. Gone Home, Papers Please, and Emily is Away are games that have felt like this for me. Emily is Away brilliantly captures all the ineptitude of adolescent and early adult relationships in a digital age where connection is so easy, but so fragile. From the limited response options, to the fumbling way in which each message is crafted, deleted and recrafted, the game captures the anxious experience of trying to love, be loved, express love, care, whatever. The game is also clever in the way it aligns your expectations as a video game 'player' with the hopes and aspirations of your avatar. You, the player, actually want to win Emily over, because you believe it aligns with some notion of 'winning' in a sense external to the game. I cannot wait to try to win Emily over again and to be heartbroken and reminded of all my past mistakes once more.

We all know what made Homeworld great. We all know Gearbox made a visually stunning remaster. What needs to be said now is what Gearbox did to make the remaster a disappointment. While the following things may sound petty, they fundamentally change how the game is played and the emotional tenor of the story:
-removing formations
-removing stances
-removing fuel for strike craft
-reworking repair mechanics (repairing is now not feasible in combat, it's more meant for between battles)
-making diffculty scaling much more aggressive
-replacing the ballistic simulation for random number generation combat
Homeworld was always a story of disempowerment. Of overcoming long odds at the brink of genocide. You were perenially starved for resources, and forced to be extremely careful when shepherding your tiny little fleet. Put your craft into evasive mode and they'll live longer. Put them into aggressive mode and they'll kill faster. Use your support craft to keep expensive ships alive from mission to mission. Use the almost Napoleonic wall formation to concentrate firepower, but don't try complex maneuvers with it. The level of care you had to put into your fleet assets, great and small, contributed a lot to the overall feel of the game.
Now, stances have been removed. Formations have no effect, and fall apart the moment your ships enter combat. Fuel for strike craft has been removed. Support ships are now so unwieldy and take so long to engage that they are only useful outside of combat. Individually these changes wouldn't be so bad, but taken together they rob Homeworld's story of it's gravitas, and it's gameplay of almost all its depth.
It's hard to care about your fleet because your ships are now throwaway items, and honestly there isn't much for you to do with them other than throw them at the enemy fleet and designate targets. What was once a game of tactics and risk management has been reduced to a laser light show. Pretty, but ultimately there isn't much for you to do but sit back and watch.
If you want a pretty game with all the familiar sights and sounds from the Homeworld we played back in 1999, then this fits the bill. If you want a game that captures either the spirit or the tactical depth of the original, then sadly you should look somewhere else.

Let me preface this eith saying that I have never played half-life or half-life 2 before this point, so the way I am reviewing this game is as if this is the original version of the game. Honestly, I have come out very very mixed about it. This is the first game on source where I have had slow down (I'm on a notebook) which has made the game extremely hard to play at some points. Another thing, for other laptop users with integrated cards, your game will be very dark, like you can't see at all. Even with the flashlight, so get out a pen and write down these two command prompts that need to be inputted on every start up so you can even see: "mat_hdr_level 2" and "mat_tonemapping_occlusion_use_stencil 1". The first level is extremely interesting as the beginning only has you adventuring around Gordon's work with a few things here and there to play with (Though I wish there was more than three voice actors for the place), but after some strange experiment goes way wrong aliens are everywhere and they want to eat your face. What's cool is the whole first area is going backwards through the intro, but now everything is on fire and alien zombie things want to eeat you. I found it very interesting that your initial weapons are a security gaurd and flares. I doubt it was in the original, but the whole throwing flares at the zombies thing is cool. Ok, so then you're given a crowbar, and it feels awful. I have never been able to hit a headcrab without the ♥♥♥♥er hitting me first. The range is so tiny for being a long tool to pry things, and the hitbox is so tiny it's hard to be effective with it. I can see why half-life is often regarded as having amazing level design, sometimes the places feel too open, as the game never really gives you feedback on whether or not you're doing the right thing. There is wuite a charm to that, but it gets frustrating after walking in circles for several minutes trying to find which way to go, or where the one button is to get to the next area. Also, holy balls, is this game hard! I set it to normal initially, but I brought it down to easy after the first encounter with the marines. It feels like every encounter you need all your health and armor to have a chance to survive, but there's not enough pickups, and recharge stations (especially for the suit) are rare. I get that this stuff is more of a retro design, and there is a lot to be appreciated here, but it all just feels really clunky.
I feel like there is a really deep story they tries to make, but like 90% of the dialogue is missing cuz all I know is kill aliens and marines, find lambda lab place. There's so much in the middle I'm missing, like what the hell is the scary tentacle monster sitting under the rocket? how did it get there? Why are these aliens so diverse? What is Xen? Why do these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s want to kill us? Why do these alian ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s want to kill us? Why are the Marines doing a cover up operation? Why do two random psychopath soldiers disobey their orders to kill me? Why is half the facility flooded? The list goes on. I noticed that sometimes the marines say stuff before an encounter starts, but it hardly fills in what is going on.
The shooting is standard "arcadey" no aim down sights kind of style, which I like, but you can get mowed down so quick it playes more like a stop and pop shooter and those goddamn marines are so strong and move fast, then later assassin ladies are intriduced that kill you way faster and jump around and are tiny. The aliens are only slightly easier and I actually have a lot of fun fighting them instead. They feel varied, and all their attacks are melee or projectile (instead of hitscan automatic fire) For instance in the variance there's little headcrabs that lunge at you and the big cousin zombies which are slower, but take more hits. There's barnacles that pull you up with their tongues, and weird explodey dog guys. One of them is an acid spitting lizard and there's a scary fish monster that shows up from time to time. And that's just scratching the surface. With the aliens I feel like theres a lot of options for combat and different weapon choices are more effective than others for different guys. With the soldiers it's mp5 and grenade spamming to hope you don't die.
Overall I think it's a game worth checking out. I am about 8 hours in and am far from finishing what they have I think. The shoehorned physics puzzles here and there bother me, and the overall experience is clunky at best and downright infuriating at worst. Get it on sale as a good weekend romp. As for me, I'm done with this game... It's just so hard and I just want to see the story through at this point more than the mediocre combat or the admittedly interesting set pieces.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for The Journey Down: Chapter 3 by SkyGoblin.
Well folks, we’ve officially arrived at the conclusion to The Journey Down. Chapter 3 picks up where chapter 2 left off with Bwana, Kito and Lina arriving in the underland. While there, they uncover the Armando Power Company’s true plot and thus set out on a journey to stop them. Bwana and Kito return to St. Armando and team up with a band known as the Resistance Rockers while Lina stays in The Underland to stop the power company’s mining.
This chapter was highly entertaining and it was definitely the funniest chapter of the 3. One thing that’s worth mentioning is that because of the original composer having died during the development 2 (Which sucks) this chapter has a very different feel music wise. It’s still very good but a lot of the Afro-Caribbean feel is lost in this chapter.
The game’s graphics are as gorgeous as ever and it’s unique hand drawn 2D backgrounds mixed with it’s 3D characters are very impressive to look at. I especially loved the backgrounds for The Underland. I also really liked the 1980’s style cyberpunk theme that was used for St. Armando. It added to the rather bleak outlook that the game took on and it fit the story very well.
Puzzle wise they were slightly more difficult this time around. Mostly because there were multiple areas for both St. Armando and The Underland which made finding some of the items a bit more difficult since they weren’t overly obvious. They weren’t too difficult to figure out but I recommend searching everywhere possible and in every nook and cranny.
Overall, The Journey Down Chapter 3 was a very entertaining end to a great journey. It was the culmination of the many years of work that went into making the series and while the music was slightly different, it features a great story and likable characters. I highly recommend playing the previous games before this one to get the most out of it. If you’re a fan of point and click adventure games like myself, I highly recommend this series, it’s pretty epic.

Managing to improve upon just about every aspect of the original title, Dishonered 2 is a gem of a game.
The story continues years after the setting of the first, Emily has grown up and become the empress, and Corve is by her side, helping her rule. Then some story stuff happens and its time for a grand new adventure of magic (If you feel like it), assassinations (If you feel like it), Stealth (If you feel, you know what you get the gist).
This time you have the choice between two different characters with different spells. This opens up to even more approaches to different instances which is of course what Dishonered was so well known and appreciated for.
The story is great, like in the first game your choices have a real weight and impact. You feel as if the desicions you make concerning the characters both big and small are reflected continiously throughout the story. I usually go for low-chaos, no kill, ghost kinds of playthroughs and in this game it was both extremely enjoyable and challenging.
The arsenal has been expanded with more diverse enemies and more diverse weapons. The foes known as "Clockwork Soldiers" can give you a proper spooking the first time they catch you sneaking around, they have different patterns of behaviour and are signifigantly harder to dispatch of if you do not know your way around them, literally.
Refrain from watching any playthroughs before playing through this game, i know it is EXTREMELY tempting but there are so many solutions to the levels that will be absolutely spoiled if you just watch a Lets Play! I get it, the levels can be tough but that is no excuse for just picking the easy way out. This game is about trial and error. And some more error, and a bit more error to boot. Now i know this is not Dark Souls "Git gud" but this game is still about you making your own way through a hostile, dangerous and outright murderous city. Make it your own.
I personally enjoyed the story, seeing it as a viable continiouation of my own choices in the original game. Some might not feel like this, but this is your own story, not theirs. I throughoutly enjoyed Dishonered 2 and i would recommend it to anyone who enjoy Stealth games, and if you just like games in general you ought to atleast play through the level known as "A Crack in The Slab" which is a masterpiece from my point of view. I do wish to stress that not everyone can run this game. I was able to complete it on a 7 year old computer with some lag.
Craft your own story in the boots of Corvo or Emily. When you are done, catch up with me over some whiskey and cigars. Have fun!

I was curious about this game and tried it during a free to play weekend. I was excited to try it because I've logged nearly 500 hours into Skyrim, and ESO is often described as "Skyrim Online".
The Good:
The game really is beautiful. The character create screen provides a ton of customization options and I enjoyed modifying my high elf exactly how I wanted her. The soundtrack is also great. The gameplay, however...
The Bad:
The UI is a mess. No minimap. Action bars only pop up if you are in combat although they can be set to always show. The alt button is used a lot and is a bit clumsy to reach, it feels like Tab would have been a better selection. The character screen "C" is confusing and not intuitive, I found myself trying to fish around to find what I was looking for. Speaking of , the skills themselves are confusing - why am I leveling class skills and weapon skills and armor skills and somehow it has nothing to do with my level yet is more important...yeah I lost track. For some reason you can immediately get a bounty on your head when you're dropped in Tamriel after the starting experience. I had a restoration staff equipped and cast it at my party member because I was curious if it'd heal him. It hit an NPC, guards were after me, he tried to help, guards were after him...we ended up paying off bounties even though we just started the game. The starting story wasn't very engaging. I didn't feel like I was immersed in Tamriel, and found myself not really caring what NPCs said and blowing through their text to (maybe) get a quest marker. Combat PvE was okay, but nothing special. I could kill stuff without too much difficulty. Combet PvP though, in a duel, was laughable. Again, my party member and I tried dueling each other just to see how that worked. We were both sorcerers who had taken the first point in each class tree. We were unable to damage each other before health regenerated and ended up watching both of our familiars shock each other impotently. Somehow that was the most amusing thing to watch.
I really tried to give this game a fair shake, and really wanted to enjoy it. Unfortunately, I was unable to and do not recommend this title to others.

Such a fun game to play around in, reminds me a lot of the old Star Wars Battlefront 2 game and the pure chaos that happened all the time. Some of the issues that have been swimming around have been fixed like kicking yourself in the foot till you die (i wanted that to stay ;-;) and bot gernade spam can be switched off by changing AI weapons. The gameplay itself is a blast with fun ragdoll physics, how every bot does something, how explosions happen everywhere, everything is just fun to me. With new content being developed by the commumity, there is seemingly no end to the shenanigans that can be had.
Although I do have some minor gripes about the game. Firstly is the aiming, for anyone who has played the game will tell you (or looked closely at youtubers using snipers), aiming is done in increments. This means trying to snipe someone from across the map is a lot more difficult as sometimes the foe is between these increments in which you can aim, forcing the player to move their character from side to side to get that final inch needed to hit the target. This is my biggest issue with the game and it really needs to be fixed. Next is the ragdoll physics which are very good already. The issues I have with them are minor and involve how they end up folding in on themselves, especially when killed in one shot. I personally find it more entertaining using a workshop SMG to get kills as the gun kills in more hits and makes the ragdolls more entertaining to look at (anyone with me on this?). Lastly there is the AI in vehicles, sometimes they will run you over or get stuck on things, I assume this will be fixed in the future but I'm including it in this review.

Best game I have played in all year (and probably one of my favorites of all time!). As an Alien fan this game caught my attention since it was announced, and I bought it as soon as I could.  I played it through in Nightmare mode (sort of as a challenge to myself). Sure it was painfully difficult (not as much as DS2 though), and frustrating sometimes, but the gameplay, plot and suspense made it an enjoyable experience. Will definetely replay it to complete the achievements and might even buy the DLC. 10/10 (would bang)

For the most part, I throughly enjoyed this game. Even though I have only actually watched Alien, it was obvious this game was designed to give you an authentic Alien horror expeirence. Personally I didn't find this game to be too scary (but I can definetly see why it would scare others), only a few things made my heart race, but I still throughly enjoyed myself overall.
Without spoiling anything, the game's story is set 15 years after Alien, and is very well written, well worth the time you have to put in. However, I was disappointed by the ending, which was most likley set up to sell a sequel or DLC, which is a shame considering the rest of the game was so good.
While I did enjoy the game play, and thought most of the mechanics were very well done, I did find parts of this game to be either repetative or enraging. It became rather tedious to have to constantly hide for long periods of time while you were only supposed to be moving across small areas. The amount of save points in the game make it obvious that you're going to die a lot, and that's exactly what happens. If it wasn't the Alien it was the damn creepy androids. The sheer amount of deaths, usually in specific areas of the game, did tend to take away from the experience the game was trying to provide.
Finally, the video game the franchise deserves.  This was a labour or Love.  Brilliant recreation of set pieces from the original movie.

Factorio is an amazingly deep and fun game. When you start out it is pretty simple, but when you start making giant mega-assembly lines you learn that every square is important. I've put numerous hours into it pre-Steam so far and have loved every moment. It is lovingly made and there are weekly blogs by the developers.

The game is a never ending stream of satisfaction, while still getting to use your brain to its fullest with gameplay never getting old, ever.
It's an endless pursuit of building, unlocking, crafting, improving, and always trying to make your productions more efficient/faster/bigger/higher yielding, all while having to constantly protect yourself and all your carefully crafted constructions and manufacturing lines from the Zerg whose numbers seem to keep increasing. You can never, ever forget to continue to keep up with defense and weapon tech or you'll slowly become overwhelmed over time.
You've played many games with systems that sound like this, but honestly nothing compares to this game. It's on another level and still manages to be extremely fun.
You'll always want to be more efficient with your building and manufacturing not for the sake of being efficient because who really cares honestly, but because you need MORE THINGS FASTER! EVERYTHING, MORE! NOW! When your inefficient hastily thrown together setup is becoming bottlenecked in various places and thus isn't making your flying robots nearly fast enough to satisfy your deep, angry hunger to see what the robots actually look like in action, it'll send you on a quest to improve each step of your manufacturing setup over several hours where you'll forget you were even making robots to begin with. From the outside you may see "tedious", but when you're on the inside, it's "adventure". You discover yourself what you need to do to fix one problem, one at a time without even meaning to. Endless discovery.
Highly recommend playing with a group of friends. After 15 hours or so you really start to get a real sense of what it must be like to run a company or manufacturing plant with so many moving parts. Get enough people together in a server and I'm sure you could simulate the insanity that is managing the LHC.
You make a server with 3-4 friends.
One friend decides to set up Iron Plate production and mining while everyone is off doing other things.
After 10 hours, you realize you've always had a steady supply of Iron Plates, Steel Plates, and Copper Plates coming in to help you build your chemical plants and batteries, but you really have no idea how the Plates are being made or are even getting to you. All you know is your friend would occasionally ask if you needed some, so he would bring you materials in the form of a conveyor belt whose path you would modify to fit into your automation you're working on, and it's working very well! You're well on your way to making robots..... But never mind how all these materials are getting to me from my friend.. How did I learn to make robots in the first place?
You realize your other friend has been unlocking new technology all this time with a lab setup, so you go to check it out and discover he has spent all this time setting up an automated lab researching process with 3 different products all being automatically manufactured and poured into the labs.. And guess what's being fed down there as well? Your other friends Plates, and your own Batteries and other things (since he needed some and you were like, oh I won't just give you some batteries, I'm going to give you an entire endless line of batteries). All while another friend has been managing a conveyor belt full of coal that circles every piece of equipment that uses coal, thus keeping all the machines operational, and loops back around for excess, where it is periodically stored into containers. And managing electricity grids. And turrets. Defenses. Exploring when you need more materials (stones, jfc). Killin Zerg any way you can... Or constantly trying to run away.
This is just the best. That's all it is. The best.
As far as Early Access goes, haven't had it crash once. Haven't run into any weird bugs yet.
Cons?
Only one. In multiplayer, the entire game pauses and waits for the person joining to download the map before resuming. If the person joining has a very low download speed, this usually equates to a having enough time to make a sandwich and some coffee for the group. A smoke break if that's your thing. Not too much of a bad thing really, but it would be great if the game could continue to function while the new player downloaded the map.
We are.. 20 hours in or so into our map? And I still don't think we're anywhere near being able to build a rocketship. But we do finally have little flying robots repairing our base now!

Was honestly hoping for a better game. After seeing this game on so many "top 10 most underrated games" and "top 10 games nobody played" lists, I had high hopes. While it wasn't bad, it was really just a little better than average. First off, the good. The story is semi-interesting and the character development and bond between the two characters is fun to watch. The voice and acting is good. The graphics are solid, except for some problems with shadows and shading (had nothing to do with my top of the line comp). The combat could have been much better. You use a light and heavy attack. But unlike god of war or most 3rd person action games, there are no combos. You literally just hit with all light, all heavy, or mix them, but any mixture of the two always comes out the same. You can use a stun attack and a wide attack to move everyone back. You also get a special attack from hitting people, although there is no meter or way to know how it is progressing. You have all that within the first hour. You literally gain nothing else all game. There is an evade attack where you just evade and attack, pretty boring. The game includes a counter ability, but it is the single worst in any game ever. It doesn't even work. You have to be blocking and then press a button at the right time, but the button takes you out of block and gets you hurt. I tried it like 10 times and it never once worked. The upgrade system is boring too. You get increased health, shields, better shooting damage, and thats about it. There is nothing interesting. There are collectible masks but they basically don't do anything besides show a random picture.
The other biggest problem is the enemies. The entire game you fight like 4 different (but basically same looking) robots. They have no personality, don't talk, and have no incentive or agenda. There is no entity you are fighting against. So the fighting is uninteresting because the enemies never change and you don't care about them. Fighting endless silent robots the entire game just takes away the fun. The game also doesn't describe the world at all. There are 3 total people the entire game, and it is never explained why. Why were there all these robots with no masters, who controls them, where are people, what has happened......none of it explained. There have been positive things said about the post-apocolyptic setting, and its ok. It doesn't feel real or lived in like the last of us. It is a bunch of same looking worn down buildings with green moss on them, thats about it. You are among buildings, in a scrapyard, in a ramshackle town, and in a facility. That's basically it. I didn't find any of them that impressive. The camera zooms in too closely in combat and it is hard to see when people are about to attack you, which is annoying. Another caveat is Trip. Instead of making her like Elle from the last of us, they make here way too feminine and damsel in distress. She needs help all the time, even making you carry her up this tiny ledge she can easily climb. She spends most of the time crying and yelling when enemies attack, even if it is you fighting them and she is nowhere near them, she'll just scream and wail because you are fighting. It gets super annoying and she's so helpless and whiny I felt like she was dakota fanning from War of the Worlds.
The platforming is kind of fun, but it is super linear. You jump from one shiny rung or foothold to another. You never have to aim or do anything besides just continually hammer jump, its not like "drakes uncharted" where you feel accomplished or like it actually took skill. Sometimes the platforming doesn't work. You will be by the edge and just roll forward against an invisible wall, because you weren't at the perfect spot to trigger the jump sequence, which makes it feel even more linear and hands-off. The game does provide good length though. The DLC is fun and a change of pace, although pigsy is made to be way too slow getting over things, activating abilities, and getting in and out of cover. It does introduce you to the best character of the game, Truffles, who is baller. The ending was sad and the most heartbroken I have been in a game in a while. As for enslaved as a whole, if the upgrade system wasn't boring as hell, the combat had variation or something more than using the same weapon with the same 2 attacks for 8 hours, and weren't fighting the same boring 4 machines with no personality, I would recommend it higher. Right now, 7/10.

I wanted to play this game, since I'd heard about it years ago when it first came out on consoles. Years later, it's on PC and I thought "Well I gotta buy it and play it now". Having bought and played the game I find it unremarkable in many ways and infuriating in others.
- Graphics are beautiful, not 100% outstanding but beautiful nonetheless.
- Excellent atmosphere, sci-fi post apocalyptic setting with a likeable main character.
- The motherfncking camera. You will know no hate like the hate for the camera during combat.
- The combat is either boring or frustrating or both. It's unimaginative and at times it even feels very laggy with its inputs.
- The controls are somehow, for the most part responsive when in combat but terrible during the platforming sections.
- Sometimes the game likes to restrict certain actions in certain zones of the given areas. For instance there are numerous sections where you can't run or roll and are forced to walk. This restriction is a major annoyance.
- Inconsistent platforming boundaries where at times you can jump what seems like an enormous gap and other times you can't even jump down a ledge to the ground directly below you.
- Powerful supporting characters in cutscenes only, during gameplay though they suck. I'm looking at you Pigsy, who one shots some robots in cutscenes but during gameplay he misses constantly.
- The story is slightly uninteresting with an inconsistent tone throughout.
- The headband feature, in early game makes sense but in late game makes absolutely no sense whatsoever. I understand why it's there in the early game as it forces Monkey into helping Trip return to her home. Having this feature in late game absolutely makes no sense as she'd gained Monkey's trust by then. This feature should've been gradually lessened to the point of non-existence by the end of the game.
- Uncalled for or crude jokes left me scoffing at the inclusion of them.
Now I'll say this it's not a bad game in any way, shape or form but it's highly unremarkable and non-memorable. It has an inconsistent tone throughout the entire game which undermines the story it's trying to tell. It loves to disable certain actions until specific areas which can lead to frustration. The story has so many unexplained events for my tastes. I often hear that it's underrated but I found it a tad mediocre, fun at times frustrating at other but mediocre throughout.

Oh yeah! This is the real deal! It feels just like HL1 but with all the visuals and appearances of a highly polished HL2 and then some. It is a must-have for any Half-Life enthusiast and a serious recommendation for anyone enjoying the genre.
I have played the original HL game multiple times. And I also enjoyed the whole anthology with Blue Shift and Opposing Forces. I call myself a huge fan of the whole Half-Life series. So I had high hopes that Black Mesa might ease the pain for never being able to play HL3 because, let's be honest to ourselves and face it: it will never come. Not from Valve Software and not from any other studio either. Ever.
Man was I lost in admiration of the job Crowbar Collective (the people behind Black Mesa) have done! This is how HL1 should have been all along. Not only did I play the game and re-live all my fond memories of the original game but stand around and simply enjoy the looks of this game. I was never happier on the money spent for a game. Such love for details! I felt like a tourist coming back to his favorite vacation destination just to see things without the visual restrictions from former visits.
I've seen youtube videos of people playing mods that show the Xen levels ported to the HL2 engine. And I see how Black Mesa differs from simply copying the maps from HL1 into HL2. There is a huge difference. Black Mesa ist re-envisioning HL1 and building it from the ground up! To me this seems to be the crucial element that makes playing Black Mesa so much more enjoyable than simply playing a HL2 mod offering a HL1 with better graphics. It is the atmosphere that Black Mesa reenacts so it feels even more genuine than the original game. A truly great feat to pull off! And I'm sure having so many of the original speakers participating in the creation of this truly remarkable remake adds yet another layer to its already high quality.
Sadly I only have the publicly available screenshots of the Xen levels to drool over since the team has decided to give the finalization of these levels more time and publish them in 2018 instead of December 2017. But since these levels will surely include a major improvement on the look & feel as well as the intended atmosphere and gameplay compared to the original game like the rest of Black Mesa already demonstrates, the time we must wait will most definitely be worth it.
Kudos to Crowbar Collective for an amazing, captivating and most convincing remake! I couldn't have asked for a better Half-Life game even if I had had the chance to ask for anything besides Half-Life 3.

A progress bar/percentage would have helped me pace myself since some levels take less than an hour and some take several hours.
It took me 21 hours to get to the end of Lambda Core on normal difficulty. I can't wait for Xen to be released. I'm going to play Opposing Force in the meantime...

A game for Torgue fans everywhere.
So, before i mention about performance i will gladly list the important parts of my pc specifications.
An AMD FX-8350
An Asrock 970 extreme 4
An Asus strix GTX 970
16gb of RAM
Note the amount of ram. This game has horrible memory leak issues so you'll definitely want 16 gigs or more. However with these specs i get 60 fps average on highest settings. Sometimes it'll be at 90 sometimes it'll go as low as 35 if a nuke was fired at 3+ explosive chaos objects. It's always at a playable frame rate.
So, this game is fun. Stupid, crazy fun and it looks gorgeous to boot. You fly around blowing up whoever you please with minimal consequence. You'll get shot out of the sky if you're slow enough. But you shouldn't ever be going slow.
It's fun going around dropping C4 (which you have infinite of) onto police and chaos objects in an unliberated town and watching the guards and army trying to shoot you out of the sky. Or grappling 5 people to a large spherical fuel tank then rolling said fuel tank into a statue of the dictator. The more gimmicks you use, the more exciting it gets. Try tethering 6 people onto an attack helicopter then attaching c4 onto those 6 people. Then, drop those 6 people onto a base and blow them all sky high. Infinite fun.
You unlock gadgets and weapons by liberating towns and bases (the little bases and towns can get a little repetitive) and by completing challenges. It's all a lot of fun.
I'd recommend it to those with a system capable of playing it. Otherwise you're left with sadness and unresponsive help staff.

The third, and last, chapter to The Journey Down has finally been released! After four to seven years since the first chapter was released as freeware and later onto Steam. With the wait of the last chapter spanning for three years, the epic conclusion of The Journey Down is finally upon us!
Like before, we come in a little bit after the events of the last chapter. When we left Bwana, Kito, and Lina just arrived at the Underland and sailed in after opening the entrance. It has been quite a while as we see all the various locations they sailed, hiked, and climbed through. Later coming across a temple that reveals that an ancient society lived in the Underland. And, sadly, they come across mining areas set up by Armando Power Company. Before going into this installment, I do recommend either replaying the previous chapters or looking up what happened as no one gives a recap.
Most of the mining areas are abandoned just so they can mine one part faster. Lina, suspecting that this will spell disaster, sends off Bwana and Kito to travel up by the bucket chain while she stays behind in the Underland. Once you get ready and jump onto the bucket chain, you arrive at St. Armando, more specifically the very place Bwana and Kito grew up in. There you see how the situation has escalated. In the previous chapter, corruption was obvious to everyone at Port Artue; here everyone in the working class either has been evicted or threatened to be evicted with many areas having their electricity turned off. Many are protesting, but that is not stopping anything. As always, it is up to Bwana and Kito to help one of the groups prominent in rebelling: The Resistance Rockers.
We also get to play as Lina, who is at the Underland. I rather not ruin anything that happens here, as it is towards the end of the game, other than there is a major reveal.
This time around, the puzzles were not focused on, as the story took most of it. This ends up to be that the puzzles are very easy. None of them make you scratch your head, or at least for long, as the solution is obvious. The only time you will get stumped if you are missing an item. This understandably brings the playtime down as the puzzles are so obvious that the story goes by fast. In terms of puzzles, this last chapter is weakest.
We get a mix of new characters and old characters. So of course, how is the new talent compared to the returning talent? They all bring in the same quality that has been present, some bringing in more comedy. The sound quality throughout is better, except in one area. A returning character in Lina’s section yells at one point, and it sounds like they tried to make her sound like she’s yelling without trying to kill headphone users...it made it worse.
The Journal of the Journey Down does not seem too important. Lina seems to already know everything that was in the book. And even then, it was not really needed to infiltrate the Underland as by the time we get there, we see that the Armando Company already built equipment and started mining areas. There is also the scene that showed the Armando Power Company boss somehow got the book, but did not show a scene that explained this. Though Lina carried on like the journal was not needed, so maybe they should of copied the pages with the map and hid the journal somewhere. It really just seemed to only be helpful in terms of bringing back Deities and the maps it provides if you decide to enter without an aircraft.
This also goes into how little we actually are in the Underland. We spent two chapters building up to this, but we only stay for two chapters of the story. It felt like there was more they wanted to show us that was not just in cutscenes. It does go in the same pattern of still mostly playing in a civilization, but there is a reveal that happens later with Lina that could have worked better if Bwana and Kito did not leave.
One of the weird changes was the soundtrack. Going for more of a rock and roll sound, going with the Resistant Rockers group, with a hint of Jazz here and there. This seems like a random change considering the first two chapters predominantly showcased Jazz. Though this does not mean the soundtrack is bad by any means. It still was mostly pleasing and really only one cliche track that played twice towards the end that sounded out of place from the other tracks.
+ Good conclusion
+ Cutscenes look better
+ Visuals
+ Sountrack
+ Good use of callbacks
+/- Easy puzzles
+/- Little time spent in the Underland
- Some dialogue seems to not of been put in correctly
- Some parts did seem rushed
The trilogy has finally been completed after many years in the making. The Journey Down: Chapter Three concluded the series in a way that was great. Despite some rushed parts and not focusing much on puzzles, the ending scene is unforgettable. Even bringing in some callbacks to chapter one that was included pretty well. Overall, I loved the series even though it may not have been perfect all the time. I do recommend this, but only if you liked the previous chapters as you will, obviously, need to have played those to understand how everything escalated.
