I have never like MOBAs, however Smite is a definite exception to the rule! Here are a few reasons why:
- Its content is much more 'free' than most free-to-play games i.e most MMOs, as you can unlock every single God without spending a penny!
- The third-person view, which is unusual for a MOBA, works very well and really makes you feel more connected to your character.
- Use of the WASD keys allows you to dodge enemy Gods' moves easier than a game which is just 'click to move'.
- You can jump!
- There is a God whose ultimate is releasing kittens! (Bastet) :)
- Each God really feels different to the next.
- The diversity of games and maps is great!
- There are regular updates.
- Every day there is a daily special game/map which is very different to the normal ones.
- And much, much more...
For those who want to hear possible negatives, then I really can't think of many, apart from:
- The community. This is a big issue, although not one Hi-Rez Studios can help. When starting off playing Smite, you probably will be called a 'noob' and reported for feeding several times. Quite a few more 'experienced' players, when matched with new players, are constantly harrassing the chat with depressing comments. However do not fear! You can block these players, report them for harrassment, and once you have practised a lot you might be a better player than the harrassers, able to defend the 'noobs'. I have found that the most harrassing happens on conquest, so maybe don't play on this map until you are more experienced.
Overall I would definitely recommend this game. The tutorials at the start can be slightly boring, however bear witht them and when you start playing it gets really fun!

I have the unpopular opinion that this game is not worth the investment, but I shall do my best to explain why. Enslaved is beautiful in graphics only. While the setting of the game is glorious, the story itself is lacking. There are several plot holes, which lack any detailed explanation, and to top it off: it’s consistent use of gender roles is insulting to both men and women. Had there been more thought put into the development of this game, I would recommend it in a heartbeat, but in my opinion it lacks tact and was not at all thought through.
The story is set in a post-apocalyptic future, although what happened to the Earth was never properly analyzed nor explained. While this fault alone can be disregarded, the fact that the entire story revolves around one young womans crusade against slavers by the means of her enslaved “Monkey” man proves more difficult to ignore. Basically, the female protagonist is a huge hypocrite who cannot take care of herself and requires the aid of a big strong man. As if the two main characters horribly written fate isn’t enough, the third character that they add in only accents the fact that the woman is viewed as a piece of incompetent meat.
There’s nothing particularly wrong with the gameplay itself, if you are the brawler type. Nor is there anything that is innovated, or outside the box. It is a pretty generic, run of the mill creation. The only bit that is even remotely interesting is the skills distribution, and even then, it’s pretty standard.
The targeting is extremely awkward, which adds an unintended level of difficulty. Apart from that, the controls are also rather generic, and there’s nothing more to say about them.
Phenomenal. In all honesty, the aesthetics of this game are pretty much its strongest selling point. It is an absolutely visually stunning game, with scenery that is worth taking in. Props for an awesome immersive setting.

Black Mesa is a remake of Valve's critically acclaimed, industry changing game, Half-Life. Following the protagonist Gordon Freeman as he tries to escape the ruins of the Black Mesa research facility after an experiment goes horribly, horribly wrong. With puzzles, aliens, and one mean military standing in your way, you will have to defy all odds in order to survive.
DISCLAIMER: I have not played the original Half-Life, so this review will be from the POV of a complete outsider, someone who has never played a Half-Life game before. Just letting you know.
Updated Disclaimer: I still haven’t played the original Half-Life, but I have played essentially every Half-Life game spare Blue shift and Decay. That won’t change the outcome of the review though, so meh.
Now, no introduction is really needed here. Black Mesa is a complete remake of the original Half-Life on the more modern source engine (yes, we know there was Half-Life source, but nobody cares about that game ok, shut up). However, it was not created by Valve, it was made by a small indie team called Crowbar Collective. As previously stated, it follows the protagonist, Gordon Freeman, through his attempts to escape the ruins of Black Mesa. However, the player will have to fight against an alien incursion, as well as some more domestic threats, in order to survive.
The graphics for the game, especially when compared to the original, are pretty damn impressive. Although, as most of us know, the Source engine is starting to show its age, the game still stands and looks absolutely amazing in a few sections. No area looks truly dull or bland. The graphics on the NPCS and other props also look quite nice as well. However, these nice looks come as a cost, because you will need a pretty tough pc to run this game with both good looks and high framerates. Even on high-end machines, stutters and slight frame-drops, while not common, do occur every now and then.
The sound design in the game is also very nice. You can tell an enemy from its sounds well before seeing it. NPCS have sounds when they are docile and inactive, and when they are aggressive and want to kill you. A prime example is the HECU soldiers (We'll get to them in more detail in a second). They chat over the radio when the don't see you, and you can even overhear some normal conversations between them. The attention to detail is quite good. And the soundtrack... Oh the soundtrack is just wonderful. Props to Joel Nielsen, he did a brilliant job on this one.
Black Mesa has two core gameplay elements to offer, those being PURE FPS MAYHEM, and puzzle solving/navigation. Enemies will also be touched on as they provide an understandably large amount to the game.
Black Mesa has a variety of weapons for the player to amuse themselves with. These can range from your standard weapons like a MP5 and Glock, to a neurotoxin-filled crossbow and an alien weapon with the most uncomfortable equipping animation in history (the screams, of god the screams). The weapons do have differences between them, meaning that a certain weapon will be much more useful in on particular area than another. I tried to run through them all in an early write-up of this review, but in my opinion, it took up way too much space (645 words of space to be exact).
The puzzles in this game don’t require an IQ of 120 or more, but they aren’t so easy that a toddler can solve them in 2 seconds either. Most of them are a perfect blend of easy enough to not be stressful, but still difficult enough to not be boring. These can range from activating two boilers to cross through a frozen storage sector, to having to fight your way through various marines and aliens for ten minutes just to flick a switch. They give the player a much-needed break from the constant shooter action and let them slow down and just admire their surroundings and put their intellect to the test.

Black Mesa has a very diverse cast of hostiles to fight against. They are all unique and require a different strategy required to deal with each enemy most effectively. Although, of course, later in the game some of these opponents can become more of an annoyance than a challenge to deal with (cough, snarks, cough).
Each hostile lifeform utilizes different tactics to cause you as much pain as possible. Zombies have a simple and not very effective way of damaging you. They stumble towards you until you are a literal arm’s length from them, and will then proceed to slash at you. While it’s very easy to avoid these attacks, they can do a worrying amount of damage, particularly on higher difficulties.
In stark contrast however, lets examine the human marines (or HECU), specially trained forces who have a very wide arrange of toys to make your life not so lively anymore. With sub-machine guns, shotguns, and grenades, a completely different strategy is required to take them out without taking too much damage yourself. They become a fair bit more difficult to deal with later in the game, attacking the player with howitzers, sniper-rifles, one frustrating to deal with Apache helicopter, and a few armoured vehicles to add icing to the enormous cake of doom.
Black Mesa is a very exciting FPS that combines puzzles, shooting, and diversity in location and foe. The graphics truly show what the source engine is capable of and the sound design is simply brilliant. This game is a perfect homage to an industry changing title, and if you are a Half-Life fan in any way, do yourself a favour and pick this game up. You will almost certainly not regret it.
8.7/10

Make no mistake- this is very much a remastering of JUST Homeworld 2, with Homeworld 1 elements thrown in (And Homeworld 1's full complement of campaign and skirmish maps as well). You could say Homeworld 1 has been Shoe-horned in depending on who you ask given the effects of Homeworld 2's engine on a LOT of the Homeworld 1 stuff.
(Formations collapse the moment combat begins, strike craft and corvettes all now act under Homeworld 2's parameters regardless of faction, harvesting and repairing both require direct-connection between ship and target regardless of faction, research now always costs resources regardless of faction, and other changes Homeworld 1 fans might be turned off by. These are all changes that most likely won't be reverted, as they're probably more engine-based issues than design choices.)
So if you're a hardcore fan of Homeworld 1 who either missed Homeworld 2 originally or absolutely hated Homeworld 2... Then stay away- as Homeworld Remastered will most likely only frustrate you.  (OR buy it for access to the classics... But if you're a hardcore fan you probably have the disc version- which honestly isn't hard to get running on Windows 7. Windows 8 I'm not as sure, but I haven't heard of it being much harder.)
Barring that? Homeworld Remastered is a worthy return for the series and does its job well: it honestly makes me excited to see what Gearbox will do for the (hopefully) eventual Homeworld 3. They put a lot of effort into this- and its not just the graphics that show for it.
The skirmish/multiplayer modes are definitely where Remastered shows its differences from Homeworlds 1 and 2 the most- and is the point where most of Gearbox's effort comes to the front. As much as Homeworld 2's engine might 'tarnish' the Homeworld 1 factions- the addition of them and Homeworld 1's maps spices things up considerably. You'll have to re-learn the homeworld 1 factions, since their balance is now completely different, but they match interstingly with the Homeworld 2 factions.
And then there's the AI- at least on Expert difficulty. Homeworld 2 suffered from having incredibly boring skirmish AI- especially compared to Homeworld 1 which actually had some excellent skirmish AI. In terms of quality, Homeworld Remastered's AI falls squarely in the middle- not as good as Homeworld 1's, but practically stellar compared to Homeworld 2's original AI. It definitely seems that Homeworld Remastered's AI is based off of Homeworld 2's original AI- but Gearbox clearly put a lot of work into improving it.
So even though Homeworld Remastered is MUCH more Homeworld 2 than Homeworld 1- its still quite recommendable overall.

In all fairness, The Journey Down doesn't feel like a game from 2017, or perhaps not even from 2007. Having played the prior TJD titles, the lack of visual / environmental detail was striking from the start. Character interactions and perspectival movement through zones looked very tacked on or more likel to be from a game from 10-15 years ago. From the Kickstarter updates, it appeared the company was in some turmoil, which explains the lack of polish. Nevertheless, the end product left a lot to be desired.
The Journey Down is not particularly challenging. One probably needn't be an old school, pixel hunting adventure game expert to breeze through the final game. Puzzles, such as they are, are often glaringly obvious or can be sorted through in relatively short time. This isn't particularly a problem. But in this genre, the puzzle challenges drive the player to observe the game world further, instead of rushing through due to the frankly entry level difficulties of the game.
Dialogues are a bit jarring. Accents are easy enough to get over with - despite being an unconventional feature, African accents were obviously necessary for an Afro noir aesthetic that Skygoblin wanted to set. Still, the affable fool sterotype in Bwana (much like the protagonist in Daedalus'
series, doesn't develop a lot and remains equally dense and  rather boring throughout. Lack of character development is actually a persistent issue throguh the game (and the series). We rarely, if ever, learn anything new about the characters - their moods and loyalties shift with no explanation or setup, feeling rather frivilous.
Music, however, is pretty impressive in this title (as well as the other two games). It is consistently in-theme and executed beautifully, and would possibly deserve a separate purchase if the OST is put on Steam.
Overall, however, TJD doesn't really make the cut. If you've played the prior two games and want to wrap the story up, it would be a choice. But in the recent revival of point & click adventure games (and remastering of some legendary titles like
, The Journey Down definitely struggles to leave a mark.
A Happy conclusion to excellent trilogy!

Perhaps I was too prepared to get involved with the story but, for it's time, I felt the facial animation and dialogue of it's characters only encouraged me to do so. Trip's story was so brilliantly executed, and I really felt for her in the hardship and regrets she suffered. The world is gorgeous and helps to set the tone of the post-apocalyptic world. If anyone has ever walked in summer you will realise how vividly coloured the world really can be, something I felt is lost in other games in favour of a "Nitty, gritty" palette where everything is mixed with grey. But the visuals are beautiful if you can forgive the relatively low-res of the game. Otherwise the combat is decent but repetitive since you face the same enemies again and again and again. But the different contexts and environments you face them in help to spice things up a little. And when you're really into such a beautiful story you can't help but be drawn along. 9/10 if only for lack of more interesting enemies.

I have never like MOBAs, however Smite is a definite exception to the rule! Here are a few reasons why:
- Its content is much more 'free' than most free-to-play games i.e most MMOs, as you can unlock every single God without spending a penny!
- The third-person view, which is unusual for a MOBA, works very well and really makes you feel more connected to your character.
- Use of the WASD keys allows you to dodge enemy Gods' moves easier than a game which is just 'click to move'.
- You can jump!
- There is a God whose ultimate is releasing kittens! (Bastet) :)
- Each God really feels different to the next.
- The diversity of games and maps is great!
- There are regular updates.
- Every day there is a daily special game/map which is very different to the normal ones.
- And much, much more...
For those who want to hear possible negatives, then I really can't think of many, apart from:
- The community. This is a big issue, although not one Hi-Rez Studios can help. When starting off playing Smite, you probably will be called a 'noob' and reported for feeding several times. Quite a few more 'experienced' players, when matched with new players, are constantly harrassing the chat with depressing comments. However do not fear! You can block these players, report them for harrassment, and once you have practised a lot you might be a better player than the harrassers, able to defend the 'noobs'. I have found that the most harrassing happens on conquest, so maybe don't play on this map until you are more experienced.
Overall I would definitely recommend this game. The tutorials at the start can be slightly boring, however bear witht them and when you start playing it gets really fun!

PROS:
- Chilling atmosphere of the movie franchise is captured to perfection
- Genuine ability to scare you, this games not for the faint hearted
- Stunning graphical style, the game looks great and isn't too demanding on your system either, the lighting effects deserve a special mention.
- Lots of single player content for the money, roughly 17 hours story mode and on top of that there is side content.
- Really good story linked tightly to the movie franchise. Easy to follow with plenty of references to please the fans.
- Alien AI is immense, its unpredictable and never gets old.
- Menacing bots offer a good alternative enemy, the way they charge at you with red eyes and take quite a beating remind me almost of Terminators.

CONS:
- I actually felt that the story was a bit too long. As the game is so tense and gameplay slow I found myself bored 11 missions in and actually revisited several months later though it was easy to get back into.
- Vsnyc big meant I got major slow down solved simply by turning it off.
- The flamethrower, whilst its a great weapon and the fire effects are stunning, it partially removes the fear factor away from the alien as its quite easy to make them back off. At the same time though you feel like an absolute badass,
VERDICT?
This is the Alien game we've always wanted, I can't believe its taken them so long to capture an obvious formula but they have delivered right down to a tee. Its a true horror experience and one everyone should experience.

As a massive fan of the Aliens movies and Aliens/AVP books, it was so good to see an installment worthy of the franchise again. The design and music was absolutely on point, resulting in a phenomenally immersive atmosphere/experience.
It took me only 25 hours game time, but over a year to finish this one, mostly because it was too terrifying to handle for any length of time. Showing clips to people really doesn't come close to conveying the true fear and vulnerability you feal playing on hard difficulty in the dark with headphones. It's the first game that actually made my hands shake from adrenaline to the point it was difficult to play.
The only major fault I found (*spoiler alert*, kinda) is in the last two hours getting a little bit sick of false endings. One or two is fine, but so many A to B via C via A again with that f**king monster *constantly* on your trail (I can see what some negative reviewers are saying there) gets pretty draining. I have to be honest there were a couple of points I kinda wished it would actually end.
Stoked I stuck with it though, even if I did need to leave the light on sometimes. Anyone who has ever enjoyed the Alien story and/or enjoys horror and/or just likes exceptionally well crafted games, I highly recommend you check this out.

Words cannot describe my joy when I saw that preview on E3.

6/10
Homeworld Remastered is gorgeous.
And dumb.
Wait, allow me to explain.
Firstly, this is primarily based on my experience in the HW1R Campaign. For me, nothing else in this release matters. At all. I don't care about HW2, don't care about HW2R, hell I don't even care about multiplayer.
Secondly, I am not going to be able to even pretend that I'm not comparing this to Homeworld, mostly because it is Homeworld: Remastered, the whole point of this game is for us to enjoy Homeworld again, so, if your stance is that this game should be measured in a void, and not held up to the Homeworld of yesteryear, then this review is not for you.
This game is riddled with bugs. The first mission crashed to desktop, the second mission didn't register a salvage corvette going to the beacon (made me send a probe), and the third mission...
The third mission.
The third mission requires you to salvage 6 objects. The programmers clearly expected you to only get 5, and when this game was released in 1999, if you got all 6 then the mission wouldn't complete. Here in 2015, far in the distant future, what should I encounter but THE EXACT SAME BUG OMFG.
I wouldn't have minded the scattering of new bugs, if they also hadn't brought back the exact same bugs from 15 years ago. I don't even understand how that's possible, you can't exactly copy and paste code from that long ago, it doesn't work, hell I don't even think they're in the same language, but I digress. The game has bugs, maybe its just new release issues, God, I hope so.
Then we move on to the AI. When this game was first released in 1999 the AI was good for the time, but still dumb, which all games then were, for example, when telling a group of support frigates to repair a bunch of ships, they'd all bunch up on one ship and repair that, ignoring any other damaged ships until the first one was fixed, even if the other ships were taking fire and about to be destroyed. Dumb, but acceptable in those heady days.
How does the modern support frigate work you ask? Simple, when you tell them to repair a group of ships, they do the exact same thing. Only NOW rather than faithfully following the fleet around, and repairing any new damage (in the same, slightly derpy way), they repair whatever damage was there when the initial command was issued, and then will float idly in space wherever they are until a new order is issued, what did they Unionize or something?
Fighters and corvettes no longer stay in formation. Corvettes now make swooping strike passes like fighters instead of maintaining their orientation on foes and engaging them continuously. The new build menu's queue system is unintuitive. The launch menu now requires you to INDIVIDUALLY SELECT SHIPS TO LAUNCH. In a game where you can have up to 72 fighters. Pick them one by one. Or launch everything. And you can't shift select groups either, hell they aren't even organized, just listed in the order that they docked, which can be awkward when you want to launch fighters but all your resource collecters are docked as well.
Oh right, resource collection. In a game where it can take HOURS to mine out an area (I'm dead serious) a bit of time dilation would have been just perfect, but no. You used to be able to tell a Resource Controller to guard your harvesters, and it would smartly place itself equidistant from all of them. No longer. Now it follows ONE around, which significantly increases the already incredibly long harvest times, and that's assuming the resource collectors actually return to the controller in the first place.
You can't pick between the Taidan and the Kushan or change your ships coloration like you used to be able to.
There is a hard limit of 14 salvage corvettes. The dynamic difficulty veers drunkenly between insane difficulty and laughable ease. Controlling vertical movement is clunky and hard to manage. Really short review. Probably won't update in the future.
The whole package is great, especially for me since I'd never played the originals. It's important to note for Classic players, though, that there are a few changes to ship behavior and mission structure in HW1R(remastered). Aggressive/Evasive tactics are out, literally removed, and some of the missions appear to have been nerfed for some reason, the Kadesh in particular. The game also hosts a dynamic difficulty setting based on your fleet size, though the specifics of its behavior evade me. Strike group behavior is also altered, making behaviors like setting a Defender squadron to Sphere Formation and guard your target behave differently from Classic. The way damage and accuracy are rolled when ships fire are also different (iirc, it's based far more on dice rolling now).
Why is it like that? Well, HW1R runs in the HW2 engine.
That being said, I enjoyed HW1R a lot. The story is very vague and built on a lot of mysticism and prophetic themes. The game itself was enjoyable, although I wish that the AI on ships were far more intelligent. You do have to babysit your units (in HW2, too).
HW2's a lot better as a gameplay experience though, although its story is a bit less interesting. I felt like a greater number of my ships were valuable throughout the course of the game, vs HW1, where the majority of the units you can build become obsolete very quickly.
HW1 had a huge pacing problem because there was no form of time-compression to harvest resources, leading to post-mission lulls lasting over 30 minutes at a time where all you're doing is waiting for utility ships to mine up the money.
HW2 solved the problem by crediting you with the resources when a mission was completed, and its overall campaign pacing is much more intense and demanding, definitely welcome, than HW1.
I wish Cataclysm was in the remaster pack, but apparently Gearbox couldn't secure the source code for the game.
Lastly, I haven't played multiplayer.

As an avid Souls player I would recommend this game to anyone who has an interest in the Souls series. I believe that Dark Souls 2 is very mechanically refined and anyone who wants to ease into the series without having too much prior experience would have more fun playing Dark Souls 2 over Demon Souls or Dark Souls (1), strictly for learning the mechanics of the game. Having logged (currently) 133 hours on Dark Souls (1) on Steam along with another 100+ hours on the Xbox 360 version, and having dabbled into Demon Souls while I had access to a PS3, I found that Dark Souls 2 has taken many positive aspects of its two predecessors, and combined them to form a very fluid style of gameplay. Dark Souls 2 feels much larger than Dark Souls (1) in terms of world size, however this may be due to the fact that the world is not as seamless as it was in the first Dark Souls. There are several locations that can only be accessed via a loading screen, or through a rather long trek through the map. I enjoyed how interconnected the world felt in Dark Souls (1) where there were many shortcuts that connected otherwise far apart areas in a fluid fashion. I am conflicted over the ability to fast travel from the start of the game, where I certainly recognize the convenience, however I feel that it might have been a quick fix to the lack of world interconnectivity. Speaking in terms of the AI, I feel that there have been improvements in most areas, and the enemies do feel a bit more intelligent, especially for the NPC invaders, however most enemies are able to be consistently cheesed once a specific strategy is discovered. That usually wouldn't be a problem except that the same strategy of "hug the enemie's left leg" works for roughly 90% of the enemies, including the bosses. Which brings me to my greatest disappointment about the game; The boss fights. I feel that a vast majority of the boss fights are simply not creative, and that they should have instead been a sub-boss or just another powerful monster, especially *SPOILER/* the Dragonriders, and you even fight a repeat version of them in another boss fight later on */SPOILER*. Overall I think that more time was spent on making the game pretty, which it is, than making the enemies and the world as interesting as it could be.
Even so, I still had fun playing Dark Souls 2 and would recommend 7.5/10

This is an excellent endless runner set in the TRON universe, with visuals inspired by the last TRON movie, TRON: Evolution, and the TRON: Uprising TV-series, though DLC characters will be made available soon from the original TRON movie. It has everything you would want from an endless runner, including two different "campaigns" of sorts consisting of 16 levels each. In the first, Disc mode, you run through a particular track towards the finish, gaining points along the way and trying to get a three-star rating. In Cycle mode, you basically do the same thing, but using a light cycle. A third mode is Stream, which is classic endless running, where you will also switch between walking on foot to driving a light cycle and vice versa.
The difficulty ramps up nicely as you play through the various modes. You have to run and jump along the track, slide underneath obstacles, run along walls, grind on rails, and defeat enemies using your disc. Enemies are either other standing programs (sometimes deployed via Recognizer) or moving grid bugs. Sometimes, a light tank will pop up and you have limited time to defeat it before getting damaged yourself. You can buy special abilities and helper programs to make life a little easier, using a currency consisting of bits (you get an ample supply of these when you buy the game and more are earned by simply playing the game).
Graphically, the game looks really nice, running on Unreal Engine 4. Everything has an electronic glow like you would expect and the surfaces are hard and reflective. In motion, it looks even more fantastic. Gameplay is solid. I have only played the game using an XBox 360 controller and I think that's probably the preferred way to play it. If there is one problem, it's that the game currently doesn't have a Quit option: you have to hit Escape on the keyboard on the title screen to quit the game, which strikes me as a curious oversight.

Previously recommended during the early access period. This game had a ton of potential during the 2-3 months of early access. The developer picked up on some of the community requested features and tried their best to implement as much as they possibly could. Unfortunately, I now see that a lot of those community ideas were instead used to generate cash grab opportunities for Disney. I won't hold this against Sanzaru Games as they have done an incredible job nailing the look and feel of this universe. Everything else is politics on Disney's end.
-Gameplay is solid. No input delay. Run, jump, glide, slide, wall run, attack, Tony Hawk 360 skatepark and light cycle your way to the finish. Supports keyboard + mouse and controller.
-Visually a very beautiful game and manages to capture the neon-glow vibrance of the TRON universe. Colour palette is buffed slightly from TRON: Evolution.
-Soundtrack is solid and adds a level of depth and dramatic feel to the whole experience.
-Steam achievements for the 100% go-getter.
-No tangible story or anything of substance to back some sort of continuity for the player. I realise this may not be a necessary feature for most runner games, but the desire to progress slowly deteriorates as repetiveness takes over soon after the first few missions (with the exception of boss encounters). The currently available 32 levels becomes a chore rather than an exhilerating journey with a justifiable cause to progress.
-Leaderboard is forever loading. This game is far from a 'finished' product.
-I previously reported randomly losing health and hero suddenly turning invisible during the running segments whilst under early access. I continue to experience these bugs.
-Performance issues continue to persist since day one of early access despite numerous reviewers and members of the community being vocal about stability issues. Some bugs (like those mentioned above) and frame rate issues continue to persist.
-Light cycle segments are an absolute drag. The developers should have focused solely on the running segments with newer and more intuitive features. The light cycle portions just don't feel right at all.
-Main menu? What main menu. There is no such thing here! No options menu unless you hit escape, and no way to exit the game unless you return to the very top menu and hit escape.
-The base game will set you back by £14.99 and an optional £19.00 for the ultimate upgrade. That totals to £33.99. Slightly overzealous, don't you think Disney? I purchased this during early access and splashed £6.99. THAT should be the price for the current content available in the base game alone. Everything else is a perfect opportunity for Disney to slag off the TRON and Steam community. Your money is best invested elsewhere.
Had I known this would be the embarrasing route Disney originally intented I would have avoided RUN/r right from the beginning. Yes, I am in love with the TRON universe and yes I did purchase this with little knowledge. However, I had no regrets at the time even with the bare bones content. I wanted to support this project and was satisfied with the content I saw and the expectations bouncing between the community. From here onwards I will be extremely vigilant towards all future entries in this universe, especially anything baring the Disney label.

Well, this is a title that I have never heard of before. I saw a friend start playing it and I felt the need to ask how was the game. The response was that it's a great game. But, I needed to try it for myself.
Let me tell you, this is a beautiful and rather charming adaptation of the chinese novel "Journey to the west".
It's a wonderful story in a post-apocalyptic world where humans are scarce and hidden, while the robots hunts them by the dozen. One of the strongest points of this game is the voice acting. Andy Serkis, Lindsey Shaw and Richard Ridings, all excelled at their jobs. They played strong, interesting characters with whom you can feel attached to.
The Premium Edition includes some outfits DLC for Monkey and Trip and Pigsy's Perfect 10 campaign, which is another story that does not include Monkey and Trip, but instead, you get to play as Pigsy in his quest to build the perfect friend, always with his sidekick, the adorable Truffles.
The gameplay is a good old beat 'em up with a mix of Prince of Persia. It's solid an very entertaining, indeed.
The graphics are fine, considering that it's a port of a game that came out for consoles in 2010. But, I must highlight the beauty of the different places where you get to visit. The desolated places are absolutely gorgeous (Just like Trip's smile).
I could buy this game on sale at, I think, 5 bucks. But, even at 50% discount is a pretty good deal.
Would I recommend this game? Hell, yes. I would give this game a solid 9 out of 10. But, in my opinion, everyone should try it by themselves and make their own conclusions.

It's like 'I Am Legend' , but with mechs and a monkey!
'Enslaved' has a solid storyline set in an intriguing post-apocalyptic landscape which is boosted by interesting characters who by the way have some of the best facial animations and expressions i've ever seen in a video-game apart from L.A. Noire. The world with it's fantastic looking backrounds makes you feel involved and part of it, and while the gameplay is fairly straightforward and isn't as exciting as done before in games like 'God of War'  and 'Prince of Persia' titles in recent years, it is entertainning enough if you don't mind casual games. In the end it's the story and performances that really make this title shine.
Performance wise it's a bit rough on PC (read: rough port), with a few annoying hang-ups here and there, but in all it's a fantastic cinematic adventure. Just be sure to play it with a controller to get the best out of it, while the mouse can come in handy with the shooting parts of the game.

Short Review
Ninja Theory knows games...
They were responsible for Heavenly Sword (a PS3 console exclusive) and DMC (series reboot) (PC/PS3/XB360) both outstanding titles in their own right.
In Short…
Enslaved Odyssey to the West is simply a great game, with high bar visuals and the title is a superior example of what a pc port should look like on the PC.
Great Story, Great Character Development (a rare thing to see), Great Gameplay and Excellent Optimization for the PC.
A game that is simply well thought out and executed to one of the highest standards for a pc title.

TJD Chapter 3 is a pretty great conclusion to Skygoblin's adventure game trilogy, and I'd certainly recommend it to fans of the other two games.  Anyone new to the series would probably be best off starting with Chapter One -- the game does summarize some of the previous plot points but it's definitely not a completely self-contained story.  The visuals continue to be quite gorgeous (though a few scenes seem a little under-detailed), and the voice acting is, in general, fantastic as well.  As with previous TDJ games, there's occasionally some poorly-recorded bits from secondary character dialog, but it's pretty minor in this one.  A couple familiar minor characters from previous games unexpectedly pop up, which was great, and the new characters are generally fun and well-written.
One of the most immediate changes from the previous games is the overall tone, which is noticeably darker.  The series has always had things like violence and government corruption lingering at its fringes, but setting this story in the heart of that corruption has definitely altered the tone.  There's actual profanity in this one, reasonably common in fact -- being verbally threatened in-game by an angry Armando Power Company employee feels a bit more dangerous when he's also swearing at you.  Your main allies in the game are armed revolutionaries, and St. Armando is beset by crowds of angry protesters.  I found myself wondering if the real world's recent politcal upheaval and unrest has influenced this shift.  It says something about Skygoblin's writing chops, though, that a puzzle involving a repeatedly-tasered protester comes across as funny rather than disturbing.
Another reason for the tone shift is in part due to the passing of their original two games' composer -- the jazzy afro-carribean grooves have largely been replaced by 80s synth and rock.  It took me awhile to get used to it, but It was probably wise to pivot rather than try to imitate the previous games' scores with another composer.  The change is even well-integrated into the story itself and makes thematic sense, both by the game's setting and the characters you meet.  By the end I'd fully come around and it was nice to see the change pay off for the final scenes.
In the end, this is a very satisfying conclusion to the series.  There's some elements I'm not as fond of -- I'd have appreciated much more time spent in the Underland, for instance -- but it's impressive that Skygoblin's created an ending for the series which delivers.  Definitely give this a go!

If you have ever played Minecraft, Terraria, Don't Starve or similar games and ended up tired of going through the complicated and tedious process of finding raw material and crafting complicated items with it, then Factorio may be for you.  Your objective is mostly the same as in those games: Find raw material, transform it into something useful, slay monsters, survive, and eventually get the heck out of there.  Yet the availability of mining drills, assembly machines, automated defenses, etc. makes the process much more fulfilling: You don't spend time crafting, but designing a factory that crafts for you.
The game is carefully designed not to bore you.  There's always something else to do.  Just when you have the perfect metal production, you need to adapt it to smelt steel; when you finally have a perfect pipeline for all your solid products, you need to make room to oil-based products and all those pipes; when you've finally nailed oil industry, suddenly the metal production is incredibly deficient and there's no way to just expand the current setup; when you thought everything was up and running, your coal production shuts down right when a hundred biters hit your now unpowered laser defense line.
Even after you have everything, there's always more to do.  And if you don't find anything to do, you can always try some mods to try to change things a bit.  you can try to create a new factory, but this time you will have everything perfectly optimized and no ugly hacks!! (HINT: You won't. Even after 10 replays. You will always forget something.)
There's also trains.  Trains are awesome.  Do you need any more reasons to buy it?

Though still in Early Access it is a really enjoyable fun game. Frustrating at times when you find you didn't plan you factory properly and have to re-arrange stuff but the satisfaction of starting from scratch and building this huge complicated machine is really fun.
Looking forward to seeing it to continue to develop.

I have never like MOBAs, however Smite is a definite exception to the rule! Here are a few reasons why:
- Its content is much more 'free' than most free-to-play games i.e most MMOs, as you can unlock every single God without spending a penny!
- The third-person view, which is unusual for a MOBA, works very well and really makes you feel more connected to your character.
- Use of the WASD keys allows you to dodge enemy Gods' moves easier than a game which is just 'click to move'.
- You can jump!
- There is a God whose ultimate is releasing kittens! (Bastet) :)
- Each God really feels different to the next.
- The diversity of games and maps is great!
- There are regular updates.
- Every day there is a daily special game/map which is very different to the normal ones.
- And much, much more...
For those who want to hear possible negatives, then I really can't think of many, apart from:
- The community. This is a big issue, although not one Hi-Rez Studios can help. When starting off playing Smite, you probably will be called a 'noob' and reported for feeding several times. Quite a few more 'experienced' players, when matched with new players, are constantly harrassing the chat with depressing comments. However do not fear! You can block these players, report them for harrassment, and once you have practised a lot you might be a better player than the harrassers, able to defend the 'noobs'. I have found that the most harrassing happens on conquest, so maybe don't play on this map until you are more experienced.
Overall I would definitely recommend this game. The tutorials at the start can be slightly boring, however bear witht them and when you start playing it gets really fun!

Someone once described Dark Souls as an abusive father that only wants the best for you. In comparison Dark Souls II would be an abusive father that abuses you not because he wants you to achieve something so you can be proud of yourself but so that he can be proud that he has a son like that. In other words, Dark Souls uses a good trail and error based system while Dark Souls 2 screws you over for no reason whatsoever all the time. In Dark Souls if you know what you're doing you could roll behind an enemy while dodging their attacks. In II they have such a ridiculous tracking that enemies will do a 360 spin if necessary in the middle of a swing.
Also the world design is just terrible. One moment you're in colonial America and then you're in the middle of Arabia. They didn't even try to make areas blend into eachother like in Dark Souls which makes it absolutely impossible to get immersed. There are no likable NPCs with perhaps the exception of the cat but then you don't actually ever need to talk to her. All other NPCs are either♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idiots or just insignificant with annoyingly repetitive dialogue.
If you've ever played Dark Souls then you might know the satisfying sensation of beating a boss. Since they're completely artificially difficult or complete pushovers in this game, that sensation doesn't exist in this game.
tl;dr Dark Souls was fun, Dark Souls 2 isn't.

Meme's aside. This game requires some viewing on the topic of lore. Going through the game I always tell myself to read the item descriptions but I end up in boss rush mode and try to beat the game as soon as possible. Because of this I ended up with a lot of questions by the end.
Story wise I will have to agree with those who dislike the circularity of the story. It makes sense in-universe, but it just didn't make the game feel that original as Dark Souls 1 was. I know that's always hard to do, but I had been hoping that maybe the second installment ties more into what happened to Gwynevere and Flan. You also never really see what happens to other NPCs. I guess since you can kill them all, it had to somehow be consistent for everyone, but we have the Ornstein cosplayer and what happened to the primordial serpents?
It's just hard to separate a sequel from it's first previous installment sometimes, but if you watch some of the lore videos that are out there you'll appreciate the narrative a bit more.
Combat wise, if you've played Dark Souls 1, you'll have to adjust to staggering, the lack of a kick and how AGL works. Everything else works as much as you'd expect it. Online is vastly superior. No hacking, a lot of coop, not that many invasions though. However PvP is difficult if you're build is not PvP focused which is kind of a shame, but always the case.
As far as PC ports goes, I think From Software did a good job, although speedruns have shown that they were a bit sloppier this time around.
The atmosphere though is weaker. The only area that recaptured that kind of DS1 feeling of new and awe inspiring was the Dragon Aerie. As a lot of people have pointed out, it's probably because of the scrapped lighting engine. There are some mods to restore some of it.
Bottom line, I don't think DS2 is a must play for gamers as much as DS1 was, but if you like the Souls games mechanics, then it's a definite buy.

In the infinite majesty of space, cruelty and beauty can be found in equal measure. A race brought to the very brink of destruction through the violation of a treaty signed millenia ago, left marooned in space clinging to a technology salvaged from ancient ancestors and a single guiding star. Home.
This sets the stage for one of the greatest space strategy games of all time, Homeworld. A game that has rarely been aspired to since, and a game filled with ideas that even to this day are rarely even touched upon. Only now a few daring indie developers dare brave the complexities that represent true three dimensional space combat and even then they have yet to come even close to what Homeworld achieved. It was lightning in a bottle, a cult classic synthesised from a pace that was stately enough to appreciate the sheer majesty that the game inspired with its' sweeping scale, a soundtrack that was borne of classical tones and distant melancholy, and a story that took you on a true campaign, where your units would carry over from mission to mission, along with your resource pool.
These are all concepts that in most current campaigns are oft ignored, set aside for flashy Michael Bay style set pieces and much shallower, more simplistic stories. Homeworld told stories of shades of grey, of culture, of alien races with diverse backgrounds and lore, of imperialism, of a nebula home to a technologically advanced enclave that sought refuge and peace within the sanctity of drifting ghostlike threads.
Homeworld Remastered is a restoration of that premise, Gearbox have carefully and considerately taken the Homeworld 2 interface (the better one) and the source assets, placed them in a more modern, more capable and more mod friendly engine, and then carefully brought the game up to current generation standards, with lighting, depth of field, better framerates, higher resolutions, better texturing, cleaned up the sound work, the whole lot. The result quite literally is Homeworld as viewed through the "rose tinted glasses of memory", it's how we always imagined it was in our heads, even if our then much less meaty PC's couldn't QUITE give us the experience that we wished for.
The change is stark when placed side by side, it's hard to imagine when you fire up remastered thinking that the ships -didn't- look that impressive before, but when you play the original you then are reminded with a shock that yes, they were kinda blocky and yes, the textures were kinda flat back in the day. That's all gone now, the ships really -do- look like their concept art, they really do move with the kind of majesty and detail that we all imagined they did, the mothership is just crammed with detail, and everywhere you look, there's something that just looks *better* than it did before. The sound too, is crisper, with all the sound assets being cleaned up and provided at a higher fidelity, with the music being remastered at a higher bitrate, again, no changes that alter the fabric of the game, but a subtle re-weaving that change the feel into the game we always remembered it as.
You do get a lot of game for your money too, for the asking cost you'll get both Homeworld 1 and 2 remastered, along with their original source games in case you feel like a trip down nostalgia lane and want to do some side by side comparisons (I suggest you do), you also get the multiplayer which brings all four factions into multiplayer together, which is sure to open up some interesting games once they get the code all sorted out and out of "beta" (for whatever that term means these days), and you'll get what is quite easily still the greatest space opera strategy ever to grace the PC.
Gearbox did good. Everyone was holding their breath because I could imagine the kind of fury that would have been issued forth had they scuffed this, but no. They did good, this has made me a happy tiger, Homeworld is a game that deserved to be brought back, it deserved this remastering, and what you get is quite comfortably the "definitive" version of Homeworld. Prepare for a journey unlike any you'll find, this one truly is something special.

This game has a cool core idea but also feels like some kind of twisted marketing experiment by Disney to see what players would let them get away with. It's shallow, it's buggy and it's full of microtransaction scumminess that would barely be acceptable in a free-to-play game but is in full force in one that costs a minimum of $20.
The basic idea is cool. It's a score attack runner game that has two modes, one on foot and one in light cycles. Each mode has their own levels, mechanics and challenges and despite a lacking sense of speed, everything feels fluid, responsive and it's actually quite fun. Though there are only 16 levels for each mode, plus a randomly generated endless mode where you race for time instead of score, you're encouraged to replay levels for better scores and there can be a decent number of hours involved in completing everything if that's your thing.
Where this completely breaks down is with the powerups and the microtransactions tied to them. Yes, this is a minimum $20 game that has microtransactions. Now, they're very much optional and grinding out in-game currency to buy powerups actually doesn't take that long. That said, the powerups are single use so you might have to grind a lot. Where this falls apart is YOU CAN BUY POWER! There are powerups that will both double your combo accumulation AND double your score! You can literally buy higher scores on the leaderboards. This completely renders the core competitive loop of this game worthless as it's not a level playing field and those willing to grind or spend money do better by default. For that reason alone, you shouldn't buy this game. This is a business model that deserves to fail.

Load times are long, even on high-end machines and as of writing, the leaderboards which you can buy your way up on don't even work! Every time I try to bring them up, it sits at Loading and never shows anything.
There's a great TRON-inspired idea here but the game is buggy, overpriced for what you get and the microtransaction strategy ruins it. I'd expect this in a free-to-play mobile game, not a $20 PC release. Such potential wasted. DON'T BUY THIS!

So, I am not a big fan of runners on the PC. In my mind they are for mobile devices...until now. TRON RUN/r is simply fantastic! One of the best runners that I have played. This game runs on the Unreal 4 engine, and looks amazing. It is a nice blend of TRON, TRON Legacy, TRON 2.0, and Uprising, with a some nice additions of it's own. In short, the game runs nice and smooth and is a total blast to play. I highly recommend this to anyone who likes runners, and TRON! Welcome back to the Grid!

First of all, this game is an absolute BEAUTY to behold! The environments are fantastic and really makes you feel like you are a program trying to get to the portal and escape from the Grid. Also, the effects and lighting that's used is perfect and it makes the Grid come alive!
The object of the game is to get to the portal. In the disc mode, this means running along, jumping and sliding, dodging attacks, throwing your disc, wall running, gliding, and even grinding on rails to get to the end in one piece. You have 3 energy (health points). If you lose all your energy, you lose. The controls handle great for this mode and it's easy to get into and learn but tricky to master especially when you're running quickly and trying to deal with everything in front of you.
The second mode is the light cycle mode and it's also a lot of fun, but very challenging. The reason it's so challenging and brutal is that you have to get to the end before the time runs out, but the catch is that you have to go through check point gates to keep the time up. The gates will have different second amounts they will add such as 2, 4, and 6 seconds. If you run out of time, you lose. This mode is tough, and it really is a try, try, and try again until beat it sort of mode.
The third mode is "STREAM" which is basically an endless randomly generated run which can switch between disc and cycle modes to keep you on your toes. It is a lot of fun and is great to come to and play if you need a break from the other two modes because instead of being pre-made like the others, it's all random as it goes. Also worth mentioning, is that this mode has a weekly challenge you can do. For example, it will ask you to survive for 1:50. This will award you for example with a badge (which I still haven't figured out what it does). Overall a lot of fun! I will be playing this mode a lot I think.
If you buy the Season Pass, you will be given a TON of new characters to play as, many new light cycles to choose from, and also an Outlands mode will appear. I still haven't been able to play this mode but it might just be a bug that needs to be fixed. The new characters and light cycles you can use include all the cycles and characters (almost) from the original TRON, TRON: Legacy, and even very surprisingly, TRON: Uprising. They are all recreated in fantastic detail and really come to life in the game.
Now for some information on how the in-game currency system works and how to get it. When you play a level in either the disc or cycle mode, all of the gold/yellow bits you gathered will be given to you as a reward for completing the level. If you don't finish the level, you don't get any of it. However, the endless mode will give you any bits aquired while in the run and you can use this to get more fairly quickly. It's quite easy to get a reasonable amount of bits by just playing the endless mode. These bits in turn allow you to purchase powerups and companions for a run. Powerups are useable items that can be activated at any time, while the companions are passive abilities like attacking enemies or drawing in nearby bits passively. Each run you can equip one of each of these. The companions are fragile however; if you get hit once, it disappears.
Overall, I am having a blast with the game and it's awesome. If you love TRON, runner games, or racing types of games, or even all of the above, you'll love it. Good luck program!
Update: It looks like the DLC such as the different cycles and characters along with additional levels have been pulled because it was prematurely released when it was still being tested. It sounds like that content will be released over time like a normal season pass works.

I'm not sure how I feel about this game? I loved Bwana. He remained the same, as hilarious as ever. And the cactus! But....the game, overall, felt less challenging then the other two. Only two parts really stumped me-the islands with Lena and the microphone bit with Bwana. That in itself isn't enough to make the game that bad but....
(cons)
-There's a moment when someone is talking about cops and they say "police beastiality." ....Was that purposeful? Or was it supposed to say "brutality"? Cause if that was purposeful, that's cool....
-This game was released a month late. But the graphics weren't quite there. At least 3 characters didn't fit with the surroundings. They didn't look right, they didn't look like the background or other characters. Apart from being different, they also looked bad. 2 were the juice ladies, and 1 was the dad (I can't spell his name) when he was with Lena. At one point he was fuzzy as all get out.
-Also on the island there was a quite clear distortion in pixels, down a straight line (when you'd sail away.)
-There was a lag on most of the cut scenes, it was really skippy. Kinda like an unbuffered streamed movie.
I'm not a computer person, so I don't know if these are just my computer and the way it downloaded (the skipping and the weird island distortion line), or actual problems with the game.
Another thing that bothered me in this game was incomplete actions and animation felt rough. For instance: When Bwana and Kito are climbing into the chain thing, you don't get to see them hop in. Bwana says "lets go!" and it cuts to them already being in it (which I think takes away from possible fun moments). Or the elevator shaft with Gabi, Bwana is by the open door way, and then it cuts to their both safe. That's just two examples. Cut scene to action was also rough. And one moment I thought was really bad was in the rubble, the rocker and gabi were on the ground and then Bwana pops in frame. Like if he was supposed to be under a rubble pile, that wasn't there either. It was two people in frame and then he popped right in, as opposed to if he had been under rubble already there. It was two people and then POP! Bwana was there too.
So for an extra month, there are a lot of rough graphics.
Pros:
-the people were cool. I couldn't believe Rose existed. I thought I had misunderstood what her job was. Nope.
-the cussing startled me. Maybe it shouldn't have. I guess I'm used to games like Nancy Drew.
-Bwana and the cactus
-Getting to see Bwanas dad.
-I didn't get stuck forever in this game like the last two. I guess it was just a lot easier. That's a win/lose.
-I adored the scenery though.
Overall, I'd say wait for any kind of sale for this game and that it's a little behind the first two games, overall polish and in terms of enjoyment. But it's worth playing!

I'm not entirely sure where to categorize this and thus got very mixed feelings about the game in and of itself.
The Journey Down: Chapter Three starts off very strong (in my opinion). It's the same characters we know and love, doing silly things and having a laugh at it. Just like in the previous episodes.
We finally find our 'heroes' in the Underland and about 20 minutes later, we're back in St. Armando. Considering that the game is about 3 to 4 hours long, being in the Underland for this short is kind of a shame. Ofcourse, the player goes back there after a while, but again... It's very short and feels more of an afterthought than an actual part of the story.
And that's what the game becomes at exactly that point.
The production value went down from there on in and it's noticable in a lot of aspects.
The voice acting, in my opinion, is really great. Bwana, Kito are done great and are very believable. Then there's always the mediocre voice acting... And then there's the phoned in voice acting.
In an attempt to avoid spoilers, when the player goes 'back' to the Underland, there are two characters, one of major importance and the other one again being an afterthought. And their voice acting is atrocious. They're reading their line from a script and sounds like they phoned it in.
Aside from the value seemingly going down, I felt like a lot of stuff was skipped. The hub area in the second part of the game felt really nice, but it didn't feel part of the world that the player is in. And it was over before I knew it. There is a puzzle there with a police officer that I had trouble with... Only to realize I missed an object. After I got the object that was needed in the puzzle, the cutscene took... 3 seconds? I couldn't even process what was going on.
And that's, sort of, how the latter part of the game is in a nutshell. It feels rushed, compared to TJD: Chapters 1 and 2. That may be due to the simplified puzzles (and in my opinion, that's nothing bad, but I can see why it's a problem for other people) but it honestly, I think that the latter part was more of an afterthought.  And that's a huge disapointment.
I would still recommend it because the game is, for what it is, pretty darn decent. Not as good as its predecessors, but it's still got its chill vibe, aside from sometimes feeling a bit 'too gamey'. (There has to be action and suspensful situations... Just more than before).
The voice actors, namely the protagonists, have done a very nice job to keep it interesting - eventhough it felt a little forced at the end of the game. One particular side character, whom wanted to fight a guard made me giggle like a schoolgirl for a long, long time. It might sound silly, but in a game like The Journey Down, I felt that the silly dialogue was part of this world and that all the serious business was secondary.
The music is actually quite good, but again, it felt like it didn't always fall into the category of the game. In the first game, the music accomodated the scene where the player was at and the same happened in the second game. Now, I know that the producer of this music had passed away during the creation of the 2nd game, may rest in peace. The music crew had done a good job in this installment, but the music oftentimes didn't fit with the mood of the game.
The scenery was really nice as well, but again, didn't quite reach the value of the previous two games. And again, mostly in the latter half of the game.
I love this series through and through and I hope that it gets the attention it deserves, because it deserves it.
It just saddens me that it's so 'mediocre' compared to the previous titles. I really hope that the developer would try to fix some of these things. It's really not a bad game at all, but it dropped the ball halfway through.

I'd been waiting for the final chapter of The Journey Down all year, and it really delivers! There are more little side stories that could be explored in future games, but this  wraps up the Afro-Caribbean mythopunk noir arc that's made the JD games so much fun to follow. The story remains imaginative and engaging, characters are just that nice little bit over the top (especially the side characters), the music is great, and the puzzles are entertaining without the danger of players getting stuck or frustrated. The solutions are all within your grasp if you're willing to chat with the surrounding characters and occasionally say, "Eh, what the heck? Let's give it a try!"
Gameplay is straightforward; the only bone I have to pick is that some of the transitions between scenes loaded slowly, so the screen was dark for all of 4 seconds. That's a pretty small bone.

There have been many articles mourning the death of the point-and-click genre. Which I always thought was strange since it has never really died. In the past decade companies like Artifex Mundi, Alawar Entertainment and Viva Media have brought us a constant stream of HOG games that play very similar to old fashioned point-and-click adventure games. And companies like 'The Adventure Company' (Book of Unwritten Tales), 'Deadalic' (Deponia, Night of the Rabbit) and 'Focus Home Interactive' (Runaway games), have been bringing us more traditional point-and-click adventure games. What the games media probably mean is that big companies like EA and Ubisoft aren't interested in producing point-and-click adventure games since it's become a niche market. Or that big publishers aren't willing to support icons like Tim Schafer (Broken Age) and Ron Gilbert (Thimbleweed Park). And they both had to resort to crowd funding in order to get their new games made. But the genre is far from dead.
And there are also indie developers, companies with a handful of programmers that are dedicated to bringing us gamers point-and-click adventure games as we remember them from the Lucasart days. Recently I enjoyed playing the final installment of the 'Dream Machine' (also made by a bunch of Swedes) and now we get the third and final episode of 'The Journey Down'. It's not perfect, some of the voice over work was kinda so-so compared to the rest, some of the background art looks rushed and the puzzles are very much on the easy side. But it is also a labour of love, created by three Swedes over a period of seven years. Is 18 Euros a fair price for a four hour game? If this would've been a game by a big studio which was obviously made in a short time with minimal effort in order to rake in some easy cash, I would have said "No way!". But this is a game with many hours of blood, sweat and tears poured into it. We need more companies like Skygoblins and buying their games is what allows them to keep doing so.
I had some conflicting feelings while playing this game but overall I enjoyed it and it feels like an appropriate conclusion of this trilogy. If you enjoy playing games reminiscent to games like Monkey Island and Full Throttle, you'll also enjoy "The Journey Down". I think it's worth the full price, because I want to support the creators. If you don't feel the same, I'm sure it will be on sale in the future, if you can get the trilogy at a decent price, go for it.

TJD3 Kickstarter backer here. TJD is a very nice point'n'click trilogy with an unique atmosphere, great characters, spot-on art and music. Really refreshing setting and humor.
However I have to say I felt TJD 3 is the weakest game of the 3, less charming than the others. TJD 2 stands out as the best episode  to me.
TJD 3 can be completed in 3-5 hours, which is more or less the same duration of the first 2 games. I wish this final game lasted more than 3-5 hours because since the game is split up between the underland and St Armando locations, it feels more rushed than TJD 1 & 2 which happen almost solely in Kingsbay (TJD1) and Port Artue (TJD2).
I didn't understand the rock'n'roll segment in TJD 3, it felt disconnected from the plot and the caribbean atmosphere of the game. Puzzles are a lot easier than in the first two games, overall I never got stuck longer than 5min, which leaves you wanting more. Imo it's a bit sad because you can't enjoy some locations (especially in the underland) as much as you would like since you won't revisit these more than once, usually.
Despite the (really talented) TJD1&2 composer has passed away, his successor does a fine job at recreating the same kind of music vibe and there's plenty of tracks as well. The cinematics are also well-made, except for the cheap explosions effects, and the voice acting is solid overall, except for a few voices such as the chief of the pirates.
TJD3 also includes some references to previous episodes, whether it's a previous character making an appearence, or an old character we can finally meet in person, which is cool. I must say I wish Kito played a larger role in the story, being able to play as him even for a short sequence would have been nice. The end is okay but I expected more of it, it's too standard/happy and not enough focused on the main characters. And the 2 vilains of the story are not really well fleshed-out characters, they are less interesting than Barlow in TJD2.
All in all it's still a pretty neat game, just a bit weaker in its conclusion than Black Epiphany for the Blackwell series for instance. Can't wait to see what devs come up with next.

This is becoming one of my favorite games of all time. I will look forward to a sequel!

Awesome graphics, good all around feel for a Total War game...
Unfortunately I've followed the series a long time and there are some drastic changes made that change the tactics too much. For a new player though, you probably feel that isn't too bad! Well, to top it all off, VERY poorly programmed AI. Traditionally (and even in this game), a quick battle click in your favour is to skip an otherwise meaningless battle (anything wasting yer time) while you can play the bigger, more important and close battles.
Unfortunately this is no longer the case in your favour. The AI cheats something aweful (they always see your hidden units waiting in ambush), they always know when a spy is coming for them and they move. And yes, their units even respond on a dime while your units take moment to respond to an order making it impossible to avoid one of their flank maneuvers. I find the auto-calc (sadly) does a far better job. I wish I could say this was all a lack of experience of my newb playing but I've had these games for many years.... no, it's lazy programming.
So if yer looking for an incredible looking board game, go for it. Graphics are amazing, auto-calc if pretty accurate and the tactical moves are top notch... but don't go looking for anything special at the battlefield level. Sucks compared to even Rome I - Total War.

to jump.  You won't fall off of -- say -- a steel girder when you're clambering across, not even if you try reallllly hard. Another nice thing the devs have added is that when you climb a ladder, it takes a single push of a button -- climbing up and down is automatic.
You have two
: Up-close combat and shooting, both of which are done with your handy staff.  Ammo is VERY limited, so be choosy on what you decide to use it on!  We have both plasma and stunning ammo. are stunningly beautiful.  The attention to detail is just incredible, with those little extra touches that really add to the scene -- the way things move in the wind, lighting effects, scratches on our characters' skin, scars, even pores!  This dystopian world is really brought to life through the amazing graphics, and you know what?  The creators didn't "cheat" on those areas where we have limited camera range.  If you try aiming to shoot something, you'll be able to see the full 360-degree view, and that the graphics are still fleshed out in areas we shouldn't be able to see.

Where to start....
Dishonored 2 is set 15 years after Dishonored 1. Dishonored 2 a good game, choppy at release but still a good game.
The game starts off pretty much the same way as the previous Dishonored, story wise that is.  But i still think that the Dishonored 2 story was very weak, Compared to the previous Dishonored. Dishonored 1 was a story about the Royal protector of the Empress who was framed for her murder. And he needed to redeem himself and Save Emily. In Dishonored 2 Emily is a young woman who loses the throne once again and needs to get it back. I'll try not to spoil the game but I can't promise anything.
I felt much more connected to the storyline in the first Dishonored than the second. The first Dishonored started with you coming home early to deliver a letter to the empress, when you get to her you gets assassinated by the one and only Daud. Your goal in the first game is to Find Emily and save the kingdom from certain doom.
In Dishonored 2 your only goal is pretty much saving Corvo (or Emily) and taking your throne back. It just feels like there was a massive hole in the story. When i finished the 1st Dishonored I really felt for the characters and the outcome of the story really mattered to me. But with the 2nd Dishonored i really couldn't care less if anyone died or how the story ended. I felt like i'd wasted my time even playing the game.
I have in total around 70 hours on the the first Dishonored. I've finished the story more times than i can count and yet it's still a great experience everytime. even the DLC is good. After i finished Dishonored 2 i was pretty much done with the game. i didnt want to play it anymore. I found it very boring actually. I mean the Gameplay was great such an improvement on the first game, obviously the graphics were good but it just didn't have the same feel as the first game.
What i'm trying to say here it that if you're looking for the same experience you had in the 1st Dishonored you're not going to find it here. What you're going to find is a good looking game with nice mechanics but a very weak story. I am going to recommend this game, But just because i had a bad experience with this game (I've still got a soft spot for the 1st game)Doesn't mean someone else might enjoy it

Bottom line: play the original first. It's cheaper, runs better, it's a more interesting and cohesive experience and although the graphics are definitely last gen it has a stronger aesthetic than its sequel.
i5-4690 and a GTX 1060 and the game chokes in certain areas. The engine is based on id Tech 5 so expect plenty of blurry pop-in and general sluggishness.
Gameplay wise Dishonored 2 is a incremental improvement over it's predecessor in most ways; more powers, more toys, more gimmicks and more options. Guards are less stupid, more alert and guard chatter is far less grating and repetitive than before. There are even a couple of levels I expect people will be talking about from years to come.
With all that praise out of the way let's move onto the bad. Dishonored 2 has a tiny core cast consisting entirely of characters returning from the previous game. Despite all of them sharing significant history together they rarely interact and have no chemistry. Even the Heart of Dunwall returns, weaker than ever (but it can conjure jedi holograms now), to say very little. The plot is similarly barren, you could describe 95% of it with your objectives checklist. Perhaps the biggest crime is the complete lack of 'downtime objectives.' Between missions in Dishonored you would often be tasked with a minor errands, through these you learn more about the characters and the world while also giving you a breather between missions. The absence is more than a little disappointing.
Karnaca as a location is not a fraction as well realised as Dunwall. I mostly blame this on the far less varied locations, although you'll be seeing the bay from different areas you'll mostly be navigating through non-descript residential areas in various states of (dis)repair. While I expect most players will remember the Clockwork Mansion long after they finish the game I expect far more will recall Dishonored's Golden Cat brothel, Lady Boyle's party, the trains of plague-dead and the water-logged slums.
tl;dr For every step forward in one area there's at least two steps back in another.

Believe me, I really wanted to give this game a positive review, I really did. But I don't think it's worth £15/$18 for the following reasons:
I loved the first and second instalment but I must say this is the weaker of the three. I was devastated to find out that the composer passed away during the development of the second game, because I feel like this chapter and its ambience noticeably suffers. The first two games had a nice feel-good Caribbean atmosphere to them and this last one just seems to take a giant leap into a different genre, as if they were desperate to push a grand plot in the last game. I watched the trailer after completing the game and was surprised to see that they chose to highlight that rock and roll was gonna save the day... it's just so far from their initial vision.
I'm also disappointed to see that they used what looks like cheap particle effects (eg. gifs of explosions) and that they've left in a bunch of jagged artefacts from the animation (wish I could include screenshots here, but oh well), which makes this game feel as if they rushed the release. The juice girl and Lina's voice acting were a bit awkward and the puzzles were less complicated than I expected.
All this being said, I did like the end and the puzzles were fun to complete. The general animation was amazing and had great frame rates, and the composition of the camera shots were nice and effective in building suspense. Generally, the backgrounds were beautifully designed, although it feels like the developers were unsure of what they wanted to do with the game so they just threw in every possible environment (beaches, evil caves, snowy mountains, cyberpunk cities... what?).
I just want to end this by saying that I know I'm being harsh on this game, but it's out of love. I know they already had to push this release back from August til now, I just wish they hadn't set a deadline and instead had taken all the time they needed to polish the small details, because this is one of the best point and click series and I think it deserved something more.
TLDR: Overall it was an alright game, but it is weak in comparison to the past releases and lacks some polish. I would have let it slide if it weren't for the price tag.
