The thing you need to know about this game is that it is, fundamentally, an MMORPG first. While Is does have a notable Elder Scrolls flavour, which sets it apart from games like WoW, it is still a fairly generic MMORPG.
Now that we've set that precedent, what makes it different to previous ES titles, and what makes it different from other MMOs?
Well, unlike previous elder scrolls titles, they have done away with the loot system for a more classic MMORPG system. To me, this is a negative, if a person I just murdered has a chest peice or a weapon I like, I should be able to take it. Considering the crafting system in this game though, I do understand that it would be rather broken had it gone that direction. The ESO team has also mostly done away with the spell system of previous titles in favor of a varient of the generic MMORPG spell system; instead of buying or finding books that you learn a spell from, any spell from, you must level up and choose which spells, out of a given set dependant on your class, that you wish you learn, and then spend skill points to learn them. Alternatively, you can choose to spend your skill points on passive skills, crafting skills, armor skills, racial skills, and a plethora of other skills. All of the skill fields available to you must first be leveled up, a la Elder Scrolls, before you can take any of the associated skills. You can also jump while sprinting, which is glorious.
Which brings us to the differences between this and most MMOs. When using spells (active skills) there is generally an indicator of some sort which allows others to interupt the spell if timed correctly. This is, to me, a must-needed addition to the ES games, in general, and more specifically to an MMO installment. It adds a nice sort of depth to physical combat that you just don't see in most MMOs. To add to that, the first person camera, blocking, and the fact that there is no autoattack, means that you are always actively a part of the fighting. And no, wizards, sorcerers, warlocks, and the like are not left out of this. Since you can cast spells while both of your hands are full, you can choose to become a spell sword, weilding physical weapons and magic alike, or if physical fighting simply disgusts you, you can also use staves that act very much the same as normal weapons, but instead cast a small spell, element dendendant on the staff itself, that does not consume magicka.
The pay shop I have heard is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I, having only played ~10 hours, have not had a problem with it at all.
The questing, collection of materials, and looting is all very MMO (though the questing does seems quite a bit more creative than most MMOs), which, as a non-MMO player, is rather disappointing, but the combat, the way you explor the world, and the lack of tens of thousands of names swarming the screen, makes for a fairly Elder Scrolls experiance.
Overall it's a good game; just enough elder scrolls to please the ES crowd, and just enough MMO to please the MMO crowd. While I might not suggest ot for full price, if you can find this on sale for ~$20, I'd certainly suggest getting it if you are at all interested in MMOs or ES.

This game kind of resembles Dota, HOWEVER IT DOESNT HAVE EVERYTHING IT HAS!!! There are more then just Lane games, or normal, pick games. Players can choose to either pick an Arena match ( A battleground in a small circle formation, like the Arena in Europe) to fight other players, or A.I. in, Assault, which players ARE GIVEN a certain god, but can change with Favor (Ingame Currency), or Gems (Money Bought Currency), Joust, a 3v3 match map (Stuck with the annoying Chinese one last checked... Nothing wrong with the Chinese, but this should have been changed back after Chnese New year, just saying, it gets rather old...), Conquest, a resemblence of Dota's gameplay, 3 lanes 2 towers, but a twist, A phoenix (Which if it falls, your side/enemy side, who ever gets the others killed, gain a buffed minion spawning till it returns.), and a TITAN (Which fight backs, and hits heavier then anything per hit, and stacks its damage boost on a target.), Siege, where your in the amazon jungle and you can summon the aid of a siege beast upon killing the middle boss, or, the number of Gods slain, and last but not least, the RANDOM challenge.... This is most odd, but fun at the same time, each week/day (Depends on the event) you can have a whacky rule changed game, such♥♥♥♥♥10000000gold upon start for Items, and other things, and other things like, God restrictions or allowance of more then once (That can be bad....) There is also an area to try items out, for building your gods.
Items, more then Dota has to offer, Smite has balanced Items that can prove most useful to the certain gods, such as melee penetration, nerfing effects(Deductiong attack power, speed, defenses, resistances... That kind of Nerf), Magical Power increasement plus after hit effects, like slowness, and decreasement of regeneration and healing abilites.... Movement and attack speed items, Crit chances and resistance. So many trinkets and odds and ends to help players kick enemy team♥♥♥♥♥ Among items, there are skins for gods, a different look from certian events, (Such as Fenrir with Xmas time event) and have Voicepacks that allow you to tell teamates with an ingame shout like your favorite god.
There Is lore on each and everygod, telling you thier story, and why they were deemed, GOD, or Godlike. Each one has a very powerful story, or, a very wise and true learning experience!

I don't think that "remastered" means what Gearbox thinks it means. While the game has had a significant face-lift bringing the graphic detail of the units and surrounding space to current resolutions. The major drawback is that they didn't really remaster many of the controls or flesh out some much-needed tactical options like "don't deliberately crash into asteroids" or "hey, guys everyone come here… except you, go chase that guy and die!". A lot of the UI feels a sloppy instead of being tightly bolted down and intuitive and much of what you didn't like about the original is still there in large parts. In a few cases it's made worse with widely variable strafing that will make you question whether your frigate captains are actually cats high on catnip. The graphics are fantastic, but the game is largely unchanged and not improved upon where it was sorely needed. As an unnecessary bonus, I can make the menu UI take up 90% of the screen.

Where to start....
Dishonored 2 is set 15 years after Dishonored 1. Dishonored 2 a good game, choppy at release but still a good game.
The game starts off pretty much the same way as the previous Dishonored, story wise that is.  But i still think that the Dishonored 2 story was very weak, Compared to the previous Dishonored. Dishonored 1 was a story about the Royal protector of the Empress who was framed for her murder. And he needed to redeem himself and Save Emily. In Dishonored 2 Emily is a young woman who loses the throne once again and needs to get it back. I'll try not to spoil the game but I can't promise anything.
I felt much more connected to the storyline in the first Dishonored than the second. The first Dishonored started with you coming home early to deliver a letter to the empress, when you get to her you gets assassinated by the one and only Daud. Your goal in the first game is to Find Emily and save the kingdom from certain doom.
In Dishonored 2 your only goal is pretty much saving Corvo (or Emily) and taking your throne back. It just feels like there was a massive hole in the story. When i finished the 1st Dishonored I really felt for the characters and the outcome of the story really mattered to me. But with the 2nd Dishonored i really couldn't care less if anyone died or how the story ended. I felt like i'd wasted my time even playing the game.
I have in total around 70 hours on the the first Dishonored. I've finished the story more times than i can count and yet it's still a great experience everytime. even the DLC is good. After i finished Dishonored 2 i was pretty much done with the game. i didnt want to play it anymore. I found it very boring actually. I mean the Gameplay was great such an improvement on the first game, obviously the graphics were good but it just didn't have the same feel as the first game.
What i'm trying to say here it that if you're looking for the same experience you had in the 1st Dishonored you're not going to find it here. What you're going to find is a good looking game with nice mechanics but a very weak story. I am going to recommend this game, But just because i had a bad experience with this game (I've still got a soft spot for the 1st game)Doesn't mean someone else might enjoy it

Bottom line: play the original first. It's cheaper, runs better, it's a more interesting and cohesive experience and although the graphics are definitely last gen it has a stronger aesthetic than its sequel.
i5-4690 and a GTX 1060 and the game chokes in certain areas. The engine is based on id Tech 5 so expect plenty of blurry pop-in and general sluggishness.
Gameplay wise Dishonored 2 is a incremental improvement over it's predecessor in most ways; more powers, more toys, more gimmicks and more options. Guards are less stupid, more alert and guard chatter is far less grating and repetitive than before. There are even a couple of levels I expect people will be talking about from years to come.
With all that praise out of the way let's move onto the bad. Dishonored 2 has a tiny core cast consisting entirely of characters returning from the previous game. Despite all of them sharing significant history together they rarely interact and have no chemistry. Even the Heart of Dunwall returns, weaker than ever (but it can conjure jedi holograms now), to say very little. The plot is similarly barren, you could describe 95% of it with your objectives checklist. Perhaps the biggest crime is the complete lack of 'downtime objectives.' Between missions in Dishonored you would often be tasked with a minor errands, through these you learn more about the characters and the world while also giving you a breather between missions. The absence is more than a little disappointing.
Karnaca as a location is not a fraction as well realised as Dunwall. I mostly blame this on the far less varied locations, although you'll be seeing the bay from different areas you'll mostly be navigating through non-descript residential areas in various states of (dis)repair. While I expect most players will remember the Clockwork Mansion long after they finish the game I expect far more will recall Dishonored's Golden Cat brothel, Lady Boyle's party, the trains of plague-dead and the water-logged slums.
tl;dr For every step forward in one area there's at least two steps back in another.

Rome 2 continues Creative Assembly's Total War franchise by revisiting the Roman Era in this latest installment. The graphics are better, the campaign map is massive, the factions are numerous, but overall the game feels soulless.
Compared to previous titles, this effort has been streamlined to the point of depriving it of the core of its Total War components.
The characters presented as generals and agents are meaningless as you recruit them from a pool of endless nobodies. The one turn per year also means they die quickly, to only be replaced by more meaningless nobodies. Armies are limited with artful but seemingly lazy unit cards. Naval battles remain broken in most aspects. Sieges remain improved but still broken. Diplomacy is improved but remains uninteresting. Their new politics system is improved but continues to struggle to be interesting.
The only thing that really saves and sells this game is the modding community and their mods. Pick through the massive selection to implement the component that the devs were either too lazy or unable to impement themselves.
Overall, I would recommend the game, but with a grain of salt. Overall, A wasted potential and shameful display.

First off let me just say that I have been a huge fan of Total War since the first time I was introduced to the game series when Shogun total war 1 came out. Since then I have been impressed with the continued advances in graphics, gamplay, politics and replayability.
With that said here is "my own experiences" of Rome Total War 2 since the updates.
Graphics - Absolutely stunning when you first start out from building to unit detail even the campaign map is very well done! You can zoom right in and see rivets in armour, dents in shields etc it really is aweome.
Gameplay - Heres where things get a little tricky. Before the updates if you didnt play as Rome you basically had the same units as every other faction however since the updates there have been improvements to unit variety, unique units and of course additional mercenaries. These updates did add to the fun you'll have during battles and give you a bit more flexibility.
Buildings have also been diversified to give you a better sense of which factions you are playing which had not been included previously.
Combat - With the new land, naval and combined battles you can have a lot of fun with very diverse tactics when taking a city, defending or just surprising an army along a coast. One thing Id like to see is greater access to rivers with navies.
Politics explained! Have you ever wondered why a faction hates you? Well wonder no more as you can just drop your mouse over the faction in diplomacy and see what you did to make the faction angry or happy which is really really helpful!
The new provincial system as I had said before the update is very different from Total War Rome 1 as multiple cities make up your province instead of one main city per province. While I do like the new provincial concept I much prefered the previous system of one main city per province due to the fact you have far more cities to take that way.
Technology - The tech tree is nothing special. pretty similar to most RTS game tech trees which saddens me because in previous games historical dates dictated when a faction recieved upgrades to units where as now you can just rush to get the tech level you want. Depending on your play style you may enjoy this change or dislike it.
Encyclopedia - Is full of information but does not have the same level of information available in previous games leaving you to search for the information yourself on whatever search engine you prefer.
Wonders - Wonders are many in this game but good for nothing. In previous games you recieved a nice little bonus for capturing wonders and even a quick bit of the wonders history however in this game you will receive no bonus and no information.
Replayability - As you can see i have logged almost 500hrs playing this game and will still play more. It is a great game with few drawbacks.
If you're a first timer to the total war series you'll love this game however if you are a returning player you'll be missing some of the older games historical accuracy.

Black Mesa is a sci-fi first person shooter game developed by Crowbar Collective for a modified Source engine. Relive the classic but fresh B-Movie-esque adventure in this polished remake of the 1998 game Half-Life, following the exploits of physicist gone action hero, Gordon Freeman, as he sets out to escape the science facility he works for after it has been overrun by aliens.
I've played this game multiple times back when it was just a 2007-SDK mod, and this most recent playthrough was still engaging and kept my attention. I appreciated the "surface tension uncut" feature, which restored some previously stripped sections of the gameplay from the Surface Tension chapter. I played this session alongside the "OaR Loop Mod (OaR Uncut Version)" as well as "On a Rail Uncut" which did the same for the On a Rail chapter, and quite frankly turned On a Rail onto my favorite, and probably best paced chapter in the game.
In terms of gameplay, we're looking at a solid campaign that lasts about 12 hours if you only kind of know what you're doing. Some of the issues that plague Half-Life 2 also crop up here, such as the bullet-spongey enemies, imprecise movement, and some other small annoyances. It is a very fun game, either way, with all the quality pacing from the original Half-Life but fine tuned and beautified. An enormous level of work went into these maps and the effort pays off. I do think the weapons could do with a bit more tangible "punchiness" since the animations and sound effects of some of the guns completely oversell their actual usefulness in-game.
From what I can tell, Black Mesa has been in development for quite a long time. Developed by an intrepid group of volunteers and fans, the slight amaturishness does shine somewhat leeringly through the seams, but at the very least it shines in a pretty lovely color, with god rays no less. This entire game is actually pretty lovely to look at, although for its ambitions, it might overload the poor old Source engine to its maximum capacity. There are plenty of lovely features to enhance the visuals of this remake/remaster, but all taken together causes some wild variance in framerate and some pretty egregious dips. Even after releasing the long promised finale fourth act of this game sometime next year, its pretty clear even more work will have to go into this product long after the finished campaign, just to fix what is some poor optimization and the occasional bug here or there. For the most part, howeverm the experience is as smooth as the Source engine would normally promise and as such allows for plenty of in game options to taper down some of the lovely effects in exchange for a more reasonable framerate situation.
As a remake of Half-Life, this is an absolutely stellar product. Reinterpretations and newly allowed elaboration makes for a polished experience, but even with the lense flare it still feels true to the original '98 masterpiece, and in many ways surpasses it. If you've never played Half-Life, I still recommend you check it out since it goes dirt cheap in almost any sale steam holds, but if the originals graphics or fidelity just don't do it for you, then absolutely consider this game as a reasonable and servicable alternative. I really did enjoy the HD models of old HL-1 exclusive monsters such as the houndeye and bullsquid. The soundtrack as well is amazing and has replaced the original soundtrack on my Half-Life series playlist.
Overall I do recommend this game. Some real passion went into this but it is as sloppy as it is masterful. Despite its occasional stumbles, however, it really is a charming little game, and occasionally thrilling and awe-stricking.

It's really cool to play HL again with better but faithful graphics. It's worth buying this on sale just for that, even without the Xen levels. There's a few things that still bug me, though.
The source engine's physics don't really benefit the game, what's the value in being able to shove boxes around? It doesn't make the game better and sometimes gets in the way. The one thing I would have enjoyed is more destructible stuff, like being able to shoot out lights and electronics (always feels cool), maybe even being able to use monitors to view cameras Duke3D style, this is stuff the source engine is good for but it's not used at all. The worst part is that YOU CAN'T GIB CORPSES WITH YOUR CROWBAR! What the hell is up with that? Just being able to throw around paint cans and CRT monitors doesn't add much to the game.
Performance on my PC is a little weird. When I get hit by a bullsquid's splash for example, it takes a second to load that particular asset and the game stutters. This only happens for certain particular things whereas the game runs smoothly otherwise.
The weapons are a little wonky, revolver isn't nearly as satisfying, using the shotgun feels strange. Sometimes it will kill in one hit from a distance but take two hits on the same enemy if I try it point blank. If a soldier hasn't noticed me yet I can throw a grenade at their head and they'll just stand there, which is kind of amusing but shouldn't work that way.
I don't really like the HL2 style zombies. Their furniture throwing mechanic is never threatening, in fact zombies are never threatening at all. This was already kind of true in the original game but somehow they feel even more sluggish in Black Mesa. They just need work. The tentacles in blast pit somehow seem to notice me no matter what I do, even if I crouchwalk. The best strategy is to just throw a grenade and rush through, taking fall damage, it used to be much more tense as you had to sneak past them. The ichtyosaur similarly isn't nearly as scary despite the cool scripted introduction scene, I didn't hear its terrifying growling noise and it's slower and less dangerous than in Half Life, kind of a let down because the ichty and the tentacles were the highlights of the game.
Most of the level changes are for the better and there's a few cool surprises, I like the look of the green ooze and the removal of some of the boring parts, but it still needs work. Reworking some of the weapons and enemies, particularly the ichtyosaur and tentacles is more important than finishing the Xen levels.
I would wait for Xen update rather than waiting for HL3.

Played the original Half Life for the first time some years back. When I heard about this, I was going through Half Life 2 for the first time and it seemed like a good opportunity to replay Half Life reskinned to look and feel similar to HL2. As much as I wanted to overlook this fact, HL1 was just dated, from the visuals to the gameplay. However, despite this, it was still a memorable experience and felt like if they just had the appropriate technology, the gameplay and story could really shine.
Well, what we have here at the moment is not THE best thing you can imagine, but it's pretty close to great. All of the horror aspects of HL1 are played up because it feels more and more like you are going through this vivid nightmare on what was supposed to be a routine day at work. The blood and lighting effects, the mutilated faces of the lab assistants, the fire and explosions, the more realistic Xenomorphs, etc. It's similar to HL2 in terms of gameplay and visuals, but the outdated character models and voice work leaves something to be desired, and that is really my only gripe to what is an otherwise stellar experience so far (and mind you, I am only in the beginning towards the end of Anomalous Materials).
Basically, they reused some of the same scientist models, including voice work that sounds distinctly like the same person having a conversation with the same person. Same with the security personnel. Same few character models and same few voice actors from the original game. This is one of those things that could really have been redone here, though I don't know if the creators plan to keep it like this simply to be true to the original. It's immersion-breaking, but it's only one part of the game, so I am going to go ahead and say that it probably will not get in the way of this being not only a faithful reskin of the original, but also an improvement on it (after all, 20 years has passed and it's destined to feel dated in some regards).
Now, most people know we don't have Xen yet, and the Dec. 2017 release date is being pushed back, but having got this on sale for around $8, I am super excited, because it's clear that a lot of love went into making it great. It's a long game and a classic experience. Of course, once I get through the game closer to Xen, I will reupdate this review. For now, it's a definite must-buy for fans of the Half Life series and 90's gaming in general.

Let me start by saying that anyone who enjoys classic platformers will absolutely love this. Whether you played Sonic, Mario, Donkey Kong, Duke Nukem, or Contra back in the day, you will love this. Trust me on this. I haven't had this much fun with a platform game for a very long time, and it's given me that same kind of rush when completing a level the old games gave me back when I was a kid.
It's basically a "run to the end and destroy everything"-kind of game, but the many different characters add a very nice touch to it. The characters, "bros", each have two different weapons. Characters change every time you liberate one, or when you die. Both happen quite a lot. This means you will have to adapt your playing style several times each level. It's a game that constantly keeps you on your toes, and most levels are surprisingly creative. The fact that you can completely destroy everything also adds a lot of depth to the gameplay.
The graphical style works really well for this game, and it actually manages to look pretty impressive when things are going wild and explosions are going off everywhere. Then there's the atmosphere... the 80s/90s action movie characters, the hard rockin' soundtrack loaded with guitar solos, the ultra-violence and non-stop explosions... it's pretty damn awesome.
Do yourself a favor and get this one.

This is a beautifully crafted point-and-click adventure game worthy of big production company like Walt-Disney. Bear in mind, this game was created by only 3 people and the finished product is astounding. The art, the sound and the music is flawless. The voice acting is the best I have ever heard by a small Indie company. This is a game for people of all ages. The Journey Down Saga continues with our three main characters Lina, Bwana and Kito. The setting starts off in cave Kwayerumoshi and you discover Thauri deities & culture with Nyakazho a Thauri King/Tyrant that ruled the world 4000 years ago. There is also humorous dialogue. It is a fun game for the whole family and a big thumbs up!

I was a backer on the Kickstarter campaign. A great ending to the trilogy, Journey Down: Chapter Three is a fun and satisfying conclusion. The writing and voice-acting are just as good as Episode 2 with some fun new characters. The soundtrack is fantastic, shifting a little bit away from the previous episodes' jazz and reggae to a straight up John Carpenter-esque 80's action movie soundtrack with synths and sax, perfect for the dystopian metropolis of St. Armando. The atmosphere is also fantastic, St. Armando looks great. Episode 3 is a bit on the linear side compared to the others but its paced well and the puzzles, while not going to keep you befuddled for long, are logical which is more important for adventure game puzzles I feel.
The only problem I had was the framerate in the cutscenes can just drop. I also had crashes during cutscenes but there is an easy fix outlined in the Steam forums by Skygoblin, but it doesn't completely solve the lag.
Overall The Journey Down trilogy is another great addition to the new age of PC adventure games. Definitely pick them up.

Chapter 3 completes The Journey Down series by delivering the same great storyline, humour and puzzles but take a giant step up in lots of places too, to make it a fitting, epic finale to a game that will surprise you when you realise the size of the indie team behind it.
The locations and the art are stunning. You might find yourself taking a few minutes just to stare at the screen. As always the voice acting is excellent but this episode adds even more top talent that work together so well. The soundtrack was in danger of being something that couldn’t live up to previous chapters with the sad passing of Simon D’Souza, but Jamie Salisbury continues the beautifully written soundtrack and, with the addition of a more 80s themed game, comes some very solid tracks that sound like they were directly plucked from that period.
The puzzles aren’t overly hard, and it could be argued that they could be a bit more difficult in places, but they are logical and fit around the story well.
The ending to the game is, in the true sense of the word, epic. I’ll be very sad to see the back of Bwana and his friends but I feel fulfilled and like that story had enough substance to make me glad it rounded out how it did.
A quality game from a very talented team that any adventure game fan should pick up. Definitely get the trilogy if you haven’t played the others because it’s all about the story. Kick back and enjoy some humour, beautiful music, stunning art and a great story.

I cannot tell you the countless hours I've put into the original homeworld series. I was a super huge fan of the entire thing, even the never mentioned cataclysm. To say I was excited to see this game remastered was an understatement.
For those that are not familiar with homeworld: It's a fantastic space strategy simulation game. You use your massive motherships as space factories and face off against other ships/factions. The scale of combat expands quickly from smaller fightercraft all the way up to massive capital ship battles. It features a harvesting economy, salvage, ship theft & invasion, and a lot of research and development to keep your fleet operating and developing in a fashion of gameplay that you enjoy. The HIGHLIGHT of this game is that it's fully 3D. You can make attacks and travel along the Z axis freely.
As a returning player, the remastered game has exceeded all my expectations.
1) The new graphics engine upgrades are gorgeous, giving you a much more believable/enjoyable visual experience.
2) Multiplayer: Has been masterfully reworked so that the kushan, higaaran, taidan & vagyr all fight in the same maps. Each one has it's own distinct (yet familiar) style of gameplay, and benefits.
3) With Steam support, the mod packs of this game are exceptionally easy to use! You can quickly "subscribe" to mods, and flick them on & off at a whim!
I HIGHLY suggest this to anyone who is either a returning player wishing to re-kindle some nostalgea, or to new players who wish to experience one of the best space tactical games out there to-date.
P.S. For those who throught homeworld was great buy easy, try the complex 9.1 mod! It upgrades the game in almost every way!

The remastered collection delivers fantastic visuals and good voice overs with the same excellent plot and unique gameplay that made Homeworld a legend. The single player mode is a true jewel with immersive gameplay and captivating narratives.
The online multiplayer features are still being developed, which is great since the OG series was very limited multiplayer-wise.
Gearbox did modify some details about the original gameplay style and I think this is a negative. I am hoping a patch can be released in the near future that can bring back the old ballistics model as well as the usefulness of tactics and formations (the remastered series is a bit sluggish with in-combat unit management) in order to return to the true homeworld tactical depth while retaining the new visuals.
All in all, a timeless classic and definatly a title worthy of any collection.

A beautiful reskin of the original, but a surprising amount of gameplay bugs are pretty readily apparent:
- formations do not work AT ALL: ships can be moved into one, but they disintegrate entirely upon combat, and strike craft are now almost a complete waste of money since they get individually picked off way too fast.
- no evasive tactics mode to harass/delay enemy units
- salvaged ships can't be retired until the next map
- friendly units will fire on ships on their way to be salvaged
- salvage corvettes can't intelligently divide up multi-ship captures anymore
- healing units don't watch over not-yet-damaged units correctly
Other surprising design choices:
- research cost a bit of money now (OK)
- LOTS more resources on maps, including salvagable capital wreck scap, means things feel MUCH easier now
- strike craft no longer use fuel, reducing need for forward support frigate/carrier deployment
This game need one or more patches BADLY.
I will be happy to change my review to recommend it once the issues get fixed, since it's still a solid design at its core.

OK I have actually had this game for 2 years and I have at least 5 hundred hours in this game (I think I'm going to break my game time in Unreal Tournament 2004 almost 2 thousand hours if I include my steam time). The game is more or less about building and maintaining a factory. The devs update this game very often which i like about them, I have yet to incounter a bug of any sort in the game. The guy they got doing the programming is a genius he will fix bugs that I havent even encountered in the game. The game is pretty damn well optomized as well on my largest factory I was only getting 8 FPS. That was with 100 or more trains running plus another 50 waiting in reserve, 2k solar pannels 2.5k accumulators and I don't even know how many smelters and assembly machines. I also built and army of logistic robots and constrution robots that would put  China's military to shame, I always get 60 FPS untill the senario mentioned above, but I digress.
The controls are what you would expect from any top down game the game world can be as large as you want it to be, all the way up to infinite (that is how I play most of my games). The music is ok even though it is only one song it tends to grow on you, but I do tend to turn the music off and play my own in the back ground. Theres also a good tech tree they kept it simple which I like not to complicated trying to use fancy names and what not ( I'm looking at you SOTS and Endless Space).
I have so much fun with this game I dont ever see myself getting tired of it anytime soon (or at all ). When you build your factory for the first time you will start to notice that you could do something better that you didnt realize before. So you will be constantly building and modifing your factory. I will say don't be afraid to completely destroy your factory and rebuild it to something better that is what the game is all about. Buy this game it may be early access but after playing it for a while you really wont know the difference It has more content and stuff to do in it than most triple A games. It may not have the graphical polish of those games, but what it has works for it very well. I hope they don't change the graphics to the game I like them the way they are.
In conclusion the game is well worth the asking price you will not be disappointed. You will have hundred if not thousands of hours of fun building different factory's. Oh and one more thing let me touch on the bitters for a minute, do not run out and start destrying a lot of their bases in the early game. From what I have seen the more of their bases you destroy the faster they evolve into higher tiers. And before you know it you are being hit by big bitters and spitters. This early access game should be the corner stone of how we judge a EA game, because if you think about it they put all other EA games and some of the devs to shame. Like said before BUY this game you won't be disappointed. 100/100 Keep up the good work gentelmen.

While normally i would nitpick and write a negative review just to get the game down from 99% i must admit that it's hard to find any serious flaws with Factorio.
I've been following it since 2014 and i can say that i've yet to encounter a broken release or a serious game breaking bug despite the game being in an alpha stage. The steady stream of decent updates and developer communication is what puts this game on par with kerbal space program, prison architect, grim dawn or craft the world and it's just one of those early access games done right for a change.
What you should understand about Factorio that it's not a minecraftesque game. It's not Starbound, it's not Terraria and it's not a crafting-survival game to begin with. It's closer to Big Pharma, Capitalism or Settlers as you are tasked with building numerous production chains rather than specific items for a specific purpose. It also has elements of tower defence/base building and just a bit of strategy gameplay for when you attack alien nests but that's it - this is mostly an economical micromanagement game which relies heavily on it's fanbase and people like me who actually enjoy micromanaging stuff.
While some will inevitably dislike the whole concept - i find having a lot of "stuff" to manage and build more liberating than having to simply dig dirt and build houses... even though i admit that i like crafting games too.
From what i've seen over the years this game can only get better as the developers seem to understand how good games suppose to work - there's balance between building, defending, expanding and recently they added an end goal as well. I can only imagine what would modders do to this game after they add workshop and in game mod support since it's quite easy to add new stuff and overhaul the game completely.
Even in it's current state it is definitely worth trying so i can actually recommend it. But if you want to wait - wait for a version 0.13 which is going to add a lot of new stuff or for a workshop support.

One of my personal favourites, I just love the story, setting and characters of Enslaved. You play as Monkey, an athletic and strong man that ends up with Trip, a technology-savvy, intelligent and beautiful woman. They must stick together in order to survive in the wilderness of post-apocalyptic America.
Story: I really like what Ninja Theory have done to modernize and put a sci-fi twist on the classic Chinese story of Journey to the West. Throughout your travels, Monkey and Trip develop a strong relationship with a hint of romance, that is both endearing and heartwarming. This rapport between the two is interrupted by Pigsy, an eccentric, fat man with a knack for technology and invention. He is very funny at times and I liked him as a character.
Graphics: The great use of the Unreal Engine 3 engine, allows the game to look stunning. The vistas are breathtaking and simply a joy to explore and collect Tech Orbs (which are used to upgrade Monkey's combat skills).
Gameplay: The game has simple yet satisfying combat for veteran and casual gamers alike. Some of the finishing moves look very cool in slow-motion and pulling off a dodge right before an enemy hits is immensely gratifying.
In summary, Enslaved is one of the most underrated games and I hope that Ninja Theory consider making a sequel to the game in the future as the story has a lot of potential to expand.

A random 3rd person action game I picked up because of praises by single reviewers (even though the average ratings were, well, average). It's an entertaining melee/climbing sort of thing with solid enough combat mechanics and a fluid climbing system where you mostly just chill and watch the acrobatics (generally you can't fall). It has a decent story as random action games go, and the dialogue/acting is rather good (e.g. Andy Serkis plays the protagonist). The setting is postapocalyptic, but this time it's not a barren wasteland - you find New York overtaken by lush plant life, for instance. Some of the enviroments are beautiful despite its age (it's a PS3/X360 game from 2010).
The game plays better with a console controller, except for the shooting parts (you get a ranged attack with very limited ammo), which become a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ There's also a couple of annoying chase sections. Generally it's an easy game.
So nothing revolutionary, no replay value (fully linear), but it's a good somewhat cinematic title with respectable writing and acting, good for a playthrough. I recommend it if you like the genre in general.
The "Premium Edition" on Steam comes with 3 DLC skins that give significant passive buffs (but can only be used after finishing the game once, unless you edit some .ini files yourself) and a shorter story mode with a more comical tone where you control a side character from the main game.

A Pleasent suprise!
Basics:
This is an "Endless Runner" style game where you are forced to run without stopping through an obstacle course of walls and barriers as well as "Grid bugs" and pick up "Bits" and power up cubes.
While running you have to do quite a bit of jumping, sliding, wall running and even gliding a bit with what looks like Parafoils which are attached to your back.
Review:
The game, though in very early access is a lot of fun. I really suck at "Twitch" type games in general, but this one is managable and a lot of fun. There are currently only 3 playable levels that introduce the different skills needed to play the game.
Level 1 is mostly jumping and throwing your disk.
Level 2 introduces wall running.
Level 3 introduces sliding and is the most challanging of the levels so far.
At the end of the level, you recieve a score that is based on how many "Bits" you pick up, how many hits you have remaining as well as other stuff im not sure about. :)
I use the keyboard and the mouse and the controls are excellent. (Rare for this type of game) and I have no problem with doing all the functions the game requires.
There are power ups you can purchase with points you get from completed levels, but so far with some exceptions I dont know exactly what most of them do. As this is in early beta, I am hoping that they add explanations to them to explain what they do later on down the road.
Once you get the hang of things, you can complete whats in the game now in about 15 minutes give or take. I am hoping they add new levels soon as I have already played the 3 missions in the game a lot of times and i am ready for more.
Summary:
This game is a lot of fun, I have already racked up 3 hours playing it and there really isnt much content yet so the groundwork for an excellent game is definetly there. If you are leary about "Twitch" games, (Hey, Im 51 years old and typically suck at twitch style games) give this one a shot and I think you will be pleasently suprised. I am sure the developers will jack up the price of the game as they get closer to completion, so get it while its cheap as I think this game will be a keeper.
According to what I am reading, they will have Light cycles soon....so that should be a hoot as well.

Homeworld and Homeworld 2 were the best real-time space strategy games ever made.  Every game made since then has tried to be them, and has fallen flat by comparison.
I am, however, still on the fence about the remastered versions of these games.  While they are graphically beautiful, without a doubt, a much needed upgrade to the visuals of the game, there are some differences in the missions, interface, and unit actions that I simply do not like.
The first thing that cheesed me off with the first game was the interface change.  While the interface for HW2 is, technically better, they changed unit behavior to match.  This is a huge problem when you assign a bunch of units to guard something important, put those units on sphere formation, and rather than surrounding the unit they are guarding and forming a ball of guns around it, they just sit there beside it in something akin to a circle and not being the defensive line you were expecting.  This is more a glitch than anything, because this tactic worked fine in the orignal HW2 (it was just harder to implement with the interface changes), and does not work at all in the remaster.
Some of the missions are very different from their original versions, making them much harder than they used to be.  There's a mission where your warp coordinates are incorrect and you warp into a moving asteroid field.  This is where I would normally turn into a wall of guns in front of my mothership, but aggressive tactics doesn't work on the asteroids in the remaster.  In addition to this, you are in the asteroid field longer than originally, so you have to prevent damage to the mothership for a much longer period of time.  This may not seem like a major issue unless you've already built several super-capitals and warp into the mission with 6 destroyers, each a fourth the size of the mothership, and these are getting taken out because they will only shoot the rocks you tell them to and it is impossible to defend them and the mothership from damage, leading to huge attrition and losses that were pointless.
Homeworld 1 and 2 were already challenging games.  There was no need to make it more challenging.  There was no difficulty selection back then.  Games had to be an acceptable challenge level right out of the gate with a smooth transition in their difficulty from the beginning of the game to end.  Putting players against BS odds is not making a game harder, it's making the player face BS.  There is a difference.  Don't believe me?  Play the first 8 levels of the original game, and then play the first 8 levels of the remaster.  Something will feel different and off.  While it may be prettier to look at, it simply won't feel as if you had as good an experience as you did the first time.
For those of you who never played this game when it first came out and felt the disappointment of games that just weren't as good that followed, you are about to enjoy one of the greatest games ever made, whether you are playing the original or the remaster.  Perhaps I'm simply jaded from waiting for similar games to even compete with this one since the death of Sierra with no good alternatives.  Perhaps my expectations are too high.  I don't know.  I will still recommend this game a million times over any other space RTS.  Relic and Sierra, I salute you for the awesomeness that were the originals.  Gearbox, I salute you for attempting to live up to the originals.

Let me start out by being fair and pointing out what Gearbox got right with HW:R - the ships look beautiful, it's quite obvious a lot of time and effort was spent lovingly crafting them and they feel very solid and real. The other eye candy like HDR and shadows is very welcome and really calls out to my first experiences of playing HW1 in 2000. Sounds and voice-overs are also remastered to a very high standard though some of the inflections aren't to my personal taste, but that's just me.
Now then, onto the bugs and why I can't recommend HW:R in its current state. If you've read the other reviews by now you'll probably have found some pointing out the bugs with formations and strikecraft in general. I am no purist, but quite frankly I think these issues have been understated so far. Not being able to put your fighters or corvettes into formations
affects the combat effectiveness of your strikecraft (less so for capitals). Since they refuse to maintain formation (regardless of tactics set) they will not fire en masse and you the player cannot position them precisely where you need and want them. A wall of just 9 heavy corvettes in HW1 would easily demolish a flock of enemy fighters if managed correctly. In HW1 the same force takes at least 3 times as long to complete the same engagement and you’ll probably take losses. I've seen positive reviews on here downplaying this issue which I find hugely disingenuous to say the least. I'm going to have to make a video showing HW1 and HW1:R side by side to really illustrate just how much this affects the game and almost everything you do in it, it really is that fundamental.
Formations aside, the path-finding for strikecraft again is quite poor. Ships like the heavy corvette with heavy forward firepower seem to insist on circling the enemy and trying broadsides to no effect, which is probably why the fights take forever to finish. Because your ships refuse to stay in formation they will also largely ignore player attack-move commands during combat (ctrl+A).
Other reviewers have already pointed out the firing system changes as well, but I really have to emphasise just how much this negatively impacts the game. Basically, in HW1 your ships would fire bullets that would actually travel through space i.e. no hitscan or RNG. Since this is no longer the case your ships are at the mercy of the Random Number Generator and setting them to evasion tactics has
no effect where as in HW1 it could vastly improve the survivability of your strikecraft.
I understand a lot of these changes were implemented to allow compatibility between HW1 and HW2 to enable multiplayer which is just fine imho. However, I consider the formations and tactics issues as bugs since they severely handicap HW1 strikecraft compared to their HW2 counterparts, not to mention that it robs the player of a huge degree of tactical control.
I love Homeworld, but being unable to control my strikecraft effectively reduces the whole thing to pumping out ships, sitting back and hoping for the best. The pathfinding and formations issues are major bugs and I hope to the almighty Gearbox get on top of this crap.

I wanted to like it but that's my fault for having high expectations from three years of labour spent on a 3-4 hour video game. Still, I honestly cannot recommend this game at anything close to original price.
As with many other projects spanning several years and several releases, this game series also seems to have lost its originally intended direction, and it's a damn shame.
- The game suffers from the same value for money spent issue as the earlier episodes (at their release).
- The puzzles are MUCH too easy and shallow, I could count the amount of long-lasting puzzles without obvious solutions on one hand; it feels like the puzzles were added afterwards to make an animated movie into barely a video game.
- The direction they went with in terms of ambiance and art style, however aesthetically pleasing to me, just seems really odd after having played the first two episodes. It's very far from having an "Afro-Caribbean" vibe. It just feels like the original direction of the trilogy was lost somewhere long ago and only the characters remained.
- Voice acting is remarkably atrocious at times. More often than not, this is due to poor mastering or recording, not due to the voice actors. Voiceovers and their scripts felt very rushed to me in several spots.
- The sountrack is great, it's absolutely amazing, actually. Jamie Salisbury did a really good job.
- The story, while forgettable and without any real plot twists, had a decent conclusion.
- While (as aforementioned) unfitting, the art is gorgeous and I found myself appreciating the scenery of the city in a lot of places, especially when accompanied by the unique soundtrack. I'm a sucker for Blade Runner-like gritty cyberpunk. Dark nights, neon lights and lit up highrises. Raised highways with cars whizzing past. Views of poverty, crime, prostitution, cigarettes, unhappy populace barely making due. I won't go more into detail in fear of spoiling parts of the plot, I think you get the idea.

A proper finale for this great series. I finished it in 4 hours and so will you, but it's definitely worth picking up anyway. The whole series has this amazing feel with fantastic locations, a great visual style and an over the top soundtrack.
Also, in my eyes, all three games surpass most point and click adventures by exclusively having logical puzzles rather than forcing you to try random thing combinations sooner or later.

Kickstarter backer here.
If you are here, you probably know about the other games at least, so I will get straight to the point. This third chapter provides a satisfying closure to the series, and that's good. It's all pretty low-budget, but the characters are ace and the story goes along nicely, and those are the most important things in an adventure game. There is a bit too much exposition this time around, especially with some stuff that was never even hinted at earlier, but it still manages to work fairly well.
Compared to the previous titles, it feels smaller. There are sveeral locations this time, rather than one bigger area to explore, but each location is very restricted. This does make it easier to see what's needed, and the hotspots are more obvious too (not to mention, "trying the whole inventory" has become easier as a result). Overall it's a bit shorter and easier than Chapter 2. This is not too bad however, since that one had me reaching for a guide a few times. No crazy logic jumps here... well, except a few, but it wouldn't be an old school adventure without a couple of those.
The trilogy overall is well worth playing. It's got highs and lows, and tends to peak in the middle, but there's as much charm as you need in an adventure and not too much brain fuming.

Chapter three is a fitting end to the trilogy. If you liked the first two, you'll like this one. Art, music, and voice acting remain just as strong.
The puzzles seemed much easier this time around––I was never stuck for more than fifteen minutes or so. This might be a good thing as inventory-based puzzle games can be illogical. While there were some clearly "absurd" solutions, it was always clear what to do. For the third game, it would have been nice to have had some harder non-inventory based puzzles. (For the record, I did have to look up some hints for both the first two chapters).
The story is satisfying yet holds no real surprises. Although everything wraps up nicely (in a climax not unlike a certain Star Trek movie, but the tone is far more appropriate here) it felt a bit rushed. It's just as long as the previous chapters, but there are so many story beats to cover that it feels at times that we're playing an abridged version of the storyline. I would have liked to have seen a bit more interaction and more dialog options among some of the heroes and villains in the endgame.
My biggest complaint is in the Underland itself: for all the buildup in the first two parts, it was a bit too generic-paradisey. I enjoy The Journey Down for its unique setting and characters, but the Underland itself didn't live up to the rest of the game, and it was a much more minor part of this chapter than I thought it was going to be.
I hope I'm not making the story sound worse than it it is. They are really minor issues all things considered, and TLJ remains my favorite of the new Lucas-style adventures that we've seen in the past few years. I certainly enjoyed it more than, say, Broken Age (and it felt much more complete than that game). I hope many people buy it so SkyGoblin can do something much more substantial next time around.

Imagine having to run for an exit, knowing that the Alien would come if you did, not knowing whether you'd make it -and have it slam into the door behind you- or whether you'd be torn to pieces. What's in the game? You run, trapping the alien behind the door, some peace. Oh look, a terminal! Let's look a what it has to say, how interesting, the Nostromo you say? *Clunk* huh?♥♥♥♥♥♥ Quick, lets hide in the cabinet to my left after I get my head out of this console. Where's the security placed here? The security is a save point that isn't logically placed or spaced, or consistent with reality. Where's the agency in this situation? The player has none. The player is stuck in an illogical animation. Where's the agency in the first example? The player's own movement.
The times this is utilised in Alien: Isolation are meaningless. You have agency to find the nearest hiding place and stay there until the Alien desides to♥♥♥♥♥♥off. That's is all. What to say about this one..?
Without giving away anything, this game is definitely an "edge-of-your-seat" thriller!
It's way better than Aliens: Colonial Marines, it does one thing that ACM didn't.., it forces you to outthink the alien rather than to "outgun" it.
In a nutshell, you are Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter, it's been 15 years since the Nostromo was reported missing, but it's about 42 years before Ellen Ripley is found in the movie Aliens. Anywho, you go to a space station in hopes of finding out what exactly happened to your mother, and it just so happens that the company (Weyland-Yutani) has found the flight data recorder, a.k.a., the black box from the Nostromo and taken it to this station for analysis.
Things are pretty quiet at first.., but not for long. Once you arrive at the station, it's obvious that something is seriously wrong and it only gets worse from there...
I haven't played all the way through the game yet, as of this writing, I've really only got started, but it's a suspenseful ride worthy of the original Alien movie!
One bit of advice that I can give on this game is, even on the easiest setting, this game is NOT easy! If you think you are going to grab this title and whiz through it in one night, I got news for ya, FORGET THAT IDEA RIGHT NOW!
You have to be cautious of EVERYONE on the station, the Alien is NOT the only threat. Some folks will help you, but they are far and few between. Most will try to kill you before you even get a chance to explain what you are doing there in the first place, and don't get me started on the "synths", or Working Joes as they are sometimes referred to. These buggers will ignore you one minute, then try to beat the living crap out of you the next, it's better to try and avoid them altogether, if at all possible.
Another little tidbit of advice.., if one synth sees you, they ALL will know where you are.
They apparently communicate with one another and will come from other areas to help the one that spotted you 'corral' you.., then they procede to beat the ever-lovin' crap out of ya... lol.
Overall, this game has a real "movie feel" to it, it really makes you feel like you are running and hiding for your life, pixellated or otherwise... lol.
You are forced to sometimes make split-second decisions on which way to go simply to escape enemies or even the Alien itself. While you can "fight off" the synths, don't even bother trying to take on the Alien, at least not in the beginning, trust me, you are no match for it early on in this game. You are better off honing your stealth skills and avoiding contact with the Alien as much as possible, at least until you can fashion a few more effective weapons later in the game... Oh, did I happen to mention that Amanda is a very skilled and crafty Engineer? No? Well, you'll find out, and don't forget to grab all the little "techie goodies" you can find, they will MOST DEFINITELY come in handy...
On that note, this game is as much an 'exploration' game as it is an 'evasion' game. To fashion those lovely techie goodies, you have to first find plans for them. These blueprints are scattered about in various places, some are easier to find than others so as not to miss any of them, it's best to look everywhere. This is where the stealth aspect comes in, some of these blueprints are in areas that are guarded by synths, or even worse, patrolled by the Alien.
The sound effects and musical score of this game really add to it's appeal in my book, it sets an atmosphere of both mystery and a strong sense of foreboding, especially in the darker areas of the station. And you know you are in major trouble when not only does your tracker say the Alien is close, but you can actually hear it banging around in the ventilation ducts and in the corridors of the station. It's not afraid of making noise, it doesn't fear you, but you sure as hell will fear it!
The A.I. (Artificial Intelligence) of this game is downright scary at times, even on the easiest difficulty. These critters actually appear to learn your habits, they begin to outthink you and cut you off from escape routes.
The A.I. for the Alien is even creepier.., this thing will track you, if you make noise, it WILL investigate it! It will also occasionally check personal lockers, so if you hide in one, be prepared to act if the Alien comes into the room looking around.
Another tidbit of advice: DO NOT try to outrun the Alien, it can't be done... This is why your tracker is your most important piece of equipment, and your best friend. It can help you keep some distance between you and the Alien.., for the most part. There will be times when you will just have to hide and wait the Alien out, so try to stay as close as possible to anything that might provide some cover, if only temporarily. Believe it or not, the best way to avoid the Alien, is to keep moving.., and most importantly, keep moving QUIETLY. When you do have to hide fast, look for crates and equipment to duck behind, look for tables and desks that you can crawl under and hide, but some of the best places to hide are closets and personal lockers. Their only drawback is that they tend to make noise when you enter and leave them, so try not to hide in these places if the Alien is within 'ear-shot' of ya, it WILL hear you and it WILL come looking for whatever made the noise.
Big thumbs up on this one, if you like stealth games like Assassin's Creed and Splinter Cell, this one is a good choice. If you also happen to like the Alien franchise, this is a double thumbs up!!

When I originally tried out this game, I had no idea it would become one of my all time favorite games ever.
When you first start playing, you join an online lobby or make a lobby with friends on a map you're not familiar with. Nothing makes sense and everything is confusing. The default controls aren't incredibly intuitive, melee feels like it's worthless, you run out of stamina as with as little as two or three swings for some weapons, and although the guns feel great, good luck finding a decent amount of ammo (especially if you're playing online). But if you just have a bit a patience, remap some of the controls and understand that this isn't meant to be a fast-paced guns blazing action game, you might find yourself enjoying the game a little. Or a lot.
Someone, maybe one of the curators, I can't remember, said this game is similar to Resident Evil 2 only in first person, and I just love that comparison. I mentioned earlier that generally you might have a hard time finding a decent amount of ammo. If you're playing online with strangers, this pretty much always applies, however if you're playing with some friends, it's very possible you could get a nice stockpile of ammo going, especially if you're playing a survival map. In objective maps, however, ammo is very scarce for the most part. Occasionally, you might be blessed with more ammo than other runs, but the thing that makes this game always interesting and stressful (in a good way!) is that it's not usually very efficient trying to take on a horde of zombies, even with all the ammo you have. You're standing there, unleashing all of your might, but the longer you stand in one place, the more zombies start to come your way. It becomes too much, so your best chance is to try and run through and dodge as many zombies as you can, saving any ammo for when you really need it. It's really satisfying making it through the small openings you're given in a horde and potentially saving tons of ammo.
I also mentioned above that guns feel good, which is very true. Guns are a lot of fun to use in this game, and popping heads with bullets into a bloody burst feels as good as Resident Evil 4. They even made the piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥Ruger gun sounds way more satisfying in the last update they did, so even though the guns are still a piece of crap, at least they feel nice to use.
One thing that I love about this game is the difficulty. It's not easy. My friends and I have beaten every single official map, with one map in particular taking what seemed like weeks to get through (FEMA) and others taking days of attempts (Junction, Zephyr, and... Most of the survival maps, actually). This might seem like a weird comparison, but this game almost has that old "NES Hard" feel to it, because even though a lot of the times your plans are  foiled by zombies growing elastic arms and somehow hitting you after you shoved them away and blasted them point blank in the face with a ♥♥♥♥ing shotgun come ON HOW DOES THAT NOT KILL YOU, there's still an incredibly rewarding feeling from beating a map that kicked your♥♥♥♥♥tons of times. Oh, but uh, get some friends if you can, at least one, because I don't think most maps can be beaten solo. Also adding to the NES hard feel of the game is that most survival maps can actually be beaten in 10-20 minutes once you know what to do. They're fun to replay through too, because every single weapon in this game has an achievement, so if you're not playing with greedy scumbag strangers online, you and your friend(s) can decide over which weapons to use, changing how the run will go, even if slightly. Also adding to the replayability factor is that a lot of the item locations on maps are randomized. Some might dislike that sometimes you can get a fully loaded FN Fal on a table and other times a ♥♥♥♥ing flashlight, but in most cases, it's just different kinds of ammo, so it's nice to have some variety for the many times you will have to try to complete certain maps.
Speaking of maps, there are a lot of custom maps for this game too, which is awesome, because sometimes you just want something different. Truth be told, a lot of the custom maps I've played, survival ones especially, are easier than official maps, so if you're new to the game and having difficulties, it might be wise to try out some of the more lenient custom maps there are. I personally recommend a map called Museum, as it has a LOT of supplies to start you out with, and I really do mean a lot, and there are supply drops every few rounds as well. Plus the map looks good.
...And if you REALLY want to have a good time, download a map called "Mansion." You'll know you have one I'm talking about if the spawn point is always around a poker table on the second floor. Here's what you want to do, open the console command with the ~ button and bind the kill command to a key, preferrably one that's away from most of your other commmonly used keys so you don't acidentally kill yourself. Anyway, jump off the balcony towards the small railing and kill yourself in midair and watch your ragdoll smack against the railing and spaz out while it does flips and twirls as it flies off. Pure comedy gold, I promise you. Even better if you have a buddy to watch/join the fun.
Aside from that, do what you want! This game has a lot to offer, and it's FREE! This game made me buy Contagion, a $20 game also about zombies and survival. It's a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ at least compared to this completely free game. A darn shame, but now you have $20 bucks that you didn't spend on♥♥♥♥♥♥ you could buy TWO copies of the soundtrack for this game if you wanted.
A couple things to mention if you're still reading and are interested in the game:
"Mastering" melee combat is essential. First off, everytime you swing, SHOVE IMMEDIATELY AFTER. This will almost always hit the enemy and push them back, stopping them from attacking you, because you see, melee hits don't always stagger zombies, so you could swing a giant fubar at a zombie, crack its skull, and it's still swinging at you. Let me start out by being fair and pointing out what Gearbox got right with HW:R - the ships look beautiful, it's quite obvious a lot of time and effort was spent lovingly crafting them and they feel very solid and real. The other eye candy like HDR and shadows is very welcome and really calls out to my first experiences of playing HW1 in 2000. Sounds and voice-overs are also remastered to a very high standard though some of the inflections aren't to my personal taste, but that's just me.
Now then, onto the bugs and why I can't recommend HW:R in its current state. If you've read the other reviews by now you'll probably have found some pointing out the bugs with formations and strikecraft in general. I am no purist, but quite frankly I think these issues have been understated so far. Not being able to put your fighters or corvettes into formations
affects the combat effectiveness of your strikecraft (less so for capitals). Since they refuse to maintain formation (regardless of tactics set) they will not fire en masse and you the player cannot position them precisely where you need and want them. A wall of just 9 heavy corvettes in HW1 would easily demolish a flock of enemy fighters if managed correctly. In HW1 the same force takes at least 3 times as long to complete the same engagement and you’ll probably take losses. I've seen positive reviews on here downplaying this issue which I find hugely disingenuous to say the least. I'm going to have to make a video showing HW1 and HW1:R side by side to really illustrate just how much this affects the game and almost everything you do in it, it really is that fundamental.
Formations aside, the path-finding for strikecraft again is quite poor. Ships like the heavy corvette with heavy forward firepower seem to insist on circling the enemy and trying broadsides to no effect, which is probably why the fights take forever to finish. Because your ships refuse to stay in formation they will also largely ignore player attack-move commands during combat (ctrl+A).
Other reviewers have already pointed out the firing system changes as well, but I really have to emphasise just how much this negatively impacts the game. Basically, in HW1 your ships would fire bullets that would actually travel through space i.e. no hitscan or RNG. Since this is no longer the case your ships are at the mercy of the Random Number Generator and setting them to evasion tactics has
no effect where as in HW1 it could vastly improve the survivability of your strikecraft.
I understand a lot of these changes were implemented to allow compatibility between HW1 and HW2 to enable multiplayer which is just fine imho. However, I consider the formations and tactics issues as bugs since they severely handicap HW1 strikecraft compared to their HW2 counterparts, not to mention that it robs the player of a huge degree of tactical control.
I love Homeworld, but being unable to control my strikecraft effectively reduces the whole thing to pumping out ships, sitting back and hoping for the best. The pathfinding and formations issues are major bugs and I hope to the almighty Gearbox get on top of this crap.

I love the Homeworld series. It is beautiful in story and visuals, and fantastic gameplay and mechanics in the classics.
(Homeworld 1 RM review)
In short:
I was fanboying over the visuals and sound and was having fun until I encounted more and more bugs and poor design decisions. I got too disappointed with the quality of the game as a whole to continue playing. It is Gearbox trying to mash Homeworld 1 into Homeworld 2's engine and failed, and feels rushed.
In long:
Homeworld RM is a HUGE upgrade in visuals and quality (stupid sexy Taiidan Heavy Cruiser)
Sounds are cleaned up and sounds so much clearer and textures are great in HD (again Taidan Heavy Cruiser, I can't get over it!). UI was also updated and now a little bit more user friendly, no longer do you need to go to a WHOLE other screen for research, construction and hanger.
However, it is not without its bugs, and there are lots of bugs and poor design decisions.
Formations and Stances do not work as intended (I.E. Sphere formation do not surround targets, strike craft just break formations rendering formations useless. Stances do not give appropriate buffs like increased speed for evasive and increased fire power for aggressive.)
Some units are unnecessarily changed (I.E repair units must now "Dock" with their targets to repair instead of repairing from a range.)
Unit A.I. isn't all that good (I.E. strike craft tend to crash into asteroids and other objects in some missions)
Units lifespan seems to be significantly shortened (I.E. A whole strike group of frigates won't last five minutes against a single heavy cruiser, same for strike strike craft to frigates. Rendering smaller ships hard to use or even worth using)
Sound bugs (I.E. strike craft engines won't disappear if you hear them while docking)
First experience with Homeworld with steam workshop mod support and sound just ceased to exist and gameplay was barely playable.
And the most game breaking bug is RANDOM DESKTOP CRASHES
it seems that Gearbox was trying to mash Homeworld 1 and 2 together when them both use very different mechanics and really messed up Homeworld 1 RM. Homeworld 1 IS NOT homeworld 2.
I understand this is still new and update are incoming but for right now and my opinion is subject to change to updates. Until the game is more polished up and bugs ironed out, I just can't recommend this remaster in its current state. I still perfer to play the CD versions because it is much more stable. Even though this is just Homeworld 1 RM review, it is still half the package.

Factorio is a factory-building game.  You are on an alien planet.  Your goals are: secure resources, clear nests of indigenous creatures, build a factory that produces the materials you need, build a rocket, and launch a satellite into orbit.  You can build mining drills, assembly machines, transport belts, power plants, chemical processors, trains, flying robots, and plenty more.  The only limit is your ability to organize such a large factory (and your CPU's ability to simulate it, but there is a continuing effort to optimize the game engine).
Not enough?  Try some of the dozens of great mods that have been created by the community, from whole-game overhauls to minor tweaks to the UI, and many that add a single feature, like my personal favorite: the Orbital Ion Cannon.
Downsides:  The game is not yet complete, and there isn't a satisfying end-game (you just launch the rocket and you win).  Also not complete is the multiplayer hub and an official mod website.  You can still install mods and play multiplayer, it's just more manual to set up.
Did I mention trains? They're awesome, for expanding your reach to more remote resources, or organizing your factory in modules, also for getting around a large base in a hurry.

Early Access Review
I'd no idea a new Tron game was in the works so seeing TRON RUN/r was a pleasant surprise.
The game in it's current state is quite enjoyable and I look forward to further levels and conent.  Currently there is one mode available entitled "Disc" with three levels accessible.  You play an unknown program fleeing the system.  This is a runner style game where you follow a prearranged set path with your movement limited to:  left/right, duck, jump and are unable to speed up or slow down.
A number of powerups are available at the start of each level that you can purchase using energy bytes that you earn in game.  This allows you to customize your character with various power-ups and companions that can affect how you play a level.
The visuals in the game are remarkable and harken back to the look of Tron 2.0 (a great fps if you haven't played) combined with the character designs from the newer Tron Evolution game.  It is also amusing to see the devs giving nods to the source material when you rack up an "MCP Combo" or "Space Paranoid" combo to name a few.
