If we continue to get these console-based ports over on PC with all released DLC set for a lower price, I’ll stay happy. This is the second game I’ve personally played with that business model and I can’t complain. (Metal Gear Rising being the other).
The story is great, its well written and well paced, keeping the humor and/or seriousness of the situation at the right level the entire time. There’s plenty of emotional moments between the two main protagonists of Monkey and Tripp as they experience the hardships of the journey. The connection doesn’t feel forced, contrived or stupid. For the most part, it doesn't seem romantically driven either. A refreshing change of pace. Though there are plenty of hints that there’s a deep connection between the two. While Monkey gives off the impression of being a survivor, he still has good humor moments. Tripp is a great character as well both in-game and from the story aspect. She never feels like a hinderance or nuisance….well...when she doesn’t fall through the floor or get stuck on ladders. That happened to me a couple of times when playing the game. But when she isn’t getting bugged up, she’s a compelling character to learn about.
Most of the challenge or antagonism comes come from the environment and machines that were designed for one purpose: to kill humans. The robots have no dialogue and little personality outside of their physical traits. On a quick side note, I wonder what these robots would do if they did succeed in their mission of killing all humans. Would they just self-destruct out of sheer boredom? Or take up knitting as a hobby? I guess we’ll probably never find out, will we. The game features two distinct gameplay areas, one involving combat and other puzzle solving with lots of “easy” platforming interspersed between and throughout the game. Given that the platforming is really hard to fail, I found that I didn't like it all that much. It’s easy though and it does add depth to each area you explore and helps pace the game out so I’ll let it slide. Even if exploration only rewards you with currency to a fairly shallow upgrade system. Keep in mind that while I sound harsh on these points, it’s only because other games have done it better. It’s not bad, it’s just nothing new.
3rd Person combat that focuses on combos and blocking shots with a few special abilities. Combat is nice and responsive with plenty of weight to each attack and reaction. Dodging is a bit funky to make work especially when you can just use your shield instead to block the shots you need to. You do see a decent number of enemies in the game but the combat ultimately lacks in variety when it’s summed up to: spam the attack button till they blow up. There’s a “dog” boss mid way through the game that is built up as this big bad robot but when the actual fight breaks out? All you do is stun it repeatedly and spam your attacks, repeatedly, until it dies. It’s rather anti-climactic. The challenge usually comes in the form of groups of robots where some will try and stun or knock you back. Still, the combat is decent enough to keep from getting stale (if only barely) throughout the four hour campaign.
I got six hours out of the game, four hours for the main campaign and two out of the included DLC short story. I think that’s just the right amount of content for the asking price. Any longer and the combat or platforming would have gotten stale or dull. Oh, right, I almost forgot to talk about the DLC. A surprising side mission where you control Pigsy, a character you meet in the main campaign, on a journey to find the perfect companion. As his physique is not designed for close up and personal combat, he can’t brawl it out with the robots. Instead, you have to use stealth, a sniper/assault rifle and tricks to get around the obstacles. It adds a different flavor to the game while showing you an enjoyable little side story. It’s a good thing it ends at two hours because the end level starts turning into a twitchy shooter arena which I didn’t find as enjoyable. What I did find more than a little heartwarming was Pigsy’s journey of self-discovery about his actual perfect companion. Kudos to the devs on this one as I enjoyed it quite a bit even after the four hours in the main campaign. It didn’t feel tacked on at all.
PC Port wise, it’s not bad but its not the greatest port from the console. Optimization seems to be decent though I did experience framerate drops at times. The textures are starting to show their age. Additionally, I noticed that the character’s mouth doesn’t always stay synced with the voice acting. If you’re having performance problems and/or shadows are broken, you can go to
and input the fixes in the
section. One other irritation I should point out is the camera. The darn thing likes to fight you in the middle of a fight to show you what it thinks you want to see, usually Monkey smashing a machine into tiny pieces. It’s not game breaking but it can be annoying at times. Also,
as the Keyboard + Mouse controls feel like an afterthought. A common problem with console-ported hack and slashes it would seem.
I recommend you pick this up if you’re looking for an overlooked, well crafted 3rd person hack and slash. It’s Sun Wukong in a post-apocalyptic, yet surprisingly colorful & beautiful world fighting robots. While the combat is a bit limited, the journey and characters more than make up for it. I enjoyed the characters, their interactions and the story overall.

Based on what I had heard, I went into this game expecting to play an action-adventure movie. I was not disappointed.
The combat, though enjoyable, can get repetitive; the platforming is on autopilot (you literally
jump to your death); and the levels are very linear, with some small side paths to find extra collectibles. The focus is on the story, and it’s a good one. Voice acting is top-notch throughout, and in cutscenes you can clearly see the emotion in the characters’ faces.
When I
, I complained about how much of it felt like I was just watching a movie, but that was in part because my expectations were totally off. With
, I had a better idea of what to expect, and its story and overall execution were far superior. I really don’t want to talk details about the story, so I’ll just say it’s about two strangers brought together in a post-apocalyptic setting, trying to get home.
If you like story-driven and emotive games, and you don’t mind brawler combat against robots, you should play
. If you can’t stand pressing buttons to smash robots to pieces, you should at least watch a playthrough.

Steam can't seem to keep track of time spent in this game properly - it was really difficult to post this review because it insisted that I'd played under 5 minutes.
Ok, wow...maybe the story makes up for a HORRIBLE graphics, control and camera system.
Maybe the story gets better and you won't notice that you're on rails 5 inches wide and actually have almost 0 control of your character.  I doubt it.
If you're prone to motion sickness, you might want to look away from my review because you might get queasy just reading about it here...it is THAT bad.  The camera fights you all the time.  Each time you get close to the edge of the 40 foot wide corridor, it yanks you back and tries to force you back to the center.  1920x1080 is the max resolution which is awesome for those with big monitors.  I know some of the settings can be changed via the .ini files:  motion blur can be disabled, AA can be turned on, VSYNC etc but the studios need to put a bit more effort into the PC port.  This is barely a usable PC port.
The game itself is at best a 2D+ platformer with open 3D combat areas, the rails I mentioned earlier are so narrow that you might as well be on a side scroller. There appears to be only 1 real way to do any of the "puzzles".  I hesitate to call them that because at each handhold, the next jump location is highlighted so you can't miss it.  As you jump, camera control is taken from you and rotated so many times during the climb/jump sequences that it is beyond annoying.
The climbing platform sections require 0 (ZERO) ability and are just an exercise in button mashing.  That huge fall below you is actually not a problem because falling wasn't programmed in, you'll just hang on the side of a burning, exploding ship while you make a sandwich...seriously.
But you're a crazy hopping climbing monkey right, that's cool - when chicky gets ahead of you up some stairs, you can just jump and catch up!  NOPE.  You have to run around and WALK UP THE FRAKKING  STAIRS.  You're not allowed to jump unless they say you're allowed to jump.  WTF.  That's the silliest thing I encountered, you can't even jump when you want to on a jumping monkey character.
You'll also be doing plenty of jumping with chicky riding on your back.  Yes, it's teenage wish fulfillment hour:  the helpless girl climbs onboard while you save her.  The sheer number of rearend screenshots I just encountered while looking at other reviews is just sad.  (It appears that Steam reviews are G/PG because you can't type the synonym for donkey)
Maybe I'll finish the other couple hundred games in my library and come back to this one but I doubt it.

Well, where do I start with this? This project is pretty much one of the reasons I'm on Steam in the first place. I remember, one day I came home after playing original Half-Life in an internet cafe, wondering how amazing it could have been if remade with the graphics of Half-Life 2. I turned on the TV and one of the gaming TV chanels literally played the trailer ( the very first one) for Black mesa. I followed the development and I must say it had been an amazing experience. And when the mod was release in 2012, it blew my mind how good it actually was. The retail is more of it and improved on many fronts. I never did rally view it as just a mod, but for me it has been equal to the official Valve games.
Presentation:
+The visuals are pretty good, considering that this is STILL the Source engine. But, ironically, this is the prettiest game in the Half Life series, and it is a remake of the old one.
+Level design is much more beliavable than HL 1. The ilogicalities that plague Half Life 1 ( hell, big part of "Freeman's mind is his questioning "Who designed this place???") if you think about it is nowhere to be seen ( as it is expected from a remake). Some parts are rally astonishing -the hydroelectric damb, the finale of the Lambda core, the resonance cascade - all look gorgeous.
+Writing is great. Most new characters and interactions are fun to listen to. I was always interested of how they changed some encounters and there are surprisingly some variety in character encounters depending on what you did previously ( the big armory encounter dialogue in "surface tension" changes differently depending on what happened to the guard running from soldiers). There has been some real personality injected into Black Mesa personel, which makes the whole experience much more immersive. ( MILD SPOILER)Kleiner addition in the begining makes total sense.
+ Visual design and modernisation of old  designs is great - all aliens are recognisable and look pretty good, weapons do too ( except for 2 mentioned below).
+ Pickup animations for weapons and H.E.V. powering up are a nice touch.
* While addition of blood getting on the weapons is neat sometimes, I would really like to at least have the option to disable it. Not to mention they cause some frame drops as well.
* Random face generation ensues there are different faces on different scientist, but sometimes they still do feel that they look the same.
- A personal  thing, but I think the mod's MP5 looks better, and the new retail model of the Tau Cannon is horrible( who thought that replacing the iconic hexagonal spinning capacitor with a cylinder or whatever was a good idea???).
- Chapter "On a Rail" ( one of my favourite chapters in the original) is cut in lenght TREMENDOUSLY. There is a mod for it tho ( from the same guy who made the extended "Surface tension", which is now a part of the game officially)
Sound
+ Great sound design all around - zombie growls are pretty scary, alien sounds are interestin to listen to, all  guns sound meaty and the voice acting is top notch - they do an amazing job of voicing characters - it's hard to believe that these are not actually the original voice actors.
+ Some might argue, but imo Joel Nielsen soundtrack is so much better in some places than original Kelly Bailey's one - the somber and sadder tones make Black mesa incident feel like a tragedy where your collegues are dying much more fleshed out, while still retaining the same feel of Half Life.

Gameplay
+ It's Half LIfe gamplay through and through, with addition of physics to it. Gotta love throwing those granades back.
+ Additional puzzles or improvements ( through physics) to existing ones.
+ Several improvements to enemies, particularly high tier Xen enemies. Controllers are actually a credible threat now. Vortigaunt and Houndye attack charge time was thankfully reduced from the mod. But for me, it's the alien grunt that is the star of the show, and for me, they subplant Marines ( who were the stars  of the orinal) - they now actually feel like  soldiers for the alien forces instead of a meatshield which could easily be beaten by the crowbar - they fight more intelligently, do actual damage and have some new tricks up their sleeves - they will use their hivehand's alt fire close range, for example. That alone made my old favourite " rush 'em and beat 'em with the crowbar" tactic innefective since I would be "insected" down before getting close.
+ You can reprogram sentry guns to attack everyone in front of them, but they do have limited ammo once you do that to them.
+ Several of the encounters have been redesigned for the better. *MILD SPOILERS* The tank in "surface tension" can now move  and destroy the environment ( most scripted, but still) and that encounter is much more dynamic and tense because of it, the chopper battle is much more interesting than just one or 2 shotting it in the original and gives better closure to the chase throught the desert. The dam battle is also a part of this.
+ Movement system is mostly untuched - crouch jump is still very much required, and you can have sprint always on to have simmilar movement speed as the original.
+ Achivements are mostly great fun. The rare specimen is quite interesting one too.
+ Multiplayer is pretty good thing to have and you can even create a custom face for your avatar too, but it's mostly empty nowadays.
* Xen isn't included in the game yet, but it devs assure us that it is commign and I personally have no reason to doubt that they have good reason to delay it. Hek, Gabe Newell himself said that it was part of the game that he felt they could have done better but didn't have time and/or the technology to do so. I have full confidence that final release of Xen will see a much deserved improvement on the original's one. Still BEWARE that the game is NOT COMPLETE a this point yet.
* Marines are much less impressive than they were in Half Life 1 - part of this is because they are slower and the power of the guns is increased too, so they die faster. They feel more like Combine soldiers than HL 1 HECU marines. They do get the addition of an actual Medic this time tho.
* Iron Sights on the Pythone feels wonky, as does the Scope on the Crossbow. The crossbow scope is also a frame rate killer on less than stellar machines.
* Placing of some weapons have been changed. Some are gotten much later in the remake than in the original.
- Several weapon rebalances are pretty bad. Most weapons had their ammo reserves reduced, especially painful on the Colt Python, crossbow  and the smg granade launcher (many times you will find more ammo for them in one place than you can carry, a leftover from old Half Life ammo cache placements, especially on the later two ). While reduced magazine and ammo reserve size is ok on MP5 because it is still enough ( and mroe beliavable too),one change is very angering - the accuracy for primary fire of the Glock is much worse in retail than it was in the mod and the original game. Granted, the alt fire is more accurate now, but the main attraction the the Glock - it's accuracy on the primary mode, the thing that made it still relevant once you got the smg in ther original - is mosltly gone. It couldn't hit a tripmine at 8~ meter range, which is absurd and made "de-tripmine-ing" with it much harder. You might as well stick to the smg. Half Life had delicate balance of weaponry - all of the weapons had purpose and were useful pretty much throught the whole game. It's just the Glock and me nitpicking,but it does stick out considering everything else is great.
TL; DR, All in all, I think this is an amazing game and a testament of what fans are capable of. It's a labor of love to Half Life and Crowbar Collective did an amazing job in remaking Half Life.I would give it a score, but,tbh,I really struggle, as I would be pretty biased on it.But,what I can tell you is that this is an amazing game and you should definitely check it out.

Black Mesa is a remake to the cult classic Half Life, with updated models, dialogue, and textures that gives players both new and old a new way to experience the PC classic.
Being a fan of the Half Life franchise (Mostly HL1 and Opposing Force) and having a slight sour taste in my mouth from not having a conclusion to the Half Life 2 saga, my interest was piqued when I saw this standalone title arrive on the Steam marketplace. I saw a Streamer play it and thought it was another way to get back into the franchise that I love.
The story and general environments have been the same or enhanced in a way that doesn’t ruin the nostalgic appeal of the game which is great, the Crowbar Collective has really taken care with the IP to ensure that the lore and feel of the game has been maintained during development.
The Developers are active in the community and are always posting updates about new tech that is being implemented in to the game such as visual effects like God Rays and Image-based Ambient Lighting, and performance enhancements.
The game also features a multiplayer mode which is a fun experience, though that is more of an afterthought as Half Life was more of a single player experience.
Though Xen has been pushed back I have full confidence that the developers are working hard to design and create an immersive and nostalgic final chapter to the Half Life story and that the delay was the best decision they could make to ensure the final product is the best Half Life experience players could ask for.
All in all Black Mesa is the definitive Half Life 1 experience but I would say play the original first, to really appreciate what the developers have done to breathe new life into this amazing title. I am really hoping to see an Opposing Force and Blue Shift remake from the Crowbar Collective in the future.

I am biased.  This game is a major part of my childhood, and to be honest, I was worried it would be less amazing now than it was ten years ago.  My fears were unfounded.
Gearbox did a phenomenal job remastering this incredible story.  The gameplay is fun without being incredibly complicated, the three dimensional aspect of the game adds a great deal of depth to the combat and strategizing if you so choose, and the growth of your fleet as time passes all forms a well rounded experience.
But that's not why we play Homeworld, we play it because there are few stories in science fiction that are told in such a compelling and heart wrenching manner as the story of the Hiigarans.  Words can't describe how immersive this games campaign is.
Regarding the multiplayer, it's still glitchy, but that is to be expected when merging two games over a decade old so people all over the world can play it together.  So far though, when it works, it is remarkably well balanced and fun.
TL;DR - Solid gameplay, incredibly compelling story, multiplayer has potential and I look forward to it's continued development.

I only played this game one other time before. I will admit, I torrented a very alpha version about a year ago. But that one time I played it, I played nothing else for about a MONTH. I just checked, my first save was on July 9th. 2015. The last save before I stopped played was August 5th, 2015. I played nothing else during that time.
When I played it then, the end goal was a Missle Defense System. Half the technologies were had copy-pasted icons. The Flying technology was a tiny picture of the alien UFO from XCOM: Enemy Unknown! Some of the textures were uncolored. Some were obvious placeholders. But now, everything is unique and beutifully textured. This is seriously some of the most gritty, realisitc, industrial, and intricate pixel-graphics I have ever seen. Everything moves. From the tiny pistons on the Inserters, to the intricate pneumatics and steams of the Boilers.
Factorio is seriously one of the most unique games I have ever played. You basically must singlehandedly build an entire infrastructure and supply chain. I have never seen anything like it. At a close up level, it's a simple puzzel of space and resource managment. How can I get these resources over this supply chain, and into this Furnace without the inserters picking up the wrong item. Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a good action/adventure/rpg-ish game. Good object scrounging, graphically wonderful, intriguing story. All in all a game I do not hesitate to recommend.
My only issue came with having to adjust resolution to get past some parts as Monkey would be unable to jump to the next pole/ledge/whatever without doing so. Not a terribly big deal, just pulled me out of the game for a bit.

This game is quite enjoyable, but it is definetly rough around the edges. Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a 3rd person adventure character action game in which you play as Monkey on the 2 core gameplay aspects of fighting robots and platforming, while journeying into some great enviroments and through a nice story which will take you around 7-8 hours to beat.
The combat feels good but it gets repetitive, there's not that much enemy variety, even a boss is reused once, and you only have 1 weapon with limted moves, I wish they expanded on it a bit more, but it does the job I suppose. The camera can be quite bad at times though, it is too close to your character so sometimes you'll get hit from enemies offscreen and whatnot, they should've zoomed it out a little bit. You can also use your staff to shoot damaging and stunning projectiles but I will warn you that aiming feels a bit sluggish with the mouse.
Now the platforming looks cool and all but it's very linear and there's not much of a challenge, you're just pressing the movement keys and the jump button at the same time following a simple path, it can get a bit fidley however, like sometimes there's just this one very specific spot to jump from to grab another ledge, and even if you're just slighly to the side of it, your jump won't work, and sometimes it works from anywhere, so it's a bit inconsistent on that note.
Right now you can probably see the game's flaws, but here's what they did right, the enviroments are really beaultiful, and it just takes you right in this post apocalyptic world that the game's trying to build, it definetly feels lonely, and the overgrown nature on New York early in the game serves to reinforce that. The story is quite good too, Monkey the main character escapes from a slave ship and crash lands on the city of New York, only to find himself wearing a slave helmet put on by another prisioner who escaped, Trip. She does this because she needs his protection to reach her home community, so Monkey is now forced to help her, otherwise he's killed by the slave helmet, and also if Trip dies, she set it so his helmet triggers too. That is quite an interesting set up for our two main characters and you can definetly see the chemistry between them as you play the game, I'd say the story is great on that regard, but on a side note I thought that the ending is kinda bad in my opinion, but to avoid spoilers that's all I'll say about it so you can check it out for yourself.
Overall, Enslaved: Odyseey to the West has quite a few flaws, but I'd definetly recommend you pick it up on sale, the story and the gourgeous enviroments will definetly make for an exciting journey into this post apocalyptic world.

JDM Tuner Racing reminds me of a Flash game, and there's apparently a reason for that. According to other gamers who've bought this game, it's virtually identical to Drag Racer v3.
Normally, I wouldn't fault a game for seeming similar to another, especially since there's only so many ways to design a game within the same genre. That said, JDMTR provides nothing new or of any value beyond the free Flash game that apparently inspired it.
The basic concept behind JDMTR is illegal racing where you take normal cars, modify them way beyond the manufacturer's specifications (which is dangerous in real life) while adding various bits of ridiculous design elements, such as an overly large spoiler.
That alone would make for a fine game (and in fact, it's worked in other games), but JDMTR breaks down immediately once you start playing it.
How so? Allow me to explain...
There is NO documentation, tutorial, or any instructions/guides whatsoever. The game itself isn't difficult to play, but many features within it — such as knowing how to fine tune your gear shift — or explaining certain acronyms (i.e. NOS) and initialisms (i.e. RPM) are left entirely up to the player to figure out.
The menu system is confusing and clunky to use. For instance, there's a section entitled "setup," which most gamers will assume means "this is the options menu." Not so in JDMTR. This section lets you tune your gear shift, but like I explained before, offers no guidance on what any of it means or how it works.
The money you earn while playing lets you purchase new vehicles and upgrade components. The problem with this is there's no "undo" function.
Some people might say, "There's a downgrade option to solve this!"
Well, yes and no. Downgrading will get rid of the last upgrade you bought and installed; however, it won't refund any of the money you spent, so downgrading leaves you worse off than before.
The graphics are passable, but static and look at least a decade out of date, if not more so. Honestly, the graphics in JDMTR are the least of its issues, which doesn't say much for it.
The actual gameplay is extremely limited and as far as I can tell, is entirely keyboard-only except for navigating the menus, which uses the mouse.
Racing consists of pushing "up" on the arrow keys, while "left shift" will shift into a higher gear (oddly enough, you can't downshift) and the "alt" key will fire NOS. Aside from clicking on menus, that's all the gameplay present in JDMTR.
Now to be fair, there is a positive to JDMTR: It's incredibly cheap (normally priced at 99 cents USD, and I got it on sale for 69 cents USD) so at absolute worst, you've wasted one solitary dollar. You can't buy anything for a dollar nowadays, not even a cup of coffee or a bottle of soda.
So would I recommend JDM Tuner Racing? Absolutely not. Save yourself some money and go play the free Flash game version instead.

While not perfect, there is little reason not to recommend this game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There are a few "unforgivable" issues which Gearbox needs to address sooner rather than later in terms of impacting an RTS game's playability.
- Mouse Input lag. This is a no-no of the highest order in an RTS. The good news is that this is not an RTS that really relies heavily on your APM. but mouse accuracy is pretty high up there, especially if you are zoomed out to control the battlefield.
- Going to black screen somewhat randomly during the campaign is hard to fathom - but based on it's behaviour with a dual monitor set up, I wouldn't be surprised if they are related.
- Speaking of dual monitor, it has some very odd behaviour related to the mouse to pan and dual screen set up. I generally don't mouse pan the camera due to a Starcraft background, but it is a bit disconcerting to nudge the screen in one situation, then have the mouse leap off the game completely in another situation with no clear reason why.
- Finally, and much like mouse input lag, a fairly unforgivable issue for an RTS player - inexplicable freezing. This is a very intermittant, seems not to impact the Frame rate which can get up to 260 if you let it, and stutters the game. The game doesn't ask all that much of the system resources that I could tell. GTX 970 with a processor that chilled right around 30% with some other software doing it's stuff... so I really can't explain the freezing.
On a non-bug topic, I find the tutorial to be woefully weak, leaving out some really pretty key fundamentals of the game - like the importance of some of the utility ships.
So not perfect, and needs to pretty significant patching and updating to get some of these fairly regrettable bugs handled.
That all out the way...
The remastering of this game is a rare case where the term remastered actually applies. The audio (which is original) has been significantly cleaned up, and the graphical overhaul is... remarkable.
Additionally, some advancements between 1 and 2 were retroactively added to 1, including some of the significant UI improvements. Some old-time players will feel this is a detriment to the game, but I think first time players of the game will certainly appreciate the changes.
The campaign is very good - but I have not played through enough of the campaign to offer thoughts on any changes they have made the story, so I assume there aren't too many, so I feel safe saying... the campaign is very good.
The game difficulty varies, during the campaign, between easy enough, and well... not easy at all. You will find the instructions for some of the objectives are a touch vague (see the point earlier about the tutorial deficiencies and say ... salvaging a larger ship), but the pace of the game is not such that you can't figure out most everything on the fly.
There is, as I recall, some level of dynamic difficulty added - so that you can't build up a powerful fleet before the mission starts.
The game is lacking it's multiplayer in any real way right now - though its in beta for a steam implementation.
All in all, a pretty stunning "remaster" of what is still a top notch RTS  that I do recommend, but offer a few caveats.
1) If you are a big fan of the homeworld series, be ready for changes in the remaster you may not entirely appreciate - but you do get a digital version of the originals so that's probably worth the cash right there.
2) If you don't want to deal with the bugs, wait for some patches before you buy
3) It is a remaster - so some old school game design elements are clearly in force, if you are looking for a slick reimagining of the RTS genre with a sci fi theme and new UI and design innovations, check out Grey Goo instead.

Black Mesa is an amazing game. Wether or not you've played Half Life in the past, I would strongly reccomend playing Black Mesa. For someone who has never played Half Life and knows very little of the story, it's an immersive experience taking you back to when story-based video games were at their peak. Now, with multiplayer being the most popular feature of most games and story often falling to a small team of people just churning out the same old repetitive obejectives, missions and stories, Black Mesa brings us all back to a time when story and the objectives were important.
The graphics are sub-par by modern standards, but they are a very, very small price to pay for the game you're playing.
The Xen chapters have also not been released yet, but I can't wait to see them remade from the shabby levels more representative of modern videogame stories into what they should have been originally. Gloriously made in the image of the rest of the game.

This game is in super early access as it is very light on content and I mean very light on content as in there are only 3 short (around 5 min each) levels. With that said it is pretty enjoyable and well done, this is a pretty solid endless runner with your typical endless runner abilities like sliding, wall running and gliding. All in all, It controls well (I used a Xbox controller) and looks fantastic, the art direction really hits the cool neon cyberspace look of the Tron franchise.
As you play you can collect the game's ingame currency called light (I think) which can then be used to purchase buffs and powerups which can then be used in each of the game's levels, abilities such as being able to improve your power disc attacks and/or the ability to automatically collect light that is nearby. First off the game looks awesome. Its appearance and atttention to detail is phenominal - everything else, well...
I hate to be on the negative side of a game I honestly looked forward to after hearing about, learned more about, and wanted to enjoy.
The trouble is - I just can't get into it.
I have tried several times since I bought it, and honestly I just can't get into it. The atmosphere, the story, the whole scope of the game should be absolutly enthralling, but to me... it feels like a soft-spoken echo I've done before.
The gameplay mechanics limit the whole danger of the game - you can't accidentally jump off a cliff, and barring really taking your time or being caught up in certain points the limited-action durations of a danger sequence really can't be that bad once you know what and where to go.  Trial and error and a bit of judgement on certain points just makes it feel too easy.
Even the whole connected-life and wandering too far issue isn't that bad, being too far from her doesn't kill you immedietly - yet unintentionally reminds me of Ico all the damn time. You gotta guard her all the time.
Certain other aspects of gameplay like the Cloud only remind me of the hoverboard in Jak 3, yet far, far less entertaining.
The combat staff/gun combo was fresh after the first few mechs but grew stale in its relative repitition over time. The fast-pased danger in some spots got sidetracked far too easily on occasion when it became clear how easy to manipulate and defeat the AI could be.
The keyboard/mouse controls are spottish - making me wish I had a proper gamepad. But that alone should not detract from such a beautiful and rich game.
No, to me the worst part is the story. I've heard it before, a dozen times over, a score of other ways. The post apocolyptic mechanical doomsday is an over-used cliche which only continually detracts from how it seems like I've been here before, helping or being coerced to help another for our mutual survival in such a hell.
Details like that, which in truth should be only mere minor quips just compound to me when they are all together like this to where I just can't get into it.
I have no doubt its well done, great intentions and a good plan - but as a seasoned gamer it honestly just felt like an echo of bad problems that just can't keep me in.
Try it if it appeals to you, but be warned - to me it seemed its all been done before, and honestly far better in many other games.

This game starts off as fun, turning into annoying, dramatic and back again!
To you people thinking about trying this out, I only have one piece of advice.
Don't play realistic mode. Not until you can get a handle of the game.
I thought it'd be like every other zombie game out there. You pick up some (conveniently placed) guns (with unlimited ammo) and start shooting the hell out of anything dead that moves.
No, I was so wrong, it hurt.
Dropping into a random server, I began with trying to figure out the game. There is no tutorial, so you have to figure everything out for yourself or someone nice enough will help you out.
No idea it was an objective map and that I had to keep moving through the map, I began guarding the starting point until they overran me. There weren't any guns, just piles of boards, a wrench, a crowbar and a hammer.
Objectives and Survival are both equally difficult, unless you're playing on an easy server.
I can't even begin to tell you what I've been through with this game.
Finally, a co-op zombie game where Teamwork is KEY to making it through., you realize that when one person dies and everything falls apart from there.
Teamwork's all you have left with actual limited supplies, only getting new ones from the military who send drops every so often.
You can get infected, bleed, shot by your own teammates (When they're not careful or just being d-bags) and just plain cornered by a mob of zombies who can do more than just attack you.
You'd better hope those people you got stuck with are willing to lend their supplies.
The music was fitting in certain parts, voice acting was really spot-on, the zombies will make you panic and the entire quality of the maps is so perfect...
So many guns, each one needing a certain type of ammo. Even then, you have limited ammo.
The only bad parts about this game, is that it's mostly multi-player.
You can play single-player, but they'll finish you before you know it.
The servers are piled together in a huge mess... good luck choosing.
And, then there's the usual try-hards and little kids who ignore what this game really means.
Teamwork. Surviving. Period.
8/10, I'd go on a few rounds with you. Get it while it's free.

Well, I just finished my first playthrough of Dark Souls II, and I can confidently say that it is a fantastic game. Although it's definitely not as good as the original Dark Souls, it's far from disappointing. I would write about my complaints with this game in detail, but there are already enough people mercilessly bashing it for not being as good as its predecessor. In short, some of the bosses were disappointing, there are too many humanoid enemies, the level design is too linear at times, and there are some cases in which mechanics are changed for the worse. There. Now for the good stuff. First of all, I love the environments in this game. They all have a unique look and feel to them, just like the first game. I also really (and I mean REALLY) loved the soundtrack for Dark Souls II. Motoi Sakuraba, who also composed the OST for the original Dark Souls, did an amazing job once again. The boss themes are all adrenaline-pumping and epic, making each fight way more fun and intense. The enhanced customization is very welcome, making your journey feel more personal since you're able to make a much more unique character this time around. Multiplayer has also been improved, as connecting with friends is far faster and easier than it was in the previous game, especially with the use of the Name-Engraved Ring. Finally and most importantly, the game is still very hard. Some might say that this game is easier than Dark Souls, but I personally think that it's not too far behind. While I can say that I would recommend Dark Souls II over Dark Souls for new players, make no mistake, this game is still quite the challenge, and I never found myself disappointed by the difficulty even once. So there you have it, Dark Souls II might not be as good as Dark Souls, but it is still one of the best games money can buy.

RATING: 3/5 stars.
TL;DR "A decent MOBA/3rd-person shooter hybrid that sincerely tries to keep it fresh, easy to slip in and out of, will only cost you your time, so it might be worth a look, especially if you like boobies!"
Pros:
- Easy to be picked up by novices or adapted by veterans with decent practice modes that will help you cover the basics and more advanced concepts
- 70+ heroes (gods) to choose from, offering a wide variety of game styles. The 3rd person approach to MOBAs makes for some interesting strategies, and some interesting combos. While I would consider this a simplification of the MOBA genre, do not mean at all a simplification of the experience potential itself!
- It's free-to-play, unlocking new heroes is relatively unexpensive in terms of game-time invested, and they have a weekly rotation/rental options that allows you to try new heroes all the time. This is the only free-to-play I can recall in the past few years where I really paid ZERO and did not feel behind the curve at all!
- Multiple game modes allows for short action matches (~15mins) up to the regular grueling grind of multi-lane pushing (> 1hr).
- They are invested in keeping you entertained, with regular updates to ensure stabilities, new match modes, daily/weekly/event-related achievements. Very well polished, the models and skins look good even on a mid-range rig. And if you're into skins, some really cool stuff in the game store.
Cons:
- BEEWWWBZ!!! Sure sex sells and it rarely ever bothers me, but come on, most of the female characters are ridiculous, and some I'd classify as erotica/softcore, especially with unlocked skins. It feels like the character design uses only horny 13 years old boys as their feedback test group. It makes it hard for me *giggles at the pun* to take the game seriously in any way or form.
- It's a team sport, so playing solo can be frustrating, especially if you run into unhelpful teammates who either don't care at all or care too much. Pretty much the same of any other competitive popular game. Also, their matchmaking random hero process could use an overhaul because often random selection matches can be spoiled by a terribly unbalanced matchup (all tanks on one side vs fragile spell-casters on the other).
- Massive and regular updates, I stopped playing this because my buddies internet connections couldn't keep up with the updates so they abandoned the game. The frustrating part is that most of these updates involve skins and aesthetics and as far as I know the dev team doesn't seem to place this as a priority for them.
- trying to appeal to demographs outside of MOBA can make veterans of the genre feel the game is "dumbed down".

I think this game is worth a playthrough, so that a person can form their own opinion of it. That's why I selected "Recommend" for this review.
Myself, I was underwhelmed. The story was pretty okay, and the acting was pretty okay. It wasn't bad, but I wasn't overly impressed.
What I really didn't get was the gameplay, in the sense that I didn't truly feel like I was "playing" anything. I felt like an actor being led around by the nose, just hitting marks in order to advance the narrative. Outside of boss battles, combat seemed like very little more than just mashing the same buttons until the enemies were neutralized. Further, I felt like Monkey's acrobatic movement capabilities were mostly wasted on environmental traversal that was  surprisingly linear and "spoonfed" to the player. At the same time, I still ended up frustrated in spots because I was playing on PC, and the "hyper-scripted" interactions in the game seem to be built to only truly work well on consoles.
I don't want to be overly harsh to Ninja Theory and the other folks involved in the production. I do think they worked hard at producing a title with good production values. (There's some interesting stuff going on in terms of visual design, that's for sure.) To be frank, though, I get the strange feeling that what they would have preferred to make was a movie - but interactive media was what they could do, so they stayed with that.
In the end, my experience was that "Enslaved" is a nominally interactive story that only gets real gameplay in a few, disjointed spots. It seems mostly meant to look pretty and tell its story, without truly asking the player to get a solid handle on actual mechanics.
I can acknowledge that the above might not be your experience, though. Lots of people like this title, and that definitely speaks in rebuttal to my own feelings about "Enslaved."

This is a biased review - let's get that out of the way early.
Having played the three originals, and having kept an eye on the progress of the remasters, it's fair to say that I was a fan before release, and one of those 'old guys' who eagerly awaited this arrival with crossed fingers and a daily prayer to the gaming gods for Gearbox not to screw it up.
Was it going to be a labour of love, a cash-in, a botch job? I was understandably concerned.
Straight out of the gate, there's a clue. When the opening titles splash, and it's introduced as a remastering of a game by Relic first and foremost, you realise that these guys are paying due deference to the source. I knew this already, as Gearbox have gone out of their way to collect original voice actors, and even original design team members to give this the attention it needs. They spent time putting everything in place to reproduce a classic. More than that, what originally started out as a simple release with a HD upgrade turned into a full-on remaster with not just improved visuals, but high fidelity sound. Gearbox had the chance to make this a cash grab. They passed up that chance of merely cleaning the windows and elected to give it a full service, respray, a new set of tyres, and replaced the engine while they were there. Sadly for some, they did mess with the handling a little, but I'll get to that.
Whenever I load up the originals, while they're still excellent in gameplay, the visuals are suffering. They don't look like how I remember them. There appears to be some gap between reality and my imagination. My imagination upgrades visuals as I go along, and I'm invariably disappointed  when I find that my memory is lying to me and the games have a lower resolution than my imagination does. Original HW2 still looked pretty good, but HW1 was showing its age badly. Apparently Gearbox thought the same. The remastered versions look like how I imagine the originals. They look better.
They're beautiful.
Nebulae are rich and vibrant, with that otherworldly quality that makes space look much more lovely than it is. Ships are detailed, explosions are impressive and Kharak and Hiigara have never looked so amazing. In one sweeping moment, all the graphical issues that come with decades old games - gone.
So far so good. How's the gameplay though?
Gearbox have modified HW1's gameplay to be more like HW2. This will be sacrilege for some, and for those who thought HW2 improved a lot of things, it will seem as simply sensible.
Fighter formations are no longer entirely static. They hold formation until they engage the enemy, and then as one would expect, they break off into one almighty hairball with contrails zipping in and out of each other to the incongruous tune of vacuum explosions. This seems more realistic (minus the forgivable space sound), and yet it unarguably removes a facet of the original that some will find hard to bear.
Some won't like it. I realise that, and I think Gearbox did too. They telegraphed it ahead of release to ease fans into the idea. Time will tell if Gearbox patch this feature back in. Also, the fuel mechanic is gone. Can't say I lament its passing. It was tedious.
Other than that, Gearbox have kept a very light touch, and have changed very little. They clearly know not to mess with a proven title too much. There are good reasons for the changes they did make however. To allow a seamless transition from the first to the second game, one of them would have to change as there were some significant differences. You can literally play them back to back now, and they feel like you're playing the same game. Nothing jars.
Also, the UI is standard across the two. It's now even more minimalist than it used to be, allowing you more screen real-estate to watch the carnage. It doesn't take long to navigate your way round, and in no time at all you'll find yourself hotkeying your way to victory.
Other than that, Gearbox have left the gameplay largely untouched, which is interesting. They must have been tempted to 'do a Lucas', but they didn't. What's even more interesting is that the gameplay from two titles which are now 16 and 12 years old respectively, doesn't suffer by modern standards. They're perfectly fine. I'm not sure of any other genre that could make that boast, but then, there really hasn't been much like Homeworld since.
People still compare it to its nearest contemporary, Sins of a Solar Empire, and that is telling. Sins is nothing like Homeworld. Both are set in space, and both are viewed from a god's eye view, and that's it.
Of course, for those who simply cannot stand the few changes that have been made, Gearbox included the two originals as well, with some fixes to enable them to run on modern machines.
There are some bugs. I've had a couple of crashes and there appears to be a persistent engine audio bug that is banished by opening the game menu. Others report more bugs than I've seen, so hopefully Gearbox will get on the case and tweak a little.
All in all, for the price, you cannot go wrong. Two games, two versions of each. One for the more strident hard-like fans, and an updated version for everyone else that is simply a joy to play. All for the price of one game.
I was starting to fear these games would be lost to the history bin, but thanks to Gearbox I've managed to walk with the Kushan once more on their cosmic caravan to regain their Homeworld, and also with the newly renamed Hiigarans, striving against overwhelming odds to preserve it. It was as much a pleasure this time round as the first.
Hopefully, now that HW1 and 2 are accessible once more to the gaming public, Gearbox will move on from here to Homeworld 3, and Shipbreakers, the latter of which is already well into development. After playing through the beautiful Remastered games, I'll be waiting eagerly.
For those who have never played these games, fair warning, they may seem harder than modern gamers are accustomed to, but they're as brilliant now as they were originally, and even though it's a much overused cliche, they deserve a place on any gamer's digital shelf.
Now, back to killing those Taiidani and Vaygr scum ...

is a
game about building up your farm on a distant planet that is inhabited by slimes.
It offers everything a good farming game should have in my opinion.
There really is a lot you can do. Where you want to put your focus is your own choice though, the game doesn’t force you to do anything.
Want to create a paradise for slimes and let them roam freely in gardens?
Want to life out your capitalist side and enslave slimes in mass animal husbandry to maximize your profit?
You kinda see what I’m getting at here. The game can be played at your own pace and you can do whatever you feel like, there isn’t really any way to mess something up. The high degree of freedom that is given to the player and the constant feel of safety are probably what makes this game so relaxing.
I originally played the game when it first came to steam and picked it up again recently. The amount of content that got added over that time is impressive. There are so many things you can do and ways to play the game that it won’t get boring anytime soon.  If you are only slightly interested in the genre or idea behind the game I absolutely recommend this one.

Okay, So I've finally got around to playing this game at length...My docket was full so I'm nearly two years late in writing a rewiew for this game.  But, as they say, better late than never.  So..here goes:
On the whole, I would say buy this game, on sale or no.  I think it's worth the money.  There has been no small amount of controversy over the bugs and unfortuneately, i think that has put many people that owuld have otherwise enjoyed this game, but instead decided to forgoe buying it all together.  For those that did not buy the game, you've missed out.  From what I can tell the bugs have largely been addressed and rectified, and the correction of these bugs (I never noticed them.  I never had one problem with the game.  I still don't know what everyone was talking about.  I started to suspect that people were playing this game on a PC or Laptop that simply did not have the chops to play and truly enjoy this game at its full potential.  And therein lies the rub.  If you have a low end PC or a laptop that did not cost you about 1100 bucks to purchase, chances are you will be very miffed.  This is a VERY high end game.  And when you experience the cinematic view during a battle, you will understand why.  While there has been every effort made to make this game agreeable to lower end PCs, you are doind yourself a disservice if you do nto have a newer model video card designed for PC gaming with it's own onboard RAM, and enough RAM otherwise to choke a yak to play this.  I know it's not the be alll and end all of computer graphics, but for Total War, their battle engine and it's cinematic mode are beautiful to behold and are singular in the TW Franchise.  If you DO have a good high end machine, buy this game, and when you are following your unit of Hastati through the woods, point your mouse so you look, so you can see the light filitering down through the leaves, and tell me tthat the sight is not beautiful.  Not only that, but it tends to put you into the game on a level  that was simply not present in the previous installments of Total War.   The DLC for this game is outstanding, and the MODing community is very active.

As far as the things that I think CA might have dropped the ball on,  I would have to say that getting rid of the family tree, along with the traits of a ruler that you could mouse over in previous TW games was a mistake.  The way characters were set up before, it was much easier to, at a glance, discern their personality.   I always though that the Devs of the Series had done well for themselves when they created that previous aspect of the game.  Lets see, what else....Oh, the Encyclopedia leaves a good deal to be desired, the unit tiles, more specificly, the artwork they use, was a poor choice.  I know what they were going for therre, but I don't like it, but there is no accounting for tasste and that shouldn't affect any one's decisions to purchase this game.  Finally, the Political system needs a complete overhall.  I like the idea of it.  It's a good concept, but too little effort was spent in fleshing the political system out, and this is reflected by the the players complete and utter lakc of  careing whether or not their  factioin leader character has enough Gravitas.  The Faction leaders seem....boring, and lifeless with no real reason to root for them, or sing happily when they finally die.     From what I have been made to understand, the new game, Attilla, which comes out on the seventh of Fedbuary,  will, at least (and hopefully much more) address this aspect of the game with the reintroduction of family trees.  I get the feeling that Atilla will evetually far outshadow Rome II as the better of the two games.
Would I reccomend this game?  Only if your PC has the chops to play it.  I give the game a solid....8.0 of of 10

Smite is a very interesting and fun game to play. I have enjoyed the game for at least 2 years. I had it installed not via Steam so it doesnt show the 1000's of hours I've put into this product. Like all free to play games, Smite has went through many changes. I get a few more graphical glitches now, still there, never went away. It's problematic with dc's and other things, we will get into that soon.
I guess I will do the pros and cons list for an easy comparison at first with a summary at the end.
PROS
#1. Very dynamic game, very in depth moba, everything is a skill shot for the most part. So, very skill based MOBA.
#2. 70 + chars. Each adding more dynamic play. Never a shortage of new chars. Hi Rez is good about that.
#3. I've had some great games and met some okay people.
#4. The game plays how it's meant to be played for the most part.
CONS - The important list to read before you spend money.
#1. Tons of skins being released with the current game play issues being over looked as always.
#2. Vey cosmetic game. Expensive skins. I've spent well over $500 on this game. Im too lazy to add it up but it's close to 1,000 dollars out of my pocket. I've supported the SPL( smite Pro League) Charity events, streamers, ect.
#3. The leveling system. In my opinion, this is the worst mechanic they put in this game. You start out at level #1. But you aren't mainly going to be playing with noobs. You will be playing against expierienced players that are called SMURFS. So, be prepared to get destroyed. Each God has a Passive with 4 Abilities and items. Takes a loooooooong time to figure out the depth of the game. You have 5 V 5. That's well over 20 combinations of abilites and such you must know how to deal with. Well, if you're new. Prepare to get stomped by smurfs. I know this, I made a new account. It's nothing new within the Smite community.
#4 Leveling system cont. Smite now gives you tons of XP booster and such when you level as a new player so you level faster. There's not really a point to getting max level except you play mainly with max level players, most are still terrible, and here's why. Smite makes it so new users have to learn the game at an extremely to steep of a learning curb. It honestly took me around a year to understand everything with all of the meta changes and such. They change items, maps, gods constantly. It's always changing. My main account has 2600 hrs played on it. So, to break it down into simple talk, new people level way too fast, end up not knowing how to play, getting to level 30 and upsetting other players because they don't have the skills to play the game and win.
#5. Most TOXIC community in any online game I've ever played. Time after time I've been harrassed in games by people doing a number of things. They feed on purpose, they AFK, they DC, they are just terrible (leveling system), or they are just punk kids in their mommies basement acting all tough. You can report, it does work, Ive been perma banned. But it doesn't stop the toxicity in the game. People ruined this game. Hi Rez not acting better, faster, has ruined this game. If you get to the point where you know how to play, well, you're going to be matched with people that dont so have fun. People ruined this game.
#6. HUGE PROBLEM. Disconnects. Get used to it. This game has had this problem ever since I started playing in 2014. DC DC DC. People either have issues with the game, dont like a god or w/e. They just DC. It ruins the game. Hands down.
It's a constant problem as well, it's not like it happens here and there, it's all the fawking time. So, good luck with that.
Summary. Final thoughts.
Like I said, it's a great game. It's worth playing. I'm warning you about spending money on it, if you get banned, bye bye money. And you will get reported, people just do it all the time because they are people. Game is very cosmetic, Hi Rez is neglegent about fixing game issues along with player issues. The DC's automatically ruin the match 4 v 5, ect. Seen whole teams DC but 1 or 2 people. Seen it all. If you play this game, play it for free only. I lost my money, will never get it back. It was a fun game for the first few hours. Great graphics and sound, and they've created an immersive universe which feels just like the films.
However, once the alien appears the gameplay gets very tedious very quickly. It only seems interested in you, it completely ignores all the NPCs wandering around. Coupled with the fact that if the alien is scripted to be in "a mission" it will just loiter around that area, suspiciously close to your character, seemingly teleporting around rather than moving along corridors/vents.
After the first few times it magically locates and kills you (the first time is indeed chilling), it just becomes a save/load fest devoid of any suspense or tension because you just wonder when the last time you saved it was and hope it wasn't too long ago. Compounding that issue the checkpoint save system will often have you redoing large portions of the game.
Another design problem worth mentioning is that when you encounter a hostile with a pistol and take them out, although their pistol drops and you can kick it about, you can't pick it up. You have to wait till the game allows you to obtain a pistol, which eventually is just sat on a desk.
I think it would have been a much, much better game if the alien didn't actually appear until much later in the game and you just heard it banging around in the vents, or maybe came across it's victims from time to time. Seeing it so often, and being killed by it so often, made the game ultimately dull and repetitive.

Theres alot of hype around this game, some of it is justified, some not so much imo.
Likes:
Nice story, nothing ground breaking though.
Decent voice acting.
Being searched for by the Alien while your hiding gives a nice sense of fear.
Decent graphics.
Superb ambient audio.
Lots of gadgets to tinker with.
True to the movies.
Dislikes:
The map, when your on a different level to your objective it can be painful to work out where you need to go. There is a marker on your hud showing your direction but no way to tell which level your on in comparison to your objective.
Once you get the flame thrower the hardest part is trying to find fuel for it or not running out of what you have.
Again the flame thrower removes alot of the suspense to the point where you can walk up to the alien blast it a couple of times and carry on.
When your using a computer or lock mechanism/mini game you can be attacked, the only way to tell is a few faint grunts from your character, no visualisations.
Towards the end for me it started to drag on a little making me hope there wasn't much left to do.( Reach point X - You made it- Oh wait no you didn't something bad is happening)
Ripley is like the grim reaper, to know her is to get killed faster than an extra on an away mission in Star Trek.
You don't really need all the gadgets, I finished the game on hard setting without using a couple of them, like the flash bangs.
Weak ending.
As many Cons as there are pros but I would still recommend playing the game, it's good for about 20 hours of gameplay, if you can pick it up in a sale.  I couldn't see myself paying full retail price for this game if I knew what it was like, probably wouldnt be too happy if I did.
Tips:
Watch the overhead vents.
Check behind you often when you hear something, the androids aren't fast but they can be damn quiet and have an extraordinary reach.
Save at every opportunity.
In Space no-one can hear you scream....or yawn once you get the flamethrower.

Even though Enslaved released on consoles in 2010, I hadn't heard about it until a few months ago during a Steam sale. Based on the Chinese tale "Journey to the West", this game will provide about 15 hours of good fun for those who like the action adventure hack-and-slash genre.
The story is interesting, and the visuals are vibrant and definitely one-of-a-kind, set in a post apocalyptic world where robots now rule the Earth. It also helps that the voice acting and motion capture for Monkey and Tripp are superbly done by Andy Serkis (aka gollum) and Lindsey Shaw respectively. The combat gets a little tiring after a while, and I wouldn't suggest this if you don't own a controller of some kind.
This Enhanced Version also comes with the Piggy's Perfect 10 DLC. It's quite different to play the more clunky and heavy Piggy who instead uses a sniper rifle with very useful equipment to stun/trap enemies. However, the DLC went on for farrr too long and was very frustrating at the end.
Overall though, I would still recommend this game if:
(1) you own a controller,
(2) it is on sale, or
(3) you don't have any better game to play at the moment.

Long story short, I bought this game for $5, and that's about what it's worth.  I recommend buying it ONLY when it's on sale for that price or lower.
Pros:
o-The graphics are beautiful and run at max on a even older machines.
o-The story isn't the greatest, but it's entertaining and interesting
o-The voice acting is top notch, though there are really only 3 characters in the whole game that talk except for maybe a minute at the end.
o-Platforming portion of the game is fun and manages to be challenging without demanding that you do every single jump perfect to the second or you die and lose 30 minutes of progression
o-Rez points are frequent, so if you die while learning an area (and you probably will at least once or twice during the multi-wave endurance fights) you just lose a few minutes.  Some of the longer multi-wave endurance fights actually haze rez checkpoints mid-battle.
Cons: Almost 100% due to being a console port, with all that implies
o-Only about 4 hours of gameplay, not counting re-playing for achievements
o-The controls are straight ported from the console version.  You can play with KB+M, but you can't change the keybindings and the combo descriptsion only tell you what buttons to press on a controller, even if you're playing the PC version with KB+M.  Many of the key configurations are impossible to use without taking your hand off the WASD keys, which can often lead to death.  For example, when changing ranged ammo (which you need to do very fast mid battle), you have to use the right and left arrow keys while aiming with the mouse and moving with WASD.  To use your power combo, you need to hit both E and F at the same time, again while using hte mouse to turn and WASD to move.  I hope you have a third hand.
o-There are only three combos and two of them (evade strike and counter strike) are useless.  I guess that's sort of a problem that solves other problems...
o-Like many console games, the controls are slippery.  In other words, fine maneuvering is very hard.  If you're close to where you want to be, but not quite there, you may find yourself overshooting it back and forth multiple times.  Additinally, direction is not attached to the camera, so you can't turn without moving, often leaving you attacking air when trying to switch targets.
o-You have extremely limited control over the camera.  It changes constantly from front to back to side views without any ability to stop it, often leading you to accidentally going the wrong direction or having to jump to an object you can't even see.  Additionally, being a console port, when you DO have control of the camera, the camera has spin inertia/acceleration, which at numerous times made me so nauseous I had to take a break for a few minutes before continuing.
o-Being a console game, you can't save, you only have checkpoints.  And though rez points are frequent, SAVE points are not.  If you die, you might lose a minute or two of progression.  If you quit for the night and come back, you can lose 20-30 minutes.  I ended up just leaving the game running overnight, which is why I have 27 hours on record for a game I only played for about 5 hours.
o-Being a console port, the resolution is upscaled for the PC.  As usual, this creates problems for multi-monitor setups, because most of the game ends up being off-screen and the little text on the screen is unreadable.  This is compounded by the fact that Enslaved automatically uses your native desktop resolution even if that resolution is unsupported, the resolution options end up offscreen at startup, and if you manage to actually fix it, the resolution resets to native every time you open the game even if you make the config files read-only.  Leaving the game open avoids this.
If you've read this far, I give you one final piece of advice: you don't need to get all the currency to finish.  Get what you can, always remember to check behind you and in dead ends, and you'll be fine.   Get 1 health regen, then both plasma damage upgrades, the rest of the HP regen then all the shield, HP, and ammo upgrades.  After that you don't really need anything else, so the rest is up to you.

This is a crappy console port (one of the worst that I have ever seen) that makes the assumption that one plays PC games exclusively with a Console controller, and not Keyboard + Mouse, and certainly not an alternative Input device such as a Trackball or a Gamepad. It does not have any options for Key or Mouse bindings, and as such if your Input device doesn't have, say a Middle-Mouse button for instance, you simply cannot play.
On top of that, the game assumes that you have an Analog stick to constantly reorient the camera. There are no camera controls for K+M or other Input devices. As such, the camera gets stuck at a weird angle making platform jumping and combat difficult at best, and at worst makes you nauesous as it constantly spins around.
I shouldn't have expected anything more than a sub-par Console port from Namco Bandai (they are as bad as Capcom). The Japanese are so rigid (and outdated) in their thinking that PC gaming nothing more than an afterthought, and simply cannot fathom why anyone would play a game with something other than a Console controller even when their business depends upon it.

600+ hours in and I still haven't come
to finishing the available PvE content.
I've played TES games since Morrowind GOTY first came out and I was initially skeptical of the idea of an online Tamriel. But ESO has everything I love about sandbox games: tonnes of quests, visually & mechanically different zones, environmental storytelling, all kinds of possibilities for creative & viable builds (if you're not a min-maxer), interesting NPCs, and a lot to do as a sneaky thief-type. And I can play with my DS4 controller on PC, so bonus. It
like an Elder Scrolls game to me, even though reviews at launch said otherwise.
This game also got me to try PvP for the first time. I spend 90% of my time in solo PvE - questing, harvesting, trying to climb cliffs - but playing PvP in a large group, raining seige weapons and support spells, is lots of fun and lets me feel useful without constantly dying to 1v1 players.
ESO isn't a perfect game, by any stretch. Every major update (every 2-3 months) re-unbalances the game, such that a lot of build advice from six months ago just doesn't work anymore. Zone chat ranges from positive to politics-related trolling, but the "Ignore" feature makes that easy to deal with; choice of guilds helps too.
(Side note: The recent One Tamriel update has made group content a lot simpler: cross-faction PvE means there are more people in the former "silver" and "gold" zones, I no longer out-level content by doing ~too many~ quests, and the battle levelling means that I can group my lvl 50 main with a lvl 20 guildie and *play* instead of steamroll all their enemies for them.)

It was a fun game for the first few hours. Great graphics and sound, and they've created an immersive universe which feels just like the films.
However, once the alien appears the gameplay gets very tedious very quickly. It only seems interested in you, it completely ignores all the NPCs wandering around. Coupled with the fact that if the alien is scripted to be in "a mission" it will just loiter around that area, suspiciously close to your character, seemingly teleporting around rather than moving along corridors/vents.
After the first few times it magically locates and kills you (the first time is indeed chilling), it just becomes a save/load fest devoid of any suspense or tension because you just wonder when the last time you saved it was and hope it wasn't too long ago. Compounding that issue the checkpoint save system will often have you redoing large portions of the game.
Another design problem worth mentioning is that when you encounter a hostile with a pistol and take them out, although their pistol drops and you can kick it about, you can't pick it up. You have to wait till the game allows you to obtain a pistol, which eventually is just sat on a desk.
I think it would have been a much, much better game if the alien didn't actually appear until much later in the game and you just heard it banging around in the vents, or maybe came across it's victims from time to time. Seeing it so often, and being killed by it so often, made the game ultimately dull and repetitive.

The dialogue must have been written by a sixth grader, as every character emotes like a rock slab with half the animation, and each one has lines ripped straight from the world's most awkward children's panto. Emily Kaldwin and Corvo Attano have finally reached the pinnacle of boring protagonists, right there with Master Chief, Nathan Drake, Marcus Fenix, and every other generic white-bread protagonist simmering with nonspecific rage. Neither character has any kind of relatable/believable goal that isn't outshined by literally any other character. I speak no hyperbole when I say that Emily is the most boring, one-dimensional character in a Dishonored game (and that's saying something). Corvo and Emily could easily have been replaced by paper cutouts with frowny faces drawn on them, and there wouldn't have been much difference. Emily comes across as a petulant teenager (her poorly written "diary" entries spring to mind), and Corvo feels alternatively like a tired dad and a generic Strong-Man Savior trope. Fun fact about the antagonist: her driving motivation, the reason why she orchestrated a coup to overthrow Emily, is because
That's the caliber of writing you can expect from the entire game.
Aside from the story, the difficulty is completely ♥♥♥♥ed. Bethesda, work-shy ♥♥♥♥♥ that they are, elected not to balance their own game, and instead left it completely up to the player. There's an in-game menu that lets you tweak every possible factor that could potentially stand to challenge or interest you in any way, from "Enemy Chase Tenacity" to "Elixir Strength". That's not to say the game is easy - it's not, because the game is woefully inconsistent with its horrible difficulty system. The Clockwork Mansion, coupled with the clunky Blink replacement they gave to Emily, made for a lot of anger that I'd really have preferred to direct elsewhere.
Speaking of the funky Blink replacement, Dishonored again shows its one and only strength: worldbuilding. Horrible characters and bad game design aside, the world of Dunwall and Dishonored in general is very engrossing. I could spend hours getting lost in the extended fiction of the world - and this makes for a much better story, too.
Truthfully, I can only recommend this game to a huge Dishonored fan - one who can get over all of the dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥that drags it down. Even then, it's hard to want to play in and know more about this world when all of the characters we're supposed to care about are essentially identical to early Arnold Schwarzneggar roles with sillier accents.
Don't bother. Buy Hitman: Blood Money instead.

Smite has become my favorite game of all time.  Even though I only have about 400 hours or so played on Steam, I've been playing the game since about September of 2014 with about 980 hours logged to date.  Smite is a third person action MOBA, with a much easier learning curve than other MOBA's such as League of Legends or DOTA 2, due to the nature of its third person perspective and plays a bit like a third person shooter.  There are multiple game modes such as Arena, which is a team deathmatch type game mode, for the more casual players, or Conquest for the more competitive players, which is your basic three lane MOBA map with a jungle, jungle camps, and objectives in said jungle. Hi-Rez Studios, the company that makes SMITE frequently adds characters to the game, and patches it every two weeks or so.  Not to mention the great deal that is the Ultimate God Pack, which gives you every existing character, and ever character to be released in the future, all for only $30 USD.  Occaisionally you will run into minor bugs, but 99/100 times they won't effect your gameplay experience. An incredibly enjoyabe story driven action adventure game. Ninja Theory have done a truly exemplary job of adapting the classic Chinese tale Journey to the West into a post-apocalyptic tale of heartbreak and an ambiguous revenge.
There are issues with the game - while always satisfying, combat quickly becomes a bit dull and the upgrade system bears no more mention than that its there. Clambouring around as the main character Monkey is good fun, but again the climbing system lacks an real nuance or depth - its a bit of button mashing with a few odd timing challenges thrown in, but thats about it. Avoiding enemies and sneaking around is more or less impossible in most instances - there are fairly regular sections of the game where you simply have to take a few bullets while diving from cover to cover, before eventually reahcing your goal or anhiletaing the bullet drones, making for some linear gameplay.
You may read that and think that this is a poor game, and in a sense you'd be right. The gameplay itself is nothing new or revolutionary - you could be forgiven for thinking you were playing Jak and Dexter or similar action adventure games of old. The gameplay is, simply put, a bit pedestrian (espcially for 2014, when I purchased it, though not too bad for 2010, its original release).
However, where this game really shines is how Ninja Theory have approached the story, characters and world. This a beautifully designed, atmospheric imagining of an America torn up by a long and brutal world war, in which nature is well along its way in recapturing those lands twisted by human toil. The result is a beautiful, lush green world - a far cry from the dull browns that dominate most post-apocalyptic settings. Whats more, our introduction to the world isn't a sad, cliched voiceover explaining the follies of human kind, or a slideshow or any other tired trope; in fact, the little we learn about Enslaveds setting is carefully dolled out through the story and world you move through. Ninja Theory are one of those rare studios that truly lives the "show, don't tell" rule, and in building the setting for Enslaved, they present an arguable master class.
The characters in this game are probably two of the best I've come across in any video game - our fairly quiet protagonist Monkey and our chatty teenaged heroine Trip are both voiced and, surprisingly, animated with an exceptional amount of depth and nuance. Slight inflections of voice, tilting of head, and stellar mocap work by the venerable Andy Serkis all come together to create cutscense and character animations that you actually look forward to watching. The one let down is that Trip, our constant companion, has clearly not recieved the same amount of attention in the animation department as Moneky - although that comparison might be slightly unfair considering that Monkey was voiced and mocapped by the unreachable Andy Serkis.
Where this game really starts to shine is in the pacing. While the gameplay has its issues, as alluded to before, they're almost entirely a non-issue because of just how well each element is balanced against the other as the story progresses. You won't find yourself becoming bored or frustrated very often - each successive section of the game offers plenty of variety with very well timed cutscenes, making for an experience that is surprisingly enjoyable, despite its lack of challenge.
Overall, Ninja Theory have created a great story driven game, let down by decidely middle of the road gamplay. However, depsite this, Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is probably one of my favourite games of all time due to its excellent characterizations, top notch story telling and beautiful atmosphere. I was bitterly dissapointed to learn that a planned sequel was canned.
