I've played TES games since Morrowind GOTY first came out and I was initially skeptical of the idea of an online Tamriel. But ESO has everything I love about sandbox games: tonnes of quests, visually & mechanically different zones, environmental storytelling, all kinds of possibilities for creative & viable builds (if you're not a min-maxer), interesting NPCs, and a lot to do as a sneaky thief-type. And I can play with my DS4 controller on PC, so bonus. It
like an Elder Scrolls game to me, even though reviews at launch said otherwise.
This game also got me to try PvP for the first time. I spend 90% of my time in solo PvE - questing, harvesting, trying to climb cliffs - but playing PvP in a large group, raining seige weapons and support spells, is lots of fun and lets me feel useful without constantly dying to 1v1 players.
ESO isn't a perfect game, by any stretch. Every major update (every 2-3 months) re-unbalances the game, such that a lot of build advice from six months ago just doesn't work anymore. Finding those last few collectibles without addons is a pain. Zone chat ranges from positive to politics-related trolling, but the "Ignore" feature makes that easy to deal with; choice of guilds helps too.
(Side note: The recent One Tamriel update has made group content a lot simpler: cross-faction PvE means there are more people in the former "silver" and "gold" zones, I no longer out-level content by doing ~too many~ quests, and the battle levelling means that I can group my lvl 50 main with a lvl 20 guildie and *play* instead of steamroll all their enemies for them.)
After fifteen years refusing to play any game wtih a subscription fee, I now have an ESO+ sub.

The dialogue must have been written by a sixth grader, as every character emotes like a rock slab with half the animation, and each one has lines ripped straight from the world's most awkward children's panto. Emily Kaldwin and Corvo Attano have finally reached the pinnacle of boring protagonists, right there with Master Chief, Nathan Drake, Marcus Fenix, and every other generic white-bread protagonist simmering with nonspecific rage. Neither character has any kind of relatable/believable goal that isn't outshined by literally any other character. I speak no hyperbole when I say that Emily is the most boring, one-dimensional character in a Dishonored game (and that's saying something). Corvo and Emily could easily have been replaced by paper cutouts with frowny faces drawn on them, and there wouldn't have been much difference. Emily comes across as a petulant teenager (her poorly written "diary" entries spring to mind), and Corvo feels alternatively like a tired dad and a generic Strong-Man Savior trope. Fun fact about the antagonist: her driving motivation, the reason why she orchestrated a coup to overthrow Emily, is because
That's the caliber of writing you can expect from the entire game.
Aside from the story, the difficulty is completely ♥♥♥♥ed. Bethesda, work-shy ♥♥♥♥♥ that they are, elected not to balance their own game, and instead left it completely up to the player. There's an in-game menu that lets you tweak every possible factor that could potentially stand to challenge or interest you in any way, from "Enemy Chase Tenacity" to "Elixir Strength". That's not to say the game is easy - it's not, because the game is woefully inconsistent with its horrible difficulty system. The Clockwork Mansion, coupled with the clunky Blink replacement they gave to Emily, made for a lot of anger that I'd really have preferred to direct elsewhere.
Speaking of the funky Blink replacement, Dishonored again shows its one and only strength: worldbuilding. Horrible characters and bad game design aside, the world of Dunwall and Dishonored in general is very engrossing. I could spend hours getting lost in the extended fiction of the world - and this makes for a much better story, too.
Truthfully, I can only recommend this game to a huge Dishonored fan - one who can get over all of the dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥that drags it down. Even then, it's hard to want to play in and know more about this world when all of the characters we're supposed to care about are essentially identical to early Arnold Schwarzneggar roles with sillier accents.
Don't bother. Buy Hitman: Blood Money instead.

It is with both sadness and joy I think back on the bankruptcy of THQ. On the one hand it meant Metro passed from competent hands into the unknown abyss, but at the same time the Homeworld franchise got hit by the defib.  Relic and Sierra both pretty much went bust after Homeworld 2. The title was sold then sold again and that was it. Stuck in economical limbo by a company that did not want to touch it with a five foot stick and rightly so, because how to tackle such a game without creating another Colonial Marines?
But it was revived, by Gearbox of all people, and again hope felt lost. Perhaps it is still lost, but this remastered edition of the original masterpieces shows competence from a company mainly associated with cellshaded gore. There's some funky voiceacting in some places, and you can tell sometimes which voicerecordings are old and which are new, but never has the Mothership looked better.
I know there's a lot of people who complain about broken mechanics, such as formations, but I have had no such issues. 15 hours to move through the main campaign at my own speed and not a single gamebreaking issue has surfaced. No broken combat mechanics, no broken triggers, both HW 1 and 2 formations work for me.
There are some graphical highjinxes though, such as commandeered taiidani ships randomly changing colours between missions, but nothing eyesore-noteworthy was had. Whatever issues people may have with random crashes it hasn't happened to me. Homeworld was a near flawless experience when it was released, one of the absolutely best strategy games ever made. What this remastered edition brings though is so much more than just a higher available resolution and support for inherent 64-bit systems. The graphics are now current generation level. Same with the sound and the classic cinematic sequences. To get that kind of update is like turning Quake into Crysis 3. The difference IS that big. Another great addition is the remade UI, the greatest improvement over the old HW 1 system. And of course let us not forget the updated multiplayer with quite a fair amount of new mechanics to spice things up.
I would say it's not just a remastered edition of the original games, but this is exactly what should be expected from a remastered edition. This is what a remastered edition of any game should actually do. It's not just a relabel of the game; it's what would be expected of an RTS title released today.
But then again, this is Homeworld. It was already a real-time strategy diamond and credit to Gearbox for all the hard work that went into this. They know what they're doing. They WANT this to be every bit as good as it can be, and it shows.

A bit of background. I purchased this game a while back when it was on half price, around $35AUD at the time. Back then they had just started releasing DLC, and the game, for lack of a better word felt 'empty'. Not of content, not of story, but of people. The game had just purged itself of its old system, and has since then gradually been crawling its way out of the abyss. Additionally, my game time shown by steam isn't a very good gauge of my time playing the game, I think at this stage it should be around 300hrs. This is primarily because I started opening the game via the direct launcher shortcut that I keep on my taskbar, rather than through steam. It's a lot faster and saves having to wait for steam to do it's thing, only to open the launcher anyway. I hear they may have changed it lately, but I'll probably still stick with my taskbar.
Anyway, on with my thoughts.
In it's story, it fulfils it purpose and earns the Elder Scrolls name. The story is rich an interesting, and has a nice amount of intrigue peppered with the elder scrolls signature emotive flair that is snuck in. Even if it's a lonely skeleton in a desert it has a purpose, and there's a lot you miss from not hearing out the npc's. Of course the story varies through each area, from the constant tragedy of the early Ebonheart Pact, to the wonder that is Rivinspire in the Daggerfall Covenent and the constant political intrigue of the Aldmeri Dominion. And lets not forget the wonderful characters that guide you throughout each story: The comically self-aware Razum-Dar, Sir Darien Gautier of the make both love and war, and the sultry tease that is Naryu Virian. It's the characters that make the story, and in that way it truly does live up to the elder scrolls name.
The game mechanics and combat system come next. Now this seems to be the part with which the game receives the most flak. So let's be clear here. This is not Skyrim. It is an MMO made utilising the elder scrolls lore as base. It's combat system is not turn based like WoW and such, and I've seen it likened to Guild Wars, particularly the PvP side of things. It runs on cooldowns and the like, with two main distinctions setting them apart. The abiltities and the spammables. The abiltites have the cooldowns, and the spammables are just that. My main criticism of the combat however, is the lack of weight that comes with it. When you hit someone, there's rarely an animation to show that. You feel like your blows are doing nothing but making the red bar above the enemies head move from full to empty. For big bosses that's fine, but when you're fighting a lone enemy or a small group, you expect for your blows to have a sense of impact and cause a reaction, and as I said earlier, this is rare. I personally enjoy the skill system, it has a lot of opportunities from the get go and doesn't force you in any particular direction. Each class has three skill trees, and you can pick and choose the weapon and armour skill trees to focus on, as well as the helpful guild ones. With the recent inclusion of weapon based ultimate abilities, this opportunity has increased further. Over all of that you can focus on three things; magicka, stamina or both, and although from patch to patch the meta around it changes, my personal belief is that if you're following the meta then you're not playing the game to its full potential (I'm looking at all of you peeps who look up the 'best' builds). My favourite thing about the skills and classes however, is that any class can fulfil any job. I'll use some of the most stark contrasts as examples. Sorcerer's and nightblades, the traditional dps classes, can tank. Even more fasinating is the fact you can run a sorcerer with a stamina build. Just think about that for a minute. It's something fresh that has really allowed me to enjoy the game, expecially considering that with in game gold you can pay to have your skills reset, and completely remake your entire character.
Finally we reach the last part, the community. When I first started, I barely saw 10 people around the main cities, and rarely saw anyone out in the wilds, although this could be chalked up to me living in Australia and having an odd timezone, it was still somewhat disheartening. So as I do, I played through the games story by myself. It was difficult at times, and I thought it would be really great to get to a boss and have help, or for someone to show me around and help me out. The real fun began when I noticed the chat for the first time. Ahhhhh, the zone chat, home of shenanigans, memes and random bouts of text based song. Of course you have the usually wtb and wts posts just like any other mmo, but the community really does just have fun. The community itself is probably one of my favourite ones in any MMO. When I first jumped in, everyone was friendly and willing to help and give advice, hell, people gave me free stuff, or offered to craft for me. I had upwards of 10 pm's in the first couple of minutes of asking people to help me out getting into the game. Looking back on the earlier month in particular, this was no more clear than during the Halloween event. This was probably one of the greatest things I've seen in the game, there were so many people, and everyone was willing to trade, or even give away duplicates of the special halloween loot. Whole groups would camp dungeons, and chat about random things while they waited for the bosses to respawn, whether it be daily life, movies, the game, progress on the halloween achievement, or just random acts of song and dance via emotes. Some of these interactions have become my most cherished memories of the game as a whole, and I hope ZOS continues these wonderful events.
Of course it has some toxicity. As anyone knows, some people are just terrible people, and as in all PvP people can get salty and hate-fueled, but that's something no MMO can claim to have avoided. Let's not mention that random game support. To be honest, the support for this game is bad, although I've never had to deal with them myself other than posting bugs on the forums. From what I've heard they have a tendency to ignore tickets, but then I also see plenty of people praising some of their solutions to particular problems, such as exploiters and loss of items. If you're playing the game right and aren't incredibly unlucky, I don't thing you'll need to worry about support. I run the game on a terrible old laptop and I've never had any performance issues that I can't chalk down to my own pile of junk laptop, with the exception of PvP lag, but when there are 60 people throwing aoe's everywhere in a small space like the forts in the PvP areas, you can't expect perfect frame-rates.
That's my thoughts anway, I hope I helped.

People often recognize Dark Souls by terms as "Frustration", but it's a game about becoming good at it and it feels powerful when you master your combat style, that being said : I love this game, It was the first one that I got every achievement. Let's begin
They supposedly fixed the input problem the first game had on pc, but playing on a keyboard is still uncomfortable, I highly recommend an xbox 360 controller.
Visually speaking, graphics are way better! it's not the mess the first game was, no mods required here. Characters and objects get a blur effect whenever they are near the screen edges, flames are prettier and particles are all over, I love when you finish off a boss and he vanishes into a million pieces, check my screenshots later! Textures are fine, except for dlc 1 boss-weapons, what the hell was that? Lights and shadows are pretty good, even if they're not the E3 promise. GeDoSaTo do the job for you if you're up for graphic modifications.
Character animations and combat, all improved in a way it couldn't have been done better, It works perfectly. I wish more games took Dark Souls 2 character/combat fluid animations as a role model.
the Difficulty is one of this saga's identity, but in this game everything comes easier to you : being able to fast travel from the beginning felt a little "too casual" for some people, also, coop make some fights easy but you can always go for the champions covenant and play solo. speaking of which, some covenants in this game reward you with unique spells and gear. New game plus is still here, obviously, and there are some unique encounters on your second playtrough, as well as player invasions and co-op system that separates new players from NG+ ones, best part is that you don't struggle to coop anymore, there is a ring working as a filter for connections, making coop quick and effective, no need for Dsfix this time!
The Lore is there, mostly hidden and open to our own interpretation, I'd say Dark Souls 1 had more impact in terms of story, but they are making this right on the second game with the DLC spisodes.
Level design...well, It fails sometimes, environments are diverse, but transitions lack cohesion. I noticed several points where one area has no logic connection to the next one, there are also Bonfires with enemy spawn points right next to it, it's just stupid.
Equipment extends from magic to steel, allowing players a great variation of builds, Soul Vessels make character respec possible, this was a very good addition to this game.
Combat against enemies (PvE) feels fair at all time, it also depends on you skill and equipement management, the problem is the online community, hackers have been all over in the last few months, expect auto-backstabs and undying foes during your online play, thankfully, Dark Souls has a Moral code that diverges from other games and sometimes, you'll be in a fight so fair and honorable, that dying only makes you want to shake the other player's hand and thank him for the fight (be that guy!)
This game runs pretty good on any computer, I even play it on my notebook sometimes ( i7 3ºGen, HD4000, 6Gigs ), but mostly maxed out with enb/mods on pc ( i5 3570, GTX650ti Boost, 4GB 1600 ) Doesn't go lower then 50fps.
If you enjoy a challenge, Dark Souls is an exhausting and rewarding experience!
tl;dr
+ Amazing co-op experience
+ Combat mechanics
+ Replay value
- Devs don't mind hackers, apparently
- Level design
- PvP Grind for covenant spells

I've played the Total War series since the first Medieval Total War (second in the series), and while Medieval II was my favorite, the Original Rome was a close second. I, for one, feel the Rome II that has emerged from countless updates is a beautifully crafted game; and not only graphically. The feel of the the turn-based campaign truly allows the player to feel like the emperor of an ancient power. Whilst, on the other hand, the scale of the battles allows the player to feel like a conquering hero. That being said, there are some aspects I didn't particularly love about the game, but perhaps only because I have been an avid fan of the series from the beginning. For instance. I am not a huge fan of the new(ish) major and minor settlement system that debuted in Empire, but not Shogun II. But, even though I'm not a fan of it, it adds depth to the strategy of the game, so I'll deal. Another mechanic that is missing, and is hugely annoying, is the inablity for the player to move their capital. This is made even more annoying when coupled with the province system, basically making certian players  stuck not only with a bad capital location, but with a minor city for their power center (ex. Sparta). So if any CA members happen to read this review, I'd suggest that if you dont (re)add the option to move the capital, add a mechanic to at least changes the political center (major city) of a province, if it is completely controlled by the players faction, in future games. (Example: Sparta conquers all of Hellas and Sparta surplants Athens as the political center of the province so Sparta in turn becomes the major settlement do to migration and commerce, etc. ...)

There are drawbacks to this remaster however including missing gameplay mechanics from the original such as physics simulated ballistics and relies on Homeworld 2's system of random number generator for combat simulation and while it has the original fleet formation coupled with the new ones the older ones tend to be bugged, alongside some pathing issues and missing fuel system, but those issues are due to remaking the original Homeworld in the Homeworld 2 some are certain to be fixed with patches while others can be addressed with re balancing.
f you're new to Homeworld none of this should bother you as the RNG mechanics of Homeworld 2 are just as playable, as for the purists who prefer the original gameplay over the newer one, the collection has the original HW1 untouched and fully compatible with modern operating systems with the trade off of having antiquated graphics.
Recommend it to anyone interested in space RTS games or a fantastic space saga in general. Truly one of the greatest games ever made and I can't be more excited for having this gem brought back to life instead of having it locked away in obscurity and intellectual property limbo.

A bit of background. I purchased this game a while back when it was on half price, around $35AUD at the time. Back then they had just started releasing DLC, and the game, for lack of a better word felt 'empty'. Not of content, not of story, but of people. The game had just purged itself of its old system, and has since then gradually been crawling its way out of the abyss. Additionally, my game time shown by steam isn't a very good gauge of my time playing the game, I think at this stage it should be around 300hrs. This is primarily because I started opening the game via the direct launcher shortcut that I keep on my taskbar, rather than through steam. It's a lot faster and saves having to wait for steam to do it's thing, only to open the launcher anyway. I hear they may have changed it lately, but I'll probably still stick with my taskbar.
Anyway, on with my thoughts.
In it's story, it fulfils it purpose and earns the Elder Scrolls name. The story is rich an interesting, and has a nice amount of intrigue peppered with the elder scrolls signature emotive flair that is snuck in. Even if it's a lonely skeleton in a desert it has a purpose, and there's a lot you miss from not hearing out the npc's. Of course the story varies through each area, from the constant tragedy of the early Ebonheart Pact, to the wonder that is Rivinspire in the Daggerfall Covenent and the constant political intrigue of the Aldmeri Dominion. And lets not forget the wonderful characters that guide you throughout each story: The comically self-aware Razum-Dar, Sir Darien Gautier of the make both love and war, and the sultry tease that is Naryu Virian. It's the characters that make the story, and in that way it truly does live up to the elder scrolls name.
The game mechanics and combat system come next. Now this seems to be the part with which the game receives the most flak. So let's be clear here. This is not Skyrim. It is an MMO made utilising the elder scrolls lore as base. It's combat system is not turn based like WoW and such, and I've seen it likened to Guild Wars, particularly the PvP side of things. It runs on cooldowns and the like, with two main distinctions setting them apart. The abiltities and the spammables. The abiltites have the cooldowns, and the spammables are just that. My main criticism of the combat however, is the lack of weight that comes with it. When you hit someone, there's rarely an animation to show that. You feel like your blows are doing nothing but making the red bar above the enemies head move from full to empty. For big bosses that's fine, but when you're fighting a lone enemy or a small group, you expect for your blows to have a sense of impact and cause a reaction, and as I said earlier, this is rare. I personally enjoy the skill system, it has a lot of opportunities from the get go and doesn't force you in any particular direction. Each class has three skill trees, and you can pick and choose the weapon and armour skill trees to focus on, as well as the helpful guild ones. With the recent inclusion of weapon based ultimate abilities, this opportunity has increased further. Over all of that you can focus on three things; magicka, stamina or both, and although from patch to patch the meta around it changes, my personal belief is that if you're following the meta then you're not playing the game to its full potential (I'm looking at all of you peeps who look up the 'best' builds). My favourite thing about the skills and classes however, is that any class can fulfil any job. I'll use some of the most stark contrasts as examples. Sorcerer's and nightblades, the traditional dps classes, can tank. Even more fasinating is the fact you can run a sorcerer with a stamina build. Just think about that for a minute. It's something fresh that has really allowed me to enjoy the game, expecially considering that with in game gold you can pay to have your skills reset, and completely remake your entire character.
Finally we reach the last part, the community. When I first started, I barely saw 10 people around the main cities, and rarely saw anyone out in the wilds, although this could be chalked up to me living in Australia and having an odd timezone, it was still somewhat disheartening. So as I do, I played through the games story by myself. It was difficult at times, and I thought it would be really great to get to a boss and have help, or for someone to show me around and help me out. The real fun began when I noticed the chat for the first time. Ahhhhh, the zone chat, home of shenanigans, memes and random bouts of text based song. Of course you have the usually wtb and wts posts just like any other mmo, but the community really does just have fun. The community itself is probably one of my favourite ones in any MMO. When I first jumped in, everyone was friendly and willing to help and give advice, hell, people gave me free stuff, or offered to craft for me. I had upwards of 10 pm's in the first couple of minutes of asking people to help me out getting into the game. Looking back on the earlier month in particular, this was no more clear than during the Halloween event. This was probably one of the greatest things I've seen in the game, there were so many people, and everyone was willing to trade, or even give away duplicates of the special halloween loot. Whole groups would camp dungeons, and chat about random things while they waited for the bosses to respawn, whether it be daily life, movies, the game, progress on the halloween achievement, or just random acts of song and dance via emotes. Some of these interactions have become my most cherished memories of the game as a whole, and I hope ZOS continues these wonderful events.
Of course it has some toxicity. As anyone knows, some people are just terrible people, and as in all PvP people can get salty and hate-fueled, but that's something no MMO can claim to have avoided. Let's not mention that random game support. To be honest, the support for this game is bad, although I've never had to deal with them myself other than posting bugs on the forums. From what I've heard they have a tendency to ignore tickets, but then I also see plenty of people praising some of their solutions to particular problems, such as exploiters and loss of items. If you're playing the game right and aren't incredibly unlucky, I don't thing you'll need to worry about support. I run the game on a terrible old laptop and I've never had any performance issues that I can't chalk down to my own pile of junk laptop, with the exception of PvP lag, but when there are 60 people throwing aoe's everywhere in a small space like the forts in the PvP areas, you can't expect perfect frame-rates.
That's my thoughts anway, I hope I helped.

Been playing this game since long before Steam release and it's amazing.
If you don't start off on the campaign (something I haven't beaten yet,) you start on an alien planet with a gun, a few bullets, a few scraps of iron, a mineral extractor, and a furnace.  Your objective is to make a colony to welcome the future of mankind while, essentially, destroying the native residents.
You will pollute the world with your lovely little machines, how much is mostly dependant on how you play the game.  Building around a forest will help mitigate some of your pollution (for a time, if I remember correctly, trees will break apart from suffering too much pollution,) but also make base production a hassle and may require a lot of time spent manually cutting trees down to get to resources.  A desert/plains allows for the easiest in terms of base production, but also the worst in terms of pollution mitigation, as well as several other potential issues (namely, not being able to find enough wood.)  You can minimize your pollution via other methods as well, maybe manually mining everything you need (you're pretty hardcore if you do this,) and only using extractors for oil, and minimizing use of electricity to only times when you really need it.
Why so much on pollution?  The aliens will not only attack more frequently as the pollution spreads on to them, but they'll also absorb a little bit of it and become stronger for it.  Are they kicking your butt and preventing you from moving forward?  Try starting a new world in a different biome, or try turning on an option so they only attack when you attack them (or get to close!)
Have you finally beaten off the natives and gotten your colony to land?  Why not start again, with a different world generation??  Try for a different starting biome, or even try for a different setup!  Maybe this time you focus more on trying to get things going through trains, or using robots more, or trying to expunge the use of coal except when neccessary?  How about playing without a care to local wildlife?
STILL not challenging or indepth enough for you?  The game is still early access, and there are updates still being done to it.  I started playing the game around the 10.0 version about a year or so ago, and it's had quite a few updates since then.  And if that's not enough for you, there are tons of mods available that will not only add more depth and complexity to the game (something it probably doesn't need much of, but there's still a joy in doing it!) but also mods that make it harder, or change the playstyle entirely!  Some that I've been interested in trying out are the no-manual mining (except for trees, but I don't often manually mine things anyway) and no-manual crafting (they give you a factory that runs on coal in the start of the game.)
Most the downsides I've encountered are sometimes a very sketchy multiplayer setup, where it's sometimes hard if not impossible to get into a game with more than one person (haven't tested on more recent versions, so take with a grain of salt here,) and the fact that I normally have to go into the save file and erase the replay data to keep the file from being 40+mb to download to the peers (I think they may have fixed this, though? Last times I've played with a friend, the replay data hasn't been too bad.)  I also tend to turn off the sound for the game since I'm often listening to music or talking on Skype with a friend while playing, so I can't comment on those aspects.
Going along with the multiplayer, it's set up in a way that may cause frustration for those who just openly allow others to join their server, maybe even among friends.  Chests are openable by anyone, resources are often sent along the world via easily lootable belts, taking buildings down is done at the same speed regardless of who put it up, or how high tier the building is, a single broken belt/track may cripple an entire system, turrets only respond to alien threats, and all players are visible on the map, etc.  So someone with a trolly personality can easily screw you over and cause many hours of work to be lost.  It's also designed more for co-op play in this respect than PvP.  Not sure if the devs have any plans to change this, though, as I haven't done much research in that regards, since I don't like PvP anyway.
All said and done, the game is really fun and interesting, and leaves things for people to do, especially if you go in with more just yourself.  Someone can sit back and work on the base, while the other can go out and try tackling alien bases if needed, or just explore the surrounding area.  If a resource management, factory building, outpost/town/city defense game doesn't appeal to you, I'd recommend checking out the demo before buying, or just skipping the game over entirely.

A decent 3D action hack and slash game ridden with bugs.
Game's beautiful, as to be expected from Ninja Theory. Very detailed background and level designs, fascinating post apocalyptic feeling. Despite being good, though, graphic settings are just few. If you're that hardcore, then enjoy the lack of AA settings for the start. Not only that, you can only set up but few only - Gamma, Quality, Blur, Motion Blur and Vsync. If you have higher res monitor, then you're out of luck... natively. There's a way to set up manually, check here:
Gameplay is similar to DmC Devil May Cry, just less chaotic. Enemies are but few in one battle, you just have to beat them using limited combo and blocking/evading.
Story wise, you will be forced to escort your annoying girl named Trip. She'll tie you down with that headband and forces you to help her. Though, despite being annoying, you can use her helping hands to distract enemies temporarily or to heal you. Some missions require you to explicitly protect her from harm or you'll die if she dies and the story will revolve around that.
Oh did I mention the game's very linear? Not open world in the slightest? Overall, no revolutionary mechanic for gameplay and/or story, far below Batman Arkham series or DmC Devil May Cry.
Then there's RPG element. If you gather enough exp, you can upgrade your abilities. Don't expect complex skill trees, but at last there's an alternative for your build and playstyle.
For playing the game controller's super recommended. Unfortunately Unreal Engine is garbage at picking up older controllers, so most likely you'll see your buttons reversed if it's Dinput. Xinput is doing fine, though. MK/B is... err.. forget it. Just play with controller.
Now here's the catch, progression blockers are everywhere. If you're caught in it, restart your game and try from last checkpoints. Game is saved automatically periodically so you won't lose much progress, it's just the blockers are beyond annoying if it's not solved as fast as possible after restart.
Overall, great game to play, but not worth full price due to rater shallow gameplay mechanic, bugs ridden game and rather poor port. At this moment of writing, it's 75% off and I can fully recommend you at that price.

A slow paced progression horror survival game in the eerie and isolated Sevastepol space station. Alien: Isolation seems to be quite overrated because of the convincingly amazing graphics and the subject matter, but I feel like many of its flaws are being forgiven and ignored which doesn't do the developers and the players justice, and the genre indirectly suffers as a whole. It's important to note that there are people who just wont like this title.
Overall though, Alien: Isolation is worth experiencing for anyone who wants to explore the incredibly detailed space station, and while the story matter isn't going to satisfy the hardcore movie fans, it's fairly well done and treats James Carmons' works with respect. Anyone looking for a convincing atmosphere and genuinely scary gameplay from a horror game is also going to want to dive right in.
If you belong to neither group, then reviewing the pros and cons should help you decide whether this should go at the top or bottom of your priorities list. Either way it's worth a committed play through for most gamers.
The setting for this game is absolutely great and the 80s product design, and detail on some of the rooms and appliances is incredible, especially early on. The mechanics and feel of the controls, when combined with the wonderful U.I. layers and concepts all add to the immersion and survival experience. The graphics and lighting too, have clearly had a lot of love and attention. It's also technically very sound, and despite a few object rendering glitches, the game as a whole feels very sturdy and reliable.
* Lighting is especially atmospheric and even beautiful in this game. At key moments in the main story you'll slowly become subtly more anxious through a combination of lighting, sound and design, only to have something startling occur, highlighted or hidden in the right way by the positioning of light in the room
The problems from this title all stem from the manner in which gameplay has been designed to fit into the world rather than the other way around. The developers have clearly either started with an amazing and detailed Sevastopol, or had an unrelenting focus on it throughout design, which has benefited the game by creating very real feeling exploration and
discovery while working through the game, but has also detracted from the gameplay in small ways.
Gameplay is often quite predictable after a point, and you know what's going to happen next based on simply the room design or text logs and the game pulls the old movie cliche of "You've reached this point, now you're safe.. No you're NOT!" which wears thin. The plot too, feels way too predictable at times and the story as a whole suffers, especially from a bad ending. It's a real shame, and feels like a let down when compared against the immense work and attention that's went into keeping the world so true to the movies. That said, it's a horror game and for the genre the story is probably above average, I just expect a little more given the production value.
There's also the mid to late section of the game, which has been criticized relentlessly for good reason, where you're given a means of circumvention against the Alien. It helps progress the game and turn it in a faster, lighter direction, but also basically makes large parts of the game, and choices, obsolete and makes for a poorer experience overall.
* The unpredictable nature of the AI helps add to the realistic feel at times, but also undermines gameplay by making some glaring mistakes like discovering you instantly or searching for you then leaving the entire section free for you to walk through safely. It can feel like you're exploiting AI weakness and may remove from the immersion.
* The mechanics, while owing to serve to the horror and survival gameplay work on the whole, but often feel very annoying and repetitive when you've held W and X then Y and Z to open a lock for the 50th time
Priced at £31.99/49.99€/$49.99, Alien: Isolation is priced at around the same point as most triple A titles and very high in terms of its other survival horror competitors. Whether you feel that price point is justified or not is up to you, and play time is very high, clocking in at around 18-20 hours for the main story. Personally I can't justify spending that much on almost any game, but considering the amount of work put into this, I wouldn't have felt ripped off. It does go up to -75% off though, which brings it to a very fair price.
The Season Pass is another £19.99/29.99€/$29.99 and is frankly an outright ripoff. Which is a shame because there are some good DLCs for the right people. All of the DLCs are incredibly short, and maps can often be completed in less than 10 minutes, they're also usually more difficult than the main story, but are almost all very nice looking and short but fun. If you like Survival Mode, look at the 3 Survival Mode DLCs. If you like slower pace, look at the 2 Salvage Modes. If you loved the movie, consider the AC DLCs. Whatever the case, be aware of their utterly ridiculous high price when compared to play time. Buying one of the three is the best way to buy the DLC, and buy more if you liked that mode.
* DLC 1. The Corporate Lockdown includes 3 maps under a time-based (ample time is given)
and optional objectives help add more play time.
* DLC 2. Trauma is very different but also includes another 3 maps in
and includes new enemies.
* DLC 3. Safe Haven includes one large map under the new
which has you venturing out to complete up to 10 objectives. Much harder than previous DLCs but with 2 hours instead of 30 minutes time limit.
* DLC 4. Lost Contact is another
playing similar to Safe Haven. 10 more objectives and also very difficult.
* DLC 5. The Trigger returns to the 3-map
model and is the least liked of the three. Very quick and small maps.
* AC (Additional Content) DLC 1. Crew Expendable is for movie fans looking to revisit and play as one of 3 crew on board the Nostromo. Gameplay is extremely short and can be completed in 30 seconds, but the setting is nicely done.
* AC DLC 2. Last Survivor also revisits the Nostromo but as Ellen Ripley trying to escape after the deaths of Lambert and Parker. Also short (around 20 minutes), also difficult, also a nice setting.

Advanced Warfare has changed the CoD series in a different way. The game is fast-paced. It was awesome at launch, but people got bored of it. It's a change and people are afraid of changes.
Anyway,
The good:
+A nice graphical improvement over CoD's old engine (2008-2012)
+Fun as hell if you don't mind jetpack spammers and laser users
+Exo perks are a nice addition(Cloak, Overdrive etc.), even though they are not OP in my opinion
+The story itself is good, has some nice "cinematic effects" and a plot twist. Not a blockbuster SP experience due to CoD being mainly focused to the MP-side of the game, but it keeps you entertained for some hours.
The bad:
-No dedicated servers ( also hackers, even thought I haven't found any at the moment)
-Maps are badly designed(too small for jetpacks, that's why Titanfall has bigger maps)
-Some guns are overpowered(BAL-27, XMG-1 akimbo etc)
-Sometimes the dialogue feels "off place"
-Jetpacks can be spammable
Personal score: 7.5/10
While this might not be the best entry in the franchise, it's still fun to play, especially with friends and it might keep you entertained for a good amount of time.

I can't recommend this game more. I played it years ago on Xbox when it came out, adored it, and rebought it instantly when it was released on Steam. I loved it that much. Played the game countless times, and it's definitely up there in my top 10 games of all time.
Let me just start by saying that for anyone that likes the old adventure games we used to have like Ratchet and Clank, Spyro, Beyond good and Evil, Rayman etc. this game is a fantastic way to get yourself into the same world you used to feel when playing those older games. It could also be compared to newer games like Tomb Raider and Uncharted.
Story:
=====
Without giving away too much of the discovery on your part, I can say that the world is a very fresh take on the post-apocalyptic setting. The cutscenes and dialogue are very gripping, polished and well spoken. All characters are very likeable, (all 3 of them).
Gameplay:
========
The gameplay consists of platforming and combat. The platforming is relatively easy, though the difficulty is ramped up during sections where you're running away from something, or you might have the ground and walls collapsing under you. It generally feels very satisfying. The combat is relatively fleshed out. At first you don't exactly have many abilities to use, but you can gain more through a rewarding level-up system. Different enemy types keep you on your feet, forcing you to deal with them differently or use them to your advantage against their allies. There are some sections before actually getting to the enemy, where you'll have to move from cover to cover using decoy abilities and such to get to the enemy before they shoot you to bits, without going into spoilers, I'll just say the boss fights are very fun to play, with intuitive ways of killing them as you implement things you have learned in the game to defeat them. There's also one very fun type of section where you use a gadget I don't want to spoil, so I'll just say it feels veeeery fun and cool to use.
Graphics, Sound and Music:
====================
As I said earlier, the game uses an unusual post-apocalyptic setting, in the sense that the environment is all lush, vibrant and filled with nature. The place is overgrown and has nice saturated colours. The Sounds all make sense and are satisfying where they need to be. From collectible-pick-up sounds to smashing-robot-faces-in-with-my-weapon.
The soundtrack is great, cueing in at the right moments, upping the emotion in certain scenes.
Controls:
=======
Although the keyboard and mouse controls are okay, I would definitely recommend using a gamepad for this game. It benefits the experience by quite a bit.
Overall:
======
This is a very rare, hidden gem that absolutely doesn't get the credit it deserves. Give it a try, the devs really deserve the money

A slow paced progression horror survival game in the eerie and isolated Sevastepol space station. Alien: Isolation seems to be quite overrated because of the convincingly amazing graphics and the subject matter, but I feel like many of its flaws are being forgiven and ignored which doesn't do the developers and the players justice, and the genre indirectly suffers as a whole. It's important to note that there are people who just wont like this title.
Overall though, Alien: Isolation is worth experiencing for anyone who wants to explore the incredibly detailed space station, and while the story matter isn't going to satisfy the hardcore movie fans, it's fairly well done and treats James Carmons' works with respect. Anyone looking for a convincing atmosphere and genuinely scary gameplay from a horror game is also going to want to dive right in.
If you belong to neither group, then reviewing the pros and cons should help you decide whether this should go at the top or bottom of your priorities list. Either way it's worth a committed play through for most gamers.
The setting for this game is absolutely great and the 80s product design, and detail on some of the rooms and appliances is incredible, especially early on. The mechanics and feel of the controls, when combined with the wonderful U.I. layers and concepts all add to the immersion and survival experience. The graphics and lighting too, have clearly had a lot of love and attention. It's also technically very sound, and despite a few object rendering glitches, the game as a whole feels very sturdy and reliable.
* Lighting is especially atmospheric and even beautiful in this game. At key moments in the main story you'll slowly become subtly more anxious through a combination of lighting, sound and design, only to have something startling occur, highlighted or hidden in the right way by the positioning of light in the room
The problems from this title all stem from the manner in which gameplay has been designed to fit into the world rather than the other way around. The developers have clearly either started with an amazing and detailed Sevastopol, or had an unrelenting focus on it throughout design, which has benefited the game by creating very real feeling exploration and
discovery while working through the game, but has also detracted from the gameplay in small ways.
Gameplay is often quite predictable after a point, and you know what's going to happen next based on simply the room design or text logs and the game pulls the old movie cliche of "You've reached this point, now you're safe.. No you're NOT!" which wears thin. The plot too, feels way too predictable at times and the story as a whole suffers, especially from a bad ending. It's a real shame, and feels like a let down when compared against the immense work and attention that's went into keeping the world so true to the movies. That said, it's a horror game and for the genre the story is probably above average, I just expect a little more given the production value.
There's also the mid to late section of the game, which has been criticized relentlessly for good reason, where you're given a means of circumvention against the Alien. It helps progress the game and turn it in a faster, lighter direction, but also basically makes large parts of the game, and choices, obsolete and makes for a poorer experience overall.
* The unpredictable nature of the AI helps add to the realistic feel at times, but also undermines gameplay by making some glaring mistakes like discovering you instantly or searching for you then leaving the entire section free for you to walk through safely. It can feel like you're exploiting AI weakness and may remove from the immersion.
* The mechanics, while owing to serve to the horror and survival gameplay work on the whole, but often feel very annoying and repetitive when you've held W and X then Y and Z to open a lock for the 50th time
Priced at £31.99/49.99€/$49.99, Alien: Isolation is priced at around the same point as most triple A titles and very high in terms of its other survival horror competitors. Whether you feel that price point is justified or not is up to you, and play time is very high, clocking in at around 18-20 hours for the main story. Personally I can't justify spending that much on almost any game, but considering the amount of work put into this, I wouldn't have felt ripped off. It does go up to -75% off though, which brings it to a very fair price.
The Season Pass is another £19.99/29.99€/$29.99 and is frankly an outright ripoff. Which is a shame because there are some good DLCs for the right people. All of the DLCs are incredibly short, and maps can often be completed in less than 10 minutes, they're also usually more difficult than the main story, but are almost all very nice looking and short but fun. If you like Survival Mode, look at the 3 Survival Mode DLCs. If you like slower pace, look at the 2 Salvage Modes. If you loved the movie, consider the AC DLCs. Whatever the case, be aware of their utterly ridiculous high price when compared to play time. Buying one of the three is the best way to buy the DLC, and buy more if you liked that mode.
* DLC 1. The Corporate Lockdown includes 3 maps under a time-based (ample time is given)
and optional objectives help add more play time.
* DLC 2. Trauma is very different but also includes another 3 maps in
and includes new enemies.
* DLC 3. Safe Haven includes one large map under the new
which has you venturing out to complete up to 10 objectives. Much harder than previous DLCs but with 2 hours instead of 30 minutes time limit.
* DLC 4. Lost Contact is another
playing similar to Safe Haven. 10 more objectives and also very difficult.
* DLC 5. The Trigger returns to the 3-map
model and is the least liked of the three. Very quick and small maps.

TL;DR
Borderlands 2 is the heart and soul of a sequel , with well developed characters and some of the best writing I’ve ever seen in a video game you will love every character, for the exact reasons they want you to like them. With an arsenal of weapons blast your way through armies of villains and monsters.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Combat in this game is where its takes a hit on pc at least, enemies tend to stand still and next to explosive barrels. But even with those it still fun to fire rockets and explode in to more rockets that explode into grenades. The guns are extremely fun to play with and driving around with your party through bandit camps is very fun. Outside of a vehicle you’ll find everything being rather slow and jumping around is like being on the moon. When main goal is to collect loot and make your character as strong as possible.
Borderlands 2 has some of the funniest and well thought out script you’ll find in most videogames. Characters from the previous game make returns as npcs and even if you haven’t played the previous game you’ll fall in love with the characters for the same reason. For the actual story your thrown in the world of Pandora with a main villain you will surprisingly love. Slowly you’ll bring arise a rebellion group to fight at your side. As you progress through the story you’ll see how the world interacts with itself as landmasses change before your eyes.
There will be no character in the game that you will hate unless the writers wanted you too. Even minor characters will have lines that’ll make you smile. You’ll also slowly learn that literally everyone in the game is insane in one way or another. There is such a diverse and plentiful array of characters each one is memorable and full of references to other games and pop culture.
The signature art style for borderlands is the cartoony style and rough outlines everything in the world has each guns looks unique with a slight focus on its effects in the design. All characters that have at least a minor role in the story or gives a unique quest has a fantastic and unique look about them, if someone showed you a picture of a random character you would recognize immediately and be able to name them even the guy that asks you to shoot him in the face.
If you are looking for an rpg with non-serious and depressing dialogue, then borderlands 2 is a fantastic pick up. With all the DLC that has been added to the game the GOTY version is a definite must and so worth the price.

Having only played 3 hours of the game at time of writing, I can confirm that the game is essentially the same as Homeworld / Homeworld 2. This is certainly not a bad thing as I have extremely fond memories of playing both of the original games, they are of the very highest quality and there really is nothing quite like them knocking around today. The remastered editions seem to use very much the same audio and gameplay mechanics just with "HD" textures, particle effects, shaders and lighting effects. Whilst graphics are not the most important aspect of this game, the remaster really does make for a fantastically beautiful gaming experience. I've had one crash so far, which is fine but the game as a whole is just as fantastic as the original(s)...There have been a few tweks, most notibly to the AI and the UI and the games are probably better for it. They are still insanely tough (if you don't have the correct unit types going into a level then you are surely going to be blown to bits) but hugely enjoyable. Trying the multiplayer once I've finished both of the campaigns (again) just gives me more to look out for. Only drawback so far? No Cataclysm, but hey, you can't have everything.

Over All I must say that it's a Nice little upgrade I'm working on HW1 (as it's my favorite) and I must say there's some good points but some bad points too.
Firstly the good points VS the origional:
+ Graphics (and resolution) are FAR superior
+ Fuel taken out, some may disagree, but I rember that as an annoyance where my interceptors would run out of fuel and just have to limp back to the nearest support ship at about 10% speed.
+ Probably my favorite game of all time not being forgotten and left in the dustbin. I mean for a strategy game, just sit down and listen to the story. None have moved me quite that way since.
+UI is Cleaned up It's a bit more useable than I remeber the old one being although...
Now the Bad points (things that they did WORSE than 15 years ago)
- Movement commands and camera control have been reworked, it's actually made it harder for me to move in #D space when I could just have hit a button to toggle moving up and down.
-Formations are now almost worthless. Formation cohesion breks down the moment in combat, not to mention not all ships (repair frigate I'm looking at you, you should NOT be leading the charge into a pair of destroyers)
-Stances are now really just a joke. It used to be that you could be in defensive stance and have your ships move a little faster and dodge a bit more at the expense of  attack power, and vice versa you could set it to aggressive for no evasion but really lay into your enemies. Now.... you just control if your ships auto engage or not... TBH rather pointless especially when some combat ships default to passive.
-No time speed up. I guess I didn't Mplay it much, but I found that a VERY useful feature when mission hopping.
TLDR They should have stayed true to the homeworld 1 engine, but it's still a fun game, even if it's only tied with the origional from 15 years ago. I'm sure that since the main focus was on 2 (can't figure out why. Alien Isolation
Alien Isolation offers more than 14 steady, smooth, terrifying hours. The game unloads slowly and it does it with surgical precision. Nothing is rushed. Which surprised me greatly. Also they really wanted to make scary game. In the same vein as older titles as System Shock 2 and newer horror classics such as Amnesia. But having much bigger budged and the time they needed, the team behind Alien Isolation created something the industry itself declared dead, on numerous occasions.
I finished it in one sitting. And it is technical spectacle. It is sad thing when you have to specify something like that – but the game is smooth, optimized to perfection and has no bugs or glitches. Throughout the whole thing I got ONCE a floating revolver in the air. That’s it. There were no crashes, no freezes, no frame rate drops, no nothing. My machine is built around AMD processor and AMD graphic card (as is the game itself) but I don’t see how any, intel/nvidia/or any strange combination of components, players would have any problems. This thing is solid.
Let’s start with the most obvious. The visuals are incredible authentic and synced with the look of the original Alien movie. The details are mindboggling. This year we have another game that might honor its movie license (Mad Max) and I can only hope they spent so much time as the team of Alien Isolation creating their world. This is more faithful to the franchise than most of the movies. From the distorted logos in the beginning to the last scene this is the Alien game fans have been wanting and waiting for for so many years. They even sent you to a relatively long stretch on the planet from the movie.
The lighting is pretty much the unsung hero of this product. Not only it creates the atmosphere it just looks natural. It feels like real light coming from lamps. Computer screens, alarm lights, flickering lamps, electricity, fire, the burning star outside the station, the soft interior lighting in the living rooms. Also rays going through mist and smoke (also greatly done). Just amazing. Which leads to…
You are in space. And you know it. Isolated and you hate it. You are in this space station and you believe it with your whole body. People say to play it with oculus rift, in the dark, with head phones and all this. NO. You don’t need to. The game is so immersive because of its thick atmosphere you will be drowning in it even if you play it on calculator, during the day with brutal glare on the screen. The only problem is there are no reflections. Most obvious with the helmets. You can see the whole room behind you but Amanda’s face is nowhere to be found when she is looking directly into it.
People don’t walk in games. They can fight and it will look great but force them to walk or sprint and watch the joint carnage. You have the occasional sliding character but most of the human animations here are superb. Impressive motion capture of the bodies. Sadly the eyes and mouths have got the short straw. The uncanny face is great for the android character, the rest… Let’s say it is best they left the face to face interactions to the bare minimum. There is the biggest damage. Sadly you don’t see Ripley’s whole body, except when she is impaled from the back, but at least her feet and legs up to her knees are there, so you don’t feel like floating around.
But the star is the Alien. The most work it seems went there and it shows. I mean, he does walk a little bit like Jurassic Park’s raptor, but it fits. The way he slides from the ceiling, or jumps back up. His movement during kill animations and overall presence scream danger and death. You want that from a top class predator and he doesn’t disappoint. And, as we have seen before, it could have been so easy to make him look funny. They didn’t. They made him menacing.
From the way the camera shakes when you walk or run, through the hacking games, to the gunplay, to the way you open doors, everything feels natural and has weight. Walking is such a basic idea but just like the animation it is easy to mess it up. The way you move is crucial and if it is done right no one pays attention but ruin it and you will hear about it. And I wanted to give props for doing great job. But you have to remember you are not a soldier or trained martial artist. Amanda is regular mechanic. She goes to a place and fix something. You know, what Dead Space was supposed to be doing but quickly turned into schlocky gore fest. Just operating with the tools that Amanda has and entering computers is great fun. Next to that you hide and evade. It was strange to have no real visibility indicator, since you can’t really rely on the motion tracker. The enemies can hear it. But it was done in much more realistic and cool way. As in real life you won’t watch a bar to see if someone has spotted you or not. So you might be in a dark corner but you are not in pitch black spot. It is reasonable to believe that the person, or alien, or robot staring right into that corner would see you. Which made the game even tenser.
The shooting, for your sake don’t overuse it, is great. The revolver and the shotgun, especially, both have that Phat heavy kick. And I guess on easy you can play with them much more. But on harder difficulty they create more problems than they solve and also ammo is really scarce.
Lastly the hacking games. I love them. Plain and simple. Great fun, intuitive and you always have your back exposed during them. You have to be fast, precise and do any sort of hack (or unlocking a door) when you are something like 90% sure there is nothing behind you.
Music is perfect. And… yeah… perfect.
The sound effects are great. They are the final component that the atmosphere needs and they deliver. Everything has a character. The buzz of the ship and its alarms are unnerving while locks, doors and panels have that satisfying click that even Borderlands 2 can struggle to get. The quiet soft footsteps of Ripley can get, in your head, deafening when she is creeping in the dark and the sound of her feet hitting metal floor is going alongside with the Alien’s stomps. The screams, the explosions, the static quality of the dialogue when delivered through microphones. And applause for the way they handled the outer space portions. Mix between no sound and muffled sounds in the helmet, broken by the breaths of Amanda.
Have you watched Alien? Everyday people, big corporation and interests, marginalizing human life, aliens in the vents. You know the story. The dialogue is normal and plausible. Like extracted from everyday life. And the characters are great and memorable. They look, act and talk like real people. Which leads to the actors themselves. This is what you say top class. Even minor characters, even logs in computers have great delivery. But Amanda takes the cake. The actress behind her gives everything that she has to bring humanity to the voice behind the camera. This is not the typical female character that looks like a super model but can bench press 200kg. She is human first. A daughter looking for her mother. That’s it. And just like her she is thrown in impossible situation where she can either stand in one place and die, or try and save herself and whoever she can. Her voice is so full of emotion and so rich you forget about yourself. She is great and immersive character through which eyes you experience the horror.
Absolutely gorgeous game. Incredibly well put together, made much more special by today’s low standards of big budget games and horror in general. It is strange combination but Alien Isolation awards, at the same time, patience and bravery.
PS. The save system is bad! I wish they can patch or someone somehow mod button saves.

Just Cause 3 is probably one of my favorite games I played this year, I've had an amazing time playing it and I'm almost done with the story, and yet still will go finish off capturing the world.
I recommend this game with a huge caveat. IF YOU CAN PLAY IT, you're going to have an absolutely brilliant time.
With that being said, I have an Alienware Alpha and put in 16 gigs of ram, and had no problems.  I did have 1 crash, and it lost my save game onces (A HUGE problem mind you, as I lost about 12 hours of progress, but got it back in maybe half the time).  It has a number of decent size bugs clearly.
However when it works?  It works!  There's a base, I soften it up with a few strafing runs with a military jet I stole, til my plane gets shot down by SAM attacks.  I eject over the base, and parachute in, as my plane "lands" in a huge explosion taking out one of the many critical targets.  I continue to work my way through the base, killing soldiers and blowing up stuff, while an attack helicopter arrives to kill me.  Sadly I haven't hacked a SAM to be friendly, and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is shooting me often enough that I don't have the time to at the moment.  I go to the tried and true method.  I use my grappling hook to tie him to the ground, and have in reel in. Pulling him out of the air, making him unstable and down he goes, directly into me.
The entire time I'm laughing and having a blast, it's so much fun to just rain hell down on an unsuspecting enemy.    The tether gun is a thing of pure magic, you can take any two objects and fling them at each other with a ton of force, this can be two structures, a building and a guard, A guard's head and another guard's butt.  Just that one weapon would have made an extremely fun game.
Some of my favorite moments are when I'm reloading, and I'm getting shot up, it's taking too long so I find the shooter and now have two choices, either zip line and kick him in the face, or tether him to the nearest object (bonus points if it's explodable) and send him face first to his death.   Waiting on a reload no longer is necessary.
Then there's the wingsuit.  I started hating the device, thinking it was impossible to use effectively.  Within two hours I was flinging myself across kilometers of land without a second thought.   Grapple the ground, pull up, reel into the ground and slingshotting between points faster than almost any other object in the game.  The speed, the excitement, the rush.     The wingsuit is to movement, what the tether gun is to combat, a redefinition of an idea that every game thinks they mastered.
There's so many moment, and there's a HUGE world to conquer in this game.   However there's a few caveats.
The missions are a mix.  Some are absolutely amazing (There's a few where the player is doing stunts worthy of James Bond, or better)  And some are defend a point missions which are frustrating or dull.    The story alongside pretty much every mission isn't just weak.  It's bad.  I mean half the time I don't know exactly what people are talking about and the other half I just don't care.   The third Island has about three to four times the first two area's landmass (Note all islands are accessible at any time, so you can truly free roam from the first moment) But about the same amount of content, so there's just more open area.
However none of that matters when you're ripping a base to shred with some wire, some guns, and a RPG, grenade launcher or any other weapon of destruction you can find, as enemies flail helplessly against you.
Overall I'd say if you can run it, it's a fantastic game.  You're going to have a good time destroying and toppling an enemy regime.  But "If you can run it" is sadly a bigger question than it should be.   If you have a computer that can handle it though, no question, hands down, this is a great game.

Why am I not able to post reviews? I hit the post review button, it says "Recommend or no?" I click YES, and it .... does nothing
Is it the lacklustre story? That is certainly part of it. Medici, which is basically just mountains and Mediterranean fields, also lacks the same wide diversity of jungle to deserts to archipelago as Panau and therefore interest. But, I think the primary reason is that despite being technically far superior and having a lot of things to do side mission-wise, and despite, I would imagine, a similar-sized map (though, it seems, a LOT more water) this game is less interesting because there is a distinct DEARTH of villages, people, cultures, activity ... LIFE!! JC2 was ABOUNDING in life, and almost every village was another place to take back from the dictatorship. By contrast, Medici consists of a bunch of coastal cities and half of the country depopulated and filled with military bases. It gets dull liberating all those bases. I know that sounds trivial, but it was why I spent 200 hours playing through that game the first time (only 66 this time, and more is doubtful). I was having an absolute blast liberating all those snow-top Tibetan villages, or those Indonesian island ones, or the ones with the huge Buddhist temples. No two seemed alike, and it was fun. Secondly, the three factions were silly cliches but they worked, they were diverse and their storylines were interesting. And the final mission was a bizarro-world blast of silliness. JC3 by comparison had a complete dud of a final boss-fight, and a lead-up that lacked. Sure, the battle missions were new and fun, but... While I think Avalanche Studios must have lost a creative writer between JC2 and 3, and it shows, maybe they listened too much to the kids now on forums saying JC2 was "boring" because it was too big and long. Maybe Avalanche decided to take the wrong advice from the internet. Wouldn't be the first time a game series has been ruined by focus groups -- aye, Infinity Ward? Or maybe a giant Italy isn't remotely as interesting as a giant South-East Asia. Either way, though it should have been more fun, being technically superior and having a lot more gameplay elements, it just... wasn't. That said, JC2 was a 5-star leviathan. That JC3 gets 3.5 stars and a thumbs-up isn't bad. Just... I hoped for lightning to strike twice.

Bro-force is without a doubt one of the best indie titles i've played so far,
The game features a wide cast of characters, which all serve as tributes to some of film and TV's greatest heroes. With this wide cast, comes a wide variety of weapons such as machine guns, shotguns, flamethrowers, high powered rifles and miniguns. Each character has their own special move. which corresponds somewhat to their character, e.g Bro Dredd has access to guided high expolosive rounds and Bro Hard gets stun grenades. Co-Op allows for 4 players to blitz through 1 level at a time, causing ludicrous amounts of chaos in their wake and is by all means great fun.
The game features fully destructable environments, and the game encourages you to use this to your advantage. Don't want to fight that rocket truck? No prob bob, just tunnel under the ♥♥♥♥er by blasting away at the ground. A few levels require you to make use of the environmental hazards at your disposal, in order to defeat certain bosses.
As for the enemies, first you'll be fighting standard ground troops, including 8ft tall guys with chainguns. Next come the vehicles, then come the aliens and after that you start fighting the spawn of hell itself.
The game can be quite difficult at times, with the game even encouraging you to play Normal mode first before playing on Hard mode. The boss battles later in the game can be quite a struggle, but ulitmately satisfiying in the end. You may find yourself starting certain levels over more often than you think and some require a small amount of problem solving, mostly around using the destructable environment to your advantage.
I was able to complete the story mode on normal in about 9 hours, so by no means is this a short game. Hopefully co-op along with the higher difficulty levels will provide me with some extra replayability, along with the custom campaigns and level editor, which I've actually yet to use.
Oh and you get to♥♥♥♥♥♥on satan's grave.
Broforce is a decent game that will probably hold up for a fair few years. I wouldn't mind seeing a sequel/expansion to this game as I would love some more unlockable characters to play as.  I can wholeheatedly recommend getting this game, even more so if its on sale.

When was the last time you played a game therapeutically? Played something to cheer yourself up? Had fun vacuuming? Slime Rancher can do all those things, especially that last point.
Story:
You just got sent lightyears away from earth to deal with a bad breakup through slime ranching. Spend your days unlocking literally every possible door your inconsiderate past landlord closed up while reading charming little digital journals he left everywhere regarding such classics as losing a boot and indecent exposure. Get bombarded with spam email from charming characters such as your obsessive ex, another successful snooty rancher that played their 30 hours to reach end game, and a corporation of construction ninjas that can add multiple things to your ranch in less than a second.
The story is non-invasive (if you can ignore the email notifications) which allows it to be organic to the gameplay. The characters are well written enough that I feel compelled to search out the journals and read the emails, they are quite amusing.
Music:
Every area has fitting background music that doesn't distract from the gameplay while doing well to fill in for wandering sessions where you're not thinking about something. Every piece fits the theme of the game very well as laid back, warm, and mysterious depending on where you are.
Style:
Slime Rancher has a wonderful simple, cute, and colourful art style that is a pleasure to experience. Everything has been well thought out to be iconic but not overly complicated, which helps make the game appear ageless while also being easy on the eyes.
Gameplay:
Slime Rancher has you wandering several unique thematic zones, sucking up all matter of things in your vac pack to bring around as you explore or take back to your ranch to help it grow and prosper. Building a well functioning ranch can be as simple as bringing a few your choice of slime back from the wilderness, plopping the slimes into a corral, upgrading a corral to keep the slimes effectively inside as well as automatically fed and have their products collected with a selective tornado. Alongside the corral tending to your slimes, you can seek out the specific slime's favourite food for double the rewards (or just give them something from their specific diet) and grow it indefinitely in a garden; upgrading its rate of production or yield with upgrades. There are ways to complicate the formula such as letting the slimes free roam instead of using a corral, and mixing two types of slimes into a largo slime at the risk of a third slime type or its products turning the largo into a tarr which would start devouring everything around it and split into more tarr until doused with water or fired into the sea.
Slime Rancher is also a game largely about exploration and rewarding your curiosity. When you're not running circles around your ranch trying to keep everything going efficiently for the sake of money or science (I'll cover that in a bit), you can go out into a world of secrets and alternative paths with the aid of dash boots and a jetpack which challenge you to try and find ways the developers didn't intend only to discover treasure capsules that reward you with various materials and blueprints for Slime Science (still getting to that). Finding the capsules without having the corresponding level of treasure cracker upgrade is rather aggravating sometimes when you're somewhere you don't remember how to get back to though. Exploration will also have you come across overgrown slimes which need to be fed a taste of their own lifestyle until they explode and reveal teleporters or slime keys which enable more exploration or make exploring more efficient.
Slime Science is the end game content that has you make more use of your slime's materials than hoarding money to dump into corporate pockets for new solid gold slime statues. Through Slime Science you can set up your own 2 way teleporters, 2 way single item banks, remote market access points, automatic tarr defence systems, decorative items for your ranch and slimes, and resource collectors to name a few major items. Most of Slime Science is designed around making managing your ranch easier and personalization which is helpful for making the long-term goal process smoother.
Slime Rancher's long-term goal is simple, invest just under 1.5 million newbucks to the money dump corporation. Completing this goal requires a very efficient ranch and a very determined and patient rancher to pump money for a long time. Just keep in mind 7Zee's Slimepedia entry: "Some ranchers point out that the whole thing seems like a way of siphoning enormous sums of newbucks in exchange for fancy colors and trophies that don't actually serve any real purpose. But those ranchers aren't sporting the latest, most fashionable vacpack colors and obviously cannot be trusted."
Replayability:
With variables such as ranching style, slime combinations (if you choose to use largo slimes), several challenge game modes, and open ended design; Slime Rancher has potential for new playthrough ideas, but completion of a playthrough with Slime Science and 7Zee's reward system largely depends on you returning to a highly efficient farm of fully upgraded corrals and gardens that include nearly every slime type then circling the ranch.
Much of Slime Rancher's replayability is the alternate challenge game mode(s) which challenge your understanding of the game. Currently the 5 Day Rush mode is the only challenge which has you aiming for the achievements or competing against friends for making the most spare money within 5 days. In the future there will be more challenges if all goes well in development.
For now, Slime Rancher is best thoroughly completed once in adventure/casual mode, returned to or replayed with large updates, and challenged in 5 Day Rush until you get the achievements or feel adequate.
Conclusion:
Slime Rancher is a thoroughly enjoyable casual adventure that I would recommend to anyone that enjoys open world games and could use a break from a hard day or a difficult game. I don't suggest trying to reach the maximum 7Zee rank without having goals to supplement your gameplay, otherwise the game starts feeling more like a chore than anything and ruins the whole experience; luckily there are large content updates on the horizon to give incentive to come back to where you left off.
tl;dr: Jumped out of a spaceship and enslaved complacent locals, fed prisoners until they filled their cells with poop before I sold that to a black market to donate the funds to a blacker market who would build a solid gold totem fuelled by my corporate greed. Pursued illegal scientific advances and now nothing can stop me, not even my ex. Indie GOTY
