Writing this pretty long after I had completed it, however, it was such that I knew I had to write it sometime and it might as well be now.
I should start off by saying I did NOT play this game when it came out. I didn't really even pay attention to it. I'm a pretty big fan of the Alien franchise (specifically the first two films--the others NEVER HAPPENED-LA-LA-LA-LA.) and needless to say, most of what has evolved from it has been garbage. Why would this be any different? When it finally went on sale for about $6.00, I figured, what the hell...
I am SO GLAD that I was SO WRONG.
This game is simply TERRIFYING. Seriously. I've never been so absorbed in the atmosphere of a videogame as I have with this. Fans of Alien will not be disappointed in the slightest. Those who haven't seen the films, this is a great way to get introduced to the universe. Play this with the lights out and the volume up and you will likely have a panic attack. I feel like this game probably gave me high blood pressure.
A few things to note:
You have to play this on the hardest difficulty. It is incredibly frustrating but all the more rewarding when you move forward. As such, you will die. A lot. This is pretty much unavoidable as you get used to the rules of the game. I hope you're a glutton for punishment.
Speaking of mechanics--while I'm absolutely impressed by the way the Alien (and all of the NPCs, really) is handled in this game, there is a predictable pattern to their behavior that eventually becomes apparent (when you're not dealing with a heart-pounding, scripted event). This means that there are certain things that will and won't attract the attention of a certain, menacing space lobster and once you realize what those are, it may unfortunately break your immersion a little (but luckily, not much).
Did I mention the atmosphere? Because it's brilliant. Every detail of the environment is spot on. The audio and visual effects are basically perfect. Seriously, if you are a fan of the films, you will GEEK OUT at basically everything. I couldn't have asked for more.
Finally, our sister from another mister, Amanda, is everything you could want in a protagonist. I was pretty skeptical that anything or anyone could ever come close to being as badass as Ellen Ripley, but they've somehow managed to do the impossible. Everything she does works within the context of her character, even down to the cadence of her voice. If you're a fan of female protagonists done RIGHT (which, as we all know, doesn't happen often enough in this industry), you will be pleasantly surprised.
I'm the last person who would want to oversaturate the world with more Alien products, but if this developer came up with something new, I'd buy it in a heartbeat.
This game ROCKS. Period. Mic-drop.

I played with the beta of TESO, then my characters were deleted. I spent about 10 hours in-game up to that point, but I never had that nice feeling with the game. I really liked World of Warcraft 10 years ago, and I really liked Guild Wars 2 in the past 4 years. TESO felt and still feels something like The Old Republic. A game with vast amount of lore and a nice amount of additions to the basic formula formed by games like Star Wars Galaxies and WoW. I would not say that I am a big fan of Bethesda's games, the reason mostly being the terrible movement and combat. In TESO they are better, - partially because of the use of a different engine (HERO) - I still did not satisfied with the clunky movement and pretty basic crosshair-based combat.
Other than that the whole MMO system here is decent, not exactly free of busy-work and unfairness, but it is more similar to the classic games of the genre. Chests and other loot in the world are shared between players, so if you are going for something that is needed for a quest you might end up spawn-camping a damn chest. While this is a pretty usual stuff with MMOs, GW2 for example already separated these objects, so everyone can gather their own. Materials can also deposited into the bank via a simple click in the inventory. These might not be everyone's favorite but other than be a little bit anti-immersive the positives are stronger regarding these changes.
Something else that I do not like about TESO is the absence of the imperial race in the base game. It was and still only available as a separate dlc. There are also a few extra content packs, like the main guilds from the previous games, but I can understand that. Cosmetics and various extra things are also available. In the end the micro-transaction system is okayish, not the fairest, but not that bad either.
This time I seriously considered buying the game, even starting a new character would not be a huge problem. But I was displeased with the game after a few hours. It is the same - or at least the start is pretty much the same - which includes the unsatisfying combat and overall movement. These are the things that I simply cannot ignore. If the gameplay is not fun then what is the purpose of those long hours filled with grind.

It was really bad before, but it got an overhaul and it's much better than it was. However, this might be okay as a F2P game, but I wouldn't even buy it on the current sale price, let alone what they are asking for it and the DLC.
The combat is generally pretty fun, and the graphics are nice too for a game that has been out a few years- the enemies look fantastic even.
However for numerous reasons I can't recommend this to anyone; because any good I find in this game is drowned out by tidal waves of problems and issues.
-Extremely grindy even for an MMO
-No sense of progression in that grind anyways, you will see players 300 levels higher than you (Yes  it seems you can go even over like 500 or 600 in levels even) but it all scales to the same anyways. You see them in the same armor and using the same skills you are pretty much.
-Spells and skills feel underwhelming, and there are not a lot of them.
-Low player count for a large MMO. This means dungeon finder takes HOURS sometimes, and you can explore incredibly barren areas for a while, it feels lonely.
-All the quests outside of some in the main quest line are boring and useless.
-Skyshards are a thing you can find from exploring, but are extremely important because they give you skill points, so your option for exploring becomes a mandatory requirement.
-Redundant skills
-Technical problems, not just with the game but with the steam integration and all sorts of issues. I only get like 25 FPS myself in some areas on a modern PC (Gtx 1080, 16GB ram, etc)
-Early dungeons are stupidly easy, and apparently though I am not that far, the later ones are way too difficult. As healer in the dngeons I've done- I never had to heal. It wasn't even a concern it is better to queue as healer with one emergency heal spell and the rest on DPS.
-Character design is limited and the bleak graphics don't help with much standing out in any way.
-UI is clunky.
Just so many flaws I can't get over them and the prices they are charging for the game right now.
I would pass on this one unless it goes F2P someday.

Take yourself back to a simpler time. A happier time. A time when PDAs were cool, people wore really high jeans, and when Homeworld was released.
That's right. Take yourself back to September of 1999. I was 7.
This was a time when strategy games were designed to be pursued and beaten over the course of weeks or months, a time when game designers weren't afraid to kick you in the balls and tell you that you were terrible at their game, and a time when thousands of Homeworld players ripped their hair out after spending hours harvesting resources only to have their fleet obliterated in one short battle.
As a 7-year-old, I did not possess the mental faculties to fully understand the majestic space banana or its purpose as the salvation of a species. I was completely unable to tactically order my fleets through the three dimensional battlefield.  As such, I had no hope of navigating the campaign, but what I could do was build hundreds of space fighters, frigates, capital ships, and carriers, and watch in awe as an epic battle between two armadas unfolded before my very eyes in all its polygonal glory. Many happy hours were spent watching interceptors swerve around capital ships while my ion frigates bombarded them from afar.
Oh that magic nostalgia feeling. How welcome it is. Homeworld remastered has taken the elegant design of the original game (something I'm now more equipped to appreciate) and made it more palatable with gorgeous visuals and streamlined interfaces while keeping the incredible atmosphere, mystery, and♥♥♥♥♥poundingly difficult strategy that we all know and love. A million thumbs up.

After 100+ hours I feel I can give a fair review to Rome II: Fixed Edition (a.k.a. Emperor Edition).
Amazingly I have not once had the game crash on me. There are a few odd display bugs with menus from time to time on the campaign map; but nothing serious. Land battles are pretty solid with probably the best A.I. to date. However the computer does have occasional pathfinding issues namely with units idling. This is most notable with cavalry units no longer dismounting to go over settlement walls. Also unit collision isn't quite as good as Shogun 2 with long lines not really suffering any penalites when they ought to.
Navy battles have at last been balanced; you can no longer abuse army transports as they are strictly limited to boarding and can't ram. However I have on an occasion or two seen retreating ships literally "slide" across the water and off the battlefield which is pretty glaring. It is rather discouraging that these issues have been totally dealt with by CA yet. However considering land+sea battles are pretty bug free I can overlook it.
I'm going to be blunt; this game probably has the best campaign map gameplay of any Total War game I've played. Factions rarely over-expand leaving you to contend with many more powerful city-states as it were. Diplomacy is easily managed by immediate negotiations with encountered factions. Settlements are much easier to manage with them being grouped into "provinces" meaning you only have to worry about public order in that province; not every dinky little settlement. Buildings and technology are also well balanced; and turns are once again resolved in quick order.
Rome II does have it's drawbacks though such as the pointless politcal system, lack of family tree, lack of easily seen skill trees. Most obnoxious is being forced to recruit a general for every army/navy with no option to assign a unit as captain when all you want to do is move some troops. Still Rome II manages to balance these negatives out with all the good changes such as battlefield line of sight, useful skirmisher units, and a good variety in siege maps with only capitals being walled. The Grand Campaign is something of a bust due to 1-year long turns leading to quick character deaths and questionable troop movements: it really takes an army YEARS to just traverse Italy or the Mediterreanean? Some also complain about the musical score not being done by Jeff van Dyck; but for me it's still alright.
In the end Rome II is a pretty solid game now. Just a shame CA didn't get to spend an extra year it likely needed to really finish and play test the game. There is no doubt CA is a very hard working and talented development studio. But it needs SEGA to support them otherwise we end up with rather
.

I have a couple hundred hours in the game, and it's awesome.
The game is about automation. You do something by hand at first, then automate it, then automate the automation. You get a lot of headscratchers when you try to get more complex stuff to flow, you rebuild your factory, you redesign everything.
Then something goes wrong, you realize you don't produce enough red circuits, you examine the problem and realize you don't produce enough plastics, because you don't have enough coal because your smeltery eats up all of it.
Or your electricity goes out and you spend half an hour getting it back up by feeding boilers by hand.
Problems are complex, because there are layers and layers of systems built on each other, and you only notice that something is wrong when the problem reaches the top layer, and you have to peel them back one by one.
If you are a completionist, you can get a ton of fun just tinkering your factory, make it more efficient, find the perfect ratios, realizing golden rules (like producing copper cable only on demand).
But vanilla doesn't make you use trains and the enemies are very easy to fend off. If you want to use the awesomeness that are huge train systems, you really need to use some mods, like RSO. Then you will get another couple hours figuring out how to place signals and chain signals to not get deadlocks. Transport Tycoon players have an advantage here.
Other mods, especially the big overhaul ones make the game fresh for even seasoned people. You have to figure out new ways to make your factory work.
Then add multiplayer to the picture, and the social aspect makes the game fun and cool again. Sharing roles means you can concentrate on the stuff that makes you tick, leaving the rest to the teammates, the more twitchy guys can go clear enemies, collecting the alien stuff, while the more planner types never even touch a weapon.
All in all, if you want fast action, this is not your game. On the other hand, if you like to tinker and think about designs.

Hello all! Looking at my hours played you may not find me a credible source for rating the whole game but nevertheless, I aim to provide a beginner's perspective into Borderlands 2.
Brief intro: I hate grinding games. I despise using up hours of gameplay going back and forth between different areas killing enemies and exploring every nook and cranny of the area to loot for items to garner xp and rely on heavy RNG for the next upgrade for my weapons and equipment. Those type of games feel like a waste of time that do not give me a sense of reward upon reaching a ridiculous level only to grind even more.
With that being said, I had a rocky start with the game, after being recommended to me by friends and it being an FPS, I thought I would overlook the grinding aspect. Unfortunately not. The first couple hours of the game was a slow and uninteresting grind of simple quests to get the hang of the game. After killing the first boss I left the game and retreated back to my fast-paced competitive FPS and RTS games. I decided to give the game a second shot, and boy I'm glad I did. Sure, you grind and grind and the reward is a slow and gradual accumulation of xp and items but I got hooked on the variety of guns, shields, grenade mods and whatever that adjusts style of play. The intruiging storylines each sidequest has is light that gives more focus to the meaty main storyline. The design of different areas that houses different creeps keeps me interested that makes me anticipate the next boss and gives hope for the drops he will leave after you finish them off. I've just started but it seems like I'm here to stay. For grind haters just try to give the game 5 hours of your precious time and I believe you shall be stuck on your chair wanting more and more of the game.
So yeah basically I've just sold my soul. Peace.

This game has the potential to be cute and fun, but ultimately, it just ends up being tedious. It constantly adds more and more to micromanage, and not scaling up automated functions to match.

All the 'challenges' in the game take what should be a fun, casual experience and turn it into video game chores (and not in the fun 'Why is it so much fun to run a farm?' way like in Stardew Valley, or the 'I am literally playing a game where I have to wash dishes, but I love it' way like The Sims).
In the end, I just come away feeling like every new mechanic or area to explore is just punishing me with more things I need to manage but not better tools with which to manage it.

The primary focus of this "game" is the story, and if you are a story kind of gamer, you'll like it. The characters are awesome and the animation and voice acting are a very big deal. I was way into the story. I would've watched a CGI movie with the story and characters in this game, and sometimes I wish that had been an option, because the game itself sort of suffers.
The game itself suffers in three ways. First, the !@#@!%! camera has a mind of its own, and sometimes it moves around at the oddest times. Moving around is sometimes trial and error, because sometimes "up" is "left" or "right" is "up". Secondly, there are occassional scenes where you have to catch Trip being carried away by something. These scenes work almost like quick-time events and you have to die until you know which way to bob and weave. Third, the way you increase your abilities has NOTHING to do with the awesome story at all. You just wander around gathering glowing orbs. You need these, so Trip may say "hurry!" and you have to decide not to. You gather orbs no matter what she says, because you need them to buy things FROM HER, but you never mention these orbs and neither does she. This is an immersion breaker.
All the frustrating lack of elegance in the game play, though, did not keep me from loving the story and the characters. The game was just the right length in that regard, or the frustrating game play might have become old.
Now.... let me say, however, that the grand finale boss fight was absolutely great fun.
I'm sad that there wasn't a sequel, because Trip and Monkey have become friends of mine. I'm gonna miss them. :)

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a third-person action game made by Ninja Theory, the guys who also made Heavenly Sword and the new DMC. It's well-made, but somewhat flawed. Overall, I enjoyed it a lot, especially the first half.
The gameplay is made up of platforming, third-person combat, and some over-the-shoulder shooting. These different aspects of the gameplay are all quite rudimentary on their own, but the game manages to weave them together into a pleasant flow--you are always propelled forward, and you're never stuck. Because of the rudimentary nature of the gameplay, doing any particular thing for long will feel very repetitive, and the game recognizes when that point comes along and switches things up. Although the game was short, I think it would have been less enjoyable if it was any longer.
I really liked the setting and the environment design.  The game definitely has a different take on post-apocalyptic wasteland, with the majority of the game taking place in a lush, jungled version of New York city. It felt like the developers really put a lot of effort into making the world unique and interesting. Though one thing that struck me about the levels was how dated they feel. The game feels to me very much like a game from 2009 with the way it segments off areas.
The character interaction is probably the highlight of the game for me. The dialogue between the main character Monkey and his companion Trip are well-written and well-acted. Their relationship felt real, and I was invested in its development. On the other hand, I found the over-arching story lacking. The ending was much too abrupt and the game didn't spend any time to establish the villain at all. A bulk of the story was just thrusted at you in the ending. The game ended in a good place in terms of gameplay progression, but not in terms of the story arc. Also, what the hell was with the ending cut scene?
Regarding the game being a retelling of Journey to the West, I don't really agree. The game makes a lot of little references to the novel, such as the names of the characters and weapons, but the story itself felt much more like a Western epic. Even though the characters in Journey to the West do go on a quest, it is not a heroic tale like most Western epics. The game makes no reference to Buddhaism, which is the central part of the novel,  and the relationship between Monkey and Trip is also completely different, among many other differences. The connection between Enslaved and Journey to the West is really quite superficial.
All in all, this game was a very pleasant surpise for me. Check it out.

At this time the game is best enjoyed single player. The campaign in HW1 Remastered is amazing and I expect HW2R's to be great as well. The story, cinematics, music and atmosphere all get 10/10
CONTROLS:
Some players have a little trouble getting used to the controls and while this is in part due to the fully 3d nature of the game I also feel it is in part down to the developers descision to keep the old control system rather than improving upon it. That said, everything works nicely and I found everythign easy to get used to. 8/10
GRAPHICS:
The game is simply stunning close up, ships are well detailed, docking ships looks awesome, the enviroments and FX are great. Could they be better.. Probably.. Are they good enough, definitly. 9/10
MULTIPLAYER:
PvP is still in beta, so it is hard to judge, but so far things seem real good. There are objectives and that is something I find very interesting as it is unheard of in other PvP games I play. AI is skilled enough for skirmish games and will give you a real run for your money, Changing tactics from game to game and really testing you. Only real issue is possibly balancing still needs to be done on some units. But hey, this is something completely new to the franchise so it was always going to take time. There is however no co-op campaign.. Something I find sorely lacking as it is my prefered game mode ussually. 7/10
OVERALL:
An exellent game, I highly recommed it to anyone who loves, RTS, sci-fi, or who is just looking to try something new or find a great story to be immersed in. 9/10

I am sorry that I purchased this game. This version of Rome Total War is greatly different than the first version which is greatly enjoyable. Rome II Total War wastes your time and resources with intrigue and factions that detract from what serious gamers like to do: fight battles.  You can never get enough soldiers where you want them as you are limited to the number of generals that you can have so you have large areas of your realm uncovered were any mutinous rebel force can come in and take them after 3 rounds of combat. That's because the garrison force depletes of manpower after every round of combat while the rebels are completely reloaded after each round that you decimate them as if nothing happened. You cannot build walls around every one of your cities either - unless it's a capital province so you may as well write of those territories to any weak invader or rebel force. The unit icons in your battle force look like a 5 year old drew them and that goes for the silly-looking faction symbols as well. My 9 year old niece may as well have drawn them. And to top it all off, your female agents look ugly. If you like to screw alround with intrigue and factions, then go play Crusader Kings II instead.

------------
Disclaimer:
------------
- Before this game, I played Total War titles Rome I and Medieval II. I am pretty sure I have 3000+ hours spent playing these. I am a TW series lover, but that alone doesn't mean I will buy everything CA has to offer me.
- The main reason I haven't played Empire is that I don't really like that era. Shogun theme was also something I don't feel especially compelled to play.
- I am an Antiquity fan. Rome, Carthage, the Hellenic nations and the Persian Empire were always of relevant interest to me. Also the Medes, Assyrians, Phoenicians, Babylonians, Ur and Ancient Egypt.
------------
On its release and subsequent months, this game had a bad reception by total war fans. I pointed out a few issues myself. Despite of its problems, I have never considered this game to be unplayable. After all the patches and DLC's, Rome II resulted in the game I spend more hours with in the last 2 years, and I am happy enough that I pre-ordered it.
Today I consider Rome II a fantastic game. Its graphics are a big step from M2TW, I like many of the new game mechanics and the way they had to make you re-think your strategy in a total war game.
Attila is about to be released, but I am not eager to buy it yet, though it is very likely that it will be much better at day 1 than Rome II was. And yet I feel I have a few hours more to spend enjoying Rome until I eventually find Attila on sale.
Things that could be better compared with the previous titles I played:
* Unit cards - not really fond of them; I currently use a mod with nicer looking unit cards (Bullgod - Style Unit Icons)
* UI in general - come on, CA. History buffs do not like modern minimalist UI's. We want the meaty thing. Where are all the stylish columns, statues, laurels, marble, coins and amphors?
* Politics - A nice idea, but not implemented at an acceptable level. If it were well forged, it could probably substitute the lack of family tree. But it just didn't work out.
* Annoying sounds - I am amazed that I have read someone complaining about this. I find the end of turn pop-up message sounds highly disruptive and too loud when leveled with the rest of the sounds in-game.
* Soundtrack - it is not bad, but it lacks more music. Culture music. A few mods attempt to overcome this, but none of them is really that good.
* Lack of hotseat - I was a hotseat fan, and I played several campaigns with friends of mine. Co-op is nice, but hotseat is a lot better. I can't understand why CA didn't develop it further.
In the end, this game is still highly entertaining, and worth every penny in my opinion.

It's Homeworld, with shiny new graphics. The ultimate space RTS. If you never played it the first time around, you need to buy this; the gameplay was never ever beaten, the story and mission variety is truly excellent, and the art direction is unique.
If you *have* played it before: BE WARNED:
At the moment, some of your favourite features from Homeworld 1 are rather broken. Formations, for example, do not work; your units will ignore them in combat completely, so no more flying balls of death with the sphere formation. Considering how a prominent a role the formations played in the original game, and how a simple formation switch mid-battle could turn the tide, this is a major issue, and one that really shouldn't have made it out of testing.
Also, remember how you could capture all those assault frigates on the third map? Nope. Not anymore. Due to Homeworld 2's unit cap rules, you cannot capture a ship if you don't have the capacity. And you don't have the capacity, if you haven't researched it yet.
Additionally, there are a few general bugs and AI mishaps, such as pathfinding being a bit dodgy (telling two support frigs to heal your ships will result in them bumping into each other and often allowing the ship to die), and engine sounds hanging (so you can hear a ship's engines really loud no matter where you are).
In other words, in spite of the word "remastered", don't expect this to be *polished*. It's great, because it's Homeworld, but it needs some patching.
That being said, despite having to launch the campaigns separately, the skirmish mode allows all content; you can play Homeworld 1 fleets against Homeworld 2 fleets if you want. Which is fantastic.

While my review will say that I recommend, I'm really closer to a mid-point between recommending and not. Having sunk over 300 hours into this game I can say I'm pretty sure I know most of what the game has to offer. While I do find the game enjoyable for the most part, it is clear that there are glaring problems, both in PvP and PvE. The problems in PvP are obvious when someone stabs you and it connects even when the tip of the weapon is clearly not anywhere close to you. Whether this is a problem with hitboxes or poor coding is up to someone else to figure out, but don't expect decent PvP even 60% of the time. PvE is enjoyable, letting  you try different builds and experiment. But the problems come with certain parts of the game that, to me, felt straight up lazy and unoriginal. It's one thing to make a section difficult to the degree where a slight margin of error leads to instant death. It's a completely different thing to make a part straight up instant death without any chance to do anything (I'm looking at you Ancient Dragon). While Dark Souls II is a fun game and I don't regret buying it, I definitely regret purchasing full price for a game that at many points feels like an incomplete product because of lazy or poorly thought out enemy/boss/level design. It may be a sequel to Dark Souls, but I find it lacking in a lot of areas. Buy it if you want. You'll probably enjoy it mostly.

It's great when it works.  Unfortunately, it doesn't always work (i.e. an ambiguous error during the online rigging process that prevents it from successfully completing --- skim through their forum for details, as it wasn't an isolated issue with me).  While this doesn't happen every time, it's happened enough to put a real kink in my workflow.  Happens in both the Steam 1.3 and Adobe CC versions.
On the bright side, when it works, it really does work well (and, if you're like me, you've gotta love that).  I can't complain (too much, I mean, I am human after all, so I still do a little) because of all of the great (unique) figures I've been able to export, rig, and animate for the Unity game engine from Fuse (for free).  A little tweaking is all it takes inside of Unity to have any number of unique and fully animated characters running around your game scene (and again, you've gotta love that --- at least I do).
And speaking of animations --- if you haven't mined the Mixamo website for all of their free animations and characters, you're really missing out on a lot of great stuff that's worth a small fortune if you were to have purchased it prior to their free releases (that I think happened when Adobe purchased Mixamo, but don't quote me on that because it may not be the case).  It's too good of a deal to pass up --- just like getting Fuse for free now, when (I believe) it used to tote a hefty price tag in the not so distant past.
As a side note, while the new CC version has higher resolution figures, it doesn't (currently) contain any medieval fantasy outfits --- so if that makes a difference to you (like it does to me), you might want to continue using version 1.3 until Adobe/Mixamo adds some updated content.  If you do use the CC version, you don't have to purchase or use any of the other CC suite of apps (i.e. Photoshop CC) since you can still export directly to the Mixamo website for rigging (for free) just like in the 1.3 version.
So while I understand the mixed reviews from other users, I still highly recommend that you try it out.  It's free after all, so you don't have too much to lose by giving it a go.  And, if like me, you just might find yourself loving it.

I want to preface this with saying, i think the animations, atmosphere, design, art, sound, and overall tone of the game is amazing, bar none one of the best in horror games, however this game has god awful AI, beyond terrible, to the point it ruins the game and makes it not fun, i'm sure if you play on easy you'll have no problem, if you play on medium you might get a little frustrated from time to time, but on hard and above it's beyond stupid how broken the AI is, to the point where the alien which is chasing you will patrol 8 meters in any direction around you, And you might think "Well it'll move away and i can swiftly move past it right?" wrong it constantly has some sort of lock on your position meaning no matter where you move it'll remain in a certain area around you which seems like 8 meters as i preluded above. You constantly have to hide and weave around it, but if it so much as see's you out of it's peripheral vision your dead, if you run or move at all, your dead, if you do anything at all besides hide, you're more or less dead, it's so badly designed i cant imagine why it was implimented, i'm all for challange but this is a horror game not something like dark souls where dying has some form of benefit or is apart of the game, here you can die for no reason other than sneaking past the alien down a corridor only for it to turn at the last moment catch a glimpse of you, run and insta kill you before you have any chance to react.
Then not to mention the game has a crafting system similar to the last of us where you craft items from junk you find around the station, however each item you can craft have very very situational uses to the point their useless to use, perhaps the items are more useful against different types of opponents? however i stress tested eached of them against the alien (The main antagonist which chases you) and none of them had any use, they couldnt even stun it for more than a split second, now i get the alien is ment to be powerful, intimidating and giving you a sense of hopelessness but what kind of game design allows you to craft items which have zero use against the enemies you face to the point of being worthless? it wouldnt be so bad if it gave you a example situation of how to use the items but if you go in blind following only what the game explains and tells you like i did, you have no idea. Heres a flash bang, oh cool that might be useful if the alien spots me right? wrong, the alien will be stuned for less than a second and still instantly murder you. Your revolver does nothing against it or the android enemies so im not sure whats the point of even having it since human enemies become scarce quite fast. Overall the game feels badly designed theres so much potential and a great love of art and atmosphere here, but at its core its  bad horror game which punishes you more than it rewards you playing on anything other than easy or medium difficulty, it's meant to be a game which rifts off of the movies, giving you the suspence and thrill the movies did when the alien chased ripley etc, but really its a case of, if the alien sees you, you're more or less dead instantly, it moves faster than you, if you run you can't avoid it, it will murder you even at full health with zero chance to break away.
Like i said earlier, the game has so much potential but the AI is so awful you might as well not bother, for a team that spent so much time crafting detail on the minor objects and details of the world, bringing it alive and giving it so much personality only to fall short in terms of the actually gameplay, it makes me sad, the most fun parts of the game are exploring the station crouching through vents and whatever else, listening to audio tapes and reading emails on computers, but encountering the alien after the initial encounter? its lackluster, dull and falls short due to bad AI, which is a shame.

I've played Factorio hundreds of hours already before it came to Steam, and can highly recommended it if you like building games. Although the game is in early access, it will already offer your dozens to hundreds of hours of fun gameplay. The early to mid game is very progressive, and you will easily pick up the basics of the game along the way.
Once you reach the (very late) endgame, the game is excellent in allowing freedom to follow your own goals. There is always something to do in your factory: acquiring more resources, building more power, building better logistics, adding more trains to your rail network, punishing the natives for living to close to your base, or adding yet more electronics production for yet bigger factories. If you have a creative mind, this will never get boring. Either you can try to create yet more novel contraptions to produce your goods, or try to go big and create clever designs to combat the growing pains of expanding to massive factory scale.
The community of the game is great, being very helpful in giving design tips and sharing their little neat tricks. Mods add yet more content to the already very diverse vanilla game, adding nice gadgets (like automatic train builders) or offer a complete overhaul of the game from resources - intermediate products to the weapons and tools you can make.
I definitely recommended this game. It is a very nice way to unwind and enjoy seeing how your contraptions do all the work for you.
If you even think this game will be your kind of game, It is.

Ive played all TW from rome 1 inc exp packs, Both medievals and their exp, shogan 2, and empire. I havent tried it with "DEL" or "Radeons" mods and frankly have no will to. Nothing against them just not my cup of tea. im happy with how it is running with a 24 turn/year and the 2 skill points per level for gens and agents. the new general and agent skill points system is a nice change from the normal asassin, diplomat, spy system. and once you have the hang of it, agents can be either your best friend of worst nightmare. ( nothing says $#!% quicker then watching your opponets cap your capital and then plunge your econmey in the the toilet, while your army just has to sit there and do nothing due to being "knocked out" by their agents)  the improved Civil war system makes for great early and long game stratagy, ( or maybe thats because i run a very long campaign.) Basicly this game IS NOT for those who are after a quick 1-2hr bull rush campaign. ie like Shogun 2. and unlike most TW titles. the factions each have a unique style of play that suits them on the normal and up difficulty. ie: what works for Britons aka icini  wont work for the Guals aka averani both are barbarian factions.  Sure the game still has bugs now and then. just like all games. Nothing is perfect. there are times when sieges will end when the player knows how to win them easily. not all factions have you beaut seigecrafting skills,. there will be times when 1 faction is more superior then another or few throughout the game but so it happens in the real world too.
as for the AI being reportedly passive. yes at the start the AI does come across passive, unless you're already at war with them off the bat. this is so. so that players are not bombarded and had their tail yanked, ripped off. shredded and spat back at them right off the bat. as the game goes further in ie: 100yrs in timeline, you will find that unless you're everyones trading partner you're going the be the guy with a bullseye target on your back.. and for those who seek to hide behind trading. yeah that just pisses the ones off who dont want to trade with you. not too mention that the longer the game goes the more it becomes harder to keep the politics in order.

Why does everyone hate Rome 2 so much?
Rome 2 has It's flaws just like any other game out there, and Isn't the first sequel to be inferior to It's predecessor, but It's still a good game nevertheless.
There are many things wrong with Rome 2 in terms of what was promised, and the fact most of the DLC were factions, and units already in the game, but I like to judge Rome 2 on what it has rather than what it doesn't have.
Rome 2 is your basic empire building game where you have a birds eye view of Europe to control your factions units, and cities. There are a variety of factions to choose from ranging from Rome, Carthage, The Iceni, and even Sparta. Once you have chosen your faction you then slowly build an empire, manage resources, fight battles, and take over land, and other factions.
The game is fun, and the battles are sometimes intense. I can spend hours on this game doing many things. I love taking over factions, and making my faction have better technology, and economics. Rome 2 is a game where you spend hours at a time on. You need to be dedicated with your time, as the time I spent on my campaign was 250 hours.
Rome 2 also has the steam workshop. At any time you get bored of Rome 2 you can always download extra content from the workshop to give you many more hours of the game. Being as Rome 2 can give you 500 hours worth of gameplay (If not more) it really Isn't a game you can speak ill of.

Thank goodness this game looks good and has an alright story, otherwise it would’ve been a piece of crap. I read a couple reviews after finishing the game, both claimed the game “never frustrates”, yet that is the defining feature of the game. It♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off many times.
Platforming is rigid. Like Thief 4 you can only jump in predetermined areas. This means I was rolling around two-three times near ledges before I happened to hit the jump area. Sometimes your character jumps automatically, sometimes you have to press a button. There’s no consistency. At one point you’re told you can’t clamber while carrying Trip, your companion. 30 minutes later you’re required to carry her while clambering in order to progress, without the game prompting you to do so. Button assignments are nonsensical. Sometimes you press A to perform an action, sometimes B. It’s constant button mashing. It’s also glitchy. Several times I was teleported outside the hidden walls, and I had to restart the checkpoint or I died by suddenly flying up in the air. The rigid platforming was intended to make the game smooth and accessible. But instead it’s the worst thing about it. It doesn’t even signpost where you’re supposed to go properly. All platforms you can interact with flash, but because the game is so bright it’s still easy to miss. Despite how controlled the platforming is it’s possible to do buggy jumps, where you fly off past platforms to somewhere you’re not supposed to be. It’s no Tomb Raider, or even Prince of Persia. It’s more like Legacy of Kain.
Even with everything that annoyed me the game is still ok. The story was written by Alex Garland and Andy Serkis, who when they make movies tend to make very nice stuff. The same is true here. The story, setting and characters are great. But because they came from film, the story feels a lot like a movie script. The big important moments are there, but all the stuff around it, the “game” bits, don’t fit naturally into the script. It has several sections which feel like drawn out busywork. I could easily see players get bored in some of the puzzle sections and never finish the game because of it. I’m glad I powered through the slow bits and finished the game. It has its moments, and the ending is good. I’m now more impressed by the quality of Ninja Theory’s work in DmC. They made huge steps forward in that game compared to Enslaved. Unlike SCE Santa Monica who make the same God of War game over and over, Ninja Theory saw what went wrong, and had the ambition to do better next time. Who knows, maybe by their next game they’ll be able to match Platinum Games.

No More Room in Hell is a cooperative first person survival horror video game, created by Matt "Max" Kazan and initially developed as a modification on Valve Corporation's Source Engine. Set in a zombie apocalypse, player assume the roles of 8 remaining survivors, with a focus on co-operation and survival, and can be played through "Objective" or "Survival" mode. The game is heavily inspired by George Romero's Living Dead series, with the title being a reference to Dawn of the Dead, as well as certain characters being a reference to other films such as American Psycho and The Big Lebowski.
It was first released on October 31, 2011 via Steam Greenlight, with an official stand-alone release following on October 2013, after a nearly seven year development, and was met with positive reviews.

Formation, for example, only work when the ships are standing, but at the first shot the ships start to doing whatever they want, and this will gonna ruin any tactic that you had planned. While it's great to have Homeworld looked at again, especially as games like No One Lives Forever fades into being forgotten as a result of publishers not giving a ****, Homeworld Remastered Collection boasts some impressive visual updates at the cost of some of the gameplay mechanics that made the predecessors what they were.
The best part happens to be the visual updates involved with Homeworld 1's remastering. It's absolutely stunning, texture detail beautiful. For Homeworld 1, this comparison is outsdanding, but for Homeworld 2 the improvements aren't as radical due to the game still being in the same engine. That's not to say that both aren't improved, but it's much more significant for the original.
Some of the audio has been re-recorded and while it sounds alright there are portions where old (albeit not as compressed) samples are used. This makes it sound jarring since the same settings aren't used between both recording as well as the actor's ages have dramatically changed since the original releases. For Homeworld 1, it's nice to not hear as much compression on things, giving better clarity.
The biggest problem with Homeworld 1's remaster is that old tactics aren't working. Formations are fundementally broken, shedding the fact that these fights are in space and momentum is a thing, instead going for a jet-fighter approach. The problem is that makes guard orders useless as you might assign a sphere formation around a target with guard orders, but as soon as enemies get within range, your ships break off and take forever to get shots on target.
The good news is that having the Classic version is great, but while the Classic version does run, it does have problems with multi-monitor systems.

Before you downvote, please take your time to actually read. I know the fanboyism is compelling you to click that thumbs down because I'm disagreeing with your opinion. But keep an open mind, aright?
Right then let's get to business. Alien: Isolation is a GOOD game. It's a really good game. It's probably one of the best surival/horror/sneaky-type games since the release of System Shock. It's gloriously designed, it has tons of atmosphere and for the most part great graphics. The sound design is the best I've heard since the opening levels of Dead Space. The only thing lacking when it comes to graphics is the inclusion of a proper anti-aliasing option. What you have in game is a limited post-processing AA that does a pretty poor job of removing the jaggies.
So why do I not recommend this? This sounds like the best game ever! It's actually quite a good game, but it just doesn't appeal to me for a few reasons, and I'll get through them below.
First off, the game is incredibly slow. It has some serious pacing issues, wildly fluctuating between intense action and absolutely mind boggingly boring hiding. Mind you, in the beginning this hiding is very tense. You feel something akin to genuine terror as the alien stalks you through the corridors. You listen intently for its footsteps, twitching at every creak of the metal around you, keeping an eye on the motion sensor.
But once you've done that for about an hour, painstakingly making your way through a large area and not seen a save station for miles...and get caught by the Alien for the fifteenth time because it decided to jump out of a vent nearby, you're starting to get a touch annoyed. The problem is that there's too much waiting around, sitting in one spot and waiting for the alien to go away so you can go about your business. So you start taking chances and you're suddenly making pretty good progress. Except the times when you accidently gets caught AGAIN.
So, in short, the distance between the save stations, combined with the absolute inevitability of death if the alien spots you cause way too much waiting around and a lot of replaying the same sections over and over again. Once you get your hands on the flamethrower you have the option of running the alien off on occasion that slightly alleviates the "instant death" scenario. Personally, I'd had a better time if getting spotted wasn't so final. If you actually had a chance to distract the alien or run and hide, it'd be more tense. But for the first half of the game it's mostly "Get spotted = Die".
Here follows spoilers!

So once the alien is out of the picture, the game actually takes a turn for the better. Since the threat of certain death isn't constantly weighing on your shoulders anymore, the game actually becomes even more scary because you suddenly don't know what is out there. There could be ANYTHING around the corner. That motion sensor beep could be friendly. It could be one of those creepy Joes. It could be dangerous human survivors. The lack of knowledge really makes it scary all of a sudden.
But then, one and a half levels later, the designers did what finally made me stop playing all together. Everything they did wrong up until this point was tolerable because the rest of the game was so good. But at this point, they decided to remove all your weapons and turn all the androids immune to EMP, Stun Batons and Flashbangs. Leading to a REALLY awkward time fighting them. In addition you are getting put in a very big area connected by single corridors, littered with these near-immortal Joes and a serious lack of hiding places. After playing this level over and over and over, hoping for the right random circumstances I really couldn't bother anymore. In the end, I tried again and again and finally got past that point. The end sections were very intense, but nothing could really make up for the lost enjoyment from that stupidly gamey part. I'm also very disappointed in the ending. Too abrupt and not at all fleshed out. I know some people do like it, but I personally don't.
Overall, Alien: Isolation is a great game with some unignorable flaws. It has great story, perfect atmosphere, great graphics and sound, but all mired by the bad pacing and annoying design. If these problems don't bother you, but you see them instead as challenges or something that adds tension, then this IS a game for you because it really is great. It's just that these design decisions ended up being complete annoyances for me personally, so for anyone like me, I do not recommend this game. If you insist on trying it, pick it up on sale. I'd say it's worth it on sale.

I think this is the best survival horror game I've ever played. No ♥♥♥♥♥♥ horror gimmicks like jump-scares or forced sequences to cause terror, just the good old atmosphere of "you're going to die, dude. Get the ♥♥♥♥ out of here".
In Alien: Isolation, you play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of the famous Ellen Ripley. Fifteen years after your mother disappeared in a strange accident involving the ship she worked on, the Nostromo, you set out for a space station at the edge of deep space to find out about what happened to your mother. When Amanda and her team reach Sevastopol, however, they quickly discover that the discontinuation of the space sation is not the only problem that people who live and work there have been facing these last few weeks. The low-quality maintenance androids are acting weird, the operational system responsible for Sevastopol's security have gone rogue and there's something far more dangerous lurking in the station, hunting people down, one by one.
To start it off the right way, graphics in this game are not only absolutely gorgeous, they're also so low-demanding that you will be able to run this game on your toaster, if you want to. Let us all take a moment of our time and pray that someday every game developer will be able to achieve such a feat of technological know-how. Talking about technology, you would not believe the AI in this game. It's like the last 20 years of stagnation in developing AIs for games never happened. The Alien will hunt you as if it is being controlled by a human. It will smell you, hear you, it knows where you want to go and it will lay traps for you. The damn thing won't leave the room until it's sure you're gone, so hiding your way out of danger will never, ever work in this game. You gotta come out of under that table and find a way around it. No safe-heaven is really safe. Hell, this is the kind of game that will tell you things like "are you sure you wanna save your game right here? I can't make sure it won't stab you right after you load". I love this kind of horror games. Not even your checkpoints are safe. To top the horror scene, there's a killer soundtrack with sounds and tracks that will make you feel like Hitchcock himself had a hand in making the game. You'll see what I mean when you get stuck in a pitch-black corridor with some intense, fast music playing.
There is crafting that works, is intuitive and it's vital for the rest of the gameplay. Craft a molotov to scare the Alien away with fire or make a noise bomb to set off alarms and call out guards while you go around. Weapons are a plenty, ranging from revolvers to flamethrowers, and you bet you'll be using every single weapon you get your hands on. Nothing is there for no reason, no loose-ends in this game. Every door, every computer, every crafting material is there for a reason. You won't find flamethrower fuel under someone's bed or revolver bullets inside an android corpse. Sevastopol is huge, beatiful and well designed. On top of everything, Alien: Isolation links up the story of the original Alien with some aspects of Prometheus really well. Hell, the game did a better job at some things that I shall not spoil than Prometheus did.
Get this game. It's a GOTY and it's worth every cent and minute of play.

First of all, lets be straight: this game isn't as good as it's predecessor, but it's still an amazing game and a worthy sequel and most of the elements that made the first Dark Souls so great are present here.
well, the game itself is pretty close in mechanics to DkS 1, although some minor tweaks have been realized, the combat feels a bit better and the adition of the power stance (you can power stance dual weapons if you have 1,5x it's stat requirements) finally makes dual wieldieng viable. the weapon and armor variety is still great, the game is long and if maybe not as hard as DkS 1 it is still pretty challenging, also the game was made a bit friendlier (not that it's easy or "casual") to new users with the addition of healing stones and a little better tutorial than the first one. also the addition of Soul Vessels for reseting your stats is really welcome since the balance patches can be an issue becouse they can mess with your build pretty bad (happened in the first also, but no way to reset).
so... I have never played any of the Dark Souls series before (including Demons Souls), so I purposefully waited a little while before doing a review of Dark Souls 2 until I broke through the initial wall I guessed I would be facing at the start.
DS2 is definitely hard to get into the swing of. The game drops you in the world, gives you a little pat on the back and then proceeds to stand and watch as you get blatted in the face repeatedly by the difficulty curve. The curve starts out reasonably enough for an average gamer. With the reputation of DS, not being careful from the get-go is pretty much your own fault if you have trouble with the first few humanoid enemies you will encounter.
To avoid any sort of spoiler at all (I love going through this knowing nothing and finding it all out for myself) I once came to a point where I thought "Holy sh#t! This must be a boss!". After several unsuccessful excursions after this particular enemy and finally taking it down for the first time, I looked past it for my hard-earned reward... only to find the remainder of the area strewn with enemies similar or the same to the one I had just face-blatted to death, surviving by the skin of my teeth and little else. This naturally felt like the game was being deliberately and maliciously as big a ba##ard as it could be.
Fast forward a bit and I have learned many things in the DS2 world. Each new wall you come across and overcome feels like an achievement, a feat of endurance, patience and skill in a dark and uncaring world. You just need to keep at it and break through. Once you get so far... you start to realise that DS2 is not as unfair as you first thought.
-=Overall=-
Keep at it and you will see that DS2 is what a game should be like. Find how to play yourself, no hand-holding, play how you want and accept the consequences. Getting further feels like an achievement because you do it all yourself. You can offer help to other players in their worlds or bring others in your world (I would recommend these, it's really a good way to improve) and this adds to the overall experience, which, for me, is a very good one.
Highly recommended, even if you have no interest in it previously. So long as you enjoy a challenge.

Clocked 219 hours of gameplay before grew totally bored with this one. Almost liked Shogun 2 more even though it is a lot older game. Here are just some of the bad aspects of Rome 2 emperor edition.
The most severe fault is the lack of proper politics(diplomacy, internal factional divides, meaningful big events, family dynasties, intelligent vassal system etc.). Compared to strategy games that specialize on the political setting, like Crusader Kings II, Rome 2 is just archaic in terms of politics.
No real faction variety. Barbarians are essentially civilized city cultures with different buildings and units. No rampaging and migrating barbarian hordes. No tribal political settings.
Mostly because of lack of politics there's little challenge in gameplay from midgame onwards. I found only the early gameplay surrounded by powerful hostile factions to be challenging with factions like Armenia and Marcomanni, though playing continually defensively tended to get boring quickly. Growing to a decent size also killed of the interest/challenge in the game. After attaining the size of about 8-10 areas and 3 full attacking army stacks with the marcomanni, I lost interest in watching the inefficent and indecisive bumbling of my Roman neighbours.
Rome 2 fails to improve much the micromanagement heavy approach to tactical combat familiar to Shogun 2 veterans. Rather the addition of specialized unit skills that need to be activated(like bracing, battle rhythm, different missiles) adds to the micromanagement. It's also annoying you can't set cavalry to automatically disengage and charge again at its chosen target. This is just silly, given that they provided skirmish mode for missile troops.
The game also doesn't really provide a proper tools to conduct army wide attacks while staying in formation. I'm assuming here that you lose the charge bonus if you just move parts of your army at running speed against enemy troops. It should be possible to just order parts of your armies to attack a point in the enemy formation and still retain the formation they're in or, if chosen units seeking automatically to flank the enemy at the sides. Now they tend to pool into a disorganized barbaric mess. As the game is, the attacking tends to devolve into a badly organized clickfest.
What I've always disliked in the Total War series is also the lack of means to turn around routing armies, the overall quickness of battles and armies, the immediate arrival of reinforcements on the map, the lack of uncertainty pertaining the enemy army size, composition and quality and the lack of any real sound use for tactical retreats.
The AI is still rather bad and is really lousy at teamwork with allied armies and when assaulting or defending walled cities.
Warfare on the strategy map is also too fast for my liking with little or no room for attrition tactics. Unless you consider using agents as part of proper attrition tactics, which I don't. Agents just turn into a game of chance, that also bloats the micromanagemental aspect of the game, features that should be achieved by armies on the battlefield and strategic map.
The stance mechanism is rather one sided pushing the player immediately towards full confrontation agains all enemy stacks you're facing. It doesn't support skirmishing tactics against overwhelming odds since your army disengages to a random point on the strategy map  after the battle. A point which usually is quite close by and accessible to enemy armies resulting in a battle to the death. The game also deems succesfull skirmishing a failure. Even if you're wildly succesfull in terms of inflicted and sustained casualties in the battle, you still "lose" the battle if you withdraw. Denying battle at lenght is usually impossible due to the siege mechanics. Especially since the settlements tend to fall quickly to sieges and wildly effective siege machines. That is, if the AI doesn't completely fail at assaulting the walled city.
Awsome espesially if you  are just about to make the jump from empire, the first rome or just starting

The collection of orbs make you dangerously greedy, and the flying disc is a hoot and a half to play with as well. If you are looking for a great game, that truly is a sleeper, you will find Enslaved to be a great fit.

Dishonored 2 is more of the same from Dishonored, with an emphasis on "more." The strengths of the first game are more pronounced, as are its weaknesses.
Dishonored's level design is second to none. Levels feel organic but retain a highly stylized sense of surealness and are wonderful playgrounds for the game's strong core mechanics and controls. The game maintains its support for multiple playstyles and allows enough room for players to stumble into solutions that not even the developer could of predicted. Played as a first person action game or stealth, the game offers numerous options for either playthrough. On some missions I felt overcome with options that the larger levels provided me and the level Crack in the Slab had me locked in spatial confusion as I struggled to navigate through two unique world spaces at once.
Both Dishonoreds struggle with player motivation and narrative voice despite a unique world and strong art style. This could largely be overlooked in the first Dishonored due to a more muted tone to the story and a lack of a single villain to carry the story. In both games I struggled to care about the motivations of the main character and instead was more concerned about the fates of my targets and the larger implications of my actions. With a spoken protagonist and omnipresent singular villain, Dishonored 2 has more of a narrative weight to bare and struggles to find its voice.
Finally you have fixed the stuttering but it doesn't change the fact that you fixed it almost a year after.
It really did stick up to the first one and is one of the best games ever.

Note that there's spoilers (Kinda, nothing too revealing but it does somewhat exhibit the progression of the game.)
Pros:
-Not too many glitches that I could really see.
-There's a really good atmosphere built, towards the end I felt a little more creeped out.
-It's the right amount of difficult, not too difficult, but when you die, you know it's your fault.
-The combat is just as good as in the first one, it's the same with the stealth system.
-While they did recycle a lot, (plot, character archetypes, sounds, all that.) it still felt fresh and new because most of the game isn't in Dunwall.
-Emily's abilities are pretty cool, I haven't played the Corvo run, but I can assume he has the same powers.
-New(-ish?) enemies, each having their own strengths and weaknesses, the most irritating being the Clockwork Soldier which seems to be like the Strider from the original but far tougher to tangle with than those long-legged, Legolas with big bow of flammable whale oil lookin' selves. (Witches aren't new, but, still.)
-While the character archetypes are all the same, basically, they're still interesting, and it's still satisfying to mess them up.
-There's new (To Corvo and Emily) characters, some with backgrounds that aren't revealed until the very end, others being unravelled as you go. (I'd suggest playing the First's DLC before playing this one.)
-There's more world interaction, although it's still linear level progression. The world feels very open, albeit still restricted.
-Arkane added a few post-mission things that basically tell you; "Hey, you did a more peaceful/stealthy approach, expect lower chaos."/"Hey, stupid, you killed literally everyone, expect a bad end."
-You can choose to play without powers.
-The baddies can be dealt with in more interesting and difficult ways. I'd suggest more time and thought into each of these approaches.
-More interesting crossbow ammunitions.
-More interesting bone charms.
Now for the Cons:
-No Drunken Whaler
-It is waaay more difficult to stealth without powers.
-Skyrim Mammoth Glitch with Sleepdart
-Getting supplies requires a visit to the Black Market(s), which, are not on every level, requiring more conservation of ammunition/weapons.
-There is a homebase type thing, but that still does not have a shop with which you can replenish your armaments/upgrade gear.
-There are some bits where you might require a Walkthrough guide, because they're either too confusing, or too difficult. If it's too difficult, I'd suggest lowering difficulty level.
-There are 'some' boss fights, the final for example. It's an actual proper boss fight, (although avoidable) unlike the end of the first, which was just running/sneaking through a horde of guards before stabbing/knocking out the end all baddie. I feel as though this detracts from the point of the game, which is to save an Empire, but moreso utilizing stealth.
-Getting to Runes takes far more time than it did in the first.
-Bloodflies are the most irritating thing ever.
-Less than stellar loadtimes.
I overall enjoyed Dishonored 2, and would heavily suggest getting it, especially since it is currently $20. Despite all the reviews claiming bad optimization and glitchiness, I felt as though the controls were smooth, and saw very few glitches worth noting. It's a good experience, especially if you enjoyed/loved playing Dishonored. Arkane, you did a good job with this one. Please don't turn into a company that pumps out Dishonored sequels (that suck) every year.

Having been a big fan of the first instalment, buying the Emily version (as I like to call it) was a no-brainer. What required more thought was how I would play it, since the game allows for both the less lethal low chaos mode and the merciless high chaos mode. The game's trailers seemed to hint heavily at how the game was designed fro high chaos, but after almost a day of gameplay, I'd say it is one of the most balanced fight or sneak games I've played till date.
Plot - The game has been billed as a revenge plot, and it excels at it. Dishonored has always been about the "grey" (epitomised by the Outsider) amidst the black and white of the exterior, and this game takes it to an altogether new level. Playing either as Emily or Corvo (I played as Emily),  you have to take down those who took your/your daughter's throne. Unlike Game 1 though, there's no murder involved (beyond of course the endless numbers of poor guards), and the enemy, Delilah, has her own somewhat dubious reasons for doing what she did. Considering that your actions give you a wide gamut of choices about what to do wtih each boss, this information actually poses moral quandries that seem to matter. So even when it lacks the twists of the first game, the plot of the second is well worth its weight in gold.
Rating - 4.5/5
Characters - I guess most gamers from the first Dishonored wanted to see what a grown-up Emily would be like. And she's a badass. Her own aristocractic upbringing and disconnect with the masses makes her character all the more interesting, something that the second coming of Corvo probably would not. Her mission is clear, but paths quite the opposite, and excellent voice acting brings that out. Sokolov returns, and Megan Foster/Billie Lurk is well fleshed out, but the villains are all new and shiny. Jindosh, Paolo, Delilah and the good Doctor are all well polished and rounded out, creating a world that is truly vibrant. Even when you're not dealing with the prime characters, the secondary ones (read cannon fodder) have their own tales to share. To the game's credit, these proved to be interesting enough for me NOT to kill off two guards while they were conversing. And this comes from someone who finished Watch Dogs 2 before jumping into this game.
Rating - 4.5/5
Gameplay - As I said, the game is well balanced when it comes to combat or stealth. While combat may look appealing from the trailers, it can quickly become tedious once you realise there are only four major types of enemies - guards, clockwork soldiers, witches and those ratty Paolo-followers. Killing off each type typically  takes one or two strategeis that you would fall back upon again and again (shooting a clockwork in the glowing orb-head disables its visual capacities for instance, turning it into a statue).
Try stealth though, and the game comes alive. The maps aren't huge, but they are marvellous in terms of depth. Moving through buildings and on pipes gives you options unlike anything the streets can offer. Once you have unlocked a decent number of abilities, each scenario with 3-4 enemies provides a ton of possibilities. Would you use far reach  to pull enemies towards you. Or chain them using domino and jump on one. Perhaps use a decoy ? Or simply throw a bottle and sneak away ? The richness of the maps and the fact that you're never faced with a barrage of never-ending enemies makes stealth a pleasure rivalled only by classics like Splinter Cell.
Rating - 5/5
Graphics - I remember the developers saying that they don't wish the game to have picture-perfect realism. Instead, the palettes and textures remind you of works of art. Watercolor pieces to be exact. Rendered well, these graphics bring out a period feel that perhaps exactness (like say Assassin's Creed Syndicate) would not have. After all, this isn't the late 19th or the early 20th Century. This is a different world, and the game brings that out through its brutal yet somewhat dreamy landscape, its caricaturish but lively facial features and light and shade effects worthy of an art gallery.
All of this, of course, means that the game is light on graphics demands compared to uber-realistic AAA titles. With a GTX 960, I could run it at Ultra with only a slight amount of lag. Cranking up the anti-aliasing would perhaps make more demands, but this isn't a game that would drain the soul from your GPU.
Rating - 5/5
Conclusion - The game is small, rich and once you've gotten off the streets and onto the parapets, pipes and balconies, filled with possibilities. It is a game that requires you to take your time, and figure out each move carefully. With a storyline that demands your moral compass and consideration at each turn, this makes Dishonored 2 a worthy successor to the first.
Overall Rating - 5/5

This is a remastered game from back in the day when RTS ruled the PC.
Back in the day i used to love this game, unlike its competitors at the time you aren't fighting on a 2d plane but in an actual 3d environment. Given this is a space game you actually get a tactical advantage from attacking enemy ships from the top of bottom, so it added literally another dimension to the RTS genre.
Another great feature of the game is you dont build a base, but maintained a fleet (think Battlestar Galactica), that fleet stays with you throughout the game. You have the mother ship that acts as production facility and when that is lost, its game over, all other ships can just be produced and captured. It adds a lot to the story.
And the story that was told is great, for those of you who have never played it, i wont spoil it, but the story itself is kind of standard, but because you are with traveling with your fleet, you feel more connected to the story!
And the best part is, that was how i remember it, and it all still holds true!! and now it looks great also.
So i do recommend this game if you are into RTS games or really atmospheric games!

No More Room in Hell is a cooperative first person survival horror video game, created by Matt "Max" Kazan and initially developed as a modification on Valve Corporation's Source Engine. Set in a zombie apocalypse, player assume the roles of 8 remaining survivors, with a focus on co-operation and survival, and can be played through "Objective" or "Survival" mode. The game is heavily inspired by George Romero's Living Dead series, with the title being a reference to Dawn of the Dead, as well as certain characters being a reference to other films such as American Psycho and The Big Lebowski.
It was first released on October 31, 2011 via Steam Greenlight, with an official stand-alone release following on October 2013, after a nearly seven year development, and was met with positive reviews.

This game is to me the definition of those 'fond fuzzy memories' of a game you once played many years ago. The way we remember the graphics being better, the gameplay tighter and more intense, the experience smoother and distilled in it's essence.
I first played Half Life in the late '90s on a weak PC, and then eagerly awaited it's (doomed) release on Dreamcast, eventually playing it again in the PS2 release that became. Back then it was almost unique in it's story-based structure as an FPS, and it is no understatement to say that it has shaped gaming history. Immersive, compelling and an enduring classic.
When I learned of Black Mesa four and a bit years back I immediately downloaded what was then (if memory serves correctly) a pre-Steam early build. Despite the certain roughness of that early build I was immediately transported back nearly 20 years, playing the game as it was remebered in the rose-tinted glow of fond memory. It's not a 1:1 rebuild; things have been condensed, reworked and tightened up - but the experience is every bit as authentic as those memories. Every event played out just as remembered, and every note hit perfectly.
As it stands now, the game has been polished way beyond that early build, and replaying again the experince is even better. You can see in every detail that this has truly been a labour of love for all those involved in it's making. It is an absolute must-have for those who played the original way back when, as well as those who have only ever read or been told about it. Soon we will have the concluding chapter of Xen which has been absent, and I look forward with great anticipation to seeing how the team re-imagine this.

I've played Factorio hundreds of hours already before it came to Steam, and can highly recommended it if you like building games. Although the game is in early access, it will already offer your dozens to hundreds of hours of fun gameplay. The early to mid game is very progressive, and you will easily pick up the basics of the game along the way.
Once you reach the (very late) endgame, the game is excellent in allowing freedom to follow your own goals. There is always something to do in your factory: acquiring more resources, building more power, building better logistics, adding more trains to your rail network, punishing the natives for living to close to your base, or adding yet more electronics production for yet bigger factories. If you have a creative mind, this will never get boring. Either you can try to create yet more novel contraptions to produce your goods, or try to go big and create clever designs to combat the growing pains of expanding to massive factory scale.
The community of the game is great, being very helpful in giving design tips and sharing their little neat tricks. Mods add yet more content to the already very diverse vanilla game, adding nice gadgets (like automatic train builders) or offer a complete overhaul of the game from resources - intermediate products to the weapons and tools you can make.
I definitely recommended this game. It is a very nice way to unwind and enjoy seeing how your contraptions do all the work for you.

Slime Rancher's two main draws are its exploration and slime farming, similar to Harvest Moon or Stardew Valley. Exploration is satisfying, as there's always something enegmatic to discover. Users who like "hands-off" narratives will enjoy the lack of explanation of the environment. Lore is dispensed through exploration and the completion of various puzzles, similar to Portal or Gone Home.
The farming is equally satisfying with sufficient strategic depth. Space management, favorite slime foods, and slime interactions make farm management interesting throughout as new slimes are obtained. Slime Rancher's aesthetic assures that you'll still enjoy exploration well into the campaign. The slimes are extremely cute, and the ragdoll physics when thrown never get old.
The player will also receive periodic mail from your ranch's previous owner (Hobson) and from a friend named Casey. Both of these contain surprisingly developed sub-plots that provide much of the title's intrigue. Why did Hobson leave his ranch, and who is Casey?
The farming aspect of the game lacks automation. You will find yourself getting bored of farming plorts from slime hatches, one plort at a time, carting them to your market stall, and depositing them one at a time. There really needs to be a slime science upgrade to let you shoot all plorts at once or automatically sell when you have more than X in storage. Also, the price of slime plorts (currency in this game) fluctuates. This usually means you can (and will) frequently get up to 30% less cash for your plorts. I don't see fluctuation as a bad thing, but when you have to sell them one at a time, it feels like insult to injury. I also frequently had MOST types of plorts selling for less than their base value.
Some "slime doors" (progression obstacles) don't unlock new areas, they simply create shortcuts to where you already go. This means you can delay your progress getting new slimes significantly by unknowingly opening doors that go nowhere. This has the potential to hamper the feeling of progression in the game.
(Possible spoilers.)
The letters left behind by Hobson and Casey could have been done better. Hobson's notes are comically sappy to the point it's hard to empathize, and his metaphors are on-the-nose to the point of absurdity. Casey's letters were written with ambiguity/uncertainty on purpose for plot reasons, but because of the way Hobson and your "stories" interact, it makes Casey's narrative (which is "the" plot point in Slime Rancher) feel contrived or like an addendum.
(Probable spoilers.)
Slime Rancher is an adorable farming adventure with interpersonal-relation subplots. Its adorable aesthetic, strategic satisfaction in farming, and emotional subtext make this a must-try-- just be wary of its ability to become monotonous in plort selling, and the execution of the sub-plot isn't for everyone. A mandatory library inclusion for any Stardew Valley fan.
