Saw it recommended due to time spent in other stealth games (mainly Hitman) but thought I wouldn't like it: that the setting was just too much "fantasy" for me; that First Person was just not for me.
I saw stealth youtubers I respect playing it and praising it, saw the awards it got and read the glowing reviews and, one day, needing to relax and try something different, I downloaded the demo.
What can I say? I fell in love with this game. You can see just how much love they put into this game. There's a fascinating world to be discovered in Dishonored 2 and you can spend - like I have - 36 hours and still not uncover half of it. There's an insane amount of lore that just adds up to the experience and, the more you read the books and journals you come across, the more you'll appreciate this game.
The story is told masterfully and your actions end up affecting its outcome (with many hidden surprises). The characters are great and Emily, the main protagonist, is perhaps the best female character I've come across in a videogame.
Voice acting is also on point - at least for Emily and Corvo.
As far as gameplay goes: classic stealth, tons of
and a delight to play through as many times as one can.
You have main objectives and scripted events - but even the latter are mostly optional, making the game a high-quality stealth sandbox.
I cannot recall the last time I've ever liked a game this much. I'm still sad it ended.
10/10.

Honestly, this game did with its potential exactly what it should have done. Playing as corvo and emily are two different experiences, giving the game some replayability. Imo it's a pretty solid game.
Better enemy AI, more options and interesting character backtories, very similar to the first one in a really good way.

I loved the original Dishonored. The lore and characters were interesting, the game was fun and kept me on the edge of my seat throughout. I've played through Dishonored three times now, twice with Corvo and once with Emily, and I can say it was a thouroughly enjoyable experience.
...As long as you have the hardware to run it.
It's a damn shame that the game shipped with such poor optimization, and it's a damn shame they haven't fixed everything yet. I was running it on my laptop-- a GTX 860M, 16 GB RAM, i7 processor-- and it stuttered something awful. Sound cut in and out.It was annoying, but not unplayable.
On my desktop? Totally smooth.
It's seriously a great experience if you can get around the technical bugs. The gameplay is just as fun and diverse as the original title, though the narrative might be a bit familar if you've played the entirety of DH1 and the DLC content.
Kept me entertained for hours, has excellent replay value, and is definitely worth the $40 price tag. (I bought it at $60 because I wanted to get it as soon as I finished Dishonored, and I don't regret it. I really feel it was worth what I paid.)
My favorite single player game I own. Dishonored was super fun, and this one surpassed the first.
Takes some high tier hardware to run. But if you have the tech to run it and love the previous game, then you're in for a great time!

Slime Rancher is a farm game where you play as a girl named Beatrix LeBeau who sets out for a life a thousand light years away from Earth on the 'Far, Far Range'. Kudos for devs and artists especially becouse their team isn't large and they still managed to release the full game. The game is still being updated after the full release. Homeworld.  10/10.  That's the easy part of a review on Homeworld.  Just itself.   Yes.   Instead of giving a basic review, I'm going to compare and contrast the Remastered edition with the originals.   I haven't played Homeworld II RM yet, so this review is subject to update.   For brevity, we'll call these "HW" for Homeworld Game of the Year edition (1999) and "RM" for the Remastered version.  Also, Multiplayer is not reviewed here.
*****HOMEWORLD 1*****
1. Audio.  HW has always been known for its amazing sound and haunting music, and the Remastered version doesn't disappoint.  The missing highs and lows that made sound "watery" (due to early day sound compression) in HW are entirely cleaned up in RM.
2. Graphics. HW's graphics have been heavily upgraded in RM, but the concept of using low polygon count models has been preserved; this is to prevent graphics problems in some truly huge battles, but mod makers may want to upgrade these further.   The textures used are beautiful and give the game a polished feel.
3. Fighter tactics.  HW gave you direct control over fighter behavior.   You could choose Passive, Aggressive, or Defensive stances.   RM has this as well, but it doesnt' do the same thing.  Setting to Passive caused them to enter evasive maneuvers that could hold together a group of fighters that ran into a Missile Destroyer.   In RM, maneuvering itself makes no changes; only combat behavior.  This makes missions like Sea of Lost Souls require a new approach.
In exchange, fighters seem to be more durable and the annoying "fuel" mechanic that could cause a fighter to be stranded in space has been removed (they work HW II style now).  This is itself a major change, as the Kadeshi Swarm (you'll know it when you see it) no longer requires fuel pods to survive.  They still exist to work as Support Frigates, though.   That completely changes how to approach the related mission.
4. Capital Ships.   Capital ships seem a little weaker to bomber attack than they used to be, which is somewhat welcome.    They also move slightly faster and you don't need the same cloud of them that you used to in order to accomplish things.
5. Difficulty.   HW took a unique approach to both cheaters and to people who had remarkable ability not to lose anything; the more you have, the more enemy ships will be in the next level.   This meant that cheating to add 90 Ion Beam Frigates or getting that many in the mission Bridge of Sighs turned the next level into hell.   You were encouraged to keep a small and manageable fleet but could go epic if you wanted.  This was handled differently in HW1 vs. HW2; it's now all using the HW2 formula.  This means the Kadeshi swarm is far easier than it was, and that if you are overpowered by the time you hit Sea of Lost Souls you are greeted by 30+ Assault Frigates.
6. Formations.  Edit: Formations don't work once combat starts; the pilots fly like they are in HW2.  They're pointless and even cause problems.  Formations were once a major part of tactics in this game. Hopefully this will be fixed.
7. Fleet Size.    RM implements the Command Point mechanics from HW II and severely limits your fleet to a realistic size.   Captured ships count toward the limit as well.  Great for continuity but you will recycle a lot more captured ships.
The enemies seem to be limited by resources and their own Command Points now as there aren't as many of them in many scenarios, and it's possible to simply outlast the opponent into starvation by eliminating resource operations.
8. Salvage Corvettes.  These get a special spot because in HW they really made the workhorses of your fleet, capturing half of your enemies and making them allies.   This is still true, but with some caveats added for balance.   Love them or hate them, they're there.
A. Ships at a higher "mission level" than you seem to be uncapturable. An example would be Mission 3; any assault frigates captured in this mission are instantly converted into RU.
B. Destroyed capital ships higher than Frigate class now leave salvageable debris.   Resource Collectors and Salvage Corvettes both can get them.
C. No mass salvaging, you have to pick the right number of SC's and pick one target for them.
D. Your defense fleet will ignore a ship has been captured if they were firing on it and continue to fire until it has been salvaged.   This causes a lot of ships you wanted to steal to get nuked.  This is hopefully going to be fixed in a future patch, as it vastly reduced the number of ships one can capture in an up-close fight.
9.Special Abilities.   It was a common tactic in HW to assign a group of ships with a "repair" ability to something you want repped every time it is damaged.  The way to do this was to put them on Defensive stance and assign them to Guard the target.   In RM they don't seem to catch on that this means repair the target if it gets hammered; even a Support Frigate will instead fire its little pea-shooter at the attacking enemy.   Once the target is repaired, they will need another repair command if it gets damaged again.  This means micromanaging your repair fleet.   Hopefully this is a bug that will be fixed.
On the bonus, some ships have new abilities.   The Scout, for instance, has a Speed Boost ability for getting out of trouble.  Dont' expect it to use it, however, without your command.
10. Other changes.   One of the most notable changes from HW to RM is that HW gave you a choice between playing the campaign as the Kushan or Taiidan fleet.  You played the same role, but as Relic had no idea what gold it had on its hands when it made HW, they never expected to sequel, so canon was not a thing.  Whichever side you didnt' choose became the bad guys.   RM doesn't offer this choice, nor does it offer ship color customization like HW I does.   You will be the Kushan (which is canon) and the ship colors will be blue, white, and gray (also canon).
If you are a fan of some of the old "nifty" things that ships did in HW1, you'll find those missing from RM.   The Kadeshi Multibeam Frigate does not roll when firing and its beams are now triangulated.   The swarmers dont' do jittery motions anymore.   Things like that.
The original HW UI has been replaced with the HW II UI in RM, giving control continuity and allowing you to control manufacturing without losing sight of the map.   You can also issue move and attack orders from the sensors manager, which used to be exclusive to HW II and Cataclysm.
Cataclysm is not included in this purchase.   It was not developed by the same developers as HW I and HW II and is only semi-canon.   The actual source code for this game has been lost.   It's my hope that a retelling of Cataclysm in a more canon fashion comes about as the next step in how Gearbox capitalizes this IP.

If you ever wondered what it would be like to actually be in the first movie (not that I do not mean the sequels, but the first Ridley Scott movie), this game will get you as close to that as you can get right now. Rather than focusing on the more action packed, space marines shooting aliens kind of an experience seen before in previous games connected to the franchise, this game replicates the horror of being hunted by just one of these things, delivering an atmosphere and gameplay that are very true to the first movie.
Whether or not you should buy it depends on what you're looking for; if you just want a more action oriented experience such as the AvP games, then you may not like this one. But, if you want to experience a good survival horror that feels like being in the first movie, then this one is for you. The level design, the graphics, the sound effects, the music, the story.. it's all perfect for an Alien game.
Fans of the first movie should also know that there are two DLC's available that actually put you aboard the Nostromo and create two sequences of the movie, and while short, I'd say these are a must have for an Alien fan. But then, so is the entire game in the first place. If you loved the movie, this is a no brainer.

This game has a ton of potential and for what it is it's pretty well done. All the other reviews focussed on the good, so I'll focus on the bad. That doesn't mean that I don't like it though...
It doesn't have a lot of replayability. For one, the match does not end, and you cannot control victory conditions, even when the game says one team won the game continues to play out. This makes it feel like the game has no point to it other than shooting blue or red figures. That is fun and all, but there has got to be an end to the game at some point. As such, the majority of games I played ended up devolving into blue holding 3 bases and red holding 2 (Island map) and the game continuing forever which in my opinion is boring. They haven't got a way to track kills or captures either. There are a lot of good workshop maps though, but many of them are too ambitious for this game I feel.
The guns are cool, and I like the TF2 meets battlefield style gameplay. The AK and the m16 are the best overall, with the DMR being very handy as well. The SMG's are useless IMO, and you will never use the pistols more than likely. The explosives however, are so overpowered its unreal. You can sit on a hill with a rocket launcher and an ammo pack and wreak havoc on the enemy team at their spawn for hours pretty much. Also, the way the enemy falls down and then stands back up after you hit them is really annoying- they should either die or continue moving until you do kill them. The swimming is ridiculous too, you have to go through the lengthy standing up animation everytime you get out of the water. There needs to be more guns though, a lot more, and the different gun classes should be good for different things.  It would also be nice to be able to cycle through the different positions in the various vehicles.
The AI could be a lot better too. When you try and take a capture point, the enemy just spam spawns on it and it's impossible to capture no matter what you do. This is how the game devolves into a stalemate 95% of the time. Rarely, your team will actually back you up and help you take the point and you will 'win' by having all the points on the map.
Overall this game is pretty cool, but you won't be playing it for very long unless they add a lot more to it and fix a lot of the frustrating issues it has. It has a ton of potential to be a great title in my opinion, but the above complaints are really holding it back.
If however, all you want to do is mindless play a simple and decently enacted FPS that doesn't take itself too seriously, this is a good choice. Do I recommend? Sure, as long as you aren't expecting this to have a CS or CoD level of playability.

This game has been quite an adventure for me.
Saw it recommended due to time spent in other stealth games (mainly Hitman) but thought I wouldn't like it: that the setting was just too much "fantasy" for me; that First Person was just not for me.
I saw stealth youtubers I respect playing it and praising it, saw the awards it got and read the glowing reviews and, one day, needing to relax and try something different, I downloaded the demo.
What can I say? I fell in love with this game. You can see just how much love they put into this game. There's a fascinating world to be discovered in Dishonored 2 and you can spend - like I have - 36 hours and still not uncover half of it. There's an insane amount of lore that just adds up to the experience and, the more you read the books and journals you come across, the more you'll appreciate this game.
The story is told masterfully and your actions end up affecting its outcome (with many hidden surprises). The characters are great and Emily, the main protagonist, is perhaps the best female character I've come across in a videogame.
Voice acting is also on point - at least for Emily and Corvo.
As far as gameplay goes: classic stealth, tons of
and a delight to play through as many times as one can.
You have main objectives and scripted events - but even the latter are mostly optional, making the game a high-quality stealth sandbox.

Players join either the Terrorist or Counter-Terrorist team and complete objectives to win the match. CS:GO’s most well-known game mode sees Counter-Terrorists fighting to stop Terrorists from planting a bomb at a designated sight by eliminating them or defusing the explosive. At the start of each round, players purchase weapons using money earned from previous rounds. CS:GO’s community has developed an abundance of custom maps and game modes that expand or reinvent default gameplay. A huge assortment of in-game weapon cosmetics can be acquired by playing the game to distinguish yourself from other players.

This game has to be the king of MMO's. No lie. I'll go straight into the pros and cons.
PROS:
- Once you buy the game, there is NO subscription fee
- Each region has around 40-50 quests to do (on average)
- DLC brings on extra content and skill lines
- Certain regions and guilds allow you to obtain collectible pets and special apparel
- Achievement system that is much comparable to Diablo III or World or Warcraft
- Tons of exploration to be completed all throughout Tamriel
- You can PVP any player 1-on-1 anywhere you are
- Among all of the Elder Scrolls titles, this game has the easiest combat, skill and leveling systems
- Once you reach level 50, you earn Champion Points - much comparable to Destiny's Light system
- The game can be modified with add-ons that change the user experience, much like the add-ons one could choose when playing games like World of Warcraft, League of Legends and Overwatch
CONS:
- Some quests you have to do solo, to where you cannot see other party members, even if they are on the same map
As you can see, the pros heavily outweigh the cons. I HIGHLY reccomend this game. Buy it ... like now, trust me - you will not regret it. Also, go for Gold Edition!

Sure it is...
So while you collecting slimes, this game collecting data and analyse your gaming experience.
Thanks to Unity engine.
There is no option ingame to disable it.
If you don't believe..
Then please look in this folder:
%userprofile%\appdata\locallow\Monomi Park\Slime Rancher\Unity
You will get an unique User-ID and more other IDs to let the Unity engine track your system and your gaming behavior.
What it collects: OS version, cpu, mainboard, graphic card, device name, system language, when you start the game and enter a level.
How long you stay in a scene and much more. And for sure your current IP.
This unique hardware setup let you also be trackable through other Unity Engine games using this technique.
Yes there are other games using this feature but there are also a lot games made with Unity engine not do this data collecting!
Game connections overview:
#If you use the feedback option.
Tracking and analytics that can be blocked


Add the last domains to your HOSTS file under %systemroot%\system32\drivers\etc\ if you want block the analytics.
127.0.0.1
127.0.0.1
Or block the SlimeRancher.exe in the game folder with a firewall!
So dear devs, please disable this analytics. Such a wonderful game like Slime Rancher do not need it.

Ah, Just Cause 3. I've waited this game for years, even before it was announced - because I knew there was going to be a sequel to Just Cause 2, I was certain, I'd played it and played it and played it on my old Xbox 360, and before that on a friend's PS3.
But how does Just Cause 3 hold up to its predecessor?
Well, I have to say, I'm enjoying JC3 more than I ever have enjoyed JC2. The setting, the graphics, the sheer destruction... even the driving was improved, even though it only went from "dreadful" to "plain bad". The wingsuit is a lot of fun, blowing stuff up is even more fun, the world is both great and large - what else could you possibly ask for from a Just Cause game? They even tried to have decent voice actors and a semblance of an actual B-movie style plot a little better than the second's, what would you know. Although I'm miffed by the lack of faction missions, the challenges, the increase in story missions and the expansions make up quite well for the lack of them. True, logging in is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you're downloading something, so you either pause it or go offline... nevertheless, there's ways around it.
So what's my final judgement for this game? Well, it's big, it's fun, and the characters have an accent an Italian like me finds ridiculously funny. I'd give this game a-a-a-a-a-a-a-a-

For those who wanted to play Homeword 1 with a new coat of paint and maybe a some UI (User Interface) improvements, this ain't it. Instead what you get is a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥mod of the Homeworld 1 capaign for Homeworld 2. Almost nothing works as expected. The UI looks awful, feels awful and is in most ways no improvement over the original one. There is a reason there was no Homeworld 3.
The graphics look good. They did a fine job remodeling the ships. Unfortunately with none of the actual behavior modeled, the ships feel like empty husks. Turrets of corvettes don't seem to independently track and shoot enemy ships like they used to, and when big ships fire their giant cannons, there is no recoil on the turret. Everything feels like a 3d-Max model making pew pew sounds.
Formations don't work. Instead of the giant walls of capital ships surrounded by spheres of corvettes and wings of fighters you get to choose between a few different amorphous blobs and any time the ships move or see an enemy, the blog disintegrates.
Battles don't work. If you follow a fighter, you see that it couldn't hit a side of a mothership if it was docked inside it, making fights between fighters and corvettes take forever. On the other hand, assault frigates swat fighters out of the sky like so many flies. It's obvious Gearbox didn't even slightly try to match the balance of the original game.
Salvaging enemy ships doesn't work. Or one could argue that in all their bugginess they work too well. Just make a few of these and capture the whole enemy fleet: fighters, corvettes, everything, and you are done. Just don't build any of your own ships because they will shoot at the captured ships. You see, Homeworld 2 had boarding frigates that captured the targeted ships in place, so the engine doesn't actually support salvage ships that take their prey back into the mothership, and it's obvious that Gearbox didn't want to make any actual changes to the engine, or do any testing.
Homeworld 1 classic works. Too bad you don't get any graphical updates or UI features while playing it. Although, it's probably for the best since Gearbox doesn't seem to care about the things that made this classic great. Homeworld 1 is still a fantastic game and doesn't look nearly as dated as they make it look in their comparison videos. All they needed to do was these things:
- Use the original physics and game simulation engine.
- Update the 3d rendering engine to support modern resolutions and shadows. Although if that was too hard, updating just the models and textures would have been fine too.
- Increase the simulation steps per second to at least 30.
- Add time control.
Instead of doing these things, they made some nice looking ship models for Homeworld 2. Hence the turd that is Homeworld Remastered.
So far, so good... Game-time doesn't seem to update properly, though.

One of the most beautifull games ever made, even before it's remastering.
It is not only visually striking, but also musically and narratively engaging, thank's to masterful art and story direction. The presentation and production value is absolutely top-shelf stuff!
The game might be based on a 15 year old title, and has changed very little, but it doesn't need to. Homeworld is still one of the most riveting strategy games of all time. The pace is slow, but manages to still feel unrelenting thank's to it's difficulty. Homeworld is a challenging game, that often forces you to take a step back and re-think your options.
It is not only mechanically excellent, as it is also emotionally engaging. I will not spoil anything, but even as the game shows no animated characters and having intentionally subdued voice-acting, the game still manages to pull quite a few heart strings. This in large parts thank's to it's audio and music, which creates some of the most memorable atmospheres  in any game ever.
If you consider yourself a fan of good storytelling, atmosphere, strategy or space games in general, this is an absolutely mandatory experience. The king is back!

Factorio is an incredbly unique mix of game mechanics that almost defines a new genre. It is perhaps inspired by production chain games such as The Codex of Alchemical Engineering or Anno 2070... but with a completely different atmosphere than those, and certainly a more complex build structure.
If you like sandbox style games which require, planning, clever thinking, and problem solving... buy it. It's super fun. Even better with friends on multiplayer.
Before it was on steam, I probably have spent over 100 hours on it. One day maybe I'll actually beat the game.

Factorio is one of the most original games you will ever play.   It does borrow ideas from a few other games but it expands on them hugely and has many ideas that are entirely its own.
This game actually falls into a completely new category of game, the realtime 5X game.
Explore
Exploit
Expand
Exterminate
+
Excogitate
This might be a bit pretentious but it is actually 100% relevant and useful in describing this game.  Yes, excogitate is a real word and means "think out, plan, or devise."
The standard 4X tasks are absolutely essential to advancing in the game.  However, coming up with cool ideas, planning things out, devising efficient factories and so on is what this game is really all about.  This is what sets Factorio apart from anything else I've ever seen.
This game can be/appear quite complex early on.  At face value it may apppeal more to people with a more technical background (programmers, engineers etc), however the beauty of it is that you can just start playing whatever your background and focus on exactly what you find enjoyable.  This is thanks mainly to the huge research tree.
It also has such depth.  There are entire systems in the research tree that may initially appear completely confusing and irrelevant.  For example it is possible to play the game for hours and hours without even looking at oil processing.  Then on a whim,  you research 'basic oil processing' for the first time and realise (maybe even with some anxiety to begin with) that you now have an entire new system to learn about and eventually master.
There are a few parts of the user interface that can be confusing until you understand the developers mindset for how certain systems should work.  For example I found the electricty information screen (when you click on a power pole) to be a unintuitive with its Production and Consumption meters.  However as I said, it does make more sense when you read a few threads in response from the helpful  people on the Factorio forums.
Overall, this is an incredibly original game that offers a huge amount of gameplay and looks like it will be improved even more.  I highly recommend Factorio.

In ENSLAVED: Odyssey to the West you will follow Trip and Monkey through the post-apocalyptic USA after you have fled from a slave-ship. Monkey, who is now forced to help Trip, protects her during their search for a way to bring her home. While Trip brings the brain, Monkey brings the muscles. To overcome all struggles you have to make best use of both. As the story progresses both characters will often interact and their relationship develops from a mere Master-to-slave-situation to a real friendship.
Because Trip is not much of a fighter you have to play the warrior. Luckily Monkey has some vast knowledge about beating up one or two mechs! During the tutorial you learn all the basic moves. And every time Monkey learns a new trick a note pops up on your screen. The fighting is very easy and intuitive. You havea strong, a weak but fast, a charged, and a radial attack. Alternativly your weapon can shoot stun and beam attacks. All viable in most situations. But enough of Monkeys skills. What does Trip actually do? Well not that much. But the developer tried to make your VIP not totally garbage. She scans the environment for traps, mechs for weakspots, and decoys enemies so Monkey can sneak away. Also she is not totally defenceless. She has a EMP which stuns mechs for a short period of time when they come to close.

civilation 5 review
My Iroquois nation spreads across the world quickly, being likened to plague by my enemies. In real life, this relatively small group of people was all but wiped out by the end of the 20th century, but in my game, they are a force to be reckoned with -- a nation wresting control of the seas with modern navies, and taking cities by force with infantry and tanks. Manifest Destiny takes on a whole new meaning; by 2010, I've slowly but surely conquered the Americans and other European nations, subduing them to my rule... or simply burning their once-haughty nations to ashes.
t's a turn-based strategy game based around building up a selected society into a world power. And, yes, Civilization V can look seriously boring to the casual bystander, but for the person at the helm of the game each turn can lead to a weighty decision, giving the player a certain feeling of power that few, if any, games match.
Civilization has no campaign, instead it simply allows the players to create a world of their devising and jump right into it either by themselves or with others in multiplayer. The biggest choice a player will make is what civilization they're going to play. Each civilization is led by a great leader from history, and gets a few special benefits and units, so its' important to consider what type of victory you're out to achieve before setting your nationality. For instance the French get cultural bonuses that give them a huge bonus towards a cultural victory, while playing Germany will give players access to powerful military units like the Panzer tank that can aid in taking over the world by force. Of course you can always pick a military-focused leader and take them on a route towards a cultural victory, but this will also present a greater challenge.Besides picking a nation, players can further customize their scenario by switching between options such as whether the world will be made of several continents or not, what era they start in (Civ moves in eras, such as Medieval, Renaissance, etc., which also influences the level of technology you have access to), and how many other civilizations they wish to compete with. It essentially makes for infinite replayability, giving players a simple tool set to craft the challenge they want in of the world over and over again.
And hell yes, this is the type of game that you want to just play over and over. Like its predecessors, Civilization V is amazingly addictive, with games commonly drawing more than five or six hours out of me in a single sitting. The reason? Because win or lose, Civilization V allows players to guide an entire society and craft their own story, taking them from the dawn of history and far into the future. I love taking the Japanese and making them into a peaceful country who wants nothing more than to make Opera houses and win over their neighbors via their culture, or take the Aztecs and fashion them into a powerful imperialistic nation that is completely fascist and obsessed with world domination. Civilization V really is what you make of it, and for me it's a good way to tell alternate stories about some of history's most interesting nations.
I say Civilization V is only "good" -- and not "great," as I would have said about Civilization IV -- at crafting stories because I feel like the game's taken away some pretty important tools for customizing your society. In Civilization IV players could force things on their country and opposing nations in the form of religions and government. In Civilization V, though, players gather up "culture" as a resource, spending it every so many turns on "policies" that give their civilization bonuses. For instance a player might choose to put policy points into the "Piety" tree, giving their nation a boost to happiness and forcing them to accept an unnamed religion. I really appreciate the way the various policy trees give players a wide array of customization options for their nation, but I miss the power and ridiculous glee I got out doing things like forcing Judaism down the throats of my enemies because my Jewish Japanese empire was out to win owning the hearts and minds of my neighbors.

I gave this game a really good swing and found it a lackluster flyball in comparison to the all too positive reviews posted for it.  Nitpickingly - it's a console port to PC and there is noticable clunkiness due to that which I'll get into later (outside of displaying prompts as B or Y when the pc hotkeys would be E or F respectly).
The storyline is extremely linear and little can be said about the basis which is heavily inspired by another work (The Monkey King and Journey to the east), the character voice acting and animations (especially facial cues) were pretty spot on but overall each one left me very little to grow attached to.  I could see the obvious portryal of tropes but I found the main character too much of a masked Marty Stu which went against the backdrop of the "badass" character.  The Extras side option from the main menu called Pigsy's perfect 10 actually found more personality in the main character albeit a bit disgusting but at least humorous one than from the main protagonist.
The female protaganist Trip went to almost Navi levels of annoying at times with her nagging but overall not too bad of a partner to have through the long escort mission that is this game due to having some abilities.... but that's where gameplay comes in.
There were so many missed opportunities to do something actually interesting with this partnership dynamic that is the center of this story that the few interactions you do get to do (sticking a syringe in my neck to heal me or using holographic decoy) were far outshadowed by the problematic issues of having the funsucking job of babysitting.  Some of the clunkiness comes out in sections where you have to "throw" your partner to a platform only to have her scrambling from the ledge due to an inadequate throw - and you having to jump across on a timer in order to haul her up and save her (consequently saving you).  The problem from that example comes when the character refuses to jump in the direction of the platform which is OBVIOUS because you are playing on a keyboard without an analog stick thus having to replay sections just to do the same nonsensical event over again.  This happened throughout the playthrough at least 3x at different sections, which is why it stuck with me at all and also showed itself on time wasting "platforming" where you basically push a direction and spam the spacebar.  The last 2(?) levels out of the 14 actually started adding in "timing" for these jumps but for the majority of this game it is a complete waste of time and adds no challenge, content or fun to the game outside of padding hours played.  One of my biggest peeves "WHY CAN YOU NOT SKIP CUTSCENES OF CINEMATICS IN THIS GAME?" It's not like this was impossible to do technically in the game since you "can" skip the epilogue by clicking by mistake and bringing yo uto the then "unskippable" credit reel.  Nothing is more annoying than continuing your progress in this game the next day to be subject to the same 4 minute cinematic or if you experience a cheap death or bug (which also happened where Trip wouldn't activate a console to progress the gameplay) that you have to watch the entire cinematic over again... WHY?
Combat has some positives - it's reactive there are quite a varied amount of abilities to use but it feels overtly easy at the beginning and progressively annoying at later stages.  The mechs are most annoying when shield types swarm you while you need to complete a specific objective quickly (namely the 12th, 13th and 14th stages) especially if they don't conveniently give you a "special" tactical mech in order to exploit (such as an explosive or electrical one).  This only ramps up the difficulty of the game in an unsatisfying way as you sit there repeating the "cheapest" of combos in order to overcome these encounters and stifles creativity in the encounters.  Which is what the game comes down to - the combat becomes very very repetitive as you push through it and rarely alleviated by sections where you use a cool "hover cloud" (nimbus tee hee) but as enemies and even bosses become repeated over and over again the levels all start meshing together into one "blah" experience.
While I enjoyed the game at the start - somewhere through the game I felt extremely uninterested by what the game had to offer and found myself wandering away to other games.  I basically forced myself to finish it once I realized the general length of the game was fairly short when I saw the achievement list - and cannot find myself recommending it for the 2014 gamer.

Enslaved: Oddyssey to the West is a passable Action-Adventure game. It does most things right -- but shines in none.
STORY:
It's passable. The game is supposedly inspired by the Chinese novel "Journey to the West" published in the 16th century -- but from what I've heard saying the game even "inspired by it" is making it far-fetched. Hey, well actually the characters names are the same.
Basically this girl named Trip has you locked on killswitch so that you'll agree to escort her west over a post-apocalyptic America infested with robotic Mechs and Slavers.
Even though the game is basically one big escort mission Trip doesn't get herself killed much and is actually somewhat useful as she gives you some extra skills that are mostly used in puzzles.
The thing that bothered me the most though was the lack of any clear villain through the very linear story. Sure, there was the mechs and some faction called the Slavers... but neither of them were really introduced or explained at any point. Yes, there is a driving reasoning for it all and yes, there is drama -- but really it all serves for just simple backdrop for a adventure no more complicated than a saturday morning Transformers episode.
COMBAT:
I'll point this out first! Gamepad is recommended if not required for this game! I highly recommend Xbox or any similar controller that uses Xinput drivers -- since the game supports them natively.
The combat is simple - you got your basic light and heavy attacks with takedowns and dodges and blocks, plus some unlockable special moves. So don't expect any God of War style combos. For the most part the combat flows nicely but the dodge move feels a bit clunky and short ranged -- and sometimes the camera can give you a bit of a trouble but nothing too bad because the game is REALLY easy. (I played on medium difficulty, on hindsight I'd pick Hard.)
OTHER GAMEPLAY:
Well the other main focus of the game is platforming. Well - if you can call it that. The game is VERY linear and on top of that the platforming is contextual -- meaning you point to a direction and press jump and your character jumps to the next point, so there is absolutely no chance of missing jumps.
Other than combat and platforming there are some very simple puzzles in the style of "Push button A -> Pull lever B -> Door opens" or "Distract the robots". It's simple but handles itself well enough.
Oh, and it barely needs mentioning. But yes there is a VERY rudimentary system of unlocking skills and enhancments for your character... however, most of it is locked away throughout the game and when the upgrades finally unlock you can afford almost everything - so there is hardly any customization or choices to make. So what's the point?
TECHNICAL ISSUES:
I've heard some people have had some issues with this game however I haven't had any problems. I'd highy recommend checking out
article on this game. They have some really simple fixes to manage the most common issues.
As for the port itself -- well it's really a half♥♥♥♥♥PC port. The options menu is laughable at best, simple resolution change and some minor settings. Nothing flashy.

I had never heard of this game before I recently saw it on sale for $5. It seemed to have a generally warm reception and looked fun enough, so I picked it up. Turns out, I didn't regret it.
I liked the developing dynamic between Trip and Monkey. She can be a tad annoying at times, always asking you for help to cross a gap, but it didn't bother me too terribly much. Andy Serkis is great at being grumpy as Monkey. Dialog is actually not bad between the two characters, and some moments between the two really felt genuine.
Gameplay-wise, I had a lot of fun. Monkey is a beast in combat, with a number of upgrades to add more moves to your arsenal like counters, etc. The camera can tend to be a bit wonky at times, but I, personally, only had minimal trouble with it in actual combat. The climbing controls felt pretty good, as you could just leap to the next handhold in the middle of leaping to the current one, so it felt smooth...didn't have to wait for his mounting animation to finish on horizontal poles, etc. The enemies are varied enough to keep things interesting at any given moment; some will have shields, some are ranged, some stun you...each of which you have to take a bit different approach to get them vulnerable.
The story length and pace feel right; not too much sidetracking. Took me about 6 total hours to beat the first time. I did feel that the end of the game was a bit abrupt, and not showing what happens after the fact (furiously trying to avoid spoilers) was a bit disappointing, but I still liked it well enough. The climactic fight was well done in making you feel that it was the end...epic and all that.
Overall, I do recommend this game. I've seen worse PC ports of console games, and I really did enjoy myself playing it. I give it a score of 8/10

I bought it because it has BANDAI NAMCO label, looked good in screenshots and had POSITIVE USER REVIEWS. After near 6hrs of playing though, I'm sooooo bored with it and sick, too (literally, camera movements in this game made me sick. Like I physically wanted to throw up, not metaphorically). But let's begin from the top:
ENSLAVED has beautiful graphics, maybe tiny bit too colorful, but still beautiful. Scenery looks awesome, made me stop at times and just look around. That's judging from moments when I had a chance to actually look at it, before camera made me sick by defying me.
I like game music, but not from this game. I really pay attention to BGM, when I watch anime or movie or play a game. When some real thing goes on out there, I think to myself "boy, I've got to get this OST". But i REALLY don't have anything to say about music in this game. Like it doesn't exist. No memory of it whatsoever. Doesn't stand out at all, all i remember is that it was there. Maybe it's all got to do with me getting sick after 10 minutes into every game session.
Gameplay is boring. BOOOORING. I'm actually amazed I put up with it for 6 hours. I just ran around half the time or jumped around the other half - and from one "jump spot" to another. All jump points are pre-determined, so you can't catually choose where to jump. You can jump back or forth or sometimes out of the way to collect one of these tech orbs. BTW, wth is a tech orb? Is it edible?!? I understand money is of no value in a post-apocalyptic world, but I could be made to collect food or soda cans for the girl so she could pump up our muscles (or reflexes, or stick), out of gratitude, or something along those lines. But not tech orbs. How does she do that "upgrading", by the way, is beyond me.
This is probably good time to write what actually made me sick. One of two things is, when I ran around, sometimes camera got pinned to the wall, instead of being 3 meters off my back, and when I got close to the point, where it was pinned, it moved uncontrollably and made the world spin. Fast. And randomly. The other thing is, when I climbed up or down, camera didn't let me observe environment, even the immediate vicinity. I moved it left and released controller, and it would brutally, with donkey's stubborness reposition itself, centered on my character's butt. It's as it would say "NO, YOU CAN'T SEE WHAT'S AROUND YOU, THAT'S IRRELEVANT, YOU NEED TO SEE THIS NEXT JUMP POINT INSTEAD SO YOU WON'T FALL, I WILL MAKE ALL OF THEM BLINK SO EVEN MORE OF REALISM IS GONE". I'm used to RPG's, where I go anywhere I want, I'm used to FPP's where I point camera wherever I want, so this repeated deprivation of camera control is just plain ANNOYING! And it makes me sick. Really. People with epilepsy should never play this game. No one should, actually, but maybe that's just my irritation speaking.
Oh, and there's fights. They're easy. REALLY. All those bots are just minor obstacle to another set of running or jumping or climbing or maybe gliding on that glowing thing, occasionally. When some bot charges at me, I just charge at it too, and I strike first, 90% of the time. Sometimes there were mini-bossess I needed to put down in a different manner, meaning repeat some sequence of actions 3 or more times until it's down. That's all. It's just tedious. Felt like I put down 10 or 15 normal bots in a row.
There's also many weap..... wait... no, there isn't. Just fists and stick, 6 hours into the game, and judging by options the Trip Shop has, there aren't any more than this. So you run around, pick up TECH POINTS and somehow your reflexes, stick power or health or other things get better, when you buy their respective upgrades from the girl (GOD, she's almost almighty, isn't she). Shop is also bugged and reeks of console, but that's just minor annoyance I could catually live with.
Anyway, all your running and jumping is interluded by neat cutscenes, which made me think of something:
This game should be made a movie. Seriously. I mean, instead of being the game. Make it a movie, like PIXAR. Or 12-episodes-long anime series. Remove running around for TECH ORBS (because that's silly, frankly), throw in some mini-boss battles, instead of having players bludgeoning them with a stick, and that's it. I'd be first to buy the BD disc.
All in all, it's one of these games that made me not care how it ends. Big disappointment. I bought it on a discount, so I'm not really feeling ripped off. Maybe I will have my nephew beat it in my stead, when he gets older. Mind you, I've played only 6 hours (by my standards this is really long, for a game that has only visuals as its PROS).

So I'll start by saying the game is 100% free! That means no microtransactions, paid DLC or marketplace to buy skins so you can't really complain.
This game started as a Half-Life 2 Mod but is literally a full conversion, there’s not much that still remains from Half-Life 2 in terms of weapons, characters, gameplay features and animations.
The game is designed to be a hardcore experience, limited resources, ammo, guns, a weight system that forces you to make choices on what you will keep and what will work better for in the long run. In a few hits you can go from being perfectly healthy to dead, either just from being hit to much, bleeding or worst of all.... Infection. Now there are medical supplies to help aid in these effects like medkits, bandages, Infection Pills and even a cure but they can be hard to find when needed the most but that’s part of what makes the game so enjoyable is the realistic experience it provides. It forces teamwork, ammo and supply conservation and many other things.
There are 2 modes, Objective and Survival. Objective is basically a campaign mode where you need to complete objectives and escape. This is a great mode and really fun to play co-op or with many other players. There are about 9 levels that offer different experiences and challenges, some very difficult with never ending zombie hordes that require quick navigation around the hordes and the objectives themselves.
Survival is the typical round by round mode that lasts for 10 rounds with a increasing rate of zombies. Not to fun on your own but enjoyable with a few others.
Professional level animations, hardcore features like no HUD, manually unload your guns and checking of your ammo means you need to be aware of how many rounds you have fired or face the consequences.
The only things I can say against it is, it would be cool to have more Objective maps or a proper campaign but I know how much work that can be, let’s hope they are working on a No More Room in Hell 2 for that :P there’s defiantly a market for hardcore zombie games.
The other is the achievements... as someone who cares about achievements, aka "completionist" I like to be able to complete all achievements but some of these are just far to time consuming or unrealistically hard, I feel as though when designing an achievement the developer should try to complete it themselves before they add it. I'm not sure that was the case for some of these, for example: "You like a good challenge? Engage 1000 zombies in fisticuffs and win" and "Complete the following maps with AT LEAST 6 players without losing a single safe zone or incurring any casualties: Favela, Northway, Flooded, Isolated, NotLD, Ransack" yeah..... the last achievement has a 0% global completion rate which means no one has 100% of the achievements for this game which is just not good enough.

Essentially Homeworld 1 skins in the Homeworld 2 engine.  If you've never played the original Homeworld, the remastered version is the game for you.  If you have, however, you'll come to realize that Homeworld 2 was a step back in terms of strategy and micromanagement of your fleet.  The formations in the original Homeworld, for example, allowed ships to move in an ACTUAL formation.  In Homeworld 2, these formations break apart as soon as you move in any direction besides forward.  Another thing is ship intelligence.  In the original Homeworld, heavy/multigun corvettes tended to strafe around the target, with their fronts facing the target.  This allowed maximum damage since no gun was obstructed by another.  In Homeworld 2, the "strafe" of corvettes is just a circular movment around the target, no fronts facing at all.  This meant that damage output is reduced, since the guns on the opposite sides do nothing.  Oh, and difficulty scaling.  Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ difficuly scaling (Sea of lost souls mission on remastered...like no..just kill yourself).  These three things are the most disappointing aspects of the remastered, in my opinion.  There are a bunch of others I didn't cover but I'm sure somebody has in the reviews of this collection.
All in all, this collection is really just a nostalgic trip down memory lane.  Graphics are top notch and so is the UI.  The original versions of the games are also included (which is freaking awesome).
Get this collection even if you have or haven't played this game.  For the old vets, it's a nostalgic trip and for the new players, its an experience you don't want to miss.

Factorio is a game where you crawl your way up from picking up iron and coal from the ground with your bare hands to having swarms of heavily fortified laser-equipped murder-bots obliterate anything in sight, as trains deliver masses of ore and other materials to your sprawling complex of pollution-belching factories.
You'll show your friends your completed factory after 30 hours of playtime and spend 20 minutes explaining how ore flows through your factory and gets processed to rocket parts. In the process of doing so you'll see multiple inefficiencies and plan a new, better factory.
When you start the next map, your friend will see what you started with and stare agape into the abyss to which you have plunged. They will then try the game to see how far down the rabbit hole you really had to go in order to spend so much time on how an arm inserts into a factory. And the cycle will begin anew.
Also, they're adding a spider-bot you create. Who doesn't want to ride a spider-bot?

Dark Souls 2.
This game is pretty good.    I enjoy the Combat, the weapons and armor system.   I even like the PVP.   Yes.   Me.   Someone who absolutely hates PVP, enjoys it in this game.     Mostly because even if you lose, it's nothing major.
Humanity has been replaced by using a consumable called a Human Effigy.   Which if burned at a bonfire, prevents online interactions for an hour.   Pro tip?  Use in the Iron Keep.   Trust me.   People invade there all day, and if you would actually like to play the game without getting griefed all day, do it.
Upgrades feel necessary and are helpful.    Soul farming has been a tiny bit nerfed what with mobs no longer spawning after you kill them 10+ times.    However the game itself is fantastic and I've never felt the need to farm.
NG+ ups the Ante times 10x with Black and Red Phantom scattered across the map, and that's where the game truly begins to shine.    It forces you to learn how to adapt and not spam, and how dodging, guard breaking, and parrying are necessary for survival.
Overall I can definitely recommend Dark Souls 2.     It's fun, has an awesome amount of content and will keep Souls Fans happy.

The experience of being in awe at what the Crowbar Collective team did to Half-Life 1 and the Source engine is definitely worth the price tag if that's something you're interested in. The lighting effect are jaw-dropping in places, especially considering it's built using an engine from 2004. The environmental design is absolutely gorgeously as well. A lot of the redesigned areas offer major improvements over the original. Certain areas are completely unrecognisable and one of the more frustrating chapters has been cut short for the better. I personally found the ai of the marines to be a bit underwhelming compared to the fearless soldiers of the original, but it's certainly not a deal-breaker.
You shouldn't be buying this game for the multiplayer. The two available modes are Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch. That is, if you even get to play it, as most of the time all the servers are dead. Thankfully gauss jumping is still in and it's as hilarious as ever, which largely makes up for the removal of bunnyhopping. The only real advantage it does offer over the original's multiplayer is that the graphics went from very dated to beautiful eye-candy. It can be a fun way to kill time with friends but don't expect much from it.
Overall I'd give this video game a "It's a yes for me" out of ten.

Very solid story, especially for the 75% off price. I thoroughly enjoyed it. Has a very likable hero, voiced by the sensational Andy Serkis. The main girl in the game is Trip, voiced by Lindsey Shaw, who is a very despicable character, but only because she's scared. In the end she does realize her flaws, and I guess Monkey forgives her because he finds he fricken attractive as hell. It's not a very long game, which is good for me since I don't have a buttload of time to keep track of a 20+ hour story in a game. The game was well made considering Ninja Theory's team on it. Some scenes feel a little empty, but all of the gameplay is lush and full of beauty. The puzzles are not overly complicated. The flaw that bugs me the most is that game holds your hand almost the whole way through, which can get a little annoying if you just want to get moving, it makes you feel a little helpless just standing there, but better than not knowing where to go/what to do. This game has the best edge grapple/jump gameplay I've ever seen. The main issues with games like Prince of Persia and Assassin's Creed is that the player would randomly jump off a ledge I didn't want them to, or storm into a random direction. Enslaved is so finely programmed that I have not run into a situation where the controls were either unresponsive, or the hero went where I didn't want him to go, or jump higher/lower than I wanted him to. The combat is very fine. Unlocking abilities simply takes resources and not levels or anything. You pick up orbs to gain resources. I thought they'd feel out of place, but in game you're more focused on finding them than realizing if they ruin the scene or not.
For those seeking adventure and a hint of romance in a post apocalyptic paradise, look no further.

Don't get me wrong. The storyline is exciting, the graphics are beautiful, the voice acting (particularly that by Andy Serkis, but yes, in general) is fantastic. It's also exciting to know that I'm playing as a character who was mocapped by Andy Serkis. However.
This is the one of the worst, and laziest, PC ports imaginable. There are game-breaking bugs throughout the game, the kind that require a walkthrough to find a workaround; and I'm not even to the end of it yet. If you can get it for console instead of PC, I strongly recommend that. However, I would not spend more than five dollars on the PC port. Video handling is atrocious, graphics are much too tightly bound to the same system as controls, and throughout the game, you will face no greater enemy than the freakin' camera angle. It felt worse than DIstrict 9. There were cases where Monkey (that's your hero) would attack at angles that had nothing to do with anything, exposing you to getting torn to shreds by a bunch of otherwise-trivial robots. There were cases in which the camera angle rotated literally 180 degrees, and it took me thirty seconds to figure out how to cross an otherwise insignificant bridge because he kept turning around halfway. There are controller instructions that make zero sense for a mouse and keyboard (I'm still trying to figure out where "X" and "B" are.) Perhaps most obnoxiously, whoever did game-camera direction seemed to think they were making a major motion picture instead of a game, because a lot of the angles serve literally no purpose other than trying to make you look cool. (While dying, evidently.)
And let's not forget the on-again-off-again problems with the scripted AI. There are many occasions in which a plot-essential event won't occur because a character has stopped in the middle of the floor, instead of completing their scripted action. The game's save mechanism is pretty much identical to Price of Persia's, except I'm not aware of any cue that appears when I get to a checkpoint. (If you've played "Ghostbusters" by Terminal Reality, think of that system.) So, when one of these disasters occurs, which might relate to something as tangential as your screen resolution, you have to reset to the last checkpoint and do everything again. Additionally, it's worth noting that the cut scenes cannot be skipped with the keyboard, to my knowledge.
Serkis deserves better than this.
It takes a lot to make me recommend a console over PC, but in this case, it is your better bet. I recommend at least having a controller around, and I do not recommend picking it up for the list price of $20.00; this product is unfinished. Wait to get it on sale, or grab the older version for Playstation. I have little faith that the releaser is making any further updates to the port.

I've tried to get into MOBAs for a while now but I just don't enjoy top-down click-to-walk games. I don't feel like I'm really a part of the action. I've played DotA 2, Heroes of the Storm, and briefly LoL, but none of them really did it for me. Smite was the perfect solution. The third-person perspective oddly enough helped me to better keep track of where everyone was, as well as really making me feel like I was in the heat of battle. The mythology theme just adds to the brilliance of this game. I've always been a fan of Age of Mythology and just mythology in general, and seeing Hercules and Odin go head to head, or Ra and Poseidon flinging spells at each other is just amazing. The skins are very creative and beautiful, and the premium currency, Gems, can be obtained through normal play, not just buying them with real money. There's a great voice command menu that's very easy to use and get used to. For instance if you press VVVR your character will say "My ultimate is ready!". This helps to communicate with your team even without the use of voice chat. The community is generally much nicer than that of other games I've played, such as WoW and TF2. People can get frustrated when a new player is playing poorly, but often times they just give them pointers to help them improve. Every day there's a new Match of the Day, which is a gamemode with unique rules. One day everyone might be forced to play a specific hero, or everyone will have infinite mana and reduced cooldowns. The Motd adds something new every day for those who are tired of the normal modes. One problem I have is the lack of maps. There's only one map per gamemode, while it's not a huge issue, it would be nice to have some new map designs. All in all I would definitely recommend this game. Good for seasoned MOBA players, or people new to the genre. If you're looking to get into this game with friends, I would definitely recommend adding one of your friends as your recruiter, or vice versa. This will give you both rewards as you level and play together.

The original Homeworld is my favorite game of all time, no joke. Look at my avatar, it's been that since day one.
Specifically, the singleplayer campaign was... perfection, everything I could have wanted as a gamer. Needless to say, I have been quite looking forward to this remaster. Keep in mind this review is from the point of view of a player of the original. Though, it IS relevant to all players.
I mostly like it. The multiplayer, even in beta, works well and seems to run good. It's neat, though I'm not sure if balanced, to have faction from both homeworld 1 and 2 fight each other. But lets get down to what they, in my opinion, did right.
-The graphics are eye porn, straight up. So pretty, and it still all looks like Homeworld. Perfect visual overhaul. I specifically noticed how much better Homeworld 1 resource collecting and missiles looked.
-The story seems to be a perfect copy, and the remastered voice-overs sound exactly the same in terms of inflection, and the music is still spot-on. The atmosphere of the game is as flawless as the origonal.
-Karan S'jet. Nuff' said.
Now, I have two main issues, and I'll address them seperately.
1. The homeworld campaign should not require resources for research. It throws off the delicate timing of how soon you can afford to build ships, as well as just makes things more expensive. In the classic I could have a much larger force at the end of mission 2, but now I'm relegated to a few measly ships because I lose a significant portion of my resources (like 10 ships worth) to researching previously free upgrades. I understand in multiplayer, but for the campaign, it can't be that hard to edit a file and adjust research costs to zero. Seriously.
2. This is... a big issue. It would appear that the AI controlling homeworld 1 strike craft is severely broken. Specifically, ships don't hold formation in combat, and homeworld 1 corvettes seem to just be unable to align themselves in such a way that they actually hit anything.
Here's an example from mission 2:
If you played the original, you know heavy corvettes in wall formation will WRECK. When I assign this as an escort and an enemy fighter shows up, they should all turn, in formation, and concentrate fire for tremendous effect.  In this remaster, they stop, turn themselves perpendicular to the enemy, and all fly off in random directions. this allowed every single enemy to quite simply fly by my expensive fleet of corvettes without taking a single hit.
I suspect this is a result of some issues related to unifying the homeworld 1 and 2 engines, but this combined with the research issue has completely soured my experience replaying the campaign, and I no longer want to since I can tell it will be nye impossible to complete with such severe drawbacks.
Also, it seems like HW1 missiles are less accurate now, not sure though.
That said, I recommend this because the multiplayer and homeworld 2 campaign are flawless as far as I can tell.
I hope they can patch the strike craft AI issues, though patching AI to that extent post-release may be more than one can reasonably hope for. Time will tell if this issue gets patched.

I think I like Factorio for many of the same reasons why I like being a programmer; Firstly, it presents you with problems that are easy to solve, but hard to optimize. And it allows you to find your own balance in how perfect you want your solutions to be. Secondly, you are given more and more basic, but powerful, tools to solve the same problems.
This is definitely one of the most fun games I've played in a long time!
(I've put upwards of 200 hours into this game before it was released on Steam.)

Short version: It's a puzzle (this makes sense as you play it) and resource management game with some very light combat thrown in. It's an awesome game if you want a non-combat challenge that pushes you to think.
Long version: Factorio is definitely not for every one. Things not to expect from Factorio: rewarding/challenging combat, in game help on what the best layouts are (there's a reason for this), easy diffuculty curve, and fun if you're not into building/maintaining networks that can be grossly complex (seriously, you won't have fun if you don't enjoy building logistic networks because that is the focus of the game).
Look at the trailer, now realize that the layout you see there is not an exageration of what's needed as you progress through the tech. Lets break it down from the begining on what the crafting tree is like and it might shed a bit of light on that thought:
Coal + Iron ore + (inserted into) Smelter = Iron plate. Same thing with copper. Then: Iron plate -> Crafted into -> Iron gear, Copper Plate -> Crafted into -> Copper cable. Copper Cable + Iron plate -> Crafted into -> Electronic circuit. Iron gear + Electronic circuit + Iron plate -> Crafted into -> Inserter.
Each time you see (crafted into) you can craft this at a machine called an assembler that will make it for you so long as it is powered and has access to all of the correct compenents, and with the inserter created, you can now move items from a chest, smelter, or assembler to another container or onto a conveyor belt.
The goal of all of the above? Trying to automate as much of it as possible, even though your character can create all of the above items mentioned, he can only create one thing at a time, and when you need at least three inserters for a single smelter (one for coal, one for ore, and one for the output) you'll soon realize making it all by hand slows the game down significantly.
Keep in mind that the resources you need will NOT be conviently placed and you will HAVE to figure out how to get resources from point A to B... and then C, and then A1, B2, and C5 (because a basic resource can be used in multiple recipes, it will need to split into different allocation lines). Then, when the resources in a particular spot has run out, it's time to pack up all that equipment in that area and move it somewhere else and then reconnect it back to the network.
Now the combat is very basic (because that's not the focus of the game). If you have a gun and ammo, you mouse in the general direction of the nasty critter you want dead and hold down space bar. Otherwise, you make gun/laser turrets to protect your network (you will need to as depending on resource locations, networks can get mas+sive) while you're not there. Then when you're ready to assualt a particular nasty nest of the beasties, create a tank and blast them to hell.
But that's it, there is no RPG elements like gaining experience, nor is there a reward for killing all of them on the map. The game does become a bit too easy if you don't have the creatures attacking you as then there's no reason to waste resources (and more importanly assembly line space) on creating defences.
The point of all this is to make it painfully obvious that if you don't like the sound of making optimal configurations for logistic networks, then pass on this game. Otherwise, take a look at the demo if it's still available.
I haven't even tried multiplayer yet, but have had this game for quite some time before the steam keys were released. It's an awesome game and would highly recommend it to any one who's interested.

Just Cause 3 is kind of a mixed bag, honestly.
In terms of gameplay, it takes all you like on JC2 and adds some more 'sense' to the orgy of destruction. While you basically could destroy most of the infrastructure of Panau in JC2, it was totally pointless. There was no liberation of the cities, soldier stayed where the were etc. Now there's actual liberation.
Also the missions are better in my opinion. There is no more 'go somewhere, protect the technician, mow down everything with the minigun' anymore.
Generally speaking, the difficulty is higher and you die more often (sometimes because the controls are not as smooth as they were in JC2).
I could totally live with that....what I can't live with, are the technical aspects of the game:
it crashes on a regular basis - you can't play two consecutive missions. While I don't suffer from the graphics issues of other players, the game crashes after about 20 minutes of play.
My system (i5 3570s/2*4GB DDR3-1600 Corsair, Intel DH77EB, Sapphire Radeon R9 380 4GB, Samsung 850Evo SSD, 450W 80+Platinum PSU, 24 inch screen@1920*1200px, Win7 Pro x64, running latest drivers, Windows patch level and BIOS).
Long story short: I want to love this game. But in this technical state, I can't.

Being a huge fan of JC2 I decided to try the third game despite the large amount of negative reviews. Turns out, JC3 runs fairly well on my PC. 60fps most of the time on high settings, with occasional dropping to 40-50 in towns and bases. The game crashed twice for no reason and, while I wouldn't call it "broken", it's definitely very badly optimized. Negative reviews are expected since Avalanche seems to be more interesed in making DLC than fixing bugs and memory leaks.
If you can get it to work, the game is actually really great. The hookshot-parachute-wingsuit mechanics work amazingly well and manage to make moving through the sandbox so much fun. Combined with an attractive tethering hookshot, tons of vehicles, a very fun physics engine and constant giant explosions (every car in this game seems to use TNT for fuel), the game truly becomes a great action movie simulator.
Definitely recomended, and you can always get a refund if you can't get it to work properly.

So... Just Cause 3, is not a bad game: just an underwhelming one. There are moments of wonderful, anarchic chaos that make you feel like the world’s coolest action hero. And it’s an amusing physics playground, letting you tether objects with your grappling hook cable and tighten it to violently smash them together. But these things, as fun as they are, can only hold your attention for so long, and boredom soon sets in. All the massive explosions in the world can’t hide the fact that Just Cause 3 is marred by busywork and simplistic design.
But maybe you don’t care about any of that, and you just want a simple action game you can fire up for an hour every other day to explode things. Reducing Medici to smoking rubble is undeniably cathartic, and it provides plenty of cheap, instant thrills. But anyone who wants anything more will be disappointed. Just Cause 3 struggles to compete with other open-world games released this year.

Edit 14/06/2017:
I've been getting a lot of comments so I've decided to write a quick FAQ of them:
1) This plan is good because modders can make money - You are completely correct that modders should have a right to make money but a better way to do this would be to have built-in donate buttons on the workshop and on
. There is absolutely no reason Bethesda needs to take a slice of the profits for someone elses original work.
2) Bethesda has a right to monetise mods that use Bethesda assets - Bethesda already profits from the sale of these assets in the first instance, a profit that is increased because people know about and expect the modding community to make stuff better. Nobody is using these assets outside of the product that was already purchased.
3) It wont effect the games with mods already - So they say. They also have a big section in the games EULA that mods can only be free. Regardless of whether or not the older games are directly influenced, you've got to look fowards.
Fallout 4 released without the very convenient Steam Workshop. It also had the standard Bethesda mod checkbox ui on the splashscreen disabled. The developers literally went out of their way to try and force people to use
mods.
Assuming Bethesda is a gigantic video games company that cares about profits this will only get worse in future release. They will begin to release games that are even less finished, have more small DLC and try and control it all through a proprietary system. When there is backlash against this they may even change the licensing on their editing software so that mods HAVE to be released through their systems or say that non-creator club mods are no longer allowed.
They would not be the first company to do something like this. Remember that this kind of thing tends to creep in over time.
4) It's good for consoles - The idea of modding for consoles is a point of discussion anyway but I don't see how having yet another storefront that uses yet another made-up currency is anything other than further exploitation of console users. If console users really want modding thats both censorship and cost free (how modding has been for years) they should also resist this new system.
5) Why put a negative review on a game that won't be affected - When you give money to a company you give a company a little bit more power. To buy something good (like Skyrim) and ignore all the bad things the company will do with your money is simply unethical. To a greater or lesser degree we are all complicit with a lot of large companies doing a lot of very bad things, but gaming is something I truly love and I won't stand by and watch one of my favourite companies do this to it's fanbase in the name of squeezing a few more dollars out of each of them.
