The second installment and sequel of the Dark Souls series (third in Souls overall) proves to be more Dark Souls goodness, but with small changes that allow the game to succeed in some areas and fall short on other aspects. The game was developed by From Software, published by Namco Bandai and directed by Tomohiro Shibuya and Yui Tanimura.
To kick things off, the game doesn't suffer from a bad PC port like its predecessor did. Don't get me wrong, the original Dark Souls game is fantastic - but it required a mod fix for acceptable visuals (nobody likes playing blurry resolutions on PC). Additionally keyboard controls and mouse (KB+M) were horrorific and basically required a controller to play. But KB+M now works acceptably for those who don't have a controller or don't like playing with controllers.
- Now that we've got that out of the way, the gameplay is pretty much as you expect from a Dark Souls game. You cut, stab and smash hollows (someone who lost their souls and sanity) and creatures in Drangleic - a Kingdom that has fallen into despair and serves as the setting of the game. There's also magic and bows for those who want to fight from a distance. There's some newer stuff like hexes and whatnot that adds more choices on how to kill your enemies, but that's not overly important in this review.
While primarily a singleplayer game, your session of the game is always interconnected with other players through messages, summonings and invasions. People leave messages for other players to see in their own, whether or not they're helpful is another question though (e.g. "Beware of giant but hole"). Summons is basically playing cooperatively with either a NPC or real player while invasions is someone there actively trying to kill players in their world for whatever reason (yes I hate invaders).
Co-op play is made easier than in preceeding games, its much easier to play with a friend or two in this game than in past installments, it has definitely been given a bigger focus this game. While I felt little incentive to help people out in DS1, I find myself lending a hand to other players frequently in this game.
It is generally ill advised to play this game like an action one - you'll simply die as the game punishes you for not adhering to its rules. In the Souls game, you're usually very reactionary and passive. Its a "wait and see" game. While many games suffer from players just rushing in and not punishing you for your recklessness, Dark Souls 2 will dearly punish and reward you with death for not learning the patterns and movesets of enemies. Recognising when there's danger will save your life. Ignoring it will usually result in your downfall. Your actions must be deliberate, you cannot simply button mash your way through the game like in other games.
In the modern era where video games hold your hands and required little thought or effort to complete, Demon Souls was prasied for its unforgiving and challenging gameplay. The same is still held true in Dark Souls 2 and it is delightful to know this fact.
- There's nothing really noteworthy to praise about the visual fidelity of Dark Souls 2 - other than its not capped at 30 frames like the original game was and required a config fix to fix the resolution. The new dynamic lighting looks great, caverns and interiors look superb with a torch in hand. There are a few interesting environments in DS2 but they never feel connected into an expansive world like its predecessor. Those who have went from Earthen Peak to Iron Keep will understand what I mean by this.
- Honestly not much to say on this one, the Souls game has never been about story. Its mostly the lore that you read from item descriptions, which has unfortunately been made more shallow in this installment.
- I have a number of complaints about the design choices in Dark Souls 2 that has negatively affected the overall experience - which resonate more strongly with DS1 veterans than newcomers of the franchise. For newcomers most of this does not apply to you.
While in Demon Souls there was the hub world and in Dark Souls they ditched that for an open interconnected world, DS2 manages to create a hybrid between the two. What we ended up was a rather disappointing treatment of the open world designs. The world felt more linear and many "bonfires" felt more like checkpoints than a smaller hub from where you travel from. As you can teleport to these bonfires whenever, they feel much more arbitrary than usual. I pretty much breathe a sigh of relief when I see a bonfire in DS1. In this game not so much.
The addition of the dynamic lighting is appreciated but it also came at a price. Because of this dynamic lighting many levels felt flat without a torch - lacking light and shadow. Players like myself find that there is usually little need to carry a torch around, because you're forced to give up one of your hand for the torch and most of the levels aren't dark enough to warrant carrying a torch. As silly as the self-illuminating lighting around the character was, the darker environments with baked lights/shadows in past games were more atmospheric and it often felt like interiors were claustrophobic.
Enemy design are poorly done. Too often you would be facing opponents that showed little weakness were relentless in their attacks, giving little room for opportunities to attack. You wouldn't be able to stagger them no matter how hard you try. I find myself poking at the enemy trying to whittle them down in fear of retaliation, taking a chunk of my health off. This made melee builds extremely difficult and sometimes unforgiving.
Random other complains include: weapons break way too easily for whatever reason (think its related to frame rate), poor tracking, bad hitboxes, forgettable boss designs, lacking an open world, etc.
- Dark Souls 2 is plagued with poor and questionable design choices. Despite this negative and lacking DS1's intricate open world levels that felt expansive and were interconnected - DS2 is still a great game that fixes the technical hurdles that came from DS1's PC port. It is the easiest Souls game to jump into for newcomers and veterans alike with welcomed quality of life improvements. If you're looking for a challenging game to play that rewards patience and perseverance, this game is definitely for you.

I'll start by saying that I have severe Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, and I tend to have panic attacks and become very anxious when I don't feel I have control over life or the many things which stress me. What I've found is that certain games are able to immerse me in a world where I have complete control and understanding over how things work, and I can just sit back and let the obsessive part of my mind use the game as an outlet for all of that pent up stress.
While the game is not "immersive" in the traditional sense of incredible graphics and realism, this game is incredible at allowing you to lose yourself, and letting your mind enjoy the fun patterns and complex systems that this game has to offer. It's a really unique game, a sort of blend of Zachtronics and Don't Starve, with the wonderful isometric graphics of Chris Sawyer.
Absolutely worth buying, even in early access. The devs should be rewarded for their incredible effort and attention to their community, as well.

Factorio is an incredbly unique mix of game mechanics that almost defines a new genre. It is perhaps inspired by production chain games such as The Codex of Alchemical Engineering or Anno 2070... but with a completely different atmosphere than those, and certainly a more complex build structure.
If you like sandbox style games which require, planning, clever thinking, and problem solving... buy it. It's super fun. Even better with friends on multiplayer.
Before it was on steam, I probably have spent over 100 hours on it. One day maybe I'll actually beat the game.

Factorio is one of the most original games you will ever play.   It does borrow ideas from a few other games but it expands on them hugely and has many ideas that are entirely its own.
This game actually falls into a completely new category of game, the realtime 5X game.
Explore
Exploit
Expand
Exterminate
+
Excogitate
This might be a bit pretentious but it is actually 100% relevant and useful in describing this game.  Yes, excogitate is a real word and means "think out, plan, or devise."
The standard 4X tasks are absolutely essential to advancing in the game.  However, coming up with cool ideas, planning things out, devising efficient factories and so on is what this game is really all about.  This is what sets Factorio apart from anything else I've ever seen.
This game can be/appear quite complex early on.  At face value it may apppeal more to people with a more technical background (programmers, engineers etc), however the beauty of it is that you can just start playing whatever your background and focus on exactly what you find enjoyable.  This is thanks mainly to the huge research tree.
It also has such depth.  There are entire systems in the research tree that may initially appear completely confusing and irrelevant.  For example it is possible to play the game for hours and hours without even looking at oil processing.  Then on a whim,  you research 'basic oil processing' for the first time and realise (maybe even with some anxiety to begin with) that you now have an entire new system to learn about and eventually master.
There are a few parts of the user interface that can be confusing until you understand the developers mindset for how certain systems should work.  For example I found the electricty information screen (when you click on a power pole) to be a unintuitive with its Production and Consumption meters.  However as I said, it does make more sense when you read a few threads in response from the helpful  people on the Factorio forums.
Overall, this is an incredibly original game that offers a huge amount of gameplay and looks like it will be improved even more.  I highly recommend Factorio.

Homeworld Remastered Collection includes all parcels of the Homeworld franchinse, except for Homeworld Cataclysm. Unfortunately I did not have the opportunity to enjoy the original in the 90s due to the lack of life. But this edition fixes that by reintroducing an amazing RTS gaming experience. Aside from the great price-to-content ratio, the gameplay and design improvements provide a spectacular set for both an interstellar epic and an interstellar war. In the remastered edition of Homeworld 1, the story appeals to every human’s instinctive desire: exploration. What would a space-game be without a voyage through the vastness of the cosmos? The skirmish mode appeals to unique space physics. Unlike many other gravity-deprived RTS games, Homeworld combines true science with fictional science in perfect proportions, avoiding a space simulation but maintaining a somewhat credible reality. For example, constant explosions during a battle enhance the gameplay, but at the sacrifice having sound travel through no medium-- violating physical principle. However, science martinets should not worry because the soundtrack and plot attract your attention perpetually. I don’t know if Barber's Adagio for strings was featured in the original Homeworld 1, but its inclusion in the remastered version definitely adds to the dramatic story. All of these aspects sum to an enjoyable experience, but not without the occasional flaw. Thankfully, only minor and often insignificant. Sometimes the 'skybox' (in context, ‘skybox’ is not concise, but you get the idea) shows a strange illustration. If there is a galaxy in the background, stars behind it will be equally luminous as ones far away from the galaxy. My reasoning leads me to think the stars should be perceived at least slightly dimmer. The units rarely break formation, but when they do, controlling combat becomes difficult. Also, in one story mission, a relatively large ship I deployed got stuck between my mother ship and a computer mother ship, rendering it unusable. Aside from these, I found the game to run smoothly. 9/10.

Being a huge fan of JC2 I decided to try the third game despite the large amount of negative reviews. Turns out, JC3 runs fairly well on my PC. 60fps most of the time on high settings, with occasional dropping to 40-50 in towns and bases. The game crashed twice for no reason and, while I wouldn't call it "broken", it's definitely very badly optimized. Negative reviews are expected since Avalanche seems to be more interesed in making DLC than fixing bugs and memory leaks.
If you can get it to work, the game is actually really great. The hookshot-parachute-wingsuit mechanics work amazingly well and manage to make moving through the sandbox so much fun. Combined with an attractive tethering hookshot, tons of vehicles, a very fun physics engine and constant giant explosions (every car in this game seems to use TNT for fuel), the game truly becomes a great action movie simulator.
Definitely recomended, and you can always get a refund if you can't get it to work properly.

Well the game runs fine with an AMD FX8350 and a GTX970, but the memory leak issue is horrible, it will crash every 10-15 minutes or so, and may even corrupt your save files, so you better have 16gb of ram or else this game will be unplayable.

So... Just Cause 3, is not a bad game: just an underwhelming one. There are moments of wonderful, anarchic chaos that make you feel like the world’s coolest action hero. And it’s an amusing physics playground, letting you tether objects with your grappling hook cable and tighten it to violently smash them together. But these things, as fun as they are, can only hold your attention for so long, and boredom soon sets in. All the massive explosions in the world can’t hide the fact that Just Cause 3 is marred by busywork and simplistic design.
But maybe you don’t care about any of that, and you just want a simple action game you can fire up for an hour every other day to explode things. Reducing Medici to smoking rubble is undeniably cathartic, and it provides plenty of cheap, instant thrills. But anyone who wants anything more will be disappointed. Just Cause 3 struggles to compete with other open-world games released this year.

Be prepared to die. A lot.
The second installment and sequel of the Dark Souls series (third in Souls overall) proves to be more Dark Souls goodness, but with small changes that allow the game to succeed in some areas and fall short on other aspects. The game was developed by From Software, published by Namco Bandai and directed by Tomohiro Shibuya and Yui Tanimura.
To kick things off, the game doesn't suffer from a bad PC port like its predecessor did. Don't get me wrong, the original Dark Souls game is fantastic - but it required a mod fix for acceptable visuals (nobody likes playing blurry resolutions on PC). Additionally keyboard controls and mouse (KB+M) were horrorific and basically required a controller to play. But KB+M now works acceptably for those who don't have a controller or don't like playing with controllers.
- Now that we've got that out of the way, the gameplay is pretty much as you expect from a Dark Souls game. You cut, stab and smash hollows (someone who lost their souls and sanity) and creatures in Drangleic - a Kingdom that has fallen into despair and serves as the setting of the game. There's also magic and bows for those who want to fight from a distance. There's some newer stuff like hexes and whatnot that adds more choices on how to kill your enemies, but that's not overly important in this review.
While primarily a singleplayer game, your session of the game is always interconnected with other players through messages, summonings and invasions. People leave messages for other players to see in their own, whether or not they're helpful is another question though (e.g. "Beware of giant but hole"). Summons is basically playing cooperatively with either a NPC or real player while invasions is someone there actively trying to kill players in their world for whatever reason (yes I hate invaders).
Co-op play is made easier than in preceeding games, its much easier to play with a friend or two in this game than in past installments, it has definitely been given a bigger focus this game. While I felt little incentive to help people out in DS1, I find myself lending a hand to other players frequently in this game.
It is generally ill advised to play this game like an action one - you'll simply die as the game punishes you for not adhering to its rules. In the Souls game, you're usually very reactionary and passive. Its a "wait and see" game. While many games suffer from players just rushing in and not punishing you for your recklessness, Dark Souls 2 will dearly punish and reward you with death for not learning the patterns and movesets of enemies. Recognising when there's danger will save your life. Ignoring it will usually result in your downfall. Your actions must be deliberate, you cannot simply button mash your way through the game like in other games.
In the modern era where video games hold your hands and required little thought or effort to complete, Demon Souls was prasied for its unforgiving and challenging gameplay. The same is still held true in Dark Souls 2 and it is delightful to know this fact.
- There's nothing really noteworthy to praise about the visual fidelity of Dark Souls 2 - other than its not capped at 30 frames like the original game was and required a config fix to fix the resolution. The new dynamic lighting looks great, caverns and interiors look superb with a torch in hand. There are a few interesting environments in DS2 but they never feel connected into an expansive world like its predecessor. Those who have went from Earthen Peak to Iron Keep will understand what I mean by this.
- Honestly not much to say on this one, the Souls game has never been about story. Its mostly the lore that you read from item descriptions, which has unfortunately been made more shallow in this installment.
- I have a number of complaints about the design choices in Dark Souls 2 that has negatively affected the overall experience - which resonate more strongly with DS1 veterans than newcomers of the franchise. For newcomers most of this does not apply to you.
While in Demon Souls there was the hub world and in Dark Souls they ditched that for an open interconnected world, DS2 manages to create a hybrid between the two. What we ended up was a rather disappointing treatment of the open world designs. The world felt more linear and many "bonfires" felt more like checkpoints than a smaller hub from where you travel from. As you can teleport to these bonfires whenever, they feel much more arbitrary than usual. I pretty much breathe a sigh of relief when I see a bonfire in DS1. In this game not so much.
The addition of the dynamic lighting is appreciated but it also came at a price. Because of this dynamic lighting many levels felt flat without a torch - lacking light and shadow. Players like myself find that there is usually little need to carry a torch around, because you're forced to give up one of your hand for the torch and most of the levels aren't dark enough to warrant carrying a torch. As silly as the self-illuminating lighting around the character was, the darker environments with baked lights/shadows in past games were more atmospheric and it often felt like interiors were claustrophobic.
Enemy design are poorly done. Too often you would be facing opponents that showed little weakness were relentless in their attacks, giving little room for opportunities to attack. You wouldn't be able to stagger them no matter how hard you try. I find myself poking at the enemy trying to whittle them down in fear of retaliation, taking a chunk of my health off. This made melee builds extremely difficult and sometimes unforgiving.
Random other complains include: weapons break way too easily for whatever reason (think its related to frame rate), poor tracking, bad hitboxes, forgettable boss designs, lacking an open world, etc.
- Dark Souls 2 is plagued with poor and questionable design choices. Despite this negative and lacking DS1's intricate open world levels that felt expansive and were interconnected - DS2 is still a great game that fixes the technical hurdles that came from DS1's PC port. It is the easiest Souls game to jump into for newcomers and veterans alike with welcomed quality of life improvements. If you're looking for a challenging game to play that rewards patience and perseverance, this game is definitely for you.

TL;DR: Hands down, the "Battlefield" game that I have always been looking for
This game has similar gameplay as the originial EA/DICE's Battlefield series before it became an online-only multiplayer.
Really nice and fun Single-Player gameplay and wide variety of gameplay styles.
Pros:
- Genuine FPS gameplay with wide varieties of customization
- Basic vehicles are already there (ground, air, and water)
- No apparent bugs/glitch at the moment
- Lightweight; even a potato rig could run this quite well.
- Bright and colorful graphics (even the blood color is PG-13)
Cons:
- None so far
Feature requests (as of September 2017):
- LAN Multiplayer (Online multiplayer with dedicated server might be nice, but LAN party is life)
- More varieties of vehicles and equipment (perhaps controllable aircraft carrier)
- More customizable key bindings (i.e. separate firing keys for weapons on ground/air/water vehicles)
- Switch seat in a vehicle
- 3rd person view in a vehicle
- Flashlight for characters and headlight for vehicles
- Battlefield support, e.g. artillery, support package drop, or paradrop
- Allow aircrafts to land (perhaps a button to toggle landing gear)
I'd say Ravenfield already qualify as a full game for its price point.

A severely underrated game. Pros involved an interesting plot, fascinating translation of setting (compared to the original material), nuanced characters and very, VERY good performance acting (voice and motion included). The combat is repetitive, but I found it to be acceptable. My one complaint about the game would be that the world and action is far too often interrupted by small unskippable cutscenes to further the puzzle/platforming in the areas. Normal, pre-rendered or plot-based cutscenes were fine, but continually halting my gameplay just to show me where an obvious switch was or the path I needed to take to progress was got to be a bit disappointing when I was trying to enjoy the game and immerse myself.
That small negative aside, the game truly is a hidden gem. It's soulful, has a lot of heart, and will grab you within the first 10min of gameplay (if it doesn't, then maybe it isn't the game for you). Purchased this with zero expectations since I had never heard of it and was absolutely blown away by the quality of writing, production, and entertainment. While there has been multiple confirmations that there is likely to be no sequel, I strongly hope that the cult following the game has garnered might help revive the effort. Your purchase of this product will help show (hopefully) that this critically acclaimed (but commercially unsuccessful) game has not gone unnoticed, and definitely not unloved.

A solid game...that's also very lazy.
The characters are very likable and the story is decent. In fact, it's what kept me playing even when the rest started to become a little tedious. The post-apocalyptic setting is well done with some nice locales mixed in.
Unfortunately, those were the only outstanding aspects to me. The rest was just mediocre. The combat, while moderately challenging on hard, is very barebones. It has a very basic moveset that doesn't get expanded upon very much. That means that you're stuck with the same 3 attacks (light, heavy, aoe) for the most part. It could've used a more fleshed out skill progression system where you actually unlock new stuff to do. What makes the combat worse is the lack of enemy variety. There are 4 enemy types that get thrown at you and that's pretty much it. The 2 bosses that get recycled over and over again throughout the game don't help much either. It's not like there wasn't enough room to be creative, since the enemy are supposed to be mechs of all kinds and sizes.
The "platforming", while cool to look at, didn't contribute much to the gameplay. It's basically climbing and parkour stuff along a very streamlined path with 0 danger of failure. I didn't mind this very much, but it could definitely have been more.
I still recommend this since I enjoyed the overall experience, but only at a discount (picked it up for 5€).

I recently got this game on a sale and was excited to play it, I had didn't have a lot of awareness about the previous issues and decided to give it a go since the Total War games I had purchased in the past were good (I have M2TW and Empire TW). For some reason the game auto-detect or my Nvidia Geforce Experience program set the graphics fairly low despite my having a decent computer (8GB Ram, GTX 760). Now I have played it enough to get an understanding of the game:
Pros: Objects in battles are an interesting way to add complexity to it, you can add things like sharp stones to slow enemies or rolling balls of fire to destroy enemies on a downward slope. As well as Catapults you can place on your walls (in some castles) to respond to the catapults of the enemies.
The battles are large and troop response time is fast
There are many playable factions.
The AI seems to have been improved over previous games I have had experience with. But in large battles (seiges) the AI will send half their force and leave the other half in their starting positions for the rest of the match (this happened in a 20 - 40 Minute game)
The building screen on the campaign map has been cleaned up a bit but does take a little learning to get the hang of.
Cons: Low performance at times, I eventually raised the graphics to about max and didn't see a big change in performance from the reccomended settings, the FPS however was still a little on the low side.
Even on the highest settings it is difficult to see what is happening at times, it is a big mess depending on what factions are fighting which. In M2TW it is clear who are your troops and who are the enemies and in slow parts of hte battle you can see them fight each other which is very cool. But I had little ability to do so in ROME II
The strategic view has little purpose besides getting your bearing at the beginning of the battle as you can't zoom in a lot or see enough detail to get a good idea of what is going on.
The in battle troop menu is overly large and the troop unit images themselves (they are almost like a silhouette) make it harder to tell what troops they are compared to an actual image of one of the soldiers.
I may have missed some things but overall the game is not as good as past Total War games in my oppinion. My personal favorite has to be M2TW (Amazing game, not perfect but absolutely great). Hopefully they will take the good aspects of Rome II and fix what is wrong)
If you like Total War games and are interested in this one I would suggest getting it on a sale.

I like farming games. I like games like Animal Crossing. I like cute things. I like slimes. I like you, too.
I did not like Slime Rancher.
If you've played an idle clicker before then the gameplay of Slime Rancher will feel familiar: you start out at the lowest tier of slime with a goal to catch, feed, and sell off their products to make money. The more money you make, the more ways you have to automate manual actions and streamline inefficiencies. This in turn allows you to catch rarer or more valuable slimes which is the entire game loop.
It's a good model that has resulted in a lot of good games. Unfortunately, Slime Rancher misses the biggest point of these games: progression has to feel good! It has to feel worth it. You need a constant stream of interesting or meaningful upgrades. You need gamechangers. You need ways to feel like a slime god.
This game has none of those things.
Here's a small example illustrating my frustration: early only you'll catch a slime that has a meat-only diet. You'll feed them a chicken and think wow, this is a pretty neat mechanic!
As you progress you'll find another chicken type, though it's just a palette swap. There are two more just like it.
You'll also find other meat eaters but they are, without exception, identical in terms of how that mechanic works
And that's it. Those are all the meat options in the entire game: 4 varities of chickens, all nearly identical in apperance, all identical in behavior and how they're raised. Your meat eaters will eat them all. It never plays with the formula. It's boring. It's not fun!
I was surprised to find that Slime Rancher isn't in Early Access, as that's exactly the vibe you get from the game. The experience feels unfinished, like it's a prototype waiting for more content.
It's certainly not worth $20.

Picked this up long ago, decided to reload it through smite to get cards for achievements. As such, I've gotten to know Smite pretty well. The game appears decptively easy, and by all rights, should be. However, because of how intensely focused the game tends to be on team fights, you'll want to quickly learn your role and what your gods will offer to your team. In terms of accessibility and tutorials, Smite does a fairly good job of introducing players to the game, with auto item buying and auto skill leveling that can easily be turned off at any time the player feels confident in their ability to make better decisions. The user interface is simple enough with a nice coat of polish, giving you accurate and helpful information, without being in your face too much and overloading you.
Smite pays homage to now 8 pantheons, I believe drawing gods and heros from Chinese, Hindu, Mayan, Greek, Roman, Norse, Egyptian, and Japanese gods, although Japanese only started several months ago, and so only has a small number as of yet. HIrez does a good job of making each god feel true to it's roots, while still giving them very responsive and satisfying kits of abilities. There are some less balanced aspects of the game, but many of these have counters that you should learn to pick or call for help from someone on your team for a gank.
Smite also trades the traditional top down view for a more personal third person view, giving you a more 'realistic' view from behind, with all the advantages and disadvantages that comes with. Refering back to the player based team fights is both Smite's most satisfying and frustrating gameplay aspects. Sometimes, as anyone in player vs player combat based games can tell you, your team can be as organized as a private military, or as disorganized and hopeless as a one legged man at an♥♥♥♥♥kicking competition. You will run into morons, elitists, and newbies who blame the team instead of their own inneptitude. However, you will also find that you can join clans in game, and join up with other players who you can friend and chat with, forming much more organized groups with much more skilled members.
In the end, you can't remove the human element, as it is Smite's greatest and weakest component, nor would we want them to. Clashing against other people in the Arena, a fun mode smite has tossed together, is fast paced, engaging, and truly fun, assuming you aren't getting completely thrashed by a bad team comp.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT - Don't buy Alien: Isolation until you've seen (and
) the original movie, "Alien," by Ridley Scott*.  Why is that so important?  I'll explain.
Alien: Isolation is first and foremost a collection of beautiful set pieces.  The game is a scenic tour of those sets, frequently and frustratingly interrupted by the alien (or "Stompy" as another reviewer appropriately names it).  The environments of the Torrens and Sevastopol station are wonderfully-crafted homage to the late '70s science fiction stylings realized in the movie.  They're spot-on, immersive, engaging, and easily my favorite aspect of the game.
But when you aren't taking in the atmosphere, what are you doing (i.e. what makes A:I a GAME)?  Sadly, it's all standard "go here and press this button or operate X device to restore power or open a door or some similar nonsense."  Mercifully, there's a good map, and viewing it pauses the game.  More often than not, you're sneaking, scavenging parts, and generally trying to avoid any kind of NPC contact/combat.  Amanda Ripley is an engineer, and always outclassed in a toe-to-toe fight.  Walking in, guns blazing, will quickly send you back to the Load Save screen.  This isn't to say you won't get the chance to heat up your arsenal, but doing so always comes with a cost, whether through the depletion of your scant resources, drawing the attention of the alien, or both.  The word of the day is "QUIETLY."  Unfortunately, despite your best attempts at stealth, you'll frequently see the Load Save screen anyway.  Alien: Isolation is HARD.
We should discuss the game's namesake, the alien.  Any old-schoolers that played Resident Evil 3 will be quickly reminded of Nemesis, the indestructible ammo sink that periodically turned the game into a total chore.  You can't kill it, and for a large part of the game can't even dissuade it.  Amanda is far more proficient at arranging distractions, but since those only buy you 15-20 seconds, they rarely feel worth the effort.  The AI is ruthless, and the alien's long stride means it can walk faster than you can run, which you should almost never do anyway.  Its appearances and search patterns are random, so there's no learning when it's safe to move.  It's NEVER safe.  You just have to be bold and hope that this time it turns left instead of right.  It's definitely effective at creating tension, but eventually all that evasion becomes tedious.  Credit where it's due: the alien looks REALLY GOOD, though, and its movements are top-notch.
OK, this is admittedly a lot of complaining for a "recommended" review.  So what else is there to love about A:I?  Working Joes.  These budget synthetics are brilliant offenders of the
principle.  They're creepy, deadly, and the most profanity-inducing part of the game you'll love to hate and hate to love.
And that's it, really.  That's a pretty complete description of what you'll experience in Alien: Isolation.  As a game, it's too often frustrating, has obscene difficulty spikes, and employs some of the most tired and cliche mechanics.  It's honestly not a BAD game, just unexceptional
.  And that should tell you just how incredible it is as an environmental experience.  The mood and atmosphere alone are more than good enough to carry the parts of the title that are lacking.  I could almost smell the humid, stuffy air, and feel the rubbery skin of the Working Joe as it choked me to death.  Any game that can craft its sights and sounds so expertly that it begins to engage my other senses as well... that game deserves my money.
If you're a fan of the movie that inspired it, you won't regret the investment.

It's really great to play this game again, especially because of the lack of good RTS games these days. At the price it is, it's really a steal as you get 4 games included (the original games and the remastered games). I still maintain that this is one of the greatest games ever made.
However I do have a few of gripes.
There are a few bugs and a few instabilities. The game crashes at the moment in multiplayer, which is seriously dodgy and shoddily made anyway. Sure it does say beta - but you'd expect glaring bugs like crashing when you connect to a game and not being able to connect to people's games, even through steam, who are in different regions than you, (unless you change your download location in Steam, but why should you have to?) to be fixed before release, or at the very least shortly after (been 3 days now without a single patch).
Another thing is that this game has been "remastered". That's great and some things have been greatly improved. BUT it still looks really old. The skins and effects have been updated, aswell as some of the sounds, mostly for the better but sometimes for the worse. Example: interceptor/scout guns used to sound great in the original; kind of like machineguns, while in the remake they LITERALLY go "pew pew pew".
Also when a game is remastered, you'd expect them to at least update the AI a bit. The battlecruisers in HW2 are STILL majorly bugged in that they simply cannot fly forward without a major headache, usually spinning around and around, very very slowly, reminding me of when I used to play homeworld 2 back in the day and never used BCs for this very reason. Ships also fly out of formation and kamikaze with harmful asteroids in a certain mission in the first game.
My biggest gripe is that the Taiidan and colour options are missing from the Homeworld campaign. In the original, you could pick from two different fleet styles and colour them however you wanted. Now you are basically shoved into the game with none of those options, really proving some of us purists right when we were worried about gameplay being changed.
In multiplayer they have merged the fleet styles from both the first and second game. I need to play some more but I can't help thinking that they are highly incompatible.
Don't get me wrong this is a great game and still well worth your cash. I will summarise thusly:
Homeworld Remastered is a great game but the remastered part is very misleading. Some key gameplay options have been changed, others removed completely. The skins and effects have been upgraded but the models themselves look old and blocky still. The AI has NOT been remastered at all, not even a little bit, and the whole thing just feels... lazy. Still an amazing deal but only because it's riding on the success of the original masterpiece from Relic. Definately worth it, but it could have been even better with a little more effort in the right places.
Postscript: Please get rid of that horrible bloody hyperspace icon that obnoxiously pastes itself on the screen at the end of a mission.

Before I get started on this I want to say, that i played both this and Dark Souls 1 for easyly well over 200 hours each and by heart, and i managed to beat the content up to NG++. So I hope I know what I'm talking about.
The first thing you need to know is, that this game wasn't made by the same producer who did Dark Souls 1. And it shows. Heavily so. If I knew that before, I would not have bought it.
Dark Souls II gets an unreal and undeserved amount of praise I can neither grasp nor understand. I can hardly recommend it to anyone, especially if you have never played one of these games before.
It's incredibly hard. And not in a good way. This whole game is an uninspired on-rails corridor third person FPS with melee weapons. The story is boring and makes no sense, is practically a direct copy from Dark Souls 1 and nothing more but a bad excuse for this game to exist. It has a disgusting amount of fan pandering and references to the last game, which have no right to exist. The Overall game feels like it was designed by fans rather than qualified personel.
The combat system did not receive any improvement whatsoever. Often i found myself battling the controls and especially the uncomfortable camera more than any enemy, which resulted in many unreasonable deaths.
The world itself feels nonorganic. Its like you are waddling through a theme park. The areas are short and feel malconnected to each other and have all way too many bonfires. There are Checkpoints almost around each corner. Graphicwise this game only received minor improvements and the music is a mayor letdown from Dark Souls 1.
The enemies in this game are a complete joke. Not only do they all almost fight the same way (large humanoid Knight-type enemies with big weapons), they also often come in packs. Either they smash you to paste if you don't single them out or you gotta run untill they reset where you can cheese them out with ranged attacks. That enemies despawn after a certain number off kills is just unacceptable.
The boss battles are uninspired and unfair and only rely on the formula: The more stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥we throw at you the better it gets. You are either facepalming because the boss battles are too easy or so ridicoulous hard and unenjoyable that its no fun to replay them. But you are expected to do so. I found myself getting tired of this neverending onslaught way over I reached the castle of the king of the game, but no, the game wants you to soldier on through 5 more levels. Why? There's no reason to stretch the game out like an old chewing gum.
Most of the weapons in this game are either ugly or no fun to use. Not to mention the multiplayer system is both in cooperative and PVP boring, timeconsuming and unsatisfying. The way players connect with this new Soul Memory makes absolutely no sense and makes nobody happy. Aside from that in the end game everybody runs around in the same cookie-cutter overpowered shitgear. You are better off playing alone.
But the worst, and i mean absolute worst gamebreaking mechanic that was reintroduced in this game is the healing system. You no longer rely on Estrus Flasks as main heal resource, but on a collection of healing crystals, that heal more slowly, but are avaiable in infinite amounts. The tense and stategic moments of planned healing is gone for good. This crystal ♥♥♥♥♥pam broke the games design and everything that could have been redeemable for this title.
The cherry on top of this whole mess is the fact that they charge for three parts of DLC at 10 Euros each. Greed knows no bounds here. Im not gonna buy this and neither should you. Speak with your wallet.
If you have even read so far to this point i'd like to thank you for your time. Even if you bought this game and don't agree with me.
All I can say is, that this game was all but a big disappointment. And I hope the producer from Dark Souls 1 will return one day to make a new game and make me forget this farce.

I've been getting a lot of comments so I've decided to write a quick FAQ of them:
1) This plan is good because modders can make money - You are completely correct that modders should have a right to make money but a better way to do this would be to have built-in donate buttons on the workshop and on
. There is absolutely no reason Bethesda needs to take a slice of the profits for someone elses original work.

3) It wont effect the games with mods already - So they say. They also have a big section in the games EULA that mods can only be free. Regardless of whether or not the older games are directly influenced, you've got to look fowards.

mods.

Cons

-Source Engine game, meaning the graphics are definitely aged.

Overall, I think this mod is very underrated for what it is, and if there's gonna be a NMRIH2 for the Source 2 Engine, I can't help but think it'll be amazing.

When your in your mid 20's and you feel like you've played every MMO the internet has the offer, everything kind of feels stale.. at some points you don't even play the damn game, you just download it for 5 hours, skim through the character creation, a quest or two and never log in again. I can guarantee anyone who has played WoW as a kid can remember the feeling of awe and feeling of adventure when you first logged in.. The sense of community, the sense of being in ANOTHER world, immersiveness, etc. Of course overtime as new games come out and new expectations are made - you look back at a game like WoW now and that sense of adventure is almost non existant.
(Not a WoW bash, I used to love the game religiously)
BUT NOW WE HAVE ESO! BOYS N GIRLS LEMME TELL YA, THIS♥♥♥♥♥♥IS AMAZING!
GAMEPLAY/INTERFACE 8.5/10
The one thing I hated about MMO's, was once you reached max level - you had a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of macros to set up and a whole lot of spells/abilities to cater for. With ESO, even though it has been simplified in a way that you won't get confused - all passive & active abilities can be tuned to how you want to play. The character customization can let you build a Battlemage Warrior to a Tanked out Rogue. (Think classes from Oblivion, that's what they've done here, and WELL!)
All combinations of abilities, class, weapon and armor type can all be tailored to how you play, but still be viable in a dungeon group or a game of PvP. The smoothness transition in combat is one to die for in MMO's these days, you'll just have fun killing mobs like you would in a game of Skyrim, having a very similar hack and slack style mechanic.
The game's interface is fluid and well taken care of, also comparable to the menu settings in Skyrim.
The following class types are: Dragonknight, Templar, Nightblade & Sorcerer
Weapon types: 1h, 2h, 1h + Shield, Dual Wield, Bow, Destruction Staff & Restoration Staff
Followed by all of your favourite playable races!
Now everything from your race, class, weapon type and even crafting proficiency will provide your character with different stats, abilities & way of playing, so have fun! Don't settle down for your first character, give em all a shot and see what fits you!
Walking around with my increased stealth stats lets me wander around city to city, scavenging through boxes and chests undetected (Yes, they have the pick lock systems just like the other games) to get cooking supplies, which I then make into high level foods and drinks which sell for high on the AH. Steal your ingredients, make more money!
Or just even be a full time thief and take it back to the Thieves guild fence for a bit of coin..
The sense of immersion I get from this game, it can sometimes feel like a singleplayer rpg. Communicating with NPC's and ACTUALLY listening to the quest storyline is actually.. fun.. which is something that's usually skipped over in most MMO's. The immense amount of lore and nostalgic references from the old games leaves plenty to the imagination, especially if you're the roleplay type.
The auction trading service is amazing - It all starts with guilds out bidding each other on NPC vendors who control spots in various places to sell their guild items to the public. If you and your guild scrap up enough gold, you can outbuy other guild traders and take their spots, enabling your guild to auction of items, lots of fun!
AUDIO 7/10
The only reason I didn't give this a higher score is because some of the music is straight out of Skyrim, but other then that - the actual music they have created for the game and the general audio of the game is beautiful. No complaints
VIDEO 8.5/10
Visually stunning, breath-taking and probably the most graphically immersive MMORPG on the market, in my honest opinion. If you have a decent computer that can run this at high settings, half the time you'll probably just stand around looking at sh*t coz how pretty it is.
COMMUNITY (VARIES, CURRENT SCORE 6.5/7 out of 10)
I've played this on PS4, PC and XBOX One.
The community on PS4 bloody brilliant, I participated in an all Orc roleplay guild who would run through cities screaming "FOR MALACATH!" on their mics. We all wore the same armor and ran through making a name for ourself. Because the only way to communicate on consoles was with a microphone, you could walk into a main city and just start talking with people like if you walked into a cafe in real life.. Not so much with the PC version, but the sense of immersion and community vibe is still there. It's a type of community I miss in MMO Games.
PVP 7/10
PVP is huge♥♥♥♥♥battlegrounds designed for big army warfare. Imagine playing a game of Age of Empires but instead of controlling the whole army, you just control your one dude. You could have 20 players attacking the south side of map taking over a castle, while another 20 or on the north side taking over a farm - and they're a good 30min walking distance from each other. THINK HUGE
There is also dueling implented as of recently, really nicely balanced!
PVE 8/10
No complaints, it feels like a singpleplayer game half the time and just feels awesome when you run into a bunch of players doing the same quest as you. Great dungeons, great loot, a good rewarding feeling after every quest.
Everything has been scaled recently, so now that old places you have outleveled months ago will be a challenge again, leaving low level places still worth adventuring for treasure.
CRAFTING  9/10
Oh man, crafting is my favoutite in this game, it feels rewarding as hell. Most of the best items created in the game is through crafting, there are unique designs from Daedric, Dwarven, Orcish, Argonian armor designs etc. It's straight forward and easy to grasp for even the most beginner player. No complaints
CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION 8/10
You're going to spend a lot of time before even logging in, just working on your dudes nose.. trust me.
You can customize your armor color (Colors unlock depending on ingame achievements)
Classes aren't bound to armor types, so go ahead and be a heavy armor rockin' mage if you like!

tldr: I did not read the user-defined tags and so misunderstood the fundamental aspect of this game. It is an exploration game that is essentially the boring parts of Pokemon mixed with the tedious parts of Stardew Valley.
From what I had heard about this game, and from the couple of videos I had watched on YouTube, I had assumed this was a farming/ranching/animal husbandry simulation game. I had assumed it was going to be vaguely similar to Stardew Valley, though I understood that there weren't crops; instead you would manage what were essentially livestock but in the form of types of slimes. Unfortunately, it quickly became clear that this is an exploration game; the actual slime ranching is wholly irrelevant. Sure, you CAN set up a ranch, for which the reward is ultimately money, but the only thing the money is actually good for is to upgrade your own gear so you can get to new unreachable places (e.g. jetpack). Actually setting up a ranch and ranching is just a means to theoretically earn money faster. Basically, the true game here is to explore the quite large map, and fill your encyclopedia with all of the different kinds of slimes you come across. Unfortunately, I am not the least bit interested in this type of game.
Ultimately, if you like that type of game, this game does seem well made, and there are lots of different slimes who each have unique looks and behaviors. If we were given a 5-star rating system I would have given it 3 stars, but instead Steam only allows us a Yes or No, and so I personally must choose to not recommend it, though I do not feel qualified to argue about whether or not it is a great or horrible representation of it's genre.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT - Don't buy Alien: Isolation until you've seen (and
) the original movie, "Alien," by Ridley Scott*.  Why is that so important?  I'll explain.
Alien: Isolation is first and foremost a collection of beautiful set pieces.  The game is a scenic tour of those sets, frequently and frustratingly interrupted by the alien (or "Stompy" as another reviewer appropriately names it).  The environments of the Torrens and Sevastopol station are wonderfully-crafted homage to the late '70s science fiction stylings realized in the movie.  They're spot-on, immersive, engaging, and easily my favorite aspect of the game.
But when you aren't taking in the atmosphere, what are you doing (i.e. what makes A:I a GAME)?  Sadly, it's all standard "go here and press this button or operate X device to restore power or open a door or some similar nonsense."  Mercifully, there's a good map, and viewing it pauses the game.  More often than not, you're sneaking, scavenging parts, and generally trying to avoid any kind of NPC contact/combat.  Amanda Ripley is an engineer, and always outclassed in a toe-to-toe fight.  Walking in, guns blazing, will quickly send you back to the Load Save screen.  This isn't to say you won't get the chance to heat up your arsenal, but doing so always comes with a cost, whether through the depletion of your scant resources, drawing the attention of the alien, or both.  The word of the day is "QUIETLY."  Unfortunately, despite your best attempts at stealth, you'll frequently see the Load Save screen anyway.  Alien: Isolation is HARD.
We should discuss the game's namesake, the alien.  Any old-schoolers that played Resident Evil 3 will be quickly reminded of Nemesis, the indestructible ammo sink that periodically turned the game into a total chore.  You can't kill it, and for a large part of the game can't even dissuade it.  Amanda is far more proficient at arranging distractions, but since those only buy you 15-20 seconds, they rarely feel worth the effort.  The AI is ruthless, and the alien's long stride means it can walk faster than you can run, which you should almost never do anyway.  Its appearances and search patterns are random, so there's no learning when it's safe to move.  It's NEVER safe.  You just have to be bold and hope that this time it turns left instead of right.  It's definitely effective at creating tension, but eventually all that evasion becomes tedious.  Credit where it's due: the alien looks REALLY GOOD, though, and its movements are top-notch.
OK, this is admittedly a lot of complaining for a "recommended" review.  So what else is there to love about A:I?  Working Joes.  These budget synthetics are brilliant offenders of the
principle.  They're creepy, deadly, and the most profanity-inducing part of the game you'll love to hate and hate to love.
And that's it, really.  That's a pretty complete description of what you'll experience in Alien: Isolation.  As a game, it's too often frustrating, has obscene difficulty spikes, and employs some of the most tired and cliche mechanics.  It's honestly not a BAD game, just unexceptional
.  And that should tell you just how incredible it is as an environmental experience.  The mood and atmosphere alone are more than good enough to carry the parts of the title that are lacking.  I could almost smell the humid, stuffy air, and feel the rubbery skin of the Working Joe as it choked me to death.  Any game that can craft its sights and sounds so expertly that it begins to engage my other senses as well... that game deserves my money.
If you're a fan of the movie that inspired it, you won't regret the investment.

Do you like games that lead you around on a short leash? Do you enjoy watching the game play itself in the most exciting moments? Do you enjoying getting slapped on the wrist when you aren't doing what the game wants you to do? Do you enjoy the same basic corridor shooting, poorly motivated character choices and good-looking but ultimately hollow and wasted graphics? Then this is the game for you!
CoD: AW has turned the "LOOK SHINY GOOD" dial up to about 9 but all that graphical polish sits atop an ultimately shallow, boring and barely interactive 'game' which defies all logic (but not expectations) by doing absolutely nothing new. While pretty, it still suffers some serious optimisation issues that have alienated a lot of users. By all reports this game is still running on a highly modified Quake 3 engine, which doesn't compare to the last few Battlefield games and their far superior Frostbyte engine. This has led to a lot of performance problems across the board. The game still struggles with my R9 390 for some reason. Why can I run BF3/BF4 on Ultra but I struggle on high with this? 8gb of video memory isn't enough for you CoD, you greedy beast? I have to assume at least 3/4 of the required graphical power of this is dedicated to rendering Kevin Spacey's eerily accurate face (minus his dead, lifeless ghouls eyes, which they seem to have forgot to animate most of the time).
You can definitely see that they spent a lot of the time, energy and money on making this game look 'next gen'. There are some truly beautiful environments and an astounding amount of props and items that some poor team of technical artists must've churned out. I can only imagine them hunched over their desktops, desperately missing their families and sobbing as they create Future Shelf #42. To be fair Future Shelf #42 is my second favourite prop, behind Future-Circle-Lamp-Which-Looks-Like-A-Tron-Disc. That was cool and I would like one for real.
The rest of the design team seems to have missed the part about making a good game to go with it however, which is dissapointing given some fairly interesting narrative and gameplay elements seen in CoD: Black Ops II (it was the exact same shooty-bang-bang stuff though). There's some interesting narrative choices that COULD'VE been made in this game, but instead it's the same railroaded "Oh no traitor who knew yes we're the good guys now" story we've seen in, oh I dunno, every CoD game to date?
The gameplay itself will be frustratingly familiar to anyone who has played a CoD game, or more accurately, any FPS since the mid 2000s. So many times playing this  game I shouted out loud "Oh come ON!" out of anger and incredulity that a game can be so narrow. Go too far from where the game wants to you stay? Die and restart. Actually go where the game wants you to go, but do something different? Die and restart. Wait too long to do something? Die and restart. Don't wait long enough? Die and restart. I tried to flank some bad guys in a mission and was told I had gone "Too far from the Mission Area". The Mission Area was literally the difference between one side of Small Future Car #3 and the other. Circle around it to take cover and you fail. This is unacceptable in this day and age, and every designer on this team should know better.
As I said, along with the $300 million in advertising (citation needed) Kevin Spacey is in there, front and centre, essentially playing Frank Underwood from House of Cards. This is no bad thing, but I can't help but think he has better things to do with his time. Troy Baker is in here too, because he is in everything now, but does an admirable job as "Grunt with a Tragic Backstory #8". Spoiler alert, someone close to him dies in a really stupid way that could've been avoided pretty easily if the world and it's technology was in any way coherent or logical. You will notice this is the main theme of the games story. "Why are we running down stairs when we have jetpacks?" "Why am I shooting these guys instead of using drones?" "Why does my grapple hook only work on some ledges?" "Why can I get hit by a car and be fine, but a single punch to the face by an enemy solider kills me?" "Why aren't I in a tank all of the godamn time?", and most frequently: "Who cares?"
The multiplayer evaporated not long after release. There's still a handful (a literal handful mind you, 5-6 people at most) still playing but it is otherwise very, very dead. I can only assume that means we'll see a lot of ideas recycled to the next BLOPS game as a result. Why do new things if the no one saw the old things you did?
Overall a 10/10 for the technical artists on this, everything looks super, but 4/10 for the rest of it is as is mostly an awful, hollow excuse for a game. I'm an idiot and I will finish it, but I am not enjoying it.
Maybe put a game in there as well as all the pretty stuff next time guys?

This software has the potential to become The Holy Grail of Character Design. Currently, it hasn't reached that point yet, but it is well on its way. In the past, there has been a lot of uncertainty about the future of this software. However, now that it is owned by Adobe, you can be sure that it has a future ahead of it. . . . .unless Adobe drops the project, but they wont. The idea is just too good to pass up, and it says on the Mixamo website that adobe is planning on releasing the software on the creative cloud. It just seems like they are supporting it pretty well.
Pros:
- EXTREMELY fast (takes 5 minutes to make a character)
- EXTREMELY simple (I just ran the program and made a character without any prior knowledge on how to use the software. I have used Blender 3D for hundreds of hours now, and Fuse is 100 times more simple to use)
- Characters have a good amount of detail to them. Not amazing, but good.
Cons:
- This is one HUGE drawback. The software works by using presets. Overall, they all look the same, there aren't enough of them, and you, very likely, won't be able to create the same look that you wanted from your character. The software is only meant for making stock characters and then editing them in 3D software.The software seems to only cater to characters based in the 21st century. The clothing, for example. There are a lot of different choices for army camo, jeans, short dresses, etc. You might be able to find 2-3 pieces of clothing for futuristic times or 3-4 pieces for midevil times. It's almost like this software is designed as a dream come true for Activision for making a bunch of generic Call of Duty characters to be shot at.
- Some models and textures are lacking in polish.
Overall, the cons are forgiveable because of how ambitious this project is. If Fuse is perfected by Adobe, I would be willing to for over A LOT of money to use it. However, at this point, I don't think that it delivers enough quality and variety to work by itself. You need to learn another 3D software program to use along with this. You might even forget about this software if you want your character to have more of an artistic look.
It's free, though. Go ahead and try it. Maybe in a year or two, it will be a 3D Character Designer's Heaven.

I find it rather depressing that I find the complete version of this game and the eventual remasters of Blue Shift and Opposing Force to be more appealing than any other AAA title being released this year or the next with the exception of something like Metro: Exodus.  But I digress: this game is an absolute masterpiece in terms of visuals and just how much it builds upon the original.  Valve, please let these guys make HL3... or HL4 if you're feeling so sensitive about the number three.  Also, just to inform the reader, I'll be reviewing the singleplayer only.  I haven't really touched the multiplayer all that much.
Pros:
-A glamorous revision of the original Half-Life.  Areas are bigger with updated textures and a side of a few additional rooms that weren't there prior.  I'm sure you'd find some issues with the textures if you looked closely enough, but I don't believe you'll care enough to stop and look unless you're trying to read the post-it notes and writing on the whiteboards.
-Well voice acted.  In addition to finding VAs who sound like the original characters like Kleiner, Barney, and Eli (to a lesser extent), the writting does surpass the original in some places. (E.g, "Though if it's one thing I know for sure is that this guy's been killing marines." instead of "Though if it's one thing I know for sure is that he's been killing my buddies.") Finally, the quality is slightly above HL2 quality where it actually sounds like there's some life and emotion to it.
-While somewhat used sparsely, the soundtrack is well conducted.  Once again, only expect it during major setpieces and for it to barely resemble the original soundtrack with the exceptions of Nuclear Mission Jam, the intro theme, and a few others.
-The suit functions are faithful to their depiction in Half-Life, meaning the flash light and sprint aren't tied to the same power source.
-Weapons are as they were with new sounds and idle animations.  While the crossbow and revolver have full-on iron sights now, there's always the option to turn that off.
-The combat is definitely not for the casual audience.  If you want to reach the end, you better pay attention and learn to play.  Basically, if you somehow found HL2 difficult, you'll go back to HL2 and find it a cakewalk.
-The usual nooks and crannies with goodies to keep you supplied and going.
-Use of the Steam community workshop.  Yes, it's rather trivial, but it's fun to mess around with the game like that.

Black Mesa is a fan-made remake of the original Half-Life game. You actually start off with your train leaving a station this time. It seems to be a little longer than in the original game, a little too long, in my opinion. But this time around, the guards and scientists have a lot more models, including… GASP… women!
So quite early in the game, I have already suffered from the wrath of loading screens. They take, like, a minute or longer to load everything. That's what I get for having a crappy laptop. It did get a lot better after the first hour of the game, though.
They’ve added a lot more dialogue for the characters. They actually have, like, real conversations with each other, instead of the nonsensical chatter from the original game. Okay, some of the nonsensical chatter is in here, but only if you have two guys following you.
And of course, among the scientists, you meet with your buddies, Isaac Kleiner and Eli Vance. The two scientists look a lot younger than they do in Half-Life 2. I remember hearing that the events of Half-Life 2 took place 20 after the events of the first game. I don’t know how accurate that is, because I think I only heard it from a mere fan of the franchise, because I haven’t seen anything else confirming it. I actually don’t remember if it was mentioned in the other games. We’ll have to wait until I get to them.
I thought at first that they got the same voice actors from the previous games in here, but it turns out they didn’t. In fact, the voice actors in this game have barely acted in anything else at all, let alone another Half-Life game. I genuinely believed that the original voice actors were in here--except for Eli, because his voice actor is no longer with us. But the voice impressions are pretty spot on.
You don’t get your crowbar in the same spot as the original game, which kinda surprised me. But I’ll be honest, I think it made the game better, especially when you don’t have any other weapon with you. It left me feeling more on edge, being so vulnerable to attacks. But it also filled me with genuine excitement when I actually did find it.
So your first means of defense turns out to be a security guard. Now, the AI of the guards is definitely better than in the original game, but apparently they still haven’t figured out how to step away from danger. And they really love to charge into battle when it’s generally a good idea to NOT.
When you reach the main lobby area, he leaves you alone and tries to call for help. So you are on your own... again… with no weapons… until you get the crowbar, that is.
The graphics are so much better than in Half-Life. Well, duh. They released this game in 2015. That’s like, seventeen years later. They put so much more detail into the objects and environments. Instead of just flat textures on panels and computers, you can actually see the knobs and buttons. And the characters actually look like people.
I love the level design in this game. Every single level is designed differently, or at least has more added to it. When I played this game, it felt like an entirely new experience… except for some areas that are pretty much the same. And some levels are more realistically designed, like some small empty rooms that exist for no reason now being slightly bigger and containing desks and stuff. Some rooms or hallways need to be accessed from a different route than the original. Sometimes you need to go through a vent, and other times you need to solve some sort of puzzle to get through an area. I honestly can’t get enough of these levels.
There are a lot more enemies in this game than there originally were. I guess it’s more realistic to have more soldiers together in one area, but man, the difficulty has gone up. Sometimes it’s batsh** crazy. But I still managed to best them, because I’m Gordon Freeman.
The weapons are slightly different in this game. They’ve completely removed the auto aim, so you have to rely more on yourself to not suck at aiming like I do. And the assault rifle or submachine gun, I’m not sure what it is, can only carry a maximum of three grenades. THREE! In Half-Life, it can hold ten. What are you trying to do, make this less fun? What I also hate is that this particular weapon shares the same ammo as the glock. However much ammo you reload into your pistol is exactly how much less you’ll be able to use for the other gun. Why did they do that? It seems kinda dumb.
The game ends just after you enter the portal that takes you to Xen. Well that kinda sucks. Oh well, I loved this game so far, I’m sure I’ll love Xen just as much.
Now for the ultimate question: Is Black Mesa better than Half-Life? Well, I think it is. Yeah, Half-Life is a classic shooter, and I love it to death, but there are things in this game that I think are improvements compared to the original. Now, I’m not saying that I would choose this game over Half-Life. If I were to suggest a good shooter game, I’d probably point more to the original, because, well, it’s the original. But this game just looks better with it’s better graphics and level design. Feel free to disagree with me, but that’s just how I feel about it.

***Original review below*** (still applicable to those without a controller):
The beginning of this game is captivating and it definitely has the beginnings of a great story, but as a PC port I find the menu and control system intolerable.  I have spent more time editing the .ini files than playing the game (which isn't much time, really) and am now giving up trying to make it functional.  At one point I was asked to press and hold a button which does not work (middle mouse button); went to change the binding in the options menu so that I could comply and discovered that bindings cannot be changed during gameplay, only from the main menu.  This prompted the loss of about fifteen minutes of gameplay which is unfortunate, but fine if it means I can have a good gameplay experience.  It happens.  While out of the game, I also took the opportunity to try to fix some of the more aggravating gameplay issues such as the inability to change the mouse sensitivity in-game (which is set exceptionally low), the abhorrent camera angles and camera controls and the observation that changing the graphics settings in-game has no effect on the graphics.   After an hour of messing around in the initialization files and succeeding only in changing the graphics settings and neither the camera controls or mouse sensitivity, I gave up.
To think that a modern game requires the editing of initialization files to effect changes that appear in the menu system but do not function is really mind-blowing.
This game looks fantastic, and the story looks great, but I have little tolerance for fighting the controls more than I'm fighting the enemies around me.
***End original review***

Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a nice game, and it is worth getting if you can get it, and its DLC, on sale.
Enslaved is a above average game, it isn't going to change your views on action adventure, or make you obsess with the source material (it is a reimaging of Journey to the West). But it is a fun experience that is easy to get into.  The main thing holding this title back is that for everything that it does right, it also kind of does it wrong.
Starting off the story for the game is a mix bag. On the positive side you have fun characters that play off each other fairly well. They have playful banter and the audio for them is good. On the negative the overall story is thin and never really explored. At best you'll have a vague idea of what is going on, why you are doing something, or what the point is. Which is a shame, since it seems like the story might have been interesting if they had bother to explain it.
Next the combat for the game is enjoyable, but very simple. You have two attack buttons and two ammo types for your staff gun thingy. And after the 3rd or 4th level, you pretty much know everything that you need to know about combat in the game. That isn't to imply that there aren't specialty moves like countering, but for 95% of the encounters in the game, you can get through them with a minimal amount of effort.
The game's environments looks nice, but most levels feel too long, like the developers were trying to increase the game's length without factoring in what they would do to it quality.  This is a common problem that a lot of games have, since pacing is hard to do.  What makes this noticeable worst is the lack of challenge on most levels. With a simple combat system, and a very simple platforming system (you push jump to pretty much do everything, and there only one correct path, so can just mindlessly push jump towards the next platform most of the time) eventually enemies and puzzles become annoyances that just slow you down.
In the end, if it was only the main game, I wouldn't recommend this title to others. But what pushes it up, is one of the original DLC pieces, Pigsy's Perfect 10, which comes standard in the steam version, so I am factoring it into the review (since it is now part of the base experience).  This DLC is several hours long and focuses on the side character Pigsy. It has different gameplay (3rd person shooter), an unique story (takes place during the main game events, but before the main cast meets Pigsy), and a different overall theme from the main game (Friendship, loneness, and lost). And while the last level in it goes on for way too long, I would argue that overall it is better than the main game, and makes the ending to the main game more significant and meaningful.
Enslaved: Odyssey to the West is a nice game that does some things right and some things wrong. I wouldn't say it a must play title, but if you can pick it up on sale for cheap, then you should. The overall experience from the main game and the DLC is fun, and who doesn't like having fun.

After almost a year I can finally give this game a proper review.
First off I want to mention that when this released it was buggy, ran poorly, and was an overall mess. I was running an i5 4690K and a Radeon R9 380 which should have been enough IMO at the time and was between the min and recommended specs for the game. Unfortunately I couldn’t even manage a steady 60Fps even at the lowest settings. The frames dropped all the time with seemingly no reason, didn’t matter if I was in a large or small area. So I waited, and waited, and tried to play again a few months later and it was still♥♥♥♥♥♥ About a month ago I was able to upgrade my graphics card to a 1060 Ti and the game is finally playable for me. However, even with a better card the game still drops frames in large areas. I could mitigate that with adaptive resolution but it honestly makes far off textures look awful.
The next thing to mention would be the bugs. I have not encountered many but the ones I have encountered were pretty frustrating. The first I one was the game crashing when I hit select to enter the character menu. This set me back a couple times since I don’t save the game every time I go to that menu. The second bug is in regards to the final upgrade for the crossbow. For some reason, no matter which one I chose, as soon as I selected it for purchase the game would crash. I even re-validated my game files since I assumed I was missing the files for it somehow. Overall not the buggiest game but definitely annoying.
I give it a 4/10 for performance, mainly due to its release day cluster♥♥♥♥.
Dishonored 2 feels very much like the first one, which is good. Controls are familiar, powers work in the same way, and the feedback from the game is smooth. Now I may be wrong here but the Blink and Shadow Reach abilities seem a bit more finnicky than in the first game (I know Shadow Reach isn’t in D1 but it is basically a variant of Blink). The one critique I have, albeit a small one, is in regards to drawers in the game such as cash registers and desk drawers. Why on earth did you make it so goddamn precise to pickup items in a drawers? When I open a cash register with 4 tiny♥♥♥♥♥items in it, why did you make it so I can close the register!? Again, it’s a small thing to complain about but honestly it made no sense to me. Just make it permanently open after I open so I don’t accidently close it when trying to take the very small contents.
I give the gameplay a 8/10 for being about as good as the first Dishonored.
I didn’t find the main plotline of the game to be anything spectacular, but it was enjoyable. The levels were well made and provided many avenues to get thru the mission, the characters were well written and didn’t feel dull, and the home base was a fresh change in comparison to the Pub in D1. I would say that of all the missions “A Crack in the Slab” was by far the best.
The games conclusion was a bit lackluster, it provided closure but not the future. D1 ended in a way that allowed for D2 to be made, but the same does not occur for D2. I am not saying that a third Dishonored needs to be made, but I would have liked there to be room for it. They may do this in “Death of the Outsider”, or just end the game there. If that is the case it kinda feels scummy to place the end of the series in a DLC. I guess we’ll just have to wait and see.

If you enjoyed Star wars Battlefront and Battlefront II (The originals, not remakes), then you will probably enjoy this game.
For the fruit bats who will inevitably ask about multiplayer:
If you are looking for a PVP multiplayer experience, this game is NOT for you. Multiplayer will NEVER be implemented. This is a SINGLE PLAYER ONLY game.
Ravenfield is a solo Battlefield/Battlefront-esque game which can involve literally hundreds of bots fighting over an expansive map. This is everything I wanted in the DICE Battlefront and never got.
Official maps are somewhat limited, but there is an active modding community which creates some truly amazing maps with professional levels of detail. The develeoper has provided a suite of free modding tools so that you can create your own battlefields, as well.
My only complaints are regarding a few nitpicky things. Vehicles are very difficult to control, especially aerial vehicles. I find the game to be difficult to play with a controller. Some level of auto-aim needs to be implemented, along with smoother movement acceleration. However, these are things which will almost certainly see some improvement in the future.
Overall, this is a fun game that fills a neglected niche in the gaming market.
